115-united-states-census-figures-back-to:
How many people lived in America in 1630, 1800, or 1950? This file lists United States population figures back to 1630, drawn from Census Bureau sources. Years before 1992 use official figures, averaged where sources differ, and later years are estimates.

Notes explain the July 1 reference dates and the one-percent growth assumption used after 1992. Raw data appear as footnotes for checking. The tables help readers see long growth from a small colonial population to a continental nation. Students and historians use them as a quick baseline. Genealogists and local historians still consult these long-run totals for context.
15619-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Harison's children's weekly for June 3, 1897 changes its premium: a favorite bicycle for any reader who sends in one hundred regular subscriptions to the Great Round World. Show the paper to friends, the offer says, and one hundred glad subscribers will soon appear. Send subscriptions as fast as received, and at the hundredth, buy any wheel from any dealer, and the paper will pay the bill.

Six-month subscriptions count as one half, three-month as one quarter, and sample copies go at half price. A notice also seeks a good agent in every town, and sets the library price at one dollar seventy-five a year. The number shows a children's paper growing by prizes, turning readers into agents with a bicycle as bait, while its news pages kept them informed week by week.
16640-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
This June 30, 1920 number of Punch, or the London Charivari, volume 158, packs jokes, cartoons, and short squibs into one weekly issue. Charivaria leads with quips on Ireland and a tiny motor car knocked down by a walker. Mustapha Kemal's call for men who will die for a cause gets a joke. Ealing folk who want Sunday bathing with Sunday concerts get one too.

Punch mocks the news of the week with dry wit and a London eye, sparing no party, town, or fashion. Golf, clubs, and colonels get their turn beside war news and home politics. The issue is a brisk dip into 1920 humor, best read a page at a time for its jokes, its targets, and its view of a world just out of war.
17038-history-of-the-english-people-volu:
John Richard Green, honorary fellow of Jesus College, Oxford, wrote this second volume of his History of the English People, covering the Charter from 1216 to 1307 and the rise of Parliament. The set runs to eight volumes, with a full index placed at the end of volume eight and later issued apart for ease of use. Pictures in the html edition are listed by file name in the text.

Green tells how charter, law, and parliament grew from John's death through Henry III and Edward I, in his famous, readable narrative style. He links kings, barons, and commons in one flowing tale. The volume gives a classic, still enjoyable history of medieval England's turn toward representative rule, best read as part of Green's great survey.
28617-astounding-stories-of-super-scienc:
Astounding Stories of Super-Science for February 1930, published by W. M. Clayton with Harry Bates as editor, promises clean, interesting, vivid tales. The Clayton standard also pledges union-shop manufacture, fair profit for dealers, and guarded advertising pages. H. W. Wessolowski's cover paints a scene from Spawn of the Stars.

Harl Vincent's Old Crompton's Secret, Charles Willard Diffin's Spawn of the Stars, and Hugh B. Cave's Corpse on the Grating lead the contents. Sophie Wenzel Ellis, Sterner St. Paul, Victor Rousseau concluding The Beetle Horde, Anthony Pelcher, and Captain S. P. Meek follow. Readers get early pulp science fiction, monstrous, mechanical, and strange.
29198-astounding-stories-of-super-scienc:
Clayton published this July 1930 number of Astounding Stories of Super-Science, volume three, number one, priced at twenty cents. Harry Bates edited the magazine, with Douglas Dold as consulting editor. The Clayton standard promised clean, vivid stories by leading writers, made in union shops by American workmen.

Contents include Captain Meek's Beyond the Heaviside Layer, Arthur Burks's Earth, the Marauder, and Tom Curry's From an Amber Block. Harl Vincent, Sewell Peaslee Wright, Charles Diffin, and Murray Leinster add terror at air-level six, a forgotten planet, power and glory, and murder madness. Readers get a full early issue of the magazine that shaped science fiction, with a three-part novel beginning inside.
29255-astounding-stories-of-super-scienc:
Clayton published this September 1930 number of Astounding Stories of Super-Science, volume three, number three, priced at twenty cents. Harry Bates edited the magazine, with Douglas Dold as consulting editor, under the Clayton standard promising clean, vivid stories by leading writers of the day.

Contents include Miles Breuer's A Problem in Communication, Ray Cummings's Jetta of the Lowlands, Sewell Peaslee Wright's The Terrible Tentacles of L-472, and Paul Ernst's Marooned Under the Sea. Hugh Cave, Captain Meek, and Arthur Burks add a murder machine, an attack from space, and Earth the Marauder. Readers get a full month of early pulp science fiction, with the start of a three-part novel, in the magazine that helped shape the genre.
29390-astounding-stories-of-super-scienc:
Volume two, number one of Astounding Stories of Super-Science, dated April 1930, opens the Clayton pulp magazine's run of clean, vivid tales by leading writers of the day. Editor Harry Bates, with consulting editor Douglas M. Dold, promises stories bought under terms approved by the Authors' League, printed in union shops, and guarded by a watchful eye on advertising. The issue cost twenty cents and went on sale the first Thursday monthly.

Inside, readers meet half-monster gods, vampires of Venus, and an entomologist named Leslie Larner, among other pulp wonders. The mix is pure early science fiction: bold ideas, brisk action, and strange worlds. Fans of the genre's roots will enjoy this first glimpse of a magazine that would shape science fiction for decades.
29607-astounding-stories-of-super-scienc:
Volume one, number three of Astounding Stories of Super-Science, dated March 1930, continues the Clayton pulp magazine's promise of clean, vivid tales by leading writers. Editor Harry Bates, with consulting editor Douglas M. Dold, kept the Clayton standard: stories bought under terms approved by the Authors' League, printed in union shops, and guarded by a watchful eye on advertising.

Its contents include The Soul Master by Will Smith and R. Robbins, in which O'Hara plunges into Professor Kell's mysterious mansion for a friend held victim there. The mix is pure early science fiction: mystery, wonder, and brisk action. Fans of the genre's roots will enjoy a second early glimpse of the magazine that shaped the field.
29768-astounding-stories-of-super-scienc:
Volume three, number two of Astounding Stories of Super-Science is dated August 1930, priced at twenty cents. Harry Bates edited it for W. M. Clayton, with Dr. Douglas M. Dold as consulting editor. The Clayton mark promised clean, vivid tales by leading writers, bought under terms approved by the Authors' League of America. H. W. Wessolowski painted the cover from a scene in The Planet of Dread.

R. F. Starzl sends Mark Forepaugh to a lifetime of castaway loneliness in the monster-ridden jungles of Inra. Victor Rousseau raises a Black Caesar on Eros, and all Earth trembles at his menace. Edmond Hamilton's Second Satellite sets Earth men at war with frog-vampires. Harl Vincent's Silver Dome opens a deep-buried kingdom of Theros. The issue is pure early pulp science fiction.
29809-astounding-stories-of-super-scienc:
Volume two, number two of Astounding Stories of Super-Science reached readers in May 1930, priced at twenty cents. Harry Bates edited it for publisher W. M. Clayton, with Douglas M. Dold as consulting editor. The Clayton mark promised clean, vivid tales by leading writers of the day, bought under terms approved by the Authors' League of America.

The cover art by H. W. Wessolowski shows a scene from The Atom-Smasher. Inside, Sewell Peaslee Wright sends two land men into the ocean depths to save Imee's race of men who returned to the sea. Murray Leinster's Murder Madness sends Bell of the secret Trade into South America after a master foe. The issue is a lively sample of early pulp science fiction.
29848-astounding-stories-of-super-scienc:
Volume two, number three of Astounding Stories of Super-Science is dated June 1930. Harry Bates edited it for W. M. Clayton, with Douglas M. Dold as consulting editor. The Clayton mark promised clean, vivid tales by leading writers, bought under terms approved by the Authors' League of America. H. W. Wessolowski painted the cover from a scene in The Moon Master.

C. D. Willard opens with Out of the Dreadful Depths, in which Robert Thorpe seeks a nameless horror sucking all human life out of ships in the South Pacific. Murray Leinster continues Murder Madness in part two, as Bell strikes into the South American jungle for the Master's hidden stronghold. James P. Olsen's Cavern World follows a great oil field gone dry. The issue is a strong sample of early pulp science fiction.
29882-astounding-stories-of-super-scienc:
Volume four, number one of Astounding Stories of Super-Science is dated October 1930. Harry Bates edited it for W. M. Clayton, with Douglas M. Dold as consulting editor. The Clayton mark promised clean, vivid tales by leading writers, bought under terms approved by the Authors' League of America. H. W. Wessolowski painted the cover in oils from a scene in The Invisible Death.

Captain S. P. Meek opens with Stolen Brains, in which Dr. Bird, scientific sleuth extraordinary, hunts a sinister stealer of brains. Victor Rousseau's Invisible Death gives America night-rays and a darkness-antidote against a terrific invisible empire. Robert H. Leitfred throws two young Earthians among primeval monsters in an electron's savage jungles. Ray Cummings sends Jetta of the Lowlands out in an invisible flyer. The issue is a full pulp number.
29919-astounding-stories-of-super-scienc:
Volume four, number two of Astounding Stories of Super-Science is dated November 1930. Harry Bates edited it for W. M. Clayton, with Douglas M. Dold as consulting editor. The Clayton mark promised clean, vivid tales by leading writers, bought under terms approved by the Authors' League of America. H. W. Wessolowski painted the cover in water colors from a scene in The Pirate Planet.

Victor Rousseau opens with The Wall of Death, a wall of viscid, grey, half-human jelly out of the Antarctic, absorbing and destroying all life it meets. Charles W. Diffin begins a four-part novel, The Pirate Planet, with a strange light blinking on Venus and a mysterious visitant hovering over Earth. William Merriam Rouse adds The Destroyer, in which Allen Parker slowly loses control of his hands and even his brain.
30691-astounding-stories-of-super-scienc:
Edited by Harry Bates, this December 1930 issue is volume four, number three, of Astounding Stories of Super-Science, a monthly pulp from publisher W. M. Clayton. Its cover art, painted in oils by H. W. Wessolowski, shows a scene from The Ape-Men of Xlotli. The Clayton standard printed inside promises clean, vivid stories by leading writers of the day, made in union shops by American workers.

Inside, Sophie Wenzel Ellis offers Slaves of the Dust, and Charles W. Diffin continues The Pirate Planet, part two of a four-part novel about two Earthmen fighting a whole planet on Venus. The issue gives a fine taste of early science fiction pulp: bold covers, serial novels, and short tales of strange worlds. Fans of the genre's roots will enjoy its pace, its ideas, and its period flavor.
34049-the-settlement-of-illinois-1778-18:
Arthur Clinton Boggess wrote this history of Illinois settlement, published in Chicago in 1908 as volume five of the Chicago Historical Society's collection. Boggess, a professor at Pacific University, applies the study of types, long used in biology, to history. Chapters run from the county of Illinois and a period of anarchy through land and Indian questions to territorial government.

Later chapters cover transportation, settler life, the first years of statehood from 1818 to 1830, slavery as it shaped settlement, and successful frontiersmen. Boggess writes with scholarly care and full notes. The book remains a standard early history of Illinois.
5933-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2:
Ducal pranks and Sancho's government advice fill chapters thirty-six through forty-three of this Don Quixote portion. Chapter thirty-six relates the strange adventure of the distressed duenna, alias Countess Trifaldi, with a letter Sancho wrote to his wife Teresa, while a facetious majordomo plays his part. Chapters thirty-seven and thirty-eight continue the duenna's adventure and tale, and chapter thirty-nine lets Trifaldi continue her marvellous story.

Chapters forty through forty-three bring matters relating to the adventure, the arrival of Clavileno, and two sets of counsels Quixote gave Sancho for governing. Readers get the duke and duchess at their most theatrical, staging enchantments for knight and squire. The part suits readers deep in volume two, since its counsels on ruling balance comedy with genuine wisdom.
6665-the-united-states-of-america-part-1:
Edwin Erle Sparks opens part one of his United States history, covering 1783 to 1830, by noting how often the tale has been told in boast or in reverence. Some praise a party, some a region, some a chosen people under providence. Sparks seeks a plainer path. He weighs the Union as both a creature of the states and a thing rooted in a new world.

From the peace that ended the Revolution to the age of Jackson's rise, the narrative moves through politics, growth, and strife. Sparks writes for readers who want a fair, readable survey, not a partisan hymn. Part one is a solid, early twentieth-century guide to America's first half-century as a nation.
a-general-history-and-collection-of-voya: Volume ten of Robert Kerr's voyages treats early circumnavigations of the world. Its chief chapter follows Ferdinand Magellan round the world from 1519 to 1522. Sections trace the voyage from Seville to Patagonia and its wintering there. Kerr's systematic history makes Magellan's great voyage plain for general readers. Young readers can follow the great voyage from start to finish with ease.
a-phrenological-bijou-1830: A Phrenological Bijou, dated 1830, is a small book of fifty-four pages on phrenology, the science that claimed character and intellect could be read from the shape of the skull. A bijou is a little jewel, and the title promises the system in miniature: a pocket gem of phrenological doctrine for the general reader. The old catalog gives its author only in a garbled form. The booklet belongs to the first wave of cheap phrenology print, when the new science was being sold to parlors across Britain and America.
arxiv-2509-00030:
Marshall Thomas, Edward Fish, and Richard Bowden present SignBind-LLM in 2025, a modular system that translates sign language to English. Signing joins hand gestures, fast fingerspelling, and facial cues that run at their own pace. One network that learns all three at once tends to miss spelled names and terms, and it wastes clues from lip movement.

Three expert streams split the work: one for steady signing, one for fingerspelling, and one for lipreading. Each is pre-trained on about two million auto-made gloss sequences, with no hand labels. A light transformer aligns and fuses the streams, and a language model then renders fluent English. Split experts aim for sharper names and fuller use of face cues.
arxiv-2509-00130:
Chang Liu, T. D. Khoa Le, Rahul Saini, Kishor C. Joshi, and George Exarchakos present VOTA in 2025, a way to run many wireless tests at once on one shared testbed. Testbed sharing is common in wireless research, but users must wait or face interference that mars results. VOTA is open-source and software-only, built to lift that limit.

Real-time virtualization and frequency tuning let distinct experiments run in parallel while interference stays in check. A demo runs two interference-sensitive 6G cases side by side on one host: a signal transform offload task and a denial-of-service attack on an open radio network. Results look near-dedicated, while sharing chances grow by more than two and a half times. Better sharing stretches scarce testbed time.
arxiv-2509-00530:
Fanxin Wang leads five authors in total, with Yikun Cheng, Chuyuan Tao, Rohit Bhargava, and Thenkurussi Kesavadas, in building a robotic platform for needle biopsy. Biopsy removes diseased tissue for study under a microscope, but manual sampling can miss the target and lab testing takes time.

Wang and his co-authors design a compact, steerable device that can guide tools of different sizes, including a biopsy needle and optical fibers for vibrational spectroscopy, a light-based method to probe tissue. They describe the mechanical design and control plan, then test positioning accuracy, admittance behavior, how the device yields to force, and tool insertion. The system aims to help surgeons reach targets for multi-modal diagnosis.
arxiv-2509-00730:
Wenkang Du and Haiping Huang propose a measure of consciousness based on neural response. They analyze recordings from inside the brains of non-human primates. The recordings cover wakefulness, anesthesia, and recovery states. A recurrent neural network model is fit to the cortical dynamics. The fit extracts how strongly the cortex responds to disturbance.

Response strength tracks the conscious state closely in their data. It is strong and widely spread during wakefulness. It is suppressed under anesthesia, while dynamics grow more chaotic. It rises again as the animal recovers. The pattern matches theory on response near a critical border. That border separates ordered regimes from chaotic ones. The pair suggests such a response may be a needed condition for consciousness.
arxiv-2509-00830:
Eunghyun Lee, writing alone, introduces a new particle system with several species. The system is an exclusion process with long-range swap. Exclusion means particles cannot share a site. This version combines a backward-push rule with a forward-jump rule. Several kinds of particles move under those rules at once. The rules are local, yet their effect is not.

Local moves induce effective long-range exchanges between particles. Lee proves the model can be solved exactly. He shows two-particle reducibility for the system. He also shows its scattering matrix obeys the Yang-Baxter equation. That equation is a key consistency test in this field. Explicit integral formulas follow for transition chances. The model opens new paths in this branch of probability and statistical mechanics.
arxiv-2509-01030:
Alexis Horde-Vo, with three co-authors, Matt Duckham, Estrid He, and Rafe Benli, presents a retrieval augmented generation pipeline for identifying origins of place names. Place names in gazetteers serve as spatial references but often lack information about their origins, and enriching them manually requires extensive exploration of archives.

Given a spatial query, their approach extracts sub-graphs from DBpedia that may contain relevant knowledge, then ranks them to generate the final answer using fine-tuned language models including ColBERTv2 and Llama2. Results highlight key challenges, especially the tendency of language models to under-use spatial information in texts as a discriminating factor. The chapter frames wider implications for geographic information retrieval using retrieval augmented generation.
arxiv-2509-01330:
Medical image segmentation, drawing the borders of organs or tumors, is often unsure at fuzzy edges, so a single answer can mislead. Fuyou Mao, with five co-authors, presents a diffusion-based framework that learns a full spread of likely segmentations for each voxel, the three-dimensional pixel. The method is guided by a prior, an early coarse guess.

Labels are embedded as one-hot targets in a continuous space to fit the diffusion process. The network then learns only the residual, the gap between the prior and the truth, which speeds training and improves calibration. Extra supervision at middle time steps steadies learning. On MRI and CT data sets, the method beat Bayesian, ensemble, and plain diffusion baselines on overlap scores and calibration measures, while needing fewer sampling steps.
arxiv-2509-01430:
When a massive star explodes, the neutron star or black hole it leaves can be flung away at high speed, a natal kick. Sergei Popov, Bernhard Muller, and Ilya Mandel review what is known about these kicks and why they matter. Neutron star kicks can reach or exceed a thousand kilometers per second, while black holes gain hundreds.

The kick's origin is tied to the physics of the supernova itself, so measuring kicks probes unsolved questions about such explosions, including rare types such as electron capture and ultra-stripped supernovae. Kick sizes and directions shape binary systems, the rates at which compact objects merge, and the gravitational wave events those mergers produce. Popov and the co-authors argue that better kick data will guide both explosion theory and the reading of future observations.
arxiv-2509-02030:
Zehra Yigit, Sefa Kayraklik, Ertugrul Basar, and Ali Gorcin propose a dual surface scheme that guards sensing and communication against a hostile drone. Integrated sensing and communication lets one base station track targets while serving users. Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces, panels that steer radio waves, ride on two drone targets here. One drone is legitimate and carries the helpful surface; the other spies and carries a malicious one.

The hostile surface both eavesdrops and fires random interference to disrupt secure links. The design assumes a worst case where the attacker knows channels and beamforming fully. An optimization maximizes user secrecy rate under that threat. A two stage relaxation method tunes base beams and the friendly surface phases. Simulations test robustness across many system settings.
arxiv-2509-02130:
Kim Hammar and Rolf Stadler present active causal learning, the first principled online method to identify causal models of IT systems from data. A causal model predicts effects of control actions and supports automation of operations, diagnosis, and intrusion detection. Experts traditionally hand build such models, a task buckling under system complexity and change. Their method estimates causal functions step by step from system measurements.

Gaussian process regression updates the dependency estimates as data arrive. A rollout based intervention policy chooses probes that are effective yet gentle on operations. The method is proven optimal in the Bayesian sense. Testbed experiments show accurate model identification with low interference. The work advances the long goal of self managing networks.
arxiv-2509-02430:
Baptiste Serraille and Maksim Stokić wrote a 2025 geometry paper on contact structures, geometric setups where a plane field twists through a three-dimensional space. They ask which surface patterns survive when maps are only assumed continuous, not smooth.

Their main result says contact homeomorphisms, continuous maps preserving the contact structure, keep characteristic foliations on surfaces intact. Singular points go to singular points, and each leaf curve lands on a leaf of the image surface. One consequence is that regular coisotropic surfaces are rigid under such maps. Contact convexity behaves oppositely: the authors build a map that sends a torus which is convex to one which is not, showing that property is flexible.
arxiv-2509-02730:
Young Kun Ko wrote a 2025 solo theoretical computer science paper proving lower bounds for data structures that compute linear operators. A vector is preprocessed once, then inner product queries against rows of a fixed matrix must be answered quickly from a small structure.

For a random binary matrix, Ko proves any such structure needs query time growing with a stated minimum of two quantities. The bound breaks a long-standing logarithmic barrier for static data structures. It also gives the first major progress toward a folklore conjecture that nonlinear preprocessing barely helps for most linear operators. Variants yield stronger circuit lower bounds for a specific operator, plus progress on the multiphase and Jukna-Schnitger conjectures. Randomness of the operator is the key that unlocks the argument.
arxiv-2509-02930:
Erik M. Lintunen presented a 2025 machine learning framework called VendiRL for teaching software agents a wide spread of skills. In self-supervised reinforcement learning, an agent practices on its own before anyone knows which real task will come. Practicing many unlike skills is a hedge against that unknown future.

Lintunen borrows a diversity score from ecology, where it counts how varied a sample of species is. Users can plug in their own notion of similarity, so diversity can mean different things in different settings. Distinct choices push the agent toward distinct families of skills. The unified setup also makes results easier to compare across studies. That flexibility may suit rich virtual worlds where many kinds of practice could pay off.
arxiv-2509-03030:
Zida Wu and 4 co-authors designed a 2025 learning algorithm for mean-field games. Such games model huge crowds of agents, where each one reacts to the average behavior of all the rest. Finding a Nash equilibrium, a stable pattern no agent wants to leave, is hard when the starting spread of agents is unknown.

Their method joins online mirror descent, an updating rule that stays close to past choices, with ideas from a reinforcement learning style that reuses its own past actions as targets. The learned policy adapts to different starting spreads and to common noise, shocks that hit everyone at once. Across seven standard test problems it converged better than leading rivals. The gains held up when common noise was added.
arxiv-2509-03230:
Silvia Noschese and Lothar Reichel analyzed network connectivity through shortest paths in a 2025 paper. Many complex systems become graphs: components as nodes, links as edges. The authors encode such a graph in an adjacency matrix, whose entries mark which nodes connect directly.

Powers of that matrix reveal routes through the network, and from them they build a path length matrix recording the shortest route between every pair. Measures built on that matrix capture how well information flows when travelers take shortest routes. One measure counts only routes of at most a chosen number of hops. New notions in the paper rate how much specific edges matter to that flow. Such ratings could guide pruning a network or judging damage from a blocked road.
arxiv-2509-03330:
Bnaya Gross and 4 co-authors used network medicine in 2025 to find existing drugs that might be repurposed against aging. Thousands of genes are tied to age-related traits, yet effective interventions stay elusive because longevity is multifactorial and genes work in interconnected webs. Their framework places over two thousand longevity genes onto the human interactome, the map of molecular interactions.

Genes for each hallmark of aging formed a connected module on that map, a discovery that lets the team measure how close any drug sits to each hallmark. They screened thousands of approved and experimental compounds. A second score checks whether a drug's effect on gene activity pushes against known age-related shifts. Combining proximity with that reversal score yielded interpretable candidates. For each drug, the framework names the mechanism it predicts.
arxiv-2509-03530:
Paul Blum and four co-authors devote a 2025 research paper to predicting future suicidal thinking from adolescents' social media posts. Suicide remains a major cause of death, yet standard risk factors predict it barely better than chance. Many young people also never reach mental health services before a crisis.

Their model, Early-SIB, reads a user's own posts and the threads they engage with, in order. It forecasts whether that user will later post about suicidal ideation or behaviour, before any such post exists. On a Dutch youth forum the model reached balanced accuracy well above chance. Explanation scores highlight which inputs drove each prediction, making outputs easier to inspect. The authors frame such tools as an addition to, not a replacement for, existing care.
arxiv-2509-03930:
Kazumi Okuyama's 2025 theoretical physics paper introduces the cap amplitude in random matrix models. Random matrix models, ensembles of matrices with random entries, encode deep information about two-dimensional gravity and the geometry of Riemann surfaces. For one-matrix models at large size, Okuyama defines the cap amplitude as a coefficient in expanding a certain differential form on the model's spectral curve.

The cap amplitude earns its name through gluing. The dilaton equation, which counts discrete volumes of moduli spaces of Riemann surfaces by genus and boundary count, can be read as gluing a cap onto one boundary. Capping lowers the boundary count by one, giving a recursion between volumes. The model's genus-by-genus free energy arises the same way, by gluing a cap onto a one-boundary volume. The picture ties matrix model quantities to the enumerative geometry of surfaces in one compact form.
arxiv-2509-04030:
Piotr Kamiński and four co-authors set out to design a wavy wall inside a channel using fluid simulations plus human-assisted Bayesian optimisation in a 2025 research paper. Wavy walls stir flow and even out temperature, but waviness also costs pressure, so the two goals compete. Their cost function multiplies the temperature variation by the pressure drop.

Bayesian optimisation drives the search, calling Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes simulations in a loop of a thousand iterations. Two shaping strategies compete: a sinusoidal wall described by four parameters, and an interpolation curve through nineteen control points. The sinusoidal design cuts temperature variation more than sixty-fold but quadruples pressure loss. The flexible shape manages a fifteen-fold temperature reduction with double the pressure loss. Turbulent kinetic energy and Nusselt number are examined. A human then refined the optimiser's result, replacing small wiggles with flat segments, cutting cost further while easing manufacture.
arxiv-2509-04130:
William Stewart, writing alone, argues in a 2025 essay-style paper that biology, not brainpower, keeps humans ahead of artificial intelligence. Future systems might out-reason people and grow hard to follow, he grants. His claimed edge lies elsewhere: the human central nervous system ties people directly into physical reality. Through it, people feel joy and pain, love and suffering, and grasp what their actions cost others.

That felt understanding, Stewart argues, is what sound ethics requires, and ethics qualifies a species to lead. A nervous system must be grown, not built or simulated, in his view. So even conscious machines would stay unfit for leadership, he concludes. DNA, not silicon, remains his foundation for the future.
arxiv-2509-04430:
Nikolay Kartashev and two co-authors argue that data uncertainty explains why modern methods for spreadsheet-style learning work so well in a 2025 research paper. Tabular deep learning predicts from rows and columns, and recent designs post strong results without a clear story for their success. The authors show that numerical feature embeddings, retrieval-augmented models that fetch similar rows, and advanced ensembling all quietly manage high uncertainty in the data.

Taking that view apart mechanism by mechanism yields one unifying account of recent gains. The same lens immediately suggested better numerical embeddings, which the team built as a practical payoff. Future tabular methods can be designed deliberately around uncertainty rather than discovered by accident.
arxiv-2509-04530:
Arash Azizi and one co-author, Reed Nessler, pinpoint an exact condition for a rare triple meeting point in a quantum light-matter system in a 2025 physics paper. The quantum Rabi model, a workhorse of quantum optics, hosts a superradiant phase transition where light and matter reorganize together. Adding a photon-photon Kerr interaction reshapes that transition into a line separating smooth, continuous changes from abrupt, first-order ones. Tempting as it is to call that whole line tricritical, the authors prove otherwise.

True tricriticality, where three phases meet, occurs at exactly one dissipation rate, a mathematically exact value they derive. That single sweet spot is the unique gateway to the higher order of criticality. Experiments must hit it precisely.
arxiv-2509-04630:
Dispersive shock waves and rarefaction waves can both emerge from one discrete lattice model. Su Yang studies that behaviour in a solo-authored 2025 paper on nonlinear dispersive waves in discrete conservation laws. The lattice model is a variant of an integrable discretisation of the standard Hopf equation.

Yang proposes two quasi-continuum models, written as partial differential equations, to capture the lattice behaviour. He applies a fitting method to predict edge speed and wavenumber for the shock wave. He also finds self-similar solutions for the rarefaction wave, then checks the analysis against model runs to test how well they fit.
arxiv-2509-05230:
Shortcuts based on broad concepts can quietly distort language models, and Aysenur Kocak and three co-authors propose a fix called CURE in a 2025 paper. Pre-trained models may lean on a topic or style cue instead of the real content, which hurts fairness and reliability.

CURE first pulls out a version of the text signal that leaves the concept aside, guarded so task content is not lost. A second step, tuned by contrast between examples, can weaken harmful cues or keep helpful ones. Tested on movie and business review data across three model types, CURE raised scores while adding little computing cost.
arxiv-2509-05430:
Choosing ground for a gravitational wave observatory with arms tens of kilometres long is the subject of a 2025 paper by Laurence Datrier and four co-authors. Cosmic Explorer, a proposed United States observatory, would pair one detector with twenty-kilometre arms and one with forty, using technology proven by LIGO.

Site hunting must weigh geology, geography, and slope for building cost, plus social and cultural factors. The authors present improvements to the project's location search code and efforts to fold science requirements into the scoring. National-level results are combined with a separate suitability analysis. The outcome is a preliminary list of promising sites for the larger detector.
arxiv-2509-05630:
Spotting trees in farm fields from airborne colour-rich images is tackled without labels by Moqsadur Rahman and three co-authors in a 2025 remote sensing paper. Hyperspectral images record many narrow colour bands per pixel, rich in plant detail, but labelled examples are scarce.

Self-supervised learning builds neural embeddings of each tree that reflect plant traits. Constructed this way, the tree representation beat direct use of the hyperspectral plant measures on downstream tasks. Farm sensing already uses other cameras from the air. Embeddings tuned to plant traits offer a stronger base for crop analysis where labels are limited.
arxiv-2509-05830:
Predicting how people will answer social science experiments is the test bed of a 2025 paper by Akaash Kolluri and three co-authors. The authors fine-tune large language models on real past responses rather than asking them to guess cold. Their dataset, SocSci210, gathers nearly three million responses from about four hundred thousand participants across two hundred ten open experiments.

Fine-tuned models beat their base versions on studies they had never seen, with the best model also passing GPT-4o in matching human response patterns. Training on part of a study made predictions for its remaining conditions far stronger still. Because the data carry demographic detail, fine-tuning also narrowed a standard bias gap between groups. The team releases data, models, and code, arguing that fields with rich archives can train simulators to screen hypotheses before running costly human studies.
arxiv-2509-06230:
A transparent plasma can turn into a perfect mirror for a strong electromagnetic wave, show Kavin Tangtartharakul and two co-authors in a 2025 paper. In ordinary electron-ion plasmas, intense waves make opaque plasma transparent; pair plasmas behave oppositely because their equal masses erase charge-separation fields. Kinetic simulations follow a wave compressing such a plasma.

Weak early reflections seed density spikes that self-organize into a moving Bragg-like grating, a stack of partial mirrors reinforcing each other. Reflection strengthens until the plasma-vacuum interface reflects completely. The authors highlight mass symmetry as the switch between transparency and reflection, a distinction with consequences for laser-plasma experiments and astrophysical pair plasmas.
arxiv-2509-06430:
Light vortices that carry twist through space and time can drive harmonics with very high twist, show C. Granados and two co-authors in a 2025 paper. The perfect spatiotemporal optical vortex keeps its ring size and intensity profile fixed whatever its topological charge, the amount of twist. That stability makes it an ideal driver for high harmonic generation in atomic gases, where extreme ultraviolet light is born.

The authors show transverse orbital angular momentum is strictly conserved through the harmonic process. Near the source, harmonic intensity patterns form tilted lobes encoding the charge; far away, the vortices share similar divergence. The route yields Bessel-Gauss spatiotemporal vortex beams with high charge in the extreme ultraviolet.
arxiv-2509-06530:
Design work that branches, merges, and forks across teams gets a new organizing idea from Sylvain Guérin and two co-authors in a 2025 software engineering paper. Real projects spawn many revisions and variants, yet modeling tools cannot manage that spread directly. Teams fall back on outside tools and habits.

The proposed Design Multiverse brings selected revisions and variants inside the modeling space itself. It stores snapshots of a design state, each made of several artifacts, so stakeholders can trace decisions, compare variants, and see how pieces depend on each other. Example uses include model product lines, where one design spawns many versions, and models that must evolve together with their own definitions. An implementation route based on model federation, linking separate model stores, is sketched.
arxiv-2509-06630:
Limits on the constants of an effective theory are drawn from heat and entropy by Xin-Yi Liu and one co-author in a 2025 theoretical physics paper. Effective field theories package unknown short-distance physics into extra terms with adjustable coefficients, called Wilson coefficients. Positivity bounds restrict those coefficients, but they are usually derived from scattering theory.

Here the tool is thermal field theory: the authors compute the entropy of a warm quantum system with higher-dimensional operators added. They argue that a basic thermodynamic expectation, that adding new degrees of freedom raises entropy, forces real restrictions on the coefficients. In particular, the leading operator at dimension eight must have a strictly positive coefficient. The approach links entropy with unitarity and causality, the usual guardians of consistency, from a fresh angle.
arxiv-2509-06730:
Branching particles spreading through curved hyperbolic space are analyzed by David Geldbach in a solo 2025 probability paper. Brownian motion in hyperbolic space wanders off to the boundary and never returns, so the cloud of descendants accumulates there. The normalized empirical measure, a record of where mass ends up, settles into a random limit measure on the boundary.

Geldbach computes the Hausdorff dimension of that limit measure in terms of the branching rate, and shows it has a density with respect to boundary volume once branching is fast enough. This behavior differs sharply from the set of accumulation points studied earlier, whose threshold is much lower. The results answer questions posed by Woess and by Candellero and Hutchcroft. The author believes the methods also extend to branching random walks on hyperbolic groups, broadening the reach of the argument.
arxiv-2509-07230:
Joining tables across databases usually demands exact matches in column names and values, which real data rarely offers. Szu-Yun Ko, with 3 co-authors, presents JOINT in a 2025 research paper. JOINT finds joinable column pairs automatically, even when names are fuzzy. It can also follow indirect, multi-hop paths that link tables through other tables.

The method mixes column name similarity with fuzzy overlap between row values. It scores each possible link, then searches the resulting graph for good join paths. Tests on synthetic healthcare-style databases show the system recovers valid joins despite renamed columns and partial mismatches. Such fuzzy joining matters for data integration. Hospitals, agencies, and companies store related records in clashing formats that no one designed to fit together.
arxiv-2509-07330:
Li-Chin Chen's 2025 paper, written with 2 co-authors, builds a pre-trained model that makes age and sex more useful in medical prediction. Foundation models for health care must work across many diseases and patient groups while staying simple enough to deploy. Age and sex are recorded almost everywhere, yet standard models may underuse what they reveal about a patient's state.

The General Demographic Pre-trained model, or GDP, learns rich summaries of a patient from age and sex alone. Adding those summaries beside the raw features improves prediction across several diseases and regions with distinct patient mixes. The team tuned how features are encoded and how visits are ordered, then compared GDP against leading tabular foundation models. Gains held up across tasks, which suggests even two basic fields carry untapped signal for clinical models.
arxiv-2509-07530:
Kiet T. Nguyen and 4 co-authors propose Universal Few-Shot Control in 2025, an adapter that gives image diffusion models new spatial controls from a handful of examples. Diffusion models generate images from text, and spatial conditioning steers their layout with maps such as edges or poses. Existing adapters adapt poorly to novel control types and cost much to retrain for each one.

Given a few image-condition pairs from an unseen task plus a new query condition, the adapter reasons by analogy between the query and the support examples. A matching mechanism and a small set of task-specific parameters build the control features. Fine-tuned with only 30 annotated examples, it achieves fine-grained control on six novel spatial tasks. With a tenth of a percent of full training data, it rivals fully supervised baselines, and it works across different diffusion backbones.
arxiv-2509-07630:
Giulia Pisegna and 1 co-author show in 2025 how nonreciprocity can create chirality in spinning mixtures. Nonreciprocal interactions break action-reaction symmetry. One species responds to another, with no equal response back. Chirality is handedness, a bias toward one sense of rotation. Mixtures of chiral active particles are a minimal setting where the two effects meet.

Their model has two species and is written only with scalar densities. Nonreciprocity and chirality enter through local and nonlocal parts of the chemical potential. At large scales, chirality shows up as localized domains, called charges. In these domains, the current between species curls. The charges move particles around and reshape the dynamics. Steady states include phase separation with steady edge currents. A disordered phase mixes both signatures. Nonreciprocity emerges as a generic route to chiral behavior.
arxiv-2509-07730:
Zexuan Li and 2 co-authors present M-BRe in 2025, a framework that mines training examples for relation extraction from unlabeled text. Relation extraction teaches machines to spot stated links between entities in sentences. Hand-labeling training data is very costly. Sentences with a target relation are scarce in raw text, and hard to find.

Large language models can help here. With many predefined relation categories, though, they often fail to capture each relation's meaning in one multi-class pass. A separate binary pass per relation fixes the meaning issue but costs too much time. M-BRe has three modules built to join the strengths of both routes. It aims for broad coverage of relations with no impractical computation cost. Cheaper training data pipelines would widen relation extraction to new domains.
arxiv-2509-07830:
A new class of topological spaces is introduced in a 2025 mathematics paper by A. R. Aliabad and 1 co-author. The authors define WCF-spaces, where certain disjoint regions described by continuous functions can be separated by special sets. The new class properly contains both F-spaces and cozero-complemented spaces, two known families in general topology.

Key results show the property passes between a space and its dense embedded subsets, and equivalently holds for two standard enlargements of the space. The concept is then carried into algebra through related classes of rings. Work of this kind refines the map of abstract space types, giving mathematicians sharper tools for deciding which separation properties a given space can have.
arxiv-2509-07930:
Small test particles drifting among the six planets of TOI-178 reveal hidden structure in a 2025 astronomy paper by J. Boskovic and 2 co-authors. Five of the planets are locked in a Laplace resonance chain, their orbital periods forming a neat ratio pattern. The authors run N-body simulations to see where extra particles can survive.

Zones sharing a planet's orbit turn out wider than classical theory predicts, especially around the innermost planet outside the chain. Between two outer planets, resonance effects carve gap-like clearings within about five hundred years, echoing the Kirkwood gaps in our own asteroid belt. Mapping stable and cleared regions helps explain how this tightly packed system formed and whether unseen small bodies could still lurk there.
arxiv-2509-08130:
Quark-gluon plasma, the fireball made in heavy-ion collisions, settles into fluid behavior surprisingly fast. Biswarup Paul studies one possible reason, wave-breaking, in a 2025 research paper written alone. He couples a nonlinear longitudinal color field to a three-dimensional viscous fluid background. The setup matches conditions at both RHIC in the United States and the LHC in Europe.

The wave-breaking threshold follows from the plasma's own frequency in the medium. At the LHC, higher temperature and density push the system over that threshold very early. At RHIC, the cooler, thinner medium delays the break. Scans over temperature, density, and timing confirm the instability is robust. Paul identifies wave-breaking as a shared microscopic mechanism for the early loss of coherence. It may explain why hydrodynamics takes over so quickly at both machines.
arxiv-2509-08230:
One shared squeezed-light source entangles a whole network of interferometers in a 2025 quantum sensing paper by Zhihui Yan and 8 co-authors. Distributed quantum sensing promises precision beyond classical limits for navigation, imaging, and environmental monitoring, but distributing entanglement optimally across many nodes is complex and fragile.

The demonstrated network links Mach-Zehnder interferometers through a single entangled resource, and it can be reconfigured as needs change. Simplicity is the point: one resource serving many sensors scales better than bespoke entanglement plumbing per node. Sensing several quantities at once, across separated sites, with quantum-enhanced precision is a capability laboratories have chased for years, and a reconfigurable single-source design moves it closer to practice.
arxiv-2509-08630:
Elena G. de Lamo and 2 co-authors build a data-driven model of schooling fish in a 2025 paper. Collective motion grows from single fish variation plus social coordination. Linking those two scales has been hard to do with numbers.

Using high-resolution tracks, the team splits motion into the school center and each fish moving around that center. The center follows an active particle model inside the tank walls. Individual motion uses stochastic equations, meaning equations with random terms, fitted from data. Synthetic schools match real ones on bursts, alignment, and cohesion. The simple framework connects experiment and theory.
arxiv-2509-09030:
Fraud and intrusion hide in tables where normal behavior depends on context: a purchase odd globally may be routine for one account. Spencer King and 5 co-authors build anomaly detection around that fact in a 2025 research paper. Traditional unsupervised methods model one global distribution for all rows. The authors instead learn how behavior varies with context, such as user, account, or device.

Their framework has three parts: a probabilistic formulation, an automatic way to pick informative context features, and theoretical support. They implement it with a conditional Wasserstein autoencoder, a compact model for tabular data. Across eight benchmark datasets, contextual learning beat global approaches consistently. Wins appeared even when the best context was not obvious beforehand. For security and finance teams drowning in heterogeneous tables, context-first detection offers a more faithful picture of normal.
arxiv-2509-09430:
Soumya Adhikari and 4 co-authors work through ways to reduce a larger supersymmetry structure in a 2025 theoretical physics paper. Their starting point is a dilaton Weyl multiplet with N=3 supersymmetry in four dimensions, which carries a rich R-symmetry. The goal is a full list of reductions down to N=2 that keep supersymmetry intact.

One route preserves every R-symmetry and lands on known N=2 vector and vector-dilaton Weyl multiplets. Another route partly breaks the symmetry and yields a large N=2 conformal supergravity representation that lives off shell. The authors also build that representation a second way, by coupling other multiplets, then prove the two versions match and connect to Poincaré supergravity.
arxiv-2509-10130:
Pietro Beri and 1 co-author give a geometric face to a symmetry of point configurations on a K3 surface in a 2025 algebraic geometry paper. For a very general polarised K3 surface of a certain degree family, the space of unordered point sets carries a birational involution, a self-map defined almost everywhere that undoes itself. Lattice theory had proved such a map exists without describing what it does.

Earlier work handled three points through an exceptional Lie group model of the surface. Beri and Manivel use broader arguments that work for four points and beyond, showing the key features persist. The map's undefined locus is described through a contraction, and the whole space is tied to a bundle over a moduli space of sheaves carrying its own induced involution.
arxiv-2509-10230:
Lilia Correa Magnus and 3 co-authors search the FLAMINGO simulations for signs of restless galaxy clusters in this 2025 paper. Clusters and groups of galaxies hold hot gas, and how disturbed that gas looks can reveal whether the system recently merged or fed. The team measured the gas profiles out to redshift one and compared several ways of judging a system's state.

They tested the true growth rate of each halo against three stand-ins that observers can measure: a stellar mass gap and two X-ray measures. The X-ray centroid shift proved most reliable. Gas and dark matter profiles tracked activity with a clear radial pattern, though the signal weakened in small groups and at early times. Scatter in the gas profiles also carried clues about feedback strength.
arxiv-2509-10930:
Dohun Kim and 8 co-authors report correlated quantum Hall states in twisted trilayer graphene in this 2025 paper. Three stacked graphene sheets, twisted in an alternating pattern by about five degrees, let researchers tune the electronic structure by geometry alone. The team measured how the stack conducts in strong magnetic fields.

At overall charge neutrality they found three low-resistance states, which theory links to spin-resolved edge channels like those of quantum spin Hall insulators. At another filling they saw suppressed resistance when two layers sat half full and the third stayed out of the action, the mark of an interlayer excitonic quantum Hall state. The results show rich many-body phases in a stack that is simple to describe but hard to predict.
arxiv-2509-11430:
Balázs Németh, Takuya Kobayashi, and Ronojoy Adhikari write laws for a strange class of materials. This 2025 physics paper treats oriented active solids. Their units push and pull with no action-reaction balance. Momentum bookkeeping must be redone.

Position and orientation serve as the basic variables. Nonreciprocal contacts yield the familiar stresses of elasticity. They also yield forces and torques spread through the body's volume. Those act as local sources of momentum and spin. Cartan's moving frames and Curie's principle give the linear law. In one dimension, the law predicts striking effects. Traveling waves appear. So do instabilities and spontaneous drift of the whole body. A chain of active particles in simulation matches the theory at long wavelengths.
arxiv-2509-11530:
Junchi Feng and five co-authors measured eye behavior while people with poor vision walked outdoors. This 2025 rehabilitation science paper asks how gaze supports mobility. Sighted walkers use steady scanning habits. Little was known about walkers who are blind or have low vision.

Four groups wore an eye tracker on outdoor routes. The groups spanned fully sighted through fully blind. The team recorded fixation counts, rates, spread, and peak spots, plus walking speed. Speed fell as vision worsened. Fixations grew more frequent and covered a narrower area. Peak spots sat at center for sighted walkers. They drifted outward, with more scatter, as sight loss grew. Gaze habits form a graded scale shaped by rehab experience as much as by acuity.
arxiv-2509-11830:
Andy Buckley and 3 co-authors present software for preserving machine learning algorithms used in particle physics in a 2025 paper called petrifyML. In the Large Hadron Collider era, machine learning has become a public, unavoidable part of many analyses, so reproducibility demands that complex models remain runnable and stable for years.

petrifyML converts configurations from commonly used high-energy physics machine learning tools into portable forms. Outputs include the industry-standard ONNX format or native Python or C++ code. That conversion enables future reuse and reinterpretation of ML-based experimental studies long after original software stacks change. The paper documents the package and the mechanisms it provides. The authors frame preservation as essential infrastructure for credible, repeatable experimental science.
arxiv-2509-12130:
Spotting subjective writing across many languages was the CheckThat! 2025 shared task, and Ariana Sahitaj with seven co-authors report the XplaiNLP entries in 2025. Subjectivity detection matters because news and opinion blur together online, and most languages lack big labeled datasets.

Two strategies competed. Fine-tuned transformer encoders, including EuroBERT, XLM-RoBERTa, and a German BERT, trained on original and machine-translated data; separately, large language models labeled text zero-shot through rule-based, contrastive-rewriting, and comparative-reasoning prompts. Highlights include first place in the Italian subtask and a strong third in zero-shot Romanian, with reliable multilingual results overall. Ukrainian and Polish zero-shot scores slipped just under their baselines, a reminder of how hard low-resource transfer remains.
arxiv-2509-12430:
Gears move because their teeth mesh, not because a designer pinned a joint, and that coupling defeats most motion prediction tools. Mayank Patel and three co-authors tackle gear assemblies in 2025 with a new benchmark and a dependency-aware learning model called DYNAMO.

The benchmark, MechBench, holds nearly seven hundred synthetic gear assemblies with exact part motion recorded. Given only a segmented point cloud of a CAD model, DYNAMO predicts each part's full rigid motion through time, reasoning about which parts drive which. It beats strong baselines on varied gear layouts, keeping predictions accurate and steady over time.
arxiv-2509-13230:
Xuanchi Li, Xin Wang and Sadamori Kojaku sample networks fast and without bias in 2025 under set degree hopes. The Chung-Lu model is fast but over-links high-degree nodes. Max-entropy models are fair but too slow for wide use.

A Miller-Hagberg tweak speeds the fair models by large factors. Tests on over a hundred real networks show ten to thousand-fold gains. Fair null models thus become practical for daily work. Network claims that rest on null comparisons gain firmer ground. Speed, not theory, had been the block; that block is now cut.
arxiv-2509-13630:
Ya-Ke Chen, Yi Pan, and Bo-Chao Liu investigate a particle reaction in a 2025 nuclear physics paper: a photon striking a proton and producing a phi meson, a pion, and a proton. Near threshold, where the reaction barely has enough energy to run, short-lived baryon resonances dominate what comes out.

Working within an effective Lagrangian approach, the team includes the Delta(1232) and several nucleon resonances plus a smooth background. The Delta excitation dominates near threshold. Their real target is the poorly known coupling between the Delta, a nucleon, and the a0(980) meson. They show that a parity asymmetry, read from the phi meson's spin patterns, can reveal the a0 exchange contribution in future experiments.
arxiv-2509-13930:
Dayeon Ki and six co-authors document linguistic nepotism in multilingual retrieval-augmented generation in a 2025 paper. Such systems answer questions with citations drawn from documents in many languages. The team ask whether the language mix itself bends which sources get cited. They hold relevance aside and ask what else drives the choice.

Using a controlled method based on model internals, they held relevance fixed. Document language varied across eight languages and six open-weight models. Models preferentially cited English sources for English queries. The bias grew for lower-resource query languages and for documents placed mid-context. Most worryingly, models sometimes traded relevance away to satisfy the language preference. Citation choices, in other words, are not driven by informativeness alone.
arxiv-2509-14130: Slawomir Klimek and Matt McBride discuss rapid decay for odometers in a 2025 mathematics paper. An odometer is a simple dynamical system built by adding one with carries on a Cantor-set space. Rapid decay is a smoothness condition on functions over such spaces, with roots in harmonic analysis. The paper connects these decay conditions to noncommutative geometry. In that field, spaces are studied through their algebras of functions. Decay estimates control how well analytic and topological information about a space agree.
arxiv-2509-14230:
Mengting Ai and three co-authors present NIRVANA in 2025, a way to shrink large language models by removing whole units rather than single weights. Cutting whole blocks speeds models up, but older cutting methods often hurt accuracy badly and need costly retraining to recover.

NIRVANA judges which units matter by how much they change the model output, using an idea drawn from the neural tangent kernel, a tool for studying training behaviour. A global ranking then spreads cuts between attention heads and the larger neuron layers, so no part collapses at high shrink rates. A light check based on output differences replaces random sampling. The aim is a smaller model that still works well with no task examples and can still be fine tuned later.
arxiv-2509-14330:
Mojtaba Najafizadeh, writing alone in 2025, builds post-Carrollian mechanics, a counterpart to Newtonian mechanics from the opposite speed limit. Newton laws come from slowing relativity down. Carrollian physics instead takes an ultra fast limit applied here to tachyon theory, a theory of faster than light particles.

New relations for energy and momentum follow from that limit. Najafizadeh derives the link between them and studies an ideal gas made of post-Carroll particles. Applying the same limit to Einstein equations with tachyon dust gives a gravitational potential for this strange regime. Geodesic equations, which trace free fall paths, then yield the matching gravitational behaviour. The work is exploratory, mapping consistent physics in a limit rarely worked out fully.
arxiv-2509-14530:
Zhenghao Fei and three co-authors teach a robot in 2025 to pick strawberries grown in tight clusters. Fruit hides among leaves, stems and other berries, so a clear reach is rare. A picking point sits on the stem just above the fruit crown.

Traditional plan then move systems struggle in that clutter. Their system learns from human demonstrations collected with a teleoperation interface for a four joint SCARA arm. An action chunking method with end pose help turns demonstrations into a visuomotor policy. The robot learns to nudge soft obstacles aside gently and approach the stem precisely. Demonstration learning suits farm tasks where modelling every leaf and berry in advance is hopeless.
arxiv-2509-14730:
Yuri Shimane, Purnanand Elango and Avishai Weiss develop guidance in 2025 for several spacecraft flying in formation on libration point orbits, the unstable parking orbits used by deep space observatories. Formation flight there needs fuel efficient control with guaranteed minimum separation at every instant, not only at sample times.

A nonlinear optimal control problem states the separation rules as continuous time path constraints. An isoperimetric reformulation enforces them inside a sequential convex programming solver. The scheme runs inside model predictive control and is demonstrated with ephemeris model dynamics, which use real solar system positions. Continuous guarantees matter for costly science fleets: a sampled check that misses a close approach between samples is not safety.
arxiv-2509-15130:
Chenxi Song and four co-authors steer video generation models with camera control, without retraining, in a 2025 computer vision paper. Video diffusion models carry rich knowledge of the visual world, but their camera motion is hard to direct, scenes drift over time, and camera and object motion tangle together. Fine-tuning per task or warping afterward adds artifacts and cost.

Their framework, WorldForge, works entirely at inference time in three cooperating parts. A refinement loop inside each denoising step injects motion guidance and corrects the output toward the target camera path. Flow analysis separates motion-related channels in the latent space, so guidance touches motion while sparing appearance. A dual-path strategy applies the corrections adaptively. The result is zero-shot camera control for three- and four-dimensional generation tasks.
arxiv-2509-15230:
Rutger Hendrix and seven co-authors design foundation models that can forget on request from the start in a 2025 machine learning paper. Privacy law, including the GDPR, can require deleting what a model learned from specific data. Retrofitting forgetting through retraining or weight editing is expensive and fragile, especially for systems that update continuously.

Their prompt learning framework makes unlearning a native capability rather than an afterthought. Class-level meaning is bound to dedicated prompt tokens instead of being baked into model weights. Training then unifies learning and removal in one phase: drop the token, and the associated knowledge goes with it. The design targets real-time and evolving deployments where deletion requests arrive as a stream, not as rare emergencies.
arxiv-2509-15330:
Min Zhang and six co-authors condition prompt learning on domain information so vision-language models generalize to unseen distributions in a 2025 machine learning paper. Contrastive models like CLIP promise representations that survive distribution shift, yet prompt-based tuning still suffers from sloppy text descriptions and weak alignment between image and text embeddings.

Their method, CoDoL, builds prompts from readily available domain information rather than generic templates. Better prompts pull the vision and language embeddings into closer alignment, which the authors identify as a driver of out-of-distribution gains. The design captures both instance-specific detail and domain-level context in the learned prompts. Stronger alignment at training time is offered as the mechanism behind the improved performance on distributions the model never saw.
arxiv-2509-15430:
Liuyuan Jiang leads a team that teaches speech models with less labeled data. Paired speech and text are costly to make, so models often learn from raw sound first. The catch is making good practice labels. Strong labels need extra models and long pipelines, while cheap labels are weak. The team wanted both speed and quality in one method.

Their method, BiRQ, reuses part of the model itself to make refined labels. A random mapping turns inner states into labels, while plain labels from the raw sound keep training steady. The whole task is set up as a two level problem that trains end to end. Tests show steady gains over the cheap method it builds on, at low cost.
arxiv-2509-15630:
Narender Khatri leads a team that tracks tiny swimmers in a lopsided channel. Such swimmers propel themselves and, in this study, also twist as they go. Gravity adds a turning pull, since these swimmers are bottom heavy. The team simulate their spread in a two way channel with uneven walls that form energy like barriers.

A resonance pops out when the gravity pull nears the swimmer's own twist rate. Particles pile up in one corner of the channel, and their spread rate peaks. The effect needs slow spin noise and fades as the twist grows. The team explain linked traits: flow sorting at low pull, steady speed growth, and odd dips near the peak. The work guides lab on chip sorting.
arxiv-2509-16330:
Agents built on language models now browse the web and run robots, but whether they keep working on new tasks is poorly defined. Minxing Zhang and five co-authors give the first full survey of agent generalizability, the skill of holding performance across new orders, tasks, settings, and fields. They set out what the term covers, using a layered map of fields and tasks.

The survey reviews data sets and measures, noting their limits, then sorts improvement methods by target: the core model, agent parts, or their interplay. It also splits reusable frames from truly general agents. Gaps and next steps close the review.
arxiv-2509-16430:
Tiny swimming organisms can get trapped for long stretches inside swirling flows, which cuts their feeding and raises their risk from predators. L. Storm and three co-authors show that such traps can be read from barrier structures in an expanded space that tracks both the flow and the swimming itself. These barriers govern when a swimmer can escape a trap.

The frame also explains when a learning swimmer can be trained to escape and when training fails. That link reaches beyond plankton to a broad class of navigation problems. Designers of artificial microswimmers can use the barriers as a map.
arxiv-2509-17030:
Hinata Tezuka and Naoya Inoue probe how multilingual models switch latent spaces in a 2025 paper. Past studies suggest a pipeline: early layers map inputs toward English-like forms, middle layers reason there, and late layers map back to the target language. The mechanism behind those shifts was unclear. The pair focus on neurons that drive the transfer.

They show that transfer neurons are critical for multilingual reasoning. Language-specific neurons, found in earlier work, help move representations between spaces. Knocking out transfer neurons hurts performance in their tests. The findings give builders a target for improving weaker languages, where latent transfers may fail first.
arxiv-2509-17230:
Alexander Giovannelli and nine co-authors wrote a 2025 arXiv paper on teamwork inside virtual worlds. Teams spread across the globe can meet in a shared virtual space, but they work either live together or at separate times. The authors name a third mode that is often missed: bichronous work, where saved records flow into a live session.

The team rethinks a classic chart of computer-supported teamwork and treats time as a smooth scale rather than two boxes. They built a system that lets a live group pull in archived material while they work. In a user study built around a joint inspection task, the mixed mode helped people process shared facts. It also changed how users moved and placed themselves in the virtual space, a cost the authors flag for designers.
arxiv-2509-17530:
Sayanta Adhikari, Vishnuprasadh Kumaravelu, and P. K. Srijith tackle forgetting inside models that never stop learning. Their 2025 arXiv paper joins two fields: machine unlearning, which removes the trace of data, and continual learning, where tasks arrive one after another. Some tasks, once learned, may later need to be erased for safety or privacy.

The authors find that standard unlearning breaks in this setting in two ways. Retained tasks lose accuracy, and erased tasks can relapse, resurfacing as later learning proceeds. Most unlearning tools also need the old data, which continual learning discards by design. Their framework, UnCLe, is data-free and mindful of future tasks. A hypernetwork generates task-specific parameters from task embeddings, which gives the system a handle for clean removal. The design aims to make erasure a normal part of a lifelong model's life.
arxiv-2509-17830:
Lekkala Sai Teja and 4 co-authors hunt AI-made text at the level of single sentences. Their 2025 paper notes that whole-doc checks miss mixed texts, where human and AI parts sit side by side. Light edits can also hide AI parts from blunt tools.

Their model tags each token as human or AI made, and marks where the switch occurs. It pairs a large pre-trained language model with a net and a chain rule layer. On two public bench sets with mixed texts, the fine tags beat whole-doc checks. Sharp bounds help users see which parts need a closer look.
arxiv-2509-17930:
Yiwen Guan and Jacob Whitehill build a tree-shaped translator that renders many tongues at once. Their 2025 paper deals with waste in multilingual translation, where each target tongue repeats much of the same work. Tongues with little data also tend to get poor results.

Their model, TET, shares middle steps among tongues that are close kin. It makes all targets in one pass, with no step-by-step output chain. Next to a plain one-to-many design, it cuts size and run cost by large shares. Paired with a speech front end, it kept good scores and ran far faster.
arxiv-2509-18030:
Justin Xu leads a large team that gathers many ways to grade radiology reports into one open tool. Their 2025 frame, RadEval, deals with AI-written reports on medical scans. Grades range from word overlap counts to doctor-level concept scores, and each lab tends to run its own mix.

The tool cleans up and standardizes a wide set of those scores. It also widens one AI-based grader to more scan types with a lighter model. A new expert-tagged set holds hundreds of key error tags on reports. The team checks how each score tracks radiologist judgement, and adds stats tests for fair checks.
arxiv-2509-18230:
Zihan Dong and 3 co-authors control desktop software with a small two-level learning agent. Their 2025 frame deals with a gap in computer use. Big vision models can drive a screen, but they run slow and learn from few tries. They are also too large for a local device. Long tasks with sparse rewards add to the strain.

Their agent splits choices into a manager and a worker policy. Screen, task, and number states feed one encoder, while meta-actions and an early stop cut wasted steps. On a suite of real desktop tasks, the tiny agent matched huge models on short tasks. It also halved run time.
arxiv-2509-18330:
Mars rovers send home thousands of images, but flat photos hide the shape of the land. Marsette Vona describes a system that builds a 3D terrain mesh for each Mars 2020 rover stop. His 2025 paper explains the Landform contextual mesh. It blends rover photos with height and color maps from the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, a spacecraft in orbit.

The meshes are built on their own during ground processing, with no hand work per site. Mission scientists open them in a planning tool called ASTTRO to pick targets and plan drives. A subset also appears on the public Explore with Perseverance website, where anyone can view the same terrain. The result links close-up ground detail with the wide view from orbit. That link helps teams read the land around the rover fast.
arxiv-2509-19130:
Sensing the surroundings helps millimeter-wave radios aim their beams, but sensing itself costs time and energy. Abolfazl Zakeri and three co-authors build a single learning system that decides when sensing is worth it. Their setup maximizes the average signal-to-noise ratio while holding average sensing spending under a set budget. A Lyapunov optimization method enforces the budget over time, turning a long-run limit into step-by-step choices.

A deep Q-network then picks which time slots to sense in, learning from rewards as it goes. When sensing happens, a pre-trained neural network maps the fresh data to the best beam in a fixed codebook. Simulations on the real-world DeepSense dataset show the system cuts sensing overhead substantially. At the same time it keeps communication quality at a satisfactory level, showing sensing can be spent only where it pays.
arxiv-2509-19530:
Flows that stretch and fold like taffy, called pseudo-Anosov flows, model chaos on three-dimensional manifolds. Ioannis Iakovoglou extends a classification method for them beyond the transitive case. Each flow casts a bifoliated plane, a sheet split by two families of curves, and the manifold's fundamental group acts on that plane. That action already pins the flow down up to orbital equivalence.

The combinatorial heart is the Markovian family: rectangles on the plane generalizing Markov partitions. Iakovoglou shows their orbit count and intersection pattern compress into a finite object, a geometric type. Finite codes for wild flows enable comparison and enumeration. The work continues the author's earlier preprint on transitive flows. Classification tools turn a zoo of examples into a taxonomy.
arxiv-2509-19630:
A hub node that broadcasts to a network can steer every other node, if its voice is loud enough. Nnamdi Daniel Aghanya studies that steering in a toy model where each node holds one of two states. He gives a sharp local test for success: at each node, the weight arriving from the hub must at least match all other incoming weight combined. When the test holds, the whole network flips to the hub's state in one step.

For uniform broadcasts, the exact loudness needed equals the largest non-hub weight anywhere, and no less will do. The result survives biased update rules and one-at-a-time update orders. All theorems come with machine-checked proofs in the Coq proof assistant. The model speaks to systems where a central authority must hold a shared setting against peer pressure.
arxiv-2509-19830:
Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks build big functions from one-variable pieces, a design that promises freedom from the curse of dimensionality. Wei Liu, Eleni Chatzi, and Zhilu Lai prove how fast such networks learn from data. Their spline-based versions settle at a precise error rate as samples grow. A matching lower bound shows the rate is best possible, apart from a small logarithmic factor.

The rate does not degrade with the ambient dimension, thanks to the structure assumed of the target. The authors trace the extra log factor to the sieve's nonlinearity, not the architecture. They also give a rule for placing spline knots and penalized selection over them. Guarantees like these tell engineers when a fashionable architecture deserves trust. The work separates real structural gains from hype.
arxiv-2509-20130:
L. R. Muftakhova and five co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on thin molecular films. Langmuir monolayers are single-molecule layers that can order themselves in striking side-by-side patterns. Grazing-incidence X-ray diffraction reveals that order as a pattern of spots. For intricate arrangements, reading peak positions alone no longer describes the structure.

The authors build a general theory for simulating such diffraction patterns from a proposed structure. They first test the framework on a simple solid monolayer case. They then extend it to the collapsed state, where the film buckles under pressure. Simulated patterns matched data taken at a synchrotron beamline. The method gives researchers a way to test structural ideas against complex patterns directly.
arxiv-2509-20330:
Spacecraft near the Moon face a new kind of threat, and Filippos Fotiadis and three co-authors model it in a 2025 arXiv paper. Cislunar space has sparse infrastructure and unstable orbits. A hostile craft could chase and jam a communication relay there, cutting the link between lunar missions and Earth. The authors frame the chase as a two-player game.

The evader must dodge the pursuer-jammer while staying near its planned path. The game is set inside the circular restricted three-body problem, the standard model of Earth-Moon gravity. Costs are shaped by the orbit's stable and unstable manifolds, and the reference orbit can shift phase to allow sharp escapes. A dynamic programming method solves the nonlinear game locally. Simulations pit the evader against worst-case and simpler pursuers, sketching defenses for future missions.
arxiv-2509-20630:
Machine-learned force fields can fake the forces between atoms at great speed, but their tests are weak. Yuan Chiang and thirteen co-authors open MLIP Arena, a public test ground, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Past tests leak data, travel poorly to new cases, and score models against a single reference method. The arena grades physics sense head-on instead.

Models face checks on chemical reactivity, on holding up under extreme heat and pressure, and on calling heat-related traits and events. Leaving static reference scores behind exposes flaws that count in real runs. Today's foundation-level fields show several such flaws under the arena's tasks. A public leaderboard and Python package keep every score open to re-checks. The aim is to steer the next wave of force fields toward speed, accuracy, and true-to-physics behavior at once.
arxiv-2509-20930:
Machine learning systems can be described in the language of category theory, where training steps compose like arrows. Mitchell Riley revisits the category of learners in a solo-authored paper from the ACT 2024 conference proceedings.
