He works with a looser equivalence between learners than the first definition used.

With learners identified up to this looser standard, the category gains a clean symmetric form. A quotient of the modified category then gives something new. It gives a fresh construction of the free compact closed category on a symmetric monoidal base. Such categories model processes with inputs, outputs, and feedback. Riley's result links the algebra of learning systems to a core construction in categorical quantum mechanics and logic.
arxiv-2509-21030:
Quantum gases of fermions obey their own Boltzmann equation, and their large-scale flow should match classical fluid equations. Ning Jiang, Chenchen Wang, and Kai Zhou verify that limit rigorously in a 2025 mathematics paper of forty-two pages. The quantum equation uses Fermi-Dirac statistics.

The authors analyze the spectrum of the linearized collision operator together with its transport part and semigroup. From that analysis, the incompressible Navier-Stokes-Fourier equations emerge as the hydrodynamic limit. Compared with earlier work by some of the same authors, the result needs less regularity in the initial data. A fixed-point argument with time iteration shows the kinetic solution lives exactly as long as the limiting fluid solution. Rigorous limits like this anchor fluid models in microscopic physics.
arxiv-2509-21330:
Optical spectra may predict how well a doped polymer conducts, sparing slow direct measurements. Its authors are Ankush Kumar Mishra and 4 co-authors. Self driving labs automate materials experiments to speed discovery. The team studies doped conjugated polymers, which carry charge after chemical treatment. Direct conductivity tests are costly and slow. Optical spectroscopy is rapid and does not destroy samples.

Their pipeline automates spectral feature extraction with a genetic algorithm and area measures. It builds a quantitative link between optical response, processing settings, and conductivity. Guided feature selection matches expert curated performance. The model could cut experimental effort by about a third by avoiding many direct tests. It also recovers known physical descriptors and finds tail state regions linked to successful doping.
arxiv-2509-21530:
Augmenting clinical text with man made cases can help models, but errors in medicine are dangerous. Dongkyu Cho and 2 co-authors guide augmentation with expert knowledge in a 2025 paper. Language models generate the man made data. A query based collaboration between models integrates expert level domain knowledge. The aim is to preserve critical medical information during making.

Generated data preserved critical information better than past augmentation methods, by their tests. Hallucinations fell at both token and concept levels. Downstream clinical output tasks showed steady gains over existing approaches. The system targets high stakes domains where clinically wrong text misleads. Expert guidance, not raw making, is the core design choice in this augmentation workflow.
arxiv-2509-21930:
Jiahui Wang and Changhao Chen present DynaNav in this 2025 paper, a framework that helps robots navigate by sight without heavy computing. Big foundation models for navigation, especially those with transformer decoders, cost a lot to run and are hard to interpret. That limits them on small robots with tight budgets. DynaNav adapts its effort to how complex the scene is.

A trainable selector picks a sparse set of features, which keeps the work light and the choices readable. The same selection feeds an early-exit mechanism: simple scenes finish in early layers, and a search method sets the exit thresholds. Tests in real-world-based data sets and simulators show the design works. Against a known navigation model, DynaNav cut computing sharply, ran faster, and used far less memory, while actually improving navigation results across four public data sets.
arxiv-2509-22030:
Odd articles in a news stream are usually thrown away as noise during topic modeling. Evangelia Zve and five co-authors argue they are worth watching in this 2025 paper, which won a best paper award at its conference. Outliers, they propose, can be weak early signals of topics that have not yet formed. The team tests that idea on news collections in French and English, focused on corporate responsibility and climate change.

The method embeds articles with modern language models, then clusters them cumulatively, following the clusters as time passes. Outliers that sat alone early on were tracked to see where they ended up. A consistent pattern appeared across both models and both languages: the outliers tended to grow into coherent topics later. The authors frame outlier tracking as an early-warning habit for analysts who follow fast-moving news themes.
arxiv-2509-22130:
Coordinating many moving agents without collisions is the multi-agent path finding problem, central to robotics and logistics. Merve Atasever and four co-authors present a decentralized planning framework in this 2025 paper. Standard reinforcement learning approaches tend to make agents self-centered, causing collisions, and their communication modules can stretch training to weeks. The team's framework is built on the Decision Transformer, trained offline on recorded experience.

Training offline cut learning time from weeks to hours, the authors report. The transformer design also handles the assignment of credit over long horizons, and it performs better when rewards are sparse and delayed. To adapt when the environment changes, the framework consults a large language model, GPT-4o, for brief guidance of the agents' policies. Experiments in static and changing environments showed clear gains in adaptability and performance over the base approach.
arxiv-2509-22330:
Jibu Tom Jose, Gal Friedmann, Dvir Feld, and Omri Ram compare what happens to turbulence when a pipe suddenly widens, gently or abruptly. Their 2025 study examines round pipe flows through two expansions with the same area jump: a gradual slope and a sharp right-angle step. Using a refractive-index-matched setup with stereo particle imaging, they resolved the full velocity field and gathered detailed turbulence statistics at two flow speeds.

Both geometries produced separated flow, recirculation zones, and a developing shear layer. The gradual expansion, though, consistently showed stronger turbulence: broader shear layers, more uneven Reynolds stresses, and stronger motion out of the main plane. The abrupt step grew a secondary vortex that interfered with the returning flow, which calmed the shear layer and reduced turbulence production. The authors trace the difference to how the return flow meets the main stream in each shape.
arxiv-2509-22630:
Xingyu Shen and 5 co-authors widen the memory of recurrent networks after training, without retraining from scratch. Recurrent models like linear attention and state-space models process long texts at fixed cost per token. But all context must squeeze into a fixed-size state, so recall of distant facts suffers. Recall grows with state size, yet training with a large state is expensive.

Their framework, StateX, expands the state of a pre-trained model as a post-training step. For both model classes, the changes add few or no parameters. Tests on models up to over a billion parameters showed better recall and in-context learning. Other skills stayed intact, and post-training costs stayed low.
arxiv-2509-22830:
Hwan Chang, Yonghyun Jun, and Hwanhee Lee attack language model agents by dressing malicious text as chat. Agents that browse and use tools face indirect prompt injection: hostile instructions hidden in environment output. Past work focused on plain-text payloads. This attack formats its payload to mimic the model's native chat template, which exploits the model's trained urge to follow such structure. A multi-turn variant primes the agent over several exchanges before the payload lands.

Across frontier models, the template attack beat classic injection by wide margins on two agent benchmarks. The multi-turn form did best of all. Payloads transferred across models, even closed ones with unknown templates. Prompt-based defenses were largely ineffective, especially against the multi-turn form.
arxiv-2509-23130:
Formal specs keep big systems honest, but writing them by hand is slow and costly. Qian Cheng and 9 co-authors built SysMoBench to test whether AI can write such models. The benchmark targets concurrent and distributed systems, the backbone of cloud services. Models are written in TLA+, the standard language for that domain. Eleven real artifacts are included so far.

The set spans Raft in Etcd and Redis, ZooKeeper leader election, and parts of the Asterinas OS. Scoring is automated on syntax, runtime behavior, code conformance, and invariants. The team aim to ground tools in this area. AI skill at full-system modeling is still unclear, and this measures it.
arxiv-2509-23230:
Graph learning works best when neighbors share traits, but a knob for that trait mix was missing. Haoyu Wang and 3 co-authors built a generative model that dials feature heterophily directly. A Lipschitz graphon generator makes the random graph. Gaussian node features pass through a smooth spectral filter of the Laplacian. Two guarantees anchor the model.

One bounds how the empirical heterophily score concentrates. The other shows the score converges to a set value from the graphon degree profile. Experiments confirm precise control across graph families and filters. The interplay of graphon and filter sets the final heterophily level.
arxiv-2509-23330:
Reasoning training grounds for language models are hard to scale when experts must write every task. Peng Yu and 5 co-authors build environments from structured data instead. Their SIE framework mines large structured sources for compositional patterns. Schemas and reasoning chains in the data give rule-based verifiability for free. No expert annotation bottleneck remains.

Models trained in these environments improved at structured reasoning in-domain. The compositional skills also transferred to math and logic tasks outside the domain. Partial environments, with data withheld, still taught robust reasoning. Models learned to infer missing data by exploring. The team frame structured data as a renewable training ground.
arxiv-2509-23430:
Black hole entropy meets quantum complexity in a gravity theory with extra scalar fields. Fabiano F. Santos and 2 co-authors work inside Horndeski gravity and the AdS/BCFT setup, which links a gravity world to a boundary theory. They refine the claim that complexity equals action, and ask how the scalar terms change the space-time region used in that claim.

For the black holes they study, including spinning and charged ones, complexity still grows in a straight line set by entropy times temperature. Shock waves sent through the system produce the switchback effect, a known delay in growth. The authors stress a limit: the result holds only where the theory's own signal cone still fits the background one used to build the region.
arxiv-2509-23530:
Lung scarring drives much of the death risk in systemic sclerosis, and chest CT scans track that scarring. Alec K. Peltekian leads a large team that built a framework to predict death from those scans. The study draws on more than two thousand scans from a Northwestern registry of scleroderma patients. Radiomics measures and deep learning models read the scans, and deaths were checked by expert physicians at one, three, and five years.

Three pre-trained image models, fine-tuned on the scans, gave fair to strong discrimination across the three time spans. The best mark came at three years. The authors argue that image-based risk scores could sharpen early detection and care planning for this lung disease.
arxiv-2509-24030:
Moving live data from a lab tool to a distant supercomputer can stall big science runs. Anjus George and 5 co-authors compare three ways to stream data across sites. The three paths send data direct, through a proxy, or through a managed service.

The team built all three on a test setup at Oak Ridge and ran fake workloads that mimic real science flows. Direct streaming took the fewest hops, so it moved data fastest with the least delay. The managed service was the easiest to roll out for many users, but it added the most overhead. The proxy path sat in between.
arxiv-2510-00030:
Ugwu and Oyeleke detect dementia directly from the timing of speech itself, arguing that the subtle, gradual. Progressive deterioration in how people produce speech is an early marker of cognitive decline that static features miss. Their full new TAI-Speech model treats spectrograms as sequences of frames and refines them iteratively, borrowing optical flow's trick for tracking change. With a convolutional recurrent unit capturing fine-grained frame-to-frame evolution of acoustic features in raw audio.

A cross-attention component aligns the spectral features with prosodic patterns such as pitch and pauses, also tying the representation to speech production deficits linked to everyday clinical functional decline. On the DementiaBank Pitt corpus the model reaches a strong AUC of 0.839 and 80.6 percent accuracy in the reported evaluation, beating text-based baselines and rivaling multimodal systems, all without needing any speech transcription at all.
arxiv-2510-00130:
Alexander Berkovich and Aritram Dhar wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on q-binomial sums, a classic topic in combinatorics. Such sums count weighted arrangements and often hide deep pattern identities. The authors study a family of these sums built with several parameters. Their main goal is to prove that certain cases have only non-negative coefficients.

Using cubic transformations that preserve positivity, plus known formulas for Rogers-Szego polynomials, they prove the claim for two infinite families. Along the way they establish new identities that equate two very different-looking sums. Such identities can later help count partitions of whole numbers, a core use of this machinery. The paper is a technical advance, but it adds firm bricks to a well-used area of algebra. Proofs here are exact, so the results stand without numerical doubt.
arxiv-2510-00330:
Z. Wang and sixteen colleagues published this 2025 astronomy paper in the oMEGACat series on the star cluster Omega Centauri. Gas between the stars leaves fingerprints in starlight, and sodium absorption lines are a clean tracer. The team used the MUSE instrument on the Very Large Telescope to map those lines. A large velocity gap separates the cluster's gas from foreground gas on the way.

That gap let them split foreground absorption from any gas inside the cluster itself. Small-scale clumps in the foreground map matched independent reddening maps from photometry. Their average reddening inside the cluster's half-light radius agreed with standard values. Inside the cluster, horizontal branch stars showed no sodium absorption at the cluster's own velocity. The non-detection sets the strongest limit yet on atomic gas inside Omega Centauri. Ionized gas estimates from pulsars run about fifty times higher than that atomic cap.
arxiv-2510-00630:
Oliva, Shaked, Carnevale, and Degani present a trajectory-based method for designing state observers in this 2025 arXiv paper on control engineering, submitted to Control Engineering Practice. An observer reconstructs a system's hidden state from limited sensor signals, and tuning one for a nonlinear system with several sensor types is usually painstaking. Their method, TBOD, starts from parameterized observer dynamics and tunes the parameters by numerical optimization against pre-recorded measurement trajectories from the real plant.

The design procedure stays modular, so new sensors can join the fusion setup without redesigning everything. The team tested it on a ground rover that localizes itself with an inertial unit and ultra-wideband ranging antennas, checked against a motion-capture system. TBOD matched an extended Kalman filter on position accuracy, the comparison standard. Its orientation estimates were better by an order of magnitude in their experiments.
arxiv-2510-00730:
Schmid and four co-authors present Maven-Lockfile in this 2025 arXiv paper on software supply chain security. Java projects built with Maven pull in many third-party libraries, and reproducible, tamper-evident builds need the exact dependency versions frozen. Other ecosystems solve this with lockfiles, but Maven has no native lockfile support. The team's tool generates and updates lockfiles that record every direct and transitive dependency together with its checksum.

Uniquely, the tool also rebuilds projects from past versions, which lets teams audit or reproduce historical releases exactly. In their evaluation it reproduced builds from old commits and successfully flagged tampered artifacts. Setup takes minimal configuration from the developer. The authors argue the tool gives Java projects modern build integrity at low cost. They also hope it spurs research on supply chain security tools such as transparency logs for the Java ecosystem.
arxiv-2510-00830:
Clément computes two hard invariants for linear Alexander quandles in this 2025 arXiv paper on algebra and knot theory. Quandles are self-distributive structures invented to build knot invariants, since their axioms mirror the three Reidemeister moves of knot diagrams. Alexander quandles come from an abelian group with an automorphism, and the linear case uses the cyclic group of order n. From any quandle one can build its structure group and its second homology group, but both resist direct computation.

Using explicit rewriting techniques, Clément shows the structure group embeds into a semidirect product whose size depends on the number of orbits, m. That embedding unlocks the second homology group completely. Its torsion part turns out to depend only on m and n, not on finer details. Worked cases include prime n, products of two primes, and prime squares.
arxiv-2510-00930:
Besserve and García-Patrón build an entropy-based benchmark for quantum advantage in this 2025 arXiv paper on quantum computing. Claims of quantum advantage keep arriving for tasks, while advantage on a useful problem remains unproven. The authors want a yardstick that connects hardware behaviour to application performance. Their idea tracks how entropy accumulates in the processor and degrades the solution of an optimization problem.

The benchmark lower-bounds the boundary of Gibbs states in energy-entropy space for the problem. Any device must operate on the physical side of that frontier, which yields go or no-go statements. The method is hardware-agnostic and needs only tractable classical numerics. Applied to the two-dimensional Fermi-Hubbard ground state problem, it returns a no-go for large instances on today's noisy hardware. Error mitigation might soften the verdict, and the authors flag that extension as future work.
arxiv-2510-01030:
Studdiford and co-authors at the University of Wisconsin–Madison and Stanford ask which design choices make language models think about concepts more like people do, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Standard benchmarks rarely measure that kind of alignment, so scores can mislead. The team instead used a triplet similarity task from cognitive science, where judges pick which of three concepts differ most, over items from the THINGS database.

They tested more than seventy models that vary in architecture, training data, and fine-tuning. Instruction fine-tuning stood out as the strongest driver of human-like representations, alongside wider attention heads. Model size, activation function choice, and multimodal pretraining mattered surprisingly little. Scores on existing benchmarks explained only part of the alignment differences. The authors argue new benchmarks are needed to track progress toward models of human concepts.
arxiv-2510-01330:
Borówka and co-authors prove that a map linking curve coverings to abelian varieties loses almost no information in their case. Cyclic coverings of degree six over genus-two curves feed the Prym construction, a classic bridge between curves and higher-dimensional tori. Whether the Prym map separates different coverings was open here.

Generic injectivity is the result, meaning distinct coverings almost always yield distinct Prym varieties. The proof recovers the covering from its Prym data by exploiting the covering's symmetries. An automorphism of order three and a companion involution carry the reconstruction. Prym theory gains a sharp new entry in its classification table. Étale coverings, unramified everywhere, are the objects under study. Line bundles on abelian surfaces explain why these coverings matter. Generic injectivity still permits rare collisions on special loci. Norm maps define the Prym variety as a kernel's heart.
arxiv-2510-01530:
Nananukul and co-authors ground language models in formal logic so their reasoning can be checked in high-stakes fields. Law and medicine run on rules with exceptions, where one new fact can void a general conclusion. Plain language models handle such defeasible reasoning poorly, however fluent their prose may sound.

Their system, LOGicalThought, pairs the model with an advanced logic language and a dedicated reasoner. Long guidelines become two compact contexts, a symbolic graph and a logic form, that shrink the inference task. Tests across four domains judged whether answers stayed accurate, verifiable, and tied to stated evidence. The design targets assurance, not just plausibility, for critical decisions. Negation and implication get explicit handling instead of being left to prose habits. Compact grounded forms also make each conclusion easier for auditors to retrace. High-assurance buyers need exactly that trail.
arxiv-2510-02030:
Kline and a large team release an open toolkit that reads animal behavior from drone footage in this 2025 paper. Field observation of wildlife is slow, labor-intensive, and limited in scope. Their package, kabr-tools, automates behavior monitoring across species in Kenyan ecosystems. Detection, tracking, and classification modules extract time budgets, transitions, social interactions, and habitat use from video.

Drone observation improved behavior detail over ground-based methods in their comparisons. Visibility loss dropped by about fifteen percent, and more behavioral transitions were captured with better continuity. Three case studies processed nine hundred sixty-nine behavioral sequences, far beyond manual annotation capacity. One finding matched Plains zebra patterns in a second species: vigilance in Grevy's zebras also falls as herd size grows. Group composition dynamics and spatial metrics come out of the same pipeline. The authors position the tools for landscape-scale ecology questions that traditional observation cannot reach.
arxiv-2510-02230:
Nguyen and five co-authors argue that reward-based fine-tuning can shrink what language models can reason about in this 2025 paper. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is the standard recipe for sharpening model reasoning. Recent evidence hints it narrows the reasoning boundary instead of expanding it. The authors dissect the learning dynamics to find why.

Two phenomena explain the shrinkage. Negative interference means progress on some training problems actively lowers the model's odds on others, dragging down pass-at-k scores. A winner-take-all effect compounds it: training disproportionately reinforces problems the base model already solves. Initially unlikely correct solutions get suppressed further, pruning the frontier. The model's sampling diversity collapses toward its comfort zone. The paper reframes a popular training method as a boundary-keeper rather than a boundary-pusher. Diagnostics from the study can flag the shrinkage early.
arxiv-2510-02830:
Uryu tests whether large language models can be trusted with species conservation data. The test bed is the IUCN Red List. The list grades how close species are to extinction. Five leading models faced checks on nearly twenty-two thousand species. The checks covered naming, status, range, and threats. Those four parts form the core of a Red List assessment.

A sharp gap appeared in the results. The models scored near ninety-five percent on naming tasks. They scored only about twenty-seven percent on judging conservation status. The gap held across all five models. The models also favored well-known vertebrates over other groups. That bias could deepen gaps that already skew conservation work. Uryu argues that models are fine for fetching facts. Human experts must keep sole control of risk judgments. A hybrid workflow is the safe path forward.
arxiv-2510-03030:
Sengupta and co-authors add a missing acid source to a global climate model. Organic aerosols make up a large share of airborne particles. They often carry acidic compounds of their own. Climate models have mostly ignored that organic acidity. The team built acid release into the ECHAM-HAMMOZ model. The release depends on concentration, as lab work suggests. Special behavior at particle surfaces was included too.

Extra acidity sped up sulfate formation inside droplets. Sulfur dioxide gas oxidizes faster in more acidic water. The added sulfate then seeded more cloud droplets. Droplet counts rose by up to about a seventh in places. More and brighter clouds reflected more sunlight away. The global mean cooling reached near one watt per square meter. Surface effects sometimes outweighed the bulk acidity effect. Ignoring organic acids thus biases climate runs warm. Aerosol acidity belongs in the next round of models.
arxiv-2510-03130:
Adams designs a type theory that schedules the pulses driving a quantum chip. Circuits describe what a quantum computer should do. Hardware, though, eats timed microwave pulses on set channels. Pulse languages like OpenPulse lack formal meanings so far. His system, PSTT, gives schedules a precise type theory. It belongs to the graded modal family of type systems. Grades on variables carry timing facts in this design.

A grade can say a qubit state lies fifty nanoseconds ahead. Another can mark a state seventy-five nanoseconds in the past. The typing rules then police the whole schedule. Two pulses can never hit one qubit at once. No silent gaps can sneak into a channel either. Only complete schedules can be written in the language. A verified quantum compiler is the planned payoff. Static checks would catch timing bugs before hardware runs.
arxiv-2510-03230:
Wang and co-authors teach interface agents to point at screen elements by giving them rulers, not guesses. GUI grounding maps a text instruction to exact pixels. Vision models usually emit coordinates as raw text tokens. That inference breaks on display resolutions never seen in training. Ruler tokens plant explicit coordinate markers across the image. The model adjusts from a visible reference instead of inventing numbers.

A second fix rebalances how positions are encoded spatially. Standard schemes treat width and height unequally in effect. Interleaved positional encoding gives both axes equal footing. Three ScreenSpot benchmarks measured the combined design. Grounding accuracy rose consistently across all three suites. The largest gains landed on high-resolution professional interfaces. Those are exactly the screens that break implicit mapping. Token overhead stayed below one percent overall. Explicit spatial guidance beat implicit learning at trivial cost.
arxiv-2510-03530:
Wang, García-Cervera, and Banerjee present a 2025 arXiv paper on how electrons oscillate in flat band crystal lattices under an electric field. Bloch oscillations swing charge carriers instead of letting them accelerate forever. Tunneling between bands, called Landau-Zener transitions, distorts those swings in ways. The authors study lattices named Lieb and Kagome, whose flat bands touch their moving bands in styles. They pair simulations with a scattering matrix analysis to cross check results.

The Lieb lattice showed half frequency oscillations, while Kagome showed the fundamental frequency, a split tied to their band shapes. In Kagome, the flat band couples with both moving bands near its quadratic touching point. In Lieb, each moving band couples to the flat band on its side, with no jumps between them. Straining Kagome toward Lieb traced how the pattern morphs. The work guides searches for flat band effects in materials and atom setups.
arxiv-2510-03630:
He and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper making multi talker recognition cheaper by merging speaker activity into two streams. Meeting transcription must handle overlapping voices, and activity conditioned systems normally run the recognizer once per speaker. Costs therefore grow with every participant. Their HEAT approach converts per speaker activity into two speaker agnostic streams, so the recognizer runs twice no matter how many people speak. The catch is that pretrained recognizers expect continuous speaker audio, so merging wrecks accuracy.

Heuristics preserve continuity while merging, keeping the streams compatible with systems. Plugged into the DiCoW recognizer, the method cut runtimes on the AMI and ICSI meeting corpora. Accuracy stayed competitive with the per speaker approach. The scheme works with perfect and model estimated speaker activity. Meeting software that transcribes calls could cut its compute bill. The authors want speaker labels restored to the output and the streams learned end to end.
arxiv-2510-03730:
Judd and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper testing which statistical methods should link crimes by a suspect's habits, judged against the UK police covenant for ethical AI use. Linking cases by modus operandi lets investigators pool evidence against offenders. Logistic regression has been the tool, prized for simplicity and interpretability. The authors compared regression, sampling, and machine learning methods against the covenant's explainability and transparency principles. Their test bed was a new data set of romance fraud reports from three hundred sixty one victims.

Machine learning improved predictive performance over the standard approach in their tests. One method, KF-ROSE-SVM, offered sensitivity with explainability and transparency. Agencies can choose their point on the tradeoff between accuracy and openness. Romance fraud linkage status was unknown, mimicking casework. Better linkage means identification of fraudsters and evidence pools. The covenant framing shows accuracy gains need not come at the price of policing.
arxiv-2510-03830:
Durkin, Stolte, and Mercangöz present this 2025 arXiv paper on automating the hardest moments of running a chemical plant. Starting a plant up or switching its product grade has long depended on a few expert operators. As those experts retire, plants risk losing know-how that was never written down. The authors aim to learn that skill from historical operating logs instead.

Their system, HOFLON, mixes offline learning with online optimization. Offline, it learns which actions stay inside the range of past practice and a critic that predicts long-run reward. Online, it picks each action to please the critic while staying near past practice and moving smoothly. Tests covered a polymerization reactor start-up and a paper machine grade change. HOFLON beat a leading offline learning baseline in both plants. It even beat the best recorded transition in the logs, on average.
arxiv-2510-04230:
Son and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on building reasoning models for languages other than English, using Korean as the proving ground. Reasoning distillation pipelines overwhelmingly use English data, leaving language-specific reasoning unstudied. Translated corpora introduce artifacts that distort the target language. The authors propose Language-Mixed Chain-of-Thought, which alternates between English and the target language during reasoning. English anchors the logic while the target language carries the content, minimizing translation damage.

They curated Yi-Sang, nearly six million native Korean prompts from web questions, exams, science, and code. A Qwen3-32B teacher generated millions of long reasoning traces, from which a high-yield subset was selected. The best, KO-REAson-35B, topped five of nine benchmarks and placed second on the rest. Smaller models gained nearly nineteen points on average across the benchmarks.
arxiv-2510-04330:
Abrão and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper demonstrating a material platform that lets spin waves propagate at cryogenic temperatures. Spin waves in yttrium iron garnet carry information with very low loss, attracting magnonics and hybrid quantum devices. The standard substrate, gadolinium gallium garnet, turns strongly paramagnetic when cold and strangles propagation. The team instead grew thin YIG films on yttrium scandium gallium garnet substrates.

In the Damon-Eshbach geometry, the films supported robust spin-wave propagation down to two kelvin, under applied fields up to one hundred fifty millitesla. Ferromagnetic resonance linewidths stayed narrower at low temperature than in films on the conventional substrate. Those traits remove the intrinsic bottleneck that kept thin-film magnonics at room temperature. Scalable cryogenic magnonic circuits could now integrate with superconducting quantum hardware. The result reopens a device direction that substrate physics had quietly closed.
arxiv-2510-04630:
Vrushank Ahire and six coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on spotting deepfake faces in images and video. Fakes grow more realistic each year, and detectors trained on one data set often fail on the next. The team built an ensemble that mixes two families of detectors. Transformer models read global face structure, while texture methods catch fine surface flaws. Their network, SFANet, adds attention over both space and frequency bands.

Several design choices target the weak points of fakes. Patch based attention zooms on high impact regions such as the eyes and mouth. Face segmentation and frequency splitting sharpen the signals that fakes distort. A staged data split and training order handle the imbalance between real and fake samples. On a test cup built from eight deepfake data sets, the model set a top score. The texture side gives interpretability for its verdicts. Hybrid designs may age better as generators change.
arxiv-2510-04830:
Paul Leask wrote this 2025 physics paper on vortices that behave as anyons inside a superconductor model. Anyons are quasiparticles whose statistics sit between bosons and fermions. The model extends the Ginzburg Landau theory with a Chern Simons term. That term ties electric charge to magnetic flux, so each vortex carries both. It changes how the fields fade with distance, adding an oscillating tail.

Superconductors split into types by how their vortices interact. One type attracts at all ranges, and the other repels. Here the screening mixes the two behaviors in a material. Vortex anyons repel at short range yet attract at range. That push pull lets vortices bind into separated clusters with a preferred spacing. The interaction energy is not monotonic, a signature of the hybrid state. The model energy is unbounded below, which makes finding these states delicate. Bound anyon clusters interest condensed matter theory and topological computing hopes.
arxiv-2510-04930:
Ali Saheb Pasand and Elvis Dohmatob examine a curious training effect called grokking in this 2025 arXiv paper. A neural network first memorizes its training data and scores near zero error. Its test performance then stalls near chance for a long stretch. Much later, test accuracy suddenly jumps to near perfect.

The authors trace the delay to uneven learning speeds across the main directions of the gradients. Their fix, egalitarian gradient descent, rescales updates so every direction advances at the same pace. On classic test problems such as modular addition and sparse parity, the method removed the plateau entirely. In other cases it shortened the wait a great deal. The change adds no new tuning knobs.
arxiv-2510-05030:
Andrius Tamosiunas extends a long-running search for the shape of the universe in this 2025 arXiv paper. Space might wrap around on itself, so distant views could repeat like a hall of mirrors. Earlier work in the series covered orientable flat shapes. This installment handles the non-orientable ones, where a trip can return you mirrored.

For each candidate shape, the paper computes how primordial ripples should correlate across the sky. It builds correlation matrices for Fourier modes and for the microwave background's spherical harmonics. The key test is whether those patterns rise above cosmic variance noise. They do when our nearest clone sits closer than about 1.2 last-scattering diameters. The rich parameter space still needs wider exploration before real searches.
arxiv-2510-05130:
Shaoyi Zheng and four co-authors improve how language models learn from examples in this 2025 arXiv paper. In-context learning lets a model copy patterns from examples placed in its prompt. Long example lists get expensive, because transformer cost grows quadratically. Splitting examples into blocks helps, but random splits waste or duplicate information.

Their framework, Sub-CP, chooses block contents with submodular objectives that control diversity. Each block can range from globally diverse to locally coherent. That fine-grained control also allows precomputation before any query arrives. Across diverse tasks and model scales, Sub-CP consistently improved performance over rival partitioning schemes. The main limits are weaker gains in one cross-attention setting and no adaptation to each specific query.
arxiv-2510-05430:
Huayi Tang and Pratik Chaudhari teach robots to explore buildings by meaning, not just geometry in this 2025 arXiv paper. Finding milk in a strange store takes semantic guesswork about where cold storage belongs. Robots map shapes superbly but lack that semantic layer. The authors call the remedy active semantic perception.

They build a compact hierarchical scene graph spanning rooms, objects, and fine geometry. A language model samples plausible scene graphs for unobserved regions consistent with partial views. Those samples score each candidate waypoint by its expected information gain. Doors and hallways proved strong cues for hypothesizing unseen rooms. In realistic simulated interiors, the method pinned down scene semantics faster and more accurately than baselines.
arxiv-2510-05730:
Lahiri and colleagues propose transport signatures of the superconducting Higgs mode. The Higgs mode oscillates the amplitude of the superconducting order parameter. Being electrically neutral, it hides from most probes. Their 2025 paper shows microwave-irradiated Josephson junctions can reveal it unambiguously.

The setting uses asymmetric, highly transparent junctions under microwave irradiation. Microwaves enhance the second harmonic of the equilibrium current-phase relation. That enhancement's sign differs from the Higgs-free expectation. Sweeping the frequency produces a resonance when it crosses the Higgs mass. A second signature appears at finite voltage bias in the alternating current. Earlier terahertz studies saw consistent hints but never an unambiguous detection. The Josephson current acts as a proxy for the order parameter itself. Standard transport measurements suffice, with no terahertz spectroscopy required. Customary Shapiro step analysis can extract that harmonic in practice.
arxiv-2510-05830:
Messias and Ide study whether DAO vote delegation truly speaks for token holders. DAOs promise shared, open rule through token voting. In practice, voter apathy and fame bias pile power into few hands. Their 2025 study links forum talk to on-chain delegation records.

The data spans five big protocols and fourteen DAO forums. Language models pull each poster's stated interests from forum posts. Those interests are checked against how the chosen reps voted in the past. The match is often poor, so holders' stated aims go unmet. Ranking screens push the already strong reps still higher. Most users post just once, so a few voices dominate the talk. Capture of the DAO and slow, stuck rules are the deep risks at stake. The authors urge adding interest match into the delegation screens. Fit with holders' aims, not raw turnout, is their test of healthy DAO rule.
arxiv-2510-05930:
Bamberger and colleagues regularize flow matching with geometry-aware noise. Generative models trade sample quality against generalization, often memorizing training data. Standard flow matching adds the same isotropic noise everywhere along its path. Their 2025 CDC-FM method varies that noise with local data geometry.

The anisotropic covariance captures the latent manifold's local shape. This geometric noise can be estimated optimally from the data itself. It also scales to large datasets without prohibitive cost. The noise encourages transport normal to the manifold, suppressing tangential collapse. Experiments span synthetic manifolds, point clouds, genomics, motion capture, and images. The framework drops into existing flow matching pipelines readily. Quality and generalization improve together rather than trading off. Memorization threatens novelty, diversity, and privacy in deployed generators. Improvements are largest in data-scarce and non-uniformly sampled regimes. Science applications with scarce data benefit most directly.
arxiv-2510-06230:
Reyes-Amezcua and five co-authors present FedAgain, a federated anomaly detection algorithm for medical imaging. Hospitals cannot pool patient data, so they train shared models across sites. Clinical clients bring corrupted images, and bad updates can quietly poison the shared model.

FedAgain guards the federation with dual-signal trust, built on reconstruction error and model divergence. The server dynamically down-weights untrustworthy clients without seeing their raw data. The system uses convolutional autoencoders trained on two kidney stone datasets from ureteroscopy. Testing covered sixteen endoscopy corruption types at five severity levels each. FedAgain suppressed expert forger clients and beat standard FedAvg under every corruption type. Precision gains reached about fourteen points, and F1 gains about ten. Kidney stone typing during ureteroscopy guides treatment choices, so robustness matters clinically. The design offers robust, privacy-preserving collaboration for medical anomaly detection.
arxiv-2510-06330:
Piarulli and five co-authors build a parametrized test of general relativity for LISA's massive black hole binaries in a 2025 relativity paper. LISA will record long, loud inspirals from merging massive black holes. Those signals are ideal for testing strong-field gravity.

The team extends the Flexible Theory-Independent framework to LISA. Generic deviations enter the post-Newtonian coefficients of the wave phase. The analysis models LISA's time- and frequency-dependent response. Fisher and full Bayesian analyses agree on the forecast. LISA could tighten constraints on agnostic deviations by at least two orders of magnitude beyond current ground-based limits. The gain depends on total mass and signal loudness, reflecting an inspiral versus merger-ringdown trade-off. The authors compare inspiral-only against full-signal analyses. Robust test design now means any later deviation can be trusted.
arxiv-2510-06430:
Kirtane, Khanna, and Relan test whether rewording a math problem breaks language models in a 2025 natural language processing paper. Models ace standard benchmarks, yet teachers constantly rephrase problems across assessments. MathRobust-LV mirrors that practice: names, contexts, and variables change while numbers and answers stay fixed.

The test set uses high-school problems, the difficulty where models serve in tutoring and assessment. Thirty-four models were evaluated on baselines and reworded variants. Accuracy declined for essentially every model when wording changed. Smaller models suffered severe drops of nine to eleven percentage points. Stronger models degraded measurably too, though GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 Pro stayed comparatively stable. Linguistic robustness, the authors argue, is a fundamental unsolved challenge. Benchmarks that never vary phrasing overstate model reliability. Classroom deployment, where no two quizzes phrase a problem alike, demands the stricter test.
arxiv-2510-06530:
Dayaratne and seven co-authors detect blind denial-of-service attacks in 5G control planes with language models in a 2025 network security paper. Control-plane protocols like RRC and NAS carry vulnerabilities blind attacks exploit. Rule-based and traditional detectors need extensive training data and predefined rules. They explain their decisions poorly.

The framework works inside the Open RAN architecture. A zero-shot language model reads unordered data beside a short natural-language attack description. No attack-specific training set is required. Detection quality depends on the description's semantic completeness, not phrasing or length. Attack descriptions can even be automated practically. The zero-shot design sidesteps the scarcity of labeled attack traffic that hampers supervised detectors. Comparisons across open-source and proprietary models show superior detection. The framework respects O-RAN's real-time constraints in validation. New attacks need only new descriptions, so the design extends to other Layer-3 attacks.
arxiv-2510-06730:
Manuel Frank and Haithem Afli design a tougher test for sentence embedding models. Their 2025 paper questions the standard benchmark suite, MTEB, which uses fixed test data. Models tuned repeatedly on the same tests can look better than they really are. Real users phrase the same meaning in many different words.

Their benchmark, PTEB, paraphrases test items fresh at evaluation time. A language model rewrites each item while preserving its meaning. Scores are averaged across several runs to keep them stable. Across seven MTEB tasks, encoder performance dropped once wording changed but meaning stayed fixed. That drop exposes weak generalization that static tests had hidden. Smaller models were not hurt more than larger ones, which surprised the authors. The team extended the check to three multilingual datasets covering ten languages. They propose dynamic evaluation like this as a new standard habit for the field.
arxiv-2510-06830:
Falko Ziebert and Igor Kulić answer an old question in a surprising way, in a perspective essay. Why do animals have no wheels? Their 2025 piece argues that animals actually do have them. The wheel is hidden inside slender, flexible bodies rather than mounted on an axle.

They call this structure the wheel-within. It appears when a body rolls or twists by reorganizing its own shape. Falling cats use it to land on their feet. Crocodiles use it in their spinning death roll, and fruit-fly larvae roll to escape danger. Even curling plant tendrils and some human movements qualify. The physics mixes elasticity, geometry, and self-organization in an unusual way. The structure stays neutrally stable while its shape keeps changing. Soft robotics has quietly adopted the same trick in recent machines. Naming the pattern may help biologists and engineers spot it in new places.
arxiv-2510-07130:
Sagynbayeva and Farr map dark spots on two distant stars in this 2025 paper, the second in a series. Starspots are cool, dark patches driven by magnetic activity. They can distort the light astronomers use to study planets. The team used old data from the Kepler space telescope. Their targets were Kepler-17 and Kepler-63, two Sun-like stars with known planets.

A planet crossing its star briefly covers spots, and those dips reveal spot size and place. The team fit the light curves with a Bayesian surface-mapping method. Both stars showed spots in two belts, one above and one below the equator. Spot sizes clustered near the limit their method can resolve. Kepler-17's spin axis sits nearly in line with its planet's orbit. Kepler-63's axis tilts far away, and its spot pattern looks more complex.
arxiv-2510-07330:
Shtern proves a classification theorem about Lie groups whose representations stay small and faithful. The 2025 note concerns continuous groups that can act as matrices. The hypotheses are strong: every irreducible finite-dimensional representation has bounded size, and together they separate the group's points. Earlier work proved a similar result for unitary representations only. Shtern removes the unitarity assumption, which widens the theorem's reach considerably.

Under those conditions, the group must be a finite extension of a commutative Lie group. In plain terms, the group is almost abelian, with only finitely many extra twists. Its continuous characters separate its elements, the paper also shows. The proof builds on the known locally compact version of the result. Classification theorems like this one bound how exotic a well-representable group can be. They tell algebraists that strong representation control forces near-commutativity.
arxiv-2510-07530:
Gallardo and Rahavandrainy study a Collatz-style game played with polynomials over the field of two elements. Their 2025 paper transplants the famous unsolved integer problem, halve the evens and triple-plus-one the odds, into binary polynomial arithmetic. Polynomial analogues sometimes yield to methods that integers resist. The authors define their variant's sequences and track the pattern of degrees along them, separating odd and even steps. Two symmetries organize the dynamics.

The mirror symmetry, taking a polynomial's reciprocal, behaves worse. A worked example shows reciprocal partners with plainly different degree patterns, so no simple transport exists there. Yet for the special family built from a pure power plus the variable plus one, the reciprocal's behavior stays regular enough to analyze.
arxiv-2510-07930:
Ma wrote this 2025 applied mathematics paper on a fractional version of the Jeffreys law for diffusion. The law describes materials whose flow sits between solid-like and liquid-like response. Its multi-term fractional equation shows rich crossover behavior, switching diffusion regimes over time. Such crossovers appear in complex fluids and biological transport. Ma rebuilds the equation from first principles to explain where the scaling comes from.

He starts from a continuous-time random walk with a generalized waiting time law. An overdamped Langevin equation with a random time change leads to the same model. Analysis with Laplace transforms proves the equation is well posed and quantifies solution smoothness. He then builds a method that is spectrally accurate in space and time. The scheme runs in near-linear time and parallelizes. Tests in one and two dimensions confirmed its accuracy, giving modelers a rigorous tool for crossover diffusion.
arxiv-2510-08030:
Danner and five coauthors wrote this 2025 quantum optics paper on catching single microwave photons. Microwave photons carry so little energy that detecting one reliably remains unsolved, unlike visible light. Yet superconducting devices speak exactly this language. The authors simulate a detector built on photon multiplication. A Josephson-photonics device uses tunneling Cooper pairs plus the incoming photon's energy to create many photons from one, compensating for the low energy.

With two multiplication stages multiplying a photon sixteenfold, simulations reached detection probability above eighty percent. The false-alarm rate stayed extremely low. A multiply-occupied output mode stands out clearly from vacuum noise in standard heterodyne measurement. The analysis gives concrete design guidelines for devices previously run only as continuous amplifiers. The authors argue the scheme promises to outperform competitors. A reliable microwave photon counter would complete the toolbox for quantum networks.
arxiv-2510-08230:
Keshvi Tuteja and colleagues introduce pyGinkgo in a 2025 arXiv paper, a Python tool for fast sparse linear algebra. Sparse matrices, which hold mostly zeros, sit at the heart of science computing and machine learning. Python is popular for this work but lacks fast sparse kernels on modern chips. pyGinkgo wraps the Ginkgo library, written in C++, so Python users can call it with ease.

The tool works across CUDA, HIP, and OpenMP backends, covering graphics chips and plain processors. It links to Python through Pybind11 and accepts NumPy and PyTorch data directly. Benchmarks compared it with SciPy, CuPy, PyTorch, and TensorFlow on hardware from several vendors. pyGinkgo beat those tools on sparse matrix-vector products and on iterative solver runs. It also matched the speed of using native Ginkgo code in C++ directly.
arxiv-2510-08430:
Ahmedeo Shokry, Alessandro Santini, and Filippo Vicentini show that a cheaper geometric approximation trains neural quantum states better, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Neural quantum states use networks to represent quantum wavefunctions for simulation. Their training relies on natural gradient steps, which need the quantum geometric tensor. Computing and inverting that tensor is expensive and often unstable.

The team replaces the full tensor with a block-diagonal version split by network layers. This mirrors block-structured Fisher methods like K-FAC in classical deep learning. The approximation keeps the essential curvature within each layer. It drops noisy cross-layer correlations that can hurt conditioning of the problem. Experiments covered the Heisenberg model and the frustrated J1-J2 model, both standard testbeds. The block version converged faster, reached lower energies, and trained more stably. The authors argue less, here, really is more.
arxiv-2510-08830:
Xu and co-authors design lightweight internal structures for parts by mixing computer search with evolution-style rules, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Engineers use topology optimization to carve material away until a part keeps its strength at minimal weight. Fine porous infill gives superb stiffness for its weight, but standard methods are costly and produce tangled shapes that are hard to manufacture or even to describe.

Their framework works at two scales at once and uses no gradients. Simple descriptors of the fine pattern are expanded into crisp, buildable geometry by a phasor-based technique, which encodes the pattern in smooth waves. A hybrid evolutionary search mixes selection, a learned latent-space crossover, and a mutation that warps images of the design. The authors report a good balance of speed and design freedom. They present the method as a scalable route to structures that factories can actually make.
arxiv-2510-09030:
Harada and colleagues let a language model rewrite its own essay-grading rubric until its scores match human judges, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Automated essay scoring lives or dies by the rubric, the written criteria the model grades against. Hand-written rubrics are laborious, and models are notoriously sensitive to their wording. The team's method closes a loop: grade sample essays, compare with human scores, reflect on the reasoning behind each mismatch, then revise the rubric.

Trials used two standard essay collections and three leading models from different makers. Agreement with human graders, measured by a standard kappa statistic, rose substantially on both collections, by nearly half a point on one of them. Starting from a deliberately simple rubric still matched or beat detailed human-authored rubrics after refinement. They argue rubric repair deserves a central place in essay scoring, since the rubric was the bottleneck.
arxiv-2510-09230:
Hong and a large team diagnose shoulder disorders from ordinary phone videos, using two AI models that split the doctor's reasoning between them, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Conditions like frozen shoulder are common among the elderly and workers with repetitive shoulder strain. Where specialists are scarce, early and accurate diagnosis is hard. The team's framework, HMVDx, feeds consumer-grade video to multimodal language models, which read images and text together.

One model judges which movements the patient performs. A second turns those judgments into a diagnosis, mirroring a clinical exam. The authors also propose a Usability Index scoring the whole pathway, from action recognition to the final call. HMVDx raised diagnostic accuracy for shoulder injuries by nearly eighty percent over asking one model to diagnose the video directly. Low-cost models, they suggest, could support practitioners in underserved regions.
arxiv-2510-09330:
Tuan Nguyen and Long Tran-Thanh address the safety of large language models in a 2025 arXiv paper. Usual safety training happens before release and is costly to redo when rules change. It can also require access to the model's inner parts, which outside users of a closed model do not have. Their goal is alignment at answer time, with no retraining and no inside access.

The authors frame the tension between safe but empty answers and helpful but risky ones as a two-player zero-sum game. A linear programming solver, a standard optimisation tool, computes the balance point of that game while the model answers. Their results show that this black-box approach can enforce safety rules in practice. The team notes it could help smaller organisations that lack the resources to retrain big models.
arxiv-2510-09430:
Hidde Jense, Marc Viña, Erminia Calabrese, and J Colin Hill check a choice every cosmology analysis must make, in a 2025 arXiv paper. The Planck satellite mapped the cosmic microwave background, the faint glow left by the early universe, and its data can be processed through several map and likelihood pipelines. The authors ask whether that choice changes the cosmological answers.

For the scales Planck keeps when combined with ground-based telescopes, the different products give very similar parameter values. Adding other microwave background datasets shrinks the remaining differences further. For extended models beyond the standard picture, the constraints gain from small-scale ground data and become fully insensitive to the Planck choice. The team also releases a cleaned dataset and a new likelihood built from the latest Planck processing. They show the extra power since the earlier release comes from polarisation at all scales and from fine temperature detail.
arxiv-2510-09530:
Generich Capuli, the sole author, studies the weather behind hailstorms in the Philippines in a 2025 arXiv paper. The work is part two of the Project Severe Weather Archive of the Philippines, known as SWAP. It examines 171 close proximity soundings, vertical profiles of the atmosphere, taken near hail-producing thunderstorms across Luzon between 2005 and 2024.

The soundings sort into three hail-prone environments. Hail was most likely when storm energy, measured as CAPE, was high, with moist boundary layers, steep lapse rates, and high cloud bases. Surprisingly, the deep-layer wind shear was often weak, unlike classic severe weather climatologies from other regions. A different shear measure, taken between cloud base and equilibrium level, restored the expected pattern and raised hail probabilities. Wind profiles were largely one-directional, with strong speed shear aloft and weak turning near the ground, while large downdraft energy pointed to damaging wind risk.
arxiv-2510-09630:
Yining Sun, Zeyu Hao, Ziyi Zhang, and Liangyun Chen introduce a bialgebra version of a deformed Lie algebra in a 2025 arXiv paper. Omega-Lie algebras twist the classical Lie bracket rule with an extra bilinear form. A bialgebra carries both an algebra and a coalgebra structure that fit together, and the authors define the multiplicative omega version.

They show the new definition is equivalent to two classical characterisations: Manin triples, which package the structure on a doubled space, and matched pairs of algebras acting on each other. They then study the omega-Yang-Baxter equation, behind many integrable systems. Its skew-symmetric solutions build Yang-Baxter omega-Lie bialgebras. Finally they define omega O-operators, show these operators can be constructed from left-symmetric algebras, and use them to produce skew-symmetric solutions of the equation.
arxiv-2510-10030:
Wang and co-authors present P-4DGS in this 2025 arXiv paper on dynamic 3D scene reconstruction. 3D Gaussian Splatting renders scenes from soft 3D blobs with high fidelity and real-time speed. Extending it to moving scenes, called 4D reconstruction, stores a fresh set of blobs for each moment.

That naive extension ignores how much of a scene repeats across time and space, so memory use explodes. P-4DGS predicts the blobs instead of storing them all, cutting redundancy. The authors report compression by a factor of ninety, a large saving for dynamic scenes. Smaller files make 4D content practical to store, stream, and edit, which storage-heavy splatting methods have struggled to allow.
arxiv-2510-10930:
Katherine M Collins and twelve co-authors ask whether AI models judge games the way people do, in this 2025 arXiv paper. AI research usually tests problem solving: how well models play chess or Go. This team flips the lens to evaluation itself, asking models to assess games rather than play them. They built a dataset of over 100 novel board games and more than 450 human judgments. Queries covered two things: the payoff or fairness of a game, and its funness.

Reasoning models generally matched human evaluations better than plain language models. But the relationship was not monotonic: as models approached game theoretic optimal judgments, their fit to human data weakened. Funness judgments were more jagged across models, matching how hard fun is to quantify. Models also used wildly variable amounts of computation per query. The authors argue models need better judgment about when to think hard.
arxiv-2510-11030:
Ji-Hoon Ha and Ibragim Alikhanov calculate whether blazar jets forge heavy electroweak bosons and neutrino traces, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Flat spectrum radio quasars are blazars whose jets accelerate large populations of electrons and positrons. Where electrons meet positrons at the right energy, they can annihilate resonantly into W and Z bosons, which decay partly into neutrinos. The authors model the electron distribution in the jet of the quasar 3C 279 during a flare and compute the reaction rates.

They then scale up to the whole cosmic population of these quasars using its luminosity function and redshift evolution. The combined diffuse neutrino flux peaks around redshift one. But the expected fluxes sit well below the detection thresholds of IceCube, KM3NeT, and Baikal-GVD. The Z boson contribution inside the jet is many orders of magnitude below the total diffuse neutrino flux.
arxiv-2510-11130:
A two-level quantum system coupled to a bath of oscillators, the spin-boson model, is a standard testbed for how environments change quantum behavior. Justin Zhengjie Tan, Nengji Zhou, and Yang Zhao study its ground state and quantum phase transitions in this 2025 arXiv paper. They focus on sub-Ohmic baths, where the coupling to slow environmental modes is strong, and use a variational wave-function method called the multiple Davydov D2 Ansatz.

The authors study three variants of the model, with one or two baths and with diagonal, off-diagonal, or mixed couplings. For the purely diagonal model, their critical coupling strengths agree with other methods, confirming the approach. In the two-bath model, competition between the couplings drives a first-order transition, and an entropy measure peaks only under exact symmetry. For the mixed single-bath case, a rotation maps the system onto the diagonal model.
arxiv-2510-11230:
Inflation explains the early universe's smoothness but leaves the big bang singularity untouched, while loop quantum cosmology replaces the singularity with a bounce. Bikash Chandra Paul and Sahil Saini combine the two in this 2025 arXiv cosmology paper. They study uniform rate inflation, where the inflaton field rolls at a constant rate, inside a loop-quantized Friedmann universe.

The potential driving it turns out to be a polymerized version of its general relativity counterpart. It mimics both a polymerized scalar field potential and hybrid natural inflation. The resulting universe is cyclic: identical epochs follow one another, separated by quantum bounces instead of a classical singularity, and the energy density and the Hubble rate stay bounded. Predictions for cosmological perturbations depend on the field value when it ends, and the authors explore the parameter space to compare the spectral index and tensor-to-scalar ratio against observations.
arxiv-2510-11830:
Yuyang Jiang and six colleagues built MindfulVerse, a virtual reality meditation app whose content is generated and adapted on the fly. Standard meditation apps follow fixed scripts, which fit users with different mental states poorly. Their paper, presented at the ACM International Conference on Multimedia 2025 in Dublin and posted on arXiv, uses AI-generated content steered by a software agent. The agent reshapes each session around the individual user's ideas and condition.

The team ran exploratory user studies and comparative evaluations inside VR headsets. Generative meditation increased neural activation in brain areas tied to self-regulation. Users also showed better emotional regulation and stronger participation than with fixed content. The authors present the work as a procedure for personalized, immersive mindfulness. Instead of forcing everyone through the same script, the system listens first and builds the session around the person meditating.
arxiv-2510-11930:
Kazi T. Mahmood and M. Arif Hasan borrow a picture from quantum computing to analyze vibrating lattices. Engineered elastic chains, springs and masses in a row, can carry waves with topological properties set by geometric phases. Their 2025 arXiv paper describes each unit cell's motion as a point moving on a Bloch sphere, the globe used for quantum bits. Two basic motions, in-phase and out-of-phase, act as the poles.

For two-atom cells, the picture makes symmetry protection plain: the phase between the two modes locks in steps, and the Zak phase jumps in quantized amounts. With three-atom cells, restoring inversion symmetry keeps the phase quantized, while breaking it lets the phase drift, even though the spectrum's origin stays fixed. The authors also mimic single-qubit logic gates by rotating the sphere. Adding space-time stiffness modulation blends harmonics and creates continuously winding phases.
arxiv-2510-12030:
David E. Kaplan and Surjeet Rajendran claim the Higgs boson's lightness needs no new particles, only stranger quantum mechanics. The hierarchy problem is the Higgs mass's stubborn smallness beside the Planck scale: quantum corrections should drag it upward unless exquisitely fine-tuned. Decades of proposed fixes predict new particles that colliders have not found. Their 2025 arXiv paper changes the rules of the theory instead.

The authors add a state-dependent term to the Higgs sector, proportional to the measured expectation of the squared Higgs field itself. Such a term makes the theory's quantum mechanics nonlinear. With it, the Higgs mass can sit parametrically below the theory's cutoff without any fine tuning, staying technically natural even if the cutoff is the Planck scale. The simplest version looks identical to the Standard Model at colliders. Other versions could show themselves, and the early-universe cosmology can differ radically.
arxiv-2510-12930:
Hilton and colleagues identify cheap wireless tags by their hardware imperfections in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their tags are deliberately minimal, just two antennas and a single diode, a one-way electrical element, meant for low-cost Internet of Things uses. Because no two diodes are manufactured identically, each tag's response carries a faint fingerprint.

An interrogating transceiver sends a set of frequency tones, and the tag's diode mixes them nonlinearly, producing a spectral response that is retransmitted. Small manufacturing differences shift that response measurably. Machine learning algorithms read those shifts to tell tags apart. The team built tags and a bistatic radar reader in the Wi-Fi band and tested several processing algorithms. They achieved real-time classification accuracy in the mid-ninety percent range when distinguishing two tags, demonstrating the concept end to end.
arxiv-2510-13230:
Khan and colleagues propose a utility-based framework for judging vehicle perception systems in this 2025 arXiv paper. Autonomous vehicles for smart cities must detect many road users at once, including distinctive local traffic such as motorcyclists and rickshaws. Operators need a principled way to decide which trained perception model to deploy. Raw benchmark scores alone can mislead that choice.

The framework combines a custom dataset with distinctive objects, a YOLOv8s detector, and a utility module that scores perception service from trained models' performance values. Three optimizer variants led on the headline detection metric, yet their class-level results told a different story. The variant with slightly lower overall score detected cars, motorcyclists, and trucks more accurately per class. The utility model correctly identified that variant as the better perception choice, validating its ability to find the right model for deployment.
arxiv-2510-13330:
Smart, Ward, and Roughan speed up entropy estimation on sequences in this 2025 arXiv paper. Non-parametric entropy estimators based on longest common substrings measure predictability, redundancy, and similarity in sequential data without assuming a model. Their core computation scaled so poorly that real-world datasets were out of reach.

Their algorithm, LCSFinder, improves the worst-case performance of longest common substring calculation from cubic time to log-linear time. It is built from standard constructs, sorted suffix arrays and persistent binary search trees, though making them deliver exactly the matches entropy estimation needs on dynamically growing sequences required care. Benchmarks on real and simulated data showed dramatic speedups over existing implementations. The authors argue the gain enables entropy estimation at scales previously infeasible in practical signal processing, from network traffic analysis to information flow studies.
arxiv-2510-13430:
Alzubaidi and co-authors survey how Arabic large language models are evaluated. Their 2025 arXiv paper is the first systematic review of Arabic benchmarks, they report. It analyses more than forty benchmarks across tasks, knowledge areas, and cultural understanding. Arabic poses special challenges, with rich dialects and scarce native evaluation data. Benchmarks decide how progress in Arabic language technology gets measured.

The authors sort benchmarks into four groups: knowledge, language tasks, culture and dialects, and target-specific tests. They compare three ways benchmarks get built: native collection, translation, and synthetic generation. Each route trades authenticity against scale and cost, they find. Gaps remain in testing change over time and in multi-turn dialogue. Translated datasets also carry cultural mismatches that weaken their value. The survey closes with recommendations for future benchmark development. The paper also reviews reproducibility standards and the metrics benchmarks use.
arxiv-2510-13630:
Ali and co-authors build AVAR-Net, a lightweight system that spots anomalies by watching and listening together. Their 2025 arXiv paper addresses surveillance tasks where video alone fails in darkness, occlusion, or bad weather. Sound can rescue recognition when the picture degrades, and the reverse also holds. Few synchronized audio-visual datasets existed to train such systems.

AVAR-Net extracts audio features with Wav2Vec2 and visual features with MobileViT. An early fusion step merges both streams before a temporal network learns long-range patterns. The team also releases VAAR, a benchmark of three thousand real videos with synchronized sound across ten anomaly classes. The system scored 89.29 percent accuracy on VAAR while lifting average precision by 2.8 points over prior best methods on XD-Violence in the authors' tests. They present it as efficient enough for real-world deployment.
arxiv-2510-13730:
Zhen and co-authors create a strongly dipolar two-dimensional Bose gas and watch its scale invariance break. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies ultracold atoms whose magnetic dipoles interact over long range. In flat two-dimensional traps, plain short-range gases scale exactly. Tilting the dipoles injects directional, nonlocal forces that may break it.

The team builds condensates in a tight trap with a tunable dipole direction. Breathing-mode measurements, which track how the cloud pulses, probe the symmetry directly. With dipoles tilted into the plane, the breathing behaviour departs clearly from scale-invariant predictions. Quantum fluctuations grow at the same time, matching beyond-mean-field theory. Near a tilt of about seventy degrees, stripe-like density patterns emerge. Those stripes hint at a roton spectrum, a dip in excitation energy at finite wavelength. The gas still flows hydrodynamically, suggesting a path toward two-dimensional supersolids.
arxiv-2510-13830:
Cai and Li harvest preference labels from ordinary users comparing two model answers, then screen out the sloppy raters. Their 2025 arXiv paper offers an alternative to paid annotation teams for aligning language models. Users know best what they wanted from their own queries. Their labels, though, arrive with no quality control attached.

The trick is asymmetry: the two responses come from different models or different versions. That design lets a habit model infer how careful each user is being. An EM routine rates a hidden quality factor per user from their choices. Labels from low-quality users get screened before alignment training begins. Downstream tests show the screening improves preference learning outcomes. The method also captures real user habits in comparison mode. Chat products already collect such choices at huge scale daily.
arxiv-2510-14230:
Hongsong Wang and co-authors present LOTA, a lightweight detector for AI-generated images that reads the noise in an image's lowest bit planes, in this 2025 arXiv paper. As generative models improve, telling synthetic images from real ones gets harder, and detectors based on reconstruction error are expensive and miss the noise patterns baked into pixels.

Bit planes split an image by bit significance, and the lowest planes carry mostly noise. LOTA refines noise extraction through bit-plane processing with normalization strategies such as scaling and thresholding, then amplifies the signal by finding the image patch with the strongest gradient score. A lightweight classification head, explored in noise-based and noise-guided variants, makes the final call. On the GenImage benchmark, LOTA averaged accuracy near ninety-nine percent, improving on prior methods by a wide margin, and generalized well across generators, as new image models appear monthly.
arxiv-2510-14330:
Yuto Nakamizo and co-authors describe their fifth-place solution to the Meta CRAG-MM Challenge at KDD Cup 2025, a visual question answering competition where wrong answers are punished, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The benchmark asks factual questions about images, including first-person egocentric photos, and an automatic evaluator scores answers, with hallucinations earning negative points, so guessing is costly.

Their strategy was to detect hallucinations from inside the vision-language model itself. They trained logistic-regression detectors on the model's internal representations, using the hidden states and the outputs of specific attention heads. They ensembled several such detectors to decide whether an answer was trustworthy enough to submit. The approach sacrificed some correct answers in exchange for fewer hallucinations, a trade the scoring rules reward. The authors present the ensemble-of-detectors recipe as a practical way to make multimodal systems abstain when their signals betray uncertainty.
arxiv-2510-14630:
Gui and co-authors propose, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a leaner way to build image generators. Most generators work in a two-dimensional latent space, a compressed image map carrying much redundant detail. The authors instead describe a whole image with a single continuous token, taken from a self-supervised vision model that already understands image content.

Their framework, RepTok, fine-tunes only that one token's embedding so it also carries the fine detail needed for faithful reconstruction. A decoder is trained alongside with a flow matching objective, the standard way to learn generation here. A cosine-similarity penalty keeps the adapted token close to the original space's geometry, so the latent space stays smooth. Despite the simplicity, RepTok matched rivals on class-based ImageNet generation. It also extended to text-to-image generation, reaching competitive zero-shot results on a standard benchmark with very small budgets.
arxiv-2510-14730:
Cano, Camarero, Martínez, and Beivide propose, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a routing method for full-mesh computer networks that needs no virtual channels. Full-mesh cores appear in high-performance designs such as HyperX and Dragonfly. Adaptive routing there normally relies on several virtual channels per link to avoid packet deadlock, where messages wait on each other forever. Virtual channels, though, cost switch area, power, and design complexity.

TERA embeds a physical subnetwork inside the mesh to supply deadlock-free non-minimal paths. Against channel-free schemes based on link ordering, TERA performed eighty percent better under adversarial traffic and up to one hundred percent better on application kernels. Against channel-based approaches it held latency and throughput roughly equal while halving buffer requirements. Early HyperX tests showed gains of up to thirty-two percent over leading algorithms using the same number of virtual channels.
arxiv-2510-14930:
Huang and co-authors present VT-Refine, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a framework for teaching robots two-handed assembly using touch as well as sight. People assemble parts by feel, adjusting to rich tactile feedback. Robots trained by copying human demonstrations inherit the demonstrators' mistakes and habits, so behavior cloning rarely suffices for precise, contact-rich work.

VT-Refine starts with a diffusion policy trained on a small set of demonstrations, fed synchronized visual and tactile inputs. That policy then moves into a simulated digital twin, where reinforcement learning refines it for robustness and generalization. The bridge to reality is the sensor: high-resolution piezoresistive tactile sensors report normal force, a signal that GPU-accelerated simulation can model in parallel. Experiments show the refined policy assembles better in simulation and in the real world, thanks to greater data diversity and effective fine-tuning beyond what demonstrations alone allow.
arxiv-2510-15330:
Tella Rajashekhar Reddy, Atharva Deshmukh, and four colleagues at Microsoft tackle a traffic problem inside AI data centers, in this 2025 arXiv paper.
