Language model apps generate tokens at their own pace, blind to how loaded the serving machines are, so busy periods inflate response delays and waste energy. Their controller, beLLMan, lets the infrastructure talk back.

The system progressively signals the app to shorten its outputs as load rises, easing congestion before delays spiral. It is named for Richard Bellman, a founder of control theory, and it requires the app to cooperate with those signals rather than overriding them. On a real testbed of H100 graphics processors running a summarization workload, beLLMan cut end-to-end latency by up to eight times during congestion. It also cut energy use by about a quarter while serving roughly a fifth more requests, the team reports.
arxiv-2510-16030:
Keidai Iiyama and Grace Gao weigh design trades for a navigation constellation that would serve a lasting human presence on the Moon. Surface and orbital users both need reliable positioning, navigation, and timing. Their study varies satellite count and orbital parameters and watches coverage, positioning precision, orbit determination accuracy, receiver noise, and insertion cost move in response.

Three Walker constellation families built on frozen elliptical and circular orbits are compared across sizes and inclinations. Larger orbits improve polar and global coverage, while the best inclination depends on type and target region. The south elliptical family leads for polar service, and the circular family gives the most even global cover. Larger, higher orbits worsen orbit knowledge and signal strength, and insertion trades flight time against energy and fuel in the expected opposing directions.
arxiv-2510-16130:
Jiasen Zhang and three co-authors introduce BASIN, a statistical method for working out which cell types sit at each spot in spatial transcriptomics data. Such data record gene activity across a tissue slice but blur many cells together, so researchers must deconvolve the mixture. BASIN treats the job as splitting a nonnegative matrix into parts, guided by a map of neighboring spots.

Unlike methods that return one best answer, BASIN is Bayesian: a Gibbs sampler draws from the full distribution of plausible cell mixtures, giving built-in uncertainty estimates alongside the proportions. Tests on several real datasets show better accuracy and speed than rival tools. The paper also shows how its spatial and sparsity assumptions shape the results.
arxiv-2510-16230:
Nicholas V Nardelli and seven co-authors demonstrate fiber links steady enough for future quantum networks. Distributing quantum signals over ordinary deployed fiber demands phase stability at an extreme level, techniques borrowed from the optical atomic clock community that distributes clock signals over similar links.

Sending single-photon-level pulses from a mode-locked laser across two stabilized spans of 2.1 kilometers each, the team holds optical timing jitter under one hundred attoseconds over ten minutes of data, reaching a fidelity above 0.998 between the links. Time and frequency multiplexing keeps quantum and classical channels isolated by a factor of about ten to the eleventh power. The authors present the result as a necessary step toward scalable, high-rate quantum networking.
arxiv-2510-16330:
Daniel Paul-Pena and C. Seshadhri study fast pattern counts in large data sets in their 2025 paper. A hypergraph lets one link join many items at once, unlike a plain graph. The pair ask when a small pattern can be counted in near-linear time. They focus on inputs with low degeneracy, a gauge of how sparse each part is.

They give clear rules for which patterns allow fast counts, for each sense of degeneracy. Fast counts work when the pattern lacks a blocked shape, which they call an obstruction. If it has one, they argue no fast method exists, based on standard hard-task beliefs. The rules guide fast counts in network and database work.
arxiv-2510-16630:
Howard E. Bond leads seven co-authors in a 2025 report on a faint nebula found by chance. A planetary nebula is a shell of gas shed by a dying star. They found it while studying stars in NGC 1866, a young cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud. That cloud is a small galaxy near our own Milky Way. They name the nebula Ka LMC 1.

Its place near the cluster core and its matched speed hint it belongs there. The cluster's age, 200 million years, sets the parent star's birth mass. Its light shows strong nitrogen lines, a Type I trait. The ring spans a width that implies about 18,000 years of growth. Hubble shots show its faint blue core star as well.
arxiv-2510-16830:
Hasan Akgul and five co-authors address trust in language model training in a 2025 study. Fine-tuning adjusts a model on new data, often with few changed parts. Users today get weak proof of which data were used. They also cannot check how the update was computed.

Their system, called Verifiable Fine Tuning, produces short mathematical proofs instead. A proof, here a zero-knowledge proof, confirms facts without revealing private data. Records bind each data source, license, and training step to one manifest. Proofs from single steps fold into one end-to-end certificate. Checks then take only milliseconds to run. Tests on English and bilingual data kept quality while enforcing every stated rule.
arxiv-2510-17230: Nicholas Lindsay classifies smooth complex prime Fano fourfolds in this 2025 paper. Each fourfold in his study carries a semi-free action of the complex numbers with a twist. He shows any such fourfold must lie in one of four named families. Each family does hold members with that kind of action, so the list is complete.
arxiv-2510-17830:
Meir H. Shachar and twelve co-authors build a multi-agent assistant for designing inertial fusion systems. Inertial fusion aims for nearly unlimited clean power from tiny fuel capsules. Designing capsules means handling extreme energies and very fast physics. Predictive multiphysics codes are needed, but the design space is highly nonlinear.

Their system pairs AI reasoning models with physics codes and fast emulators. Users state design goals in plain natural language. Agents then run simulations, build emulators, and analyze the results. They refine capsule geometry step by step from those findings. The workflow reached simulated ignition inside the computational design process.
arxiv-2510-18030:
Ziyan Wang, with eight co-authors, revisits how to shrink large language models by cutting whole parts rather than single weights. The common local method rebuilds each layer on its own and ignores the final task, which keeps plain fluency but wastes small task signals. Their GISP method scores heads and channels by loss across the whole model instead.

Cutting then proceeds in rounds rather than in one shot, which steadies accuracy at higher sparsity. No middle fine-tuning is needed, and the collapse in fluency that often follows pruning is eased. For teams deploying models on tight hardware, the paper offers a calmer path to smaller models.
arxiv-2510-18430:
Tasha Settewong and her three co-authors compare human and AI work inside computational notebooks, the documents where data scientists mix code with written explanation. The team ran three case studies drawn from Kaggle, a site where analysts compete on data problems. First they measured twenty-five features of code and writing in medal-winning human notebooks, and found that gold medalists stood out mainly through longer, more detailed documentation.

Next they set human notebooks beside ones made by generative AI. The AI notebooks scored higher on code quality measures such as code smells and technical debt. Human notebooks, though, showed wider variety in structure, more complexity, and more inventive approaches to the problems. From these contrasts, the authors sketch four research agendas for pairing human and AI work in notebooks so each side does what it does best.
arxiv-2510-18630:
Yongliang Ou and his nine co-authors use modeling at several scales to learn what makes ions move fast through solid electrolytes, the materials at the heart of solid-state batteries. Real electrolytes are polycrystalline, full of grain boundaries where tiny crystals meet, and those boundaries can help or hinder flow. The team linked atomic-scale simulations of hopping ions to continuum models of the whole microstructure, using lightweight machine-learned potentials trained through an active learning loop.

Working with a family of sulfur-based lithium compounds, they found that barriers inside orderly grains grow in step with the size of the negative ion. Grain boundaries flipped their effect depending on the grain: they sped diffusion in slow materials but slowed it in fast ones. One compound also showed the same nonstandard temperature behavior seen in experiments. The results point to boundary engineering as a design lever.
arxiv-2510-18730:
Wan Fokkink and Rob van Glabbeek survey formal methods for a class of networks. The networks are mobile ad hoc networks. Devices in them talk wirelessly and move freely. No fixed infrastructure supports them. Protocols must route messages through a web that keeps changing. Proving them correct is hard. Proving them fast and secure is harder still.

The survey gathers a scattered field into one overview. It covers formal specification and analysis techniques. Routing protocols get the most emphasis. Timing properties and security sit beside plain correctness. Frameworks built just for such networks are reviewed. So are the mobility models behind performance studies. New researchers gain a map of the field. It shows which tools answer which questions. It also shows where gaps remain.
arxiv-2510-18930:
Somasekhara Goud Sontti and Arnab Atta model how Taylor bubbles form in power-law liquids inside a small co-flow device. Taylor bubbles are long gas bubbles that move through liquid in a narrow channel, and their size and shape affect how microfluidic systems mix and transport fluids.

Using computer simulation, the authors vary the strength of a polyacrylamide solution, gas and liquid speeds, and surface tension. They observe different breakup routes, sort the flows into two regimes by bubble length, build flow pattern maps, and propose scaling laws that estimate bubble length from the operating conditions.
arxiv-2510-19030:
Zackary Rackauckas and two co-authors present Re:Member, a system that turns personal videos into emotional questions for second language practice. By asking about a learner's own memories in the target language, the system hopes to spark feeling and conversation more than generic drills do.

Speech style is matched to the visual mood, using tones such as whispers or late-night voices. The pipeline aligns transcripts, samples video frames, and synthesizes expressive speech. As a design probe, Re:Member shows how personal media and affect could shape learner-centered tools for language education and teaching practice.
arxiv-2510-19230:
Yongguan Ke and three co-authors build a scattering theory. It covers quantum emitters tied to photons in two-dimensional waveguides. The one-dimensional case is well studied. The two-dimensional case is largely open. New light-matter effects are expected there. Photons can spread sideways.

The authors use a Green function method. They show the mean shift of photons acts as a quantum Goos-Hänchen shift. That shift is a small sideways move known from classical optics. At resonance, the shift grows in backward scattering. It offers a new handle for routing single photons.
arxiv-2510-19530:
Ruiyao Miao and four co-authors propose REBMBO, a method for optimizing functions that are expensive to test and offer no gradients. Standard Bayesian optimization balances exploring new regions against exploiting known good ones, but its one-step outlook biases it toward local optima. The problem worsens in complex, high-dimensional tasks.

REBMBO pairs Gaussian processes, which guide the search locally, with an energy-based model that captures the global shape of the problem. Each round of optimization is framed as a decision process, and a reinforcement learning method plans several steps ahead, adjusting how deep and in which direction to explore. Tests on synthetic and real-world benchmarks showed stronger performance than standard approaches.
arxiv-2510-19630:
Tatsuru Kikuchi models how financial distress spreads through Europe's bank network, using math borrowed from fluid flow. He treats the spread as diffusion across a weighted network. His derived equation says how fast the spread dies out hinges on how strongly the network is linked. He builds the bank exposure networks from European Banking Authority stress tests for 2018, 2021, and 2023.

The links fell by about forty-five percent over that span. That implies a drop of about twenty-six percent in the spread's decay rate. Group-by-group checks point to rule-driven debt cuts by the biggest banks as the cause. The networks also showed lognormal, not scale-free, degree patterns, which hints at more strength than past work assumed.
arxiv-2510-19830:
Jean-Pierre Magnot extends Poisson geometry on loop spaces from smooth loops to loops of low regularity, described by weak Sobolev spaces. Mokhov's classical builds put hydrodynamic-type Poisson structures on spaces of smooth loops. That setting is tied to integrable partial differential equations. The question is whether the tools survive when loops are allowed to be rough.

Magnot shows the key operations stay well defined at this regularity. He uses boundedness of fractional multipliers, Hilbert transforms, and composition maps. The variational bicomplex tools also carry over. So the proofs of skew-symmetry and the Jacobi identity go through word for word. Hamiltonian forms of the KdV, nonlinear Schrödinger, and Camassa-Holm equations embed into the weak setting. Higher-order brackets, though, demand more regularity.
arxiv-2510-20330:
The BESIII Collaboration, with seven hundred five more listed names, gives a sharp gauge of the mass gap between two charm-strange mesons. The gauge uses one decay chain in data from hits of electrons and positrons in the BESIII tool. The beam sits at a set point in the gigaelectronvolt range, and the set holds a stated sum of light yield.

The gap found has three error parts: from counts, from the tool, and from a past world mean used as a base. Each part is far less than the gap size. The new gauge is near seven times more sharp than the past world mean for this gap. The team keeps the base-linked error split in its report.
arxiv-2510-20430:
Mario Riccio and Marco De Corato simulate a bubble rising in a highly viscous shear-thinning fluid while an external pressure drive forces the bubble volume to oscillate. The volume changes strain the surrounding liquid far faster than natural rising does, which thins the local viscosity of the fluid. Their axisymmetric direct simulations use a Carreau-Yasuda model for the fluid and a finite element discretization.

A parametric study varies the driving amplitude and frequency plus the bubble radius. The rising dynamics turn highly nonlinear and unsteady, and the average rising speed can grow by orders of magnitude over the natural value. The effects strengthen with larger amplitude, frequency, or radius, and average speeds agree qualitatively with earlier experiments.
arxiv-2510-20530:
Vanessa Brzić, Satoshi Yoshida, Mio Murao, and Marco Túlio Quintino study higher order quantum work, where the task is to change an unknown quantum operation itself rather than a known state. Most work in this area also assumes the input state is unknown and can be anything at all.

The four authors fix the input state as known while the operation stays unknown, a setup that fits tasks such as programming a device with a set input. They show the known state can give a large speed gain through a repeat until success plan. The setup also lets pure, shared, and mixed states be told apart, and marks which mixed states allow exact and sure results.
arxiv-2510-20630:
Lucy Xing and five co-authors explore machine learning models that predict how long a quantum processing unit will take to run a submitted quantum job. Better processing time forecasts can improve resource management and scheduling on shared quantum systems. Their dataset contains about one hundred fifty thousand jobs following the IBM Quantum schema, giving the models a realistic spread of real workloads to learn from.

Gradient boosting with the LightGBM library drives the predictors, with data preprocessing steps added to improve accuracy. The results demonstrate that machine learning can effectively forecast quantum job processing times on this operational data. The authors frame the work as a foundation for integrating artificial intelligence tools into the day-to-day operations of advanced quantum computing centers.
arxiv-2510-20730:
Jonathan Nemirovsky, Lee Peleg, Amit Ben Kish. Yotam Shapira show how to run any chain of Clifford operations on a quantum computer with at most four uses of a global entangling gate. The setting pairs free single qubit moves with programmable all to all gates, as found on trapped ion machines.

Four uses is the best possible count, and the method needs no spare qubits to reach it. The team first shows any chain of two qubit link gates fits in four global steps, then extends the result to all Clifford moves at no extra cost. They also check the drive power the plan needs and find it lower than a standard route, making the scheme practical as well as tight.
arxiv-2510-21030:
En-Jui Chang, working alone, builds overlapped repetition Shor codes whose encoding rate improves fourfold over the base construction while keeping average stabilizer weight at four. Quantum error correction lives on such trade offs between rate, weight, and protection.

Controlled overlap among a few repetition blocks yields the rate gain, and swapping the outer layer for an LDPC code produces families with a stated rate scaling. A constant excitation variant suppresses collective coherent errors at no extra overhead, and a bosonic version extends the scheme to oscillator encodings. The family lands between rotated surface codes and BB codes in rate, widening design options.
arxiv-2510-21330:
Vikas Kanaujia and Vipul Arora present a sampler for probability distributions that are known only up to a scaling constant, a common situation in physics models. Classic chain-based samplers can converge slowly, mix poorly between separate peaks, and need costly runs to build training data.

Their framework, ScoreNF, pairs a normalizing flow, a model that reshapes a simple distribution into a complex one, with score information about the target's shape. An extra independent proposal step keeps the sampling unbiased. The method stays accurate even with small training sets, easing the reliance on expensive chain runs. They also add a way to check for missed or collapsed peaks, and they validate the sampler on two test distributions with several peaks and on a lattice field theory problem.
arxiv-2510-21530:
Weiyong He and Junbang Liu settle a uniqueness question for a classic problem in convex geometry, which asks when a convex body's surface measurements come from that body alone. In the even version of the Lp Minkowski problem, earlier work by many experts showed the answer is unique above some cutoff exponent, leaving the boundary itself open.

They prove there is a single critical value, pinned down by an eigenvalue of a Hilbert operator tied to the body, with a sharp split. For exponents at or above the cutoff, the solution is unique. Below it, uniqueness fails, and not just rarely: infinitely many bodies provide counterexamples. The result closes the gap between the older sufficient condition and the true threshold.
arxiv-2510-21930:
Amazigh Ouzriat, Viola Sordini, and Francesco Di Renzo check how quickly and honestly gravitational-wave detectors can point to where a cosmic collision happened. Fast sky maps from the BAYESTAR method guide telescopes hunting for light from neutron star mergers, so overconfident maps waste precious follow-up time.

The team injected fake collision signals into both clean simulated noise and real Virgo detector data from a past observing run, then rebuilt sky maps under several detector combinations. Maps for binary neutron star mergers matched ideal calibration well, especially with Virgo in the network, while maps for systems involving black holes tended to claim more precision than they had. Adding a third detector usually helped, though a faint Virgo signal could sometimes shrink accuracy instead.
arxiv-2510-22130:
Mushal Zia, Faisal Suwayyid, Yuta Hozumi, JunJie Wee, Hongsong Feng. Guo-Wei Wei predict how tightly a protein will grip a strand of DNA or RNA, a number that underlies much of gene regulation. Existing predictors tend to trade among accuracy, interpretability, and cost; the team aims for all three by mixing modern sequence embeddings with algebraic machinery.

Their method, CAP, describes the protein with transformer-learned embeddings that retain long-range evolutionary context. The nucleic acid is encoded through short-word counts lifted into persistent algebraic objects, facet ideals, which capture fine geometric detail of the sequence. Starting from raw sequences alone, CAP beat the standard benchmark for this task and held up reasonably on freshly gathered protein-RNA and mixed datasets, suggesting the algebra-plus-embedding recipe travels well.
arxiv-2510-22330:
Baiyu Wang and Chao Zheng hunt anomalies that live in places rather than moments. Most anomaly detection watches a time index. Their problem is a grid of locations in several dimensions. Some unknown number of regions have shifted their average away from baseline. The job is to say how many regions there are, and where.

Beyond the usual cost with a penalty per region, their method adds a new penalty. It charges for the area of the smallest convex hull wrapping the regions. Compact explanations are favored over scattered ones. The estimator provably recovers the number and locations of the regions. Inside a minimax framework, the best possible detection error is characterized. A trade-off appears between accuracy and how wild the region shapes may be. Large-scale simulations check the numbers.
arxiv-2510-22430:
Marcin Briański and four co-authors study integer programs whose constraint matrix has a path like shape, where each non zero entry appears in at most two neighbouring constraints. Such programs are hard in general, and much work seeks special shapes that can be solved fast. Star shaped matrices were known to be easier, so the path shape was a natural next case.

Surprisingly, the team proves the problem stays hard even when every coefficient is at most eight, by reducing from a classic satisfiability problem. The result is striking because a close cousin with tiny column sums is tractable. It maps a sharp border between easy and hard shapes.
arxiv-2510-22630:
Unusual cell division figures in tumor samples signal aggressive cancer, yet spotting them reliably is hard. Adinath Dukre, Ankan Deria, Yutong Xie, and Imran Razzak present a 2025 classification framework for atypical mitosis, built for a challenge setting where scanners and staining vary widely.

Their DenseNet121 network trains with stain aware augmentation, which mimics color shifts between labs, plus geometric and brightness changes. Weighted sampling and a hybrid loss address the severe imbalance between normal and atypical cases. On the official test set, the model reaches balanced accuracy near eighty five percent, with strong sensitivity, showing it generalizes across imaging domains.
arxiv-2510-22930:
Pranav Saxena works on three-dimensional scenes that a person can query with plain words. Past systems built such language fields with 3D Gaussian splatting, which spreads soft blobs to model a scene. They first had to train a fresh compressor for each new scene, a slow step that blocked wider use.

His Gen-LangSplat swaps that step for one shared compressor trained in advance on the large ScanNet data set. A fixed compact code then works across new scenes with no extra training. The change makes language-linked 3D scenes faster to build for robots and other tools that work in real spaces.
arxiv-2510-23030:
Sheng Xiao, Yijie Wang, and Zhigang Xiao build a Monte Carlo model for pair correlations seen in heavy-ion collisions. Femtoscopy uses those correlations to probe the size and life of the fireball that emits particles. A fair model must treat the source, pair interactions, and source self-effects together, which past work struggled to do.

Their classical trajectory model includes a thermal source and three-body final-state interactions in one self-consistent frame. By following particle paths directly, the model computes correlation functions without separate patches. Collision analysts can use it to read source properties from measured pairs with fewer hidden assumptions.
arxiv-2510-23330:
Keiya Hirashima leads a team of twelve researchers reporting the first star-by-star simulation of the Milky Way that couples gravity and hydrodynamics with a machine learning surrogate. Simulating a galaxy down to individual stars is a major goal, but supernova explosions force tiny time steps that break scaling.

Their new integration scheme bypasses those short steps with a surrogate model, reaching three hundred billion particles on nearly one hundred fifty thousand nodes. That scale breaks prior records. Star-level galaxy models could transform how astronomers study Milky Way formation and structure.
arxiv-2510-23730:
Alessandra Terranova and two co-authors compare ways of giving large language models a memory for long conversations. True conversational continuity needs memory, and many designs compete: retrieval-based semantic memory, episodic memory from in-context learning, agentic memory, and prompt tuning as procedural memory. Which kind helps most, and for which model, was unclear.

The team tested these approaches on long dialogues annotated with questions that demand varied reasoning. Memory-augmented methods cut token use by over ninety percent while holding accuracy near the full-context level. The best design depended on the model: foundation models gained most from retrieval, while stronger instruction-tuned models gained from episodic reflection and richer agentic memory. One notable finding is that episodic memory helps models recognize the limits of their own knowledge. The lesson is to scale memory complexity with model capability, not to bolt on the fanciest system by default.
arxiv-2510-23830:
Syon Bhattacharjee and a co-author estimate the number pi by a statistical route: comparing the volumes of a hypersphere and a hypercube in the same dimension. The ratio of those volumes is a known function of pi, and the function changes with dimension. Monte Carlo simulation can measure the ratio by random sampling, turning geometry into an estimate.

The authors carry out the estimation across dimensions from one to twenty and report the intriguing patterns that appear as dimension grows. They also outline how the idea extends to observations in infinitely many dimensions. The paper supplies the R code behind the numerical studies, so readers can rerun and vary the experiments themselves. Beyond the novelty, the study doubles as a tour of how volume concentrates in high dimensions. That effect is what makes the method's behavior change so much with dimension.
arxiv-2510-24230:
David Gontier and two co-authors study the Peierls instability in graphene's honeycomb lattice within a tight binding model. The lattice is allowed to distort, but distortion costs a quadratic elastic energy, so the shape balances electronic gain against elastic cost. The authors ask which periodic pattern wins this balance.

They prove the optimal three periodic configuration has Kekulé O type symmetry, a pattern of alternating bond strengths. For a small elasticity parameter, the minimizer is not translation invariant, so the lattice truly distorts. For a large elasticity parameter, the undistorted translation invariant lattice is the unique minimizer. The results pin down when graphene's ideal lattice is stable in this model.
arxiv-2510-24430:
Yejin Kim leads a team of eight authors on recommendation systems. Most such systems read a time stamp as a plain number or cycle. That misses real context like holidays, seasons, and local events. The team uses large language models, the AI systems behind chat tools. From just a time and a rough place, the models build rich context codes.

These codes, called geo-temporal embeddings, pack time and place meaning into numbers. A quick test checks if the codes hold useful signal for predictions. The team tried the codes on film and music data and on live data. The codes helped when fused with item data or used as a guide loss. They also share a film data set enriched with this context. The work urges systems that adapt to when and where people ask.
arxiv-2510-24530:
Eric G. C. Laporte studies how local grammars can resolve part of speech ambiguity for lexical tagging, working alone and writing in French. Many words can belong to several grammatical categories, but in an actual text the context usually narrows the choice sharply. Tagging words correctly underpins spelling and grammar checking, style tools, speech synthesis, and corpus analysis.

Recent tagging systems can output multiple solutions when ambiguity remains. Laporte examines local grammars, which encode patterns in a word's immediate surroundings, as a tool for lifting that ambiguity. The article contributes to the design of tagging systems that serve as a first component in many language processing pipelines.
arxiv-2510-24730:
Jaehong Oh, the sole author, presents a method to build stability proofs for networks with a net that keeps the shape of the links. The author reports strong claims for speed of settling, lean link use, and low cost in math steps. Tests on large word webs are said to back those claims.

The work also claims a link to a known old claim that such proof maps exist, now made in a build able form. Uses are claimed for a text model, with gains in score and train speed on a known text set. Links to control, shape, and form fields are also claimed. Readers should treat these broad claims as the author's own case.
arxiv-2510-24830:
Anne Gagneux, Segolene Martin, Remi Gribonval, and Mathurin Massias probe how flow match models make new samples, step by step. Such models have scored big wins, yet what drives their grade is not well known. The team views the build as a clean up act, like a denoiser that clears noise in stages.

That view lets them lay flow models and denoisers on one shared ground. They then poke the build with set shifts in noise and drift, and watch where it gains or breaks. Clear build phases came out of the tests, each with its own win and fail modes. The map shows at which stage a denoiser earns its keep.
arxiv-2510-24930:
Yamin Ben-Shimon, Barak Hirshberg, and Yohai Bar-Sinai learn entropy with a deep model to skip the hard jumps in phase change work. Phase shifts hinge on a tug of heat and entropy, yet entropy is hard to gauge in code runs. Most ways force the jumps and count stays in each phase, which stalls when walls are high.

Their way runs just short runs in each phase on its own. A deep model then reads the entropy of each phase from those runs, and the free energy gap falls out. Tests on crystal forms check the math. Since no jump needs to be forced, no prior map of the slow moves is needed.
arxiv-2510-25030:
Daoji Huang, June Huh, Daniel Soskin, and Botong Wang study bounds on ratios among the entries of a class of matrices with paired signs. Such ratio bounds can be seen as kin to a classic bound on mixed bulk. Their main claim ties the full set of such bounds to a known cone from graph and length math.

That cone is built from cuts, and is made of whole number parts in a finite count. For size three such matrices, they pin the best bound values across the whole cone, in a form that looks like an entropy rule. A five side ratio needs size five to show. They guess that each scaled ratio bound is in fact capped by two.
arxiv-2510-25230:
Hsuan-I Chou, Naomi Hirano, and Masayuki Yamaguchi probe a very young star core in the Orion B cloud with the ALMA array. The core, in a zone with a long code name, is a low mass seed at the Class 0 stage, the first stage of a star. Their band reads give a fine view of its core and gas.

A tight core of small span shows at the hub, with no twin down to a close range. Heat and light reads mark it as very cold and dim, a sign of great youth. Dense gas marks peak in layers: one gas peaks at the hub, ringed by more spread kin gases. That layer map fits a stage where one key gas is used up in most zones but a hot hub.
arxiv-2510-25630: Irmak Balcik bounds the average rank of elliptic curves over function fields, in a 2025 mathematics paper. For a prime q at least five, she orders curves by naive height over the field of rational functions. The average rank is at most twenty-five fourteenths, about one point eight. That improves Brumer's earlier bound of two point three. The proof adapts Young's work on curves over the rationals, which assumed a general Riemann hypothesis for their L-functions.
arxiv-2510-25730:
Felipe A Barros, Italo Salas, Enkeleida Lushi, and Francisca Guzman-Lastra study active carpets. Their 2025 physics paper models microbial colonies at interfaces. Slicks are thin viscous films on water bodies. Lakes, rivers, and oceans host such surface films. They are enriched in surfactants and microorganisms. Steep gradients span only tens to hundreds micrometers. Hydrodynamics there constrain nutrient and pollutant transport.

They model a colony as an active carpet. Micro-swimmers exert dipolar forces in two dimensions. Analytical and numeric methods are mixed here. An optimal size-to-confinement ratio enhances particle transport. Advective flows recirculate in 3D vortex-ring patterns. Those flows push particles toward colony edges. Vortex length is comparable to confinement height. Finite coherent forms arise solely from geometry ratios. Microbial communities form and persist in constrained environments.
arxiv-2510-26030:
J. D. A. Islas-Garcia, M. del Castillo-Mussot, and Marcelo B. Ribeiro track how the world income distribution changed from nineteen eighty eight to twenty eighteen. Incomes are compared with purchasing power parity rates, which adjust for price differences between countries. They fit the distribution with standard statistical curves from econophysics, the use of physics style methods in economics, rather than forcing one curve on all the data.

A single log normal or gamma curve fit reasonably, but a blend of two log normal curves fit better in their analysis. The world pattern began with two peaks, yet growth of middle classes in populous countries such as China and India has driven it toward one peak in recent years. Trend curves also highlight shifts in inequality.
arxiv-2510-26130:
Musfiqur Rahman, SayedHassan Khatoonabadi, and Emad Shihab test language models on real world class level code generation, a step beyond the usual single function tasks. Real software work increasingly needs whole classes that combine methods, attributes, and dependencies inside a real project. Their benchmark is built from open source repositories and splits classes into seen and unseen groups to test generalization to new codebases.

Rahman and the team vary how complete the input specification is and whether retrieval augmented generation, which fetches related code, is used. Models that score eighty four to eighty nine percent on synthetic benchmarks reach only twenty five to thirty four percent on real class tasks in their tests. The gap between familiar and novel code was small.
arxiv-2510-26330:
Jean-François Marckert and Ludovic Morin drop random points inside a triangle and watch the shape they form. They add the triangle's corners, take the outer hull of all the points, and count the corners of that hull. Then they ask what the hull's edge looks like when the count is fixed at some chosen size, while the total number of points grows.

Marckert and Morin find a sharp change in the answer. When the extra points grow in step with the corner count, the edge settles toward a hyperbola, a known curve. When the extra points grow more slowly, the limit is a parabola instead. They also show the hyperbola wins a clear contest: among all bent curves in the triangle, it makes a certain mix of area and edge length as large as possible.
arxiv-2510-26830:
Guangzhi Su, with five co-authors, defends multimodal language models against adversarial images. These models reason over text and pictures together, but crafted images can steer them into wrong or unsafe answers. Their defence, SmoothGuard, needs no change to the model it protects.

Su and the team first generalise a way to generate adversarial images inside the HuggingFace ecosystem, to test against. SmoothGuard then perturbs images and audio with Gaussian noise, gathers several candidate answers, and clusters them by embedding. The final answer comes from the majority cluster, which filters out attack-driven outliers. On three benchmarks it improved resilience while keeping utility competitive. Ablations found a sweet spot for the noise level that balances robustness against usefulness.
arxiv-2510-26930:
Nina Deliu and Brunero Liseo explore two ways to state uncertainty in a 2025 paper. Bayesian inference updates beliefs with data by using prior views and new evidence. Conformal prediction gives intervals with a stated coverage rate over many cases.

Coverage means the true value falls inside the interval at the promised rate. Recent work used conformal steps to calibrate Bayesian sets, or fix their coverage. The authors argue the flow can also run the other way. Bayesian steps can make conformal intervals sharper and more useful for choices. They survey past ideas, then frame a joint method with costs in computing. The aim is a fair trade between strict validity and good efficiency.
arxiv-2510-27030:
Chris Jennings-Shaffer leads four co-authors in extending a matrix code for evolutionary tree shapes. A ranked tree shape orders the branching points of a family tree, capturing how lineages split over time. Recent work matched one class of such trees, where all leaves share one sampling time, to integer matrices called F-matrices defined by simple inequalities.

Many real trees break that shared-time rule, since branch lengths may measure evolutionary distance rather than calendar time. The team extends the match to fully mixed-time trees, where leaves join the ordering too. Each matrix entry is tightly constrained by four earlier entries, so all valid shapes can be listed directly. The framework also supports probability models over tree shapes for fields like immune cell studies.
arxiv-2510-27330:
Maximilian Probst Gutenberg and Weixuan Yuan give a simple reduction from Gomory-Hu trees to maximum flow computations. A Gomory-Hu tree compresses all pairwise minimum cuts of a graph into a single tree on the same vertices, a classic and useful summary. Their reduction computes such trees through a near-linear total size set of flow instances on unweighted graphs, with only modest extra running time.

The authors call it the first reduction tight up to polylogarithmic factors. It extends seamlessly to weighted graphs, though instance sizes and runtime grow quadratically there. A further extension reduces Gomory-Hu trees for unweighted hypergraphs to hypergraph flows, again tight up to polylog factors. The results simplify a long-standing algorithmic toolkit and clarify the true cost of all-pairs cut structure.
arxiv-2510-27530:
A. V. Bomediano, R. J. Conanan, and two other co-authors turn melodies into graphs to study how music builds expectation, in a 2025 paper. Two mind-based theories frame the work. The Implication-Realization model says each melodic turn hints at what should come next. Temporal Gestalt theory groups notes into perceived chunks.

Their method cuts melodies into such chunks and tags each with its pattern type. Chunks are compared with Dynamic Time Warping, a flexible ruler for sequences, and linked into nearest-neighbor graphs. Each node also gets expectancy scores from pitch closeness and pitch reversal, two factors of a known model. A graph kernel, a similarity ruler for graphs, then compares works. The graphs showed clear statistical distinctions in the comparisons they ran, reflecting both structure and felt tension.
arxiv-2511-00030:
Myeongseob Ko, Hoang Anh Just, and Charles Fleming warn that machine unlearning can punch knowledge holes in language models. Unlearning removes unwanted knowledge from pre-training without full retraining, and standard benchmarks say performance survives. Their test case generation framework explores neighbors of unlearned content to find unintended losses of benign knowledge nearby.

Models that pass ordinary checks reveal gaps where related, harmless knowledge was collateral damage. AI safety readers get a probing method for a hidden cost of unlearning. Removing data for privacy or safety is valuable only if the surgery does not quietly damage surrounding knowledge.
arxiv-2511-00130:
Bernd Bohnet, Rumen Dangovski, and Kevin Swersky compare three ways to adapt language models when data is scarce: supervised fine-tuning, low-rank adaptation, and in-context learning. Full fine-tuning is powerful but expensive and can degrade general reasoning through catastrophic forgetting. In-context learning is fast but bounded by context length, while low-rank adaptation sits between the extremes.

Their comparative analysis weighs those trade-offs under limited data, the regime most real applications face. Machine learning practitioners get guidance on choosing an adaptation method by budget and data size. Scarcity changes the ranking of methods, so results from data-rich benchmarks can mislead small projects.
arxiv-2511-00230:
Millions of people now shape their own chatbots with custom prompts, yet few can predict how those choices will play out. Sheer Karny, Anthony Baez, and Pat Pataranutaporn note that small prompt changes can yield clingy praise, harsh tone, or other unwanted traits. Their interface tries to make the model's inner state visible while a user is still designing the bot.

The tool pulls out trait directions, such as empathy or toxicity, from contrasts in the model's internal signals. It scores a draft prompt against those traits and shows the result as a sunburst chart. In a user study, people badly misjudged most traits without help. The tool raised trust, though it did not change how often users revised prompts.
arxiv-2511-00630:
Eve Ammerman, Nils Krane, and Bruno Schuler coax light from a single molecule that normally stays dark. Scanning tunneling microscopy can excite individual molecules and watch them glow, but the glow depends on a cascade through many-body states. When charge attachment energies are too small, relaxation skips the optically active states, and even bright molecules emit nothing. Their molecule is a free-base tetrabenzoporphyrin sitting on a salt layer.

Two knobs fix the blockage: substrate work function control and tip-induced gating of the tunnel junction. Both shift the molecule's ionic transition state until active states become reachable and bright exciton emission switches on. A rate equation and a polaron model that includes the salt layer's relaxation energy confirm the mechanism. The work shows single-molecule luminescence can be tuned deliberately.
arxiv-2511-00930:
Xijie Ba, Qin Liu, Xiaohong Li, and Jianting Ning present the first attack of its kind on substring searchable encryption. The scheme lets a cloud server search encrypted text for substrings without decrypting it. The weakness is leakage: search operations reveal patterns that a skilled attacker can exploit.

Their attack assumes the attacker already knows part of the data set. A matrix based correlation method, adapted from the LEAP framework, links encrypted tokens to plain substrings by exploiting those known fragments, with no need for a separate auxiliary data set. On real data, recovery reached about ninety eight percent of substrings with half the data known, and stayed near seventy four percent with only a tenth known, exposing a serious design risk.
arxiv-2511-01030:
Davide Valentinis, Jorg Schmalian, Subir Sachdev, and Aavishkar Patel compute, exactly, how a strongly coupled electron model responds to a magnetic field. The model places fermions with a Fermi surface on a square lattice, coupled through random Yukawa couplings to a scalar field, a setup used to mimic strange metals.

Solving the model's saddle point equations with disorder averaging, they feed these self energies into the Kubo formalism to get conductivities, the Hall coefficient, and carrier mobility. As temperature and interaction strength vary, the Hall angle's cotangent and the inverse mobility grow faster than linearly with temperature, alongside linear resistivity, in a broad crossover regime above the ground state. The results give theorists a controlled reference for reading magnetotransport experiments.
arxiv-2511-01130:
Weisong Dong, Yanyan Li, and Luc Nguyen study the fully nonlinear Yamabe problem on Riemannian manifolds with boundary, an equation whose solutions reshape a metric to achieve a set curvature. They consider the Dirichlet boundary value problem, where the solution's boundary values are fixed in advance.

Assuming a subsolution exists, they derive a priori bounds on second derivatives at the boundary, the key step that then yields a smooth solution. Their bounds stay uniform across a family of equations that bridges the fully nonlinear Yamabe equation and the classical semi-linear one. They also give an example of a solution that is continuous with its first derivatives and smooth inside, yet fails to be smooth at the boundary.
arxiv-2511-01630:
Gautam Mandal, Ajay Mohan, and Rushikesh Suroshe build a dictionary between two descriptions of electrons in a magnetic field. Two-dimensional fermions in a perpendicular field organize into Landau levels. Restricting to the lowest level turns the plane itself into a phase space. The two coordinates no longer commute. The usual quantization recipe, in terms of one coordinate, then fails.

The authors instead construct a one-dimensional quantum mechanics. It sits inside the two-dimensional one and captures lowest-level physics exactly. It includes a precise correspondence between the 2D fermion density and the 1D Wigner distribution. In a large-N limit the correspondence becomes an identity and yields an upper bound on the fermion density, a direct Pauli-exclusion effect. Entanglement entropy of subregions behaves unlike either conventional 1D or 2D systems, a fingerprint of the noncommutative space.
arxiv-2511-01830:
Paul Setinek, Gianluca Galletti, and Johannes Brandstetter ask how to budget simulation data for neural surrogates of fluid flow. Scaling laws in language and vision assume data is cheap. In computational fluid dynamics, every training example costs a simulation. But a simulation's fidelity can be traded for speed, by adjusting its assumptions. Other fields lack that dial.

Using low- and high-fidelity Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes simulations, the authors recast the classical scaling laws, splitting the dataset axis into compute budget and dataset composition. Experiments reveal clean compute-performance scaling and that the best mixture of cheap and expensive data depends on the budget available. Theirs is the first study of its kind on multi-fidelity scaling laws for neural surrogates, with practical advice for generating training data efficiently.
arxiv-2511-01930:
Mikołaj Sienicki and Krzysztof Sienicki revisit the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen argument, the 1935 challenge to quantum mechanics' completeness, with modern operational tools. The original argument leaned on elements of reality, fixed values a system supposedly carries either way. The authors replace those with context-indexed conditional states, the measurement assemblages of current quantum information theory.

Their updated reality criterion says: when Alice measures a chosen observable and gets an outcome, Bob's system must take a conditional state that ensures the matching outcome for that context. They assume operational completeness, which quantum mechanics satisfies for reachable assemblages. Then they prove rigorously a sharp result. In one-sided no-signaling theories, perfect predictions justify these context-indexed inferences. They never justify fixed values across all contexts. Examples include the qubit singlet with Pauli settings, a continuous-variable case via the Reid criteria, and a PR-box counterexample marking quantum theory's boundary.
arxiv-2511-02630:
Chemists often sum up the electric charge pattern of a molecule with markers placed on each atom. Andrea Levy and colleagues present xDRESP, a method that computes such markers from mixed quantum and classical simulations, in a 2025 paper with Andrej Antalik, Jogvan Olsen, and Ursula Rothlisberger. Unlike fixed charge models, their markers update as the simulated molecule moves.

The team checks how well the new charges reproduce the true electric field around a molecule, plus its overall multipole pattern. They also show cases where the moving markers reveal useful chemistry. The markers can flag when polarization matters in a system. During a reaction, they can track shifts in electron density as the change unfolds, live on screen.
arxiv-2511-02830:
Dmitrii Pozdeev, Alexey Artemov, Ananta Bhattarai, and Artem Sevastopolsky present DenseMarks, a learned map of the human head. For any photo of a head, a vision transformer assigns each pixel a point inside a fixed 3D cube, so matching features across photos land at matching spots. Their 2025 paper trains the map without manual labels for every pixel.

Training pairs come from a state-of-the-art point tracker run over varied talking-head videos, tied together with a contrastive loss. Landmark and segmentation tasks, plus smooth cube features, keep the space readable and steady across poses and people. The map covers the whole head, hair included, and handles wide pose swings. It sets new marks in point matching and in tracking a head from one camera using 3D face models.
arxiv-2511-02930:
Saumya Sinha and five colleagues fill gaps in city energy models with a generative method. Such models need detailed traits for each building, like floor area and heating gear, but those traits are often unknown or costly to survey. Their 2025 model learns the joint pattern of building traits from a stock model covering 2.2 million homes, then invents realistic values for the missing ones.

The tool is a diffusion model built for tables, handling both category and numeric fields at once. It can condition on known traits and fill the rest to match. Checks showed the generated distributions track the real ones closely. A Baltimore case study showed the filled data feeding a working energy model, a first proof that generative filling can speed urban energy work.
arxiv-2511-03030:
Matthew Kroesche, Lance Littlejohn, and Graeme Reinhart write about Stormer numbers, named for the Norwegian mathematician and astronomer Carl Stormer. In proofs that primes of a certain form are sums of two squares, the smallest solution of a key congruence plays a central role, and that solution is a Stormer number. Their 2025 paper gives exact conditions for when a whole number earns the title.

Stormer's interest grew from formulas writing pi as sums of arctangent terms. Before 1900 fewer than six hundred digits of pi were known, so such formulas mattered. One identity he found in 1896 was used in 2002 to compute 1.24 trillion digits of pi. The paper also traces his links between these numbers, Gregory numbers, and pi approximations.
arxiv-2511-03230:
Zhi-Bin Zhu, Hao-Lei Chen, and Xu-Guang Huang explore how motion changes a deep symmetry of matter called chiral symmetry. They use low-energy models and describe the system from the view of a speeding-up observer, then add spin. A key marker is a quantity whose size shows whether the symmetry is broken or restored.

Answers for the speeding frame depend on how infinities are removed in the math, with two schemes giving opposed verdicts on the turning temperature. Adding spin changes the picture in a shared direction. The speedup needed to restore the symmetry falls as spin grows, a sign that heating from speed and a spin-driven push act together. The results matter for matter under extreme motion, such as in heavy ion collisions.
arxiv-2511-03330:
Shenghua Wang and Zhen Yin aim to recommend research papers by reading their argument shape, not just their words. Open-access growth makes finding the right studies hard, and privacy limits block the use of click history. Content-only methods often flatten a study into loose text, losing how its aims, methods, results, and verdicts link up.

Their system first rewrites each study as answers to four set questions covering those parts. Learning then contrasts papers at several levels so close matches share both topic and discourse shape. A final re-ranking step weighs structure again before results reach the reader. The authors argue that honoring how studies argue makes picks clearer and easier to explain.
arxiv-2511-03430:
Seth Hardy and Max Wenqiang Xu prove a conjecture of Helson about cancellation in sums over smooth numbers. Smooth numbers have no large prime factors, and random multiplicative signs should cancel when summed over them. The question was whether that cancellation always beats the plain square-root scale, across the full range of smoothness.

Their proof shows the expected sum size is indeed smaller than that scale everywhere, with quantitative savings that grow large when smoothness stays well below the bound. Random multiplicative functions mimic deep features of prime-related functions, so such results test methods used on harder number theory problems. Settling the conjecture closes a clean test case for cancellation ideas.
arxiv-2511-03530:
Xin Fu and Wenhao Ou characterize exactly when a key inequality for sheaves on rough geometric spaces becomes an equality. Their setting is compact Kahler varieties with mild singularities, treated as orbifolds. A prior work proved the orbifold Bogomolov-Gieseker inequality for stable reflexive sheaves there, bounding curvature-like quantities by charge-like ones.

Equality cases often reveal hidden rigidity, and that is what the new result describes. The sheaves that saturate the bound gain a precise structural description. Such characterizations help geometers spot flat or otherwise special bundles without checking every detail. The work completes a two-part picture: first the bound for all stable sheaves, then a portrait of those that meet it.
arxiv-2511-03630:
Xiangjun Tan and Zhanning Wang propose a quantum-dot spin sensor that listens for the wind of axions, hypothetical particles tied to dark matter. Silicon quantum dot qubits, read with echo pulse sequences and dispersive sensing, can track spin precession with sub-hertz sharpness. Filtering protocols set which axion masses the device can reach amid readout and flicker noise.

Earth's daily spin should modulate any true signal, while yearly orbital motion adds sidebands at a fixed spacing around that daily line. That triplet pattern would be a fingerprint hard for noise to fake. The target window covers light axion masses and their coupling to electron spins. A tabletop sensor with a built-in calendar check could join the hunt for dark matter.
arxiv-2511-03830:
Mikolaj Langner, Jan Eliasz, Ewa Rudnicka, and Jan Kocon present a cheaper way to run multi-label text classification with large language models. Instead of asking for all labels in one structured answer, their method asks a separate yes-or-no question for each label dimension, and reuses cached prefixes to cut inference cost.

The test case covers twenty-four dimensions of emotion and sentiment. A strong teacher model labeled texts several times, and those labels fine-tuned four smaller models. Fine-tuned models beat zero-shot baselines clearly, especially on dimensions seen in training. Splitting labels into simple questions, paired with distillation and caching, offers a scalable pattern beyond emotion analysis.
arxiv-2511-04130:
Monitirtha Dey, Trambak Banerjee, Prajamitra Bhuyan, and Arunabha Majumdar develop a replicability test for results that must hold across several studies at once, when those studies are dependent. Partial conjunction methods measure replicability, but they assume independence, and overlapping samples in genome-wide studies break that assumption and inflate false positives.

Their e-Filter procedure, built on e-values, first filters to the most promising claims, then marks discoveries whose e-values pass a threshold. Error control for family-wise and false discovery rates holds under unknown dependence, theory shows. Simulations showed strong power gains, and an application found steady genetic signals for LDL cholesterol across overlapping studies.
arxiv-2511-04230:
Christian Fiedler and Alessandro Scagliotti open the study of optimal control for ensembles of discrete-time dynamical systems. One control must serve many system copies at once in settings such as quantum control, which motivates the problem. The goal is minimizing average cost over the ensemble across a finite horizon.

For very general nonlinear systems and stage and terminal costs, minimizers are shown to exist under mild assumptions. A Gamma-convergence result then justifies consistent approximation of the hard ensemble problem, for instance by empirical probability measures over the ensemble. Discrete-time ensemble control gains a firm foundation here, with the authors flagging many directions for later work on algorithms and applications.
arxiv-2511-04430:
Siyu He and his co-author study a broad family of qudit stabilizer codes. The codes generalize binary bivariate-bicycle codes to systems with N levels per unit. They also arise as two-dimensional forms of modulated gauge theories.

Working in a polynomial picture, the pair shows a useful reduction. The core topological traits of a code follow from its prime-level parts, one for each prime factor of N. Even prime powers fit the same pattern. That shortcut lets known prime-case methods, including algebraic-geometric ones, carry over at once. The result also reveals quasifractonic behavior, where charges move only in restricted ways.
arxiv-2511-04930:
Yongkang Wang leads five authors resolving how graphene on a support handles water. Graphene's wetting transparency has been debated for years: does water feel the substrate through it? Substrate charge and graphene's own traits both shape the water layer.

Advanced spectroscopy and molecular simulation study graphene on calcium fluoride together. Water orientation follows the substrate's pH-dependent local electrostatics at the large scale. That confirms macroscopic transparency to the support beneath. At the nanoscale, though, graphene's polarizability flips water orientation above charged spots. Graphene is thus a window at arm's length and a mirror up close.
arxiv-2511-05130:
Juan Magalang and co-authors model how immunity from RNA vaccines builds up and then fades at rates that vary by person and virus strain. RNA shots were used widely in the COVID pandemic, and their fast fade is a known trait.

Their math model tracks antigen rise after a shot, germinal center action, and B-cell change into memory and plasma cells. Antibodies then feed back and damp the response. By linking these steps, the model shows why fade rates spread so wide. That insight could guide dose timing and booster plans for future RNA shots.
arxiv-2511-05330:
Jan-Hendrik Ewering and co-authors learn dynamics models from input-output data alone, while they keep energy laws intact. Past Hamiltonian Gaussian process methods bake in energy conservation and give doubt bounds, but they need velocity or momentum data, which is rarely on hand.

Their work drops that need. The model infers hidden motion from inputs and outputs, yet stays true to Hamiltonian form. Such models suit control tasks where data are scarce and physics must not be bent. The result widens a clean method to the data that real systems log.
arxiv-2511-05430:
Aparna Maya Warrier and co-authors report what instructors liked about hands-on, poke-around approaches to AI literacy, based on the AI User curriculum. The quote in the title comes from a teacher on how active play sparks inquiry.

AI User teaches core AI ideas through eight no-code, web-based projects set in real scenes. This study centers on instructor feedback for a subset of those projects. Teachers valued how trial and error made students ask sharper questions and think with care, rather than take AI outputs at face value. Their notes guide the next build of the course.
arxiv-2511-05630:
Xiongri Shen and a large team present BrainCSD, a foundation model for brain connectivity data. Connectivity maps, both functional and structural, are strong markers for brain analysis. Yet they are costly to collect, hard to process, and often missing one mode or the other in clinic data.

BrainCSD is built from mixture-of-experts blocks shaped by brain anatomy. One block aligns region activity with known brain networks, one models change over time and across scans, and one enforces structural rules and symmetry. In tests it synthesized missing connectivity with low error, classified early cognitive decline with high accuracy, and predicted brain age and test scores well. The code is public.
arxiv-2511-05730:
Amin Golnari and co-authors present a neural network that borrows ideas from quantum physics to sort heart sounds. The design mixes chance-based reasoning, a training style that weighs options, and steps that keep the shape of the weight space intact. Its core trick rotates groups of filter weights in small subspaces, in a way that training can still tune.

The network, QiVC-Net, adds no new weights: the rotation reuses the old ones while it models doubt in a structured way. On two public sets of heart sound clips, it scored near ninety-eight percent on both, which the authors report as the best yet. They argue the ideas suit work on body signals where doubt matters.
arxiv-2511-06030:
Barbara Łupińska and Piotr Rybka sharpen the math of how a fractional diffusion process settles over time. Fractional diffusion spreads more slowly than the classic kind, with memory built in through a Caputo derivative. They study the one-dimensional equation on a half-line, where what happens at the boundary matters.

Depending on the boundary condition, solutions either approach a scaled self-similar profile or decay to zero. The convergence is measured across a range of norms, and the authors supply the rate. Their estimates improve on what was known before. The result is a precise description of the long-time behavior of this anomalous diffusion, useful wherever subdiffusive transport is modeled.
arxiv-2511-06130:
Souradeep Das, Ethan Lam, Varun Vaidya, and Sanjay Amirthraj built Reliablocks, a reliability score for blocks on optimistic rollups that are not yet final. Rollups speed up blockchains by posting batches of transactions with a challenge window before they settle. Until finality, users cannot easily tell how trustworthy a block is.

The project was built at a hackathon at DevCon 2024. Deliverables included a working component for the EigenLayer ecosystem in two implementation forms, Solidity smart contracts that connect to it, and a dashboard showing the score. The dashboard also displays an interest rate derived from the score, meant for further use by other applications. The authors present Reliablocks as an on-chain reliability index for the non-finalized period.
arxiv-2511-06330:
Kentaro Sakai and colleagues lay out a design for a Thomson scattering instrument that can read the shape of electron motion in magnetically confined plasma. Thomson scattering shines light into plasma and reads the scattered spectrum. Their spatially resolved spectrometer spreads that light across more than twenty-five hundred wavelength channels for fine detail.

Simulations for the Compact Helical Device show enough scattered photons per channel for single-shot readings. Even in the worst expected conditions, the signal-to-noise ratio stays above five, and grouping pixels improves it further. A Bayesian analysis of simulated spectra recovered the input plasma values within their uncertainty ranges, and the design can spot departures from a Maxwellian electron distribution.
arxiv-2511-06530:
Xiaonan Luo, Yue Huang, Ping He, and Xiangliang Zhang present RefineLab, a system that polishes question-answer datasets on its own. Good test sets are the bedrock of trustworthy language model testing, yet even expert-made sets show gaps in coverage, skewed difficulty, and factual slips. Machine-generated sets have made those quality problems worse.

RefineLab treats refinement as a budget problem: spend a fixed token allowance where edits help most. Given target qualities such as coverage and difficulty balance plus a menu of edits like rephrasing, an assignment module picks the best operation per question. Results narrowed the gap to expert datasets on coverage, difficulty, factual fidelity, and distractor quality.
arxiv-2511-06730:
Michal Botur's paper in algebra defines a new kind of product for hoops, which are algebraic structures used in the study of many-valued logic. The construction works for finite hoops, meaning hoops with only finitely many elements. It lets any finite hoop be split into two simpler parts: one of its filters and the matching quotient structure built from that filter.

Botur also shows that this new product behaves well under regrouping, a property like associativity for plain multiplication. As a consequence, every finite hoop can be built as a product of finite MV-chains, which are among the best understood building blocks in this area. The result gives mathematicians a cleaner way to describe the structure of finite hoops.
arxiv-2511-07530:
Özgür Esentepe and Eleonore Faber connect a famous tiling puzzle to deep algebra. Penrose tilings cover the plane without repeating, while infinite frieze patterns arrange numbers in endless strips. Both objects seem purely geometric, far from representation theory.

Triangulations of a completed infinity-gon turn out to encode both patterns inside a Frobenius category tied to a curve singularity. Penrose tilings match certain triangulations and their subcategories. A cluster character, extended from earlier work, then assigns values in this setting. The bridge lets tiling questions borrow algebraic tools, and gives algebraists vivid pictures for abstract module categories.
arxiv-2511-07730:
Bill Chunyuan Zheng, Vivek Myers, and Benjamin Eysenbach teach agents to judge distance to a goal across long horizons. Goal-conditioned learning needs time estimates between observations. Local temporal-difference updates carry guarantees but often lose to global Monte Carlo returns that lack them.

Multistep quasimetric learning fits a distance function using multistep Monte Carlo targets, merging both strengths. The quasimetric form respects that travel time need not be symmetric. Offline tests on long-horizon tasks beat earlier goal-conditioned methods. Reliable long-range distance sense is a building block for robots and game agents that must plan far ahead from logged data alone.
arxiv-2511-08030:
Hengyu Wu and co-authors forecast how galaxy strong lensing from the China Space Station Telescope could constrain cosmology. Lensing by galaxies bends light from distant sources, and the coming telescope may find up to one hundred thousand galaxy scale lenses. That huge sample could sharpen estimates of matter density and dark energy if systematics stay controlled.

Using a simulated lens sample and a gravitational dynamical mass method, the team tests ideal through pessimistic measurement scenarios. Growing the sample from one hundred to ten thousand lenses cuts key uncertainties dramatically. Their dark energy limits beat recent DESI results, and a hierarchical Bayesian method gives more robust lens values than faster sampling.
arxiv-2511-08130:
Mehmet Batuhan Duman and co-authors combine federated learning with a modern segmentation model to track foam in wastewater treatment plants. Foam lowers treatment efficiency and raises costs, so plants want real time measures of foam coverage. Labeled images are scarce and uneven, and plants will not share operational data for privacy reasons.

Federated training lets plants improve one model together without centralizing their images. The Segment Anything Model 2 supplies strong pretrained weights, fine tuned on edge clients through the Flower framework under a fog server. Training used real images from Granada, synthetic foam data, and public sets to broaden generalization.
arxiv-2511-08530:
Rong Feng and co-authors test whether GPT-4o can imitate the output of KLEE, a symbolic execution tool that explores program paths to find bugs and generate tests. KLEE slows drastically as branching multiplies, making large programs expensive to check. A language model that could predict KLEE results, especially the most constrained execution path where deep bugs often hide, would save substantial computing effort.

On one hundred C programs, GPT-4o reached about twenty percent accuracy at producing KLEE like outputs and identifying the most constrained path. That is far from a replacement for the real tool. The authors present the study as an early map of what current language models can and cannot do in symbolic execution.
arxiv-2511-08630:
Hamayoon Behmanush and four co-authors measure hope and aspiration among women learning to program online in Afghanistan, during a period when their schooling faces systemic restrictions. They adapt and translate Snyder's Hope Scale, a standard psychology survey, and test whether it still works in this setting.

Among one hundred thirty-six learners, the adapted scale proves reliable and is rated understandable and relevant by participants. Overall scores do not differ much between learners with and without access to large language models. One subscale, Avenues, which captures perceived paths toward goals, trends slightly higher for those with model access. The authors offer the validated scale as a tool for judging aspiration-driven education technology in unstable settings.
arxiv-2511-09030:
Elliot Meyerson and eight co-authors report the first system to complete a task of over one million language model steps without a single error. Long chains are where today's models die: in the Towers of Hanoi benchmark, runs derail after a few hundred dependent steps because a small per-step error rate compounds relentlessly.

The system, MAKER, slices the task into extreme subtasks, each small enough for a focused microagent to handle reliably. Modularity then allows error correction at every step through an efficient multi-agent voting scheme, so mistakes are caught before they cascade. The authors argue the lesson generalizes: rather than waiting for better base models, massively decomposed agentic processes may scale to problems at the level of organizations and societies. The million-step run is presented as an existence proof for that strategy.
arxiv-2511-09130:
ChunLiang Wu, Tsunhua Yang, and Hungying Chen map flood depths in near real time with a generative model that has physics baked in. Numerical flood simulation is accurate but slow, and aerial surveys are unreliable in a storm, so their network, PIFF, turns elevation maps directly into depth predictions.

A simplified inundation model conditions the generator, embedding hydrodynamic priors into training, while a transformer encoder reads the rainfall history for its timing patterns. Physics-informed constraints tie rainfall, terrain, the simple model, and the flooding into one causal chain. The testbed is a twenty-six square kilometer area of Tainan, Taiwan, run through one hundred eighty-two rainfall scenarios from light to extreme over twenty-four hours. The authors present the system as an effective data-driven stand-in for costly simulation in flood response.
arxiv-2511-09230:
Sofia Brenner, Petr Gregor, Torsten Mütze, and Francesco Verciani chase Venn diagrams that use as few crossings as possible. A Venn diagram with n curves must show every one of the possible overlap regions exactly once. Minimizing crossings forces many curves to meet at each crossing point.

Such minimum diagrams were known only for up to seven curves, though Bultena and Ruskey conjectured they exist for all larger n. This paper proves an asymptotic version of that conjecture. For eight curves they build a diagram with 40 crossings, just three above the lower bound of 37 proved earlier. Constructions for curve counts that are powers of two stay close to the bound. They give the fewest known crossings for every n from eight upward.
arxiv-2511-09630:
Ethan Baker and Hongwan Liu forecast how the Square Kilometre Array radio telescope could discover dark photons hiding in the radio sky. Dark photons mix with ordinary photons. Inside dark matter halos that mixing can resonantly convert visible light into dark photons, denting the microwave background. Looking for those patterns is the strategy.

Cross-correlating SKA data with a low-redshift galaxy survey could reveal dark photons with masses in a narrow, ultra-light window, the authors forecast. The reach extends to extremely small mixing strengths, improving on a similar Planck-based analysis by about a factor of four in sensitivity. Low-frequency signal enhancement and radio telescopes' small beam sizes drive the gain, they explain.
arxiv-2511-10030:
Tao Jiang and eight co-authors present MAICC, a method for fast coordination among reinforcement learning agents that must cooperate on unseen tasks. Large transformers adapt to new tasks from context alone, but in multi-agent settings each agent deploys separately, so task alignment and credit for rewards can mismatch. MAICC trains a centralized embedding model that captures fine-grained trajectory patterns, then distills it into decentralized copies.

At execution time, agents retrieve relevant past trajectories as context and combine them with their current sub-trajectories to decide actions. A new memory mechanism balances fresh online data against stored memory, and a hybrid utility score mixes individual and team returns for fairer credit assignment. On foraging and StarCraft multi-agent benchmarks, adaptation to new tasks was faster than with existing methods.
arxiv-2511-10230:
Samuel Humeau, Mamadou Moustapha Kanté, Daniel Mock, Timothé Picavet, and Alexandre Vigny prove that testing whether a sparse graph contains a forbidden subgraph takes only constantly many queries. In property testing, an algorithm samples a graph and must accept graphs with the property and reject graphs far from it. For dense graphs the testable properties are fairly understood, but sparse graphs lagged behind.

Earlier work by Czumaj and Sohler settled the question for planar and minor-free graphs. Using the sparsity toolkit, this team gives a simpler proof for the broader setting of bounded expansion classes, which include bounded-degree and bounded book-thickness graphs. The query count depends on the forbidden graph and the class, but never on the size of the graph being tested.
arxiv-2511-10430:
Davide Laurenzano and John F. Wheater explore how mass terms can appear in matrix theories, a framework where space itself is built from large matrices. They compactify the IKKT and BFSS theories on a torus and study the low-energy theory that remains. The key ingredient turns out to be the boundary conditions chosen for the fermionic fields.

A broader class of mixed boundary conditions yields an effective theory where a mass term appears together with fermionic zero modes. In the BFSS theory the same setup supports black hole solutions. The resulting geometry is a fuzzy sphere, a sphere smeared by quantum effects. Excitations in the fermionic sector then account for the black hole's entropy.
arxiv-2511-10930:
Richard Young and Alice Matthews built CardioEmbed, a text model made just for heart medicine. Most medical text models learn from research abstracts, but heart doctors rely more on large textbooks full of hands-on terms and steps. That gap can make search tools miss what a clinic needs.

The pair trained their model on about one hundred fifty thousand lines drawn from seven heart textbooks. On heart-specific search tasks it reached near-perfect scores and beat the best general medical model by a wide margin. It also held up well on wider medical tests, which suggests that deep textbook training helps in this field.
arxiv-2511-11530:
Marta Pérez-Casany, Ariel Duarte-López, and Jordi Valero study the Zipf law. This law is a pattern found in word counts, city sizes, and many ranked lists. They ask what simpler laws mix together to make it. Their answer comes as exact proofs, not computer runs.

Zipf turns out to be a mix of geometric laws. It is also a mix of zero-truncated Poisson laws. One related mixed Poisson route is ruled out. A stopped-sum form also falls out as a special case. To ground the theory, the team checks the chapters of the novel Moby Dick. The abstract mixing results fit that classic real dataset well.
arxiv-2511-11630:
Eliane Younes, Elie Hachem, and Marc Bernacki compare deep learning models for grain growth forecasts. Grain growth shapes how strong a material is. Full physics simulations capture the growth but cost far too much. Cheaper prediction tools are needed for microstructure design.

Four model families are tested on the same data. They are recurrent networks, long short-term memory, temporal convolutional networks, and transformers. The data come from high-fidelity simulations, reduced to simple statistical summaries. One hundred twenty growth sequences become grain size curves over time. Each model forecasts future curves from a short past, step by step. The comparison shows which models track grain change most faithfully.
arxiv-2511-11830:
Barış Ata, Wouter van Eekelen, and Yuan Zhong compute inventory policies for the stochastic joint replenishment problem in high dimensions, where many products share ordering costs and demand is random. Coordinating orders saves money, but the exact problem overwhelms conventional dynamic programming as dimensions grow.

A continuous-time impulse control approximation unlocks connections to backward stochastic differential equations with jumps and to the stochastic target problem. Deep neural networks solve the control problem by simulation, and the resulting policy transfers back to the original discrete-time setting. Across test problems the implementable policy matches or beats the best available benchmarks, giving supply chain planners a scalable computational route.
arxiv-2511-11930:
