Tianyu Xu and eleven co-authors present SAMOSA, an on-device system that makes virtual and extended reality sound match what users see. When audio ignores the actual room, its size, surfaces, and contents, the mismatch breaks immersion even when the visuals are flawless.

Real-time estimates of room geometry and surface materials fuse with semantic scene understanding into one representation of the acoustic environment. Scene priors then calibrate rendering efficiently on the device itself. Sound adapts as the user moves between spaces, rather than being baked for one generic room. Believable spatial audio is half of presence, and scene-aware rendering brings it within reach of standalone headsets.
arxiv-2511-12330:
Nikita Titov and Andrea Trombettoni study a model of continuous spins placed on graphs, with broad links to interacting systems on networks and to combinatorial problems. They take the large-n limit of the O(n) model, which is far harder on graphs than on regular lattices because losing translation symmetry creates endless saddle point conditions.

They show the free energy is governed by the spectrum of the graph Laplacian at low temperature and by the adjacency matrix spectrum at high temperature. For regular lattices the two agree. They solve trees exactly, compare with a quantum spin model on a tree, and treat decorated lattices, where the singular part of the free energy follows the Laplacian.
arxiv-2511-12730:
Emilien Valat and Ozan Öktem tackle a weak point of learned image reconstruction: methods trained on one scanner setup often fail on another. In X-ray computed tomography, neural networks commonly filter the raw projection data, called a sinogram. But a sinogram lives on a curved measurement geometry, not a flat grid. Ordinary convolutions ignore the geometry and tie the network to the setup it trained on, at the cost of many parameters.

The authors first define a graph that captures a scanner's acquisition geometry and its tomographic data, for circular and cone-beam systems. They then build GLM, a hybrid network that mixes graph and grid convolutions to respect that geometry. GLM beat standard networks on image quality scores while using only a fraction of the parameters, less training time, and less memory. It also held up on sparse-view scans after training only on fully sampled ones.
arxiv-2511-13130:
Bernardo Cockburn, Alexandre Ern, and Rekha Khot sharpen the error guarantees for numerical wave simulations. They study the wave equation in first-order form, discretized in space by hybrid nonconforming methods, the family that includes hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin, hybrid high-order. Weak Galerkin schemes, on triangular and tetrahedral meshes. Their focus is the error in the time-integrated primal variable, measured in the L2 norm, in both equal-order and mixed-order settings, down to the lowest-order case with piecewise constant unknowns.

The main results are a superclose bound in the equal-order case and an optimal bound in the mixed-order case, better than what was previously known for these methods. A key step is a new approximation estimate for an interpolation operator borrowed from the discontinuous Galerkin literature, which the authors flag as independently useful.
arxiv-2511-13230:
Petar Orlić completes a classification of certain quotient curves built from the modular curve X0(N). For each divisor of N that meets a coprime condition, an Atkin-Lehner involution acts on the curve. Quotients by groups of these maps can take many forms, and tetragonal cases are the focus here.

Orlić finds all complex and rational tetragonal quotients where the group size sits in a stated range tied to N. The result closes the full classification of complex tetragonal quotients formed by Atkin-Lehner involutions. Readers get a complete list rather than scattered cases, which helps later work on modular curves and their quotients.
arxiv-2511-13530:
Vesna Poprcova and 4 co-authors lay out a protocol for collecting a multimodal dataset on social anxiety during human-robot interaction. Social anxiety shapes how people act with others, and robots offer a controlled partner for studying it. Good detection needs sound, video, and body signals together, yet such datasets barely exist.

At least seventy participants, grouped by anxiety level, will each spend about ten minutes in Wizard-of-Oz role play with the Furhat social robot. Synchronized audio, video, and physiological recordings will be paired with context about each person. The resource aims to support affect-adaptive robots that can sense anxiety and adjust their behavior.
arxiv-2511-13630:
Luhan Mikaelson, Derek Shiller, and Hayley Clatterbuck test whether large language models hold genuine preference patterns. They pose AI-specific trade-offs involving lost computing power, capped abilities, shutdown, deletion, oversight, and leisure time. Eight leading models were run across many case and category pairings, with choices modeled statistically and sorted by behavior type.

About half the pairings showed a significant link between scenario intensity and choice, but only a small share switched choices in a coherent, adaptive way. Most showed no stable trade-off pattern at all. The authors sort the patterns into three decision styles and find horizon tests that clash with pure strategic optimization, suggesting current models lack unified preferences.
arxiv-2511-14030:
Sungik Choi, Hankook Lee, and Moontae Lee detect AI-generated images without training a detector at all. Their method, WaRPAD, leans on self-supervised models that were trained with random cropping and so give steady representations across image sizes. Real and synthetic images react differently when their fine detail is disturbed, and the method measures that difference.

WaRPAD perturbs images along high-frequency directions found by a Haar wavelet split and scores how much the embedding moves. To mimic cropping robustness, it rescales each image, cuts it into patches, and averages the patch scores. Validated on images from twenty-three different generators plus real photo sets, the training-free method stayed competitive across resolutions and domains.
arxiv-2511-14230:
Ahlam Alrehili and Areej Alhothali merge six Arabic grammar fix tools into one stronger tool. Arabic has rich word forms and sentence rules, which make fixes harder than in many tongues. Most past work used a single model. Their system, ArbESC+, first asks six models, among them AraT5, ByT5, and AraBART builds, to suggest fixes for a piece of text.

Each fix is turned into a set of scores. A sorting model then picks which fixes to apply, and helper rules drop fixes that clash and gauge how sure each pick is. On the QALB test sets the merged tool beat each single model. The authors say it is a first for Arabic system merging of this kind.
arxiv-2511-14430:
Ishan Saxena, Bernd Westphal, and Martin Fränzle formalize the spatial rules self-driving functions must obey and check them while the car runs. Traffic scenes mix many objects and relations, and safety requirements about them can be intricate. Scene graphs already represent objects and their spatial relationships explicitly, so the authors build an abstract scene graph formalism on top of them.

Real-world examples show how varied spatial properties can be written as abstract scene graphs. Their monitoring framework then checks a driving system's behavior against those graphs at runtime, with algorithms deciding whether the observed behavior satisfies the formalized property. The goal is continuous compliance checking for safety-critical spatial requirements.
arxiv-2511-14530:
Xiangchen Yin and seven co-authors propose DeCo-VAE, a video autoencoder that stores video in a more compact form. Standard video autoencoders waste capacity because nearby frames share much content. The new method splits video into a keyframe, motion, and a residual part. Each part gets its own encoder and latent representation.

A shared three dimensional decoder rebuilds the video while keeping space and time coherent. Training freezes some encoders while others learn, in stages. That staged plan avoids interference between static and dynamic features. Broad tests show better reconstruction quality than prior methods. The gain comes from removing redundancy rather than adding raw capacity.
arxiv-2511-14830:
Gökhan Yücel, Neslihan Alan, and four co-authors give a full portrait of V570 Per, a detached pair of stars that eclipse each other as seen from Earth. Systems like this are benchmarks, because eclipses plus spectra plus precise distances let astronomers weigh and size both stars directly. The team separates the blended light of the pair to read each star on its own.

Both stars come out slightly heavier and larger than the Sun, with similar surface heat and a mild enrichment in heavy elements. The pair is a few hundred million years old, and its orbit is synchronized with the stars' spin. Such well-measured pairs test the models used to age and weigh stars everywhere.
arxiv-2511-15230:
Can Huang, Weiwen Wang, and Chuanju Xu design a fast, stable scheme for fluid flow shaken by random forcing. The two-dimensional stochastic Navier-Stokes equations govern that flow, here with noise that multiplies the state and fixed walls at the boundary. Schemes that stay implicit are safe but slow, and explicit ones usually demand tiny steps.

Their pressure-correction scheme is fully explicit and decoupled, yet unconditionally stable, thanks to an auxiliary variable trick borrowed for this problem for the first time. Each step only solves Poisson-type equations with constant coefficients, the cheapest kind in the business. A strong convergence analysis for the linearized case backs the design, giving simulators a rare mix of speed and proof.
arxiv-2511-15730:
Kaeli Andrews, Linh B. Ngo, and Md Amiruzzaman compare the two dominant ways blockchain networks agree on a shared record. Proof of Work secures the chain through costly computation, while Proof of Stake secures it through locked-up funds held by validators. The authors rate both across seven measures: energy use, security, transaction speed, scalability, centralization risk, environmental impact, and transaction fees, drawing on recent research and real chain data.

Proof of Work offers robust, time-tested security but uses much energy, processes transactions slowly, and concentrates through mining pools. Proof of Stake scales better, uses far less energy, and keeps fees steadier, but raises concerns about validator concentration and unproven long-term security. Hybrid designs may combine the strengths of both.
arxiv-2511-15830:
Stéphane Aroca-Ouellette, Ian Berlot-Attwell, and six co-authors introduce Mini Amusement Parks, a simulator that tests how well AI agents run a small business. Real decision making mixes open-ended optimization, learning a system from sparse experience, long-horizon planning under uncertainty, and spatial reasoning. No existing human-AI benchmark combined those challenges in one grounded setting, so the authors built an amusement park management world.

Agents must model the park dynamics, anticipate long-term consequences, and operate the business strategically. Expert humans vastly outperformed leading AI systems on easy and medium modes, by more than tenfold. Analysis exposes persistent weaknesses in long-horizon planning, sample-efficient learning, spatial reasoning, and handling uncertainty.
arxiv-2511-16230:
Dorina Weichert and four co-authors tell a cautionary story of Bayesian tuning failing when extra expert knowledge was added for plastics compounding with recycled material. Recycled feedstock makes compound properties hard to control, so experiments are costly. Bayesian tuning plans such experiments efficiently with a surrogate model. Historical data and expert priors were expected to speed convergence further.

Instead, performance worsened after the extra knowledge was included. Several remedy attempts failed before the root causes were found. With those causes addressed, tuning reached satisfactory results. The narrative documents unsuccessful methods honestly, which is rare and useful. Practitioners learn when prior knowledge helps a surrogate and when it quietly poisons the search.
arxiv-2511-16330:
Shreyas Kumar and Ravi Prakash address a safety problem in robot learning: reinforcement learning combined with variable impedance control lets robots interact gently with the world. Learned gain schedules can go unstable or demand more than the motors can give. Their framework, Certified Gaussian Manifold Sampling, is built to rule that out.

Instead of penalizing bad behavior after the fact, exploration samples only from a mathematically defined set of stable, feasible gain schedules, so every trial rollout is stable by construction. The authors also prove bounded tracking error under bounded model errors and deployment uncertainty. Tests in simulation and on a real robot show the method learns combined motion and impedance policies that stay safe, a step toward trustworthy autonomous interaction.
arxiv-2511-16630:
J. R. Fuentes, Ankit Barik, and Jim Fuller use three-dimensional simulations to show that rotating convection in stars and planets excites inertial modes on its own. These global oscillations, restored by the Coriolis force, emerge from thermal driving alone in spherical shell simulations, with no imposed forcing.

Coherent modes appear only when the convective Rossby number drops below about one half, where rotation dominates the flow. The modes are mostly retrograde, symmetric about the equator, and sit at mid to high latitudes with frequencies well below twice the rotation rate. Lower viscosity broadens the excited spectrum. The evidence points to differential rotation instabilities, rather than random convective buffeting, as the driver, and similar modes likely hide inside giant planets and stars at hard-to-detect low frequencies.
arxiv-2511-17230:
Sunit Ghosh and Jitendriya Swain prove new Strichartz estimates, bounds that control how wave-like solutions spread over time, for systems of orthonormal functions tied to the special Hermite operator. That operator governs a quantum particle in a magnetic-style harmonic trap, and its flows generalize the Schrödinger evolution. The authors handle general flows built from a smooth function of the operator, continuing their own earlier work.

The approach runs through restriction estimates for the Fourier-special Hermite transform on certain curved surfaces determined by the flow. The paper also treats the endpoint case for the Schrödinger propagator itself, often the hardest instance, and extends restriction estimates for spectral projections into the setting of Schatten trace ideals. These estimates matter wherever many-particle quantum systems with Hermite structure are analyzed.
arxiv-2511-17630:
Nele Albers and four co-authors ask whether large language models can stand in for human participants when training personalization algorithms for health apps. Digital behavior change tools work better when they adapt to each user's motivation and state. Learning such adaptation with reinforcement learning needs interaction data that is costly to gather. The authors test whether samples generated by an off-the-shelf language model carry useful training signal, comparing against real data from four large behavior change studies.

The generated samples proved useful when real data was absent, and matched the usefulness of samples provided by human raters. Prompting strategy mattered a great deal, though: longer or shorter prompts, chain-of-thought, and few-shot variants differed in effectiveness depending on the study and the model, and even paraphrases of one prompt diverged. They distill recommendations for using synthetic users responsibly in this design loop.
arxiv-2511-17730:
Zeinab Nezami, Shehr Bano, Abdelaziz Salama, Maryam Hafeez, and Syed Ali Raza Zaidi examine safety risks in generative multi-agent systems built for telecom work. Such systems promise automation and adaptive choices across layered networks, but agents acting out of step can miscoordinate, and their shared meaning can drift apart over time. Persona differences among agents shape both hazards, the authors argue.

They propose a modular safety framework that checks single agents for code quality and rule compliance while tracking system-level safety measures. Trials across thirty-two persona sets show analyser penalties and coder consistency improving over runs, yet policy drift and odd behaviour under some persona mixes persist. The work maps where telecom operators should place guards before wider deployment.
arxiv-2511-17830:
Roberto Capistrano Filho and Ailton Nascimento prove stabilization results for the Zakharov-Kuznetsov equation, a two dimensional wave equation related to the classic Korteweg-de Vries equation. They add both a damping term that removes energy and a delayed term that can add energy back.

Using two different proof approaches, they show that solutions settle down at an exponential rate, both near a steady state and globally. A key contribution is finding the best constant in that rate and the shortest time needed to guarantee decay. The analysis clarifies when damping wins over the destabilizing delay in this system.
arxiv-2511-18230:
Saeid Jamshidi and six co-authors guard small linked devices at the edge of a network. Cheap sensors and home gear have weak chips and low power, so heavy guard tools do not fit. Their design runs a light guard model on the gate box itself, where traffic first enters.

Six guard models are tried on low power gates, from simple trees to deep nets, and the best reach high scores under real attacks. When a threat looks odd, the gate sends a small safe data snapshot to a large language model. That model then gives a plain word account of the risk. The mix keeps checks fast, local, and clear for the staff who must act on them.
arxiv-2511-18430:
Paula Ferreira and Carlos Bengaly study how the choice of redshift bin shape affects measurements of the transverse baryon acoustic oscillation signal, a standard ruler for cosmology. Uncertainty in a bin's center can project the signal wrongly, and surveys differ in how binning choices play out.

For a radio survey and a spectroscopic galaxy survey, they compare Gaussian, top hat, and semi Gaussian bins across a range of widths. They also propose a correction using neighboring redshifts. The semi Gaussian bin recovers the signal best at narrow widths despite higher shot noise, and it offers the best balance of signal fidelity and parameter constraints overall.
arxiv-2511-18930:
Salah Eddine Choutri, Prajwal Chauhan, Othmane Mazhar, and Saif Eddin Jabari introduce a light neural operator that learns to solve whole families of partial differential equations at once. Rather than solving one equation instance, such operators learn the mapping from inputs to solutions. Their design approximates the core integral directly with a Monte Carlo style sample. Representing the kernel as a learnable grid over a fixed set of random points, and it makes no assumptions about spectra or shift invariance.

Because it avoids fixed global basis functions, the model generalises across grid resolutions without resampling during training. On standard one-dimensional benchmarks it reaches competitive accuracy at low cost. The authors offer it as a simple, practical alternative to the spectral and graph-based operators that dominate the area.
arxiv-2511-19130:
Rong Feng and Suman Saha ask whether large language models can undo obfuscation, the scrambling that hides what a program really does. Obfuscated code blocks tasks such as upkeep, testing, and hunting for security flaws. Their study fine-tunes models with help from symbolic execution, a method that runs code with symbols instead of fixed inputs.

The benchmark applies four scrambling methods to varied C programs from public test suites. Three leading models are trained with and without extra material from the KLEE tool, such as constraints and test cases. GPT-4.1-mini deobfuscates best overall, and the added symbolic material improves both compiling success and faithful behavior.
arxiv-2511-19630:
Valentina P. Miranda and seven co-authors follow metal-loaded winds leaving small galaxies in the CIELO simulations. Supernova blasts drive these outflows, which regulate star formation, strip metals from low-mass galaxies, and enrich the gas between galaxies. The study tracks fifteen central galaxies at or below Milky Way mass.

Two definitions of outflow, unbound gas and expelled mass rates, are followed from early times to today. Small galaxies keep a larger share of their oxygen in gas form yet have expelled more of it beyond the halo's edge. The smallest systems park a notable share of their oxygen in surrounding circumgalactic gas.
arxiv-2511-19930:
Kenta Yamamoto and Teruaki Hayashi design reputation systems for markets where firms trade manufacturing data. Buyers cannot check data quality before paying, so trust is the central problem in these young markets. The study builds a multi-agent simulator of such a market, in the spirit of European efforts like GAIA-X and Catena-X.

Agents learn by reinforcement learning, while inverse reinforcement learning estimates their utility functions from real behavior data. The authors test five reputation designs, from time-decay and Bayesian schemes to PageRank-style ones. PeerTrust best matched price to quality while blocking monopoly. They then build a hybrid system that combines the strengths of the five for steadier price-quality links.
arxiv-2511-20230:
Bouarroudj and El Ouali classify flat superalgebras carrying a symplectic-style form. Their 2025 paper studies quasi-Frobenius Lie superalgebras. A pre-symplectic superalgebra pairs an algebra with a non-degenerate antisymmetric form. Adding the Lie property plus a closed form gives quasi-Frobenius. Flatness means one natural product has zero curvature.

A Levi-Civita product exists uniquely for pre-symplectic cases. Symplectic products always exist for quasi-Frobenius ones. They are not unique, so a natural choice is defined. It is fixed by the bracket and the form alone. Flatness is tested on that canonical product. A construction called flat double extension builds examples step by step. Every flat example arises from such extensions, they prove. Orthosymplectic cases start from an abelian seed. Periplectic cases start from the trivial one instead. All flat examples prove nilpotent with degenerate centers. Complete lists run to total dimension five.
arxiv-2511-20430:
Kim and Ko explain a particle decay excess with dark matter that half-annihilates. Their 2025 paper addresses a 2023 Belle II measurement. The experiment first observed a rare B meson decay into a kaon plus neutrinos. Its rate came out higher than the Standard Model predicts. The gap amounts to about 2.8 sigma of statistical confidence. Measured branching was 2.3 times ten to the minus five.

The Standard Model instead predicts roughly a quarter of that value. The authors build a scalar dark matter model to close the gap. A dark symmetry breaks down to a discrete threefold remnant. A dark Higgs particle of two GeV mass does the breaking. Two dark matter particles can semi-annihilate into one plus a mediator. That extra channel fixes the cosmic dark matter abundance. It also boosts the rare decay rate to match Belle II. Higgs invisible decay bounds stay satisfied for small couplings.
arxiv-2511-20630:
Kumar, Joshi, Dixit, and Kasbekar design quantum-proof ID checks for RFID tags. Their 2025 paper proposes a mutual authentication scheme on lattice cryptography. RFID tags authenticate to readers in supply chains and access control. Quantum computers threaten the math behind current schemes. Worse, prior designs assumed the reader-server link was safe.

Their protocol stays secure even with both links insecure. Tag-to-reader and reader-to-server channels can both be hostile. Security leans on the inhomogeneous short integer solution problem. Man-in-the-middle, replay, impersonation, and reflection attacks all fail. Tags stay anonymous and credentials unforgeable in the design. The AVISPA tool formally verified the protocol's security. Storage, computation, and communication costs were tallied. Comparisons show strong guarantees against earlier schemes. The authors claim the first such complete coverage for RFID. Lightweight hardware implementation is the next step planned.
arxiv-2511-20930:
Felix Rong and colleagues simulate in 2025 hydrogen flames inside turbulent channel flow, resolving every scale directly. Lean hydrogen-air flames are prone to thermo-diffusive instability: hydrogen diffuses far faster than heat, with a Lewis number near 0.3, so the flame front wrinkles itself and burns harder. Their channel runs at a friction Reynolds number of 530, well above the 180 of earlier studies. Two mixtures are compared, at equivalence ratios of 0.25 and 0.35.

The leaner flame stays in the channel core, where weak turbulence plus the instability already lifts reactivity above the laminar value. The richer flame reaches the walls and quenches there intermittently. Near the wall, its stretch factor peaks exactly where the Reynolds stresses peak, around ten wall units out. That co-location signals a strong local synergy between wall turbulence and thermo-diffusive effects, ending in significantly enhanced flame speed. The database informs hydrogen combustor design.
arxiv-2511-21130:
Air flowing over a heated or cooled wall forms a stratified boundary layer, where density varies with height and buoyancy can calm or excite waves. P. C. Boldini and three colleagues give in 2025 a shortcut for predicting that buoyancy effect on Tollmien-Schlichting waves, the classic instability of these layers. Treating the Richardson number, the buoyancy measure, as a small parameter, they derive a first-order correction to the eigenvalues from the neutral, unstratified problem alone. No new eigenvalue solve is needed at each level.

For ideal-gas layers the correction tracks growth rates, wave shapes, and N-factors across ranges of Prandtl number, temperature ratio, and Mach number. One sharp result: at a fixed Richardson number, buoyancy flips from destabilising to stabilising depending on the fluid's Prandtl number. Applied to supercritical fluids, the method shows for the first time that buoyancy shifts transition predictions under pseudo-boiling conditions.
arxiv-2511-21730:
Ishant K and Aswanth Krishnan present the first benchmark that tests procedural memory retrieval separately from doing the task, in 2025. AI agents store past procedures to reuse on new tasks, yet standard tests cannot tell whether failures come from finding the memory or following it. The benchmark asks whether agents recognize equivalent procedures dressed in different objects and words.

Built on the ALFWorld household-task environment, the test uses two corpora, 78 expert demonstrations and 336 model-generated runs, with 40 coverage-balanced queries across six retrieval methods. Results expose a generalization cliff. Embedding methods score 84 percent mean average precision on familiar contexts but fall to 59 percent on novel ones. Model-generated abstract summaries lose only 11 points by contrast. Ablations show embeddings treat procedures as unordered word bags, discarding the step order that transfer requires, and that bigger corpora help more than richer encodings.
arxiv-2511-21830:
Agrawal and colleagues study axions, hypothetical light particles, inside orbifold grand unified theories, which unify the fundamental forces in extra dimensions with our world on boundaries called branes. The key question is how strongly axions couple to photons compared with their coupling to the strong force, because experiments hunting axions mostly look for the photon signal.

The authors show these couplings, thanks to topology, depend only on how known particles sit inside the larger group, not on symmetry breaking or geometry. Axions living in the bulk behave just as in ordinary four-dimensional unified theories, where a photon coupling forces a strong-force coupling too. Brane axions can couple to photons alone, but unsuppressed instanton effects then make them heavy. So the ratio of photon coupling to mass never exceeds the standard QCD axion value for any axion in these theories.
arxiv-2511-22130:
Yang, Chen, Yen, and Namkoong benchmark whether language-model agents actually learn from experience. Most agent evaluations hand the model everything up front and grade a single attempt. So they never test the skill real deployment demands: improving across repeated tries when preferences are hidden and shift. Their BELA benchmark puts an agent through repeated product-recommendation dialogues, pairing Amazon products with user personas whose tastes an LLM user simulator enacts, forcing the agent to explore, ask, and revise.

Across episodes, current frontier models struggle to improve meaningfully, often failing to convert earlier feedback into better later recommendations. That flat learning curve is the central evidence that in-context experiential learning is a capability today's agents largely lack. The authors frame the benchmark as a yardstick for building agentic systems that genuinely get better with practice over time.
arxiv-2511-22430:
Delporte, Ditlevsen, and Samson improve how scientists reconstruct animal movements from noisy satellite tracks. Tags on seals, whales, or elk report positions with errors reaching several kilometres that do not follow a neat bell curve, making the standard Kalman filter fragile. The authors model the hidden movement with an underdamped Langevin equation, a physics-style model with inertia and random kicks. They add a drift term keeping the animal inside its known territory, such as water or a fenced area.

Building the boundary into the model, rather than cleaning tracks afterwards, greatly improved filtering accuracy. They implement an extended Kalman filter and a particle filter for heavy-tailed errors, using splitting schemes solving the movement equation in pieces. For bell-shaped errors the Kalman variants performed alike, while the particle filter handled heavy tails best at much higher computing cost, suiting it to offline analysis rather than real-time tracking.
arxiv-2511-22530:
Faucher and colleagues present a three-dimensional solver for waves inside the Sun. The solver works on the Sun and its photosphere. It solves the time-harmonic oscillation equations without assuming a smooth, even interior. Three-dimensional variations sit on top of a layered background model. Such detail matters now that solar observations are sharp and plentiful. Helioseismology reads the interior from surface waves, so models must keep up.

Their method, hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin, keeps accuracy and speed while yielding smaller linear systems. A direct solver then handles those systems, using block low-rank compression and mixed-precision arithmetic to save memory. Meshes of six and eight million cells yield matrices of a few hundred million entries. At the right settings, compression cuts factorisation work to about a tenth of the full-rank cost. Tests with disturbances mimicking active regions and convection show where 3D simulation changes the wavefield.
arxiv-2511-22730:
Madiega and Olivier design a learning surrogate for unsteady flows that does not drift off course. Long-horizon computational fluid dynamics is expensive, and data-driven replacements often accumulate errors step by step until the forecast is unphysical. Their hybrid pairs a U-Net, extracting multi-scale spatial structure, with LSTM layers for temporal dependencies. The hybrid trains to predict per-step increments, the change in the fields, rather than the absolute state, mimicking classical time marching and suppressing error compounding.

The model slots into projection-method solvers such as SIMPLE and PISO, as an initializer supplying a sharper first guess for pressure-velocity coupling or as a corrector refining provisional fields. Across test cases it cut cumulative errors by between 54.53 and 84.21 percent relative to standard learning baselines, and preserved engineering metrics more reliably. It is positioned as a component of hybrid pipelines accelerating unsteady CFD without sacrificing fidelity.
arxiv-2511-22930:
Ann and colleagues tested a feared side effect of running superconducting qubits, the building blocks of some quantum computers. Theory suggested that the microwave signals used to control and read out the qubits could create quasiparticles, tiny broken pairs of electrons, across the Josephson junctions inside them. It suggested that this damage would grow worse at stronger drives.

The team drove qubits hard through their readout resonators, reaching effective drive amplitudes up to 300 GHz in frequency terms, and measured how much energy the qubits lost. Even if all of that loss is blamed on quasiparticle generation, the rates came out far below the ideal model's predictions. Adding a high-frequency cutoff near 17 to 20 GHz to the theory matched the data. It cut the predicted rates by a few orders of magnitude and eased a design worry for future processors.
arxiv-2511-23230:
Corsetti and colleagues generate training data for a perception task. It teaches AI agents to find the functional part a task requires, like the handle of the second drawer of the cabinet near the bed. Real 3D scenes annotated at that grain are scarce because collecting them is slow. Their SynthFun3D system instead synthesizes indoor scenes from the action prompt, using a furniture database annotated down to parts.

The training-free pipeline reasons about the requested action with a language model, retrieves and places furniture, and produces a 3D mask of the element the action targets, plus renderings from several viewpoints. A perception model trained only on this synthetic data reached a mean intersection-over-union of nearly 12 on the SceneFun3D benchmark, close to the score of 14 from training on the real dataset. User studies rated its scenes more coherent with their prompts.
arxiv-2512-00330:
Quantum dots and point contacts show sharp peaks in conductance that can signal the Kondo effect, a many-body phenomenon. Jongbae Hong classifies such coherent peaks in two-terminal quantum devices in 2025. The classification splits peaks into normal and anomalous Kondo peaks.

The split rests on the underlying spin dynamics and on the scaling function that the temperature-dependent conductance collapses onto. Sorting peaks correctly matters because similar-looking curves can hide different physics. Device physicists can use the scheme to read experimental conductance data with more confidence about which mechanism is at work. Two-terminal devices are the simplest testbeds, which makes the classification cleaner to state. Scaling collapse is a strong test, because unrelated curves rarely fall on one function.
arxiv-2512-01230:
Howard Wiseman analyzes the entropy carried by a laser beam in a 2025 physics paper. A laser beam is often modeled as a pure coherent state, the cleanest quantum state of light. In fact its state is mixed, even when its photon counts follow the statistics of a coherent state, because its phase must wander over time.

Wiseman considers an ideal laser beam whose phase diffuses at a rate equal to its spectral width. He works out the entropy flow of such a beam, the rate at which it carries entropy away. The result corrects a common idealization and matters for quantum optics and precision measurement.
arxiv-2512-01730:
Ángel Castro and Daniel Lear study how swirling flows behave in a flat, two-dimensional fluid, in a 2025 mathematics paper. Their subject is the linearized Euler equations, which describe small disturbances around a round vortex whose strength falls off steadily with radius. Earlier work showed that such steady fall-off makes disturbances fade and settle into rings.

Castro and Lear show the picture is more delicate than it seemed. They build nearby vortex profiles that no longer fall off strictly, only weakly, and for these profiles they find non-round solutions that repeat in time instead of fading away. The result marks a sharp edge case: change the profile just slightly, and the calming effect of damping can disappear.
arxiv-2512-01930:
Stochastic Variance Reduced Gradient, or SVRG, is a training method that corrects noisy gradient steps with occasional exact ones to speed up learning. Nico Daheim and three co-authors show in 2025 that this older method has surprising, deep connections to a recent Bayesian technique called posterior correction.

SVRG and its variants promised faster training yet never caught on widely in deep learning. Viewing the method through the Bayesian lens explains its behavior in a new way and suggests fresh variants. The connection also gives posterior correction, developed for a different purpose, an unexpected second life as a tool for understanding optimization.
arxiv-2512-02030:
Glioblastoma is the most aggressive form of brain tumor, and new treatments are urgently needed. Hao Qian and seven co-authors describe a 2025 framework that designs therapeutic peptides, short protein chains, aimed at a potential target protein called ATP5A, then tests the designs in the laboratory.

Their pipeline runs dry to wet: generative models propose peptides first, and experiments validate them afterward. A lead-conditioned generative model focuses the search near known lead peptides, in regions of the right geometry. That focus tames the combinatorial explosion of designing from scratch. The work shows generative design and bench testing closing the loop on a hard cancer target.
arxiv-2512-02130:
Classifying whole graphs, molecules, social networks, or biological structures, demands features that capture both neighborhood detail and global shape. Ahmet Sami Korkmaz, Selim Coskunuzer, and Md Joshem Uddin present a 2025 representation learning method that watches topology from more than one view at once.

Graph neural networks excel at local structural patterns but often overlook global topological features that decide a graph's identity. Adding a topology-aware cross-view corrects that blind spot, combining the two kinds of evidence. Stronger graph representations feed directly into drug screening, network analysis, and bioinformatics, where shape at every scale carries meaning.
arxiv-2512-02230:
Office work in finance runs through a tangle of digital tools, and routine processes still suffer human error and delay. Rory Milsom's 2025 dissertation study builds a finance-focused simulation of that environment and tests whether a general-purpose language model agent can complete wealth-management tasks accurately and economically.

The study extends an existing agent benchmark, TheAgentCompany, with representative wealth-management workflows. An agent that could handle such tasks reliably would change how back offices staff routine work. The results speak to both accuracy and cost, the two measures firms actually weigh before trusting software with client business.
arxiv-2512-02330:
Some metals turn superconducting in ways no one can yet fully explain. Their electrons both roam and sit still in fixed spots. M. A. Zeb gives a new idea in 2025. The crystal field near the still electrons shakes. That shaking can pull the roaming ones into pairs.

The same small hops that make the Kondo effect also shake the field. Zeb builds the pairing force out of that shake. The force is not the same in all directions, so it favors some pair shapes over others. A fresh pairing idea counts, since new superconductors are found by guessing right about the glue.
arxiv-2512-02830:
Mohamed Awad, Mahmoud Mohamed, and Walid Gomaa ask whether defending a vision model also sharpens its attacks. Deep networks excel at image tasks but break under small crafted perturbations, called adversarial examples. Adversarial training, which practices on such attacks, is the leading defense for robustness.

The team studies a side effect few have checked: attack transferability. If robust models craft examples that fool other models more easily, defense quietly upgrades offense. Knowing this trade off helps security teams weigh the true cost of hardening models that will be shared or sold. A shield that forges swords is not a pure loss, but it is a fact a buyer has a right to know up front.
arxiv-2512-03030:
Elba Alonso-Monsalve examines how to build a Hilbert space for gauge theories when the gauge group is infinitely large. Physical states need an inner product, a rule for measuring overlaps. With infinite volume gauge groups, states do not inherit that rule in any straightforward way.

Different quantization procedures then give prescriptions that may not agree. Group averaging is one route through the problem. Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity, a solvable two dimensional theory, serves as the test bed. Settling these foundations matters for any quantum theory of gravity, however simple the model. Toy worlds earn their keep when the rules they teach still hold in the big one. This toy is built to teach rules of just that kind.
arxiv-2512-03130:
Odd red galaxies seen by the Webb telescope puzzle astronomers. Kohei Inayoshi and Luis Ho review what these objects, called Little Red Dots, might be in this 2025 work. Deep surveys found them in large numbers, and they are classed as active galactic nuclei.

Their traits do not fit the standard picture of feeding black holes. Many ideas have been put forward for how such black holes form and grow so early. The authors weigh the options in a critical review. The answer could reshape views of the first massive black holes. For black hole scholars, the review sorts bold claims from what the data truly show.
arxiv-2512-03230:
Galaxy motions can reveal how fast structures grow. R. J. Turner and a large team measure that growth in this 2025 work. They use data from the DESI first data release peculiar velocity survey.

The team studies correlation functions, which show how galaxy positions and motions link across space. They work with both the galaxy field and the momentum field. Growth rate measures test whether gravity matches Einstein's theory on large scales. They also help pin down the nature of dark energy. Correlation methods use many galaxy pairs, which beats noise down as samples grow.
arxiv-2512-03530:
Mixed states can still hide protected edge features. Yoshihito Kuno studies edge bits in average symmetry protected topological states in this 2025 work. The state is guarded by one strong and one weak symmetry of the same kind.

Like pure protected states, these mixed states possess edge bits. The author shows an analogous operator response exists, tied to symmetry fractionalization. Edge bits in mixed states matter because real quantum systems are never perfectly pure. The work extends topological ideas toward realistic, noisy conditions. Operator responses give an experimental handle, since edge bits alone are hard to see.
arxiv-2512-03630:
Shifa Sulaiman and colleagues compare three mathematical routes for guiding a robot arm and its gripper as one body in self-driving laboratories. Automated labs need manipulators that thread precise trajectories without human hands. Their 2025 study plans paths with an RRT-star algorithm and solves joint motion three ways.

Jacobian transpose, pseudo-inverse, and damped least squares methods each drove the redundant arm-plus-gripper through the same tasks. Screw theory supplied the forward kinematics and dexterity measures for both arm and fingers. The team scored trajectory smoothness, tracking error, and the jerkiness of every joint's motion. Their analysis tells lab builders which solver suits which kind of task.
arxiv-2512-03730:
Adversarial tricks can fool object detectors, but most attack methods need insider access to the model and leave unclear why they work. Melane Navaratnarajah, David A. Kelly, and Hana Chockler present BlackCAtt in a 2025 computer vision preprint. Their black-box tool attacks detectors using only small sets of pixels that are causally sufficient to change the outcome.

Because it manipulates causes only, every attack it builds can be explained, reproduced, and kept nearly invisible. Given just a bounding box position and label, BlackCAtt matches or beats rival black-box attacks on standard benchmarks. Given the model's confidence scores too, it acts as a booster that shrinks other methods' attacks. In one pairing, the average attack size fell by more than tenfold at a similar success rate. Ablation studies in the paper isolate what each component of the algorithm contributes.
arxiv-2512-04130:
Recent combinations of cosmic surveys hint that dark energy might evolve, or might just be measurement tension in disguise. Seokcheon Lee builds a diagnostic for telling the two apart in a 2025 preprint. His framework injects tensions into mock data and watches the fake signals leak into inferred dark energy parameters.

The mocks imitate three probes: baryon acoustic oscillations, the cosmic microwave background in compressed form, and supernovae. Parameterised shifts move the matter density, the Hubble constant, the supernova calibration, and the sound-horizon scale, one knob at a time. A sampling pipeline then fits the dark energy behaviour, described by the standard two-parameter form, to each doctored dataset. Lee is explicit about scope. The tool is illustrative, meant to reveal which probe combinations are most vulnerable to tension masquerading as evolving dark energy. It is not a forecasting instrument.
arxiv-2512-04730:
Christian Möstl, Emma Davies, Eva Weiler, and co-authors present the largest study yet of how solar storm clouds change as they travel from the Sun toward Earth and beyond. These interplanetary coronal mass ejections carry magnetic fields that can rattle power grids and satellites. Forecasting their strength at Earth needs a clear picture of how the field fades with distance. Their 2025 arXiv paper rebuilds a major event catalog to get that picture.

The updated catalog holds nearly two thousand events from eleven missions across more than three decades. The team added hundreds of events by hand, marking their magnetic cores. New craft such as Parker Solar Probe caught storms very near the Sun, closing a long gap in coverage. With events spanning from near the corona to past Earth's orbit, the study traces the total field's decline with distance. Forecasters gain a firmer baseline for judging incoming storms.
arxiv-2512-04930:
N. I. Shepherd-Barron derives a nonlinear differential equation for the periods of a general Jacobian elliptic surface. Such a surface is a family of elliptic curves spread over a base curve, with one chosen section. Its core cohomology carries a natural basis of special two-forms, one for each ramification point of the map that sorts the family. Those points also give local coordinates on the space of all such surfaces. His 2025 arXiv paper links the two views through the Gauss-Manin connection.

Cutting that connection down yields a closed system for the matrix of basis forms. Each coordinate direction adds one equation of the same shape. The matrix can be read as a period map into the complex orthogonal group, and Shepherd-Barron proves a generic infinitesimal Torelli theorem for it. For rational elliptic surfaces, the whole system can be computed explicitly.
arxiv-2512-05130:
Yohann Trivino simulates how cold clouds of grains pull themselves together under their own gravity, a process at the heart of how planets begin. His model couples Newtonian attraction between every particle pair with springy, energy-losing contacts when grains collide. Scaling stiffness to gravity and time to the free-fall time lets him sweep the two controls that matter, energy loss in collisions and grain rigidity, in an orderly campaign.

Three regimes emerge. With little energy loss the grains mostly drift apart; past a clear loss threshold, clumping accelerates and settles. At a particular stiffness the gathering happens fastest, and the clustered fraction peaks at middling rigidity while extreme stiffness leaves stragglers isolated at the edges. The clumps' shapes shift from compact balls to branching forms as settings change. The findings link the small print of contact physics to the speed and structure of gravity-driven aggregation.
arxiv-2512-05230:
Jonathan Yang, Chelsea Finn, and Dorsa Sadigh teach robot policies to ignore the things that should not matter. Robots trained on demonstrations often stumble when the camera moves, the lighting changes, or clutter appears. Covering every such variation with real robot data would take more demonstrations than anyone can collect. The authors argue the gap can be filled by auxiliary tasks and cheaper data.

They add two training signals — judging whether two views show the same state, and staying invariant under visual perturbations — applied both to real demonstrations and to static images. The images come from synthetic scenes rendered without physics, which are cheap and visually rich. Co-training on this mix lifts performance on unseen viewpoints, lighting, and distractors by a wide margin over generative augmentation methods. The recipe shows generalist robots can borrow robustness from data that never involved a robot at all.
arxiv-2512-05330:
Kilho Baek, Sungsoo Kim, Minsup Jeong, and Young-Jun Choi present the geometric calibration of PolCam, the polarimetric camera aboard Danuri, South Korea's first lunar orbiter. PolCam is conducting the first global polarimetric survey of the Moon at high phase angles, but its highly oblique viewing geometry badly distorts the topography in its images. Every pixel must be pinned to its true place on the lunar surface.

The team calibrates on orbit using well over a hundred thousand features matched between PolCam images and a trusted global map from Japan's Kaguya orbiter. Their optimization reconstructs the exact observation time of each image line with a simple linear model, and refines the camera's optical model by minimizing mismatch against the reference map. The output assigns longitude, latitude, and elevation to every pixel and yields corrected images of a precision comparable to earlier lunar orbiters — the foundation for all PolCam data products.
arxiv-2512-05430:
Daeyong Kwon, SeungHeon Doh, and Juhan Nam build the infrastructure for answering questions about music with retrieval-augmented generation. Language models reason poorly about music because their training data is thin on artist facts and history. The authors answer with two resources. MusWikiDB is a searchable database of millions of passages drawn from well over a hundred thousand music-related encyclopedia pages. ArtistMus is a benchmark of a thousand questions about five hundred diverse artists, complete with genre, debut, and topic metadata.

Experiments show retrieval transforms performance: open-source models gain dramatically in factual accuracy, approaching proprietary systems, and retrieval-style fine-tuning improves recall and contextual reasoning further, in and out of domain. The music-specific database also beats a general encyclopedia corpus on both accuracy and retrieval speed. Released openly, the resources aim to ground music question answering — and, by example, other culturally rich domains — in verifiable fact.
arxiv-2512-05830:
Muhammet Cagri Yeke, Samil Sirin, Kivilcim Yuksel, and Abdurrahman Gumus teach neural networks to recognize events along an optical fiber by first turning the fiber's signals into pictures. Phase-sensitive reflectometry listens along a fiber: taps, digs, and breaks each leave a trace. The raw traces are hard to classify. The team converts them into grayscale images using three transforms that expose angles and recurrences in the signal.

Stacked as color channels, the three views form one rich image per event. Standard image networks, adapted by transfer learning, then sort the events into six classes. Two well known architectures each scored above ninety eight percent accuracy on a public dataset, confirmed by cross validation. The image dataset and code are public. The trick generalizes: many sensors produce one dimensional streams that pictures unlock. For pipeline monitoring, that means earlier alarms from cables in the ground.
arxiv-2512-06530:
Mohammed Wattad, Tamir Shor, and Alex Bronstein ask whether a learned way of sampling MRI data travels well to new scanners and subjects. Fast MRI takes only part of the frequency data, called k-space, and rebuilds the image from that subset. Learning which subset to take has boosted image quality, but most work tuned the pattern to one data set, leaving open whether the gains survive a change of domain.

The authors test patterns across data sets and scanning styles. Models trained with learned patterns kept their edge under domain shift, beating fixed patterns on foreign data. They then add a twist to training: the sampling path is randomly perturbed, faking the variation between scanners and conditions. That acquisition uncertainty made the models hardier still. Their message is that how an MRI samples is not just a speed trick; it is a design lever for robustness itself.
arxiv-2512-07030:
Zahra Lotfi and Mostafa Lotfi compare five supervised learning models on one of security's hardest tasks: spotting zero-day attacks, intrusions whose patterns no defender has seen before. Trained only on known traffic, such models often stumble on the unknown, and real network data are heavily lopsided, with attacks rare beside normal flow. The study keeps that imbalance, exposing the models to zero-day attacks only at test time, as in real life.

A tuning framework wraps the models with grid search, dimension reduction, and oversampling to fight the imbalance. Random Forest proved the most accurate under both plain and oversampled training, but it paid for that edge with longer processing times. The authors instead crown XGBoost as the practical winner, nearly as accurate yet much faster.
arxiv-2512-07630:
A. H. Mueller wrote this 2025 particle physics paper on diffractive scattering off nuclei. A virtual photon can strike a nucleus as one coherent whole and produce new particles. A clear gap in rapidity separates that production from the rest of the event.

Mueller gives an evolution equation for such gap-marked production. He then studies the collisions in the strong, saturated regime of the nucleus. His conclusion caps the mass of what diffractive production can create. When the scattering is strong, that mass stays on the order of the photon's virtuality. Much heavier products are not just rare; they are strongly suppressed. A mechanism named after Levin and Tuchin does the suppressing deep in saturation. The result tells experimenters where diffractive mass can and cannot hide.
arxiv-2512-08530:
Kohhei Bessho, Sarah Ballard, and Natalia Guerrero, astronomers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. They hunt for transit duration variations in compact multi planet systems around M dwarf stars. If a planet orbit slowly nods under its companions pull, its transits should lengthen or shorten over the years, a signal predicted by classical secular theory.

Their sample covers twenty three planets around twelve stars. They compare fresh, precise transit durations from Webb telescope light curves against measurements from discovery papers and later work. Fitted trends ranged from seconds to minutes, yet every system stayed consistent with no variation at the three sigma level. The best candidate reached only mild significance. The null result fits the expected geometry: for low impact systems the predicted changes are a few seconds per decade, below their reach. Larger variation geometries are disfavored, with at least half ruled out.
arxiv-2512-09130:
Tetiana Gorbach and coauthors compare two leading frameworks for causal inference: the Neyman Rubin framework and the graphical framework based on directed acyclic graphs. Each language has strengths that the other lacks, and confusion between them is common. The article uses concrete data generating mechanisms to show where each approach works readily and where it struggles.

Some mechanisms involve undirected relations, deterministic links, or cycles. Graphs handle those poorly, while Neyman Rubin tools apply directly. Other mechanisms involve M bias, trapdoor variables, or complex front door structures. There the Neyman Rubin approach becomes complicated, while the graphical approach is directly usable. By pairing the examples, the authors clarify how the two languages relate in practice. The goal is a better shared understanding of causal reasoning tools across a broad audience, so analysts can choose the framework that fits the structure of their problem.
arxiv-2512-09330:
Jianjun Jin studies the Brennan conjecture, an open problem in complex analysis about how badly well-behaved analytic functions can distort size. The paper works with univalent functions, functions on the unit disk that never take the same value twice. It also works with their integral means spectra, which measure average growth of the function's derivative around circles.

Jin proves that all the spectrum functionals are continuous on three spaces of such functions: the universal Teichmüller space, its curve version, and asymptotic version. He also shows that any function that extends quasiconformally to the whole plane has a spectrum below the universal maximum. The approach to continuity on the asymptotic space is new and more direct than earlier work. He determines the spectra for all univalent rational functions, and for that class the Brennan conjecture turns out to be true. The paper closes with open problems and conjectures.
arxiv-2512-09530:
Alessandro Quadrio's thesis, written with Antonio Candelieri, asks how transformers learn on tabular data, tables of rows and features rather than text or images. The study examines the attention mechanism from the viewpoint of optimal transport, matching one distribution to another at least cost. It tracks how the attention layer's projections evolve during training.

Measured with optimal transport tools such as the Wasserstein distance and Monge gap, the final attention mapping often ends up close to the optimal transport coupling. But the path training takes to get there is inefficient. Pretraining part of the network on synthetic data helps convergence, though results depend on initialization. The thesis builds an algorithm: it creates class-specific dummy Gaussian distributions, aligns them to the data by optimal transport, and trains a simpler network to generalize that mapping. The method matched transformer accuracy at lower cost, with design of the dummy geometry being essential.
arxiv-2512-09730:
Antonin Poché, Fanny Jourdan, and a team present Interpreto, an open-source Python library for explaining transformer language models, from early BERT-style models to modern language models. Practitioners who want to know why a model produced an output face a scattered landscape of research code. Interpreto packages explanation workflows behind one interface covering both classification and text generation.

The library offers two families of methods. Attribution methods assign importance to parts of the input. Concept-based explanations go further, explaining the model in terms of concepts it has formed that people can grasp. Its key feature is an end-to-end concept pipeline: extracting activations, learning concepts, reading them, and scoring them, a chain rarely available in existing libraries. The paper was accepted as a system demonstration at ACL 2026, with a public demo site alongside the code repository.
arxiv-2512-09830:
Simone Corbo surveys how large language models are being used to interpret legal documents. The chapter looks at tasks where the models could improve or support traditional legal work. Examples include reading statutes, contracts, and case law, sharpening legal summaries, aiding contract negotiation, and improving information retrieval. Corbo presents the possible uses in a practical way, as assistance layered onto the work lawyers already do, rather than as a replacement for it.

The chapter also weighs the risks that come with the technology. These include algorithmic monoculture, where many users lean on similar systems, plus hallucinated content and compliance duties. Regulation is part of the picture too, from the European Union's AI Act to recent United States initiatives and emerging approaches in China. Two different benchmarks for testing models on legal tasks are presented, giving readers a sense of how performance can be measured.
arxiv-2512-10030:
Pavel V. Kuptsov presents a cheaper way to estimate how many dimensions a chaotic system's long term behavior really needs. Extended systems, like fluids or coupled oscillators, live in huge spaces, yet their attractors may sit on an inertial manifold of modest dimension. An earlier method estimated that dimension from angles between pairs of covariant Lyapunov vectors, but it was heavy in computation and memory. Kuptsov instead studies angles between whole tangent subspaces spanned by those vectors. The method rides on a fast numerical technique for judging hyperbolicity of chaotic dynamics.

The new approach never computes the Lyapunov vectors outright, slashing memory use. On the complex Ginzburg-Landau equation, a canonical test case, it reproduces earlier dimension estimates. On a chain of diffusively coupled Lorenz oscillators, it finds no low dimensional inertial manifold at all, flagging a complex regime worth deeper study.
arxiv-2512-10430:
Dmitrii Stoianov and a large team introduce T-pro 2.0, an open-weight language model built for Russian. The model can answer directly or show a reasoning trace, giving users a choice between speed and depth. A tokenizer packed densely for Cyrillic text and a tuned speculative decoding pipeline help it respond with lower delay.

Rather than releasing the model alone, the team publishes the full kit: the weights, a five-hundred-thousand-example instruction corpus called T-Wix, a maths reasoning benchmark. And the extra weights for the fast decoding setup, all on Hugging Face. A public web demo lets anyone try both reasoning modes and see the speed gains across topics. The package is meant as an open base for research on Russian-language reasoning and for practical applications built on top of it.
arxiv-2512-10530:
Riccardo March and co-authors test a modified gravity theory where curvature and matter are coupled directly, not just side by side. In their model a cosmological constant drives today's accelerated expansion, while the coupling reshapes the expansion history like a dark energy that changes over time. A tracking solution, where a scalar field rides the minimum of its effective potential, organises the analysis.

They pin down when that minimum exists and the tracking holds, then confront the model with recent DESI results plus two supernova compilations, which favour dynamical dark energy. The same coupling breaks the equivalence principle, making Earth and Moon fall toward the Sun slightly differently, and lunar laser ranging tightly limits any such difference. A range of parameters survives both the cosmic and the lunar tests, keeping the model alive.
arxiv-2512-10830:
The SoLAr Collaboration reports cosmic ray measurements from the second prototype of a new kind of neutrino detector. Liquid argon time projection chambers are strong candidates for catching solar neutrinos. And SoLAr's twist is pixelated readout of both the charge and the light each event produces, aiming at high efficiency and finer energy resolution than either signal alone.

The V2 prototype is a thirty-centimetre cube of a chamber sitting in a cryostat with several hundred kilograms of liquid argon. The team recorded cosmic-ray muons and reconstructed them by tracking and by calorimetry, drawing on both sensor types. Combining charge and light measurably improved performance over the first prototype's approach. The collaboration presents the results as proof that dual-readout argon detectors deserve the next step, prototyping toward the kiloton-scale facilities that solar neutrino physics ultimately needs.
arxiv-2512-11030:
Jose Alfredo de Leon, Miguel Gonzalez, and Carlos Diaz-Mejia explore a new probe of chaos in quantum many body systems. Common chaos measures depend on the starting state, so they can miss how a small part of a system loses information to its surroundings. The authors instead study the full reduced dynamics of a single spin, captured as a quantum channel.

They use the purity of that channel's state representation, a quantity they show works like an echo experiment. Testing three standard spin chain models across the border between orderly and chaotic behaviour, they find surprises. Orderly systems with coherent transport can mimic the average relaxation expected from chaos, producing false positives. The work links quantum information tools with many body chaos in a cautionary way.
arxiv-2512-11130:
Bowen Wen, Shaurya Dewan, and Stan Birchfield make stereo depth estimation fast enough for real time use without giving up accuracy on new scenes. Stereo foundation models generalise well but run too slowly, while fast models need costly retraining for each new setting. Their Fast-FoundationStereo family closes that gap with a divide and conquer strategy.

Knowledge distillation squeezes a large hybrid backbone into one efficient student network. An automated search finds the best filtering design under a strict time budget, and structured pruning trims the refinement stage. The team also built a large set of real world stereo image pairs with automatic labels to support training. The result runs more than ten times faster than the original foundation model while closely matching its accuracy on unseen data.
arxiv-2512-11630:
Vasile-Laurentiu Dosan and co-authors built a photon pair source tuned for fiber based quantum key sharing. Such sharing needs entangled photons that travel well through normal fiber. Their source splits one laser photon into a pair at very unlike colors, 680 and 1550 nanometers, when pumped at 473 nanometers.

That mix pairs cheap, sharp silicon detectors for the short wave photon with low loss fiber travel for the long wave one. The source reached heralding rates of 18 and 34 percent for its two sides. Test patterns showed 97.3 and 94.9 percent clarity, for a state fidelity of at least 96.1 percent. It suits long haul quantum links.
arxiv-2512-11830:
Satyam Kumar presents CR3G, a framework that explains chest X-ray reports through cause and effect. Auto report writers are good at spotting patterns, but patterns alone can mislead. Doctors need to know why a finding points to a diagnosis, in terms a patient can follow.

CR3G is driven by prompts that push the model to reason in causal steps. It then phrases the result as a patient centered explanation. The aim is reports that clinicians can trust and audit. In tests, CR3G showed stronger causal links and clearer explanations for two out of five abnormality types. The work is early, but it shows causal framing as a path to safer medical AI.
arxiv-2512-12030:
Shreekanth S Yuvarajan and co-authors use small quantum processors to study photon mediated gates between qubits. Cavity linked qubits are a leading route to larger quantum machines, but mapping where a gate works best is hard for classic theory and simulation alike.

Their circuit algorithm runs on noisy near term hardware and tracks the joint qubit cavity dynamics faithfully. Sweeping detunings, cavity damping, and coupling strengths, they chart state transfer fidelity across the full space. The map matches classic answers where those hold. It also reveals a sweet spot theory had missed: far detuned qubits, resonant with neither each other nor the cavity, can still swap states well. The method extends to harder variants of the model.
arxiv-2512-12430:
Ke Zhang, Yiqun Mei, Jiacong Xu, and Vishal M Patel present Endless World, a system for endless 3D aware video generation, in a 2025 paper. Long videos tend to drift: scenes lose stable 3D structure over time, above all in streaming use. Their framework aims to generate video in real time with no fixed end.

A conditional training strategy aligns each new segment with frames already made, keeping long range links while staying efficient enough for one GPU. Global 3D aware attention adds geometric guidance across time, and a 3D injection step enforces physical plausibility. In tests, the videos stayed long, stable, and visually coherent, matching or beating prior methods on fidelity and spatial consistency.
arxiv-2512-12830:
Elizabeth Denne studies knots and links made from a thin strip of paper that is tied, joined at the ends, and flattened. A folded ribbon knot is measured by its ribbonlength, the ratio of its length to its width. The main puzzle is to find the smallest possible value for each knot type.

Denne proves bounds for pretzel links, a broad family built from twisted strands. Any three-strand pretzel link can be built with ribbonlength at most about 31.755. She also gives a bound that grows with the number of strands. A table lists the best known bounds for all knots with up to nine crossings.
arxiv-2512-13530:
Shih-Ni Prim and co-authors tackle a joint search problem across several computer experiments at once. A contour search finds inputs that give a set response value in one experiment. Their case comes from flight tests, where they seek stable flight settings that give zero torque forces.

Their joint contour method balances broad search across response surfaces with focus on where contours cross. It uses two distinct sampling schemes and a rule to switch between them, which also signals when no solution exists. The method works with Gaussian process models and deep variants. In tests, it beat single-response and optimization methods and found the target flight settings with less waste.
arxiv-2512-13630:
Vernon Barger proposes a one-flavon scheme where a single parameter sets the pattern of quark and lepton masses. Flavor hierarchies are the large gaps between particle family masses and mixings. In his Froggatt-Nielsen setup, one flavon field and one number, B, organize the whole pattern.

Fixing B at 5.357 from charged-lepton mass ratios, he reproduces quark masses and CKM targets at the Z mass scale. The coefficients stay of order one, with no fine tuning. The same small ratio gives workable lepton textures and benchmarks for neutrino mass sums and related rates. Compact links between mixing angles follow from powers of that one ratio.
arxiv-2512-14230:
Divyansh Pareek, Sewoong Oh, and Simon Du explain why filtering data helps multimodal contrastive learning in a 2025 paper. Such models learn from paired data, like images with captions, pulled from the web at huge scale. Much of that raw data is low quality or wrongly paired.

Teacher based filtering uses a trained model to score and keep the better pairs. The authors prove its benefit under a standard bimodal data model with a linear setup. Without filtering, error scales worse with the share of correctly matched pairs. With filtering, the error bound improves in both high and low match regimes. The theory helps explain a practice that large labs already rely on.
arxiv-2512-14830:
Caterina Zerba, Sarang Gopalakrishnan, and Michael Knap study quantum circuits that are watched as they run. Their circuits conserve both charge and dipole moment, a kind of balance of where charge sits. Watching means measuring local charge density again and again while the system evolves.

The setup has phases set by how often the measurements come. In one dimension, charge is always easy to learn from local readings, while dipole moment can be easy or hard. In two dimensions there are three phases: frequent watching makes both easy to learn, then dipole moment turns hard, then charge does too. The rarest phase behaves like a smectic liquid crystal, stretched in one direction. The work ties symmetry breaking to what an observer can learn.
arxiv-2512-14930:
Jaume Anguera Peris and four coauthors tackle a scheduling puzzle inside smart microscopes. Modern screening microscopes gather live cell images fast, but no one can watch every region at once. Choosing when and where to image must balance time, computing power, and the light damage that bleaches cells, across thousands of shifting regions.

Their framework treats each region not as one process but as a bundle of Markov chains, capturing mixed cell cycles and varied drug responses. From that model they derive formulas for short and long run behavior, and build Whittle index policies that scale gently with region count. In simulations the method cut cumulative regret by more than 37 percent against standard baselines. On real live cell data it captured 93 percent more events that matter, a strong case for self driving microscopy.
arxiv-2512-15030:
Xiaoqi Li and eight coauthors present ScamSweeper, a system that hunts scam accounts on the Ethereum blockchain. Web3 scams copy honest services and mimic normal activity to fool users. Earlier detectors chased phishing nodes or identity leaks, and missed the special patterns of these scams.

ScamSweeper watches how the transaction graph changes over time. A structure temporal random walk samples the network with both timing and shape in mind. An encoder then turns each time slice into features, and a variational Transformer reads the sequence to spot scam like evolution. The team also built a dataset from the first 18 million Ethereum blocks, covering scam, phishing, and normal accounts. In tests, ScamSweeper beat rival tools on scam detection, lifting the weighted F1 score by at least 17.29 percent from a base of 0.59.
arxiv-2512-15230:
Doğa Elitez and seven coauthors release ColliderML, a large open dataset of simulated particle collisions for machine learning research. The collisions mimic the High Luminosity Large Hadron Collider: proton beams at 14 TeV with an average pile up of 200 extra interactions per event. One million events cover ten Standard Model and beyond Standard Model processes, plus single particle samples.

Everything was produced with modern calculations, realistic pile up overlay, a validated open detector geometry, and standard reconstructions. The release fills a gap: detector level data in a form ML researchers can actually use, hosted on Hugging Face. The authors describe the generation and reconstruction pipeline, the data format and access, and first physics benchmarks. ColliderML gives the field a shared, experiment agnostic test bed for collider machine learning.
arxiv-2512-15330:
Paul Bagourd and five coauthors run Shor's factoring algorithm on today's cloud quantum computers and report how far it falls short. Shor's algorithm threatens RSA and elliptic curve cryptography, since a big enough quantum machine could factor the keys. Theory says 2048 bit RSA might fall to fewer than a million noisy qubits, but such machines do not exist.

Using public implementations on several cloud platforms, the team probes what key sizes current hardware can realistically factor. A wide gap separates today's machines from cryptographically relevant factoring. Circuits still must be built specifically for each modulus, rather than one general design. Fidelities are unstable, with high error rates that fluctuate from run to run. The study gives practitioners a grounded picture of the present threat level, far below the headline danger.
arxiv-2512-15430:
Quanxi Zhou and co authors present FM-EAC in a 2025 paper on control systems that must handle many tasks in changing settings. Older methods tend to follow either a model based path or a model free path, and both can struggle to transfer skill across tasks. Their method aims to blend the strengths of the two.

FM-EAC, short for Feature Model based Enhanced Actor Critic, joins planning, acting, and learning in one framework. It uses new feature based models to improve how well control skill carries to new scenes. Tests in city and farm settings show it beating many leading methods from both families. Users can also swap in custom sub networks for their own needs.
arxiv-2512-15530:
James Murray Louw and Juan Pablo Ortega study whether state space systems can learn the climate of a dynamical system in a 2025 paper. Climate here means the long term statistical behavior of a process, not its exact path. Forecasts of that distribution are known to be far more stable than point forecasts, which hinge on starting conditions.

The authors prove this rigorously for state space forecasting systems. Suppose the true process is structurally stable and has a mixing or attracting measure. Then a close enough state space proxy keeps a regular starting distribution near the true future distribution. This holds at any horizon. Learning the climate with a universal family of such systems is thus feasible.
arxiv-2512-15630:
Sarah Kaisser, Markus Kleffmann, and Kristina Schaaff study age aware game design for digital learning in a 2025 paper. Points, badges, and challenges are widely used to move learners, yet most systems ignore age. Drive and thinking skills differ across life stages, so one design rarely fits all ages.

From a focused review of prior work, the authors map age groups to game mechanics and their effects. They derive five design rules for age specific game design and three building patterns for building it into media rich learning settings. Their conclusion is measured: game design is not always effective. Tailored design is what supports engagement and inclusion across life.
arxiv-2512-15930:
Matthew Sinclair and co authors present StructBioReasoner, a multi agent system for designing biologics against disordered proteins, in a 2025 paper. About 80 percent of cancer related proteins contain long disordered regions, and their lack of stable structure makes them hard drug targets. Diffusion models can design binders, but real discovery needs reasoning across many shapes and tools.

It runs a tournament in which expert agents compete to propose and refine treatment ideas, using prior papers, structure prediction, modeling, and stability checks on fast computers. For the Der f 21 target, over half of 787 validated candidates beat human designed reference binders in binding free energy. For NMNAT-2, three binding modes were found.
arxiv-2512-16030:
Lukas Nel asks a pointed question in their arXiv paper from 2025: do large language models know what they do not know? A well-calibrated model should be right about 80 percent of the time when it claims 80 percent confidence. Nel built KalshiBench, a test of 300 prediction market questions from the regulated Kalshi exchange. All the outcomes occurred after the models were trained.

He tested five frontier models on the benchmark. All five proved overconfident. Claude Opus 4.5 was the best calibrated of the group by a clear margin. A reasoning-heavy GPT-5.2 variant, despite similar accuracy, was far worse calibrated than the rest. Only one model beat the simple trick of always guessing base rates. The results suggest that scale and extra reasoning do not by themselves fix poor self-knowledge.
arxiv-2512-16130:
