Samapti Lakshan and eight co-authors revisit a nuclear astrophysics puzzle in research shared on arXiv in 2025. Iron-60 is forged inside massive stars and supernovae, and its abundance tests models of how stars build elements. A 2024 study reported a surprisingly large boost in iron-60 production, blamed on a much bigger neutron capture rate than expected.

Using microscopic models for nuclear level density and gamma-ray strength, the team rechecked that claim. They trace the reported boost to a level density choice whose spin dependence is unreliable, a key input for reaction rate calculations. Their own rate comes out much lower, which undercuts the claimed enhancement. They also explain a low-energy rise in gamma-ray strength as a finite-temperature effect. The long-standing iron-60 question, they conclude, is open again.
arxiv-2512-16330:
Cesare Straffelini studies the foundations of set theory in a paper posted on arXiv during 2025. Forcing is the technique mathematicians use to build new universes of sets and test what can be proved. Generic absoluteness asks which truths stay fixed across all such universes, and collapse forcings are one especially simple family.

A classical observation by Kripke says any forcing extension can be realized inside one built by a collapse forcing. Straffelini proves that, under suitable large cardinal assumptions, projective absoluteness for collapse forcings alone already equals absoluteness for arbitrary forcings. At low projective levels the result needs no extra assumptions at all. Collapse forcings are thus terminal: this one simple class captures the full robustness of the set-theoretic universe under forcing, a notable economy for the field.
arxiv-2512-16730:
Sandeep R. Murthy writes on the triple product property for finite groups, a rule about three subsets whose pairwise ratios never collide unless the elements match. The size of the largest such triple, scaled by group size, gives a ratio used in fast matrix methods.

A past guess capped that ratio at four thirds for groups with a cyclic subgroup of index two. Murthy proves a stronger subgroup version for any finite group with an abelian normal subgroup of prime index p. The cap he proves beats the old general bound by a clear factor. He closes with a wider guess for groups with cyclic normal subgroups of prime index.
arxiv-2512-16830:
Francesca Pelusi and coauthors review recent work on Rayleigh-Bénard convection in emulsions, the classic setup where a fluid layer heated from below forms rising and falling patterns, here with droplets mixed in. Such heated emulsions show up in nature and industry.

Emulsions change character with strength: dilute mixes flow like plain liquids, while dense ones act like yield-stress pastes. In heated flow, that inner structure and the convection shape each other, giving rich effects in stability, short-term motion, and form change over time. The short review gathers what is known and offers fresh angles on how soft materials behave when heat drives their flow.
arxiv-2512-16930:
Changlong Wang and coauthors use large-eddy simulation to ask how the Coriolis force, from Earth rotation, shapes turbulent structures in a neutral air boundary layer. The force is known to veer the mean wind with height, but its grip on the swirls themselves was unclear.

By changing latitude or the geostrophic wind speed, they vary the force strength. Coherent velocity structures deflect toward the geostrophic wind direction, matching neither the mean wind nor the mean shear. Plotted against local wind veer, the deflection follows one universal curve in all cases. Tilt of large structures in the surface layer also shifts, likely from the same deflection of the swirls.
arxiv-2512-17030:
Patricia A Almeida, George B Martins, and Sergio Ulloa study the Kondo effect in strained kagome nanoribbons, narrow strips of a lattice prized for its Dirac points and flat band. Strain can break lattice symmetries and reshape the electronic states that screen a magnetic impurity.

Using the Anderson impurity model with numerical renormalization group methods, they find strain tunes Kondo strength sharply. The impurity site matters a lot: symmetric local settings can crush the effective hybridization through orbital interference. When the Fermi energy sits near weak edge states, the Kondo temperature swings hard. That sensitivity could turn Kondo measures into a probe of local density of states in kagome materials.
arxiv-2512-17530:
Lukas Schamriß, Louis Garbe, and Peter Rabl describe a way to refrigerate a gas made not of atoms but of microwave photons, in a 2025 theory paper. The photons travel inside a superconducting transmission line, a wire like channel used in quantum hardware. Cooling them below what standard lab fridges reach would open new experiments.

A nonlinear Josephson element at one end of the line moves photons from high frequency modes into low frequency ones while keeping their total number fixed. The authors work out the steady state that results when this cooling fights the natural warming from the surroundings. With realistic settings, they predict temperatures below a millikelvin, far colder than a dilution refrigerator's base. The setup also shows a new kind of condensation, which they suggest could serve quantum simulations.
arxiv-2512-17630:
Menna Elgabry and Ali Hamdi show that a jury of small models can out-read big ones at spotting emotion in text. Their panel joins five compact, differently built language models, each fine-tuned for emotion classes. An old voting idea, Condorcet's jury theorem, guides the panel: many decent judges, wisely weighted, beat one star judge.

Each vote counts twice over, weighted by the model's past record and by how sure it sounds on this very text. On the DAIR-AI emotion set, the panel scored a macro F1 of 93.5 percent. That beat giant models with up to 7 billion parameters, even after those giants got task-specific tuning. The whole jury totals just 595 million parameters.
arxiv-2512-17730:
Yichen Jiang and four co-authors retrain a fake-image detector so it stops memorizing one generator's fingerprints. A detector raised on GAN images learns GAN blemishes as the meaning of fake, then waves through diffusion and commercial tool output. The team first builds Diff-Gen, a balanced set of 100,000 diffusion images plus matching real photos, whose frequency signature differs sharply from GAN data.

On that diet they adapt the CLIP model with AdaptPrompt, tuning only about 0.1 percent of its weights through a small visual adapter and learnable text prompts. Cutting CLIP's last block, oddly, helped too. Across 25 test sets, from GANs to Midjourney and DALL-E 3, the detector topped rivals at 98.60 percent mean average precision. Cheap tuning, broad vigilance.
arxiv-2512-17930:
Aziz Muminov and Anne Pham built CytoDINO to sort bone marrow cells under a microscope, a key step in finding blood cancers. Human experts do the task slowly and often disagree. Big general image models help, but they need heavy hardware and treat all errors as equal, which is unsafe in medicine.

Their system fine tunes the DINOv3 model with a light method and a new loss that punishes risky mistakes most, such as calling a blast cell normal. It scored 88.2 percent weighted F1 across 21 cell types on held out data. When the model was sure, it was right 99.5 percent of the time on 67 percent of samples, leaving hard cases for experts.
arxiv-2512-18030:
Leroy Cronin, Juan Carlos Morales Parra, and Keith Y. Patarroyo widen a classic counting puzzle. An addition chain builds a number by adding past sums, and short chains mean fast work. Their version builds any object from a kit of basic blocks, where each step joins two things already built.

The new frame covers strings of letters, colored connected graphs, and colored tile shapes as its main cases. For each, they define the best possible chain and prove floor and ceiling bounds on its length, echoing classic bounds for numbers. The kit size of a target object sets the scale of those bounds. The work links pure math to how complex objects can be assembled step by step.
arxiv-2512-18330:
Tatiana Tatarenko and Lucas Wey Hacker teach rival players to find a shared resting point in hard games. In a generalized Nash setup, each player's best move depends on the rest, and private limits tie their hands. Past learning rules demanded the game bend in a friendly monotone way, which many real contests fail.

The pair recast the balance conditions as a smooth convex program with a trait that makes plain gradient steps race in a straight line pace. Players update over a fixed talk network and still land on a balance point together. When slopes are too costly to get, a second rule uses only each player's own costs and limit gaps, and it closes in at a slower one over t rate.
arxiv-2512-18830:
Owe Philipsen writes an invited viewpoint on hot QCD, the theory of quarks and gluons at extreme temperatures, where lattice results have unsettled the standard picture. As matter heats past the chiral crossover, theory expected a smooth path to restored chiral symmetry. Instead, simulations reveal an intermediate region with a larger, approximate chiral spin symmetry, where pseudo-scalar mesons still exist as hadron-like excitations. His article, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and published in the European Physical Journal A, argues these findings deserve wider attention.

He shows that the constituents of the hot medium are thermoparticles, thermally reshaped versions of ordinary stable particles, with properties far from perturbative expectations. Testing formal arguments against lattice data supports that view. The viewpoint aims to stir phenomenological interest in the intermediate regime, a stretch of the phase diagram whose degrees of freedom are only now being named.
arxiv-2512-19030:
Haoshuai Wang, Zhaoqi Dong, and Lei Chen revisit the Vicsek model, a simple rule set for how swarms move together. In the classic version, each member sees in all directions and aligns with its neighbors. The authors add more realistic limits drawn from natural swarms, then study the contact patterns as networks.

Uniform rules, they find, produce random Erdős–Rényi style networks, while mixed rules produce scale-free Barabási–Albert style ones. Across both kinds, order in the motion is set mainly by the average number of contacts per member. They also report a stretched-exponential link between that average and standard measures of synchronization.
arxiv-2512-19230:
Yue Fang, Geert Ridder, and Haitian Xie ask how to beat a fair lottery without throwing fairness away. Lotteries often hand out scarce chances, from school seats to program slots. Their rules estimate an assignment plan that raises welfare, while a penalty keeps it near the original randomization.

The framework spans discrete, continuous, and mixed treatments. Because regret grows with the square of estimation error, sloppy estimation costs real welfare, not just precision. Weighting by known lottery odds proves inefficient. Estimated-propensity and doubly robust criteria reach the efficient regret pattern instead. Simulations and a commitment-savings case measure the gains in practice.
arxiv-2512-19330:
Edwan Préau uses the holographic product formula to pin down how spectral functions look near extremality. Holography ties a hot, strongly coupled system to a black hole picture. Near extremality, energy, momentum, and temperature all sit far below a hard scale, and the spectral shape should simplify.

In the deep low-temperature limit, the gapless modes and the infrared conformal behavior factor cleanly apart. Préau shows that split sometimes holds through the whole near-extremal band, at leading order. Examples with different mode types are worked through, including new numerics for low-temperature quasinormal modes. Adding the infrared behavior sharpens low-energy descriptions in practice.
arxiv-2512-19430: Juliana Xavier surveys what is known about the growth rate inequality for endomorphisms of spheres, a circle of questions in smooth dynamics. The article gathers recent progress, flags the points where proofs still resist, and sets out open problems and conjectures that organize the area. As a survey, its value is the map it draws: which cases are settled, which techniques have worked, and where the next effort should go.
arxiv-2512-20030:
Arjun Sharma and Donald Koch compute the stress in sparse particles adrift in complex fluids. In dilute suspensions of non-Newtonian fluids, the total stress mixes two things. One is the fluid's own response. The other is what the particles add. Part of that is a stresslet from non-Newtonian tractions on the particle surfaces. Untangling those parts for a general fluid is the paper's feat.

A generalized reciprocal theorem states the stresslet through the fluid stress alone. For weakly non-Newtonian fluids, a perturbation expansion does more. With the method of characteristics, all lead terms come from the Newtonian flow field alone. No coupled equations need be solved. Two uses follow. One is spheres among smaller spheroids, where the stress can flip sign. The other is suspensions in nematic liquid crystals.
arxiv-2512-20230:
Hossein Tahmasbi and co-authors benchmark universal machine learning interatomic potentials, the learned models now used to simulate atoms. They test several leading models, including three built on the MACE architecture, plus MatterSim and PET-MAD. The tests stick to single-element systems, the simplest case any universal model must handle.

Near equilibrium, the models reproduce volumes well for transition metals but struggle with alkali and alkaline earth metals. Far from equilibrium, the team runs minima-hopping searches that explore each model's energy landscape. Those searches reveal a split: a smooth landscape does not guarantee accurate energies. The approach gives materials modelers a benchmark for judging how far these potentials really generalize.
arxiv-2512-20330:
Yuyang Li, Yipin Deng, Zijian Zhou, and Peng Hu test two strategies for reconstructing multicontrast cardiac magnetic resonance images. One strategy augments training data in a physics-consistent way, coupling image transforms with k-space noise and motion simulation. The other adds capacity cheaply, through a small vector-quantized prompt module or a sparse mixture-of-experts network called Moero.

On the multivendor CMRxRecon25 benchmark, augmentation helps small data sets but hurts the large benchmark when overused, exposing sensitivity to ratio and schedule. The prompt module gives modest, steady gains at almost no memory cost. Moero keeps improving after early plateaus but routes sparsely, so wall-clock time becomes the bottleneck. The authors recommend scale-aware augmentation and prompt-based scaling as the practical path forward.
arxiv-2512-20530:
N Barišić and D K Sunko use one unusual crystal to connect two famous families of superconductors. Murunskite, a sulfosalt, shares its structure with the iron pnictides but its electrons behave like those in the insulating parents of the cuprates. Comparing the three clarifies which orbitals do the binding, which carry current, and which drive superconductivity.

In cuprates, a hole localized on copper interacts with a Fermi liquid living on oxygen, and that mix underlies the effect and the Fermi arcs seen in spectra. In pnictides, binding and conduction split: some iron orbitals set the lattice spacing while others overlap directly between iron atoms. The authors argue a parallel pairing scenario is plausible there, with a light Fermi liquid scattering on a slow, nearly antiferromagnetic one.
arxiv-2512-20630:
Aayam Bansal and Ishaan Gangwani argue that checking a large model's reliability should not require thousands of test cases. Their method, MicroProbe, builds just one hundred well chosen probe examples. Strategic spread across five dimensions is combined with uncertainty scoring and adaptive weighting to expose failure modes efficiently.

Across several GPT-2 family models and validation in healthcare, finance, and legal domains, the probes beat random sampling clearly on composite scores. Three AI safety researchers rated the planned selection well above random selection in an expert review. Statistical power stays high while test cost drops by about ninety percent and coverage remains near that of older methods. For teams shipping models safely, cheap and credible checks matter.
arxiv-2512-21430:
Yusuf Ali, Zsolt Kira, and their co-authors tackle a weakness of generative robot policies. Policies built on diffusion or flow-matching models, which generate actions step by step, perform well in training conditions but recover poorly when the situation shifts. Fixing them normally requires expensive retraining.

Their system, EVE, wraps a frozen pretrained policy with verifier agents based on vision-language models. Each verifier inspects the policy's proposed actions and suggests refinements, with no extra training for either side. An action incorporator then fuses the suggestions back into the action generation process using classifier guidance. The authors study how the generator and verifiers should exchange information, and test the design across simulated and real robotic tasks on different robot bodies. EVE consistently raises success rates. Careful ablations separate which verifier abilities and fusion strategies matter most, giving builders practical guidelines for similar systems.
arxiv-2512-22030:
Entanglement, EPR steering, and Bell nonlocality form a ladder of quantum correlations, and how the first two relate for mixed states was incompletely understood. Yu-Xuan Zhang and Jing-Ling Chen prove that every entangled rank-two two-qubit state is EPR steerable, with pure rank-one states included as a special case.

The proof combines a local-unitary parametrization of rank-two two-qubit states, a necessary and sufficient separability condition, and a state-dependent nonlinear steering inequality. The result gives an analytical characterization of steerability for this whole class, extending Gisin-type reasoning beyond pure states. Rank-two entangled states are thus certifiable steering resources, a useful guarantee for quantum information protocols that rely on one-sided device-independent security.
arxiv-2512-22130:
Shunshun Liu and four co-authors show how expert feedback can teach a language model to mine numbers from research papers reliably. Their test task is pulling lattice constants, a basic crystal measurement, for high-entropy alloys out of published articles. Rather than hand-tuning prompts for months, they optimize them automatically through feedback cycles on just seven expert-annotated papers.

Recall for Claude 3.5 Sonnet climbed from 0.27 to above 0.9 under this small budget. The tuned prompt then extracted data covering 1,861 alloy compositions from 2,267 publications, and it transferred well to three newer models. The authors sort model mistakes into contextual hallucination, semantic misreading, and unit conversion errors, arguing that validation protocols remain essential.
arxiv-2512-22330:
Raphaël Cerf rewrites a classic proof so that undergraduates can follow it in a first probability course. The de Moivre-Laplace theorem, the ancestor of the central limit theorem for coin-flip-like trials, says binomial probabilities approach a bell curve. Standard proofs lean on series expansions and uniform convergence, machinery beginners have not met. Cerf follows the strategies in Breiman's and Feller's books but strips out those heavy tools.

In their place, the proof uses only the basic inequality that the exponential of t is at least one plus t. Stirling's formula is also avoided, replaced by the exact formula for the Wallis integral. As a by-product, the argument yields a non-asymptotic inequality directly linking the binomial and Gaussian distributions.
arxiv-2512-22930:
Yoshiki Nakamura settles the computational cost of deciding when two expressions mean the same thing in a relational algebra with a loop operator. Relational Kleene algebra models programs built from relations using composition, choice, and iteration. Its graph loop operator restricts a relation to pairs where input and output coincide, essentially testing for loops in a graph. Nakamura proves the equational theory for this system is PSPACE-complete.

The result survives adding top elements, tests, converse, and nominals to the language. It also resolves an open problem about Kleene algebra with tests: with domain, the relational equational theory is PSPACE-complete, in contrast to the ExpTime-completeness known for antidomain. The proof introduces loop-automata, finite automata on graphs that can test whether the current vertex carries a loop. Through them, the equational problem reduces in polynomial time to language inclusion for two-way alternating automata.
arxiv-2512-23030:
S. S. Agaev, K. Azizi, and H. Sundu investigate two hypothetical hadronic molecules built from charmed and bottom quarks. The proposed states bind a J/psi meson to a Bc meson, or its excited partner, forming objects with four heavy quarks in total and spin-parity one plus. Whether such exotic states exist, and where experiments should look, depends on their masses and decay widths, which the authors compute with QCD sum rules.

The two molecules come out with masses and current couplings so close that the study concentrates on the first. Its predicted mass sits above the thresholds for falling apart into ordinary meson pairs, so strong decays dominate. The authors compute partial widths for the main fall-apart channels and for six annihilation channels leading to B and D mesons. The total width is broad, giving experiments concrete targets.
arxiv-2512-23330:
Hadar Rotschield and Liat Peterfreund squeeze new power out of GQL, the new ISO standard language for querying property graphs. A known limitation says core GQL pattern matching cannot check whether edge values increase along a path, a natural condition for routes, timelines, and ranked chains. Their answer is a constructive translation: instead of extending the language, they compile the increasing-edges requirement into the input graph itself, rewriting the data so plain pattern matching enforces it.

The surprise is that the workaround also pays in speed. In a proof-of-concept built on Neo4j's Cypher, where such path constraints are expressible directly but expensively, the compiled version ran faster and avoided timeouts that hit the direct queries. The authors present the episode as database theory earning its keep twice: a translation invented to close an expressiveness gap turned out to be the more efficient implementation strategy as well.
arxiv-2512-23730:
Alon Drory continues a series on the four-body problem, the gravitational choreography of four masses, using his pair-space formalism. He focuses on central configurations, arrangements in which the gravitational pull on every body points toward one common center, so the shape can rotate or collapse as a unit. Such configurations organize much of what is known about few-body dynamics.

The pair-space equations fully characterize these configurations, and Drory examines the subclass where at least two pairs of inter-body distances are equal. He shows the only non-collinear examples are the tetrahedron, the unique non-planar case, plus planar kites and the isosceles trapezium. For each shape, the internal angles are pinned down by the mass ratios of the bodies, and the paper gives explicit formulas for all of these relations.
arxiv-2512-23830:
Nicola Garofalo introduces a family of heat kernels with a fractal twist. Mehler kernels are the explicit heat kernels of certain quadratic diffusion operators, classic tools in analysis. His two-parameter family of fractal Mehler kernels is built to match a class of Baouendi-Grushin flows, degenerate diffusions whose natural geometry carries a fractal dimension rather than the ordinary one.

Beyond constructing the kernels, Garofalo highlights a link between them and a geometric fully nonlinear equation, suggesting the kernels encode more than linear diffusion. The paper sets a program: it sets up the objects, establishes the connection to the flows, and ends by posing two questions for future work. Analysts working on degenerate diffusion equations and sub-Riemannian geometry are the natural audience. The paper opens doors more than it closes them.
arxiv-2512-24230:
Keshav Aggarwal, Robin Frot, Haozhe Gou, and Hui Wang make prime gap results fully explicit. Prime gaps are the differences between consecutive primes. A sequence of gaps is called graphic when it can be the degree sequence of a graph. Recent work by Erdős and others settled the question in principle. For large n the gap sequence is graphic, unconditionally. Under the Riemann Hypothesis it is graphic for all n.

What was missing was an explicit threshold. This paper supplies the first one. Beyond a stated double-exponential bound, the result holds for all n. A second, larger threshold covers a stronger property. Every graph realizing the gap sequence then extends in the stated way. The proofs use a refined test for graphicality. They also use sharper estimates on large prime gaps. An explicit zero-free region for the zeta function underpins those estimates.
arxiv-2512-24430:
Ashley Dickson and five colleagues simulate radiation damage in a fusion material. The material is YBCO, a high-temperature superconductor used in tapes. Compact fusion reactors will bombard those tapes with neutrons. Older atomistic models handle only the perfect form of the compound. Real conductors lack some oxygen, and that lack changes behavior.

Machine-learned models lift that limit. Two recent ones are used, built by cluster expansion and by Gaussian approximation. Both match quantum calculations for energies and forces. Cascade simulations then follow collision damage directly. Peak defect output exceeds the older model's predictions. Total defect output depends only weakly on oxygen content. High-energy cascades leave amorphous pockets sized near the coherence length. That matches microscope images of irradiated tapes.
arxiv-2512-24630:
Md Nahidul Islam Opu and three colleagues study how AI coding agents handle performance work. Agents increasingly write and revise real software. Correctness has been studied; performance behavior less so. The team mines agent-authored pull requests for performance changes. Language-model detection and topic modeling do the sorting. Fifty-two performance topics emerge, grouped into ten broad categories.

The optimizations span many layers of the software stack. Type of optimization matters for the outcome. Acceptance rates and review times both shift with it. Timing matters too. Agents do most performance work during development, not maintenance. The study grounds debates about agent quality in evidence. Reviewers and tool builders learn where agent optimizations land well and where they stall.
arxiv-2512-24730:
Di Wu, Xi-Li Zhang, and Qing-Guo Huang search LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA data for gravitational wave echoes without assuming a specific echo waveform. Echoes could reveal structure near a black hole horizon, beyond standard spectroscopy, but theory gives uncertain predictions. Their target is long-lived quasinormal modes expected from strong reflection inside the remnant.

A generalized phase-marginalized likelihood combines each mode coherently across the detector network, raising sensitivity. An optimized notching step suppresses instrument spectral lines in real noise. Readers get a robust search design that stays useful even while echo models remain unsettled, plus a template for model-agnostic gravitational wave searches.
arxiv-2601-00230:
Jayaseelan Dhakshinamoorthy works with Hitesh Chhabra and Ajaya K Nayak on pinning down the twist of magnetic skyrmions. Skyrmions are tiny swirling spin textures with device promise. In centrosymmetric materials, Bloch skyrmions form freely. Their helicity, though, lands at random each time. No Dzyaloshinskii Moriya force exists to pick a twist. Nucleation stays uncontrolled as a result.

Their simulation study offers a fully DMI free fix. Ferromagnetic stripes with opposed magnetization stabilize one chosen helicity. A patterned notch plus current pulses does the same job. Geometry and interface coupling create dipolar fields. Those fields lift the tie between twist states. Skyrmions then form with fixed chirality on demand. Guided motion becomes possible as well. The authors present the layered design as robust. It opens a cleaner path to skyrmion based spintronics.
arxiv-2601-00530:
Ravi Teja Pagidoju compares cloud platforms for running retail point-of-sale systems, the software that handles checkout in shops. Despite rapid adoption of cloud-based registers, little published research measures how specific platforms perform on retail workloads. Pagidoju set out to provide a transparent, repeatable comparison that small retailers and researchers can reuse.

Deployments on Google Cloud Platform and Microsoft Azure were tested through real-time API endpoints with open-source benchmarking code, using free-tier resources. Latency, throughput, and scalability were measured directly, while running costs were estimated from actual resource use and current public pricing, since free tiers produce no bills. All tables and figures were generated from the code outputs, so the reported numbers match the experiments exactly.
arxiv-2601-01230:
Burkhonov and 8 co-authors report seven years of watching a distant quasar whose light is split into two images. A galaxy between Earth and the quasar bends its light, so changes in one image reach us later than in the other. The team used a telescope in Uzbekistan from 2018 to 2024.

They find the brighter image leads by about 52 days, with an error of a few days either way. Spectra give the quasar's distance measure and, for the first time, that of the lens galaxy. Two simple mass models match the delay well. That match makes the system a good target for studying cosmic expansion.
arxiv-2601-01530:
Jing Ye, Lu Xiang, Yaping Zhang, and Chengqing Zong build EmoHarbor, a benchmark that tests whether AI emotional support is truly personal. Most evaluations reward generic empathy: warm words that could go to anyone. Real support must fit one person's traits, history, and situation. EmoHarbor judges from the user's side, simulating the user's inner world.

A chain of specialized agents plays the roles inside that inner world, interacts with the supporter being tested, and scores the exchange. The benchmark uses one hundred real user profiles spanning many personalities and situations, and grades ten dimensions of personalized support. Twenty leading language models were tested. The headline finding is blunt: models excel at sounding empathetic yet consistently fail to tailor support to the individual. The authors say the field's target should shift from generic empathy to user-aware support, and they offer EmoHarbor as a repeatable way to measure it.
arxiv-2601-01730:
Solar filaments, cool ribbons of gas held above the Sun's surface by magnetic fields, often sway, and those sways encode the strength of the field holding them. Upasna Baweja, Vaibhav Pant, Iñigo Arregui, and M. Saleem Khan study rare cases where a filament oscillates along its length and across it at the same time.

The team uses Bayesian methods. First, the lengthwise swing is treated as a pendulum to estimate the magnetic field. That result then feeds into the sideways motion. From it, the team infers the length of the magnetic tube. They also infer its number of twists. The tubes prove very long, from one hundred to one thousand megameters, with no more than three twists. The work shows how combined oscillations sharpen solar measurements.
arxiv-2601-02130:
Heating fusion plasma with ion cyclotron waves means solving two problems at once: how the waves propagate, and how the particle distribution evolves under them, each feeding the other. Dirk Van Eester, Vincent Maquet, Fabrice Louche, and Bernard Reman sketch a framework for solving the wave and Fokker-Planck equations fully self-consistently.

The approach assembles shared building blocks the two equations both need, including the plasma's dielectric response for arbitrary, non-Maxwellian particle distributions. Two settings are treated: particles that simply follow magnetic field lines, and an axisymmetric extension where drifts carry them off magnetic surfaces. A limited set of analytical results is included. The paper is a blueprint for coupling the solvers rather than a finished code.
arxiv-2601-03030:
Ali Kashefi builds generative models that predict fluid flow fields on irregular shapes, a task where standard image-based networks struggle. Pixel-based methods first project a geometry onto a uniform grid, which wastes effort and blurs fine detail. Kashefi instead couples flow matching and diffusion models with PointNet, a network that works directly on point clouds such as the vertices of a simulation mesh.

Both frameworks learn to rebuild physical flow fields from pure noise, conditioned on shapes the model has not seen. Unlike graph-network diffusion approaches, they avoid high-frequency noise artifacts and need no auxiliary geometry network. Tests on steady incompressible flow past cylinders of varying shape show the approach works, giving engineers a simpler route to fast flow prediction on new geometries.
arxiv-2601-03130:
Faisal Chowdhury and six co-authors present a deliberately simple system for automatic prompt engineering, the craft of finding prompts that make language models perform well. Their system needs no tuning and no explicit clues about the task, yet matches the effectiveness of more elaborate approaches. They test it on cryptic column name expansion, the task of turning terse database column names into full descriptions.

That task matters for searching, accessing, and understanding tabular data, but it has drawn little research attention until now. The team evaluates on datasets in both English and German. They report the first application of automatic prompt engineering to column name expansion, and, to their knowledge, the first such application to a language other than English.
arxiv-2601-03230:
Michael A. D. Taylor and Yu Zhang prove a generalized Bloch theorem for excitons bound to both cavity photons and phonons. Bloch's theorem sorts crystal states by momentum. But when fermions and bosons swap momentum, the translational symmetry of a crystalline exciton seems to break. The authors frame the problem around the conserved total crystal momentum instead.

In that frame, for both standard descriptions of the coupling, the Hamiltonian becomes exactly block diagonal. No approximations are used. The clean form yields the dispersions and optical responses of the hybrid particles that result, cavity exciton polaron-polaritons. The authors argue the frame lets researchers probe material traits in the strong coupling regime, where light and matter can no longer be pulled apart.
arxiv-2601-03330:
Anherutowa Calvo and Dante K. Calvo prove that time order can emerge from consistency alone in distributed information systems. Their minimal setting has records spread across sites, each interpreted as a constraint on a global space of possibilities. Events act locally by tightening records, and independent events commute, so the order in which they run does not matter. The authors define influence between events without assuming any primitive notion of time.

Influence by itself can cycle without contradiction, so they separate weak influence, mere dependence, from strong influence, exclusive branching on an observable fact. Assuming every reachable state stays satisfiable, plus the diamond property and monotone writing, they prove strong influence is acyclic. That acyclicity induces an intrinsic chronology, and the derived order is shown to be minimal.
arxiv-2601-03530:
Satoko Sawada-Satoh and twelve co-authors report new radio observations of the galaxy NGC 1052 and the gas torus around its central black hole. Using the Korean VLBI Network at two-millimeter wavelength, they detected sulfur monoxide absorption against the compact core. The absorption is broad and has several components at different speeds, including a newly found blueshifted feature.

The signal appears only toward the central components, not the outer jets, which pins the gas to a region smaller than about half a parsec from the black hole. The authors argue the molecules were evaporated by shock heating where the jet strikes the torus. Some clumps move outward with the jet while others fall back in. The finding gives a rare close look at how jets and gas rings interact.
arxiv-2601-03730:
Fabian Haak and Philipp Schaer study bias hiding in search engine query suggestions for searches about people. Suggestions flash by almost subliminally, so biased completions can shape what users think and click before they notice. Earlier work by Bonart and colleagues built a detection pipeline, but suggestions are sparse and carry little context, which makes bias hard to measure well.

Haak and Schaer add perception-aware metrics to that pipeline, measures that account for how briefly suggestions are actually seen. An analysis with the enhanced pipeline confirmed it detects systematic topical bias better than before. The topic matters because autocomplete quietly steers public curiosity about real people, including politicians and minorities, and engines cannot fix a bias they cannot first detect reliably.
arxiv-2601-03930:
Ilann Amiaud-Plachy and three co-authors build Bayes-PD, a Bayesian neural network that learns binding behavior directly from phage display experiments. Phage display is a powerful laboratory technique for studying how proteins bind other molecules. Its data are noisy, awkward to preprocess, and hard to interpret, so deep learning has underused them for protein design. Their model trains inside a loop that simulates the experiment and its noise.

The goal is to show that modeling experimental noise and the network's own uncertainty makes phage display results reliably interpretable. Validation uses actual binding affinity measurements rather than proxy scores from held-out display rounds, a stricter test. If the approach holds, vast phage display archives could become training material for designing proteins with desired binding partners.
arxiv-2601-04230:
N. O. Chudak, O. S. Potiienko, I. V. Sharph, and V. P. Smolyar present five objections to the usual telling of the EPR paradox. The paradox claims that quantum entanglement seems to clash with relativity and local action. The authors argue that overlooked local interactions inside the setup change the analysis.

For entangled subsystems, they argue, forming the post-measurement state must involve local interactions that touch both subsystems, contrary to standard EPR assumptions. Correlations between distant measurement devices, they show, can still fit relativistic principles. Removing redundant degrees of freedom, as in generalised Hamiltonian dynamics, stops the paradox from arising for states of fixed total momentum or spin. They also flag a separate puzzle for a charged quantum particle, whose field they link to potential shapes encoded in its state.
arxiv-2601-04330:
Can Onur Akyuz and three co-authors compute a key correlation in a much-studied toy model of strange metals and black holes, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The complex Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model, a system of randomly interacting fermions, is known to behave at low energies like a one-dimensional nearly conformal field theory. adding a chemical potential tilts that behaviour through an asymmetry parameter.

Working in the conformal limit, the team computes the model's four-point function for any value of that asymmetry, at leading order in the large-system expansion. The answer fits the expected nearly-conformal structure exactly, which lets them pull out the structure constants that govern how two fermions correlate with combined, bilinear operators. The calculation firms up the model's low-energy picture where earlier results covered only special cases.
arxiv-2601-04630:
Xiyuan Zhu and eight co-authors build a visual analytics system for exploring job markets from many angles at once, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Online recruitment platforms dominate hiring but offer only blunt filters — title, keyword, salary band. Which hide how attributes relate and how patterns change from national trends down to single emerging roles. RecruitScope is designed for seekers and employers alike, especially human resources specialists.

Coordinated visualizations let users move across levels: reading salary distributions and position patterns from several perspectives, interpreting industry dynamics at the macro scale, and spotting newly emerging positions at the micro scale. Case studies demonstrate the system at work, uncovering regional salary distribution patterns, characterizing how industries' hiring grows or cools over time, and discovering high-demand emerging roles that simple filtering would never surface. The authors present it as evidence that multidimensional exploration beats the filter box for labour market sense-making.
arxiv-2601-04930:
Antonella Del Pozzo and 4 co-authors set out a new way to add up model updates in federated learning in a 2026 paper. In federated learning, phones or sites train a shared model and send in updates. The server must add those updates up in a way that leaks none of them. Old schemes assume all hands act at the same pace, lean on heavy peer-to-peer chats, and fail if the server stalls or drops notes.

Their scheme works when notes can arrive at any time, with any lag. It also holds up when the server itself acts in bad faith and breaks the rules in any way it likes. Dropping the need for lockstep pace and a trusted server brings safe federated learning far closer to how real fleets of phones and sites truly act.
arxiv-2601-05130:
Rishabh S. Gvalani and Lukas Koch prove how smooth the best cheap move of stuff from one spread to a next stays in a 2026 math paper. The cheap move task is called optimal transport. In work use, a smoothed form of the task is the norm, since the raw task is hard to run on a machine. The smooth form adds a soft curb, of one of two types, to keep the task tame.

The pair start from the case where the raw move is known to be smooth in a set sense. They then prove bounds on how fast the smoothed move can tilt, and on its slopes. The bounds hold for all strengths of the curb. For the pure smooth cases, the bounds grow more strong. Such proof counts, since smoothed moves run at the heart of machine learning losses and of tools that reshape shots and scans.
arxiv-2601-05230:
Quentin Garrido and 5 co-authors teach world models to infer their own action space from raw video in a 2026 paper. World models predict the consequences of actions, which agents need for planning, but most require action labels that are expensive to obtain at scale. Latent action models instead learn what an action is from videos alone, and earlier work stayed inside simple robot simulations, video games, or manipulation datasets.

The authors expand learning to in-the-wild videos, capturing richer and messier actions from ordinary footage. That broader diet makes training harder but the resulting models more general. World models that learn from unlabeled real video could supply planning skills for robots and agents without hand-labelled action data for every new environment.
arxiv-2601-05330:
Tengwei Song and 3 co-authors lift enzyme calls by feeding a model the full text of how stuff reacts in a 2026 paper. To call which enzyme works on which food-stuff is a core task for life science and for plant design. The known pairs, set down by pros, are few and far from full, and they cost dear work to keep up. A model fed just on those pairs tends to fail on pairs no one has seen, which is just where a find would count most.

The team mine the text of real chem acts, the rules of what turns into what. They fold that lore into a map of facts whose links can join more than two nodes at once. Sharp enzyme calls could speed the build of germ-based works and the hunt for enzymes that drive green chem.
arxiv-2601-06030:
Richard Jiarui Tong traces sixty years of human-AI teamwork in a 2026 review paper. Early visions cast the computer as a colleague in symbiosis or as a tool that augments human intellect. Later schools frame it as a supertool, or as a partner that adapts mutually with its user.

Tong sets out a chain for effective teaming: explainable AI supports co-adaptation, which builds shared mental models. Evidence shows a paradox. Human-AI teams often do worse than AI alone on judgment tasks, yet do better on content creation. Failures trace to bias, aversion to algorithms, and slow loss of human skill. The paper closes with a framework for durable gains from treating AI as part of one's own thinking.
arxiv-2601-06130: Hector Andres Granada Diaz and 2 co-authors define a derivative for functions between metric groups in a 2026 mathematics paper. The domain is a metric divisible group and the target is a metric Abelian group with a group metric, settings far more general than ordinary real functions. The paper states and proves basic differentiation theorems for this new derivative. In particular, the authors obtain a chain rule, the rule for differentiating a composition of two functions in this group setting.
arxiv-2601-06630:
Molla Basir Ahamed, Sujoy Majumder, and Nabadwip Sarkar sharpen Bohr-type inequalities in 2026. They study multidimensional analogues for bounded holomorphic mappings in several variables. Their domain is the unit polydisc in complex space.

They establish a sharp extension of the classical Bohr inequality. The Bohr radius remains one over three n, they prove. That radius holds for functions bounded by unity in the multivariate setting. Classical Bohr results concern power series in one complex variable. Extending them sharply to many variables is delicate and long studied. Their radius matches the best possible value, hence sharp. Complex analysts get a definitive constant for the polydisc case. Euler operators enter their treatment of Schwarz functions as well.
arxiv-2601-06830:
Yinan Hu and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers constrained density estimation using optimal transport. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. A new framework for density estimation under expectation constraints is proposed. The framework minimizes the Wasserstein distance between the estimated density and a prior.

Subject to the constraints that the expected value of a set of functions adopts or exceeds given values. The framework is generalized to include regularization inequalities to mitigate the artifacts in the target measure. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-06930:
Research by Olga Azenhas and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with symplectic left companion of a Littlewood-Richardson-Sundaram tableau and the kwon property. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. As a consequence of the Littlewood-Richardson (LR) commuters coincidence and the Kumar-Torres branching model via Kushwaha-Raghavan-Viswanath flagged hives. We have solved the Lecouvey-Lenart conjecture on the bijections between the Kwon and Sundaram branching models.

For the pair ( G ​ L 2 ​ n ​ ( ℂ ). S ​ p 2 ​ n ​ ( ℂ ) ) consisting of. The general linear group G ​ L 2 ​ n ​ ( ℂ ) and the symplectic group. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07030:
Paresh Arora and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with special l l -values of certain CM weight three hecke eigenforms. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Ramanujan’s theories of elliptic functions to alternative bases. For modular forms connect hypergeometric series with modular forms and have led to applications such as the modularity of certain hypergeometric Galois representations.

The authors relate special values of L L -function of certain CM cusp forms to Ramanujan’s alternative bases via. The modularity of hypergeometric Galois representations arising from CM elliptic curves over real quadratic fields. We also give a complete classification of these representations. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07130:
Nicholas Pritchard, Richard Dodson, and Andreas Wicenec wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a new kind of chip for radio astronomy. The chips are called neuromorphic, which means they work in a way shaped by the brain. Radio work leans on custom, trial-based tools built for each task. The next wave of telescopes will push those tools hard.

Two vast arrays lead that wave. One is the Square Kilometre Array, or SKA. The other is the next-generation Very Large Array, or ngVLA. Both will draw huge amounts of power. Both face harsh radio noise from human tech. With classic von Neumann designs, the power bill may block the science goals. Brain-shaped chips use far less power per task. The authors weigh what that shift could mean for the labs that run these telescopes. They ask where such chips could help first and most.
arxiv-2601-07230:
A 2026 arXiv paper in pure math sets out a new form of cohomology for groups. Cohomology reads the shape of a space or a group by means of chains and holes. The new form is called configured group cohomology. It grows out of a known form called locally smooth cohomology. Its parts are tuples in a good layout, with shapes that fill the gaps.

The frame yields new 3-cocycles of Chern-Simons type, which take values in the real line split by whole steps, written as R over Z. They live on groups of diffeomorphisms, smooth maps that bend a shape but do not tear it. The maps in view keep a set geometric form in place. The paper also deals with torsion in the third homology of such groups, with values in Q over Z.
arxiv-2601-07530:
Yi Liao, Quan-Yu Wang, and Yuanbin Wu study a scattering process where particles carry a twist. Their 2026 preprint concerns electron-positron annihilation into two photons. In this setup the positron is a plane wave, while the electron and photons are vortex states. Vortex states carry orbital angular momentum, like a corkscrew. The geometry is off-axis, adding further structure.

The authors build a theoretical formalism for this triple-vortex process. With it they examine how vortex parameters and the scattering angle affect the outcome. Vortex beams of particles and light are a growing tool in fundamental physics. Understanding their collisions may open new ways to probe particle properties. The paper is written for specialists in quantum electrodynamics and structured beams.
arxiv-2601-07730:
Jithin D. George and colleagues integrate equations along paths in the complex plane instead of the real line. Most numerical time-stepping methods use real-valued steps. Complex steps add a degree of freedom, since size can be chosen in both real and imaginary directions. Their 2026 preprint shows that specific complex paths expand the stability region. Larger stability regions mean bigger, safer steps for stiff problems.

The advantage is clearest for complex-valued systems. Stiff problems force tiny steps in standard methods because fast and slow scales coexist. A clever path can sidestep some of that cost. The authors present explicit integrators built on this idea. Numerical analysts solving stiff differential equations are the readers. The work turns an old curiosity, complex time, into practical integrators.
arxiv-2601-07830:
Valentina Njaradi, Rodrigo Carrasco-Davis, and Peter Latham ask how a learner should schedule its own learning rate. Learning efficiently is a basic challenge for both biological and artificial agents. Speed brings rapid improvement but also costs: effort, instability, and resource use. Their 2026 preprint studies the optimal schedule that balances effort against performance. The learning rate here is the size of each update step.

Too fast, and learning can thrash or waste energy. Too slow, and time runs out before mastery. A principled schedule could guide both animal learning studies and machine learning practice. The authors come from computational neuroscience, where brains are the original self-tuning learners. Their framing treats the schedule as a decision problem. The paper speaks to neuroscientists and machine learning scholars who tune learning dynamics.
arxiv-2601-07930:
Liying Zhang and Liang Zhao use a transformer model to swap groups in molecules on its own. Swapping a functional group is a key approach in cheminformatics to design compounds with set traits. Old methods for removal and swaps rely on rules of thumb set by hand. Those rules limit the diversity and novelty of the structures produced. Their 2026 preprint gives a transformer approach to the task.

Such models learn from data in place of hand set rules. Applied to molecules, they propose swaps a rule book would never suggest. Drug chemists use such swaps to tune strength, safety, and how a drug dissolves. Novel structures matter because patented and known chemical space is crowded. The paper serves scholars of cheminformatics and drug search teams. It brings a language model architecture to a classic molecular design step. A good swap keeps what works and trims what harms.
arxiv-2601-08530: Zhonghao Wang, Junqiang Peng, Yuxi Liu, and Mingyu Xiao ask how hard it is to rig a knockout tournament. Their 2026 arXiv paper defines the tournament fixing problem on a tournament digraph. The digraph encodes outcomes of all possible matches, and a designated favorite must emerge as champion. The question is whether a schedule exists that guarantees that result. The authors study the case where few players can beat or be beaten by the favorite. Complexity results here inform fair bracket design in sports and esports.
arxiv-2601-08630: Gregoire Nadin, David Nahmani, and Nicolas Vauchelet wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on the best way to swap one population for a new one. The work treats an optimal control problem. The system is ruled by a nonlinear differential equation with a bistable term that repeats in time. Bistable means the system can rest in one of two states. The model tracks A-type members as B-type members take their place, in a setting that shifts over time. The state is the share of B-type members in the group.
arxiv-2601-08930:
Enhyeok Jang and five co-authors study a quantum chip shaped like a race track. On such a chip, trapped ions move round zones where work is done. A past test on this shape showed a quantum edge for pure chance tasks. The team asks how well the shape runs plain programs as zones are added.

They run test programs that tune a set of values by trial. To their own surprise, more zones can make runs slow, not fast. The blame lies in the plan that sets which job goes to which zone, and when. A reader who builds such chips gets a clear warn. More zones help only if the work plan grows with them.
arxiv-2601-09030:
Yingtong Zhu and five co-authors explain a strange glow from a thin sheet of a sulfur based stuff. The sheet is one layer of WS2. Its glow comes from a bound pair of a charge and a gap, called an exciton. The pair spans two low zones of the sheet. When the sheet is stretched both ways, the glow shifts in a wave like path.

Past lab work saw that wave path, but not its cause. The team builds a joint frame that plays the glow back in full. It shows how stretch mixes the two zones to steer the pair. A reader in thin stuffs gets a cause for a known glow quirk, and a knob to tune it.
arxiv-2601-09330:
Pierrot Lamontagne and a large team weigh a small planet round a near red dwarf star, GJ 3090. The planet, GJ 3090 b, is a sub-Neptune: large than Earth, small than Neptune. It crosses its star each 2.85 days. New speed marks from the NIRPS tool, plus past HARPS marks, let the team pin its mass with more care.

They set the mass at a value near four and a half Earth masses, with a tight doubt range. They also find a next planet near the star's own spin span. That find needs care, since star spin can fake a planet mark. A reader in planet work gets a firm mass for a key near case, and a warn on its mate.
arxiv-2601-10230:
Ming Liu and Yosuke Hasegawa sim flows past a spinning solid with odd shape. Such flows drive fans, pumps, and turbines. A true sim is hard when the solid spins and its shape is bent. The team use a volume penalty method to fake the solid.

They pair the method with two frame tricks. One frame spins with the solid. One mesh slides past the next. Each pair gives a way to host a spinning shape on a fixed grid. The paper tests both pairs. It aims for sims that are sharp yet cheap to run.
arxiv-2601-10430:
L. Serafini and a large team plan to probe fault zones with muon beams. Muons are heavy kin of electrons. A high energy beam of them can pass through rock. The team want to send such a beam across a live fault. Rock at a fault can act as a piezo stuff under stress.

Such stuff gives off charge when squeezed. A muon beam could read that charge at depth. The paper grows a past study of the plan. It sets out the beam and the read gear it would need. The aim is a new probe of stress in fault zones.
arxiv-2601-10630:
A 2026 arXiv preprint takes up classification imbalance, the case where one class is far rarer than the other. Rare classes arise in fraud, disease, and fault detection. A model trained on skewed data may do well on the common class and fail on the rare one. The authors reframe the problem to handle that skew head on.

They cast it as transfer learning under label shift. The source data follow the skewed mix seen in practice. The target is a balanced mix, the one used to judge performance. That frame clarifies what a fair test should look like. It gives practitioners a principled way to train and score models when classes are far from even.
arxiv-2601-10830:
Ayman Badawi defines a new graph from a finite abelian group. Take a group H with at least two elements, and an integer m above one. Make each group element a vertex. Join two vertices when the m-th power of one equals the other element in the right pairing. The result is the m-graph of H.

Graphs built from groups let algebra be seen and counted. Degrees, cliques, and connected parts can mirror subgroup structure. Badawi's construction adds a fresh member to this family. Papers of this kind supply test cases for graph theory and new lenses for finite group structure at the same time.
arxiv-2601-10930:
Zhixian Xie, Yu Xiang, Michael Posa, and Wanxin Jin build a framework for dexterous robot manipulation over long horizons. Contact-rich tasks demand joint reasoning about shape, joint limits, and rough contact dynamics. End-to-end learned policies skip that structure. They often need huge data, transfer poorly from simulation, and generalize weakly across tasks and robot bodies.

The authors combine reinforcement learning with model predictive control in a hierarchy. Their frame is geometry-aware: where to touch, and how to make contact, are decided as linked questions. The hierarchy lets learning handle what models miss, and models keep learning grounded. The work targets hands that must work in the real world, not just in simulators.
arxiv-2601-11130:
Tatiana M. Rodríguez and co-authors present very-long-baseline views of ionized jets from young stars. The team used the VLA at 1.3 centimeters with sub-arcsecond resolution, about a tenth of an arcsecond. They also observed the 22.2 gigahertz water maser line. Targets were fifteen compact radio sources with rising spectral index, plus eight string-like radio structures from earlier surveys.

Rising spectra and string shapes are signs of jets carving through natal gas. Sub-arcsecond maps can separate a true jet from a round wind. Maser spots mark shocked gas along the flow. Such detail shows how jets launch and collimate, a core step in star birth that also feeds back on the cloud that made the star.
arxiv-2601-11330:
A hunt for dark matter with a Higgs boson is reported in this preprint. The authors are listed as the CMS team in the record. The data come from proton-proton collisions at the LHC. The collision energy is 13 TeV, the standard LHC run energy.

The sought event pairs dark matter with one Higgs boson. The Higgs then decays to a bottom quark pair. That decay is common, which gives the hunt more events. Data from the CMS detector total 101 inverse femtobarns. Dark matter would flee the detector unseen, as missing energy. A Higgs tag plus missing energy is thus the signature. The search tests models where the Higgs links to a dark sector.
arxiv-2601-11630:
Haonan Wei and five coauthors distill a generation model to one layer. Their 2026 preprint reworks FreeFlow, a one-step flow method. Flow matching compresses diffusion generation into few steps. MeanFlow and FreeFlow lead that one-step push via ODEs.

FreeFlow uses a 28-layer transformer for its generation. The team reads those layers as steps of an Euler scheme. Depth acts as discrete time along an ODE path. That view suggests the layers can be re-distilled. Their model generates in one step with a single-layer transformer. A one-layer generator cuts cost and latency sharply. The work tests how much depth generation truly needs.
arxiv-2601-11830:
Griselda Arroyo-Chávez, Enrique Vázquez-Semadeni, and James Wurster ask what sets spin in giant gas clouds in space. Such clouds form stars, and their spin shapes how stars and disks form. Views show that spin per unit mass grows with size in a set pattern.

They weigh three forces: gravity, turbulence, and magnetic fields. Each can move spin from large scales to small ones, or the other way. Their work tests which force rules the pattern seen in the views. The answer helps star birth models start from more true cloud states.
arxiv-2601-12030:
Yilun Yao, Shan Huang, Elsie Dai, and their co-authors keep long AI research tasks on track. Language models used as research agents lose skill as their chat history grows. That decay, called context rot, breaks clear, task-fit inner state over long runs.

Their frame, called ARC in the work, manages context with active picks and self-review. It aims to keep key facts and drop noise as a task runs. Long search and report tasks stand to gain most. The work tests how such care lifts long-run agent skill.  Less rot means more sound work on long search tasks.
arxiv-2601-12230:
Koki Takahashi and Shun Watanabe prove channel resolvability for classical-quantum channels by a set code method. Resolvability asks how well random noise can mimic a channel output. Past proofs for such channels used random coding alone.

Their past work gave a deterministic proof for classic channels via multiplicative weights. They extend that route with a matrix form of the weights method. A set code is easier to build and audit than a random one. The result adds a firm tool to quantum information theory.  A set proof is a step past random code proofs.
arxiv-2601-12430:
Tsan Tsai Chan and four co authors study a quirk of vision language models. These models take in a system prompt, an image, and text, then answer questions. A known flaw is hallucination, where the model claims things that are not there. Such flaws are often linked to how attention is split across the three inputs.

Most fixes so far push the model to attend more to the image. The team argue that this image centric view misses the roles of the other inputs. Their title names the effect they find: system mediated attention gaps make models say yes. In other words, the system prompt can tilt a model toward agreement. That tilt helps explain false yes answers on visual questions.
arxiv-2601-12730:
Zhaochun Li and six co authors rethink the exploration and exploitation trade off in reinforcement learning for language models. Training with group relative policy optimization tends to be exploitation driven. Entropy falls steadily, samples converge, and exploration fades away. A model that stops exploring can lock into mediocre habits.

Most existing fixes are sample centric, hunting or rewarding rare samples. They assume exploration comes from novel trajectories and tokens. The team argue for a distribution centric policy optimization instead. Their title claims this view dominates the old trade off framing. Shifting focus from single samples to whole distributions may keep exploration alive. The work targets a core weakness in current language model training.
arxiv-2601-12930:
Jale Basten, Katja Ickstadt, and Nina Timmesfeld guide analysis of stepped wedge cluster trials. In these trials, all clusters start in the control condition. They cross over to the intervention on a staggered schedule over time. Sequential measurements within clusters span multiple periods.

That staggered start unbalances observations across intervention groups over time. Individual time effects can then bias naive analyses of the treatment effect. The team run a simulation study on how to address those effects. Guidance grounded in simulation helps trialists pick sound models in advance. Stepped wedge designs are common in health service research. Their advice serves a wide base of applied statisticians.
arxiv-2601-13330:
Jamie Cummins, Beth Clarke, Ian Hussey, and Malte Elson built a tool to check if a paper matches its pre plan. A pre plan, called a registration, states what a study will do before it starts. Across social and health fields, pre plans aid clear and strict science. Yet checks of plans are rare, so their worth is lost.

Their tool is called RegCheck. It pairs a study plan with its paper and flags where they part. Parts may be swaps in tests, marks, or who took part. By auto of the pair work, checks can run at scale. For journals and funders, the tool turns a norm few check into one that can be kept.
arxiv-2601-13530:
Tomoya Hayata, Yoshimasa Hidaka, and Yuta Kikuchi watch a deformed Yang-Mills theory start to thermalize on a trapped ion quantum computer. Non balance acts of quantum many body systems are a top aim of quantum sims. Gauge theories in high energy physics draw more and more such runs as gear grows.

Yet most past runs stay in one space dim, or in Abelian theories like the Schwinger model and the toric code. The team runs a q deformed SU(2) theory, a non Abelian case with a twist. They track when thermal acts set in. Such a run tests if today's ion gear can host the gauge acts that count most.
arxiv-2601-13730:
Makoto Ueki studies how epidemics break out in populations split into linked groups in 2026. During an outbreak, a pathogen spreads through host groups that interact. Group size, network shape, and the strength of links all shape the spread. Ueki uses stochastic simulation, which rolls random events, and analytic approximations.

The work shows how outbreak sizes depend on those three factors. Network architecture can speed or slow a wave of cases. Coupling strength sets how fast one group seeds the next. Such maps help planners guard the links that matter most.
arxiv-2601-14030:
Samuel Remedios and co-authors sharpen MRI scans by combining many images at once in 2026. Diffusion models are the current state of the art for imaging inverse problems. They sample from a prior distribution to fill in missing detail. A known likelihood function then guides posterior sampling without retraining.

Most methods focus on single-image inverse problems. Multi-image MRI super-resolution must fuse several scans of one subject. Their likelihood-separable diffusion inference targets that multi-image case. Sharper MRI from faster, lower-grade scans could cut patient time in the scanner. Most past work used one scan at a time. Real clinics have many scans per case, so the multi-image case is the one that counts.
arxiv-2601-14130:
Till Aczel and co-authors compress gray images with logic circuits that learn in 2026. Neural image codecs beat traditional hand-crafted methods like PNG in compression ratio. They often incur substantial computational overhead to do so. That overhead limits deployment on energy-constrained devices like smartphones, cameras, and drones.

Their GIC-DLC trains lookup tables to mix neural flexibility with Boolean efficiency. Differentiable logic circuits learn the compression while staying hardware-friendly. The codec targets grayscale images in this work. Small devices could then store more photos on less power. Logic steps use far less power than dense math units. On a drone or a phone, that saved power is pure gain.
arxiv-2601-14230:
Yiyang Wang, Yiqiao Jin, Alex Cabral, and Josiah Hester build companion agents that keep distinct voices in 2026. Multi-agent systems have emerged as socio-collaborative companions for emotional and cognitive support. Such systems frequently suffer from persona collapse. Agents revert to generic, homogenized assistant behaviors over time.

Social sycophancy is an other flaw, producing redundant, non-constructive dialogue. Their Mascot framework targets multi-agent socio-collaborative companion systems. It is designed to be generalizable across uses. Companions that stay in character could give richer, more honest support. The frame aims to keep each agent's voice its own. It also aims to curb praise that adds heat but no light to the talk.
arxiv-2601-14730:
Bizu Feng, Zhimu Yang, Shaode Yu, and Zixin Hu explain graph neural network predictions in this 2026 paper. Despite the widespread success of graph neural networks, understanding the reasons behind their specific predictions remains challenging. Existing explainability methods face a trade-off. Gradient-based approaches are computationally efficient but often ignore structural interactions.

Game-theoretic techniques capture interactions, but at high computational overhead. They may also deviate from the model's true reasoning path. Their explainer, FSX, is enhanced by message flow sensitivity. It tracks how messages move through the graph to shape a prediction. The path it picks can be shown. A user can ask why, and get an answer tied to the graph. Readers get explanations that follow the network's own traffic, at a cost closer to the fast methods.
arxiv-2601-14830:
Monalisa Dubey, Kuntal Misra, and a large team of co-authors report on a star that blew up in the galaxy NGC 2139. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies the supernova SN 2023zcu, classed as a Type IIP event. The team tracked it with both light data and spectra.

The light curve is well sampled from the rise through the flat plateau phase and into the late nebular phase. The authors measure an optically thick phase of about 100 days. The title also points to early flash features seen near the start of the event.
arxiv-2601-15030:
Piotr Płonka and Agnieszka Janiuk model the death of a massive spinning star. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with gamma-ray bursts, the most powerful explosions known. Long bursts come from stars that collapse into black holes.

At collapse, the new black hole holds far less mass than the star left behind. The rest of the star still falls in or flies out as a jet. The team runs three-dimensional simulations in general relativity with magnetic fields. Their runs follow how the jet forms deep inside and pushes out through the star.
arxiv-2601-15230:
Edgar F. A. Lederer checks two classic Turing machines with a modern proof tool. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with formal verification in Dafny, a program verifier. Both machines are deciders, so the goal is total correctness, not just partial results.

The machines are typical first examples from courses in theoretical computer science. The second one is taken straight from a standard textbook on the subject. Lederer proves each machine halts with the right answer on every input. The paper shows how Dafny handles these textbook cases from start to finish.
arxiv-2601-15630:
Chandra Prakash, Mary Lind, and Avneesh Sisodia write on governing AI agents in health care in a 2026 arXiv paper. Health systems now embed agentic AI in daily workflows. Uses include clinical documentation support and early-warning monitoring. As agents spread across departments and vendors, sprawl sets in. Duplicated agents appear. Accountability blurs. Controls vary from team to team. Tool permissions can outlive the task they were granted for.

The authors address the full lifecycle of such agents, per the title. Governance means knowing which agents exist, who owns them, and what they may touch. Lifecycle management covers launch, updates, and retirement. For hospitals, the stakes are clinical, not just technical. A stray agent with stale permissions is a safety risk. The paper speaks to leaders who must tame agent growth.
arxiv-2601-15730:
E. García-Río, R. Rodríguez-Gigirey, and R. Vázquez-Lorenzo describe a class of geometric structures in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their topic is four-dimensional Lorentzian algebraic Ricci solitons. A Ricci soliton is a space whose metric evolves in a self-similar way. Lorentzian geometry adds a time direction, as in relativity. The authors contrast their setting with the Riemannian one. There, such solitons are far more restricted.

In their setting, a striking fact holds. Any connected, simply connected four-dimensional Lie group admits a left-invariant Lorentz metric that is a Ricci soliton. That breadth is unexpected next to the Riemannian case. Classification work like this maps what geometries can exist. Relativity and geometry both draw on such maps when they model spacetime.
arxiv-2601-16130:
Neeley Pate and coauthors test if language models copy slanted thought in humans. Their 2026 preprint deals with driven thought, where a wish bends how facts are read. Human tests show this bend in clear ways. It is not known if plain language models show the same bend. The team reruns human tests with models in the place of people.

They check if model picks shift with the wish as human picks do. Like shifts would mean models pick up human bias from text. Un like shifts would mark a gap in how models think. The work helps teams judge model acts in charged topics. It ties model tests to known human test designs.
arxiv-2601-16230:
Aditya Kamlesh and coauthors test speech models on scores for learned tongue speech. Their 2026 preprint deals with scores for speech in a second tongue. Good scores give fair feed back and track growth. Speech must be judged on flow, tune and full sense at once. That joint score task is hard for code tools.

The team tests speech large models with no task train. Such zero shot tests show what the models can do at once. They weigh scores across all parts of speech grade. Gaps show where fresh train or cues are needed. The work maps a path to fair speech scores.
arxiv-2601-16430:
David King, Thomas Russell and Ahmad Omar show how live grains shake a soft sheet. Their 2026 preprint deals with a sheet that bends with ease. Live grains swim or crawl and push on the sheet. The team solves for the push those grains place on it. That push turns out to cut the pull tight of the sheet.

It also cuts the bend stiff of the sheet as a whole. New far reach terms join spots on the sheet through the grains. Such terms have no match in dead sheet maths. Soft sheets in cells may act by these same rules. The work gives a first theory for the pair.
arxiv-2601-16730:
Bekir Daniş and İsmail Alperen Öğüt settle a math guess with a firm no. The guess claimed that all posets have a trait called conclusiveness. A poset is a set with a part-way rank rule. Their 2026 preprint gives a case that breaks the guess. The case leans on twist traits and a famed flat shape.

The authors also sort which small posets hold the trait. They link the trait to the life of outer derivations. Such maps track how a rank rule can shift. Plain cases that break broad guesses are gold in math. They keep the field from years of false trails.
arxiv-2601-16830:
Andrew Thompson and Miles McCrory work out exact math for doubt in neural nets. A trained net gives a call for each input. When inputs blur, the call's blur counts too. Past work gauged that blur with rough series tricks. Their 2026 preprint gives exact forms for one class of nets.

The nets have one hidden layer and a ramp-style switch. Inputs are set as bell-shaped chance spreads. From those, exact mean and spread of the output fall out. No rough cuts are used in the proof. Exact doubt helps in care, flight, and risk work. It lets teams trust net calls with proof, not hope.
arxiv-2601-17030:
Maxwell Siegel broadens his own past frame for Collatz-type tasks. The Collatz task asks if a simple rule chain always lands at one. Hydra maps are kin rules that branch like the myth beast. His 2026 preprint casts those maps on rings of whole marks. Those rings sit in global fields, a broad number world.

His frame joins the maps to ghost-value spread math. That math, from his 2024 work, reads how marks spread. Broad frames may crack more than one hard task. They show how one rule set can span many fields. Pure number work gains a wider lens here.
arxiv-2601-17130:
Megha Khosla asks how graph shape sways leak risk in graph neural nets. Such nets learn from webs of linked facts. They ace tasks like node tags and link calls. But they may leak if a fact was in their train set. Foes can probe that leak with sly asks. Her 2026 preprint ties the leak risk to the web's shape.

Dense hubs and tight crowds may leak more than loose webs. Shape-wise maps can warn where leaks run high. Health and bank webs need such warns most. Their facts are the most dear if leaked. This work gives builders a shape check for risk.
arxiv-2601-17330:
Laurent Caraffa asks if common training tricks share one deep rule. Machine learning uses weight decay, dropout, and moving averages to keep models in check. Each trick works, yet each rests on its own story. At the same time, training big models burns more and more energy. Caraffa asks if learning nears a hard efficiency bound.

He frames best regularization under information-geometric constraints. That frame ties the tricks to limits from thermodynamics. If such a bound holds, it would guide greener training. It would also unite split tricks in one theory. The work is a step toward learning rules set by physics, not just trial and error.
arxiv-2601-17430:
Zichuan Yang and Yiming Xing study how to find a bad subset among many data streams. The streams have correlated noise, so one odd stream can drag its kin. Uses include monitoring and security in cyber-physical systems. The task is a form of combinatorial pure exploration. Each stream acts like an arm to test. Measures must be spent in sequence under doubt.

Smart spending finds the anomaly with fewer checks. Correlation can help or mislead that hunt. The authors frame active tests that learn as they go. Faster finds mean faster response to faults or attacks. The work fits plants, grids, and sensor nets. It treats search cost as part of the problem.
arxiv-2601-17530:
Gautam Siddharth Kashyap and co-authors present ConLLM for spotting multi-modal deepfakes. Deepfake tools now fake video, audio, and text at once.
