Fakes threaten trust in news, courts, and daily talk. Single-mode detectors miss cross-mode clues. The authors aim at fakes that span modes. Their system uses a language model at its core, as the name ConLLM states.

Cross-mode checks can catch what one stream hides. A voice may not match lip work or text tone. Tools that fuse those signs raise the bar for fakes. The work serves platforms and newsrooms that vet media fast. It adds to a growing shield against synthetic fraud.
arxiv-2601-17730:
Ting-Yan Li, Zi-Yue Bai, and Xiang Liu study a hard corner of particle physics in this 2026 preprint. They look at how high-spin mesons form when a pion hits a proton. The mesons in question are the omega and rho families with spin values of three, four, and five. States with such high spin are rare and hard to pin down.

The team uses an effective Lagrangian method to work out how these mesons are made. That method turns the forces between particles into terms that can be solved step by step. The study covers each spin value in turn, so the states can be compared side by side. Work like this gives experimenters a clearer guide for searches at hadron facilities.
arxiv-2601-17830:
Mengmeng Wang and co-authors work on making diffusion models cheaper to train. Their 2026 preprint presents VAE-REPA, a method for diffusion transformers. These models build images by clearing noise step by step, and they perform well. Their training, though, converges slowly. Past fixes lean on outside encoders or on running two models at once, and both add heavy cost.

VAE-REPA instead aligns the model's inner features with those of a variational autoencoder. That gives the training a guide that is already inside a light setup. The aim is faster convergence without the extra weight of external parts. Cheaper training matters as these models grow in size and use.
arxiv-2601-17930:
Antonio Falcó, Daniela Falcó-Pomares, and Hermann G. Matthies give a strict, self-contained proof of a key quantum method. Their 2026 preprint covers the Grover-Rudolph state preparation algorithm. Many quantum methods need a state whose heights encode a known probability list. Loading such a state is a basic first step for tasks like amplitude estimation. The Grover-Rudolph method builds that state step by step from the list.

A proof that stands alone, with each step checked, serves students and builders alike. It also guards against hidden gaps in a much-used method. The authors lay out the full argument in one place. Readers can verify the method without chasing other sources. That kind of care keeps core tools sound.
arxiv-2601-18030:
Markus N. Rabe, Judith Clymo, and Zheren Dong give language models a sense of spelling. Their 2026 preprint changes the embedding layer, the part that turns tokens into numbers. The change feeds each token's letters into its embedding. Models trained this way do better not only on spelling tasks but across standard tests as well. The team runs scaling studies with models from forty million to eight hundred million parameters.

Spelling is usually invisible to a model that sees only whole tokens. That blindness hurts on names, rare words, and typos. Letter-aware embeddings attack the problem at the root. The gains across broad tests suggest the fix helps general skill, not just spelling bees.
arxiv-2601-18530:
Aliasghar Sarizadeh studies how a set of maps acts when it is run again and again on a tight space. Each map in the set is a two-way move that keeps the shape of the space whole. Run as a group, the maps build a kind of cloud of forms. A twin set, built from the back moves, runs the cloud in reverse.

The work asks when the group act stays smooth as the start point shifts a bit. It also asks how keen that act is to small shifts in the maps them-selves. Smooth acts are a base for the maths of fractals, where clouds of forms grow from plain maps. Keen acts can break a fractal with a breath. Proofs here help sort which map sets give calm clouds and which give wild ones.
arxiv-2601-18630:
Abeer Badawi and eight colleagues grade how well language models help with health of the mind. More people seek help than there are trained staff to give it. That gap makes smart chat tools a tempting path to help at scale. A chat tool can be warm and quick, yet warmth is not the same as good care. Its words must be safe, apt, and in line with what trained staff would prize.

The team grade chats on more than one trait at once, with human judges. Traits can pull in unlike ways: a warm reply may still be unsafe. A score per trait shows where a tool is strong and where it is frail. Such grades could help clinics pick tools with care. They could also set a bar that tools must clear before they meet the public.
arxiv-2601-18730:
Henry Bell and five colleagues build a way to teach language models a set of writ rules in the open, with the chain of thought on show. In the main path, rules are taught by score-based training that hides why a reply counts as good. Staff who must trust the tool can't see which rule drove a call. That gap counts when the rules touch fair play and harm.

Their tool, named Reflect, has the model state the rule it uses as it works. The chain can then be read, checked, and fixed by staff. A tool that shows its rules could be held to them in a real way. It could also serve at scale, since the check is part of the run, not a next step. The work aims at trust by sight, not by faith.
arxiv-2601-18930:
Seiji Shaw and three co-authors teach agents to learn worlds they cannot fully see. In such worlds, called POMDPs, the true state stays hidden and the agent sees only partial clues. Their test cases include things like locking mechanisms, where the inner state is not shown.

The agent starts out knowing what acts it can take and what it might observe. It does not know the states, how they change, or how clues link to states. Learning past those limits would let robots and software cope with hidden machinery in the real world, not just in clean lab setups.
arxiv-2601-19030:
Philip Amortila, Audrey Huang, Akshay Krishnamurthy, and Nan Jiang unify a key idea in judging policies from logged data. Off-policy evaluation asks how well a new rule would do, using data logged under an old one. In the linear case, error bounds hinge on a coverage number that says how well the old data covers the new rule's path.

Many past bounds each define coverage in their own way. The team gives one view that ties them together. A single lens on coverage helps researchers compare results and spot which assumptions truly drive the error in such studies.
arxiv-2601-19130:
Zexu Pan and four co-authors pull one voice from a crowd using hands as well as lips. Most tools that isolate a target speaker lean on lip motion synced to the speech. But people also gesture as they talk, and those gestures line up with stressed words and beats.

Adding gesture cues gives the system a second clock to lock onto. That should help when lips are hidden, blurred, or turned away from the camera. Cleaner single voice tracks serve hearing aids, meeting tools, and any setting where many people talk at once.
arxiv-2601-19230:
Dimitrios M. Thilikos and Sebastian Wiederrecht study what happens when a graph is banned from containing a whole surface's pattern. The great Graph Minors Structure Theorem covers graphs that avoid a fixed minor. Such a graph splits into pieces that almost lie on a surface. That surface is one where the banned graph cannot sit.

Their work refines that picture by excluding surfaces themselves as minors. Structure theorems of this kind are the backbone of graph theory: they turn a ban into a blueprint. Algorithms often ride on such blueprints, since a graph with known structure is far easier to search and color.
arxiv-2601-19530:
Ettore Budassi and eight colleagues refine a measurement tool used at electron-positron colliders. The tool is called radiative return. Instead of scanning many beam energies, physicists run at one energy and use radiated photons to sample lower ones. The target is the pion form factor, a function that describes how pions respond to electric charge.

That function feeds into a key calculation: the hadronic part of the muon's anomalous magnetic moment. Small errors there matter, since the muon value is a sharp test of known physics. The authors bring the radiative return method to a high accuracy standard that mixes fixed-order results with resummation. Sharper inputs mean a cleaner verdict on whether the muon hides new physics.
arxiv-2601-19630:
Matías G. Delgadino and Scott A. Smith study a classic model from statistical physics. The O(N) linear sigma model describes fields with N components and a symmetry between them. They place the model on a two-dimensional plane and scale it following the large N expansion. In that limit, many quantities become computable.

The authors show that correlations in the model decay exponentially fast. The model also acquires a mass, a gap that controls how far influences reach. That mass itself decays exponentially as the temperature parameter varies. Proving mass generation in such models is a long-standing goal in mathematical physics. The result adds a rigorous case to a field built on formal arguments.
arxiv-2601-19730:
Hongxu Chen, Ke Wei, Xiaoming Yuan, and Luo Luo study how machine learning models train under messy noise. In practice the random noise in gradient estimates has heavy tails, meaning extreme values occur often. That picture fits real training better than the usual bounded-noise assumption. Most theory under heavy tails covers how fast training converges.

Far less is known about generalisation: how well the trained model does on new data. The authors analyse stability and generalisation bounds for nonconvex optimization with heavy-tailed noise. Nonconvex problems are the norm in deep learning. Bounds like these explain when training will transfer to unseen examples. The work closes a gap between optimisation theory and learning practice.
arxiv-2601-20130:
Haoxuan Wang and five colleagues work on making robots act in real time. A robot that pauses to think can react too late, since the world keeps moving while it plans. Recent systems use asynchronous inference: the next chunk of actions is predicted while the current chunk still runs.

The authors present a method based on masked action chunking for this setting. The aim is smooth control with no gaps between what the robot does now and what it plans next. Fast, steady action matters for robots that handle objects or move through changing spaces, where even small delays can spoil performance.
arxiv-2601-20230:
Haoyuan Yu, Yuxuan Chen, and Minjie Cai present a framework for full-duplex voice dialogue, where a system listens and speaks at the same time. Natural conversation needs this overlap; turn-taking systems feel slow by contrast. The authors break dialogue into minimal conversational units, so each unit can be processed on its own.

Their system predicts when to move from one unit to the next. It is built around a multimodal large language model, with voice activity detection and speech synthesis as supporting parts. The setup works without task training, in a plug-and-play manner. Smoother voice dialogue would help assistants feel more like talking with a person.
arxiv-2601-20330:
Zhuang Chen and six colleagues present PsychePass, a way to judge how well large language models do therapeutic work. Models show promise in mental health care, but judging their skill is hard because counseling is unstructured and unfolds over long sessions. The authors say current evaluation has an unanchored defect.

That defect shows up as process drift, where a simulated client wanders off the counseling goal, and standard drift, where fixed scoring stays unstable. PsychePass anchors evaluation in trajectories and compares models in tournaments. Steadier measures matter before any model is trusted near real patients.
arxiv-2601-20630:
Wen-Tao Lyu and Eulogio Oset propose a reaction to search for a predicted exotic particle. It is a pentaquark-like state with strangeness, near a mass the authors give in energy units. The state is expected at lower mass than comparisons with known pentaquark states would suggest. The authors argue that coupled channels play an important role in setting that mass.

They propose a specific decay of the lambda-b baryon into a phi meson, an eta-c meson, and a lambda baryon. Giving experimenters a concrete channel to measure is how predicted states get found, or ruled out.
arxiv-2601-20830:
Waldyn Martinez builds a detector for odd points in messy process data. The 2026 paper presents VSCOUT, a hybrid method based on a variational autoencoder. Modern plants and services produce data that defy classic control charts. The data are high-dimensional, skewed, and prone to contamination. Heavy tails and multiple modes break the assumptions of classical statistical process control.

The setting is retrospective monitoring: looking back over past data. Rare special-cause points can warp the baseline itself. That warp can mask true anomalies and hide them in plain sight. VSCOUT aims to find a clean in-control reference set despite the mess. A sound reference set is the base for all later alarms. The method serves industries that must spot real faults in noisy records.
arxiv-2601-20930:
Emilie Burnham and a large team model how galaxies built their stars over time. Their 2026 paper gives a forward model for star formation histories. It targets galaxy groups seen in the early universe. JWST shows such galaxies with a wide range of brightness and color. The question is whether their star formation ran smooth or in bursts. The title warns the answer is more complex than it looks.

A forward model starts from a proposed history and predicts what telescopes would see. Matching those predictions to data tests the history. Bursty growth leaves traces that steady growth does not. The model infers the recent history of whole groups, not single galaxies. That shapes how we read the JWST census. It helps decide if early galaxies were calm builders or flickering ones.
arxiv-2601-21330:
Avijit Mandal and Henry D. Pfister extend a quantum message-passing method for reading signals sent as quantum states. The method offers a cheaper option than measuring all signals jointly. Until now, its design and analysis covered only binary alphabets, where each signal is one of two states.

The authors generalize it to alphabets with many symbols. They focus on symmetric channels whose output structure has a tidy circular form. That form lets the analysis tools carry over to the larger alphabet. Cheaper decoding for richer alphabets matters for future quantum links, where each signal should carry more than a single bit.
arxiv-2601-21530:
S. Simón-Díaz reviews how large spectroscopic surveys have reshaped the study of massive stars. These surveys gather spectra, the fingerprints of starlight, for huge numbers of heavy stars. Spectra reveal a star's heat, makeup, spin, and motion.

The review lays out the main surveys and what their data have shown. Several familiar readings of the signals turn out to be far more tangled than once thought. Massive stars drive the life cycle of galaxies, forging elements and ending as supernovae. Sharper readings of their spectra feed better models of how they live and die.
arxiv-2601-21630:
Metha Prathaban, Charlie Hoy, and Michael J. Williams speed up the analysis of gravitational wave signals. Full Bayesian analysis of a wave event is rigorous but very costly. Fast methods exist, yet their results are rarely used to guide the full analysis.

The authors present a way to reuse the fast estimates inside the final inference. Their repartitioning keeps the prior independent of the data, so the statistics stay rigorous. That balance gives speed without cooking the books. Faster final answers matter when telescopes must chase a fading source within hours of a detection.
arxiv-2601-21930:
G. Théret, D. Sugny, and C. Latune compare ways of counting entropy production in small quantum systems. Entropy production measures how irreversible a process is. For two-level systems open to an environment, the literature offers several definitions, born from different settings and motives, and they do not always agree.

The authors set those definitions side by side and analyze how each relates to memory effects, where the environment feeds information back into the system. They use a concrete example: a qubit coupled to a single bosonic mode acting as a finite environment. Their 2026 preprint helps physicists choose the right entropy measure for quantum thermodynamics experiments, where sloppy definitions can flip conclusions.
arxiv-2601-22030:
Chengyi Cai and co-authors refine a popular trick for making language models forget private information. Task arithmetic unlearns by computing a task vector, the change in parameters caused by tuning on the private data, and subtracting it from the model. The method is fast and simple.

Its flaw is over-forgetting: one blanket subtraction can damage parameters that other knowledge depends on. The team's 2026 preprint proposes per-parameter task arithmetic, scaling the subtraction parameter by parameter. Surgical forgetting matters because privacy requests, from personal data to copyrighted text, increasingly require removal that does not lobotomize the model. Finer control could make unlearning a routine operation rather than an emergency procedure.
arxiv-2601-22130:
Lakshya Gupta and co-authors build a proving ground for language model agents inside enterprise software. Frontier models excel as autonomous agents in many domains. They remain untested, though, in complex business systems where hidden workflows trigger cascading effects across interconnected databases.

Their 2026 preprint introduces World of Workflows, a benchmark that brings world models to enterprise systems. An agent must predict how an action in one system ripples into others, much as an employee learns that one form updates five records. Enterprise automation is where agent failures get expensive and quiet, so a benchmark that exposes hidden dependencies could prevent costly surprises in deployment.
arxiv-2601-22230:
Peijia Qin and co-authors improve the judges that pick the best generated code. Test-time scaling for code generation often samples many candidate solutions and lets a language model judge select the best. Training a reliable judge is hard because the candidates shift in distribution, with severe imbalances between good and bad samples.

Their 2026 preprint presents DaJ, a data-reweighted language model judge for test-time scaling in code generation. Reweighting the training data counters those imbalances, so the judge learns to spot the faults that actually appear at test time. A better judge multiplies the value of every extra sample, making test-time scaling cheaper for coding assistants.
arxiv-2601-22430:
Rudrajit Choudhuri, Christopher Sanchez, Margaret Burnett, and Anita Sarma ask what daily AI use does to how students think. Their 2026 preprint notes that many students now use generative AI in coursework. Past work looked at one-off help-seeking; this work asks about habit-level shifts.

The team study whether routine use ties to weaker cognitive engagement, the deep work of thought itself. The stakes are high: habits formed in school can last for years. Clear evidence can guide teachers, not just ban or bless the tools. The work frames the right questions. It seeks facts over fear.
arxiv-2601-22530:
Tung Sum Thomas Kwok and five co-authors train table-question agents with rewards for each checkable step. TableQA asks a model to answer from a table, but the answer needs a chain of changes to the table state. Their 2026 preprint notes that this chain, not a static read, is the hard part.

Rewards tied to each table change give the agent true feedback as it works. That should cut wild leaps that land on a lucky answer. It should also yield a trace a human can audit. The work aims at agents that do data chores with proof. Each step can be checked.
arxiv-2601-23030:
Gefan Yang, Frank van der Meulen, and Stefan Sommer infer hidden processes that evolve along trees. Observations may exist only at the leaves, as with species traits at the tips of an evolutionary tree. Exact smoothing for nonlinear dynamics is intractable, and particle methods weaken in high dimensions.

Their neural framework, NBFFG, guides sampling forward using a backward filtering pass learned by a network. It handles both jump transitions and smooth diffusions in one scheme. Better tree inference helps biology, epidemiology, and other fields with branching data. Sparse, leaf-only observations define the difficulty: everything between the root and the tips must be inferred, not seen.
arxiv-2601-23230:
Adrien Cogez and seven co-authors assess whether the space observatory LISA can detect gravitational-wave memory. Memory is a permanent deformation of spacetime left behind after a wave passes. It is a direct prediction of general relativity that has never been observed.

LISA, a future laser interferometer in space, may record signals strong enough to show the effect. Their Bayesian approach weighs how confidently memory could be claimed from noisy data. A detection would confirm a subtle, lasting fingerprint of gravity itself. A Bayesian treatment suits the question, since detection claims for memory must weigh signal evidence against instrument noise.
arxiv-2602-00530: Adam Mammoliti studies coline graphs, whose vertices are a graph's edges, joined exactly when those edges do not join originally. A graph is tough when cut sets leave at most as many components as the set's size. Mammoliti gives a new longest-cycle proof of Wu and Meng's and Liu's characterisations of Hamiltonian coline graphs. He proves a tough coline graph is Hamiltonian unless the graph is one of four examples, including K5, whose coline graph is the Petersen graph. He characterises tough coline graphs with a Hamiltonian path.
arxiv-2602-00930: David Gao and colleagues show handle constructions are always full, without using Property (T) phenomena needed in all earlier works. They plainly compute the bimodule shape for von Neumann algebra inclusions in handle constructions, built as inductive limits of stacked amalgamated free products. Their computation uses fine normal form decompositions for amalgamated free products built in steps. Their bimodule machinery works for any von Neumann algebras with faithful normal states, yielding full III_1 factors via handles.
arxiv-2602-01230: Masayuki Nagai and co-authors probe how to make DNA-to-function models both readable and travel-ready in regulatory genomics. Such models read DNA letters and predict regulatory readouts, used for variant calls, mechanism reads, and sequence design. Though they score high on held-out genome chunks, they travel unevenly across variants and cell contexts. The team pulls together how build, train data, and job shape conduct, and why high scores can hide weak grasp. They urge self-bettering loops of probe tests, fair checks, and updates.
arxiv-2602-01330: Mei Ian Sam and Tai-Yu Li build a scalable tensor-net frame for a quantum-classical dual kernel, easing costs as qubits grow. The frame runs a linearly mixed dual kernel up to 784 qubits, with one qubit per trait. On Fashion-MNIST, the dual kernel beat both single-kernel baselines across trait counts from 2 to 784. It held steady as traits grew and dodged the large-scale fade seen in the pure quantum kernel. Learned mix weights show quantum gains ruling below 128 traits, classical gains mattering more past that mark.
arxiv-2602-01530: Parsa Esmaeilkhani and Longin Jan Latecki study vision-language models losing visual-token patch ties. Autoregressive models answer fluently while visual tokens drift from regions, limiting explainability. Logit Lens maps project visual-token embeddings through the vocabulary head, measuring each patch's link to queried concepts. They introduce Logit Lens Loss, a lightweight objective aligning tokens with vocabulary concepts for their regions. It needs no architectural change or retraining. On LLaVA-v1.5-7B and a Qwen VL model, maps sharpen, grounding and hallucination improve, zero-shot pointing transfers, and VQA holds.
arxiv-2602-01630: Bohan Zeng and colleagues argue that world model research should stop at tricks and adopt one unified design. Current work injects world knowledge into visual prediction, 3D estimation or symbol grounding, gaining performance without a definition or framework. The authors analyze those limits and propose a unified design specification. A robust world model is a framework joining interaction, perception, symbolic reasoning and spatial representation, not a bundle of skills. That view aims to steer work toward models of the world that are more general, robust and principled.
arxiv-2602-01830: Cheng Cheng and colleagues test the 3+1 laws in Teleparallel Equivalent of General Relativity for hyperbolicity, using the Hamilton VAST split. At the level in 1D, one sector of the principal symbol carries imaginary eigenvalues, so the system is not hyperbolic. The sectors form a lone set removable by gauge fixing, and the rest is strongly hyperbolic. They present the 3D system, the first use of Hamilton's equations in TEGR, usable for spherical symmetry and numerical relativity setups. That opens a path to computer runs in this gravity theory.
arxiv-2602-01930: Felix Igelbrink and colleagues build LIEREx, joining vision language models with scene graphs for target directed robot exploration. Semantic maps let robots reason about surroundings to navigate, find objects and explore unmapped areas, but traditional maps use geometry and fixed vocabularies. Fixed object classes fail on knowledge not defined at design time, limiting robots to known categories. Vision language models like CLIP encode objects as embeddings rather than fixed labels, enabling open mapping. LIEREx integrates these models with established scene graphs so an agent can explore unknown environments toward targets.
arxiv-2602-02130: Lukas Zimmermann and colleagues study how flawed alignment warps scans made by machines that turn cone beam X-ray views into CT-like images. Perfect matching of scans taken apart can never be reached, so flaws seep into trained models and skew scores. They build pairs with a physics based simulation that lines views up by design, judging results by how well shapes line up with the input scan. On two pelvic data sets, models trained this way matched shapes better, and readers picked their outputs in most cases.
arxiv-2602-02230: Ziyu Zhou and others present SEDformer, a spiking transformer for forecasting irregular telemetry time series from large-scale connected systems. Such series show a sparsity-event duality: long sparse stretches punctuated by short dense bursts where most notes occur. Existing forecasters ignore this structure, either padding sequences onto uniform grids, or recasting relations in ways that disrupt local continuity. SEDformer couples an event-aligned spike encoder, an event-keeping downsampling module, and spike transformer blocks with membrane-based linear focus, reaching leading score with lower energy and memory.
arxiv-2602-02330:
Konstantinos Horaites and 12 co-authors study how magnetic events at Earth's edge affect electric fields on the ground in a 2026 arXiv paper. Flux transfer events happen when magnetic field lines at the magnetopause, the boundary of Earth's magnetic bubble, briefly connect and form twisted ropes of field. The team uses Vlasiator, a global computer simulation recently extended to include the ionosphere.

Inside the simulation, special points where the magnetic field vanishes can split one event into several flux ropes. Currents flowing along field lines toward Earth line up with passing events. Near the footpoints, rotating electric field patterns form around noon and drift toward the night side. Such fields matter because they can drive currents in power grids.
arxiv-2602-02530:
Saurav Singh and 3 co-authors automate two of the hardest design choices in reinforcement learning for human-robot teams, in a 2026 arXiv paper. A learning system needs a state representation and a reward function, and both are usually hand-crafted through costly trial and error with live interaction. Safety-critical settings make that interaction expensive or impractical.

Their framework uses off-policy evaluation, which estimates a policy's quality from logged data alone, to select both choices. Candidate state spaces and reward functions each train offline agents, and evaluation scores estimate which combination yields the best policies. No real-time environment access or human-in-the-loop feedback is required. Validation covers the Lunar Lander simulator and a NASA human-subjects teaming environment. The method aims to make offline reinforcement learning formulation systematic, repeatable, and cheaper to deploy.
arxiv-2602-02730:
Fam Shihata and 2 co-authors rebuild autonomous racing software as interchangeable layers, in their 2026 paper on the AROLA design. Scaled racing platforms have moved fast, leaving tangled, monolithic codebases behind. AROLA splits the driving workflow into sensing, preprocessing, perception, localization and mapping, planning, behavior, control, and actuation.

Standard ROS 2 interfaces connect the layers, so modules can be swapped rapidly and benchmarked fairly without custom message definitions. A paired Race Monitor logs lap timing, path quality, and compute load in real time, then generates standard post-race analyses. Testing ran in simulation and on RoboRacer hardware, including deployment at a 2025 competition. The authors argue modularity, clear interfaces, and steady testing jointly speed development and repeatable results in scaled autonomous racing research.
arxiv-2602-02830:
Sourajit Das and 2 co-authors present SC3D in a 2026 paper on finding causes in time series data. A time series records values that change over time. Causes can act after a delay, or at the same moment, which makes the search very large.

SC3D works in two stages. First it preselects likely links between variables. Then it refines those links while enforcing that instant links form no cycles. Tests on synthetic systems, chaotic benchmarks, changing dynamics, and real datasets follow. The authors report steadier and more accurate recovery of both delayed and instant causal links than earlier methods.
arxiv-2602-03030:
A distant dusty galaxy gets a corrected distance in a 2026 paper by Mengyuan Xiao and 23 co-authors. The galaxy, called S1, had seemed exceptionally efficient at turning gas into stars. That claim rested on a redshift from slitless grism data, a method that spreads light without a slit and can suffer contamination.

New observations with JWST and the ALMA telescope tell a different story. Multiple emission lines give a secure, much lower redshift. The earlier value came from a nearby galaxy whose spectral trace overlaps S1. Updated modeling shows S1 is still very massive and heavily obscured. Its star formation is moderate, however, resembling typical massive galaxies more than extreme ones.
arxiv-2602-03230:
Event cameras need leaner language models, and Shaoyu Liu heads a team of 6 others tackling that efficiency problem. Event-based vision records changes rather than full frames, suiting high-speed and low-light perception. Current event-based multimodal models process data densely like ordinary images, ignoring the spatiotemporal sparsity of event streams and paying high computational cost for mostly empty information across time and space.

Their model, EventFlash, sparsifies tokens in time and space. A large, scene-diverse dataset with over half a million instruction sets supports curriculum training. An adaptive temporal window module compresses temporal tokens while keeping key cues. A density-guided attention module selects informative regions and suppresses empty ones. Throughput improved more than twelve-fold over the baseline at comparable performance, with far longer stream support.
arxiv-2602-03330:
Philip Kennerberg's solo analysis finds an extremal principle for reconstruction under covariance domination. A residual norm measures how well a reconstruction fits a signal, in mean-square terms. In centered cases those norms reduce to trace forms with covariance operators. The non-centered case is harder. Mixed terms appear that covariance order alone cannot recover. That shift is the source of the extra terms.

Kennerberg shows the worst-case squared residual norm over such an envelope is attained at one canonical representative. That representative may lie only in the closure of the admissible class. The identity holds uniformly over all admissible operators. It needs no convexity, compactness, or global Hilbert space structure. The minimax problem then reduces to checking that single representative. So one case stands in for the whole class.
arxiv-2602-03430:
A proactive agent does not wait for orders; it watches the environment and decides when to step in. Xiaomeng Zhu and 10 co-authors support that research direction with ProAct-75, a benchmark described in their 2026 paper. It covers 75 tasks in assistance, maintenance, and safety monitoring, with step-level annotations and explicit task graphs.

The graphs record which steps depend on each other and which can run in parallel, giving agents structural grounding. On top of the bench, the authors build ProAct-Helper, a multimodal model baseline that detects state and searches over the graph for actions. It beats strong closed-source models on trigger detection and runs more parallel actions than human-style step following.
arxiv-2602-03830:
Jiaping Lu studies how many generators iterated wreath products need, in a 2026 paper on group generation. He starts from a sequence of almost simple groups and builds wreath products step by step. Each new group wreaths the previous product, acting through its regular action. The question is the minimum number of generators of each product in the tower.

Lu determines that minimum exactly for every stage of the construction. Generation numbers matter because they measure how economically a group can be presented and controlled. Wreath products are a standard way to assemble complicated groups from simple ones. Iterated wreath products over almost simple groups form a rich test family. An exact formula here closes the question for the whole tower at once.
arxiv-2602-04030:
Text in the wild is often broken, tilted, or half-hidden. Leeje Jang and 3 co-authors built TiCLS, a scene text spotter that reads with linguistic help. Their 2026 system tightly couples detection and recognition with a character-level pretrained language model.

A linguistic decoder fuses visual features with language knowledge and can start from the pretrained model's weights. Ambiguous fragments get resolved by what characters plausibly follow. On ICDAR 2015 and Total-Text benchmarks, TiCLS reached state-of-the-art results. The lesson generalizes: perception systems read better when they know the language they are looking at.
arxiv-2602-04130:
Game crowds need paths that are fast to compute and pleasant to watch. Tiroshan Madushanka and 1 co-author present a multi-threaded pathfinding framework in a 2026 paper. Standard A* search on navigation meshes from the Recast library forms the core.

Bezier curves smooth the jagged search output into natural trajectories. Density analysis coordinates crowds so agents stop colliding. The system was evaluated across ten phases, from 2D mazes to multi-level dynamic worlds. It reportedly held high frame rates with a thousand simultaneous agents while keeping navigation collision-free. The work targets game studios needing believable crowds without hand-tuned movement.
arxiv-2602-04230:
You may not need the network map to measure a treatment's total effect. Albert Tan and 3 co-authors validate causal message passing against network-aware methods on real experiments in a 2026 paper. Spillovers between connected people usually make network data essential, yet such data are often missing or noisy.

Causal message passing instead exploits temporal structure in outcomes. On two large field experiments, its estimates matched a network-aware bipartite graph method in direction on every metric, and in significance on the primary one. The finding matters for platforms and policymakers who run experiments but cannot observe who influences whom.
arxiv-2602-04430:
Queries that mix database tables with language model judgment need an engine that budgets accuracy. Gabriele Sanmartino and 3 co-authors present Stretto, an execution engine for semantic data systems, in a 2026 paper. These operators can run in many ways, each trading speed against accuracy.

Unlike earlier systems, Stretto promises accuracy across the whole query plan, not per operator. Planning becomes constrained optimization: a gradient-based optimizer picks implementations and splits error budgets jointly. A KV-cache compression trick supplies a spectrum of execution strategies with controllable trade-offs. The design targets analysts querying structured and unstructured data together without uneven quality.
arxiv-2602-04630:
Tim Kunt and 5 co-authors map world science as both a graph and a text collection in a 2026 paper built on the Web of Science database. Publications link to each other through references and shared attributes, while their words carry meaning that newer embedding models can capture numerically.

The dataset covers tens of millions of scientific publications. Applying their embedding method, the authors reveal a self-structured landscape of texts, where fields and topics arrange themselves through language and links together. Established graph algorithms handle classification and prediction on the link side. The paper demonstrates that combining both views is practical at very large scale. It offers a resource for studying how research fields connect and evolve.
arxiv-2602-04730:
Christopher Amey, Bala Sundaram, and Andrew C. Poje analyze how stirring and diffusion compete in flows whose phase space mixes orderly and chaotic regions, in a 2026 paper. They work at very large Peclet number, where advection dominates diffusion.

Combining Fourier methods with symmetry reduction and iterative solvers, they computed about one hundred leading eigenpairs reliably. The slowest mode is diffusive and sits on the largest regular region. The broader spectrum is organized by local phase-space geometry. Chaotic regions mix exponentially and suppress correlations, while orderly regions host long-lived structures. Three mode families appear, including tunneling modes coupling separated regions. The authors argue that competing families govern finite-time behavior rather than any single mode.
arxiv-2602-04830:
Karina Kohl and Luigi Carro argue that software work must reinvent itself as AI makes code cheap, in a 2026 position paper. Automation is cutting the cost of writing code, while hardware and energy limits raise the cost of failures. The old focus on building and process no longer fits.

The authors propose remaking the field around three human strengths: stating intent, keeping control of system structure, and checking work in a systematic way. They name accountability collapse as a central risk when generated code outruns human judgment. The shift has deep effects on research aims, degree programs, and industry practice. The field becomes one centered on human judgment under automation rather than output volume.
arxiv-2602-05130:
Black hole thermodynamics usually treats pressure and volume loosely, borrowed from ordinary gas physics. Silvester Borsboom and Manus R Visser argue for a holographic definition in this 2026 theoretical physics paper, the published version running to 62 pages. Their starting point is a black hole enclosed by a finite boundary, where a quasi-local first law already holds a surface pressure tied to the boundary's area.

If a dual quantum theory lives on that boundary, the geometric pressure and volume become the dual system's own. For static, spherical black holes the authors work out when the system counts as extensive, the thermodynamic notion of scaling cleanly with size. Small flat-space black holes fail that test while large ones pass. The picture for anti-de Sitter black holes is similar, with an extra twist in how the energy splits. The paper supplies a careful base for finite-size black hole thermodynamics.
arxiv-2602-05330:
Panoramic cameras see everything at once, but labeled panoramic data for training scene understanding is scarce and warped by projection. Jingdong Zhang and 7 co-authors present MTPano in this 2026 computer vision paper, a multi-task foundation model for panoramic scenes trained without any panoramic labels. The trick is borrowing supervision from perspective images, where foundation models are already strong.

Each panorama is cut into perspective patches, labeled by off-the-shelf models, and reprojected to serve as patch-wise supervision, sidestepping the domain gap. Tasks are then split into those unchanged by rotation, like depth and segmentation, and those changed by it, like surface normals. A dual-branch network shares information between the groups while blocking conflicting gradients. Token mixers handle the equirectangular distortion. Across benchmarks, MTPano reached state-of-the-art multi-task results and stayed competitive with single-task panoramic specialists.
arxiv-2602-05630:
Verifiable rewards have sharpened language model reasoning, but Zepeng Zhai, Meilin Chen, and 4 co-authors find two flaws in how the leading GRPO method uses them. Positive examples get their gradients misassigned, while negative examples dominate the update, and together these skew learning. Their framework, called REAL, treats rewards as categorical labels instead of scalar weights, turning policy optimization into a classification problem.

Anchor logits are added to strengthen the learning signal. Analysis shows the new setup gives a monotonic, bounded weighting of gradients, which balances updates across sampled attempts. On math reasoning benchmarks, REAL trained more stably and beat GRPO and strong variants such as DAPO at two model sizes. Even a plain binary cross-entropy version stayed stable and ahead of one strong rival. The authors argue that rethinking what a reward is, not just how it is weighted, can fix subtle training pathologies.
arxiv-2602-05730:
Small and distant objects are the hardest for image detectors, and the misses matter most in safety critical uses like driving. Moussa Kassem Sbeyti and Nadja Klein ask why depth information helps, and whether it must be fused into the detector itself. Their answer is a framework called DepthPrior, which uses depth as prior knowledge during training and inference while leaving detector architectures untouched.

A theoretical analysis explains how depth drives systematic performance loss, and why depth informed supervision counteracts it. The framework weights and stratifies the training loss by depth, and adjusts confidence thresholds by depth at inference time. The only added cost is an initial depth estimation step. Across four benchmarks and two detectors, small object detection and recall improved clearly, with strong recovery of true detections at inference. No extra sensors or architecture changes are needed, and code is available.
arxiv-2602-05830:
Neural networks built only from Boolean operations promise nanosecond inference on cheap hardware, but learning compact and accurate ones is hard because their structure is discrete and combinatorial. Shengpu Wang, Yuhao Mao, Yani Zhang, and Martin Vechev attack the problem with three complementary ideas. The result is a learning method for Boolean networks aimed at resource constrained deployments.

First, a parameter free strategy learns effective connections. Second, a compact convolutional Boolean architecture exploits spatial locality with fewer operations than existing kernels. Third, an adaptive discretization procedure shrinks the accuracy loss when a relaxed network is converted into a discrete one. On standard vision benchmarks the method improved the accuracy efficiency frontier, reaching higher accuracy with far fewer Boolean operations. On dedicated hardware, their MNIST model hit high accuracy with single digit nanosecond latency and a much smaller circuit than the prior best.
arxiv-2602-05930:
Fake cites made by language models slipped into papers at a top AI meeting, and Samar Ansari lists how they were built to deceive. The study looks at one hundred made-up cites that showed in papers accepted at NeurIPS 2025, despite review by several expert researchers per paper. The fakes were spread across dozens of published papers.

A five group sorting puts the fakes by failure mode, led by total lies and partial rot of real traits. The key finding is that every single fake mixed several failure modes at once. Side traits, above all sense-truth and stolen IDs, layered onto lies to create a gloss of trust. That mixed build, the author argues, is why peer review missed them: each check is beaten by another layer. Most tainted papers held only one or two fakes, while a few held many.
arxiv-2602-06030:
Language-model multi-agent systems reason richly but cost too much to scale and drift out of step in time-aligned simulation. Kavana Venkatesh and three co-authors answer with PhysicsAgentABM, a physics-guided frame that moves inference up to clusters of behaviourally similar agents. Symbolic agents encode mechanistic transition rules, a multimodal neural model tracks time and interaction, and uncertainty-aware fusion yields calibrated cluster transitions.

Single agents then realise transitions stochastically under local limits, so population inference stays separate from individual noise. A clustering method called ANCHOR, driven by a language model, groups agents by cross-context behaviour and cuts language-model calls six to eight times. Tests across public health, finance, and social science show better event-time accuracy and calibration than mechanistic, neural, and language-model baselines. The frame makes large agent simulations both cheaper and better calibrated.
arxiv-2602-06730:
Siyi Wang, Zifan Wang, and Karl H. Johansson study predictions that change the behavior they predict. Once a model is deployed, people adapt to it, shifting the data distribution in ways that depend on the model itself. The paper builds a framework for this performative setting that stays robust when only limited data is available.

They place an uncertainty set around the observed data distribution, measured by Wasserstein distance, and train the model against the worst case inside it. The problem is recast as a tractable min-max task, and two iterative algorithms are given for reaching a stable point where retraining no longer moves the model. Both are shown to converge quickly under standard conditions, with bounds on how far the stable point sits from the true optimum. A credit scoring simulation illustrates the approach.
arxiv-2602-06830:
Soonbin Lee and seven co-authors make 3D Gaussian splatting models smaller without hurting how they look. Existing pruning methods rank Gaussians by importance scores, such as blending weights or sensitivity, but those scores are not tied to visual error, so the compactness-quality trade-off is often poor. GaussianPOP instead derives an error criterion directly from the rendering equation, measuring exactly how much each Gaussian contributes to the final image.

A fast algorithm computes that error in a single forward pass, which makes the method practical. It supports pruning during training as well as after training, with iterative re-measurement for stability. In experiments it consistently beat state-of-the-art pruning methods in both settings, achieving better rendering quality at the same model size, or smaller models at the same quality.
arxiv-2602-07030:
Young Jin Ahn and three co-authors treat baseball as a world a language model can simulate, pitch by pitch. Classic sabermetrics boils long histories into compact stats. Those stats serve valuation and hindsight, but they do not generate how a game unfolds. The team's world model casts each game as a long autoregressive event sequence. One model is pretrained without pause on over a decade of Major League Baseball tracking data, covering more than seven million pitch sequences and near three billion tokens.

In one frame it predicts many facets of game evolution. On regular-season data and on postseason games outside the training mix, it beat strong neural rivals. It got about 64 percent of next pitches right within a plate appearance, and 78 percent of batter swing choices. Language models, the work suggests, can serve as unified world models for sports.
arxiv-2602-07230:
Moving supplies to demands through a network usually allows splitting shipments across paths, but some cargo cannot be split.  Srinwanti Debgupta and two co-authors present the unsplittable transshipment problem on directed graphs with many sources and sinks, where each source-sink pair gets at most one path.

Their main result generalizes a classic 1999 theorem: any transshipment can be rounded to an unsplittable one while increasing flow on each arc by less than the largest demand.  Further results bound how many rounds are needed to satisfy all demands under capacity limits.  Network builders get both a theorem and methods for shipments that must travel whole.
arxiv-2602-07730:
In reinforcement learning, Laplacian vectors give a compact basis for describing rewards, but policies built only from that basis cannot express all. Siddarth Chandrasekar and Marlos C. Machado offer the Laplacian Keyboard, a layered method that goes beyond the linear span of those vectors.

It builds a library of behaviors from the eigenvectors that is guaranteed to contain the best policy for any reward inside the span. Then a meta-policy stitches those behaviors together on the fly. Theory bounds the error of the zero-shot approximation, and tests show gains over the plain zero-shot approach. The paper offers a sound way to reuse learned structure for new tasks without fresh training from scratch.
arxiv-2602-07830:
Time series data fill finance, medicine, and industry, but language-model thought for such tasks lags behind text thought for lack of good training data. Jiahui Zhou and eight co-authors present VeriTime, a method that tailors language models to time-series thought through data synthesis, scheduling, and reinforcement learning.

Their pipeline builds a text-and-series dataset with annotations that can be checked step by step. It orders training examples by a principled difficulty and task hierarchy, and trains with reinforcement learning suited to that data. The combination aims to make models reason reliably about trends, patterns, and forecasts rather than guess. Users working with sequential data gain a full-stack recipe, not just another benchmark.
arxiv-2602-07930:
Command-tuned language models follow commands well, but how they show commands inside remains murky. Irina Bigoulaeva and three co-authors trace command-specific codes through two post-training stages, guided fine-tuning and direct preference tuning, using causal tracing to see where commands live in the model.

They find command codes are fairly local and cleanly split, yet interact by cause in curved ways, a mix that questions the common linear-representation idea in model-reading research. A new finding method free of linear patching assumptions helps undo that interaction. The paper gives model-reading teams a sharper picture of command processing and a tool for studying it without assuming linearity.
arxiv-2602-08030:
Reasoning models improve by thinking longer, yet beyond a point extra thinking tokens can hurt, accumulating redundant steps with no way to discard them. Yilun Zheng and seven co-authors diagnose this as a malloc-only flaw and propose Free()LM, a model with an intrinsic self-forgetting ability.

A plug-and-play adapter called the Free-Module lets the model alternate between reasoning and cleaning modes, pruning useless context chunks to maintain a compact, noise-free state. Experiments across model scales from 8 billion to 685 billion parameters show consistent gains, averaging 3.3 percent over strong reasoning baselines, with a new state of the art on an IMO-style answer benchmark. Long-horizon reasoning benefits most, where clutter otherwise compounds.
arxiv-2602-08430:
Image matching models pair points across photos, but their training hides a key design choice. Qiang Wang revisits attention-based sparse matching across many local feature types and finds an overlooked setting that strongly affects the LightGlue model. His arXiv paper then asks whether detectors or descriptors drive performance gaps.

Detectors, not descriptors, turn out to be the main culprit in many comparisons. Wang proposes fine-tuning existing matchers on keypoints from a diverse detector set, yielding a universal, detector-agnostic model. As a zero-shot matcher for new detectors, it matches or beats models trained specially for those features. Readers get practical guidance for deploying matchers in the wild.
arxiv-2602-08630:
AI safety via debate pits two models against each other so a human judge can verify complex tasks, but how much must the judge actually read? Jonah Brown-Cohen and five co-authors introduce debate query complexity: the minimum bits a verifier must inspect to decide correctly. Their arXiv paper turns a question about oversight cost into precise complexity theory.

Surprisingly, the class debate can decide efficiently is exactly the class decidable with logarithmically many queries. Even very hard problems need only logarithmic checking, and functions depending on all inputs need at least that many. A circuit-size bound links debate complexity to central questions in circuit theory. Readers get a reassuring result: debate is remarkably cheap to oversee.
arxiv-2602-08730:
Adapting a trained model to a new domain without the original data is valuable for privacy, but fine-grained classes confuse the process. Shanshan Wang and six co-authors study asymmetric, shifting class confusion, where similar classes are misclassified unequally over time. Their arXiv paper proposes CLIP-Guided Alignment to model and mitigate that confusion explicitly.

Three parts do the work. One detects directional confusion pairs from source-model predictions on the target. Another builds confusion-aware text prompts with CLIP, such as a truck that looks like a bus, for context-sensitive pseudo-labeling. A third aligns confusion-guided feature banks by contrastive learning. Tests show consistent wins over leading source-free methods, especially on confusion-prone fine-grained tasks. Readers get a clear case for modeling confusion rather than ignoring it.
arxiv-2602-09130:
Shrinking large language models is key for use, but tests usually cover only pruning and number-shrinking on knowledge tests. Jonathan von Rad and two co-authors introduce UniComp, a unified test setup that also adds teacher-student teaching. It judges models on scores, trust, and speed together, across more than 40 data sets and seven shrinking ways.

Three patterns emerge. Factual recall survives shrinking while multi-step thinking, multi-language skill, and following orders degrade, a knowledge bias. Kept scores do not guarantee kept safety, fairness, or privacy. And task-specific tuning can improve pruned-model thinking by up to 50 percent. UniComp gives users a fuller, hardware-aware picture of what shrinking costs.
arxiv-2602-09230:
Weak-lensing cosmos work with the Roman Space Telescope will live or die by how well redshift doubts are modeled. Diogo H. F. de Souza and nine co-authors run a tuned main-part study of the full redshift-spread shape inside the Roman High Latitude Imaging Survey setup, CoCoA. It follows a method lately used in the Dark Energy Survey's sixth-year analysis.

Checking uses Cardinal simulations covering mixed Roman setups, rating bias on the cosmos numbers S-eight and Omega-matter. When fake data are not badly mistuned, mean-shift and main-part approaches agree. Under mild to strong mistuning, adding parts progressively removes bias, matching the nine-bin mean-shift model with fewer numbers.
arxiv-2602-09330:
Leonardo P. G. De Assis asks what quantum gravity may do to the Standard Model once its effects are written as a low-energy effective theory. Phenomenological models often add free parameters to mimic Planck-scale deformation, but gauge symmetry sharply limits which interaction structures are allowed. His single-author 2026 paper shows those limits acting as selection rules that admissible quantum gravity models must obey.

From non-Abelian Ward identities plus a covariant mapping of operators onto the dimension-six basis, an on-shell link emerges in the paper between terms describing motion and terms describing three-way interaction. As a test case, it examines the Levy-Helayel-Neto framework, a candidate effective picture of loop quantum gravity, and finds it meets the requirement only when its parameters satisfy one specific algebraic relation. The apparent freedom in writing the Hamiltonian, the author argues, is illusory once gauge structure is preserved.
arxiv-2602-09430:
Robot laboratories promise continuous autonomous experiments, but long tasks chain many atomic skills, and existing vision-language-action models stumble when skills are reordered or composed. The failure has a name: the skill-chaining gap, where one skill's ending robot state falls outside the next skill's valid starting states. Yiwen Pang and nine co-authors propose AtomBridge, a 2026 inference-time plugin that bridges those gaps without retraining.

AtomBridge attaches to a vision-language-action policy already fine-tuned on atomic tasks, leaving its weights fixed. Whenever one task gives way to the next, transitional actions are slipped in between them through reasoning about transitions by a language model together with generated code for robotic actions. Across simulated scientific manipulation sequences and a real experimental setting, the plugin improves execution continuity and per-step success. On eight-step composed tasks, full-sequence success rises by ten to twenty-five percent.
arxiv-2602-09530:
Zihang Liu and three co-authors present AutoSpec, a 2026 neural design that finds step-by-step spectral methods for large-scale linear algebra and tuning. Self-taught models adapt to input matrices using coarse spectral clues, such as eigenvalue guesses and leftover sizes, then predict recurrence numbers for a formula fitted to the task at hand.

Three parts drive the design. First, a design whose use pass runs short, runnable number steps. Second, fast training on small fake problems that transfers to large real matrices. Third, task-set goals enforcing the wanted fit or setup behavior across spectral shapes in the training set. Uses span matrix function fit, sparse linear solvers, and spectral sifting for eigenvalue tasks. On real matrices, learned methods improve quality or cut step counts by up to an order of magnitude, with links to classic Chebyshev theory.
arxiv-2602-09930:
Upgrading old Java code by hand is slow, repetitive work, and language models promise to speed it up. A 2026 paper led by Nishil Amin, with four co-authors, builds JMigBench, a test for moving functions from Java 8 to Java 11. An early collection of function pairs proved too noisy, so the team rebuilt the set around eight groups of deprecated interfaces.

The team tested Mistral Codestral with measures of wording, meaning, and migration correctness. The model handled simple one-to-one swaps with middling success, matching the reference migration in about one case in nine, but stumbled on harder cases such as CORBA or JAX-WS. The verdict is partial help: the model can trim routine effort, but it cannot yet replace a human on this benchmark.
arxiv-2602-10130:
Japan's shrinking, aging population squeezes public finances from both ends: fewer workers pay taxes while more retirees draw pensions and health care. A 2026 paper by Goshi Aoki builds and tunes an integrated system dynamics model linking demographics, labor supply, output, and public finance. The model tracks historical trends reasonably well and tests which policy combinations stabilize fiscal indicators.

Productivity gains and per-person cost control offer the strongest near-term relief, acting quickly through revenue and spending. Raising fertility, by contrast, worsens the medium-term picture, since newborns take decades to reach the workforce. A combined scenario of moderate productivity gains and moderate cost control nearly erases the deficit by mid-century.
arxiv-2602-10230:
Audio language models turn sound into rich frame-level forms. Yet temporal localization usually emits timestamps as text tokens, discarding those forms for slow, non-parallel decoding that hallucinates outside the training distribution. A 2026 paper led by Joseph An, with four co-authors, proposes internal frame-level reuse. It trains audio models to reuse their own inner forms for finding directly, bypassing token generation entirely.

A light prediction head is trained with two frame-level goals: a binary frame classifier and a new inhomogeneous Poisson process loss modeling temporal event intensity. Across word finding, speaker diarization, and event finding, the approach runs over fifty times faster than token-based generation and holds up across audio lengths where token models collapse. Finding accuracy matches or beats fine-tuned token baselines.
arxiv-2602-10530:
Xiucai Ding and two co-authors build a principled way to fuse multiple noisy data views in a 2026 paper. Multiview datasets are common in science and building, but current fusion methods offer weak promises when views carry heterogeneous, large noise. One view's noise can swamp another's signal.

Their system, GRAB-MDM, uses kernel-based spread shape with a bandwidth chosen per view, adapting to each view's shape and noise level. Under a common-surface model, the authors prove asymptotic settling. They also prove robust recovery of the shared intrinsic structure, even when noise levels and sensor sizes differ across views. Number tests support the theory, showing stable fusion where fixed-bandwidth methods falter.
arxiv-2602-10830:
Christian de Correc and two co-authors simulate large qubit registers with a phase-space method in a 2026 paper. The approach uses a number ensemble of independent mean-field paths, substituting older fluctuations for quantum ones at the qubit level. Cost grows at most quadratically with system size, allowing simulation of several thousand qubits on a older computer.

The method describes one-qubit observable evolutions qualitatively accurately, making it a useful reference against methods limited to small qubit numbers. Forward power weakens for multi-qubit observables, a limitation the authors state plainly. Benchmarks on the transverse-field Ising model across local to all-to-all contacts map where the approximation succeeds and where it strains.
arxiv-2602-11030:
Most black-hole population studies assume near-circular orbits, leaving eccentric cases aside. Muhammad Zeeshan and two co-authors run the first population fit that treats mass, spin, redshift, and eccentricity jointly. They use setting values for over one hundred fifty black-hole binaries from the GWTC-4 catalog.

Inferred population traits broadly match earlier circular-orbit results. Dropping the most eccentric event leaves the picture intact, and the authors bound the eccentric share at a low level under a mixture model. Across four eccentricity models, the eccentric rate stays weakly pinned down and highly model-sensitive. The paper thus opens eccentric populations to study while warning against over-reading their rate.
arxiv-2602-11130:
Tiny nudges to a point cloud can shatter a 3D rebuild. Maximilian Plattner and three co-authors study that failure, which they call Meltdown, in point-cloud-conditioned diffusion models. Small on-surface shifts fracture outputs into hundreds of disconnected pieces.

Adversarial search triggers Meltdown in nearly all shapes tested across two leading open-weight models and both common samplers. Tracing the forward pass, the authors blame how evenly points spread on the surface, carried through the encoder and locked in by one early cross-focus write. A test-time fix called PowerRemap reshapes that write's spectrum and rescues most cases. The study links a circuit event to a path-level failure.
arxiv-2602-11330:
Fair division asks each agent to receive close to a proportional share. Sushmita Gupta and three co-authors prove that partitions where every part pleases every agent hit a discrepancy barrier growing with the square root of agent count. Their goal is to beat that barrier with stronger individual guarantees in polynomial time.

They succeed by letting agents arrive in an agreed order and pick autonomously and rationally. Each agent then gains at least its proportional share minus a logarithmic term, an exponential improvement over the barrier. Better guarantees follow for three restricted valuation classes: near-unanimous orderings, bounded value multiplicity, and bounded-influence hypergraphs. The work turns a barrier result into a practical sequential protocol.
arxiv-2602-11730:
Vision-language models often hallucinate when text must line up with visual coordinates. The problem sharpens in dense video grounding tasks that track objects across space and time. Xiaowen Zhang and four co-authors sidestep coordinate alignment with a visual prompting trick. Each object gets a unique identifier that stays consistent over time. That identifier is embedded in the video as a prompt, turning per-frame coordinate prediction into an instance identification problem.

Their framework, STVG-R1, is the first reinforcement learning approach for this video grounding task. It rewards temporal accuracy, spatial consistency, and structural format together. On six benchmarks it beats its baseline model by about 21 percent on a key overlap metric. That sets a new state of the art. It also generalizes without training to multi-object video segmentation, reaching a strong score that sets another best mark.
arxiv-2602-12130:
Inversion sequences encode permutations, and pattern dodging in them is a classical combinatorial theme. Benjamin Testart introduces minimal inversion lists for a pattern: the smallest set whose dodging is equivalent to dodging the pattern itself.

He characterizes these minimal lists exactly by the pattern occurrences they contain, then derives upper and lower bounds on their lengths. Full counting results follow through a bijection with increasing trees plus exhaustive generation, giving exact counts for some patterns. Finally, he counts lists equal to their own reduction and uncovers a connection with poly-Bernoulli numbers.
arxiv-2602-12530:
Item ranking systems must infer changing user tastes and rank items by intent, a task needing deeper thinking than pattern scoring alone. Kehan Zheng led this work with six co-authors, giving Reasoning to Rank, an end-to-end training frame that builds ranking utility tuning into step-by-step thinking in large language models. How to tune such models well for ranking utility was still new.

To avoid place bias and enable direct tuning of thinking, the frame reasons at user-item level and uses RL for end-to-end training. Tests on three Amazon data sets and a large factory data set show steady gains over strong old and language-model rivals. In-depth checks confirm the need for key parts and shed light on future ways for thinking-driven ranking.
arxiv-2602-12630:
Most large language models run on outside clouds, where users must trust that a remote GPU runs the model without hostile tampering. Oguzhan Baser led this work with seven co-authors, asking how to achieve checkable LLM inference. A prover must convince a checker that an inference ran correctly without rerunning the model. Old crypto works are too slow at LLM scale, while non-crypto ones require a strong checker GPU.

Their scheme, TensorCommitments, binds LLM inference to a tag, an irreversible mark that breaks under tampering, organised in multivariate Terkle Trees. For LLaMA2, TensorCommitments add only 0 point 97 percent prover time and 0 point 12 percent checker time over inference. They improve toughness to tailored LLM attacks by up to 48 percent over the best prior work requiring a checker GPU. Readers get a light, tensor-native proof of inference for cloud language models.
arxiv-2602-12730:
Proteins fold into shapes that drive life, and comparing their sequences has long been the way to trace evolution and function. But the best-scoring alignment can hide other stable shapes tucked into slightly worse alignments, and those hidden regions may carry unexplored biology. Andrei Preoteasa and three co-authors built EMERALD-UI, a free interactive web app that visualises those suboptimal alignment regions so researchers can inspect them directly.

The app reveals stable structural forms and protein regions that optimal-only methods tend to ignore, turning a usually invisible corner of alignment space into something biologists can explore by eye. It is open source and available online, aimed at anyone studying protein evolution or function. The goal is modest but practical: make hidden structural clues easy to find, rather than leaving them buried in alignment scores.
arxiv-2602-12930:
Interstellar objects are rare visitors, and only the third known, 3I/ATLAS, lets astronomers watch a foreign comet wake up. Gregory Paek and ten co-authors monitored it with the 7-Dimensional Telescope from July to September 2025, using medium-band images to separate gas from dust. In the 400-nanometre band, cyanogen emission emerged clearly once the object came within 3 astronomical units of the Sun.

Several signs agree on that onset: a break in the light curve, excess reflectance, coma growth from about 11,000 to 19,000 kilometres in half-light radius, and a fast rise in cyanogen production. Fitting inner dust and outer gas components shows the gas profile holding its shape while growing brighter, implying fast expansion. The shift from dust-dominated to gas-dominated light resembles 2I/Borisov, suggesting both active interstellar objects switch on near 2 to 3 astronomical units.
arxiv-2602-13030:
Smart textiles need gesture recognition, but power, compute, and size limits make standard deep learning impractical. Daniel Schwartz and five co-authors present a convexified focus workings for wearable e-textiles that weights traits while preserving convexity through simplex projection and convex losses. Unlike softmax focus, which is non-convex, their approach uses Euclidean projection onto the probability simplex with multi-class hinge loss, guaranteeing global convergence.

On a textile capacitive sensor with four connection points, the method hits 100% closeness on both tap and swipe gestures across cross-checks and held-out tests. It uses only 120 to 360 settings, a 97% cut from conventional approaches. Fitting takes under a millisecond with under 7 kilobytes of storage. The testing used one user in lab rules, so real deployment still needs multi-user, multi-setting checks, but feasibility for basic gestures is established.
arxiv-2602-13430:
Chest X-ray classification in clinics suffers from imperfect supervision: diseases follow a steep long tail, and rare or unseen findings lack labels. The CXR-LT 2026 challenge frames the problem on a PadChest-based benchmark with 36 classes, 30 for training and 6 held out for zero-shot testing. This paper offers task-specific answers for each regime.

For long-tailed multi-label classification, an imbalance-aware strategy lifts tail-class recognition while holding steady on common findings. For zero-shot recognition, a prediction method scores unseen disease categories without any supervised labels or examples from those classes in training. The method ranked first on the public development leaderboard. Ha-Hieu Pham leads the work with six co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13530:
People remember concrete episodes in time and place and reason across them. Language agents, by contrast, mostly store semantic facts and struggle to recollect and reason over their own interaction histories. REMem closes that gap with a two-phase design. Offline indexing turns experiences into a hybrid memory graph linking time-aware summaries and facts, and online inference uses an agentic retriever with curated tools to search that graph step by step.

Across four episodic memory benchmarks, REMem beat leading memory systems such as Mem0 and HippoRAG 2. It gained 3.4 percent on recollection and 13.4 percent on reasoning tasks in absolute terms. It also refused unanswerable questions more robustly, a sign of genuine memory rather than fluent guessing. Yiheng Shu leads the work with seven co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13730:
Quality-Diversity algorithms seek diverse, high-performing solutions across behavior niches, but search often stalls as gradual variation tools struggle to spread building blocks across large groups. Existing mutation tools rely on gradual variation, limiting search of regions distant from parent solutions and spread of helpful genetic material. This paper augments variation-based tools with discrete, gene-level crossover, allowing rapid mixing of elite genetic material.

The crossover mirrors the biological principle of meiosis, allowing direct transfer of genetic material and search of novel gene patterns beyond the existing elite space. Tests on three movement settings improved quality-diversity score, coverage, and maximum fitness, with notably strong late-stage results once building blocks were established in the archive. Joshua Hutchinson leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14330:
Khalil Harrabi and two co-authors build a 2026 arXiv artificial neuron from superconducting wirelets. Brain-like hardware seeks the energy thrift and flex of living smarts, and cold devices offer ultra-low loss with fast flips. A resistively shunted cold wirelet serves as a minimal neuron for time-based brain-like work.

The simple design allows plain fab, electronic control, and high scale-up. Tests and runs show spiking voltage motion from resistive flips and rest, with threshold, firing rate, and rest time tuned by current, heat, and shunt resistance. Synaptic training on time voltage signals shows net work, with trainable time weights acting on full time-based wirelet-neuron responses rather than static outputs alone.
arxiv-2602-14530:
Shi Chen and one co-author names a 2026 arXiv universal observable for the chiral anomaly in lattice Weyl fermions. The Adler-Bell-Jackiw anomaly keeps its Lorentz-safe form, with axial current split matching E dot B, in lattice Weyl systems past mid magnet fields, where neither Lorentz nor spin symmetry holds. Along and Hall magnet flows split into a shared anomaly part and a non-shared part tied to state density at the Fermi level.

A spin-safe seen mark kappa, equal to flow times (heat density over heat) squared, serves as a tough anomaly sign. It follows a shared B-squared trend and scales as absolute cos theta, where theta is the angle between E and B. Analytic proof and full number runs show kappa stays shared regardless of system knobs and field aim at fixed theta, with a new SO(3) symmetry.
arxiv-2602-14630:
Cosmic voids are vast low-density regions that carry clues about the universe. Leander Thiele notes that finding them from sparse galaxy maps is uncertain by nature. Standard finders give one fixed catalog and hide that uncertainty.

Thiele trains a graph neural network to sample from the mapping between galaxy catalogs and any chosen void definition. Test particles evolve under a flow-matching goal, and the trained model beats its teacher on cosmological signal. The method can mimic old finders cheaply or aim at the Bayes-optimal mapping. That includes definitions based on simulated matter and velocity fields.
arxiv-2602-14930:
Sebastian Golat and Francisco J. Rodriguez-Fortuno give a firm, quick plan for working out electromagnetic modes on a tube step-index nano-fibre, a task key to nano-light work from quantum links to vector light sense. Book plans solve a four-by-four grid eigen task, but finding field strengths then needs the null nook of a sick grid, a shaky step that spoils small yet key lengthwise field bits.

Their half-math plan starts from base mirror traits to dodge that flaw, giving modes with far less miss. Nano-fibre work thus gains a count it can trust in each field bit, not just the big ones.
arxiv-2602-15330:
Yang and Wang offer Curiosity-Driven Game-Theoretic Multi-Label Learning, a setup turning tail sorting into a multi-player game. The long-tail spread, where a few head labels rule while rare tail labels teem, brings a lasting hurdle for sorting in data digging. Current new-sample and re-scoring plans break inter-label links or need fragile setting tweaks.

Each sub-guesser, or player, works in a slice of the label space, teaming to raise scores while chasing prizes based on tail fewness and clashes. This setup feeds cues into under-shown tail labels without hand evening. The team shows their method settles to a tail-aware balance and strictly ties tuning motion to Rare-F1 gains. Tests across 7 benchmarks, datasets with 30,000 labels, show their method beats state-of-the-art methods, with wins up to about one and a half percent P at 3 on Wiki10-31K.
arxiv-2602-15430:
Zhao and Xia track Schrödinger cat state transfer in a quanta take of Newton's toy in a non-Markovian setting. Built on a non-Markovian main rule, they show that the cat state can be moved only through the recall impact of the non-Markovian shared setting. This works even without any plain links between nearby boxes.

The trick of the setting caused cat state transfer is studied by math and by numbers to show that the transfer is a one-off event in the non-Markovian mode. From this case, the non-Markovian setting is shown to be in kind from the memory-free setting shown by the set over nil rest linkage. They show the sway of setting knobs are key for the transfer. They bet the cat state transfer probed here may shed light on the deep gap between non-Markovian and memory-free settings.
arxiv-2602-15630:
Sharma and colleagues control polariton links in a polaritonic Luttinger liquid built on a superconducting circuit platform. Their system is a multi-connected Jaynes-Cummings lattice, a one-dimensional chain of mixed qubits and resonators with unequal left and right couplings. An engineered cross-Kerr coupling, put in place dispersively through ladder-type qutrits between neighbouring mode pairs, mimics attractive nearest-neighbour interaction.

Projecting onto the lower polariton branch yields an extended two-mode Bose-Hubbard-like model with on-site and neighbour interactions. Bosonisation then splits the system into symmetric and antisymmetric collective modes. When the antisymmetric sector gains a gap, the system reduces to a single-component liquid.
