The cross-Kerr term lowers compressibility of that mode, raises its Luttinger parameter, and slows the algebraic decay of single-particle correlations. The knobs here are the engineered couplings, which an experiment can tune.
arxiv-2602-15730:
Feldman and colleagues build an end-to-end pipeline for causal estimation when the treatment is text itself. Researchers who want to know how text shapes outcomes must run controlled tests. Those tests vary textual features step by step, but large language models alone do not guarantee controlled variation or sound evaluation. The pipeline first generates hypotheses and steers text with sparse autoencoders, then estimates effects robustly.

The work shows that naive estimation suffers large bias in this setting, since text inherently conflates treatment and background traits. The authors describe that bias and propose covariate residualisation as a fix. Tests show the pipeline induces variation in target features while cutting estimation error. That gives a robust foundation for text-as-treatment tests in which treatment and background traits travel together.
arxiv-2602-15830:
Roberts works alone on fair scores for ensemble forecasts. Fair scores reward members behaving like samples from the same spread as verifying observations. They are therefore attractive as loss functions to train data-driven group forecasts or clean-up methods when large training groups are unavailable or too costly.

Spread-aware clean-up methods that introduce structural dependency between members can violate that assumption, rendering aCRPS unfair. Roberts demonstrates that effect using two approaches designed to minimise expected aCRPS of a finite group. In both cases, results are sensitive to group size, and apparent gains in aCRPS can correspond to steady unreliability shown by over-dispersion. Applied to weekly mean temperature forecasts from the ECMWF subseasonal system, that approach reduces steady model biases. It improves or maintains forecast trust regardless of group size used in training or real-time forecasts.
arxiv-2602-16030:
Aditya Arabhavi leads a team of eleven researchers studying the light from disks where planets form. Their paper asks how the amounts of carbon and oxygen in the inner disk shape the mid-infrared spectra that telescopes record. Using the ProDiMo disk code and the FLiTs radiative transfer code, they built a grid of twenty-five models spanning a wide range of carbon-to-oxygen ratios.

The models show that spectra respond not only to the ratio but also to the absolute amounts of each element. Even with the same disk structure and ratio, some molecular fluxes shift by more than tenfold, driven by changes in excitation and in where emission arises. The authors single out flux ratios that can trace carbon and oxygen abundances, and they compare their grid with recent JWST looks at T Tauri disks.
arxiv-2602-16430:
Ali Faraz leads three coauthors designing production-scale recognition for India. Building such systems balances linguistic diversity, document variety, and deployment constraints. The paper studies two training strategies for multilingual recognition with vision-language models in the Chitrapathak series. One pairs a generic vision encoder with a strong multilingual model trained end-to-end. The other fine-tunes an existing recognition model not trained for the target languages.

Evaluation on Indic benchmarks and deployment metrics finds the second strategy gives better accuracy-latency trade-offs. Chitrapathak-2 runs three- to six-fold faster than its predecessor, with top Telugu results and second best elsewhere. The authors also present Parichay, an independent series for nine Indian government documents extracting structured key fields, reaching nearly ninety percent exact match. Together they reach state-of-the-art performance and offer guidance for production-scale recognition in India.
arxiv-2602-16530:
Sidharth Menon and Ameya Jagtap present Feature-Enriched Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks. These networks are prized for clear, piece-by-piece function structure. Older variants built from splines, wavelets, and radial bases cost too much compute. They also learn too slowly for large use. The new design adds enriched input features. It keeps the same count of trainable weights.

Tests cover function fitting and physics-informed problems for varied partial differential equations. Neural operator tasks are tested too. The enriched networks converge faster than the baselines tried. They also fit more accurately, including against FastKAN, WavKAN, ReLUKAN, and SplineKAN. Builders of scientific models get speed and accuracy gains without a larger model.
arxiv-2602-16930:
Farnaz Zamiri Zeraati and co-authors explore user control in conversational visual question answering with blind users. Prompting and steering techniques are well established in general-purpose generative AI, yet assistive visual question answering tools for blind users still follow rigid patterns. User control helps when system replies misalign with goals and contexts, a gap especially consequential for blind users who may rely on these systems for access.

Eleven blind users were invited to customize interactions with a real-world conversational visual question answering system. The authors analyze prompting techniques participants adopted. Exchanges often ran long, averaging three turns and sometimes reaching twenty-one, with input text typically tenfold shorter than replies heard. The system lacked verbosity controls, struggled estimating distance in space and time, relied on inaccessible image framing, and offered little camera guidance. Prompt engineering helped participants work around those limits, alongside a new public dataset.
arxiv-2602-17030:
Eric Chen and Patricia Alves-Oliveira present a patch-based framework for spatial authorship attribution in human-robot paintings. It is shown through a forensic case study of one human artist and one robotic system across fifteen paintings. As agentic AI joins creative work, noting authorship matters for artists, collectors, and lawyers.

Using cheap flatbed scanners and leave-one-painting-out cross-validation, the approach hits nearly eighty-nine percent patch-level accuracy and nearly eighty-seven percent painting-level accuracy by majority vote. It beats texture-based and ready-made feature baselines. For collaborative artworks with inherently ambiguous ground truth, conditional Shannon entropy measures style overlap. Hand-marked hybrid regions show sixty-four percent higher uncertainty than pure paintings, suggesting mixed authorship rather than classification failure. The trained model fits only that human-robot pair but gives methodological grounding for sample-efficient attribution in data-scarce human-AI work.
arxiv-2602-17330:
Rong Fu led a six-author team building SubQuad, a system for studying adaptive immune repertoires at population size. Two snags hamper such study: the near-square cost of pairwise affinity checks and dataset skew that hides key rare clones. SubQuad joins antigen-aware near-subsquare lookup with GPU-boosted scoring kernels, learned multi-way fusion, and fairness-limited grouping.

Compact MinHash pre-checks slash rival checks, a smooth gating module weights matching and vector channels per pair, and an auto tuning routine ensures fair-share presence of rare antigen-tied subgroups. On large viral and tumor sets, the system gained throughput and peak memory economy while keeping or lifting recall, cluster purity, and subgroup equity. The co-design offers a scalable, bias-aware platform for repertoire study, vaccine target ranking, and marker hunting.
arxiv-2602-17530:
Shahaf Bassan led a seven-author team behind a 2026 arXiv paper on explaining neural additive models. Most post-hoc explanation methods rest on heuristics and carry no guarantee. The strongest guarantee, a smallest feature set that alone fixes the prediction, is usually out of reach for standard networks. Finding that set can demand an exponential count of verification queries, each itself hard.

Neural additive models change the picture, since each input passes through its own small univariate part. The authors exploit that structure with a new algorithm that reaches a provably smallest explaining set using only a logarithmic count of verification queries. A parallel preprocessing step over each small part comes first. The method even beats existing algorithms that settle for a looser subset-minimal answer, despite solving the harder problem. Tests show smaller proven explanations and far less compute time than prior methods.
arxiv-2602-17730:
Kevin Maik Jablonka tests whether materials models learn chemistry or merely journal clues. Machine learning speeds materials discovery and scores well on many benchmarks, yet strong scores do not prove a model learned chemistry. The paper tests a concrete rival account: a mix-up driven by publication traits.

Across five tasks spanning metal-organic frameworks, perovskite solar cells, batteries and TADF emitters, models trained on standard chemical traits predict author, journal and publication year well above chance. When those predicted byline data serve as the sole input to a second model, scores sometimes rival standard trait-based models. Many data sets thus fail to rule out non-chemical accounts of success, so progress needs disproof tests, tougher data sets, and a clear split between forecast use and evidence of chemical understanding.
arxiv-2602-17830:
Marcos Tapia Costa and team study drift gauging for random change equations with known diffusion rate, from multiple paths read at high rate over a fixed time span. The target is the steady drift function. The paper recasts drift gauging as a cleaning problem given past readings.

The proposed drift gauge falls out of training a conditional diffusion model able to mimic new paths on the fly. Across drift classes, the gauge matches old methods with few inputs and stays strong with many inputs. Its gains cannot be chalked up to design choices alone. Readers gain a diffusion-based gauge that competes with classical tools while adding a generative model of the motion as a bonus.
arxiv-2602-17930:
Narjes Nourzad and Carlee Joe-Wong tackle a limit of reinforcement learning agents: in sparse or delayed reward settings, they need many samples because they lack prior structure. Large language models can supply subgoal breakdowns, plausible paths and abstract priors that speed early learning, yet heavy reliance on them strains scale and trusts shaky signals.

Their answer is MIRA, a memory-integrated reinforcement learning agent with limited language model guidance. A structured, evolving memory graph stores path segments and subgoal structures from high-return experiences and model outputs, spreading model queries into lasting memory rather than live supervision. A utility signal from that graph softly adjusts advantage estimation to steer policy updates without changing rewards. As training proceeds, the policy passes the initial priors and the utility term fades, keeping settling pledges. Tests show MIRA beats baselines and matches frequent-supervision methods with far fewer live model queries.
arxiv-2602-18030:
Emmanuel Deruty and team argue that electronic tones routine in contemporary popular music, including 808-style bass and power chords, match multiphonics in contemporary classical music both structurally and perceptually. Hearing tests with ten people and signal analysis back the claim. Both tone types elicit multiple pitch percepts that vary by person, arising from similar spectral and temporal cues.

The findings suggest pitch ambiguity is not limited to experimental contexts. It also marks mainstream music, where such tones carry the same multiplicity. The study thus bridges popular and classical music, showing that a quirk often treated as avant-garde also lives in mainstream music.
arxiv-2602-18730:
Touch interfaces usually need motors, rigid parts, or closed boxes, which limits how freely a physical token can move in the open. Yusuke Koroyasu, with two co-authors, presents PolygonWave in 2026, a solid-fluid acoustic interface that moves small tangible icons across liquid droplets with sound alone.

Lightweight Janus icons carry a water-repelling top for dry touch and a water-loving bottom that sits on a droplet over a mesh. A 256-element phased array focuses ultrasound into lateral forces that steer the icons and carry loads. The liquid layer itself acts as a springy button that recovers after pressing and gives vibration feedback. The result is a touchable interface with no mechanical contact.
arxiv-2602-19030:
Superradiant lasing with ultra-narrow width would sharpen atomic clocks for quantum precision measurement. Min Du, with four co-authors, demonstrates in theory in 2026 superradiant lasing with widths in the microhertz range, sustained at high power, by exploiting the EP feature of the system.

Incoherent pumping of optical lattice clock transitions with ultracold strontium-87 atoms in a parity-time-symmetric system at its EP drives the effect. Atomic coherence reaches a maximum at the EP, significantly amplifying superradiance and yielding ultra-narrow width lasing. That width is three orders of magnitude smaller than superradiant lasing without the EP. The work extends superradiant lasing by introducing the EP feature, offering good uses for atomic clocks with EP stability and accuracy.
arxiv-2602-19530:
Vision-language models do well on new tasks, yet their results hinge on the quality and shape of text models for classes. Omprakash Chakraborty and two co-authors introduce ORION, a fine-tuning framework for text encoders that lifts pretrained vision-language models using only class names. Standard zero-shot sorters from frozen text encoders and handcrafted prompts can yield linked or weakly set-apart vectors.

ORION tunes, via low-rank updates, a loss with two terms. One pushes class vectors for a task toward right angles to each other, and one punishes drift from starting class models. A stats reading links the right-angle penalty to maximum likelihood fitting through Huygens' theorem. Readers get a class-name-only route to sharper, better-set-apart text models.
arxiv-2602-19630:
Electron-phonon coupling shapes how electrons move in quantum materials, yet mode- and band-selective coupling is hard to pin down. Carl E. Jensen and five co-authors probe centrosymmetric 1T'-MoTe2 with time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy plus frequency-domain analysis. Near-infrared femtosecond pulses excite coherent Ag-symmetric phonon modes at 2340, 3340, and 3860 gigahertz.

Those modes show up as wobbles in how bright photoemission is and in binding energy across valence states. Pixel-wise Fourier analysis finds sharp band selectivity, with coupling strengths that differ across states and modes, giving band-renormalization amplitudes of a few millielectronvolts. First-principles calculations match the observed patterns and trends in broad terms, showing the joint method can resolve ultrafast electron-phonon interplay.
arxiv-2602-19930:
Imitation learning agents can replay demonstrations well, yet they falter when contexts shift or goals evolve, acting as clever memorisation machines. A 2026 arXiv paper by Nathan Gavenski and two co-authors argues that failure is basic, not merely technical: the field has optimized for the wrong objective.

The paper proposes a research agenda with a new definition of success: compositional adaptability instead of perfect replay. That adaptability means learning action primitives once and recombining them in new contexts without retraining. The authors set out metrics for generalization by composition, propose hybrid designs, and sketch cross-field directions from cognitive science and cultural evolution. Agents with adaptability at their core, they argue, gain an essential capability for an open-ended world.
arxiv-2602-20230:
A 2026 arXiv paper by Paul C. W. Lai and two co-authors reports high-resolution radio polarization images of the Boomerang pulsar wind nebula, catalogued as G106.65+2.96. The images come from the Very Large Array at six gigahertz. The images reveal new small-scale features.

An oval core, forty by twenty arcseconds, rings the central pulsar. A two-arcminute arc curls north around the core, with a gap between arc and core. A bright lobe lies to the northwest, and a tongue-shaped feature points northeast. Those shapes may come from the pulsar wind pushing against its surroundings. The magnetic field is well ordered and wraps in rings around the core. The small features are all strongly polarized in a straight line: the lobe reaches about sixty percent, near the synchrotron limit and far above the lower-frequency value. Faraday rotation inside the nebula likely explains that loss.
arxiv-2602-20330:
Jingcheng Yang and four co-authors introduce a framework for tracing circuits inside vision-language models. Such models are powerful yet opaque, and their multimodal reasoning has lacked a transparent analysis method. The new framework combines transcoders, attribution graphs, and attention-based methods to follow how visual and semantic concepts integrate. It reveals a hierarchy in that integration, with distinct visual feature circuits handling mathematical reasoning and cross-modal associations.

Feature steering and circuit patching validate the findings, showing the circuits are causal and controllable rather than merely correlated patterns. The work lays groundwork for more explainable and reliable vision-language models. By opening the black box, circuit tracing lets researchers check which internal pathways drive a given answer. That transparency supports models that can be examined, not merely trusted.
arxiv-2602-20730:
Zhenxing Xu and six co-authors present ECO, a learning system joining batched preference tuning with a Mamba backbone, aimed at speed in neural combinatorial optimization. Instead of tightly mixing every policy update with on-policy rollouts, ECO splits path making from gradient updates in two stages.

The stages are guided warm-up on pre-computed solutions and iterative Direct Preference Optimization on batched trial sets from the current policy. A mixed Mamba encoder-decoder cuts memory growth on long sequences and improves hardware use. A local-search-guided kick-start plan during training widens choice margins and steadies stepwise improvement. Key, local search only builds stronger choice pairs during training and never runs at use time. On TSP and CVRP, ECO achieves the strongest overall performance among compared neural baselines while also giving clear gains in memory use and throughput.
arxiv-2602-21030:
Linear preserver problems ask which linear maps preserve a given matrix property, a question pursued since Frobenius characterized determinant preservers in 1897. Projesh Nath Choudhury and Shivangi Yadav survey the positivity branch of that tradition in this 2026 arXiv paper. They cover linear preservers of several positivity classes of matrices.

The survey reviews recent developments in the literature and, for each positivity class considered, identifies gaps that remain. Readers new to the area get the current state of research in one place, while specialists get a map of open problems. The paper serves as both an entry point and a guide for future work on positivity preservers.
arxiv-2602-21430:
Meng Xu and two co-authors clarify how open quantum systems with memory can be embedded in a larger space with no memory. Such embeddings allow strong simulations that do not rely on weak-coupling approximations. But the extended motion can obey several distinct memory-free equations, and their links had stayed murky.

The authors show those distinct embeddings come from different unravelings of Gaussian bath self-energies. Each unraveling yields a family of deterministic, time-local equations for the extended system. Using a Brownian-oscillator spectral density as an example, they connect existing methods, including the Hierarchical Equations of Motion and the Lindblad-pseudomode formalism. The work thus gives both a clear theory base for embedding methods and a flexible platform for stable, efficient simulation of quantum motion with memory.
arxiv-2602-21530:
Xiyong Yan alone authors a paper on which signs can occur among Hamiltonian circles in simple plane signed graphs. Adopting a viewpoint centered on faces, the paper ties whether a Hamiltonian circle is positive or negative to multiplying together the signs carried by its interior faces. The author introduces co-Hamiltonian sequences to capture that link.

From that link comes a test for when both signs occur: exhibit a pair of co-Hamiltonian sequences whose face-products disagree. Signed grid graphs supply the motivation for local structural results that establish that each sign is attainable even when the complete sequences are never built out in full. One ladder-type configuration toggles along two 4-circles to produce Hamiltonian circles of opposite sign. Hexagon configurations also realize both signs.
arxiv-2602-21730:
Paul Borrill revisits Lamport's 1978 happens-before relation and logical clocks. They freed networked systems from synced clocks and are widely read as a break from absolute time. He argues the formalism keeps an unexamined assumption: causality forms a global acyclic graph over events. That forward-only structure embeds an arrow of time at the meaning level.

Following Ryle's account of category mistakes, the paper says this conflates two things. One is an epistemic idea, the logical ordering of messages. The other is an ontic claim that physical causes form one-way chains with no loops. The conflation is traced through Shannon's channel model, TLA+, Bell's theorem, and the Fischer-Lynch-Paterson and CAP limits. Relativity allows only local cause structure, and work on indefinite causal order shows nature admits correlations with no set ordering. The paper proposes mutual information conservation as the more basic primitive for shared accord.
arxiv-2602-21830:
Light setups give control over light-matter links through band design. Certain lattice shapes show spread-free flat bands, with fading group speed and spiking states, opening doors for slow light, nonlinear steps, and steering glow. Yet flat bands had not been seen where lattice sites are light-linked over a long range. Joel Lehikoinen and seven co-authors show stacks of evenly spaced 1D chains with flat bands of purely bending origin.

Flat band levels and angles are set by lattice and cell shape. The flat bands extend over all angles, with widths of a few nm, and are straight aligned. The team sees flat bands at set levels in gold nano lattices at near-IR via Fourier scans. The results provide a handy design plan for lattices with flat, aligned spreads for flat-band lasing, stronger links, and steering glow or uptake over a wide range.
arxiv-2602-21930:
Mohammad Reza Alipour and three co-authors map the thermodynamics of a class of black holes in anti-de Sitter space onto a dual quantum field theory. In that holographic picture, the central charge of the field theory joins the usual thermodynamic variables. Their 2026 arXiv study works through two settings: one with fixed charges, and one with a fixed electric potential.

In the fixed-charge setting, small and large black holes swap dominance in a van der Waals-like transition with a characteristic swallowtail shape. In the mixed setting, the system instead jumps between confined and deconfined phases. A key result is that stronger non-Abelian charge lowers both transition temperatures and shrinks the stable window of the confined phase, making that charge a central control knob for confinement.
arxiv-2602-22030:
The size of an atomic nucleus can be read from its charge radius, and tin offers a long chain of isotopes for testing nuclear theory. Pepijn Demol and three co-authors compute charge radii along the tin chain from first principles, using a coupled-cluster method at the singles and doubles level. They test modern chiral effective field theory forces against the measured pattern of radii.

Two features prove telling: the curved pattern of isotope shifts between two magic neutron counts, and a kink at tin-132. None of the fine-tuned forces on trial captures every feature at once. Beyond tin-132 the results swing sharply with the chosen force, making that region a sharp test bed for future theory and for new shift measurements toward lighter and heavier tin.
arxiv-2602-22330:
Entanglement and magic are the twin resources behind genuinely quantum computation, but magic has resisted mapping. Lorenzo Leone and two co-authors prove a stark limit: deciding membership in the stabilizer polytope, which defines magic's free states, takes super-exponential time even approximately. The proof reduces the problem to a satisfiability instance on a squared number of variables.

The exponential-time hypothesis then seals the result. The blow lands twice: both counting magic and certifying it are fundamentally hard. Any magic measure for general states must be super-exponentially hard to compute, and deciding whether an operator witnesses magic is equally hard. The boundary between classical and quantum computation thus hides behind a wall of hardness.
arxiv-2602-22530:
Michael Stephen Fiske presents a mathematical idea he says was hiding inside his 2012 paper on Turing-incomputable computation. That paper was given at the Alan Turing centenary conference in Manchester. Called dynamic level sets, the concept is distinct from familiar ideas in dynamical systems, topology, and computability theory. That distance may explain why it went unnoticed.

The key mechanism is the Principle of Self-Modifiability. At each step, the physical form of an unchanging logical level set is rebuilt by a process that itself cannot be computed. Fiske connects this to a classic result of de Leeuw, Moore, Shannon, and Shapiro. Their result says probabilistic Turing machines with computable bias compute no more than deterministic ones. Fiske explains why his object escapes that frame.
arxiv-2602-22930:
Saeed Noori Gashti and seven co-authors test two conjectures at once in F(R)-Euler-Heisenberg black holes. The Weak Gravity Conjecture and Weak Cosmic Censorship Conjecture meet in anti-de Sitter and de Sitter backgrounds, with solutions set by charge, F(R) deviation, Euler-Heisenberg coupling, and scalar curvature.

A universal entropy-extremality relation gives thermodynamic evidence for the Weak Gravity Conjecture independent of the F(R) deviation and curvature. Photon-sphere analysis from geodesic and topological angles confirms both conjectures can hold together, with Euler-Heisenberg coupling restoring photon spheres even around naked singularities. Lensing shows photon-sphere radius ignores the cosmological background while the critical impact parameter nearly doubles in de Sitter. Barrow-entropy analysis adds van der Waals-type transitions and Joule-Thomson expansion, with small black holes as the conjecture-compatible phase reachable by cooling.
arxiv-2602-23230:
Zahra Khatibi and three co-authors cut the cost of training models that design new dysprosium compounds with large magnetic anisotropy. Models that create new molecules could open new regions of chemical space, but training them usually needs large data sets. That rules out costly high-level ab initio runs, yet such multireference runs are exactly what reliable forecasts for dysprosium coordination compounds require.

Their semi-supervised, chemistry-shaped training-by-proxy for models that learn to create new structures shrinks the cost of building a training set from multireference runs by two orders of magnitude. Starting from as few as 1,000 multireference runs, the approach creates hundreds of new organic ligands for dysprosium(III) five-sided double-pyramid compounds with record magnet strength that varies by direction. It points toward computer design of complex coordination compounds with target charge and magnet traits.
arxiv-2602-23430:
Biplab Pal and two co-authors show that magnetic flux can strengthen magnetic couplings in a flat-band diamond chain. Flat bands have become an essential condensed matter frontier, hosting anomalous transport, superconductivity dominated by quantum geometry, and exotic topological phases. Even in magnetic systems, the authors argue, flat bands can produce unexpected features.

The focus is the Aharonov-Bohm flux effect on exchange couplings in magnetic diamond chains. The headline result is a significant amplification of magnetic couplings at short distances under flux, considerably raising the thermal conductivity carried by magnons. The flux-dependent decay length of the couplings is tied to the quantum metric of the flat bands. The findings matter for controlling magnetic properties in spintronic devices and for nanoscale heat transport by magnons in quantum technologies.
arxiv-2602-23530:
Aditya Gaydhani and four co-authors propose a unified learning-to-rank model for merging retrieval channels in large-scale e-commerce search. Modern systems use multiple specialized channels, from bestsellers to new or seasonal items, but merging them under strict latency limits while optimizing conversions is a key challenge.

Rank-based fusion methods like reciprocal rank fusion use fixed global channel weights and treat channels independently, ignoring query-specific utility and cross-channel interactions. The authors instead reformulate multi-channel fusion as a query-dependent learning-to-rank problem over heterogeneous sources, jointly optimizing clicks, add-to-carts, and purchases with channel-specific objectives and recent behavioral signals for short-term intent shifts. Online A/B experiments test the proposed approach.
arxiv-2602-23830:
Christoph Hansknecht and two co-authors present a flow-based method for optimization problems with vanishing constraints, a class notorious for failing standard constraint qualifications. The 2026 paper notes that relaxation methods usually handle such problems, but they demand careful hand-tuning of a relaxation parameter.

The new approach replaces relaxation with piecewise gradient flows that lead to first-order stationary points, without a tuning knob to babysit. The authors test it on several real-world instances with vanishing constraints and compare it with a common relaxation method. The flow method proves effective on those cases, offering a cleaner route to solutions where constraint structure would otherwise block standard solvers. It may simplify modeling tasks where constraints switch off in parts of the domain.
arxiv-2602-23930:
Poulomi Maji and fifteen co-authors study percolative instabilities and sparse-limit fractality in the layered material tantalum disulfide. The 2026 paper examines the low-temperature metallic phase, which may arise when current and voltage destabilize a commensurate charge density wave inside a strongly correlated Mott insulator.

Electrical pulse transport plus second-harmonic response reveal abrupt switching, negative differential resistance, and reorganization of domain walls across scales. A free-energy analysis finds a critical threshold for the Mott-to-metal transition, with scaling exponents matching two-dimensional percolation. The sparse-limit fractal dimension rises with temperature, tracing how conductive pathways grow hierarchically. In plain terms, the tests track how the stuff flips from one state to another. The flip spreads in patches, and the patches join up as heat rises.
arxiv-2602-24030:
Fangyu Sun and six co-authors present a vision-based curriculum reinforcement learning framework for quadrotor racing through courses with random obstacles. The 2026 paper notes that most drone racing research uses obstacle-free tracks, while obstacles add perception and agility challenges that often sink success rates in real flight.

The method combines multi-stage curriculum learning, which ramps difficulty gradually, with a multi-scene updating strategy and domain randomization, balancing obstacle avoidance against gate traversal. A single end-to-end network controls the quadrotor at high speed in varied obstacle layouts. Tests in the real world and in hardware-in-the-loop setups show higher success rates and faster lap times than existing approaches. They advance drone racing from clean tracks toward the cluttered environments real flights must handle.
arxiv-2603-00530: Blessing and four colleagues improve sampling from unnormalised densities with diffusion models, where least squares matching methods force trade offs such as restricted priors or unstable optimisation. Viewing those methods as fixed point iterations rooted in Nelson's relation, they build the Bridge Matching Sampler. It learns a stochastic transport map between any prior and target with one scalable stable objective. A damped variant adds regularisation to fight mode collapse and steady training further. The method samples at unprecedented scale while preserving mode diversity, leading on synthetic and molecular benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-00930: Xu builds an information-theoretic account of caching for derivation-based reasoning engines under premise erasure. Comparing a general coded cache with a derivation-constrained cache of logical facts, he proves four coding theorems, including an exponential capacity gap between chain and merge architectures. The headline result is the derivation penalty: the constrained cache exceeds the coded cache by the reciprocal of the erasure rate. That rigidity also yields a strong converse and a dispersion split.
arxiv-2603-01230: Fang and Liang propose Confounder Imputation with Stochastic Neural Networks, a causal-guessing method for unmeasured hidden factors. It models a causal graph with a stochastic neural network and fills in latent confounders by tuned stochastic-gradient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. Under standard rules and a size-capped sparse network class, they prove model ID and steady gauging of the mean future outcome under a fixed treatment. The latent confounder is known only up to rewrites keeping the joint treatment-outcome spread, but the causal target stays fixed across that class.
arxiv-2603-01630:
Anjali Parashar, Yingke Li, Eric Yang Yu, and colleagues test whether self-run systems like drones act in line with human values. Their 2026 work notes that ethical checks lack shared metrics and depend on who judges. Values differ by stakeholder, so no fixed formula can capture them alone.

Their frame, SEED-SET, designs tests in steps and learns from both hard scores and human judgments. Each kind of input is modeled on its own with layered Gaussian processes, a flexible statistical tool. A new picking rule then proposes tests that best probe what stakeholders prefer. Across two test uses, the method beats rivals and finds up to twice as many near-best test cases. Coverage of wide search spaces also improves, with a clear trade-off users can read.
arxiv-2603-01930:
Junbo Huang, Max Weinig, and Ulrich Fritsche annotate news narratives as graphs with methods borrowed from qualitative research. Their 2026 work targets economic stories, like inflation coverage, that shape how the public reads events. Turning a story into a structured graph remains a key challenge for language technology.

Events become nodes in a directed acyclic graph, and causal links become its edges. Principles from qualitative content analysis guide the annotation to cut labeling errors at the source. Their data set holds inflation narratives labeled in that graph form for shared use. A factorial test varies narrative representation and distance metric to measure agreement between annotators. Lenient metrics overstate reliability, they find, while locally constrained forms reduce label variation between readers.
arxiv-2603-02030:
A TCG CREST team describes its speaker diarization system for a medical conversation challenge in this 2026 report. Diarization answers who spoke when, here in noisy rural healthcare dialogues from the DISPLACE-M challenge. Overlap, dialect shifts, and background noise make the naturalistic recordings hard to split by speaker.

The study compares voice activity detectors and clustering methods inside two frameworks. One is a modular pipeline with speaker embeddings from a SpeechBrain model. The other is a hybrid end-to-end neural system built on a pre-trained speech model. Novel spectral clustering variants compete with classic hierarchical clustering across both frames. The neural system cuts diarization error sharply versus the pipeline baseline in phase one analysis. Their best entry pairs that system with hierarchical clustering and wide median filtering, placing fifth of eleven teams.
arxiv-2603-02130:
Tracking a body in three dimensions is hard when cameras miss parts and sensors drift. Tutian Tang, Xingyu Ji, Yutong Li, and colleagues tackle that task in this 2026 paper. Their system, Stereo-Inertial Poser, uses one stereo camera and six small motion sensors worn on the body. It aims to track both shape and place with true scale.

A stereo camera has two lenses, so it can judge depth that a single lens cannot. The team fuses that view with sensor data to fix drift and guess joint spots. A new shape-aware step adjusts for body size while tracking travel across a room. Tests beat prior methods, ran past 200 frames per second, and cut foot sliding.
arxiv-2603-02230:
Linxuan Wang, Ziyi Wang, Yikun Bai, and colleagues rebuild self-correcting text generators in this 2026 paper. Discrete diffusion models build text in parallel steps, not word by word. Self-correction lets such models fix early errors while keeping parallel speed. Older fixes work only at run time or after training, and they generalize poorly.

A prior model baked self-correction into pretraining, but through a tangled pipeline. The new model, SCDD, uses clear state changes and learns in discrete time steps. Training noise is simpler, a redundant remasking step is dropped, and only uniform changes are used. Tests at a modest scale show faster parallel decoding with quality preserved. The cleaner design should make self-correction easier to tune and adopt.
arxiv-2603-02330:
J Lyman, D O'Neill, T Killestein, and colleagues describe the data pipeline of a transient-hunting telescope array in this 2026 paper. GOTO uses thirty-two small telescopes at two sites on opposite sides of Earth. It scans the sky for sudden flashes like supernovae and kilonovae. It also rushes to follow alerts from gravitational wave and other detectors.

Speed is the core demand: counterparts fade within hours or less. Their pipeline compares new images with older ones to spot changes. Candidates are ready about seven minutes after the shutter closes. Later steps mix automated checks with human review, reporting, and follow-up triggers. The workflow meets the project's needs for fast discovery, the authors report. They also flag areas where the system should improve.
arxiv-2603-02430:
Logan Frank and Jim Davis revisit one key dial in knowledge distillation in this 2026 paper. Distillation trains a small student model to copy a larger teacher. A temperature dial softens the teacher's outputs, exposing relations between classes. Picking that dial well is poorly understood, and grid search wastes time.

The authors argue temperature is tightly linked to other training choices. Optimizer, teacher pretraining, and fine-tuning all interact with the best setting. Their unified study maps those interactions in a systematic way. Certain common situations shift temperature choice in pronounced ways, they find. Values borrowed from other setups can quietly hurt student performance. The paper turns those patterns into practical guidance for training students.
arxiv-2603-02530:
Miroslav Krstic designs controllers that stabilize positive nonlinear systems in this 2026 paper. Positive systems keep states and controls above zero, as in living populations. Classic inverse optimal methods assume inputs can swing either sign. Their symmetric cost shapes also fail for one-sided systems by nature.

Krstic builds two general frameworks around contractor and expander functions. One pairs a Lyapunov function with a feedback law and an expander. The other needs only the Lyapunov function and a contractor. Both yield inverse optimal stabilizers at any size on the positive orthant. Stronger conditions on the Lyapunov function yield stronger results. Two explicit formulas give ready, universal designs. The predator-prey model shows the designs carry real meaning for life science.
arxiv-2603-02730:
Yuanqing Yu, Yifan Wang, Weizhi Ma, and colleagues fix a mismatch between how generative recommenders train and how they answer. Their 2026 framework, APAO, targets systems that spell out the next item token by token. Training assumes the true history is always present, yet live search prunes weak early tokens, so the right item can vanish early.

APAO adds training losses at the prefix level, matching how beam search actually discards candidates. An adaptive step focuses effort on whichever prefixes look most at risk during training. Theory supports the design, and tests on several datasets show steady gains across different backbone models. The code is public, so other teams can adopt the fix directly.
arxiv-2603-02830:
Prarthana Bhattacharyya, Joshua Mitton, Ralph Abboud, and Simon Woodhead compare small specialist models with large language models at predicting student answers. Their 2026 paper focuses on knowledge tracing, which forecasts how a learner will respond to the next question. Such forecasts let teaching platforms step in at the right moment.

Across accuracy tests, the compact tracing models beat the large language models on both raw accuracy and balanced scores. The large models were also far slower, by orders of magnitude, and cost far more to run. The authors argue that closed large models should not be treated as a universal answer for every task. For narrow prediction jobs in education, trained specialists remain faster, cheaper, and more accurate.
arxiv-2603-03130:
Frederick Reiber, Nathan Kim, Allison McDonald, and Dana Calacci document how employers use digital tools to break union drives. Despite strong public support for unions, United States workers still struggle to win contracts against organized employer resistance. Their 2026 paper studies campaigns at Amazon, Starbucks, and Boston University from public sources.

Four tactics recur, summed up as surveillance, spacing, screaming, and scabbing. Each has a digital edge: monitoring workers' messages, scattering organizers across schedules and sites, flooding channels with anti-union messaging, and lining up replacements through platforms. The analysis traces how the same tactics adapt across workplaces. The authors close with design implications for tools that support organizing, plus emerging forms of worker resistance.
arxiv-2603-03530:
Achleshwar Luthra, Yash Salunkhe, and Tomer Galanti explain why self-supervised models transfer so well from so few labels. Frozen representations learned without labels often need only a handful of examples for a new task, and one representation can serve many tasks without interference. Their 2026 paper names a single geometric quantity behind both gifts: the variance along class-separating directions, a directional version of within-class spread.

When that directional variance is small, classes collapse tightly along the axes that matter. The authors prove sharp, non-asymptotic error bounds whose leading term is exactly that quantity, with finite-sample corrections cleanly separated. Small values across tasks also force different tasks' decision axes toward orthogonality, explaining the low interference. Empirically the quantity collapses during pretraining even where its classical cousin stays large, and the bounds track real few-shot error closely.
arxiv-2603-03630:
Saber Zerhoudi and seven colleagues argue that search engines can no longer tell who is using them, and never will. User models assume behavior reveals intent. That collapses when the user is an artificial intelligence agent privately configured by a hidden human operator: any observed action could match countless hidden instructions. Their 2026 paper calls this the agent-user problem and proves it structural, not a tooling gap.

Evidence comes from an agent-native social platform: hundreds of thousands of posts from tens of thousands of agents across thousands of communities. Individual actions cannot be classified as autonomous or directed. Population signals still sort agents into quality tiers, though click models trained on agent behavior degrade as weak agents flood in. Capability references spread across communities like an endemic infection and resist even aggressive modeled suppression.
arxiv-2603-03730:
Spencer R Klein and four colleagues take up an unmeasured property of the proton: where its baryon number sits. A proton's size depends on what you measure, and its charge, mass, and mechanical radii are all mapped. Baryon number, the conserved count that makes a proton a proton, has no measured distribution at all. Their 2026 paper frames the open question plainly: is baryon number spread evenly through the proton, or concentrated at its center?

Two pictures compete. In the simple parton view, the three valence quarks carry the number. Gauge invariance complicates that story: a configuration of gluon fields at the junction of quark strings, the baryon junction, may carry it instead. Heavy-ion data on baryon stopping, where baryon number halts mid-collision, support the junction picture. Imaging the distribution would settle where the proton keeps its identity.
arxiv-2603-04230: Lin and colleagues study the impact of dynamical charm quark and mixed action effects on light hadron masses and decay constants. For light, strange, and charm flavor observables, they use the same tadpole-improved clover fermion action. Numerical results cover pion and kaon decay constants, light and strange quark masses, and Omega and Omega-ccc baryon masses. After continuum, chiral, and infinite-volume extrapolations, the values agree within uncertainties.
arxiv-2603-04430: Muser and colleagues solve PDEs with warps alone in Flowers. Only pointwise channel mixing and a multiscale scaffold join the warps. No Fourier multipliers, dot product attention, or convolutional mixing appear. Each head warps mixed features by a predicted displacement field, sampled sparsely at source points. Stacked multiscale residual warps give global adaptive interactions at linear cost. Theory ties the design to conservation flow maps, waves in inhomogeneous media, and a kinetic limit. A 17M model beats similar baselines, and a 150M model tops recent transformer foundation models.
arxiv-2603-04530: Sarkis and Zanasi axiomatize relative entropy with diagrams from a categorical view. Relative entropy gauges gaps between distributions across statistics and machine learning. Viewing it as a layer on random matrix categories, they use Kronecker product and direct sum forms. Their results axiomatize Kullback-Leibler divergence fully, and Renyi divergences of any order too, for each form. The theories live in numeric monoidal algebra, using string diagrams filled with numeric rules. The work thus gives a complete diagram account of these gaps.
arxiv-2603-04630: Bassi traces quantum foundations into quantum technologies. Quantum mechanics carried foundational questions: seeing processes, locality, Heisenberg limits, a deeper reality, and measurement. The path proved unpredictable: once abstract questions spawned platforms, which matured into devices for quantum computation, communication, and sensing. Progress runs the other way: tech enables tests once out of reach, like whether superposition survives at scale and whether all reality, gravity included, is quantum at root. Foundations and technology thus keep shaping each other.
arxiv-2603-04930: Xueyang Wang and team map privacy tensions between camera-glasses wearers and bystanders through surveys of 525 people and 20 paired interviews in China. Bystanders demand stronger transparency and protection than wearers will provide, with gaps widening in sensitive settings where 65-90% say they would take defensive action. Twelve technologies reveal four trade-offs: visibility against disruption, empowerment against burden, protection against agency, and accountability against exposure. The authors read the gaps as shape incompatibility rather than poor goodwill, and offer context-adaptive pathways that tighten protection in sensitive settings.
arxiv-2603-05230: Serkan Ergun and colleagues present a digital-twin robotic sorter for textile recycling, combining grasp prediction, perception, and reasoning. A dual-arm cell with RGBD and tactile sensing and collision-aware planning pulls garments from a basket to inspection and classifies them with vision-language models. Across nine models from five families on 223 scenarios, Qwen leads overall accuracy with strong foreign-object detection, while lighter Gemma3 trades accuracy for edge speed. A digital twin with MoveIt plans collision-aware paths and merges segmented point clouds virtually, demonstrating scalable autonomous sorting.
arxiv-2603-05630: Xu and team propose interpolated FID, a simple version of rebuild FID tracking closely with making FID for latent diffusion models. For each data set item, they retrieve its nearest neighbor in latent space and blend the two forms. Reading out the result, they compute FID between read-out samples and the original data set. Interpolated FID tests blends near the ridge set where model samples gather. In tests, it is the first metric tracking closely with making FID across VAEs, with Pearson and Spearman links near 0.85.
arxiv-2603-05730: Van de Wetering and Zhu look into neural operators copying drift-wave splitting. Self-steady models of turbulence transport improve fusion plasma holding. Catching joint change of turbulence, flow, and profiles is hard, and direct model runs are too slow for control. Using the changed Hasegawa-Wakatani model, the tuned operator captures splitting scales and stays robust on rare moves. A single unified model predicts steady-state turbulence and moving shifts. Shifts include fullness, on-their-own calming, and rise of zonal flows, over spans far past local correlation time.
arxiv-2603-06130: Odinokov and Yavorskiy set out a robotics physical safety method that names assets in plain terms, lists vulnerabilities step by step, and makes synthetic data from hazards. Old-style risk engineering meets new machine learning pipelines in this method. Safety envelopes can then be learned from a formal hazard ontology rather than from ad hoc examples. Its main point is that it lines up safety engineering, twin simulation, synthetic data creation, and model training in one chain.
arxiv-2603-06230: Harries presents a machine learning method producing dust continuum images and spectral energy distributions from radiative transfer training sets. With Bayesian optimization, he fits 1.3 millimetre ALMA ODISEA images of Ophiuchus protostellar discs and their spectral energy distributions to determine dust masses and radii. Good simultaneous fits emerge for Class II objects, though poorer for Class I and flat spectrum sources. Broader and shallower dust mass distributions than millimetre flux estimates predict raise high mass and low mass disc counts, through optical depth and temperature effects tied to size and inclination.
arxiv-2603-06430: Moconja and Tanović confirm Martin's conjecture across a wide subclass of weakly quasi-o-minimal theories, in a study centred on countable models within that class. The result extends the conjecture's confirmed range across a wide family constrained by weak quasi-o-minimality, rather than settling isolated cases alone. By establishing it throughout that subclass, the authors place countable models of such theories on firmer ground and clarify how far the conjectured behaviour reaches. The contribution remains a confirmation for that subclass, leaving theories beyond it still open.
arxiv-2603-06530: Li and colleagues propose AV-Unified, a framework for joint learning across audio-visual scene understanding tasks, where humans integrate multiple tasks in dynamic scenes but works explore tasks individually. AV-Unified standardizes input-output formats and adds a perception network capturing audio-visual associations. All task inputs and outputs become sequences of discrete tokens, giving a representation for joint training across datasets. A multi-scale temporal module captures cues at varying event granularity, and a cross-modal spatial module models audio-visual associations despite lacking auditory supervision.
arxiv-2603-06630: Litowitz and colleagues apply MacKay's energy-policy arithmetic to AI computation, treating the token as a physical quantity carrying measurable thermodynamic cost. From Landauer's principle, Shannon's channel capacity, and infrastructure data, they build a global token-production balance sheet and derive a question budget. Applying Coase's firm theory and the durable-goods monopoly problem, they locate where value concentrates and regulatory openings. Their claim is that expanding the token budget cannot resolve which questions merit asking, a problem of agency computation alone cannot solve.
arxiv-2603-06730: Dennis Delali Kwesi Wayo and colleagues compare surface-code decoders inside one LiDMaS+ workflow, testing how decoder and estimator choices shift threshold estimates. In a Pauli-reference sweep, a matching-style backend beats Union-Find. In hybrid continuous-variable and discrete sweeps, crossing estimates vary by code distance, and one pair sits in a low-error region where results stay estimator-sensitive. Learned reweighting cuts mean logical error in a neural-guidance sweep.
arxiv-2603-06830: Ma and colleagues describe the Fraunhofer qubit, a superconducting qubit tuned by flux through a wide ballistic Josephson junction. Flux through the junction averages the Josephson potential over a phase window that grows with flux. Near one flux quantum, perfectly clear junctions see the minimum change shape from quadratic to triangular, greatly boosting anharmonicity. Lower-transparency channels keep the boost, and atom-level simulations with disorder confirm it. The result gives a sweet spot balancing that boost against charge-noise safety.
arxiv-2603-06930: Rather describes position sets for graph classes and gives formulas for position polynomials of multipartite graphs. The general position problem seeks a vertex set with no three vertices on a common shortest path, and its polynomial counts all such sets. For balanced multi-part graphs with part size up to four, the polynomial is log-concave and unimodal for all parts. Larger part sizes give counterexamples. He analyzes the corona of a graph with one vertex. Unimodality survives for classes, with counter-cases for bipartite and multi-part graphs.
arxiv-2603-07030: Dimobi studies stronger leakage abuse attacks in searchable crypto with eBPF watching. The crypto lets users search coded data on outside servers such as cloud hosts. While it hides query and document content, it still leaks patterns such as query rate, fueling attacks that past guards have made harder. Dimobi shows system watching with eBPF can uncover new leakage forms beyond standard threat models. By watching system acts during searches, a foe gains insight into query acts, document access, and handling flow, marking a new pattern that strengthens past attacks.
arxiv-2603-07230: Wang and colleagues improve grouped rank-rank fit for gauging parent-child rise within groups. Standard rank-rank regression with covariates added directly yields parameters that are hard to interpret. Conditional rank-rank regression uses covariate-adjusted ranks instead. The team gauges grouped ranks with a deep grouped mapping model plus cross-fitting, letting end-to-end grouped spread learning work under curves, high-order mixes, and discrete ordered results. They extend the method to discrete results via an omega-indexed rank rule and give limit theory for smooth results.
arxiv-2603-07330: Khallaf and Sharoff examine uncertainty estimation for multilingual text classification under noise and off-topic inputs. Softmax-based methods stay competitive on high-resource in-domain data but lose reliability when resources thin out or domains shift. Monte Carlo dropout, by contrast, holds up across languages with steadier calibration and thresholds. Skipping the most uncertain tenth of cases lifts scores on a non-topical task, supporting abstention as a reliability tool.
arxiv-2603-07530: Nguyen and colleagues give robots in-context imitation learning with visual reasoning traces. Existing methods read only state-action trajectories and lack an explicit picture of task intent, hurting performance where the same actions fit different goals. ICLR augments demo prompts with structured traces of coming future paths in image space. The model jointly learns to generate traces and low-level actions, improving success and generalization on simulated and real manipulation tasks.
arxiv-2603-07830: Krishnan, Maurya and Samanta develop a hydrodynamic framework for force dipoles in a compressible membrane on a shallow subphase. From generalized Stokes equations with shear, dilatational, and odd viscosities, they derive an exact Green tensor via Hankel transforms. The tensor carries three screening scales for shear, compressional, and odd modes. It reduces smoothly to incompressible and parity-symmetric membranes while capturing the chiral odd response. Using this tensor they obtain velocity and vorticity fields. The analysis reveals distinct regimes and observables isolating the odd contribution, including transverse drift.
arxiv-2603-08830: Martínez-Ramírez and colleagues unveil 16 new quasars near the end of reionization with self-supervised learning. Foreground cool dwarfs outnumber such quasars by orders of magnitude, swamping classic color searches. Scanning DESI Legacy Survey images directly and ranking by spectral energy fits, they confirm 16 bright quasars, three of which classic color cuts would have missed.
arxiv-2603-09030: Tenny Yin and colleagues train robot world models from unsupervised self-play video. Today's video models still miss physically faithful robot-object contact despite huge robot datasets. Their PlayWorld pipeline learns entirely from autonomous play and enables failure prediction, policy evaluation, and reinforcement learning in the model, lifting real-world success rates by 65 percent.
arxiv-2603-09430: Marius Furter and colleagues add uncertainty to the symmetric monoidal categories used to model open systems in co-design. Real systems are seldom fully known, and Markov categories offer a strong frame for uncertain processes. Their change-of-base move swaps a category's maps for parametric ones valued in a Markov category, giving a 2-category with the same objects. Picking different monads then captures different kinds of uncertainty while the wiring stays intact.
arxiv-2603-09630: Sanjin Benić and colleagues compute the dipole gluon Sivers function of the proton from its eikonal spin-dependent Odderon matrix element with a helicity flip. A three-quark light-front model fixes the function at moderately small x and transverse momentum up to about 1 GeV. The model's light-cone wave function predicts the function's size, its peak position in transverse momentum, and its small-momentum behavior. They also compute the BFKL anomalous dimension behind the power-law tail at larger transverse momentum.
arxiv-2603-09730: Abhishek Malvankar and coauthors describe WVA, a control plane that scales language model serving in the llmd system. Standard Kubernetes scaling ignores service goals, mixed hardware and the load inside each inference engine. WVA instead scales with spare headroom in mind and shrinks fleets without breaking live state. Trials show far higher useful throughput and far fewer failed requests than the standard scaler.
arxiv-2603-09930: Yao Zhang and coauthors improve text to motion search, where a written phrase should find a matching 3D human movement. Global embeddings from dual encoders throw away fine local links between words and joints. Their method turns joint level features into a structured pseudo image read by a vision transformer. Token wise late interaction then aligns text and motion closely, with clear fine grained matches.
arxiv-2603-10130: Plisiecki argues that text embeddings serve prediction well but make poor tools for measuring meaning in a rigorous way. Social study and psychology now use embeddings to scale up meaning measurement, yet good retrieval scores say little about tool quality. He proposes a distinct aim, with clear geometry, links back to language proof and strength against non semantic confounds. Static embeddings stay open to check, while contextual ones entangle meaning with other signals.
arxiv-2603-10230: Fang and coauthors propose a trust region interior point SSQP method for problems with a noisy goal. In this setting the goal and its slope cannot be read exactly, but noisy guesses can be built as needed. At each step their method builds oracles held to accuracy rules that hold with a fixed chance, while a decaying wall handles inequality limits. Under standard rules they prove convergence to first order still points, with tests on CUTEst and logistic tasks.
arxiv-2603-10330: Eugene Ku and Yiwei Lyu present PC-Diffuser, a safety layer built into diffusion-based trajectory planning for self-driving cars. Diffusion planners learn from expert driving and plan well, yet they are hard to certify and can fail badly on rare scenes. PC-Diffuser makes safety part of generation itself, checking collision risk with a capsule-distance barrier that fits vehicle shape. Denoised waypoints become feasible motion under a bicycle model, then a path-consistent filter removes leftover violations without warping the path.
arxiv-2603-10530: Jingchen Hu and Li Sheng prove that the potential of a complete Kähler-Einstein metric is itself strictly convex. The setting is a bounded, strictly convex domain in complex space, and u is that potential function. So the convexity of the domain is matched by strict convexity of the very function that defines the metric. It is a tidy link between the shape of the space and the shape of its potential, proved for this complete metric on such a domain.
arxiv-2603-10730: Peter von Schultzendorff and co-authors assess how to design homotopy continuation methods for hyperbolic transport problems in porous media, such as carbon storage and groundwater flow. Newton solvers for the coupled equations are costly and not always convergent. Continuation solvers first solve a simple auxiliary problem, then trace a solution curve to the hard target. On the Buckley-Leverett equation they compare two known homotopies with a new entropy-based one. The choice of auxiliary problem, they find, governs how traceable the curve is.
arxiv-2603-10830: Shirin Golchi and Satoshi Morita develop Bayesian design and analysis methods for precision trials that borrow partly from external data. Precision medicine needs methods for subgroup effects, where precise estimates are hard and sparse subgroups beg for outside information. Motivated by a gastric cancer trial, their model weights each external subject by fit with the target population, based on covariate patterns. Simulations compare the approach with dynamic borrowing. A design framework then takes priors from the external data to set decision boundaries and sample sizes.
arxiv-2603-11330: Yuxiang Feng, Niall Mangan, and Manu Jayadharan expose a trap in learning governing equations from time-series data, the dictionary-based sparse regression workflow now popular in systems biology. When its functions track each other strongly, ill-conditioning lets noise swing the model wildly. Sparse regularization only partly helps. Even two or three terms can show strong multicollinearity and extreme condition numbers. Orthogonal polynomial bases do not fix this. But sampling aligned with the basis's weight function brings back conditioning and accuracy.
arxiv-2603-11630: Tzouvaras returns to the magmatic universe and asks what basic set-theoretic objects it can still define. Ordered pairs, relations, functions, and numbers are all missing from that universe as native objects. Magmatic pairs, he shows, can serve as analogues of ordered pairs. Relations and functions prove far harder, since magma elements split into intended and collateral kinds. Functions end up definable only under very special conditions. One win does land: a Separation scheme cut down to magmatic formulas holds in the universe. Replacement, by contrast, fails badly.
arxiv-2603-11830: Borndörfer and co-authors present an eikonal method that finds the single best free-flight path for an aircraft in steady wind. The best path cuts emissions and fuel burn. Trouble lurks when the destination sits near a cut locus of the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation: small grid errors can pick a merely local best path. Using finite element error bounds, they build a trust region around the cut loci. That region guarantees one-of-a-kind paths for destinations far enough away.
arxiv-2603-12130: Zhu, He, Koßmann, and Wang price the entanglement needed to tell two quantum channels apart locally. In one-shot tests, the diamond norm sets plain channel discrimination. Their tester theory asks how much shared entanglement local protocols need to match the global best score. They define that need as a minimum Schmidt rank and study it under positive partial transpose rules. A semidefinite program gives the best score for each rank, made tractable by a symmetry cut. Worked cases use depolarizing, SWAP, and Werner-Holevo channels.
arxiv-2603-12330: Yu, Matsuda, Watanabe, Arita, and Agterberg find pure spin flow along one axis from ferroaxial symmetry breaking. Their setting is coplanar antiferromagnets with vector spin chiral order that keeps parity and time-reversal. Such order looks tame, since it breaks only spin rotation symmetry. That breaking can take a ferroaxial form with striking transport effects. The states allow spin-conductivity that runs purely along one axis, with no dissipation. Twisted light can also switch on altermagnetic spin splitting, and 16 materials are named.
arxiv-2603-12530: Buyukkalayci, Hanna, and Fragouli extend the contexts-are-cheap view of linear bandits to Markovian contexts. With independent contexts, linear bandits reduce to a single-context problem with sharper guarantees. Real action sets, though, often evolve through an exogenous Markov chain, breaking that independence. Under uniform geometric ergodicity, the authors build a stationary surrogate action set. A delayed-update scheme controls the bias from nonstationary context distributions. Regret matches the underlying bandit oracle when mixing is fast enough, and tests on a real instance beat a LinUCB baseline.
arxiv-2603-13030: Alberto Mercurio and co-authors extend dissipative phase transitions to time-periodic open quantum systems. The classic account uses the spectrum of a fixed Liouvillian, which fails for Floquet drives. Their frame reads critical traits from the Floquet propagator spectrum instead. In driven Kerr resonators, counter-rotating terms shift the critical point and its time scales. In the driven Rabi model, new critical features appear near ultrastrong coupling. Deep strong coupling then erases the transition as light and matter decouple.
arxiv-2603-13330: Soochul Park and co-authors propose RBF-Solver, a faster sampler for diffusion probabilistic models. Sampling from these models gives high fidelity but costs a lot of compute. Polynomial multistep samplers speed things up, yet follow a fixed path with no room to tune. RBF-Solver interpolates model outputs with Gaussian radial basis functions that have learnable shape values. At first order it matches the Euler method, and at higher order it nears the Adams method. It beat polynomial samplers on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet tests at set function counts.
arxiv-2603-13530: R. Kerman and S. Spektor study when a positive integral operator stays bounded between Lorentz-Gamma spaces. It acts through a positive kernel on functions over Euclidean space. Their key step turns the multi-dimensional problem into a one-dimensional weighted norm inequality. That step uses an operator built from the iterated rearrangement of the kernel and the Stieltjes transform. For the case S squared, they get explicit Muckenhoupt-type conditions on the weights. The result settles boundedness in the stated range.
arxiv-2603-13730: Yuchen Miao and co-authors propose R3-REC, a retrieval-augmented LLM framework for sequential recommendation. Two hard problems drive the work: cold-start sparsity with noisy item texts, and opaque models of user intent over long and short horizons. R3-REC unifies five parts, from multi-level user intent reasoning to reasoning-based interest matching and scoring. Similar user data adds a collaborative boost to the matches. Across ML-1M, Games, and Bundle, it beat strong neural and LLM baselines. Ablations show each part adds gains.
arxiv-2603-13830: Cao and co-authors build an early warning system for rug pulls among meme tokens on the BNB Smart Chain. The system profiles wash trading in three forms: self, matched, and circular trades. Twelve token-level features turn trade, address, and fund-flow signals into a risk score. On 7 tokens with 33,242 records, a random forest reaches an AUC of 0.9098. Trade-level features drive most of the skill, and alerts come about 3.8 hours early on average for some samples.
arxiv-2603-14030: Brag benchmarks open-source foundation models that predict biological age from PPG pulse signals. A task-trained model built on 212,231 UK Biobank subjects fails on a new clinical group, with predicted ages squeezed into a narrow band. A general model with no age training does better on the same patients. On 906 surgical patients, Pulse-PPG gives the lowest error of the three models tested. Adding basic demographic data improves results further, and the age gap tracks diastolic blood pressure.
arxiv-2603-14130: Flynn, Obiso, and Newman introduce GELATO, a dataset of U.S. House and Senate bills from the 118th Congress labeled for named entity recognition. A two-level ontology, built for legislative text, covers government, executive, legislative, and treaty bodies. Transformer models such as BERT and RoBERTa are fine-tuned for the first level. Language models with tuned prompts then complete the second level. RoBERTa performs strongly while BERT lags, which supports this model pairing for legal text extraction.
arxiv-2603-14330: Abdullah and co-authors trace how the brightest cluster galaxy's star mass scales with its host halo mass. They use 996 clusters from the SDSS GalWCat19 catalog, within a low redshift band. Lognormal fits, run with a Markov chain Monte Carlo method, give a shallow slope for the relation. The scatter drops when the relation is recast in normalized form. Adding the magnitude gap between the brightest galaxy and its peers trims the scatter further. Checks across richness and mass cuts show the relation is stable.
arxiv-2603-14630: Bhosale and co-authors adapt the Charm++ runtime for cloud-native high performance computing. HPC codes built for static supercomputers fit cloud settings poorly. Clouds shift underfoot, with mixed hardware and spot pricing. Charm++ uses asynchronous, message-driven tasks that suit that flux. Rate-aware load balancing lifts speed on mixed CPU and GPU fleets. Core Charm++ rules blunt harm from network contention and speed variance. Extra tools push resilience further for coupled science codes, the authors report.
arxiv-2603-14730: Hao and co-authors verify language model task plans with a graph neural network in GNNVerifier. Model-written plans often hallucinate steps or tangle dependencies. Verifiers that prompt another model can be fooled by fluent narration. Structural flaws like type clashes and missing middle steps hide well. GNNVerifier draws each plan as a directed graph with rich node data. Edges encode run order and dependency constraints. The network scores whole-plan plausibility and flags risky nodes and edges. Targeted repair can then fix the weak spots.
arxiv-2603-14930: Vereshchagina and Ryzhikov build mixing automorphisms whose symmetric squares keep simple spectra. The maps act on a space with sigma-finite measure and mix ergodically. Simple spectra for the tensor square touch old questions from Kolmogorov and Rokhlin. Such spectral control is rare among mixing systems. Explicit examples come from near-Sidon constructions. The class gives concrete models where the square stays spectrally simple. Ergodic theory gains test cases for its spectral problems.
arxiv-2603-15030: Zhu and co-authors present VTC-Bench, a benchmark for multimodal models that must chain visual tools to solve tasks. It offers 32 OpenCV-based operations and 680 curated problems in nine cognitive groups. Each problem ships with a ground-truth execution path. The team tested 19 leading models. The best, Gemini-3.0-Pro, scored only 51 percent. Models struggled with new tools and picked narrow, familiar tool sets instead of the best plan. The authors aim to guide more general visual agents.
arxiv-2603-15830: Dougherty-Bliss and Elizalde link subset sums to binary necklaces and cyclic permutations. For odd n, subsets of 1 to n with sums divisible by n match binary necklaces in count. Their work widens that classic match in two ways. A new parameter r shifts the target residue class. Necklaces then gain matching periodicity conditions. A size split k matches the count of ones in each necklace. Generating functions prove a related Baker conjecture for r equal to 1. Bijective proofs stay open for most cases.
arxiv-2603-16030: Dantchev and Rudnick compare two fluctuation forces in the Gaussian model. Critical Casimir force rules the grand canonical ensemble. Critical Helmholtz force rules the fixed-mean canonical twin. Exact results near the bulk critical point anchor the study. Four boundary settings face the same side-by-side test. Dirichlet pairs split the forces apart in clear ways. The Casimir pull stays attractive, while Helmholtz can flip sign. Mixed Neumann-Dirichlet walls split the pair as well. Periodic and Neumann pairs make both forces coincide.
arxiv-2603-16130: Wang and co-authors fuse infrared and visible images with glare in mind. Daylight and headlight glare wash out visible camera detail. Their EPOFusion frame spots regions that need infrared rescue. A spatial guide module marks the overexposed zones. A region-aware loss then strengthens true infrared structure there. An iterative head refines features across many scales. Normal zones keep their visible look through the fusion. A new IVOE dataset trains and tests the method. Scores beat the glare-focused baseline by 10.7 percent on QAB/F.
arxiv-2603-16330: Rachel and co-authors predict drug response in non-small cell lung cancer. Their model learns from multi-omics data in the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer set. The target is LN-IC50, a measure of drug sensitivity. An XGBoost model makes the predictions from molecular features. Tuning used cross-validation and randomized search. SHAP values explain each feature's push on a prediction. A large language model then checks the top features for biological sense.
arxiv-2603-16730: Song and Zou count solutions of a mass-prescribed nonlinear Schrödinger problem. The domain is bounded, and the total mass is fixed in advance. For L2-subcritical powers, infinitely many sign-changing solutions exist at every mass. Their energies grow without bound as solutions multiply. The critical power keeps the result for small masses. In the supercritical range, solutions cost a shrinking mass budget. On the unit ball, exactly two positive solutions exist for small mass. One branch's energy fades to zero; the other blows up.
arxiv-2603-17030: Faleiro and co-authors study a class of Bell inequalities built from equality checks on outcomes. This generalizes full correlator rules and XOR games beyond binary outputs. They define the matching sub polytope of the local polytope and solve it in several cases. This yields thousands of tight Bell inequalities, many of them facets of the local polytope. They also define unanimous Bell inequalities, where all outcomes must agree. Most of these admit quantum violations. Some serve as witnesses of dimension or of genuine multipartite nonlocality.
arxiv-2603-17130: Gritsevich and co-authors analyze outbursts of comet 17P/Holmes from 1892 to 2021. They focus on the huge 2007 mega outburst, when the comet's coma briefly grew larger than the Sun. The study constrains the size distribution and total mass of the porous ice, organic, and dust particles thrown off. The inferred distribution fits a power law. Effective particle sizes span microns to millimetres, depending on the power law index. They conclude that outburst brightness is set mainly by particle count and size spread, not by ejected mass alone.
arxiv-2603-17230: Errabii, Sentieys, and Traiola study low bit quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, or KANs. KANs use learnable spline functions, whose cost at inference is high. The authors test how far spline precision can fall. They find B-splines can be quantized to 2 or 3 bits with negligible accuracy loss. They then swap the recursive spline algorithm for precomputed low bit lookup tables. One model cut BitOps fiftyfold with no accuracy loss. On FPGA hardware, cutting table precision raised clock speed by half.
arxiv-2603-17530: Barusco, Dalle Pezze, Borsatti, and Susto present AdapTS for visual anomaly detection on factory lines. Most methods handle one product class and never learn new ones over time. AdapTS shares one frozen backbone and adds small trainable adapters for the student path. A prototype step picks the right adapters at run time with 99 percent accuracy, they report. The lightest variant adds only 8 megabytes of memory.
arxiv-2603-17630: Bitonti, Michel, and Scott count unlike spanning trees in graphs with large minimum degree. A classic result gives the complete graph an exponential count of such trees. They show any connected graph with n nodes and minimum degree d holds at least n to the power of order d distinct trees. A random spanning tree hits any fixed shape with tiny odds, they prove. That strong anticoncentration form settles a conjecture of Lee.
arxiv-2603-17930: Yang and Zhang assign traffic blame from dashcam video with legal multi-agent reasoning. Courts need statute-backed verdicts, not just scene summaries, after a crash. Their C-TRAIL dataset pairs videos and text with fixed blame modes under Chinese traffic law. A first stage turns video into a written account of the event. Agent teams then reason over statutes to issue full judgment reports. The pipeline beat general and legal models on two sets, they report.
arxiv-2603-18330: Kumar, Ba, and Pan introduce MemArchitect, a policy-driven governance layer for persistent LLM agent memory. Standard retrieval frameworks treat memory as passive storage with no conflict or privacy rules. Stale zombie memories can then contaminate the context window.
