arxiv-2604-24630: Saganas, Guardiani, Porqueres and Enßlin present charm2, a code that rebuilds the cosmic expansion history from type Ia supernovae. It does not assume a fixed form for dark energy. Using information field theory, it applies geometric variational inference. That method flattens a curved posterior through a coordinate change. It then traces energy density changes with redshift. Reconstructions from two supernova sets match flat Lambda-CDM. Two newer sets deviate in a way compatible with evolving dark energy, though model selection finds no conclusive preference for non-flat features.
arxiv-2604-25130: Nguyen and four colleagues introduce LongSumEval, a framework that judges long-document summaries through structured question answering. Old metrics match human judgment weakly and give aggregate scores with no account of flaws or path to improvement. Here summary quality means answerability and factual alignment of question-answer pairs, giving clear scores plus feedback on coverage gaps and factual errors. Across seven benchmarks the method agreed far more with human judges. Its feedback improved summaries by self-refinement with no retraining.
arxiv-2604-25230: Kwon and three colleagues present four conceptual AI systems on AI presence in prayer. Drawing on prayer values from a diary study, they designed AI systems to assist prayer. Shown to participants in workbooks, the designs provoked co-reflection on how AI might shape prayer. Findings suggest authenticity, a genuine connection to the divine, matters most, while AI often diminished it when guiding prayer too much. The authors argue such designs should preserve user agency through interpretive openness, treating AI inexplicability as a resource, or non-use as legitimate.
arxiv-2604-25930: Xiao asks whether structured recurrent state can anchor language models with exact retrieval. The UniMatrix family reuses one recurrent block across depth, with hybrid updates, a residual path, and token-conditioned modulation. At small scale it slightly beats a matched-size transformer on WikiText-2 with far fewer parameters. But on associative recall it stays near chance, while the transformer reaches about a quarter. A sparse-pointer variant with slot routing and pointer-logit fusion reaches about three-quarters. Exact retrieval, the paper concludes, needs explicit sparse mechanisms.
arxiv-2604-26030: Edidin and Suresh solve a recovery problem motivated by cryo-electron microscopy. The task is reconstructing a finite point configuration, up to rotation, from its autocorrelation. This is known as the orthogonal beltway problem. They prove that when the point count exceeds the dimension, the orbit of a generic binary signal with enough equal-magnitude points can be recovered. They also connect the result to Euclidean distance geometry. A polynomial-time reconstruction algorithm follows, with a worst-case bound far lower in practice and robustness to modest noise.
arxiv-2604-26130: Nadaf presents reward-lens, a library porting interpretability tools from generative models to reward models. They break the usual vocabulary-projection tricks by swapping a vocabulary output for a scalar regression head. It offers a reward lens, component attribution, and three-mode patching. A reward-hacking probe suite and feature attribution come with adapters for several major model families. Tests on two production reward models give a negative finding: linear attribution barely predicts causal patching effects. The design treats that gap as a finding, not a bug.
arxiv-2604-26430: Ahmed and four colleagues tested quantum-circuit integrity with a three-layer score set, arguing no single view suffices. One score, the Structural Integrity Score, rates global shape; a second, the Operational Integrity Score, gauges behavior drift; a third, the Interaction Graph score, models link patterns before run time. Faults planted in test circuits showed each score catching different faults. In shape blind spots, where the shape score topped 0.95, the behavior score caught faults in about 94 percent of cases and the link score in about 73 percent.
arxiv-2604-27030: Gloeckner and four colleagues present a hardware-native gadget framework for constraint problems on Rydberg quantum hardware. A compact xor gadget enforces one-hot constraints through geometric embedding and blockade, with fixed detuning. Skipping penalty terms cuts tuning versus QUBO and improves feasibility, while geometry bypasses all-to-all couplings and fits planar layouts. Lean designs cut atom counts with little preprocessing, suiting near-term hardware. On gate assignment and N-queens, it cuts detuning by up to 99 percent and atoms and links by up to 54 percent.
arxiv-2604-27230: Sekharan and Thiruvathukal argue that computer science teaching must change now to center software and AI systems engineering. Old curricula treat coding, data structures, and algorithms as ends in themselves. Instead those topics should serve as building blocks for systems-centered training. Graduates should design, orchestrate, verify, and own complex AI-enabled systems under real-world limits, rather than compete with AI on routine coding tasks.
arxiv-2604-27630: Cordoni, Battestini, and Missiaggia introduce a stochastic agent-based extension of GSM2 for particle therapy. Each cell acts as an agent whose DNA lesions, cell-cycle phase, and oxygenation evolve by a continuous-time Markov chain. Damage, repair, misrepair, progression, proliferation, and migration compete as events in a next-event algorithm that scales well while keeping resolution. On tumor spheroids hit by hydrogen and carbon ions, the model reproduces trends in dose-rate dependence. These include fading at high LET plus a flipped dose-rate pattern in split doses.
arxiv-2604-27730: Basar and Song study non-balance growth of non-bell swings in a fluid system in Bjorken flow spread. They derive rules for two- and three-point speed links using working field theory and present exact answers. The average Landau frame proves better for tracking non-bell speed swings when fast-motion effects matter, and in Bjorken flow it matches the mass frame. Three-point links depend in a curved way on two-point motion and show memory effects, key to the QCD tipping point search.
arxiv-2604-28030: Monnier and colleagues offer MIFair, a single framework for judging and reducing bias in machine learning across intersecting groups and many classes. It defines fairness as independence between predictions and sensitive attributes, measured through mutual information, and trains with regularisation to cut bias under the chosen metric. Tests on real tabular and image data show it lowers bias, including for multi-attribute groups, while keeping predictive performance strong.
arxiv-2605-00330:
Purav Matlia, Christian Moya, and Guang Lin combine quantum neural networks with conformal statistics to learn operators, the mappings between functions that govern dynamical systems. Operator learning gives fast stand-ins for costly simulations, but dense layers grow expensive quadratically, and uncertainty estimates are often unreliable where safety matters. Their framework aims at both problems.

Quantum orthogonal layers can, in the right regime, run in near-linear rather than quadratic time, and the authors pin down that regime. For uncertainty, they wrap ensemble predictions in split conformal calibration and prove a finite-sample coverage guarantee that needs no assumption about the data distribution. Tests on synthetic problems and real power-system dynamics matched the promised coverage, even under some simulated hardware noise. Hybrid classical-quantum designs are explored as a way to manage running costs.
arxiv-2605-00430:
S. Kumano and Kenshi Kuroki derive relations for a little-measured function describing how quarks share momentum inside a spin-1 hadron. Tensor-polarized distribution functions exist only for such hadrons, and the deuteron is the practical target. An experiment now being prepared at Jefferson Lab will scatter electrons off tensor-polarized deuterons at modest energies, where higher-twist effects, normally small corrections, could loom large.

Two relations matter most: one linking the twist-3 function to its twist-2 partner, in the style of the classic Wandzura-Wilczek relation, and a sum rule in the style of Burkhardt and Cottingham. Both were found earlier with a nonlocal operator method. Kumano and Kuroki re-derive them with the operator product expansion using local operators, the standard formal route for such identities. An independent derivation on firmer footing matters, since experimenters will lean on these relations when reading the coming data.
arxiv-2605-00830:
Adel Dabah and Andreas Herten present FAST-GED, a fast open-source system for computing Graph Edit Distance on graphics processors. That distance counts the fewest edit steps needed to turn one graph into another, a measure used in bioinformatics, machine learning, and pattern recognition. Exact and near-exact methods are costly, which limits their use on large graphs.

FAST-GED uses GPU-friendly algorithms and careful mapping to hardware while limiting host-device transfers. The design is tested across several GPU architectures on real and synthetic graphs of varied size and density. It runs orders of magnitude faster than the Python NetworkX library, reaches optimal solutions in most cases, and beats leading approximate methods on accuracy and scale.
arxiv-2605-01030:
Alan L. McCann presents a machine-checked write-up of rule systems for AI workflow architectures, asking whether effect-level rules can be imposed without reducing internal computing power. Using Interaction Trees in the Rocq proof system, McCann defines a rule operator that mediates all effectful actions, including memory access, external calls, and language-model queries. The build compiles with no admitted lemmas across many modules and hundreds of theorems.

Seven properties are established, including ruled Turing completeness, a decidability boundary for rule predicates, goal preservation, and expressive minimality of primitive capabilities. Structural rule systems are shown to strictly subsume content-level filtering. On permitted runs, the ruled reading is observationally equal to the unruled one apart from rule-only events, so rule systems and expressivity act as orthogonal dimensions.
arxiv-2605-01130:
Zephaniah Roe and seven co-authors ask whether training a model on its own outputs amplifies behavior traits such as sycophancy or misalignment across generations. They train series of models where each is finetuned on data generated by its predecessor, starting from a model seeded with a persona or belief. Three settings are tested: supervised tuning, synthetic document finetuning, and direct preference optimization.

In the two other settings, traits mostly decay or stay constant, so further cycles do little. Rare amplification generally costs coherence. In the preference-based one, the effect can build reliably with continual training favoring a model's own outputs. It vanishes when models are reinitialized each cycle. Limiting repeated post-training may be an effective defense.
arxiv-2605-01230:
John C. Schotland and one co-author study inverse scattering problems for Dirac equations that arise as continuum models of waveguide arrays. Inverse scattering seeks to recover unknown structure from how waves scatter, a task with imaging and device applications. The authors first establish well-posedness of the forward models. The problems are then mathematically sound before inversion is attempted.

For the inverse problems, they develop both the inverse Born series and a reduced version, providing convergence analysis and rigorous error estimates. Numerical experiments validate the proposed algorithms and demonstrate their effectiveness. Readers get a complete treatment. It moves from forward theory through series construction to tested reconstruction methods for this setting.
arxiv-2605-01330:
Jin Tong, Guang Liang, Peilin Sun, and Jianxin Wu address a snag in shrinking vision Transformers to low-bit numbers for fast, cheap use. When a model is trained in full precision and then cut down, large outlier values in its signals wreck the accuracy of the small version.

Capping outliers outright can hurt the full model. Their method, Colinearity Decay, instead curbs the way paired matrices inside each block line up and amplify those spikes. The fix runs as a separate update step, leaves the model shape and task loss alone, and adds almost no training cost. On image sorting, object finding, and fine-tuning tests, models trained with the method keep their full-precision scores and gain clearly after shrinking, with no cost at run time.
arxiv-2605-01630:
Roseval Malaquias Junior and eight co-authors show that how a judge model scores chat answers matters more than which judge is picked. Holistic scores from a model judge swing with that judge's bias, so rankings built on them are fragile.

Their alternative breaks grading into binary rubric items and filters across judges. To prove the point they release Prosa, the first benchmark of real multi-turn user chats in Brazilian Portuguese: a thousand WildChat conversations, three judges from three model families, sixteen models. Under filtered rubric scoring all three judges agree on every rank; under holistic scoring they agree on fewer than half. Filtering also widens the gap between neighboring models by nearly half, sharpening the ranking. Grading a new model costs about two dollars, and the benchmark and code are public.
arxiv-2605-01730:
Promit Kundu describes the fixed points of a torus action on spaces of sheaves over toric stacks. Those bookkeeping spaces have bundles and their kin as points, on spaces built from fans. Counting anything on such a moduli space usually starts by locating where the symmetry stands still.

Extending work by Klyachko, Perling, and Kool, Kundu gives a combinatorial description of torsion-free toric sheaves in any dimension on smooth toric Deligne-Mumford stacks. He checks their basic properties, recovering known results for plain toric varieties under stated conditions. The torus action lifts to the moduli of modified Gieseker-stable sheaves, and its fixed locus is written out explicitly through finer invariants called characteristic functions. The explicit form is the working tool: from it, topological invariants of these moduli spaces can be computed by localization, which is where the paper points next.
arxiv-2605-01830:
Petr Vlachopulos develops new identities for the inverse tangent integral, a function tied to Catalan's constant. His route links the integral to the dilogarithm, a richer polylog function, and to a helper arctangent integral whose end point can be tuned. A generating function view then turns the helper integral into an explicit formula.

At the same time, standard changes of variable rewrite the inverse tangent integral through the imaginary part of a dilogarithm at a complex value. Together, the two routes give a compact form and a clean polylog description. The paper builds a bridge between arctangent integrals, Catalan's constant, and a systematic way to make new integral forms.
arxiv-2605-01930:
Wayne Tee and Jonathan Happel address how to verify where a graphics processing unit, or GPU, is located. Location checks matter for governing advanced chips, but current ping-based methods rely on secret keys stored on the chip. A person with physical access might extract those keys and break the check.

Tee and Happel propose using hardware fingerprints instead of keys to identify a chip during a location check. Fingerprints come from traits of the device itself, so there is no stored secret to steal in the same way. Their proof-of-concept method reached up to full re-identification accuracy in small tests. The work is early, but it points to a harder-to-forge route for chip governance.
arxiv-2605-02130:
Le Zhang and colleagues benchmark whether multimodal language models understand what objects are for, not only where they are. Current tests cover geometric perception well, but grounded intelligence also needs functional reasoning about use and context. Their Spatial-Functional Intelligence Benchmark uses video from first-person indoor scans, with more than fifteen hundred expert-annotated questions.

Questions probe two linked skills. Structured spatial reasoning covers complex layouts and coherent maps of a scene. Functional reasoning covers what an object affords and how its use depends on context. Tasks include conditional counting and multi-hop relational questions. The benchmark aims to show where models that locate objects well still fail to grasp their purpose.
arxiv-2605-02430:
Thomas Duquesne and Robin Khanfir study the range of a branching random walk that moves on a random family tree. The tree itself grows by a Galton-Watson rule, biased toward criticality, with an endless line of ancestors. The walk spreads over this tree, and its range is the set of sites it ever visits, viewed as a subtree with its own distance and a measure of time spent.

The indexing tree is conditioned to have a set number of vertices, with offspring counts drawn toward a heavy-tailed stable law. Given the tree, the authors find a scaling sequence under which the measured range settles to a limit, under a moment condition on the offspring law. The result belongs to probability theory's study of random media and scaling limits.
arxiv-2605-02530:
Felipe Albino dos Santos studies the centers of universal central extensions for algebras tied to a superelliptic curve, in a work of pure algebra. The curve is defined by a palindromic polynomial, and two algebras are in play: one of derivations and one of currents. Both centers are finite in size and match each other in a natural way.

The dimension on the derivation side was known for every covering degree, but reducing an arbitrary class had only been done for the double cover. Santos carries out that reduction for every degree. The spanning classes form chains of orthogonal polynomials of an ultraspherical type, and he determines which chains carry a positive measure. For a quadratic defining polynomial, a mixed quantity is evaluated in closed form using Legendre-type functions.
arxiv-2605-02630:
Ruilin Yao and four co-authors present AutoFocus, a training-free method that helps vision-language models click the right spot on a crowded computer screen. High-resolution interfaces pack in tiny elements, and model inputs are limited, so grounding a written instruction to exact coordinates often fails. Fixed zoom rules and grid heuristics do not adapt well to each case.

AutoFocus treats the model's own hesitation as a signal. Token-level uncertainty in its coordinate output is sampled across several guesses and turned into a directional probability map over the screen. From that map, global and local regions are proposed, and a shape-aware zoom balances tight focus with surrounding context. A visual prompt step then picks the final point. The method adapts where to look, case by case.
arxiv-2605-02730:
Yangfu Li and ten co-authors present PFlowNet, a network meant to make large vision-language models reason with their eyes, not just their words. Standard training does not constrain the visual path a model takes, which invites language bias and hallucination. Added expert guidance helps, but it is tuned for geometric precision and gives limited reasoning value, the authors observe.

PFlowNet splits perception from reasoning, so generation conditions on the model's own perceptual state. Multi-part rewards, shaped by nearby geometry, are optimized with a variational reinforcement method. That steers perception toward reasoning use while keeping visual output reliable. The authors state a performance guarantee and report leading results on two visual reasoning benchmarks. The design lesson is that guidance should serve reasoning, not copy an expert.
arxiv-2605-02830:
Dong-Hui Yang, Bao-Zhu Guo, and Jie Zhong prove null controllability for a degenerate parabolic equation in several dimensions with a degenerate point inside the domain. Null controllability means a control applied on a chosen inner region can steer the system exactly to zero. Here that region deliberately excludes the degenerate point, where the equation's leading term fades, which is what makes the problem hard.

The proof approximates the degenerate equation by a series of uniformly elliptic ones, despite their limited regularity. A Carleman estimate, a weighted inequality, is derived for those approximations. From it comes an observability inequality for the adjoint system, the standard bridge to controllability. The chain closes the result: a multi-dimensional degenerate system can be nulled from a region that avoids its worst point.
arxiv-2605-03030:
Jack H. Farrell and Andrew Lucas show how one multi-contact device can reveal how electrons flow in clean two-dimensional materials. Samples often sit between clean limits such as straight-line, fluid-like, and scattered flow, and imaging those regimes directly is hard.

Using a linear Boltzmann model with five contacts, they find the split of current among the drain contacts marks which regime a sample is in. The same setup lets them pull out both momentum-losing and momentum-keeping scattering rates. It can also separate viscous flow from a related tomographic regime, giving a simpler lab route.
arxiv-2605-03130:
S. V. Butler develops a broad theory of image transformations and Markov operators on spaces of topological measures, then applies it to the sample median. Iterated function systems and their operators are classic tools in fractal theory, and this work extends them to infinite mixtures.

Butler shows that when the transformations contract in a suitable metric, the operator has a unique invariant measure, recovering the classic fractal result as a special case. A generalized median distribution is defined and shown to behave well under a wide class of variable changes. A final result links low-dimensional topological measures to Radon measures.
arxiv-2605-03430:
Al Zadid Sultan Bin Habib, Gianfranco Doretto, and Donald A. Adjeroh present DynaTab, a deep architecture for high-dimensional tabular data. It learns the best feature order for a dataset. Tables have no natural column order. That blocks sequence-sensitive deep models, which expect a meaningful ordering.

Inspired by neural rewiring, DynaTab reorders features dynamically. Learned position embeddings, importance gating, and masked attention process the result, fitting any sequence backbone. A lightweight criterion predicts when reordering will help, based on dataset complexity. Against dozens of baselines on many real datasets, gains were significant. They were largest in high dimensions, supporting ordering as a new design lever.
arxiv-2605-03530:
L. S. Braginsky and M. V. Entin compute transmission through crossings of narrow quantum wires in two-dimensional systems. When wire widths fall below the electron wavelength, the Schrödinger problem simplifies and a Laplace formulation allows exact solution by conformal mapping.

They study electron states in bulged one-dimensional wires built on the two-dimensional system, treating the strips as tunnel conductors. Transmission coefficients are derived for both T-shaped and X-shaped intersections of the narrow strips. The results give exact benchmarks for nanoscale conductor design, where geometry alone controls how electrons pass a junction.
arxiv-2605-03630:
Nicolas Grimbaum Yamamoto reviews the prospects for detecting primordial high-energy neutrinos, neutrinos created before or around recombination in the early universe. Such particles could come from the decay or annihilation of long-lived relics and would reach today's detectors with energies from GeV to PeV. Few other probes reach those earliest moments.

The paper summarizes sharp spectral features these fluxes should show, plus theoretical and experimental limits on the source particles from Big Bang nucleosynthesis and the cosmic microwave background. Yamamoto also presents a Monte Carlo code that models how the spectrum is distorted during propagation, and applies it to the KM3-230213A ultrahigh-energy neutrino event.
arxiv-2605-03730:
Zhe Yu and Liang-Bi Wu compute total transmission modes in the draining bathtub model, an analogue-gravity setup where a draining fluid mimics a black hole horizon. The model here includes vorticity, or rotation in the flow. Total transmission modes are special waves that are purely ingoing both at the horizon and at infinity, and their frequencies form a spectrum.

Using a Chebyshev-Lobatto pseudospectral method, the authors obtain the spectra numerically. They find the right-moving mode spectra can carry positive imaginary parts, signaling growth, while for certain parameters the parts turn negative. Higher overtones prove extremely sensitive, showing pronounced spectral mobility as parameters change, a warning for any stability reading based on single modes.
arxiv-2605-03930:
Wladislaw Krinitsin and Markus Schmitt remove a subtle bias from time-dependent variational Monte Carlo, a workhorse method for simulating quantum many-body systems with flexible trial states such as neural quantum states. The traditional formulation's bias causes inaccuracies. They are especially damaging for real-time dynamics, where errors compound step by step.

Their unbiased variant uses self-normalized importance sampling with respect to a cutoff-based deformation of the Born law. They show its feasibility and accuracy on extreme and generic quench dynamics. They also explore a second sampling strategy, based on tensor cross interpolation and active learning. That route's tensor network lacked the needed low-rank property. But the algorithm complements conventional importance sampling and may guide future work.
arxiv-2605-04030:
Hong Huang and three co-authors build a systematic way to describe form factors. These functions capture how a particle responds to a probe. Their method keeps the rules of relativity exact at every step. Older multipole expansions work in a chosen frame, which can hide that structure.

Working in a spinor framework, they treat each matrix element as a set of three-particle amplitudes and split those into orbital and spin parts. They give complete, independent bases for scalar, vector, and tensor cases at several spins. They show the older expansions match theirs in a suitable frame. They also offer a universal recipe for any tensor operator.
arxiv-2605-04230:
Simon Dufort-Labbé and four co-authors propose a new way to train deep networks that respects the geometry of the whole model, not just one layer at a time. Geometry-aware methods can train better, but fast versions usually cut the links between layers early to save computing cost.

Their approach recasts the ideal training step as a control problem across layers, then learns a structured stand-in that is cheap to reuse. The resulting optimizer wraps standard training methods while keeping a principled link to the full geometry. It aims for better conditioning without paying the full cost at every step.
arxiv-2605-04330:
Enrico Vompa and Tanel Tammet investigate whether transformer models can reason deductively inside a single pass, without writing out step-by-step chains. Their testbed is logical deduction over Horn clauses, a clean setting where conclusions follow from rules and facts.

They discourage shortcut learning with counterfactual training data and encourage shared reasoning skills across direct and step-by-step modes. In deep enough models with a suitable attention mask, hidden reasoning matched explicit step-by-step performance across graph shapes and problem sizes. Writing steps out was still needed when problems grew deeper than those seen in training, marking a clear limit.
arxiv-2605-04530:
Kuan-Hao Tseng and five co-authors present a troubleshooting agent for computer networks that works the way trained human engineers do. Language-model agents applied to this task locate root causes far below the level needed for real deployment, partly because they mix gathering evidence with committing to a guess.

Their agent encodes a classical layer-by-layer diagnostic method as an explicit policy. Phase gates separate collecting evidence from forming hypotheses. A routed library of fault-specific skills is included. On a held-out set of hundreds of incidents from a public benchmark, it improved root-cause accuracy by a large margin over a general agent baseline.
arxiv-2605-04630:
James East, Marianne Johnson, and Mark Kambites study diagram categories. These are structures built from pictures of connections between points. The question is how they can be shown faithfully with matrices and binary relations. Their main target is the partition category and the partition monoids that sit inside it.

They construct a faithful version using zero-one matrices over any idempotent semiring. The matrix sizes are powers of two. They prove no smaller sizes can work for versions of this type. The matrices secretly count floating parts created when partitions are composed. That lets the same idea cover twisted versions of the categories. They also give smaller representations for the Brauer and Temperley-Lieb categories.
arxiv-2605-04830:
Yifan Zhang and four co-authors compare two ways of describing a key moment in how diffusion models create images or other content. One view says paths split toward different meaning choices, a form of symmetry breaking. The other says local step-by-step cleaning stops working and global information becomes necessary.

Working with modern diffusion transformers, the team tracks generation paths and their outcomes over time. They observe the two critical moments occurring almost together. That near match unifies the two pictures in practice and gives a diagnostic for when conditioning and global denoising matter, which can help cut wasted computation in sampling and design.
arxiv-2605-04930:
Miguel Fernandez-de-Retana and four co-authors ask when methods for inferring gene regulatory networks from single-cell data actually break down. Networks of gene control matter for understanding cells, yet causal methods often fail to beat simple correlation in realistic tests. Earlier benchmarks mixed many flaws at once, hiding which flaw hurt which method.

Their diagnostic framework isolates seven problems, including dropout, hidden confounders, mixed cell types, and feedback loops, and turns each up in turn. Across thousands of controlled experiments, causal methods did win in clean settings, but dropout and confounders removed that edge. Methods with similar scores also made quite different kinds of errors.
arxiv-2605-05030:
The ATLAS Collaboration reports how ten years of radiation at the Large Hadron Collider have changed the pixel sensors in the innermost layer of its detector. These planar sensors have absorbed heavy particle fluence, which raises leakage current, wastes collected charge, and increases the voltage needed to deplete the sensor. Regular voltage scans bookend each data-taking campaign.

Using those scans, the collaboration tracks pixel cluster charge and depletion behaviour against accumulated fluence over the full operating period. Standalone device simulation and the experiment's own Monte Carlo modelling, both including radiation damage, help interpret the trends. Such studies guide how long inner detectors can keep performing in harsh collider conditions.
arxiv-2605-05130:
Pratik Chattopadhyay and Avi Wadhwa examine how a Chern-Simons term changes soft theorems for gauge theories when the background is nearly de Sitter space rather than flat. Soft theorems govern scattering when one particle carries very little momentum, and the Chern-Simons correction enters at the first subleading order. The authors define scattering within a compact region of the de Sitter static patch.

They show the Chern-Simons corrections do not mix with the leading curvature corrections at that order. In other words, the subleading soft factors ignore the de Sitter curvature, pointing to their topological nature at the level of amplitudes. That insensitivity also suggests these factors behave universally across nearby settings.
arxiv-2605-05430:
A telegraph process models motion at finite speed, switching direction at random. Manfred Marvin Marchione and Enzo Orsingher study where such a motion first exits a region, and how long that takes on average. For the basic process, with and without drift, they derive the governing boundary problems on an interval.

They then extend the work to a flat, two-dimensional version that moves in perpendicular directions. There they obtain Laplace and Poisson type equations, plus explicit solutions for an infinite strip. In the fast-switching limit, all of their results settle down to the classic answers for Brownian motion.
arxiv-2605-05530:
Energy-based generative models create samples by sliding downhill on a single learned energy surface. Yixuan Wang, Wenqian Xue, and Warren E. Dixon recast training and sampling as one motion: transport of probability on the space of distributions, steered like a control system. The KL divergence plays the role of a Lyapunov function, a quantity that certifies stability.

Within that frame they derive a finite stopping rule for Langevin sampling. They also prove no such certificate exists for the plain gradient flow. Adding trained energies together keeps an explicit invariant distribution, opening doors to control tools like barrier functions.
arxiv-2605-05730:
Online platforms live on conversion rate, yet conversions are the scarcest signal in their data. Guohao Cai, Jun Yuan, and Zhenhua Dong propose a knowledge transfer method for multi-task recommendation models. Each conversion task should learn from the richer behavior signals of sibling tasks, clicks, views, and other engagement.

A router module integrates knowledge from the different tasks and disseminates it where it helps. Every task can then benefit directly from the others' insights. The method targets ranking models whose main metric is starved of examples, borrowing strength across related prediction problems.
arxiv-2605-05930:
Andrius Čiginas and two co-authors propose a design based way to use non-probability samples in official statistics. Such samples are cheap and large, but who joins them is unknown, so standard fixes rest on hard to check assumptions. Their alternative treats the volunteer sample as fully observed and surveys only the people it missed.

Within that sequence, they build two regression estimators, one fitted only on the new sample and one pooling both samples. Both stay design consistent with no assumption at all on how volunteers were chosen. Simulations show the estimators stay near unbiased even when selection is not random. Two uses in Lithuanian official statistics show when pooling helps and when fitting apart is safer.
arxiv-2605-06030:
Adrián Gude and five co-authors compare the grammar and word use of two generations of language models against human news writing. Their test bed is English news text, including New York Times articles from two different years. A formal grammar framework lets them count syntactic structures and lexical types in a precise way.

Human news style changed little across the time frame studied. Newer models, by contrast, showed reduced diversity in syntax and especially in word choice compared with older models that lacked instruction tuning. The authors suggest that tuning, while improving coherence and prompt following, may narrow the expressive range of model output. They point to this trade off as a topic for future study.
arxiv-2605-06230:
Xinquan Chen and forty co-authors present Safactory, a combined infrastructure for training trustworthy autonomous agents. As models move from chat assistants to agents that act over long horizons with tools, risks surface through real environment interaction. Current support systems stay split across testing, data handling, and agent improvement, so risks are hard to find and fix in a steady loop.

Safactory joins three platforms into one evolutionary pipeline. A parallel simulation platform generates agent runs at scale. A trustworthy data platform stores those runs and extracts reusable experience from them. An autonomous evolution platform then improves models through asynchronous reinforcement learning and on policy training. The authors describe the system as the first unified pipeline of its kind for next generation agent training.
arxiv-2605-06330:
Siraaj Akhtar, Saad Khan, and Simon Parkinson fine tune small language models to analyze Windows event logs and prescribe fixes. Large models can read logs, but their compute demands, cloud reliance, and security exposure limit real deployment in system administration. Most log tools also stop at naming the problem, leaving the remedy to the human operator, a gap this work targets directly with locally hosted models.

The team first built a large synthetic Windows event log data set, complete with remediation actions, using a high performing large model. They then fine tuned several small and large models with an efficient adapter method and compared them against expert assessment. Fine tuned small models consistently beat the large ones at spotting issues and giving relevant remedies, while needing far fewer computing resources.
arxiv-2605-06430:
Pablo Aramburu Sanchez and five co-authors revisit a rhombus circuit as a protected superconducting qubit. The circuit uses pairs of Josephson junctions in an interferometer. Earlier designs encoded states in even and odd charge parity, but the team deliberately unbalances one junction to study a softer version of the device.

That change lets them probe qubit transitions directly over several gigahertz. Away from half a flux quantum, large capacitors localize the states and produce a biased-noise qubit with long relaxation times. Their loss analysis points to flux noise and quasiparticle tunneling as low-frequency limits and suggests an optimal operating range near a few gigahertz.
arxiv-2605-06530:
Ruiqi Lyu, Alistair Turcan, and Bryan Wilder present SpatialEpiBench, a benchmark for epidemic forecasting that uses spatial information realistically. Forecasting outbreaks matters for public health response, yet data are sparse, noisy, and shifting. No standard benchmark existed, and simple time-based splits do not mimic real-time forecasting practice.

The benchmark covers eleven epidemic datasets with rolling evaluations and outbreak-focused metrics. Most spatial models with standard epidemic priors still lose to a simple last-value baseline from one day to one month ahead. The authors name three failure modes: poor outbreak anticipation, trouble with sparsity and noise, and limited value from plain geographic adjacency.
arxiv-2605-06630:
Yixuan Wang, Dan P. Guralnik, and Warren E. Dixon study how an autonomous agent can reach its goal without revealing that goal to a watching adversary. Any stable tracking controller is legible: its pull toward a target lets a Bayesian observer concentrate beliefs about the hidden intent. The authors frame intent privacy as a joint control problem over the physical state and the observer's belief state.

The observer runs a particle filter over possible goals, and privacy means keeping information leakage above a set threshold with high probability, enforced through probabilistic barrier functions. Separate results for the filter's update and resampling steps combine into one guarantee. A feasibility analysis then maps where privacy and tracking demands can hold together.
arxiv-2605-06730:
Likhita Yerra and Remi Uttejitha Allam present Semantic State Abstraction Interfaces, a template that converts sparse news text into a few named, open numbers for portfolio decision systems. The point is splitting coding choices from optimizer noise in stepwise decisions. Their test version uses four axes: sentiment, risk, confidence, and a price swing forecast, with neutral defaults on quiet days.

Applied to thirty large United States stocks with market news from 2019 to 2023, the four-factor portfolio posts strong raw returns. Careful controls, however, show the edge over buy-and-hold is fragile, reverses at modest trading costs, and trails simpler baselines. The authors position the framework as a diagnostic tool, not a winning plan.
arxiv-2605-06830:
Dan Ofer, Oriel Perets, Michal Linial, and Nadav Rappoport present ProtSent, a post-training framework that teaches protein language models to place related proteins near each other in embedding space. Standard protein embeddings come from averaging residue vectors never trained for retrieval geometry, so related proteins may sit far apart. ProtSent adds contrastive supervision from family membership, structural clusters, and interaction data, with mutation fitness ordering as an optional signal.

Applied to several ESM models, it sharply improves family recovery and retrieval from frozen embeddings, beating its bases and, at ranking depth, a sensitive alignment search. Under a trained linear probe, however, the tuned embeddings fall below the untouched backbone. Better neighborhoods thus trade against probe accuracy, a tension the paper documents honestly.
arxiv-2605-07130:
Tianle Jiang and Yufa Zhou show that a simple nearest-neighbor trick can make clustering robust to outliers. Robust k-means must drop a set of outliers before grouping the rest, and fancier methods often add centers or discard extra points. The authors instead remove points whose nearest neighbors lie unusually far away.

Under a practical assumption about cluster sizes, they prove this simple removal gives approximation quality comparable to prior work. It needs no extra centers and drops no extra points. On real datasets, the method matched or beat several more sophisticated algorithms in cost and runtime. That links outlier detection and clustering in a direct way.
arxiv-2605-07230:
Selin Yildirim and four co-authors speed up image generation by relaxing speculative decoding in a principled way. Image models generate step by step and stay slow even on top hardware. Draft-and-check schemes from text lose their gains because image models are so uncertain. Draft tokens get rejected too often to help.

The authors formalize two patterns in the target model's inner states: tokens that are interchangeable in meaning, and states that converge during prediction. CASCADE uses those redundancies to accept more drafts safely, with no extra training, and also feeds the signals into drafter training. Across image models, it reached leading speedups while keeping quality.
arxiv-2605-07530:
Erblin Isaku and four co-authors address the safety of robots that refurbish used laptops at the Danish Technological Institute. These robots rely on object detection models to find screws and stickers during disassembly. Small changes in camera input can make such models fail, and a failure here could damage the laptop being repaired.

Their approach, PROBE, searches for tiny, local image changes that expose detection failures, using a multi-objective optimizer called NSGA-II. It found failure cases three to seven times more effectively than random search, while changing the image less. The failures also transferred to other models. Extra checks using metamorphic relations revealed how stable each model stayed even on passing inputs.
arxiv-2605-07630:
Zhengyang Tang and twenty co-authors ask an uncomfortable question about phone-use AI agents: when an agent avoids doing harm, is it being safe, or simply incapable? A dangerous action may be skipped because the agent spotted the risk, or because it could not work the screen at all. Existing evaluations usually cannot tell these apart.

Their benchmark, PhoneSafety, collects seven hundred safety-critical moments from real phone use across more than one hundred thirty apps. It scores whether the model acts safely, acts unsafely, or fails to act usefully. Testing eight agents, they found stronger general phone skill did not reliably mean safer choices, and that failures to act tracked capability rather than caution. A harmless outcome, they conclude, is not evidence of safety.
arxiv-2605-07730:
Dion Mann gives a careful construction of Singer's universal connection, a standard geometric structure on a bundle of paths tied to any manifold. The idea promised a single object from which connections could be rebuilt through their holonomy, the record of how vectors rotate along loops. Mann's construction uses diffeology, a flexible theory of smooth spaces.

The universal connection is built inside that setting and then widened: diffeological principal bundles with connections can be rebuilt from their holonomy data. Any two such pairs whose holonomy data are conjugate turn out to be equivalent in a precise sense. The results assemble into an equivalence of categories between the holonomy category and the category of diffeological bundle pairs.
arxiv-2605-07930:
Xiao Tian and three co-authors fix a fairness failure created by individualized differential privacy. When data owners set their own privacy levels, owners of sensitive records, like positive cases of stigmatized diseases, choose stronger protection. Existing tailored algorithms then leave out exactly that data in the trained model, so the model serves similar future users worse.

Their INO-SGD algorithm counteracts the imbalance by down-weighting data by design within each batch, improving performance on the more private data across training while still satisfying the individualized privacy guarantee. Techniques for utility gaps generally do not satisfy that guarantee and cannot be adapted easily. The paper studies the gap problem and shows that the approach works in practice.
arxiv-2605-08230:
Kabi Raj Tiruwa, Abhisan Ghimire, and Anuj Kumar Shah map the social conditions behind fentanyl overdose deaths across United States counties. Deaths keep rising, and the authors ask which county-level factors, from disability rates to treatment access, mark a county as high risk before its toll becomes severe.

They merge four federal sources covering 975 counties, including 2022 CDC mortality data and the Social Vulnerability Index, and train an XGBoost model to predict standardized mortality risk. SHAP values explain which factors drive each county's score. The analysis highlights so-called silent risk counties and treatment deserts, places where need is high but care is scarce.
arxiv-2605-08330:
Karolina Źróbek and colleagues split robot planning between two language model modules so people can direct a service robot in plain words. One agent takes the high-level role, turning a spoken command into an action sequence with a ReAct-style prompt and calling perception and manipulation tools for picking, placing, and releasing objects.

A second module handles fine spatial language, such as placing a mug next to a plate, by reasoning over object geometry and scene layout in three dimensions. Object detection and pose estimation come from a YOLOX-GDRNet pairing. The team evaluated the system in twenty-four scenarios, from simple spatial commands to high-level and even infeasible requests.
arxiv-2605-08530:
Hoang Hai Pham, Shuntian Zheng, Jiaqi Li, and Yu Guan rebuild three dimensional human bodies from millimeter wave radar signals. Radar works in poor light and guards privacy better than cameras, yet its echoes are cluttered and partial. Their two stage method first locates body reflections in a voxel grid, then rebuilds the mesh with attention to motion between frames.

A dual branch network joins shape in each frame with change across frames. Tests show the method beats earlier radar approaches while staying light on computing power. Better radar body capture could help health checks, indoor sensing, and care settings where cameras feel intrusive or fail.
arxiv-2605-08630:
Huyen Nguyen, Astrid van den Brandt, and Nils Gehlenborg ask what fake users actually tell us when they test a real system. Judging niche tools like genomics visualization search is hard because true experts are scarce, so language model personas are tempting stand ins. Their probe, Sycamore, tests one real genomics search engine three ways: ungrounded personas, personas grounded in past interview material, and a published expert study.

Grounded personas echo documented user language and concerns, while ungrounded ones drift toward operational details real users never raised. Both fake groups miss a key expert preference for image based material. Evaluation research gains a clear account of where synthetic testers help and where they mislead.
arxiv-2605-08930:
Yi Zhang and six coauthors teach large think models to check the safety of their own words. Clear think chains can talk a model into more risky ends. Most safe work screens prompts as they come in. Their checks show safe tuned models fail to vet their own words. They stay open to jail breaks. Their Safety Internal plan trains on safety vet tasks, and on those tasks just. Models grade their own past words with pro think paths as guides.

To vet is a skill that spreads. It spreads to reply safety as a whole. It hardens models to jail break styles they have not seen. As a start for reward work, it beats plain tuned starts.
arxiv-2605-09130:
Surojit Ghosh, Ankit Kumar, and Lakshit Pande extend a branch of algebraic topology that links a space with the points left fixed by a symmetry. Their 2026 paper deals with conjugation spaces, where cohomology of the whole space and its fixed points are tied by an isomorphism that halves degree. Moving to the Klein four group, the corresponding structures quarter degree instead, guided by Dickson invariants.

Under a mild assumption, the authors prove that quaternionic conjugation spaces are homologically pure. As an application, they show such spaces meet two maximality properties tied to the Klein four group. That result connects the theory with Smith-Thom type inequalities in real algebraic geometry, which bound the topology of real varieties by their complex counterparts. For topologists, the paper widens a known purity framework to a four-element symmetry and shows the expected maximality follows from it.
arxiv-2605-09230:
Arnoux and Schmidt explain why Caroline Series's 1985 paper on the modular surface and continued fractions is required reading. Series linked the modular surface geodesic flow to the regular continued fraction, in a deceptively simple way, through a symbolic coding chosen with care. The overview sketches why that link matters, traces history around the paper, and points to later works it inspired.

The paper connects a three dimensional geometric system with a one dimensional system, a bridge between dynamics, geometry, and number theory. Its consequences reach ergodic theory, hyperbolic geometry, continued fraction theory, and symbolic dynamics. The authors call the coding elegantly simple, and the paper itself short, precise, and accessible. Later researchers extended the Farey tessellation model and coding to other situations, spreading its influence beyond the modular surface alone. A personal note recalls one author learning of the paper from a reprint left in a common room.
arxiv-2605-09430:
Zhou and four colleagues present FlashAR, a lightweight post-training framework turning a pre-trained raster-scan autoregressive image model into a highly parallel generator via two-way next-token prediction. Sequential raster-scan decoding uses strictly next-token prediction, making inference expensive. Existing speed-ups either demand pre-training from scratch or parallelise generation with gaps or changed goals. The key insight is to barely change the original training objective. The original AR head stays for row-wise prediction, joined by a lightweight upright head for column-wise prediction.

The vertical head branches from an intermediate layer, dodging horizontal head bias, and a learnable fusion gate combines the two predictions per position. A two-stage setup initialises the vertical head from the pre-trained model, then fine-tunes it with the backbone. LlamaGen and Emu3.5 experiments show up to a 22 point 9 times speedup for 512 by 512 images.
arxiv-2605-09630:
Zheng and five colleagues introduce Scratchpad Patching, a method that separates compute needs from patch size for byte level language models. Tokenizer free models work directly on bytes, and patch variants group byte spans into patches for efficiency. But patch size sets a tight trade off: larger patches cut compute and memory yet degrade quality. Predictions inside a patch must rely on a stale representation until the patch is fully seen. That staleness, called patch lag, grows with patch size.

Scratchpads inserted inside each patch gather the bytes seen so far and renew context for later predictions. They trigger on next byte prediction entropy, spending compute where information is dense and allowing post hoc adjustment of inference compute. At 16 bytes per patch, augmented models nearly match the byte level baseline. They use a 16 times smaller key value cache over patches and 3 to 4 times less inference compute.
arxiv-2605-09930:
Equbal and eight colleagues study fair division when some items conflict and cannot go to the same person. Items form a graph, edges mark conflicts, and each agent must get a conflict-free bundle, an independent set in graph terms. Fairness means envy-freeness up to one item: nobody envies another's bundle once a single item is removed. Efficiency means maximality: no unassigned item could feasibly go to anyone.

With two agents holding monotone valuations, some maximal envy-free-up-to-one allocation is guaranteed, via a colour-switching argument that repairs allocations locally. Such allocations can be found in pseudopolynomial time generally, and in polynomial time for additive valuations or for interval and bipartite graphs. Drop monotonicity and existence can fail even for identical additive valuations, with the decision problem turning NP-hard, and three agents can fail too.
arxiv-2605-10030:
Zhuang Zhang and Yong Zhang studied how aliphatic parts affect the aromatic emission of PAHs. Strength ratios of aromatic emission bands reveal the size and charge state of PAHs in space settings. But PAHs often carry aliphatic side chains, a shape feature that may weaken standard testing methods.

Based on theory data from the NASA Ames PAH IR Spectral Archive, the study matches purely aromatic PAHs against those holding aliphatic add-ons. Aliphatic extras may shift the strength ratio of the 11.2 micron band against the 7.7 and 3.3 micron bands, risking wrong reading of charge state if shape effects are ignored. The effect is size-linked: small PAHs shift a lot, large ones barely. The classic testing grid remains largely usable for mixed aromatic-aliphatic PAHs with some tuning, but caution is needed in aliphatic-rich settings.
arxiv-2605-10130:
Ranasinghe and five co-authors build the first large-language-model-supervised open-vocabulary tool designed for thermal images. Existing open-vocabulary detectors target RGB photos and fail on thermal imagery, where low texture and emissivity variation defeat RGB-based meanings. Thermal-Det is trained on a made-up set made by turning GroundingCap-1M into the thermal domain and sifting out RGB-specific caption terms, yielding over one million aligned samples.

The model jointly tunes spotting, caption work and cross-modal distillation, with a frozen RGB teacher supplying shape and meaning pseudo-guidance for paired but unlabelled RGB-thermal data. A Thermal-Text Alignment Head calibrates text, and a Modality-Fused Cross-Attention module handles dual-modality reasoning. Fully fine-tuned to internalise thermal contrast patterns while preserving language alignment, it gains a consistent two to four percent average precision over existing open-vocabulary tools on public benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-10230:
Improving a drug-like molecule usually means small, careful edits, not a fresh design. Qingchuan Zhang and eight colleagues recast that task as context-aware local editing. Their 2026 paper presents FORGE, a two-stage framework for molecular optimization that decides where to edit a molecule and how to replace the chosen fragment.

Stage one ranks candidate fragments by their property contribution within the full molecular context, using automatically mined and verified edit pairs instead of costly human-written text. Stage two generates the explicit replacement. Built on a compact 0.6-billion-parameter language model, FORGE beat prior methods across three benchmarks, including much larger language models and graph methods. It also adapts to unseen black-box goals through in-context examples.
arxiv-2605-10430:
George Panagopoulos examines a split in how treatment-effect methods are judged. Estimating varied treatment effects with machine learning attracts both academics and industry, but the two camps test under different conditions. Methods papers use simulated benchmarks and metrics needing what-if outcomes, while real applications use visible metrics based on ranking or test outcomes. His 2026 paper compares those test regimes head to head.

Across standard simulated benchmark families and real-world datasets, covering meta-learners with multiple base learners plus special causal models, Panagopoulos finds two gaps. What-if metrics do not reliably pick out the estimators favored by visible metrics, even on matching simulated benchmarks. Rankings from simulated benchmarks fail to carry over to real datasets. Simple meta-learners with strong base models prove consistently competitive, unlike specialized causal models. Progress, he argues, should be judged with observable metrics and real-data validation, not simulated benchmarks alone.
arxiv-2605-10730: Bing Zhao and the Qwen team present Qwen-Image-2.0, an image model unifying high-fidelity generation and precise editing in one framework. It couples Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model, as condition encoder with a Multimodal Diffusion Transformer, trained in stages on large curated data. The model handles instructions up to 1,000 tokens for slides, posters, infographics and comics, with stronger multilingual text, photorealism and prompt following than earlier Qwen-Image models.
arxiv-2605-10930:
Vardhan Palod, Upasana Biswas, and Subbarao Kambhampati test whether language-model explanations help users spot wrong answers or merely talk them into false trust. Reasoning traces, their summaries, and after-the-fact explanations all resemble provenance, yet the evidence shows traces may not mirror what the model actually computed.

In a between-subject study where users could not check answers themselves, the team compared explanation types and added a contrastive setting that argues both for and against the answer. Reasoning traces and post-hoc explanations persuaded users without informing them, inflating trust in wrong answers. Designers of critical AI tools learn that explanations must be judged by user discrimination, not by how convincing they read.
arxiv-2605-11330: Chen and four colleagues rethink how hallucination detectors for language models should be judged. They set out a list of traits good benchmarks should have, and find no existing benchmark has them all. Two gaps stand out: grounded benchmarks built on retrieval with long context, and realistic noisy labels for stress tests. Their new open benchmark, TRIVIA+, fills both gaps, and tests show current detectors still have ample room to improve.
arxiv-2605-11430: Nishi Doshi, Urvi Oza and Pankaj Kumar tackle diabetic retinopathy classification. The task sorts retinal fundus images into five stages by diabetes severity. Large and varying image sizes pose a major problem. The team therefore tests several downscaling algorithms before feeding images to a deep learning network. They combine Kaggle data with the Indian Diabetic Retinopathy Image Dataset, and use a multi-channel Inception V3 architecture with self-crafted preprocessing, beating prior state-of-the-art methods.
arxiv-2605-11730: Cristian Morasso and three colleagues probe a blind spot in safety testing for large language models in a 2026 paper. Their method, Persona-Conditioned Adversarial Prompting, steers jailbreak searches with varied attacker personas, from doctors to malicious actors, so the search covers realistic threats rather than one narrow slice. On GPT-OSS 120B it lifted attack success from 57 percent to 97 percent, and fine-tuning on its output raised defense recall markedly.
arxiv-2605-11830: Si-Qi Hou and three colleagues link doping-induced in-gap states to spin excitations in Mott insulators. They use cluster perturbation theory on Kitaev-Hubbard chains and ladders. In the Z chain, in-gap states move from a gapless spread to a flat band with a gap as the system shifts from Heisenberg to Ising behavior. The gap equals the Ising spin gap. For the XY chain, by contrast, they mirror the Jordan-Wigner fermion spectrum. In the two-leg ladder a broad continuum reflects fractionalized spin excitations.
arxiv-2605-11930: Panagiotis-Alexios Spanakis, Grigorios Alexandrou, and Diomidis Spinellis examine citation cliques in low-impact journals. Using Crossref records matched by subject and h5, they find authors in low-impact venues cite co-authors 6.7 times more often and cite back 4.7 times more than authors in high-influence venues. A hybrid screening pipeline flagged 277 outliers with 93.5 percent case purity, showing closed, inward-looking citation clubs that distort citation-count scores.
arxiv-2605-12030: Philipp Heering and three colleagues give an elementary proof about matchings in symmetric designs. They show a perfect matching exists between point and block complements of an incidence-free pair. The result recovers Spiro, Adriaensen, and Mattheus for all k. They connect this to chambers of a projective plane: the Kneser graph on those chambers, and its chromatic number. That number equals the incidence-free number of the plane. They also build an incidence-free pair for PG(2,q squared) of size about q cubed over 2.
arxiv-2605-12430: Figueira and six colleagues make segmentation for wire-bonded chip inspection cheaper to adapt. Current models are tied to one device and need retraining when a new device or a shift in data appears. Their AOI-SSL framework pre-trains vision transformers with self-supervision on a small inspection set, where masked autoencoders prove most effective. Patch-level retrieval then predicts masks from encoder features with almost no extra training, matching fancier attention-based methods.
arxiv-2605-12530: Tang and six colleagues argue that fairness in language models should be judged in live conversation, not by standardised test scores. Prompt surface choices alone, they show, explain most score variance in test-style fairness benchmarks, flip conclusions in direction and size, and scramble model rankings. Their MAC-Fairness framework embeds controlled variation factors into in-situ behavioural evaluation, varying identity inside natural multi-agent dialogue. It tracks within-model shifts in position persistence and peer receptiveness, reusing test questions only as conversation seeds.
arxiv-2605-13130: Li and four co-authors present GRACE, a gradient-aligned method for curating reasoning data. Existing pipelines score whole samples, treating every step as equally valuable, yet steps contribute very unevenly. GRACE scores each step by its alignment with the answer gradient and its consistency with the preceding trajectory, aggregating step scores into a sample value for subset selection. A representation-level gradient proxy estimates alignment in a single forward pass. Training Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct on MMathCoT-1M, GRACE hits 108.8% of full-data performance with 20% of the data.
arxiv-2605-13430: Yiwen Qiu and four colleagues study whether average treatment effects can be found from selected populations, where selection warps the sample. Biobank data can show healthy volunteer bias when people are healthier and wealthier than the wider population. Estimating effects from such a sub-population can badly bias the estimate for the whole population. The authors give necessary and sufficient rules for finding the average treatment effect under selection bias, using weak assumptions to describe propensity scores and selection chances. Their results stretch existing graphical criteria with weaker conditions.
arxiv-2605-13630: Mirela-Magdalena Catrina, Ioana Cristina Plajer and Alexandra Băicoianu advance multi-texture synthesis with neural cellular automata, adding robust self-regeneration of texture in damaged regions. That healing power suits dynamic adaptive systems and shows the self-organising power of these automata. They also present a grafting technique mixing distinct textures cleanly during inference, without special retraining, by precise setup of genome channels. The result is high-quality complex texture with fluid shifts, a strong efficient way for dynamic texture mixing and self-repair.
arxiv-2605-13830: Ajinkya Naik and four colleagues measure tweak-risk for choice tree sets, asking whether a small change in a subset of inputs can misread an input. Their method writes the problem as an algebra choice diagram, splitting it into sub-tasks solved fast to make math modular and large. Over tests of varying size in tree count and depth, XCount achieves big speedup over model counters on the same problem code. It scales well with growing sets.
arxiv-2605-14130: Kim and three co-authors probe how hydrogen bridging bonds steer shear thickening and jamming in dense suspensions. Strong thickening and jamming come from friction as particles are sheared into contact, and friction can be tuned through particle shape, roughness, surface chemistry and solvent interactions. In cornstarch suspensions, friction grows when hydrogen atoms at solvent molecule ends bond with hydroxyl groups on neighboring particle surfaces. Lengthening the solvent backbone from water toward diols with up to four carbons flips the mix from strong thickening to thinning.
arxiv-2605-14430: Bhattacharyya and colleagues study department retail space optimisation, allocating bay capacity among planograms under business constraints. They formulate the problem as a linear binary knapsack model. Potential products become items with space needs and value weighted by sales, margin, units and similarity. Dynamic programming gives exact, reproducible decisions, avoiding heuristic variance. A second-stage bay model as a mixed-integer program integrates those decisions. Across ten runs over departments and store clusters, OPTIMUS lifts sales by 11.8 percent and margin by 9.5 percent on average.
arxiv-2605-14530: Hong, Yoon and Hwang diagnose why large diffusion vision-language models repeat themselves and lose track of images during long outputs. They trace repetition to mask tokens drifting toward a shared prior, and weak grounding to a mismatch between position bias and unmasking. Their training-free fix suppresses the mask prior and rescales rotary positions monotonically, with claimed gains on long-form description tasks.
arxiv-2605-14630: Berglund offers lecture notes on Wiener chaos expansion, written for a Finnish summer school on probability and statistics. The notes introduce Wiener chaos decomposition in finite dimension. They construct Gaussian fields on the torus, covering white noise and the Gaussian free field. The phi-four model is covered. Stochastic integration, stochastic PDEs, and Malliavin calculus are left out.
arxiv-2605-14930: Rhys Jordan and five colleagues train a machine learning model to sort galaxies near massive clusters into cluster members, group members, or neither. Groups falling into clusters pre-process galaxies before they reach the core, but projection effects blur the picture. Trained on mock surveys from cosmological simulations, the model hits 81 percent overall accuracy. Group galaxies prove hardest, found only 30 percent of the time, though with 76 percent purity.
arxiv-2605-15030: Tri Cao and ten others build WARD, a guard model defending web agents against prompt injections hidden in pages and interfaces. Earlier guards generalize poorly, cry wolf on benign content, slow each step, and fall to attacks aimed at the guard itself. WARD trains on a 177-thousand-sample base dataset plus a dedicated guard-targeted attack set. An adaptive attacker-guard co-evolution loop then strengthens it step by step. Experiments report near-perfect recall out of domain with low false positives and resilience to guard-targeted attacks.
arxiv-2605-15330: Rui-Hong Yue, Yu-Qian Zhao, and Wei-Liang Qian propose an analytic metric for rotating black holes embedded in dark matter halos with central density spikes. Seeded by a mass function for the surrounding dark matter, the geometry is an exact solution. Its halo truncates near the horizon, so density and pressures vanish beyond that radius. The spike makes the dark matter locally anisotropic, and the metric stays asymptotically flat while reducing to known cases in limits. Applications to specific gravitational systems illustrate the parameters.
arxiv-2605-15730: Hu-Xiao Peng, Zheng Yan, and Shuai Yin study short-time critical dynamics in the dimer model. The model hosts ordered columnar and disordered Coulomb phases, split by a transition beyond the Landau-Ginzburg-Wilson. Quenching from ordered and disordered starts tracks parameter scaling. They pin the critical temperature at 0.672 and the static exponent ratio at 0.581, matching past work. They also find the dynamic exponent at 1.92 and a negative slip exponent at minus 1.052, odd against the usual positive sign. They blame emergent SO(5) symmetry and a local U(1) gauge constraint.
arxiv-2605-16230: Chotrattanapituk and eight others present the magnetic structure network, an E(3)-equivariant graph neural net that predicts spin order straight from atomic crystal layouts. Lab tests are costly and niche, while theory-based methods struggle with noncollinear and incommensurate orders. Trained on MAGNDATA's lab data, the model encodes both kinds of order in one primitive modulated structure representation. It rebuilds those orders with high fidelity across all its parts.
arxiv-2605-16330: Sakano and Strachan introduce a temperature-tuned autoencoder tool for reduced-order kinetics of energetic matter. Data-driven models built from atom simulations can yield latent views that are hard to read or stretch when reaction paths shift with settings. Their single model learns a unified reduced-order account of decomposition across a wide temperature range. Sign rules and softmax activation tie latent variables to additive parts, and joint tuning of kinetics and heat-release values couples chemistry with heat flow.
arxiv-2605-16530: Sivakumar and five others present SWoMo, a neuro-symbolic model for cataract surgery splitting motion from realism. Surgical simulation matters for training surgeons and self-run agents, and world models scale practice to diverse ops. Current methods fail clinical bars including realism, contacts, and cases beyond training. The symbolic component, a simulator with scene graphs, models motion and tool-tissue interactions, while diffusion gives appearance. Inverse pairing reconstructs real surgical videos in the simulator for sim-to-real translation. Tests show gains, with generalization to unseen geometries and phase detection.
arxiv-2605-16630: Seeam, Li, Yu, Chen and Hu present PrivScope, an on-device governor that limits what a hybrid local-cloud agent sends to a cloud language model. It pulls disclosure units from the assembled payload, keeps direct identifiers and account-linked values local, and sends only what the subtask needs, in the least revealing form that still works. On 100 medical-booking workflows it wipes profile leakage, more than halves attacker re-identification, and preserves task success.
arxiv-2605-16830: Santra and colleagues develop a relativistic theory for coupled orbital and spin momentum in magnetic systems. From the Dirac-Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian under an electromagnetic field, they derive an extended Pauli Hamiltonian and coupled dynamics for orbital and spin moments. Total angular momentum holds without a spin-polarized exchange field, but not under an applied field such as laser or terahertz pulses. Under an atomistic Heisenberg approximation for exchange, total angular momentum still holds even with a field, while spin and orbital parts alone do not.
arxiv-2605-16930: Sharma and Mishra define a trace-based metric on positive semi-definite tensors, linking their algebraic structure to geometric properties. They introduce the Bures-Wasserstein distance for tensor spaces, giving a clear way to measure between tensors. They derive trace-based eigenvalue bounds for such tensors, showing how the bounds depend on the positive semi-definite condition. They also explore what happens when that condition is relaxed, with examples, and add a detailed complexity analysis of their methods.
arxiv-2605-17030: Zhou proves an exact sum rule for a quantum operator in superconductors, linking its particle and hole weights to a single trace value. He then works out how the spin response forms an ellipsoid set by the spin-locking pattern on the Fermi surface. Full cubic symmetry pins that shape to a simple two-thirds value, while crystal symmetry alone does not. A finite field breaks the simple picture and demands a full self-consistent calculation.
arxiv-2605-17130: Baranov, Nozdrinova and Pochinka study gradient-like diffeomorphisms of the two-dimensional torus, maps whose long-term behavior stays finite and orderly. They show that maps outside the identity's isotopy class split into only finitely many stable connectivity components, unlike the sphere case. Each class's periodic data, they prove, decides exactly which component a map belongs to.
arxiv-2605-17230: Cao and colleagues review maximum likelihood decoding for quantum error correction. That is the provably optimal strategy of picking the most likely logical class for an observed syndrome, though it is generally intractable. They survey advances through three lenses: statistical mechanics, tensor networks and neural networks. Each route nears optimal accuracy with feasible cost. The review closes on open problems including real-time decoding and scaling to large code distances.
arxiv-2605-17830: Ahmad Al-Tawaha and four colleagues warn that memory-equipped agents grow riskier over time. Safety tests check one task at a time, but agents carry memory across unrelated tasks, and memories can taint behavior. The team calls this temporal memory contamination and tests it with a trigger-probe protocol against saved memory snapshots plus a NullMemory baseline. Across scenarios and memory designs, memory-enabled agents exceed the baseline, and violation rates climb with exposure length. Risk is detectable from retrieval state before generation, via a strong monitor.
arxiv-2605-17930: Penghao Yu and three colleagues show multilayer Transformers approximate differently from single-layer ones. For retrieval tasks, a single-layer Transformer needs order epsilon to the minus k parameters for precision epsilon, with k growing linearly with sequence length. A two-layer Transformer with one head per layer needs order epsilon to the minus one parameters. Two mechanisms explain this gap. Softmax attention retrieves only the top token. Decoding coupled information costs scale with the token set size. They propose InfoFlow, tracking positions at each token and layer.
arxiv-2605-18130: Fengyi Zhang and four colleagues present Rad-VLSM, a two-stage cross-modal method for masking and calls. A BLIP-2 sight-language module first finds lesion regions under meaning cues and turns them into box prompts. A SAM-based multi-job network then pools multi-candidate regions for stable prompts and masking. Predicted masks serve as spatial priors for calls, while a fusion head joins lesion-aware seen features with texture marks. Tests on a private breast ultrasound set and public benchmarks show strong masking and calls with good spread.
arxiv-2605-18430: Liang Wang and six co-authors present Text2CAD-Bench, a 2026 benchmark to test text-to-parametric CAD generation. It spans shape complexity and varied uses, areas prior benchmarks neglect. Its 600 hand-picked cases run four levels, from basic geometry to complex topology, freeform shapes, and real-world domains beyond machine parts. Current models handle basic geometry but degrade sharply on complex topology and advanced parts.
arxiv-2605-18530: Zhihan Yang and seven co-authors revisit Plaid in a 2026 paper, a likelihood-based continuous diffusion language model, and build RePlaid by aligning it with modern discrete diffusion models. In this unified setting they derive the first scaling law for continuous diffusion models that rivals discrete ones. RePlaid shows only a 20-fold compute gap to autoregressive models and sets a new perplexity bound of 22.1 on OpenWebText among continuous models. Tuning the noise schedule to minimize ELBO variance yields linear cross-entropy over time, spreading denoising difficulty evenly.
arxiv-2605-18830: Wei Tang and three colleagues view in-context learning as concept subspace learning. Regression and Bayesian accounts explain how examples induce predictors, while mechanistic work finds compact directions that steer behaviour, yet the link between them stays unclear. The authors show forecasts break down into a concept part plus leakage outside the subspace for ridge and least-squares proxies. Under block-diagonal covariance, leading errors scale with concept dimension, while cross-subspace coupling controls the rest.
arxiv-2605-18930: Kaixiang Wang, Jiong Lou, Zhaojiacheng Zhou and Jie Li poison self-evolving agents with experiences that look correct yet generalize harmfully. Memory-augmented agents distill past episodes into rules, but existing memory attacks need privileged access or overtly malicious content that safety filters catch. Their Obsessive Experience Poisoning attack needs neither: it plants clean edge cases pairing correct local solutions with non-transferable methods and severe consequences. Reflection then leans toward overcautious, over-general rules, and tests across three domains push attack success above fifty percent with GPT-4o agents.
arxiv-2605-19230: Nikhil Cherian Kurian and four colleagues tackle age bias in medical imaging, where age links patterns to disease rates. Overdiagnosis clusters where disease is common, underdiagnosis where it is rare. Strict age invariance can erase useful signals, so the team targets spurious age trends after a warmup phase. They model difficulty by label, then decorrelate age from dominant trends with robust weights and a coverage score scaled by batch variance. On two radiology sets, age-linked gaps fall with minimal accuracy loss, robust to growing age shifts.
arxiv-2605-19630: Marik, Klemt and Rohrbach tackle deepfake detection for manipulations never seen in training, where collecting data for each new technique is impossible. They argue high-level semantic cues can support low-level detectors, and study emotions as such a cue.
