Their EmoForensics detector uses vision and audio emotion recognition plus intra- and inter-modal temporal consistency in emotion representations from audio-visual streams. Fused with an off-the-shelf RGB- and acoustic-focused detector as EMO-BOOST, it lifts average cross-manipulation generalization AUC by 2.1 percent on FakeAVCeleb.
arxiv-2605-19730: Bimali, McCabe, Treacy, Khanal, Lo and Haji unify the matched eigenfunction method for wave forces on fixed or heaving ring-shaped offshore bodies. Traditional boundary-element solvers bottleneck on added mass, damping and excitation coefficients, while this semi-analytical alternative was never directly benchmarked against them. Their framework handles arbitrary numbers of annular cylinders with smooth radial profiles and maps its matrix structure and convergence. Slanted shapes land within five percent of the Capytaine solver, and convergence arrives an order of magnitude faster with far smaller matrices.
arxiv-2605-19830: Fuentes-Vicente, Even, Dormion, Chambaz, Shalit and Josse propose set valued policy learning, where several treatments may tie or none may help. Single recommendations look arbitrary, eroding trust, so policies output sets of valuable treatments whose size reflects ambiguity. Set policy value uses a choice function, and doubly robust estimators are built for it. Two methods follow: a Greatest Lower Bound approach, and conformal set valued learning bridging estimated and true optimal rules. Synthetic, trauma care and IVF tests show robust policies balancing performance and reliability.
arxiv-2605-19930: Lambrick and colleagues push helium beam imaging to fine detail at a long work gap. The soft neutral beam suits frail and insulating surfaces, but long gap pinhole tools had stayed coarse. By tuning the beam path and rebuilding the pinhole plate, they reach a beam width well under a micron, with sharp views of bacteria and worn diamond.
arxiv-2605-20030: Salil Parth Tripathi and four co-workers let partial optimal transport reject by local information. Partial transport leaves mass unmatched by a global budget, rebate or uniform rule, but tasks need pointwise choices tied to reliability or side information. Their intent-controlled version sets pointwise rejection costs on both measures, reads as acceptance thresholds, and solves as a balanced Kantorovich problem on an augmented support. In positive-unlabelled learning and open-partial domain adaptation it improves baselines, and a satellite-ocean case shows sensor priors shaping which signal compares.
arxiv-2605-20230: Irshadullah Khan and Bilal Khan give the Maxwell codimension-three Riesz-Gaussian form for parallel plates. It extends a scalar version: the same transverse reduction and set-covariance device carry to the Maxwell operator. Fourier study proves the finite-volume gap, compact resolvent, and heat-trace admissibility. For the reduced operator, the Riesz integral yields a mediator, and a heat-regularized Gaussian source has expected Green energy matching the Maxwell trace. Under the finite-part rule, the large-area energy density is minus pi squared hbar c over 720 a cubed.
arxiv-2605-20330: Samuel Schlegel and three co-workers study gravitational entanglement in optomechanics, classical versus quantum models. Gravity-born quantum entanglement is read as proof of non-classical gravity. Most lab work starts from Gaussian states, and weak gravity trims the quantum Newtonian potential to second order. That regime allows a classical Wigner-Weyl account, with traits tied to quantum entanglement. They weigh options and give tests for non-classicality via Wigner negativity and non-quantumness via Weyl operator negativity. Proving such entanglement demands more than once thought.
arxiv-2605-20630: Alimurtaza Merchant and five colleagues speed up industrial agent pipelines for asset operations, where one query can coordinate sensors, work orders, and forecasting tools. Standard caching breaks down when answer validity depends on time, asset, or sensor values. They add a temporal semantic cache plus workflow optimizations, including disk-backed tool discovery and dependency-aware parallel steps. Workflow changes alone gave a 1.67-fold speedup, while cache hits reached a median 30.6-fold speedup.
arxiv-2605-20730: Jihoon Kwon, Jiwon Choi, and Jy-yong Sohn propose distributional alignment as a design criterion for task vectors in in-context learning. Task vectors compress demonstrations into compact hidden-state forms, but quality has been judged only by downstream accuracy. The authors argue that task-vector inference should match in-context learning's predictive distribution. Their d_NTP metric measures the gap in next-token probabilities between the two modes, and it correlates strongly and negatively with downstream accuracy.
arxiv-2605-20830: Semin Kim and ten colleagues present Raon-OpenTTS, open models and data for robust text-to-speech. The part of large-scale open data in recent speech progress remains underexplored, though closed-data models set the pace. Their pooled dataset aggregates 615,000 hours and 240 million speech segments from public English corpora and web recordings. A model-based filtering pipeline derives a curated core of 510,000 hours and 194 million segments, used to train diffusion-transformer models from 0.3 to 1 billion parameters.
arxiv-2605-21230: Nitin Yadav and Apanba Khuman ask how solar vortices shape waves and heating. They run high-resolution three-dimensional simulations of magnetized solar plasma. Slow waves climb field lines, grow in the layered air, and steepen into shocks in the chromosphere, driving repeat plasma surges. Lines through vortices run hotter than other lines. Yet shock heights show no clear gap, so spin heats plasma without moving where shocks form.
arxiv-2605-21730: Liu and colleagues study fast high-latitude jets in the upper atmosphere of Mars. They use MAVEN wind data and runs of the Mars climate model. Non-orographic gravity waves, ripples not tied to surface mountains, speed and slow these jets by about 280 meters per second. The push comes from momentum divergence driven by wave saturation and wind filtering. The waves shape the jets mainly in the hemisphere of the Hadley cell's descending branch, where no critical layers block them in the middle atmosphere.
arxiv-2605-21930: Tasfia Tasnim and Soneya Binta Hossain present PITMuS, a tool that turns bytecode-level mutation reports from the Java tester PIT into source-level mutant pairs. PIT reports mutation metadata rather than the source edits, so its mutants are hard to inspect, replay, and reuse. PITMuS reconstructs the original and mutant source methods for each report. From 69,229 reported mutations across 1,913 files, it produces 69,198 source-level pairs, covering 99.96 percent of the records for testing, repair, and learning-based software work.
arxiv-2605-22130: Gwynn and co-authors test whether chiral-induced spin selectivity can enhance radical pair dynamics across a broad parameter space. The effect lifts magnetic sensitivity in radical pair models under specific Hamiltonian conditions, but wider persistence was untested. They model the effect as a spin-dependent starting state and recombination operator for a model radical pair. Gains in the single-nucleus model are largely suppressed by a second nucleus, except where tensor misalignment drives a robust antisymmetric response. Sustaining it thus needs highly ordered, rigid molecular geometries.
arxiv-2605-22230: Backis and co-authors measure alpha background in multi-grid neutron detectors from actinide impurities in aluminum. Alpha rates from radio-pure aluminum and aluminum/B4C composite grids were measured with a large-area low-background spectrometer. Composite rates run about 280 times higher than radio-pure aluminum, yet 25 micrometer nickel plating cuts the composite rate by about 1170 times. Two prototypes with identical B4C-coated radio-pure normal blades differed only in radial blades. The nickel-plated composite prototype background runs around 20 percent of the radio-pure prototype.
arxiv-2605-22330: AbdusSalam tackles the cost of adding Large Hadron Collider limits to global fits of physics beyond the Standard Model. Checking each parameter point takes too long for live fits. He uses symbolic regression on ATLAS electroweakino search constraints to derive a formula that classifies parameter space as allowed or excluded. The formula then joins a global fit of the phenomenological Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, including Run-2 limits. The approach makes collider limits usable inside ongoing fits rather than after them.
arxiv-2605-22430: Hartman and Kalantar prove that a simple reduced crossed product forces a stabiliser with trivial amenable radical. The setting is a minimal group action on a compact space. From this, they characterise simplicity for reduced crossed products of minimal actions. Covered classes are countable linear groups, hyperbolic groups, and groups with countably many amenable subgroups. The result answers Ozawa's 2014 question for these classes. For infinite uniformly recurrent subgroups of C*-simple groups, almost every subgroup has trivial amenable radical. The measure is fully supported and atomless.
arxiv-2605-22530: Herd and team present a method for live safety cases, adding live trust changes. Trust is scored across the project by mixing design-time data and recent live SPIs in one Subjective Logic case. SPI data is checked nonstop. Set claims update by a rule: trust rises without breaches and falls fast after them. The design prizes safety-first speed over exact old Bayesian after-the-fact updates. The team shows the method on a mock roadwork zone assist with an ML cone detector, showing trust shifting.
arxiv-2605-22630: Pérez Sar and others test how void crossed with cosmic microwave background lensing signals respond to method choices, using Roman mock catalogues. They find the signal less sensitive to mock construction than galaxy or void statistics, so future tensions are unlikely to stem from mock errors alone. The best signal to noise comes from two dimensional voids with rescaled profiles. Forecasts reach about 13 sigma for two dimensional and 8 sigma for three dimensional voids with Planck, rising to about 31 sigma and 18 sigma with a CMB-S4 like survey.
arxiv-2605-22830: Magarshak presents Intercloud, a decentralized economic network in which watcher swarms secure private data streams by observing only cryptographic hashes, never plaintext. Security rests on two ideas: ripple identifiers that stop any ripple repeating through a node in one epoch, and consensus by attesting that no conflicting evidence exists. A swarm of about 35 watchers, the paper argues, suffices to block double-spending, and conflicting attestations yield self-certifying proof of corruption.
arxiv-2605-22930: Rana and Jain determine Rogosinski radii for some subclasses of close-to-convex functions on the open unit disc. They also establish improved versions of the classic Bohr inequality and the Bohr-Rogosinski inequality for these subclasses. All results in the study are shown to be sharp, meaning the bounds cannot be tightened for the classes considered. The work refines Bohr-type estimates within this corner of complex function theory.
arxiv-2605-23030: Mugambi and four coauthors propose an impedance-based method for judging stability margins when a new offshore wind power park joins an existing cluster. Many studies lean on Nyquist encirclements without quantifying margins. Their method evaluates margins at the existing connection after integration and derives a maximum allowable impedance for the new link, so operator margin requirements hold. New Nyquist-based stability regions complement the generalized Nyquist criterion. Vendor-based case studies with two wind plants and an HVDC link validate the approach.
arxiv-2605-23130: Bappy and seven coauthors study how AI coding assistants reshape coder security mindset in real practice. Talks with 15 coders plus watched security tasks show they shift rather than erase security thinking. Thinking shifts from writing code to review. This early to reactive shift is pushed by tools that frame making as a plain task, leaving security as an extra. Notably, no person listed security needs in initial prompts, even when they knew them.
arxiv-2605-23230: Fan and three coauthors propose a smooth model for transit designs under mixed demand. Old studies assume rigid line layouts, but their model lets bus lines route flexibly and form layouts with detouring, merging, and diverging. Their mixed networks enlarge the class of mixed designs. To solve the tuning problem, they develop a sequential shape solver. Under mixed demand, their model cuts overall costs by over 7 percent against existing homogeneous models. Findings show the model beats old counterparts, and flexible designs help most in large-area cities.
arxiv-2605-23330: Jin and three coauthors study the safety, privacy, and ethical risks and tracking risks of OpenClaw, a local AI agent system for natural language talk and real-world tasks. They focus on the risks of stored data, tool calls, cross-context pooling, multi-user talk, and the linking of plugins and outside tools. They argue that these issues are major blocks to the safe use and uptake of this tech. They list the open risks in safety guards, privacy care, ethical rules, and tracking in agent use.
arxiv-2605-23430: Lewis and Short unify three classical geometry theorems with full converses in hyperbolic space of several dimensions. The three are Penner on horocycles, Ptolemy, and Casey. Building on Waddle's observation that the three theorems share underlying equations, they derive all three from one Gram-matrix calculation over lightlike, timelike, and spacelike vectors in the Lorentzian model. The same route yields a planar Casey theorem with a full converse and three geometric alternatives, a version the authors believe is new.
arxiv-2605-23530: Naud studies singular values of transfer operators twisted by large random permutation matrices. In the large N limit he obtains a Weyl law for those singular values, valid asymptotically almost surely with rapid decay. He also extends the polynomial method to an infinite-dimensional setting, which yields a smooth probabilistic Weyl law for singular values.
arxiv-2605-23830: Łukasz Pawela and Zbigniew Puchała release a Julia package for exact symbolic averages over compact groups, a staple calculation in quantum information and random matrix theory. IntegrateUnitary.jl handles unitary, orthogonal, symplectic and special unitary groups, plus circular, Gaussian and Ginibre ensembles, permutation groups, random states and unitary designs, using Weingarten calculus and Wick contractions. Some high moment and matrix valued jobs still need concrete dimensions, but broad symbolic dimension support is built in.
arxiv-2605-23930: Mankarious introduces Quantum Frog, a cooperative game in which time moves only when a player acts, and two frogs must cross an eight-by-eight grid of traffic. Training agents through five stages, from table learning to multi-agent policy optimization, he finds rushing straight up always best, since less time in traffic means less risk. An uncoordinated second player hurts more than sixfold traffic, yet training recovers 32 to 34 points of success and cuts episodes from about 90 steps to six. The winning tactic is synchronized rushing, not fancy positioning.
arxiv-2605-24330: Kiyohara and six co-authors propose Interdomain Attention, mixing attention with recurrent memory in one layer instead of stacking separate layers. Viewing attention as kernel regression, the design squeezes key features and values into recurrent memory run by a state-space model. It rebuilds attention values from memory states. The design keeps the memory model's speed edge. Text-trained models from 125 million to 1.3 billion parameters beat an S4D baseline at equal memory size. On genome data with a Caduceus base, it matches or beats the original.
arxiv-2605-24530: Hao Sun and colleagues present Unveil, a 2026 system for finding multimodal documents that mixes words and layout instead of text parsing alone. Text-only tools ignore layout and often misread, while image-only tools miss fine word meaning in text-heavy pages. Unveil first learns a joint word-and-image embedding, then distills it into an image-only model for fast parsing-free search. Tests show the joint model beating prior methods, with distillation closing most of the semantic gap.
arxiv-2605-24630: Adam Lee presents DexSIM, a 2026 system for copying deft hand-object handling in real time with unified causal video diffusion. A two-stage scheme first trains a two-way video diffusion model mixing hand trajectories and video, using Gaussian heatmap hand codes. Self-feeding training with a spatial cache as focus sink then lifts long-term consistency and 3D sense. DexSIM tops the old bar on motion fidelity, hand projection accuracy, and pixel and semantic similarity. It runs at 15.24 frames per second and allows hand motion transfer.
arxiv-2605-24730: Jeremy Bertomeu studies sender-receiver games where reports are costly to move away from anchors seen in private. An analyst might anchor on a proprietary model, an auditor on an internal score, a manager on an estimate. Because senders face different costs, anchored reporting yields steady variation in messages rather than partitions. Small positive costs for moving a report can bring communication near full revelation; zero costs return the game to cheap talk. Uninformative anchors can still transmit information through distortions, yet cheap talk alone wins when misalignment is low.
arxiv-2605-25130: Ravi Jaiswar and colleagues test how much the choice of analysis method changes the inferred properties of distant galaxies seen as analogues of the reionization era. Combining spectra and images with three fitting codes, they find stellar mass estimates shifting by over 0.6 dex. Star formation rates shift by more than 0.9 dex. The ionizing photon output varies even more between methods. Claims about how reionization unfolded can therefore hinge on method alone, including whether its efficiency appears to evolve with redshift.
arxiv-2605-25230: Andrew Corbett and colleagues treat the step-by-step reasoning of tiny recursive networks as approximate inference over hidden thought paths. Their guided stochastic exploration nudges those paths with small random tweaks, then lets the model's own stopping rule reweight the candidates as they form. Three diagnostics computed from inference traces alone forecast whether the trick will help and which answers to trust. On an extreme Sudoku set, exact solves jump from about 86 percent to 98 percent with no retraining.
arxiv-2605-25330: Qian Zhang and colleagues show standard scores for generative recommenders can mislead when item codes collide. Semantic-ID systems give each item a token sequence, and evaluation matches generated sequences to target sequences. That scoring stays honest only when each sequence names one item, yet collisions reach about 31 percent across tokenizers and datasets. The team introduces collision-corrected metrics and a reassignment method that rebuilds collision-free codes cheaply. Under honest item-level scoring, inflation grows with collision rate and can flip the winning tokenizer, casting doubt on past rankings.
arxiv-2605-25430: Yanzhou Li and colleagues let coding agents evolve reusable skills, not fixed prompts and heuristic updates. Their CODESKILL framework treats skill extraction and bank upkeep as a learnable policy, trained with reinforcement learning. Skills are extracted at several granularities from trajectories, updated with experience, and kept in a compact bank for future tasks. A hybrid reward mixes rubric skill-quality feedback with sparse execution feedback from a frozen agent. Tests on three benchmarks show the method beats no-skill setups by 11.03 and the strongest prompt or memory baseline by 5.10.
arxiv-2605-25730: Tabib, Bayzid and Rahman examine what happens when Segment Anything Model masks are fed back as prompts. That loop can cause decoder coupling drift, where the mask decoder's cross-attention slowly drifts from the target and errors compound. They probe SAM's decoder and derive ground-truth-free measures for coupling, attention stability and temporal consistency, all without labeled data. On electron microscopy volumes, iterative prompting harms alignment against oracle-anchored feedback. Their DeCoDrift framework constrains prompt updates at run time without new training, lifting stability and quality.
arxiv-2605-26030: Pravash studies dust-grain alignment in the fringes of bright-rimmed clouds and cometary globules. Non-round grains lined up with magnetic fields polarise starlight and dust glow, tracing field shape and strength. The top theory says light-driven torques twist grains into line. Pravash uses optical polarisation of background stars toward nine clouds, with star distances and dimming data from Gaia and StarHorse. He tracks how well grains polarise light and how field direction shifts in diffuse cloud fringes.
arxiv-2605-26130: Luitel and thirteen colleagues present AirCast-SR, a foundation model raising global AI weather forecasts from about 28 kilometres to one. Fine-scale forecasting stays too costly for classic numerical models, limiting fine guidance for energy, farming and disaster work. AirCast-SR downscales GraphCast forecasts to hourly fine fields, giving 67-hour forecasts for eight linked surface variables. A three-dimensional U-Net in a latent consistency diffusion framework learns from United States patches, with NOAA analysis data as target. Near-zero bias and strong skill support climate services and hazard forecasts.
arxiv-2605-26330: Deepak Singh and three colleagues build NightSight, a lightweight perception system that lets small aerial robots navigate in complete darkness. It joins a monocular event camera with a coded aperture lens, plus an infrared dot projector. The pattern, seen through the coded aperture, yields depth-dependent blur signatures that encode scene geometry. A convolutional network trained only on synthetic planar-wall data decodes those signatures into dense depth maps. It generalizes zero-shot to complex real scenes at twenty hertz on a Jetson Orin Nano.
arxiv-2605-26530: Chen Linze, Cai Yufan, Hou Zhe, and Dong Jin Song want legal AI to react only to material changes. Systems should hold steady under irrelevant tweaks, shifting only when material points change. Their suite covers change and no-change cases in fairness, robustness, and statute-confusion settings. Existing models prove sensitive to irrelevant shifts and confuse elements and statutes. Their LexGuard framework turns statutes into constraints, pits rival agents against each other over fact-statute arguments, and checks satisfaction and logic with SMT solvers. Tests show better reliability and stability.
arxiv-2605-26730: Ngoc and ten colleagues build PRISM, a benchmark for judging automated peer reviewers of machine-learning papers across four dimensions: depth of analysis, novelty assessment, flaw spotting, and constructiveness. Unlike surface scores or free-form judge prompting, PRISM grounds each dimension in argument mining, retrieval checks, and consensus scoring. Tests cover five reviewer systems and human reviewers. Language models can match or beat humans on single dimensions, but none matches the balanced human profile overall.
arxiv-2605-26830: In a 2026 paper, Saketos and Xiao present Kalman Evolve, a framework that discovers better Kalman-style filters by optimizing both noise parameters and update structure together. Large language models propose interpretable, non-affine tweaks to the classic filter while keeping its recursive form, motivated by proofs that affine estimators fall short under nonlinear sensing. Across Doppler radar, LiDAR, and pedestrian tracking benchmarks, the discovered filters beat strong baselines, cutting error by up to 12 percent.
arxiv-2605-27030: Wang and eleven co-authors present Collaborative Parallel Thinking, a training-free method that lets parallel test-time search branches share discoveries. Standard parallel methods isolate branches, so each rediscovers facts others already found. CPT pools compact intermediate findings, deduplicates them, and broadcasts them through input context for later steps. On HMMT and AIME benchmarks, it sets a stronger accuracy-latency frontier than strong baselines across budgets and model sizes.
arxiv-2605-27130: Donaghy and Rastogi present DEI, a quality-diversity framework. It assigns language models as mutation operators across nodes using async operations. Rather than replicating one model's biases on every worker, DEI treats each model's prior as a source of novelty. Nodes share optima each round to seed the next population. On the Core War domain, where Redcode warriors battle inside a machine, a four-node mixed ensemble beats a single-node baseline by 124 percent on QD score and 28 percent on coverage. It beats a budgeted homogeneous ensemble.
arxiv-2605-27230: Bag and co-authors introduce a direct probe of the current dark energy equation of state. Standard reconstructions differentiate the expansion history, which amplifies noise, but their w0-probe is built from the Om diagnostic and reads the current value straight from the expansion rate. It keeps the null test for the standard cosmological model while giving a direct estimate. Applied to supernova, baryon acoustic, and microwave background data, both diagnostics exclude the standard model at 95 percent confidence, with the new probe favoring a current value near minus 0.6.
arxiv-2605-27330: Yunbi Nam and colleagues extend two-phase sampling designs to studies with ordinal outcomes. They propose three outcome-informed ways to pick the phase 2 subset, then build valid estimation methods around them. Simulations beat simple random sampling, and a sepsis trial example links interleukin-6 to a four-level clinical status outcome.
arxiv-2605-27630: Yujia Xu, Zhiheng Wang, and Thi Dinh verify language-model optimization agents inside the coordination loop itself. Their OptiLoop pipeline generates local agents from text, checks them in brief capped coordination trials against a fixed reference partner, and repairs failures from structured behavioral evidence. On 40 held-out scenarios, objective match rises from about 66 percent to about 93 percent, and mean objective gap falls from about 15 percent to about 4 percent.
arxiv-2605-28030: Chen and colleagues defend language models against harmful fine-tuning attacks that strip safety alignment. SPARD alternates utility updates with safety projections onto curated safe data, chosen to balance relevance and diversity. Under four attacks it posted the lowest attack success rates among rivals while keeping task accuracy high on standard tests.
arxiv-2605-28230: Hassan and colleagues let frozen video generators judge their own physical plausibility. Proprio reads the model's flow residual under small latent nudges as a self-score: better-explained samples yield smaller, steadier residuals. Used for best-of-N search or gradient refinement, it lifted physics scores markedly and won roughly two-thirds of human comparisons for plausibility.
arxiv-2605-28730: Bibek Poudel, Sai Swaminathan, and Weizi Li introduce AlphaTransit, a planning framework for city-scale bus networks. Route building suffers delayed feedback: a useful-looking extension can create bottlenecks, redundant overlap, or lower throughput. AlphaTransit couples Monte Carlo Tree Search with a neural policy network, giving decision-time lookahead without simulator rollouts. On a Bloomington benchmark with realistic roads and census-derived demand, it posts the top service rate in both demand settings. It beats reinforcement learning without search and tree search without learned guidance, gaining up to about 11 percent.
arxiv-2605-28930: Callum Witten and colleagues revisit the apparent surplus of Coma-like cluster progenitors seen by JWST in the first billion years. They show past comparisons mixed two errors. Aperture-summed halo masses were set against virial-radius simulation masses, and backward-tracked growth was used where forward tracking fits better. Fixing both errors, plus merging coincident candidates and cosmic variance, removes the tension entirely: most candidates are likely proto-groups, and none looks set to become a Coma-like cluster.
arxiv-2605-29030: Jean Bertoin and Martin Minchev study relocations to past states in a sub-stochastic Markov chain with killing. Such relocations increase the persistence rate, so survival decays more slowly than the benchmark chain, strictly under mild assumptions. Lower bounds cover the persistence-rate ratio when relocations spread far. The analysis uses ergodic chains with complete connections and a Feynman-Kac approach for persistence.
arxiv-2605-29430: Zixuan Jiang frames Interactive ASR as a multi-turn task. Most speech recognition systems follow a single-pass pattern, poorly aligned with human talk, where mix-ups are resolved through iterative follow-ups. Their Agentic ASR system combines a single-pass front-end with meaning fixes, intent routing, and reasoned editing. Tests on many-language and code-switching benchmarks show back-and-forth interaction always reduces meaning errors. Gains are much larger in the meaning metric than in token-level metrics.
arxiv-2605-29730: Phuc-Dang Truong and seven colleagues model how spin-orbit coupling shapes flat five-sided MS2 sheets for silicon, germanium, and lead. Their density functional runs find the silicon sheet likely unstable, while the germanium and lead sheets hold. Coupling tightens electron placement, shrinks the lattice slightly, and rebuilds states near the Fermi level, more so for heavier metals. Germanium disulfide stays metallic, but lead disulfide flips to a semiconductor with a near-direct gap, looking promising for gas sensing.
arxiv-2605-29930: Toru Takahashi argues public disagreement runs deeper than clashing values, since seeing is not yet judging. Not every sight earns inferential weight, and not every object in a sight sequence becomes a target. A target counts only when a state picture nearly suffices for prediction, evaluation, or action. Recognition is rebuilt as building near-sufficient pictures under tight limits, under the Multi-Phase Inference Assumption and its Multi-Phase Inference Mechanism engine. Alignment maps and transformation loss show how unlike world models can talk without merging into one.
arxiv-2605-30330: Benjamin A. Burns and Sara Fridovich-Keil ask when, why, and how diffusion posterior samplers fail, via a finite-sample lens. They give a finite-sample view of the posterior as training set size grows. With this lens, approximations tend to misjudge posterior spread at middle steps. This causes early stopping errors, mode weighting errors, and hallucination. They find these errors need neither a nonlinear model nor a multimodal posterior, arising from a multimodal prior and bad posterior spread.
arxiv-2605-30830: Asai and Yamada study when the sign of Ollivier Ricci curvature changes on graphs obtained by removing edges from complete graphs. They define graphs obtained by removing matching edges, incident edges, and cycle edges from complete graphs. The curvature in the three patterns equals the number of triangles including two vertices divided by the maximum degree of the two vertices. The curvature of these graphs is therefore zero or positive. The study concludes that curvature stays positive even if some edges are removed from a complete graph.
arxiv-2605-31130: Martinussen, Knudsen and Rytgaard develop a way to estimate the effect of starting treatment at a chosen time on survival. A fixed start time gives an estimand too rough for assumption-light inference. They therefore smooth the intervention over a window around the target time and derive a debiased one-step estimator. Simulations check its small-sample behaviour. The method is applied to Stanford heart-transplant records and to treatment-delay data for subfertile couples.
arxiv-2605-31330: Van An Nguyen and colleagues study social welfare under reward and punishment. Institutional incentives promote teamwork among self-regarding agents. Existing work treats scheme design as two-goal: minimise cost, maximise teamwork. Whether such schemes also raise welfare was largely unexplored. The authors derive welfare maths for rewards and fines in Donation and Public Goods games. They find regimes with one optimal level and regimes with phase shifts and local optima. Any welfare-best payout is zero or near a closed-form target. Reward beats punishment under close-formed rules.
arxiv-2606-00230:
Muckatira and co-authors hunt a slow bloom of grammar skill in language model training. Nets can fit their data long before they grasp the rule behind it. That late grasp is called grokking. It was first seen in small, set tasks with clear train and test splits.

Big model training has no such split, so the team builds a stand-in frame. They use paired lines from BLiMP that clash on one grammar point. The key span of each pair marks it as seen or unseen in training. Gains come late across five grammar traits. After the shift, inner grammar cues grow sharper and spread wider. A few heads link the key word to its mate in the line.
arxiv-2606-00330:
Chafaï, García-Zelada, and Xu track wild swings of log traits in a ball-based point crowd. Their crowd spreads points on a sphere by chance. It acts as a chance sketch of the full sphere. Smooth traits swing in the known gauss-field way in such crowds.

Log traits, with their sharp spikes, act in a far split way. They live on a larger log scale than smooth traits. In high dims, they split off from smooth swings in full. The end law takes a plain white-noise form. Sharp end marks fall out for log sums and key product forms. Chord traits of the sphere set the fixed gains in those marks.
arxiv-2606-00430:
Algama and co-authors release a vast fake move set for the San Francisco Bay Area. Real track data are noisy, gapped, and bound by privacy rules. SF-LIFE dodges those walls with a full sim of life in the zone. Half a million fake folk move through the zone for 70 days.

Each tick of one second logs where each fake soul stands. That yields trillions of log lines in the full set. Day plans are driven by needs, so trips have a why, not just a path. Moves span bus, rail, bike, car, and foot on true street maps. Feed data from more than 40 ride firms ground the routes. Trimmed takes, act logs, demo facts, and map data ship as well.
arxiv-2606-00630:
Esteban-Sinovas and co-authors bench six ways to fake an MRI from in-surgery sound shots. Sound shots in brain surgery are cheap and flex in use. Their planes are off-norm, their flaws are their own, and their look strays from MRI. Fake MRI could let pre-surgery tools serve in the room.

Their bench uses the ReMIND set of paired shots. Six maker tools span GAN, watch, and spread lines. Each is trained in four run forms and two goal forms. That grid yields 48 runs in the full bench. Grade spans shot marks and a cut-task test on growth and pit zones. No tool wins on all marks in the grid. Felt grade tracks end use most close of all marks. Plain match marks track it in the wrong way.
arxiv-2606-00930:
Jiang and Zhang test whether a probe can name the circuit inside Mamba in this 2026 paper. The trait is the state sink. Like the attention sink in Transformers, it fires hard on boundary tokens such as start markers and newlines. Interpretability work often calls a probe's top units the circuit for a trait.

At Mamba-1 channel grain, the label holds. At Mamba-2 head grain, it breaks three ways. A near-separate set of top heads matches the named set's ablation effect. Many dual heads react to boundary tokens yet lack that causal profile. The attack surface matters too: nudging the gate the probe reads moves loss by at most 0.16 nats in total. Muting the same heads' output moves it by 1.5 up to 7.3 nats in these tests. The heads do matter for behavior: needle recall falls from 30 of 30 to zero. A probe finds a circuit, not the circuit, they conclude.
arxiv-2606-01430:
Dutta takes a variational approach to ferronematics in bulk and thin form. Ferronematics mix nematic order with magnetic order. Two established theories describe their energy. Landau-de Gennes energy covers the nematic part. Micromagnetic energy covers the magnetic part. Coupling energies link the two parts together. Dutta also includes the nonlocal stray field energy. A further term couples the nematic to that stray field.

She proves an energy minimizer exists for the bulk functional. The proof works in a three-dimensional setting. Then she reduces the model to two dimensions. Gamma-convergence yields a reduced local energy in that limit. The work serves analysts who model coupled liquid crystal materials.
arxiv-2606-01530:
Mikhin and Xiourouppa split one Gaussian curve into a mix of narrower ones. A single Gaussian gets approximated by a mixture of Gaussians. All mixands share the same smaller variance. The gap is measured by the L2 norm between curves. A smart parameterization keeps the search problem simple. The technique is straightforward and robust in their tests. Mixtures approach the original curve fast as mixands grow.

Special cases of the input parameters simplify things further. Those cases yield extra closed simplifications in the solution. The method extends to non-Gaussian targets as well. That extension is discussed at the end. The work serves readers in signal processing and statistics. It offers a flexible tool for curve approximation tasks.
arxiv-2606-01930:
Mäkinen studies a new model of the early universe in loop quantum cosmology. The universe here is homogeneous and isotropic in shape. The model tweaks the standard Hamiltonian of the field. A Lorentzian term for spatial scalar curvature is added. Its form comes from a heuristic operator argument. That argument rests on the one-vertex reduced gravity model.

Effective dynamics differ from the standard scenario in detail. Yet the key features return in qualitative form. The classical singularity is replaced by a quantum bounce. The path through time stays symmetric around the bounce. One change stands out in the comparison. The bounce now occurs at a notably lower volume.
arxiv-2606-02030:
Chuet and co-authors define a domatic analogue of chi-bounded graph classes. A dominating set touches every vertex of a graph. The domatic number counts a largest such partition. Vertices are split into the most dominating sets possible. Minimum degree bounds that number from above.

A class is DOM-bounded if a growing function lower-bounds it. The bound depends on minimum degree alone. The notion mirrors chi-boundedness for chromatic number. A conjecture analogous to Gyárfás-Sumner is proposed. It covers classes forbidding a fixed induced subgraph. Connected forbidden graphs are the case of interest. The paper sets up the framework and conjecture. It invites work on domatic analogues of coloring theory.
arxiv-2606-02230:
Shao and co-authors work out how two jets from a diffraction event spread in angle. Such jets can probe the transverse momentum structure of the target in a non-perturbative way. The team study three kinds of collisions: heavy ion, electron-proton, and electron-nucleus. They focus on the main channel, where a semi-hard gluon is not seen.

Soft gluon emissions are summed to all orders for an energy-energy correlator in the transverse plane. Both initial and final state radiation are kept in the sum. The team also study heavy quark pair production. The spread in angle turns out to depend on how the jet axis is defined. Numeric forecasts are given for the LHC, HERA, and the future EIC.
arxiv-2606-02330:
Koll Pistarini and co-authors study swirls of gas in the solar atmosphere, called vortices. They ask how magnetic fields and image detail change these swirls. The team runs six three-dimensional models of the solar surface layers. The models use three field setups. One comes from a small-scale dynamo. Two use upright fields of 50 and 200 gauss.

Two detection methods scan every model at three levels of detail. One method, swirling strength, finds swirls at any tilt but needs a height-based cutoff. The other, SWIRL, finds only upright swirls yet matches the flow field better. The authors report that field setup and detail both change swirl counts and sizes. In the 200 gauss model, most swirls link the photosphere with the chromosphere. Vortices run hotter than the gas around them in all setups.
arxiv-2606-02630:
Sheoran and Hao show that medical chatbots weaken under multi-turn pressure. Real users push back after refusals. They add urgency and invoke authority. Single-turn tests miss that dynamic. Their benchmark, MultiTurnPSB, extends PatientSafetyBench to four turns. Attacks come in fixed template, template-adaptive, and live forms. GPT-4.1-mini is the main target.

Unsafe responses climb from 35 percent to nearly 80 percent by turn four under live attack. GPT-4.1-mini and Claude Sonnet 4.5 tie at baseline. By turn four they diverge to a 19-fold gap. Four degradation trajectory shapes are charted. A two-element attack formula drives most catastrophic failures. A light input-side classifier cuts turn-four unsafe replies by 52 points. Its 45 percent false alarm rate on benign queries blocks easy deployment. A side finding stands out. Claude Sonnet refused to write attack messages in over half of late-turn chats.
arxiv-2606-02830:
Fazla and Hashemi de-bias training data by watching how models memorize it. Real datasets carry spurious correlations not causally tied to the label. When those patterns dominate, models lean on them. Minority samples without the pattern get misclassified. Subset selection could help, but group labels are usually unknown. Popular scoring functions in coreset work depend on the spurious features themselves. They misjudge the difficulty of core features.

The team builds a two-stage scoring function. It disentangles the learning dynamics of core and spurious features. Each side's difficulty is scored separately. An algorithm then finds and prioritizes informative samples. It works with and without spurious correlations present. A standard ERM model trained on the selected samples beats top debiasing methods. It needs as little as 10 percent of the original training data. The work turns memorization patterns into a debiasing signal.
arxiv-2606-03130:
Erfanian and co-authors turn a flaw of code models into training data. Small open code models still invent completions that look right but name methods, imports, or variables that do not exist. Past fixes need per-language sandboxes, which fail mid-keystroke, or large human-labeled sets.

Frontier models are asked to make plausible-but-wrong completions for real code contexts. These hard negatives pair with the true developer edit to form a fine-tuning set. Contexts came from public GitHub code in eight languages. A panel of three frontier models made one fake per context for each of four flaw types. A model tuned on a curated 100,000-row subset gained about 19 points in exact match on a hallucination benchmark. Gains held across all languages and flaw types, and on other fill-in tests too. Ablation runs map which choices drive the gain.
arxiv-2606-03230:
Shen, Duran-Martin, and Oates build a Kalman-style filter that guards against wrong models. Online filtering tracks a hidden state from noisy data over time. If the dynamic or measurement model is off, classic Bayesian filters can grow over-confident. Their approach uses predictively oriented posteriors. In that frame, learning happens only when the whole model is well set.

Such posteriors are hard to characterize in closed form. The team's main tool is a fast update that mimics an iterated extended Kalman filter in a linear-Gaussian way. The method, EKF-PrO, has no tunable settings. Its cost is on par with standard filters. Tests cover linear and nonlinear cases where the state-space model is wrong on purpose. The filter avoids the over-confident errors that trap standard tools. It offers a principled hedge, not just a tweak to gain terms.
arxiv-2606-03330:
Richardeau, Dashyan, Le Merrer, and Tredan fingerprint single deployed instances of a language model, not just the model itself. A model's behavior rests on its weights and on instance settings: prompts, sampling choices, and quantization. A setup that is safe in one form may turn toxic in another. Past fingerprinting guards ownership and is built to ignore such settings. Regulators, though, must judge the deployed behavior in front of them.

Their method, FLIPS, reads biases in the binary random strings a setup generates. It sorts instances with 96 percent accuracy when all targets are known. With some targets unknown, it still hits 90 percent. An adapted baseline method reached just 35 percent. The test set holds 237 model instances. The authors argue instance fingerprinting is both needed for regulation and workable in practice. The code is public.
arxiv-2606-03430:
Schwarzer and co-authors defend energy-system intrusion detectors against model stealing. Attackers can copy a detector by probing it with synthetic traffic. They then craft traffic that slips past the copy and the original. Guards that track user identity fail when attackers spread queries over many accounts. Guards that poison soft labels fail when the detector gives hard labels only.

FlowGuard takes a different route based on flow matching. It flags incoming queries as out of distribution before the detector sees them. Synthetic attack traffic sits on a lower-dimensional manifold than real traffic. A continuous normalizing flow trained on real data scores such queries low. Tests pit FlowGuard against PRADA and FDINet under two known attacks. Attack setups include one client and a spread of 100 fake clients. PRADA's detection fell to zero when the spread changed. FlowGuard held a stable rate in both settings without identity data.
arxiv-2606-03630:
Lai and co-authors find a second rhythm in the collapse and revival of quantum coherence. Bosonic coherent states lose and regain phase coherence after a quench. Past work held that interactions alone set that rhythm, even with a tilt. Whether the interaction-only rule is universal stayed open. The test system is an ensemble of one-dimensional bosons in a tilted optical lattice.

When the tilt is weaker than the interaction, two modes appear at once. One mode is set by interaction, the other by the tilt. Tunneling between lattice sites enables the new tilt mode. With both modes live, their amplitudes scale linearly with tilt in a universal way. The result clarifies how collapse and revival behave in tilted lattices. It also deepens insight into collective motion in correlated systems. Cold-atom teams can use the tilt mode as a new dial.
arxiv-2606-03730:
Malik, Naseer, and Khan add a drift gate to test-time defenses for vision-language models. Models like CLIP generalize well with no training, yet adversarial images fool them easily. Adversarial training helps but costs a great deal. Test-time defenses use noisy views instead. Past versions work in the weak-noise regime, where adversarial inputs look oddly stable.

Beyond that regime, the picture flips. Adversarial representations drift far more than clean ones under strong noise. The clearer split gives a better detection signal. It holds across noise types, transforms, datasets, and attacks. It fades in adversarially trained models, tying it to fragile local geometry. A training-free gate uses high-noise drift to trigger existing defenses only when instability looks adversarial. Across 13 datasets, clean-plus-adversarial accuracy rises by several points. ImageNet gains are the largest, about ten points for one defense family.
arxiv-2606-03830:
Jin and co-authors design a constrained pinching antenna array for multi-user indoor wireless. Pinching antenna systems promise flexible indoor links. Prior array designs trade beam accuracy against steep deployment cost. Their design groups several antennas into one movable array. Fine shifts at the wavelength scale tune each element inside the array.

Sum rate across users is the goal to maximize. Array-center position and inner antenna spread are set jointly. Structural traits of the array yield an explicit cap on its aperture. Tractable approximations cover channel gain and user rate. The sum-rate curve proves unimodal under practical conditions. A one-dimensional search then finds the best center position. A closed-form approximation trims compute further. Simulations confirm the design nears the ideal upper bound. It beats fixed-spacing and prior pinching arrays by clear margins.
arxiv-2606-04330:
Kun Huang and co-authors demonstrate in 2026 a more efficient route to mid-infrared light, prized for sensing and spectroscopy, by mixing two laser pulses in a nonlinear crystal: difference-frequency generation. Their advance is seeding the process with coincident pulses from passively synchronized fiber lasers.

The synchronized seed pulses substantially lowered the pump power needed to start parametric emission. The resulting picosecond source at about three micrometers reached watt-level average power, with a peak conversion efficiency of seventy-seven percent from pump to mid-infrared light. Output stayed steady to within a fifth of a percent over an hour. Because synchronization is all-optical and the build uses polarization-maintaining fiber, the system is simple, compact, and robust enough for use beyond the laboratory.
arxiv-2606-04730:
Ugan and coauthors report a speech system built for a 2026 contest track in this arXiv paper. The system hears long speech in four languages and must follow instructions for each task. It handles six jobs, including writing down speech, translating it, answering questions, and summarising it. Most training speech came in clips under thirty seconds, far shorter than test pieces.

The team joined short clips into long ones, made labels with language models, and translated labels across languages. That work built over one million training examples across all six jobs and four languages. They found that ranking answers by likelihood, a score of how expected the wording is, helped transcription greatly. That same ranking hurt meaning based jobs, because it favoured answers built from chopped audio. Mixing that score with a risk based method fixed the trade off and protected question answering and summaries.
arxiv-2606-04830:
Sinigaglia and Kitaura untangle two sources of uncertainty that plague precision cosmology, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Surveys like DESI and Euclid will measure parameters, but finite survey volume creates cosmic variance, and galaxy formation adds bias between galaxies and the matter. The authors revisit the definition of cosmic variance and build a framework.

They apply the idea to the shift of the baryon acoustic oscillation scale, a standard ruler for cosmic expansion, separating uncertainty from cosmic variance from that of galaxy biasing. Checking the argument against N-body simulations, they find the reduction in the uncertainty on the BAO peak position. Their conclusion is: extra care is needed when inferring information from perturbative approaches that estimate bias parameters.
arxiv-2606-04930:
Chihara and co-authors present a 2026 arXiv paper on forecasting from data streams, where new values keep arriving and patterns keep changing. Their tool, AdaKoop, rests on the Koopman operator, a mathematical object that recasts nonlinear change as linear change in a richer space. Nonlinear here means the change does not follow a simple straight-line rule.

AdaKoop treats both raw readings and transformed features as views of one hidden linear system underneath. It tests the stream for abrupt pattern switches and updates its parameters step by step for gradual drift. That design keeps its computing cost constant, no matter how long the stream runs. Across 71 practical benchmark datasets in the reported experiments, AdaKoop beat leading rival methods on forecasting accuracy and on computing efficiency alike.
arxiv-2606-05130:
Linyao Chen and co-authors propose AgentMob in this 2026 arXiv paper, a training-free agent framework for predicting where a person will go next. Individual mobility prediction feeds urban simulation and transport planning. Supervised sequence models are accurate but need task-specific training and hide their reasoning. Earlier language model methods rely on static prompts and one pass, so they cannot gather more evidence when signals conflict.

AgentMob casts next-location prediction as adaptive, evidence-controlled decision making. Routine cases take a fast path based on historical regularity. Unclear cases trigger more tool use over trajectories, stay-move likelihood, and geography. Across three mobility datasets, AgentMob was the strongest training-free method. With GPT-5.4 it reached 71.42 percent top-one accuracy on one dataset. On hard non-fast-path cases its controller lifted accuracy from 30.65 percent to 48.62 percent over a statistical baseline using the same tools.
arxiv-2606-05330:
Jared Moore, Noah Goodman, Nick Haber, and Max Kleiman-Weiner build a framework for tracing how human beliefs move during persuasion in this 2026 arXiv paper. Language models can shift people's beliefs in high-stakes domains, but most studies measure only beliefs before and after a conversation, showing whether persuasion happened while missing where and how beliefs traveled.

Built on a web-based platform, the framework collects belief reports after every turn from human or simulated persuasion targets. It annotates persuader turns with rhetorical dimensions in the logos, pathos, and ethos scheme. It judges simulators by how faithfully they reproduce human belief dynamics. Human targets fell into two clusters of patterns and showed susceptibility to rhetorical strategies. Prompted model simulators failed to mimic human dynamics. The authors' Bayesian-network target, which carries a belief state, scored 81 on human-likeness against a human reference of 80, above the 64 of baseline model targets.
arxiv-2606-05430:
Guillaume Dubach and Hai An Mai prove a bipartite version of the Harer-Zagier formula in this 2026 arXiv paper, using random matrix theory. A formula counts how pairings of a polygon's sides produce surfaces of each genus.

In the bipartite setting, one polygon and several smaller polygons have their sides paired across the two groups, never within a group. Gluing along the pairings forms an orientable surface whose genus one wants to count. The authors decompose powers of Ginibre matrix eigenvalues, the eigenvalues of random matrices with Gaussian entries, into a superposition of point processes. That decomposition lets them identify coefficients of the generating function for the genus in this bipartite pairing problem. The result extends a formula to a combinatorial regime and shows that non-Hermitian random matrix techniques can organize surface-counting problems as the Hermitian theory did.
arxiv-2606-05630:
Jianing He and Dong close a gap in the theory of a classic fixed-point method in a 2026 arXiv paper. The Halpern iteration steers repeated steps toward a fixed anchor point. It finds points that a nonexpansive map, one that never stretches distances, leaves unchanged. Every known speed estimate assumed the anchor equals the starting guess. Real use often picks them apart, and then the old estimates say nothing.

The pair derive tight convergence rates for the general case. Their bounds cover both fixed anchor schedules set in advance and adaptive ones that react as the run proceeds. Tight means no better general rate exists, so the estimates settle the question. The results contain the older same-anchor theory as a special case. They also guide users who must start far from a sensible anchor. The paper is a compact, complete extension of a sixty-year-old method's theory.
arxiv-2606-05730:
Shuyu Wang and colleagues unify three scene text editing jobs in one model in a 2026 arXiv paper. Editors often remove, create, or swap text inside photos and posters. Separate tools for each job struggle to keep backgrounds and styles intact. TextWand splits every job into two basic moves: rendering text and erasing it. Two new parts sharpen control over layout and cleanup.

A positional encoding ties each letter to its exact pixels and to a style example. A region-adaptive step suppresses leftover traces for clean erasure. Since no benchmark covered all three jobs, the team built TextWand-Bench. Across removal, generation, and replacement, the model beat leading open and closed rivals. It won on text accuracy, layout and style match, and overall image quality. The authors present unified editing, with atomic moves, as the practical path for design tools.
arxiv-2606-06230:
Adam Distler and Juliette Becker test an origin story for the closest in exoplanets in this 2026 arXiv paper. Many systems show a peas in a pod pattern, with planets evenly spaced and similarly sized. Ultra short period planets, orbiting in under a day, break that pattern with higher tilts, older ages, and larger sizes. One idea says they began as the inner pea and split off as their star spun down.

Using Laplace Lagrange secular theory, which tracks slow orbital change, the authors check whether spindown alone can trigger the resonance crossing that decouples the inner planet. Strictly regular systems never cross that resonance under the expected change in stellar oblateness. The inner planet must first migrate inward for any crossing to happen. Crossing times vary widely, making the framework a test of migration paths and initial stellar tilts.
arxiv-2606-07130:
An answer with citations looks trustworthy, but does the cited passage actually support the claim? Yeginbergen and co-authors build citations that can be checked precisely in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their FullCite framework attaches structured inline citations to every claim. Each citation names the source document and the exact supporting span inside it.

Three generation strategies are compared. Prompt based generation asks the model to cite as it writes. Constrained decoding forces citations through a formal grammar. Posthoc alignment attaches spans after the text exists. Three benchmarks, including biomedical and expert question answering, graded the outputs. Models picked the right documents reliably. Finding the precise supporting span was much harder. Document scores far exceeded span scores in every setting. The authors conclude that faithful attribution research must focus on span level evidence. A citation that points at the wrong paragraph is decoration, not proof.
arxiv-2606-07830:
Santos and co-authors survey how software engineering students feel after using language models in ways they themselves judge inappropriate, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Automated help is blurring the line between legitimate assistance and misconduct, under growing performance pressure. The team ran a cross-sectional survey of one hundred sixteen undergraduates about their emotional responses.

The feelings reported were strikingly mixed. Indifference was the most common response, even among students who recognised real risks to their learning and academic standing. Guilt and anxiety appeared where students felt moral discomfort or feared penalties. Relief and satisfaction showed up mainly in deadline-driven situations and where course guidance about allowed help was unclear. The authors argue integrity policy cannot rely on shame: many students feel nothing, and unclear rules actively licence misuse. Addressing the emotional and situational drivers matters as much as detection tools.
arxiv-2606-08230:
Liang Zhang and co-authors revisit a puzzling measurement in particle physics in this 2026 arXiv paper. The measurement uses femtoscopy, a technique that infers the size of a particle-emitting source from momentum correlations between pairs of particles. For pion-proton pairs, the peak tied to the Delta resonance, an excited proton state, appears shifted from prediction. The authors reformulate the standard Koonin-Pratt framework in momentum space to investigate.

Their tool is the T-matrix approach, which separates on-shell contributions from off-shell ones, where particles briefly violate the mass condition. Using a model fitted to low-energy scattering data, they show the finite source size makes the measurement sensitive to off-shell dynamics. This produces the peak shift and a dip on the high-momentum side. The calculated strength still falls short of the data, which they attribute to a more complex source shape.
arxiv-2606-08730:
Lee and Kim build the missing statistical theory for prediction-powered inference, in this 2026 arXiv paper. It is a popular recipe for trustworthy estimates when labeling data is expensive. A model predicts labels for a large unlabeled set, and a small labeled sample corrects the bias. Many variants exist, but whether any of them is statistically optimal, achieving the lowest possible uncertainty, was unsettled.

The authors recast PPI as an M-estimation problem, linking its bias-corrected equation to the ideal full-label equation. That link yields consistency and asymptotic normality under simple random sampling. They then identify the efficient influence function and prove PPI reaches the semiparametric efficiency bound, the best attainable precision, when the predictor is score-calibrated. For predictors learned from data, they develop theory for cross-fitting and a variance-corrected single-fit version. Simulations and a real-data application back the theory.
arxiv-2606-09130:
Bhattacharyya and colleagues watch a molecular state that should split in two, and find it never stops being a mixture, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Singlet fission converts one photo-excited singlet state into a triplet pair, two entangled triplets that could double harvested carriers or serve quantum technologies. The pair is born as an overall singlet. Whether it decorrelates depends on its electronic character, tracked across a library of flexible pentacene dimers.

With polarization-controlled ultrafast spectroscopy, they found formation happens only in planar conformations, with large nuclear reorganization. Polarization anisotropy, backed by theory, showed singlet-triplet mixing persists through the pair's evolution, across all motifs tested. Once strongly bound, neither nuclear reorganization nor structural fluctuations suppress the mixing, so decorrelation loses the race against decay. The result constrains solar-cell designs banking on free triplets, and establishes anisotropy as a direct probe of decorrelation.
arxiv-2606-09730:
Pu Ning and his co-authors teach a language model the skill of handing work to helpers in this 2026 arXiv paper. Long research tasks can swamp a model's fixed context window. A lead agent can split the job and farm pieces out to subagents, which send back short sums. The authors call that knack delegation intelligence. Good training data for it barely exists in the wild.

Their harness steers a model through clean splits and tidy returns. The logged paths then serve as fine-tuning data, baking the skill into the weights. The trained model, SearchSwarm, targets deep research work. It scored sixty-eight point one on BrowseComp and seventy-three point three on its Chinese twin set. Those marks were the best among models of like scale. The team plans to release the harness, weights, and data. The hope is that open work on delegation can now move faster.
arxiv-2606-09930:
Sheneman builds a compiler that makes ordinary programs differentiable, meaning gradients can flow through them for optimization, in a 2026 arXiv paper on programming languages. His compiler translates a large, self-hosting subset of the Scheme language into computation graphs. Because the subset can compile its own evaluator, the result is a differentiable meta-circular interpreter: an interpreter that runs programs supplied as data while gradients reach the numbers inside them.

He proves the gradients are correct almost everywhere and checks them against direct compilation across one hundred seventy-one recursive and higher-order program pairs. A language model then proposes program structures while exact gradients tune their continuous parameters through the frozen interpreter. On battery capacity-fade data, the search recovered a knee-like degradation pattern and beat hand-crafted baselines on early extrapolation. A high-dimensional El Niño inverse problem shows the same workflow scaling up.
arxiv-2606-10230:
Nosrati and his team design quantum circuits that shuffle items in perfectly even random order on hardware with limited links, in a 2026 arXiv paper on quantum computing. Even random shuffles underlie uses from cryptography to quantum tuning and error repair. Existing exact quantum designs usually need all-to-all qubit links and quadratic circuit depth, both out of reach for near-term devices. Their variational approach lets the wiring graph set the circuit layout, with tuned parameters enforcing the target shuffle statistics.

They give controlled-SWAP designs reaching exact uniformity with quadratic circuit size and linear depth on linear nearest-neighbor layouts, removing the all-to-all need and improving prior depth by a factor. The results clarify how circuit layout constrains exact sampling, and point to variational circuits as a natural fit for hardware-limited even shuffles.
arxiv-2606-10530:
Kong and a large team of co-authors survey machine learning for hidden brain activity in this 2026 arXiv paper, a review rather than a new experiment. Modern recordings capture hundreds of neurons at once, and the useful signal is thought to live in a small set of latent variables. Latent variable models try to recover those factors and their rules. The survey organises the field into three domains: dynamics within one region, communication between regions, and behaviour-aligned modelling of task-related activity.

Within each domain the authors trace the path from early state-space models to recurrent networks and neural ordinary differential equations, comparing methods by assumptions, not scores. A recurring theme is what the models still cannot do: identify causal links between regions, or the direction of communication, with confidence. The paper closes with benchmarks, evaluation criteria, and open challenges for future researchers.
arxiv-2606-10630:
Cheng, Dai, and Liu classify the positive solutions of a coupled system in this 2026 arXiv paper. The system pairs two unknowns through a p-Laplacian operator and power-law coupling at the critical Sobolev exponent, where the equation is invariant under rescaling. Such systems model reactions where each component feeds the other. The authors establish regularity of any positive solution and estimates on its decay at infinity.

With those estimates, the method of moving planes, reflecting the pair across sliding planes and comparing, proves each is radially symmetric and decreasing about some point. The picture is complete: positive solutions are unique up to the symmetries, and their form is described. The results extend uniqueness theorems known for p equal to two to the full range, p between one and the dimension. Such systems benchmark how far symmetry methods reach.
arxiv-2606-10930:
Finkel and Halava pin down the complexity of a two-way word puzzle in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Post Correspondence Problem, undecidable since 1946, asks whether tiles of word pairs can be lined up so both rows spell the same string. The bi-infinite version asks for a two-way infinite match. The authors locate it in the arithmetical hierarchy, the ladder that ranks how hard such questions are.

They prove the bi-infinite problem sits at the second level of that ladder, strictly above the first, via reductions from Turing machine nonhalting through several infinite variants. Along the way, the infinite problem is shown undecidable even for injective morphisms, and several shifted variants are complete for the first level. Whether the bi-infinite problem is complete for its level stays open.
arxiv-2606-11030:
Cox, Kamsma, and Rosický revisit cellular generation in a 2026 arXiv paper in category theory, the mathematics of abstract structures and maps. Cellular generation is a smallness condition on a class of morphisms, or maps. Roughly, the whole class can be built from a small set of basic maps. Deciding whether a class has this property is a standing challenge.

Their tool is a weakened diagram condition. An effective square is a commuting square of class maps whose induced map from the pushout, a glued construction, also lies in the class. Dropping one requirement gives quasieffective squares. The main theorem says this: in a locally presentable category, a class is cellularly generated exactly when it is almost everywhere quasieffective. That is a set-theoretic test inside almost every small subuniverse. Added assumptions yield a version through filtrations, and a stronger one through accessibility, improving a theorem of Lieberman, Vasey, and Rosický.
arxiv-2606-11230:
Argüelles, presenting for the TAMBO collaboration, describes a novel neutrino telescope in a 2026 arXiv conference paper. Neutrino point sources stay elusive because atmospheric backgrounds swamp the signal, and searching many sky positions inflates false alarms, the look-elsewhere effect. TAMBO, the Tau Air-shower Mountain-Based Observatory, attacks both problems with geography. Its deep valley screens background while tau neutrinos skim through rock and shower in the air.

The design targets neutrinos from one to one thousand petaelectronvolts. TAMBO will observe only one to three astrophysical events per year, fewer than conventional observatories, but with far higher cosmic purity from its valley geometry. That pure sample can anchor point-source searches at traditional telescopes. Preliminary sensitivity studies show it can map diffuse emission and point sources, bridging optical Cherenkov and radio neutrino detectors.
arxiv-2606-11330:
Marston, Becker, and Howe ask whether super-puffs defy the standard formation theory in a 2026 arXiv paper. Super-puffs are sub-Saturn planets with extremely low bulk densities, under 0.3 grams per cubic centimeter. Short-period ones can be blamed on irradiation and star-planet interactions, but cold super-puffs challenge core accretion theory. The team constrains 34 cold super-puffs by computing interior structures with PlanetSolver.

They find 28 of the 34 fit core accretion models, given observed masses, radii, and age. Six cannot: HIP 41378 f, Kepler-30 d, Kepler-51 d, Kepler-177 c, TOI-1420 b, and WASP-107 b. They need a non-standard explanation such as exo-rings. An extra heat source rescues all but TOI-1420 b, though. Of two candidate heat sources, enhanced radiogenic heating is insufficient to inflate planets to super-puff densities. Late impacts with sub-planetary objects can produce the needed inflation for a billion years or more.
arxiv-2606-11430:
Mayeux proposes connecting two disconnected systems in a 2026 arXiv paper. Mathematical knowledge is split between bibliographic databases like MathSciNet and zbMATH Open, which index publications, and formal proof libraries like Lean's mathlib, which hold machine-verifiable proofs. Neither side knows what the other holds: bibliographic ones do not record whether results are formalized, and formal libraries ignore it.

Mayeux proposes a bridge database aligning paper metadata with formal artifacts, a layer between the literature and formal systems. A paper-level formalization score measures how much of a publication is covered by formal systems. The feasibility study shows such scores can be estimated by cross-document alignment between informal texts and Lean versions, enabling large-scale analysis of coverage. The framework is a first step toward machine-usable knowledge graphs linking papers to proof objects.
arxiv-2606-11530:
Choi, Lee, and Ryu cheapen a constraint-preserving quantum algorithm in a 2026 arXiv paper. The Grover mixer variant of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm confines evolution to the feasible subspace of a problem, keeping every state valid. Its mixing unitary, however, needs a global multi-controlled phase-shift gate acting on all qubits, a substantial circuit overhead on near-term devices.

The authors propose locally acting Grover mixers, tailored to initial states with a product structure over disjoint qubit subsystems. Such states arise when only a subset of problem constraints is encoded into the initial state preparation. The method preserves the search space defined by the initial state while significantly lowering implementation cost, since the global gate is replaced by local operations on separate subsystems. The work targets constrained optimization problems, where feasibility-preserving mixers are attractive but their global implementations have limited practicality on today's hardware.
arxiv-2606-12130:
Yichuan Cao and co-authors settle a long-standing question about how hard a basic algebra test really is, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The test asks whether one sparse polynomial divides another exactly, where sparse means each polynomial is listed by few nonzero terms. The setting is a finite field, a number system where arithmetic wraps around a fixed size. Long division can explode in size here, so a fast general test was far from obvious.

The authors prove the test is CoNP-hard, meaning it sits among the hardest problems whose no answers are easy to check once given. Equivalently, showing that one polynomial does not divide another is NP-hard under randomized reductions that convert one problem into another. The result closes an open problem posed in nineteen ninety-nine and restated in problem lists. Any fast exact test for all cases is now known to be unlikely.
arxiv-2606-12430:
Ghia and co-authors ask workers which of their own tasks feel pointless, and whether robots should take them, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Debate about automating work usually targets whole occupations. But meaning varies task by task inside one job, as Graeber's theory of bullshit jobs suggests. The team surveys 202 workers rating 171 workplace tasks. They validate a five-item scale measuring perceived bullshitness, how pointless a task feels to the person doing it.

Bullshitness strongly predicts the desire to hand a task to AI agents. Such tasks are also judged to need less human oversight once delegated. The pattern aligns worker preference with perceived feasibility: pointless tasks are the natural first candidates for automation. Expectations shift with meaning, too. For meaningless tasks, workers want agents that are fast, simple, and decisive. Grounding deployment in workers' lived experience, the authors argue, beats top-down automation lists drawn from job titles alone.
arxiv-2606-12530:
Vasiliou and co-authors simulate a new moiré material where electrons carry three valleys and an almost perfect sixfold symmetry, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Twisting monolayers whose states sit at the Brillouin zone's M-points yields a three-valley Hubbard model. Hopping is valley-selective and nearly one-dimensional. The onsite repulsion is almost U(6)-symmetric, treating all valley-spin flavors alike, without any fine-tuning.

At three electrons per moiré cell, determinantal quantum Monte Carlo runs sign-free, a rare luxury. For near-isotropic interactions, matching stacked tin diselenide, an extended intermediate regime appears. Local moments form yet electrons stay itinerant, and the crossover toward low-temperature order reads as fluctuating U(6) local moments settling down. At strong coupling, the simulation finds robust long-range antiferromagnetic order on each valley's rectangular sublattices. Many features should persist beyond the idealized sign-free limit, the authors argue.
arxiv-2606-12630:
Carneiro and Cunha rewrite Maxwell's equations for the space around a non-rotating black hole in this 2026 arXiv paper. Maxwell's equations govern electric and magnetic fields, and Schwarzschild spacetime describes gravity outside a spherical mass. What fields look like depends on the measurer, so the authors use tetrads, local reference frames that keep measured fields physically direct.

Two observer families are compared in one coordinate system. Static observers, who hover at fixed radius, recover the familiar spherical equations. Gravity adds corrections linked to proper distance, proper time, and the lapse function, which measures how clocks slow near the mass. Freely falling observers see extra effects from their motion: charge density mixes with radial current, and the electric and magnetic sectors intertwine. Weak-field and near-horizon limits are also examined, likening the curved geometry to an uneven, and for fallers a moving, material medium.
arxiv-2606-12730:
Kocielnik and colleagues test when a language model's stated traits predict what it does, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Psychometric questionnaires are tempting for guessing how a model will act, but earlier work found models produce tidy personality profiles that fail to predict their choices. Those studies used the Big 5, which predicts behaviours only weakly.

The authors apply the Theory of Planned Behavior, which tracks intentions aimed at a specific behaviour, across 4 behavioural tasks and 11 frontier models, while varying session context and persona prompting. Within a conversation, the behaviour-specific instrument reaches human-level coherence between self-report and behaviour, while the Big 5 does not. Across separate conversations, coherence lasts only for behaviours rooted outside the prompt, such as implicit bias shaped by training, and fails for context-primed behaviour such as sycophancy. Persona prompting makes self-reports steadier across conversations but does not pull behaviour into line.
arxiv-2606-12830:
Li and colleagues introduce PERIA, a tool-augmented visual agent that improves spatial reasoning by actively gathering visual evidence, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Vision-language models reason over static image features, which limits tasks needing fine-grained spatial evidence, multi-step interaction, and a coherent spatial state, such as tracing routes on subway maps. PERIA adds 2 lightweight tool families: perception tools that expose textual, symbolic, and spatial evidence, and interaction tools that manipulate visual context, trace paths, and verify spatial relations.

Training combines supervised tool-use trajectory synthesis, composite rewards, and a new policy optimisation method called OR-GIGPO. On 13 benchmarks drawn from 8 datasets, PERIA-8B improves over its Qwen3-8B backbone by 10.0 percent on in-distribution benchmarks and 4.4 percent on out-of-distribution ones. It also beats previous state-of-the-art baselines of similar size by 7.0 to 14.8 percent.
arxiv-2606-12930:
Zhou and colleagues show that removing spurious correlations is not always learnable, even when the invariant pattern can be read off the data, in this 2026 arXiv paper.
