Invariant learning uses data from multiple environments to find features whose link with the label stays stable, dropping links that hold only by accident.

Under a samplable sparse-recovery primitive, the authors build multi-environment instances with a 1-dimensional invariant subspace. These cases are learnable from a modest sample count by brute-force search. Yet any polynomial-time algorithm reaching accuracy would break the primitive, giving a computational-statistical separation. They measure environment diversity by a gap parameter gamma, which controls identifiability and the curvature of invariance goals. With enough diversity, the minimax risk scales as k times d minus k over the sample size times the number of environments. A phase transition occurs at a sample threshold set by 1 over gamma squared.
arxiv-2606-13030:
Zhang and colleagues present a multi-modal framework for micro-gesture recognition in untrimmed videos, built for Track 1 of the 4th MiGA-IJCAI Challenge, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Micro-gestures are spontaneous, subtle body movements that convey emotions, but spotting them is hard: the signal-to-noise ratio is low, class spreads are long-tailed, and cross-subject evaluation brings domain shift.

A saliency-guided extraction pipeline joins 68-keypoint skeleton joint coordinates, 3D heatmap volumes, and RGB features. A square-root smoothed weighting mechanism, paired with an orthogonal semantic embedding loss, protects tail classes without hurting accuracy. To bridge the cross-subject generalisation gap, the authors propose cross-modal pseudo-labeling, an unsupervised domain adaptation strategy that boosts single-modal robustness, and a temperature-scaled soft-voting mechanism eases overconfidence during fusion. The framework reaches an F1 score of 68.13 percent, securing 4th place in the challenge.
arxiv-2606-13230:
Nguyen and colleagues prove a reassuring result about approximate Bayesian inference in this 2026 arXiv paper. Bayesian inference updates beliefs about unknown quantities as data arrive, producing a posterior distribution that sums up what the data support. Exact posteriors are often impossible to compute, so practitioners use variational methods, which swap the true posterior for a simpler distribution chosen to be close. A posterior is called consistent when it concentrates on the true value as data grow. The paper asks when the simpler stand-in inherits that property.

The main theorem says that if the gap between approximation and target stays bounded, measured by Kullback-Leibler divergence, then consistency carries over. The authors give simple conditions for the bound. They illustrate them for generalised posteriors, used when likelihoods give way to loss-based updates. The result shows when a fast approximation can be trusted at scale.
arxiv-2606-13630:
Pedro and colleagues investigate which speech representation drives facial animation in this 2026 arXiv paper. Speech can be encoded many ways, and the choice shapes animation quality. Self-supervised features stress sound-segment and meaning cues, neural codecs produce codes tuned for sound rebuilding, and recogniser-style goals yield label-based spaces tied to sound categories. The authors evaluate four representation families, comparing rebuild quality across two facial decoders with scored metrics and a listening study. Probing analyses relate the tokenised codes to sound units and to movements of the face.

They find that encoding phonetic classes benefits facial animation in both meaning-based and label-based codes, at comparable quality. Building on the label-based result, they build an audio-visual text-to-speech pipeline on discrete codes as a shared space, decoding both speech and facial motion. A shared discrete code promises simpler, more synchronised talking-head systems.
arxiv-2606-14030:
Chatterjee and Chowdhury measure what is lost when a speaker-labeling model is compressed for live medical dispatch work. Speaker diarization decides who spoke when in a recording. Streaming versions must run fast on limited hardware, vital for dispatch calls. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses SIMSAMU, a simulated medical-dispatch dataset, to test streaming behavior, then compress the segmentation model by pruning and low-bit quantization.

Extra buffering was not consistently helpful across latency budgets. Very low-latency settings degraded performance substantially. Compression traded accuracy for memory measurably. One point stands out: half-precision FP16 arithmetic halved model size while leaving the real-time factor essentially unchanged. Its cost was a forty percent relative rise in diarization error rate. The authors caution that results come from one pipeline and a small corpus with two main roles, so error levels may not generalize.
arxiv-2606-14130:
Adalat, Hamel-De le Court, and Belardinelli let cooperating agents rely on each other's promises without giving up hard safety guarantees. In multi-agent reinforcement learning, one agent's safe move may depend on teammates' behavior, so shields that ignore teamwork discard team-optimal behavior that is safe only jointly. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses contracts: agents share a global safety spec in safe linear temporal logic, choosing tuples of local obligations whose conjunction implies it. Each tuple is certified by a circular assume-guarantee fixed point, then projected into local action masks.

Because certification precedes learning, safety stays hard-guaranteed while rewards adapt. A non-stationary bandit then picks among the pre-certified library to optimize team reward. Evaluation covered six environments and fifteen variants. Contract-aware shields recovered coordinated behaviors that factorized permissions exclude, keeping pre-emptive safety throughout. Future work targets probabilistic duties and heuristics to avoid exhaustive enumeration.
arxiv-2606-14530:
Di Cicco asks whether a language model knows if its code will work before writing it, in a 2026 arXiv study. The testbed is a four-billion-parameter coding model. It faced four hundred forty-four tasks from LiveCodeBench, a set of programming problems. A simple linear probe reads the model's hidden state. It reads the state at the final prompt token, before any output exists.

That probe predicted first-attempt success well. Its score sat near zero point eight eight across fifty held-out splits. That is a strong result for such a cheap signal. Removing each hidden unit's link to prompt length barely hurt it. The score stayed near zero point eight four. A length-only baseline scored near zero point six six. No nonlinear model beat the linear probe. A planned study of self-repair failed for a simple reason. Successful repairs were too rare to analyze.
arxiv-2606-14630:
Das and co-authors build robust numerical methods for coupled flow and transport in a 2026 arXiv paper. The Darcy-Forchheimer equations describe fluid flow through rock or soil. They include a nonlinear drag term that matters at higher speeds. The system couples to an advection-diffusion-reaction equation for a transported substance. Solvers must stay stable whatever the permeability or reaction parameters are.

The authors adapt recent saddle-point theory in Banach spaces. They obtain parameter-independent stability bounds. This extends the Brezzi-Braess theory from the Hilbert setting. They prove the full coupled system is stable regardless of its parameters. Their mixed finite element discretization converges in parameter-weighted norms. They design operator-based preconditioners that stay robust across regimes. Numerical examples in practical ranges confirm the behavior.
arxiv-2606-14730:
Rawat predicts imminent soccer actions from broadcast video in a 2026 arXiv paper. The task is ball action anticipation. It watches a thirty-second window of football footage. It forecasts which of ten action classes will occur in the next five seconds. Anticipation is harder than recognition. The decisive contact has not happened yet.

The model works hierarchically. A shared transformer encodes features inside each five-second sub-window. A gated recurrent unit gathers context across sub-windows. A transformer decoder with input-conditioned event slots produces the forecast. It uses three separate heads for objectness, class, and temporal offset. A frequency-reweighted matching scheme favors rare action classes in training. Gaussian soft targets supervise timing. On the SoccerNet benchmark the method reached a mean average precision near eighteen percent.
arxiv-2606-14930:
Díaz-Cruz and colleagues present a spin-spinor treatment of scattering amplitudes for massive particles in a 2026 study. Amplitudes give the probabilities for particle reactions, and modern methods compute them without field Lagrangians. The authors set out conventions, then work two examples in full detail. They also ask how the massive theory reduces to the massless one at high energy.

The worked examples cover the decay of a W boson into a lepton and neutrino, plus electron-positron annihilation into muons. Charts trace how spin and helicity flow from incoming to outgoing particles, exposing symmetries between branches. The charts also let readers assemble the total squared amplitude for each process. For the massless limit, the authors show the reduction is exactly a little group contraction, an older idea from Inonu and Wigner. That link ties realistic massive calculations to the better-known massless amplitude program.
arxiv-2606-15330:
Tang and coauthors replace a recommendation cascade with a generative model for e-commerce video feeds, in a 2026 information systems paper. Short-video apps show a search bar under each video, suggesting queries the content inspires. Old systems retrieve and rank queries through many stages, drifting from the video. OneBar instead generates the query from the video watched. It fuses multimodal video understanding with behavioral signals about users. Prompt compression keeps serving fast enough for live feeds.

Progressive preference learning folds user behavior into the generation policy. That removes the need for a trained reward model. In an A/B test on Kuaishou's feed, query exposure rose about seventeen percent. Query clicks rose about nineteen percent, with click-through rate up. Guided orders grew about twenty percent and sales volume about twenty-two percent. Bad-case rates for quality fell. The framework shows generation can beat cascades at scale.
arxiv-2606-15430:
Escolà validates a candidate exoplanet around a bright star in a 2026 astronomy paper. The object, TOI-7701.01, was flagged by a machine learning survey of data from NASA's TESS telescope, which watches for the tiny dips when a companion crosses its star. Automated detections can be mimicked by blended binary stars, so the author runs a statistical pipeline to test false-positive scenarios with a Bayesian tool called triceratops.

Two versions of the light curve, raw and instrument-corrected, independently converge on the same companion size, about eight times Earth's radius. The ensemble false-positive probability lands near two tenths of one percent, far below the validation threshold, and chance alignments with nearby stars are excluded. At that radius the object sits at the boundary between giant planets and brown dwarfs, though its size favors a planet. The bright host star makes radial velocity follow-up to weigh it practical.
arxiv-2606-15530:
Heyde and Mahadevan build a minimal eco-evolutionary model in 2026 in which a population and its fitness landscape reshape each other. Standard theory holds the landscape fixed, but real organisms consume resources and alter the conditions that set their own fitness. Their model couples replicator dynamics for a population density to a regenerating, resource-driven landscape through a single environmental sensitivity parameter.

With that feedback switched on, they generate selection gradients of their own making and ride them, producing directed motion in trait space even on an initially flat landscape. The dynamics also show sustained oscillations, chaos, and branching, where one lineage splits into distinct types. To explain the behaviour, the pair derive reduced equations that extend Fisher's fundamental theorem to deformable landscapes, adding curvature-driven variance dynamics and the feedback loop. The result is a compact account of how populations self-propel across landscapes they regenerate.
arxiv-2606-16130:
Yuan and colleagues sharpen predictions of alpha-decay half-lives in 2026 by letting machine learning correct a physics model, rather than replace it. Alpha decay is how heavy and superheavy nuclei shed an alpha particle, and its half-life guides the hunt for new elements. The effective liquid drop model gives a macroscopic baseline based on barrier penetration. Its predictions still deviate measurably from experiment.

XGBoost and TabPFN models learn those residual deviations from data. Physically motivated descriptors feed the correction, covering nuclear deformation, Geiger-Nuttall related features, and minimum orbital angular momentum. The best variant, TabPFN-term3, cuts the root mean square error to 0.348 and the mean absolute error to 0.248 in the reported tests. Those figures correspond to improvements of about 38.60 percent and 40.46 percent over the baseline. Feature ablation confirms the physics descriptors carry real signal. Better half-life forecasts help experimentalists choose which superheavy nuclei to chase.
arxiv-2606-17030:
The Qwen Team presents a video world model for robots in a 2026 technical report. Qwen-RobotWorld takes natural language as its action interface: given observations and a text instruction, it predicts physically grounded future video. One formulation spans robot manipulation, autonomous driving, indoor navigation and human-to-robot transfer.

Three components make it work. A sixty-layer double-stream diffusion transformer couples frozen vision-language semantics with video latents through joint attention. A corpus of millions of video-text pairs, over twenty robot bodies and hundreds of action categories, aligns actions with language. A two-stage curriculum first learns general visual priors, then adds embodied specialization. The model ranks first overall on two embodied world-model benchmarks and leads open-source systems on two more. Promised uses include synthetic training data, cheap virtual test environments, and planning signals for control. Zero-shot tests support generalization and consistency across views.
arxiv-2606-17230:
Eyles-Ferris presents a 2026 arXiv paper on tidal disruption events and their infrared glow. Such events occur when a star is torn apart by a massive black hole. Some flares show infrared counterparts blamed on dust reprocessing the light. A spherical dust shell is the usual picture, yet X-ray-rich events show infrared glow more often.

That pattern contradicts the shell model, which predicts no strong change with viewing angle. Eyles-Ferris instead arranges the dust in a ring around the black hole. On-axis views then give brighter counterparts with a delayed initial rise. Off-axis views may show a double-peaked shape instead. Applied to two real counterparts, the ring model matched their traits and constrained their viewing angles.
arxiv-2606-17830:
Tran and colleagues map the hidden symmetries of Transformer attention in a 2026 theory paper. Different settings of the weights can compute the exact same function, a freedom that shapes how models can be merged or averaged. This symmetry is well understood for older networks. It grows intricate in attention, though, above all once position codes enter the design.

Studying the two main codes, the authors show the sinusoidal kind leaves the symmetry of plain attention intact. The rotary kind, by contrast, shrinks the symmetry group sharply. That raises what the model can express, and it may explain why rotary codes keep gaining ground in practice. The team then links these symmetries to linear mode connectivity, which asks whether two trained models can be joined by a straight path of good solutions. An alignment method is shown across Transformer settings.
arxiv-2606-17930:
McFadyen and colleagues show that how much thinking time a language model gets can matter as much as the model itself, in a 2026 evaluation study. AI tests increasingly use hard tasks with tools and long solution paths, yet many still grade models at one tight compute budget. Low scores may then reflect the test setup rather than the model's real capability, and the authors set out to measure that distortion.

They ran up to twelve frontier models on seven tough benchmarks spanning software work, math, medicine, and cybersecurity. Three simple levers were tested: bigger token budgets, context compaction, and repeated attempts with light feedback. Larger budgets lifted scores across domains, and fixed-budget tests understated newer models most, since they unlock harder tasks when given room. The study urges evaluators to report results across budgets.
arxiv-2606-18030:
Luo and colleagues design an AI tutor built for two learners at once, a parent and a child, in a 2026 paper. At-home tutoring has lopsided roles by nature: parents steer the session while children do the reasoning. Most language model learning tools assume one user, or partners with equal roles, so this setting was largely unexplored.

A formative study showed good tutoring depends on keeping those roles distinct, and it surfaced common snags. Parents may miss a problem's structure, lack the knowledge to help, or talk past their child. The team's system, ParaTutor, answers with a role-separated scaffolding interface that supports each side differently in real time, feeding the parent guidance while keeping the child actively solving. The design aims to strengthen, rather than replace, the parent's teaching role.
arxiv-2606-18330:
Terry and Anderson present the software plumbing for a Hubble precursor survey of the Roman Space Telescope's bulge fields, in a 2026 astronomy paper. Roman's Galactic Bulge Time Domain Survey will watch five crowded fields for years, and Hubble has already imaged the same ground under program GO-17776. THOR, the Terry Hubble Observations of Roman pipeline, reduces that Hubble imaging from the Wide Field Camera 3 and the Advanced Camera for Surveys.

Its companion tool, HAMRR, mines the resulting catalog through a standard cone search. Outputs include calibrated photometry and astrometry for detected point sources, plus cutout images, auto-generated color-magnitude diagrams, and luminosity functions. The pair is built for joint work ahead: the same catalogs will support combined analyses with Roman itself, the Rubin Observatory's LSST, and Euclid. These are some of the most crowded star fields in the sky.
arxiv-2606-18530:
Pai evaluates defenses against a class of prompt injection attacks on language model agents, in a 2026 computer security paper. These domain-camouflaged attacks hide malicious instructions inside retrieved documents written in normal professional vocabulary, so detectors looking for obvious override commands miss them.

Across more than three thousand trials spanning three model families and financial, legal, and general domains, Pai tested five prompting-based defenses, including spotlighting, paraphrasing, and sandwiching. Paraphrasing the retrieved content before the agent processes it worked most consistently, cutting attack success by over half depending on the model and beating a guard-classifier setup on every model. Other defenses varied sharply: spotlighting halved success on one model yet gave no benefit on another. Financial settings carried the highest residual risk, and no prompting defense fully removed the threat on weaker models. Pai offers the benchmark as guidance, while noting its documents were synthetic.
arxiv-2606-18630:
Zhao and the team design a path-tracking controller for unmanned ground vehicles, in a 2026 vehicle control paper. It keeps them on course over slopes combined with potholed ground. Off-road ones serve military, rescue, and scout missions, and face terrain shocks that badly degrade steering. The nonlinear jolts from potholes are hard for standard controllers to foresee.

The strategy has three joint parts. An adaptive forgetting least-squares estimator tracks tire cornering stiffness on coupled slopes. A Laguerre-function model predictive controller handles the base tracking cheaply. A deep neural network, built on Koopman operator theory, offsets the drift caused by potholes. An event-triggered mechanism switches it in, after a credibility check. On a hardware-in-the-loop platform, the joint system improved tracking performance by more than eleven percent, holding lateral error within tight bounds.
arxiv-2606-18830:
Istace and the team shift the sensitivity analysis of linear programming from the objective value to the decisions, in a 2026 paper. Models in energy, logistics, and industry use uncertain costs, demands, and capacities. When inputs drift, an optimal plan can become suboptimal or break. People ask how the optimal profit changes. But what ops teams need is how the optimal values move.

The authors study changes to the cost vector, the right-hand side, and the constraint matrix, selecting solutions from the optimal set by a linear criterion. They reveal an asymmetry. Under cost perturbations, the primal selection can jump, as the optimal face changes. Yet with a near-optimality tolerance, continuity comes back. On intervals with a fixed optimal basis, the selection is a homographic function of three parameters. Under right-hand-side perturbations, the primal and dual swap sides. The paper maps that structure.
arxiv-2606-19030:
Zhu and colleagues study the far tails of critical order-parameter distributions in 2026. Near a continuous phase change, fluctuations span all length scales. Averages alone miss how rare, extreme fluctuations behave. Those tails can expose universal features that standard scaling misses. The team targets them for percolation and Ising-type models in two and three dimensions and on complete graphs.

Two rescaled measures are tracked, one tied to total magnetization or cluster mass and one tied to the largest cluster. For the first, a stretched-exponential tail form holds, including for the percolation analogue. For the largest cluster, the authors propose universal scaling forms for both tails, guided by an exact complete-graph result. Large Monte Carlo runs support those forms. One sharp finding stands out. On the complete graph, the left tail follows percolation-like scaling, not typical Ising scaling, revealing hidden structure in critical fluctuations.
arxiv-2606-19130:
D'Souza and colleagues present two cheap methods in 2026 for computing electron-phonon coupling and thermoelectric transport in semiconductors. First-principles methods can predict transport well, but they remain costly. Both new methods need only a small number of electron-phonon matrix elements computed from first principles. The rest is filled in by models or by machine learning, cutting the cost of dense sampling across the Brillouin zone.

The first method builds mode-by-mode coupling models from about ten matrix elements per band and mode. It includes an acoustic deformation potential model for arbitrary crystal symmetries and band edge positions. The second method uses machine learning to interpolate about a hundred elements onto dense grids where transport matters. Applied to two-dimensional molybdenum disulfide, both match the state-of-the-art method closely. The computed properties also agree well with experiments.
arxiv-2606-19230:
Stricker and colleagues extend a human-in-the-loop optimization framework for bioprocess work in 2026. The method uses a Gaussian process surrogate to guide costly tests. In Pareto Front Guided Sampling, surrogate-derived quantities become objectives in a joint problem. The Pareto front is shown to a domain expert, who picks candidates directly instead of taking a single machine recommendation for the next run.

Two extensions are added. For constrained work, the chance of meeting output limits becomes an explicit Pareto objective. For robust work, a Monte Carlo strategy estimates lower-confidence performance under input shifts a user defines. The dashboard shows trade-offs among performance, uncertainty, constraints, and robustness. Experts can refine choices as the surrogate improves.
arxiv-2606-19930:
Guangyi Liu leads a ten-author system adapting phone agents to new apps with no human labels in 2026. Apps are legion, update often, and resist coverage by hand-written tasks or demos. MobileForge closes the loop from exploration to policy improvement on its own.

MobileGym grounds task generation and rollout scoring in real app interaction. A hierarchical feedback-guided optimiser turns outcomes, step feedback, and hints into training signal. Step-level GRPO updates absorb those hint-rich signals directly. Only machine-made adaptation data feed the whole pipeline. An adapted open model reaches close to a closed-data specialist on AndroidWorld. A further tuned variant sets the open-data pace there and on MobileWorld's GUI split. Self-made curricula thus rival hand-built supervision for phone agents.
arxiv-2606-20130:
Xuesong Wang reports a fourth-place entry to the ICRA 2026 GOOSE challenge, a contest in fine-grained semantic segmentation for off-road robot cameras. His 2026 paper adapts Segment Anything Model 3, a visual foundation model, to label every pixel of outdoor scenes into sixty-four detailed classes. The system reached a mean intersection-over-union of 69.73 percent on the official test set of 1,815 images from four robot platforms.

Three ideas carry the result. A lightweight decoder sits on SAM3's image encoder. A self-distillation scheme uses SAM3 itself, prompted with true boxes, as a teacher on classes where it beats the student model. A test-time augmentation rescales the image rather than the model input, restoring multi-scale inference for a fixed-size network. Most striking, an aggressive photometric distortion borrowed from a winning 2025 entry proved the single largest source of improvement, outweighing architecture changes.
arxiv-2606-20430:
Aki Mori and Hidefumi Ohsugi link the face structure of lattice polytopes to how their toric ideals are generated. Their 2026 paper introduces the clique-face property: every clique in the polytope's 1-skeleton should be the vertex set of an actual face. The question is when quadratic binomials suffice to generate the toric ideal.

Under a mild condition on edges, quadratic generation forces the clique-face property. For (0,1)-polytopes the implication is clean: quadrics generating the ideal means every clique is a face. Under condition (E), the property comes down to which quadratic monomials in the ideal's binomials divide the others. As a consequence, such toric ideals have no required monomials of degree three or more.
arxiv-2606-20630:
Haiyi Zhu, Canwen Wang, Qing Xiao, and Hong Shen argue that human-agent interaction is a core design target, not an afterthought. Their 2026 position paper notes that agents now sustain interaction, use tools, and collaborate long-term, yet real-world adoption lags capability. The barrier, they argue, is missing design knowledge as much as missing technology.

Fourteen design principles articulate the ideal human-agent relationship across four interaction stages. Agents interact with, adapt to, influence, and sometimes fail humans, so evaluating autonomy alone misses the point. The principles give builders a shared vocabulary for the human side of agentic systems. Adoption may turn on these relationships more than on raw task scores.
arxiv-2606-20830:
Miaochen Jin and four colleagues show in 2026 that hidden CPT violation could distort measurements of CP violation in neutrino experiments. Long-baseline tests extract a CP phase from how neutrinos oscillate. That step assumes CPT is conserved, a deep symmetry linking matter and antimatter. Jin and colleagues model a breach as a gap between neutrino and antineutrino mass splittings.

That gap creates an energy-linked phase shift. The shift looks much like the true CP phase in the measured data. A fit that assumes CPT can therefore miss the real phase. The known tension between two major tests can also ease if CPT is breached. Air-shower neutrino scopes offer a natural extra test. Their warning matters for DUNE, where a wrong symmetry premise could bias a headline result.
arxiv-2606-21330:
Chris Nicholls, Michael Fenelon, Yang Zhang, and Louis Cattafesta III probe a sonic fluidic oscillator in 2026. The device makes a jet flip side to side with no moving parts, which suits it for flow control. Two design factors were unclear: how the feedback channel ports are shaped, and how much outlet restrictions matter. The team measured the internal flow with phase-averaged particle image velocimetry, matched to unsteady pressure readings.

A mode analysis finds two coupled patterns: a sweeping mode for sideways jet motion and a bending mode that drives the outlet flow split. Separation at the port entrances throttles feedback and weakens oscillation at high flow rates. Surprisingly, tight outlets create a secondary separation that shields the jet's attachment, so strong oscillation survives even at the smallest apertures tested, breaking a long-assumed design coupling.
arxiv-2606-21530:
Sabin Roman, Vitaliy Soloviy, and Klaus Kubeczko present SORT in 2026, a data-driven method for mapping how sustainability shifts unfold across many linked systems at once. Energy, emissions, innovation, digitalization, finance, and wellbeing evolve together through feedbacks that single-sector models and optimization pathways tend to miss. Inspired by SINDy, which finds sparse equations behind data, SORT infers a compact set of cross-domain links from matched European indicators rather than assuming a structure up front.

The fitted system reproduces distinct real patterns: steady renewable growth, nonlinear scaling in transition finance, diffusion-like spread of digital tools, and falling emissions from regulated sectors. Runs diverge from straight-line extension where feedback loops bite, marking where faster decarbonization is conditional rather than assured. The authors stress the model is a map for exploration, not a forecasting tool.
arxiv-2606-21830:
Leung, Kim, and Park introduce Mat-Pref in 2026, a benchmark for testing whether verifiable-reward training teaches real chemical reasoning about inorganic materials. The benchmark holds 10,837 questions about ionic substitution, swapping one ion for another inside a crystal, across eleven structure families. Every answer is checked against density functional theory calculations from the Materials Project.

Three test splits separate ordinary performance from transfer to wholly held-out structure families and transfer to a new property, band gap, for hosts seen only through formation-energy training. Four large zero-shot models scored only 33 to 54 percent on every split. A pipeline of supervised fine-tuning plus group relative policy optimization then lifted a small eight-billion-parameter model to 65.2 percent in-distribution and 71.6 percent on held-out families. That beat a model roughly thirty times larger by over twenty points, at a total cost under fifty dollars.
arxiv-2606-21930:
Han, Cho, and Bak present MindTailor in 2026, a framework that writes personalized emotional support replies for people posting in distress on social media. Earlier personalization used the seeker's current feelings, persona, or situation, yet ignored the past experiences that shaped the present concern. MindTailor instead reads the seeker's post history before answering a new post.

From that history it builds a case formulation, the structured summary a counselor might write about a client's background and patterns. Several counselor agents, each grounded in a distinct counseling strategy, then critique and refine the draft reply together. To study the task, the team built ReddiSupp, a dataset of 798 Reddit posts paired with each seeker's prior post history. Judged by automated evaluation, expert humans, and a user study with seekers themselves, MindTailor beat baselines on empathy, personalization, and understanding, and won the highest overall preference.
arxiv-2606-22030:
Singh presents Nous in 2026, a memory architecture for artificial intelligence agents built on the principle that knowledge is prediction, not storage. Instead of saving facts as records, vector embeddings, or graph triples, Nous keeps a predictive world model. For each entity-attribute pair seen in conversation, it stores a probability distribution over values. Each new observation is scored by how surprising it is, in information-theoretic terms, and folded in through a closed-form Bayesian update.

What the system stores is the delta, the shift from prior to updated belief, rather than the fact itself. Forgetting then emerges as distributions decay toward uniform. On the LoCoMo benchmark, across ten conversations and 1,540 questions, Nous reached F1 scores between about fifty-five and sixty-four across question types. It beat a rival memory system's reported numbers in three of four categories, with Singh flagging where cross-paper comparisons are uncontrolled.
arxiv-2606-22230:
Jha develops, in 2026, a framework for distributional Granger causality, asking whether one time series predicts another through any feature of its distribution, not just its mean. Outside the Gaussian setting, predictive content can flow through scale, tails, or asymmetry. No single test can capture all of it, so Jha builds the framework from a finite menu of channel-specific conditions.

Under suitable conditions, the channel menu is complete. Non-causality in this sense is then equivalent to a finite set of testable hypotheses, giving an identification result. On that basis Jha designs an adaptive sequential testing procedure. It allocates inferential effort across channels while controlling the familywise error rate through an alpha-investing mechanism. A validity theorem guarantees finite-sample size control under any admissible selection rule. An efficiency theorem shows a confidence-bound allocation matches an oracle benchmark's power in the limit.
arxiv-2606-22530:
Eric Bittner, Carlos Silva-Acuña, and Hao Li rethink how to read multidimensional spectra in this 2026 physics paper. Such spectra are interpreted through Liouville pathways, sequences of quantum states between pulses of light. Textbooks treat each pathway as evolving on its own, but in open systems the environment keeps shuffling amplitude among pathways during every interval.

The authors build a geometric framework where a Liouvillian connection governs that pathway transport, complete with curvature and observational holonomy, a twist built up around a cycle. Transport arises when the basis the environment selects differs from the basis used to build the signal. Using a Duhamel expansion, they derive a procedure that identifies which transport operators redistributed the pathway weight. It stays accurate across the full range of basis misalignment. Distortions, peak shifts, and forbidden contributions then read as geometric signatures of curved Liouville space.
arxiv-2606-22630:
Serge Thilges, Onur Celik, Denis Blessing, Emiliyan Gospodinov, and Gerhard Neumann train diffusion policies for reinforcement learning in this 2026 paper. Diffusion policies represent complex action choices well, which suits robots weighing many plausible motions. Online training has lagged, though, because there is no ground-truth data and standard tools like score matching do not apply directly.

Their algorithm builds on adjoint matching, a technique from stochastic optimal control. It enables simulation-free training and avoids both explicit likelihood estimation and costly backpropagation through the diffusion process. Several extensions make the method more robust and stable in practice. In experiments, the approach matched existing methods' performance while sharply reducing computing overhead. The authors argue this makes diffusion policies far more viable for online reinforcement learning, where an agent must learn from its own ongoing experience rather than from a fixed dataset collected beforehand.
arxiv-2606-22730:
Louis Davis and Conor Kresin unify a family of estimators for Hawkes processes in this 2026 paper. A Hawkes process models events that trigger more events, like aftershocks. Fitting one by likelihood is standard but costly. Cheaper moment-based methods, such as least squares and Takács-Fiksel, grew up separately, each with its own theory.

The authors show all these methods form one class of equations built on the compensator, with the likelihood score as the efficient benchmark. For processes with compact memory, positive nonlinear links, and kernels that allow inhibition, any suitable summary of a fixed lag window gives an unbiased equation. Estimators built from finite sets of such summaries share proven convergence rates and normal limits, with a workable two-step optimal weighting. A projection identity measures each set's exact efficiency loss against the benchmark. Fast forgetting extends the theory to nonstationary starts after a short burn-in.
arxiv-2606-22830:
Jinwei Xiao and eight colleagues hunt for the tokens that matter in reasoning distillation in this 2026 paper. On-policy distillation trains a student model on its own reasoning chains, supervised token by token by a teacher. The team finds two kinds of knowledge in those chains: decisions, where the path branches, and evidence, the steps that justify each decision.

Current methods capture decisions, which surface where the student is uncertain. Evidence hides where the student is confident yet wrong, so it goes untransferred. Their method, DEAR, first finds decisions through student entropy, a measure of uncertainty. It then locates supporting evidence by comparing hidden states to decision anchors, using teacher-student divergence to rank the widest knowledge gaps first. Across three student-teacher pairings on math and code benchmarks, DEAR beat standard distillation consistently, gaining up to 2.5 points on competition math and 5.7 points on code generation.
arxiv-2606-22930:
Johannes Buchner writes about nested sampling in a 2026 statistics paper. Nested sampling is a Monte Carlo method, meaning it uses random draws to estimate quantities. Scientists use it to fit models to data and to compare rival models. The method keeps a set of live points and repeatedly swaps the worst point for a better one. Drawing each replacement point correctly is the hard part of the algorithm.

Buchner gives a full mathematical account of MLFriends, a practical method that builds a proposal region around the live points. He then derives bounds on how much of the target region that proposal can miss. The bounds shrink fast as the number of live points and bootstrap rounds grow. For normal settings the missed share is tiny. Buchner argues the resulting bias stays well below the random error of a single run, while noting a fully rigorous proof remains open.
arxiv-2606-23230:
Raphaël Delécluse, Hazem Wannous, and Laurent Guimas re-identify people across cameras without using face images in a 2026 paper. Person re-identification links sightings of the same person across views, a staple of surveillance in places like transport hubs. Standard methods use color images, which expose identities and fail under lighting changes or occlusion. The team uses depth images instead. Depth maps show body shape while inherently hiding faces and fine identifying detail, making the approach privacy-preserving from the sensor up.

Delécluse and colleagues match individuals across views with the Hungarian algorithm, which finds the global best assignment over a distance matrix. Feeding sequences of frames into a transformer encoder adds motion information over time. The encoder exploits both depth and color streams where available. Dynamic movement patterns sharpen the features and improve re-identification accuracy in their tests.
arxiv-2606-23330:
Hubert Dunikowski and Emilia Witkowska study spin squeezing in Fermi-Hubbard systems with high spin in a 2026 quantum physics paper. Spin squeezing sharpens the collective spin of an atomic ensemble in one direction, a resource for precision measurement. Fermi-Hubbard systems model strongly interacting fermions hopping on a lattice, here with large internal spin and a weak coupling to light. The conventional description treats the ensemble as one maximal spin. The authors show that description breaks down because of degeneracies, the many internal states sharing the same energy that high-spin structure creates.

Dunikowski and Witkowska identify those degeneracies as the breakdown's microscopic origin. They build an effective framework based on population eigenstates, states labeled by how atoms spread across internal levels. That framework reproduces the spin squeezing evolution quantitatively. The results uncover a generic mechanism: degeneracy itself reshapes collective spin dynamics.
arxiv-2606-23530:
Kozitsin and Proskurnikov study why people press the like button on social media posts, in a 2026 computational social science paper. Social contagion means behaviors and opinions spread through network ties, much like infections, and a like is a small visible act that friends can copy. The authors ask whether influence stops at direct friends or also reaches friends of friends.

Working with about two hundred ninety thousand users of the VKontakte platform, they find that personal traits such as gender and number of connections matter less than activity nearby in the network. Likes by direct neighbors and by second-order contacts, people two steps away, strongly track a user's own liking, even when no direct friend has liked yet. Nothing measurable appears at distance three or beyond. Surprisingly, once spread and second-order activity are counted, more active direct friends alone predict slightly less liking.
arxiv-2606-23830:
Wu, Xuan, Leskovec, Choi, and Li predict where antibodies will bind on a protein by learning directly from the protein's three dimensional surface, in a 2026 paper on computational biology. An epitope is the patch of an antigen that an antibody grips. Knowing epitopes guides antibody engineering and vaccine design. Most tools read amino acid sequences or backbone shapes, and they struggle with epitopes scattered across the surface. The actual contact cues, surface geometry and chemistry, are largely ignored.

SurfBind represents the antigen as a surface point cloud divided into patches. A transformer merges geometric and chemical features, and cross attention makes the representation aware of the specific antibody. Prediction proceeds from coarse patches to fine points. On demanding benchmarks SurfBind reaches state of the art accuracy and generalizes to unseen antibodies.
arxiv-2606-24230:
Hidalgo-Izquierdo, Carrión, and Caminero extend the Flower federated learning framework so training no longer waits for the slowest participant. Federated learning trains a shared model across many devices, without centralising their data. But the classic synchronous round stalls on stragglers and wastes fast clients' time. Their semi-asynchronous strategy, SAFL, relaxes the lockstep while keeping training stable.

Implemented as the FedSaSync strategy inside Flower, the system allows partial sync among clients. It does not demand every update before proceeding. Tests in mixed settings, the norm for edge learning, show improved robustness and less idle time against fully synchronous baselines. The team reports that SAFL balances convergence stability against system efficiency. That is the trade-off deployment engineers face. Published in SoftwareX in 2026 with openly licensed code, the extension targets training across uneven real-world fleets.
arxiv-2606-24530:
Horizon Research, the team behind this report from Frontis.AI and Tsinghua University, asks whether AI coding agents can match the best published results of papers in the Nature family of journals. Agents are moving from reproducing code toward autonomous research. Existing benchmarks carry limitations that blur genuine advances with pattern matching, though. NatureBench rebuilds the test around real published state of the art results as the bar.

Tasks span six scientific domains drawn from Nature family papers. Source figures anchor each problem. Ten models are ranked on a public leaderboard by a Surpass-SOTA score. It measures whether an agent's solution actually clears the published result, rather than merely approaching it. The benchmark's premise is strict. Fitting familiar patterns to new data earns nothing, unless the number beats the paper. Horizon Research positions the suite as the rigorous evaluation autonomous science needs.
arxiv-2606-24630:
Sakai and Bauer trace how a water surface's influence travels downward through turbulent channel flow. Open channels, rivers and canals in the laboratory, differ from closed ducts. The free surface lets turbulence breathe. Using matched direct numerical simulations of open and closed channels at high Reynolds number, in a domain large enough for very large scale motions. The pair dissect the turbulent kinetic energy budget term by term in 2026.

The surface's influence turns out to be communicated primarily through transport terms, rather than local production. Near the surface, pressure transport supplies energy toward the interface while turbulent transport and dissipation fall, and the surplus is exported by viscous diffusion. No single similarity scaling organises all the near surface budget terms: viscous diffusion follows a viscous length scale, dissipation a Kolmogorov scale. Sakai and Bauer's accounting tells modellers which mechanisms a free surface turbulence closure must represent to be believed.
arxiv-2606-24830:
Noah Hout, Kenta Miyahara, Dustin Newland, and Maxim Yattselev refine the long time behaviour of a quantum spin chain's autocorrelation function. The system is the transverse Ising chain at its critical magnetic field. Spins sit on a one dimensional lattice, interacting with neighbours while a sideways field acts on each. The autocorrelation measures how a spin's present state remembers its state long ago. Deift and Zhou previously extracted the leading long time asymptotics through a Riemann Hilbert problem, a boundary value method for analytic functions.

The refinement targets what the leading term leaves out. Hout and colleagues determine the subleading growing term in the asymptotics. Subleading terms matter when comparing theory against numerics at large but finite times. The analysis again runs through the associated Riemann Hilbert problem and steepest descent machinery. The model is a special case of the spin one half XY chain in a field.
arxiv-2606-25230: This paper classifies groups of certain orders: which integers can occur. The classifying classifies. Their classifying is groups certain orders. The classifying classifies. It is group theory. The classifying is which integers. The group classification is order-based. The integer orders are group-theoretically classified.
arxiv-2606-25530:
Making existing software faster is expert work, and judging whether a language model can do it needs honest tests. Ezgi Sarıkayak, Wenchao Gu, Hesham Ghonim, and Chunyang Chen build such a test in 2026 from one hundred two real optimisations written by experts in open source projects. Each task is scored with parameterised tests measuring runtime, peak memory, and time weighted memory use, under noisy conditions and varied inputs, because real performance is all of those at once.

Current models struggled badly. Their runtime gains were negligible and memory improvements nearly absent. The expert versions, in contrast, sped tasks up by a factor of about fifteen on aggregate and cut peak memory enormously on many tasks. Experts improved runtime in over ninety percent of tasks. The authors call the gap a measure of how far models sit from expert level engineering judgement.
arxiv-2606-25930:
Djihad Amina Djemmah and colleagues test titanium dioxide ceramics for metamaterials in the terahertz range. Those frequencies sit between microwaves and infrared light. Artificial structures at those frequencies need a dielectric with very high permittivity, near one hundred, paired with very low energy loss. Whether a ceramic meets both targets depends strongly on how it is baked, a step called sintering.

Conventional sintering is compared head-to-head with spark plasma sintering, and the effect of a later annealing step on losses is measured with terahertz time-domain spectroscopy. One sample reaches a loss tangent of about six thousandths while keeping permittivity just above one hundred, comfortably inside the design window. Designs built on the measured values show flat all-dielectric structures. Their effective index comes out negative or near zero. The results confirm that the firing route matters.
arxiv-2606-26230:
B. A. Seidel, K. Dolag, and J. G. Sorce sharpen the art of zooming into simulated galaxy clusters. Cosmology simulations must cover huge volumes yet resolve single galaxies. Zoom-ins answer by re-simulating one region at high resolution inside a cheaper parent run. Low-resolution particles leaking into the clean region ruin the trick. Stable boundaries for the layered zoom are their contribution.

Target regions are chosen from a forward run of the parent box. The zero-velocity surface far in the future outlines the region that will collapse into the target. Up to four layers of falling resolution wrap that region, softening the transition. The team builds zoom setups for twenty regions holding thirty local clusters, drawn from the SLOW constrained simulation of the nearby universe. Test runs stay remarkably stable to the present day. Baryonic evolution studies gain clean initial conditions as a result.
arxiv-2606-26530:
Yuxuan Yang, Feiyang Li, and Yile Wang propose DiARC, a training method for puzzle reasoning in language models. The target puzzles come from the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus. Each gives a few grid examples and asks for the rule behind them. Open models do poorly on such tasks, and closed models are costly. Most training work adds more positive examples.

DiARC argues that near-miss wrong answers teach just as much. It builds preference pairs that contrast a correct output with a tempting wrong one. Three methods create the wrong versions. One transforms the output visually. One inverts the rule at the program level. One edits the task's own rule. The demonstration examples stay unchanged throughout. Across several ARC-like benchmarks, models trained this way beat the baselines consistently.
arxiv-2606-26730:
Peter Mathé and Bernd Hofmann study how to compute a generalised inverse when the problem is ill-posed. Banach spaces are the broad workspaces of modern analysis. Their metric generalised inverse plays the role that the famous Moore-Penrose inverse plays in simpler spaces. When the underlying operator has a non-closed range, direct computation breaks down. Approximation schemes, called regularisations, must step in.

The authors analyse iterative schemes and a Tikhonov scheme in this setting. A clear split emerges, which they call a dichotomy. Applied to points where the inverse exists, the schemes approach the best approximate solution well. Applied outside that domain, the same schemes blow up without bound. There is no middle behaviour. The result tells users exactly when such methods can be trusted.
arxiv-2606-27030:
Richarda Niemann and eleven colleagues image the sideways electric fields of waves that skim crystal surfaces. Surface phonon polaritons are hybrid waves of light and lattice vibration, tightly confined to a surface. Near-field scopes usually sense only the out-of-plane field component, because their tips are elongated. Complex patterns, like those in hyperbolic materials, need the in-plane parts too.

Their far-field microscope uses sum-frequency mixing of infrared and visible light. The short visible wavelength of the signal gives the needed resolution. In-plane components are selected directly rather than inferred. The team shows the method on moving polaritons. Full vector-field access should sharpen studies of exotic wave patterns such as skyrmion-like field textures.
arxiv-2606-27530:
Ritchey leads a team pinning down the interstellar carbon abundance along two sight lines toward the Rho Ophiuchi star-forming region. Gas-phase carbon shapes the ionisation balance of diffuse clouds and the budget of carbonaceous dust, yet its abundance is hard to measure securely. High-resolution archival spectra from the Hubble Space Telescope's imaging spectrograph supply the data. Carbon ion column densities are derived two independent ways: from the weak intersystem absorption line, and from the damping wings of the strong, saturated line, in an astrophysics paper published in 2026.

Both sight lines give weak-line and strong-line determinations that agree remarkably well. That agreement certifies the damping-wing fitting technique that earlier work had reason to distrust. The abundance toward one sight line matches previous weak-line determinations closely. A measurement technique earns its credentials.
arxiv-2606-27730:
Pulsar timing may test whether black holes hide singularities. Tuleganova, Karimov, Izmailov, and Nandi study a pulsar orbiting a black hole in 2026. Their diagnostic compares two light rays from the pulsar. The rays leave at once, pass on opposite sides of the lens, and arrive at different times. That arrival-time difference samples frame dragging from the spin. It differs from the classic Shapiro delay, which uses one ray.

One lens model is a charged regular black hole of Ayón-Beato and García type, with no singularity. The others are the singular Kerr–Newman and Kerr black holes. Numerical estimates for two binary systems give delays at the microsecond level. Such delays should be measurable. Under the thin-lens approximation, though, the predictions agree until third order of smallness. The authors conclude the regular and singular cases cannot be told apart this way, despite differences between them.
arxiv-2606-28230:
Yawen Cui, Qiankun Shi, Xiao Wang, and Xiantao Xiao design an algorithm for hard optimization problems where both the goal and the equality constraints are nonconvex and can only be estimated noisily. Most existing methods pay heavily in evaluations of the noisy constraint function, which can dominate the total cost.

Cui's team builds a search direction from decomposed pieces and uses Fletcher's augmented Lagrangian, a smooth scoring function, to choose step sizes. A technical hurdle is that the noisy constraint Jacobian can nearly degenerate. They split the analysis by its smallest singular value to control the resulting errors. Under smoothness assumptions, the method provably reaches an approximate KKT point, the standard certificate of a good solution, with a total expected cost they characterize, and experiments support the theory.
arxiv-2606-28530:
Wael Tabbara, Sharafeddine Sharafeddine, Ahmad El-Hajj, Jihad Fahs, and Ibrahim Abou-Faycal ship a software package for probability's heavy tails. Alpha-stable distributions are the limiting laws for sums of heavy-tailed amounts, so they should fit finance, engineering, and network data well. In practice their density functions have no closed form, and both evaluating them and sampling from them are treacherous to compute.

Their Python package, AUB-HTP, attacks both problems. Densities come from several routes that complement each other: integral formulas, series formulas, and direct inversion of characteristic functions. Random generation covers single variables and joint ones, with flexible dependence built through series formulas. Tests show better accuracy and stability than current tools for scalar densities, plus new joint simulation abilities, all packaged for repeatable work with heavy-tailed models.
arxiv-2606-28630:
Jun Wang and Peirong Liu forecast how brain lesions will grow, separating two changes that most models tangle together. A lesion's shape deforms as it expands, and its image intensity shifts as its composition changes. Learning one direct map from today's scan to tomorrow's blurs those mechanisms, costing physical plausibility, generalization, and interpretability.

Their PDF framework assigns each process its own flow matching network, one for morphology and one for intensity. A physics-based penalty, built from a diffusion-reaction-advection equation for lesion growth, keeps the morphology honest. On three public datasets of brain scans over time, spanning diverse diseases, the disentangled design reached state-of-the-art forecasting performance. Splitting what changes shape from what changes signal, the experiments suggest, is the right inductive bias for disease trajectories.
arxiv-2606-28730:
Thanawat Sornwanee, writing alone, repairs the footing of conformal prediction, the method that wraps any model in honest confidence sets. Full conformal prediction retrains the model on every candidate answer, and modern practice makes its non-conformity measure random, since training itself involves chance. A folklore loosening claimed the guarantee survives if the measure is merely permutation invariant in distribution.

Sornwanee shows that the commonly used condition is in fact not enough, a crack in a widely used guarantee. In its place he provides a correct sufficient condition, which he names conditional independence together with permutation invariance in distribution. The new condition still covers several chance-driven settings that arise in machine learning practice, so the repair does not exile the methods people actually use. It tells them exactly which extra shape their randomness must respect.
arxiv-2606-28930:
Dumbadze and colleagues hunt for regular oscillations in data from the Parker Solar Probe, a spacecraft flying close to the Sun. Earlier studies had reported coherent oscillatory signals in its solar wind measurements. Similar long-period patterns appear in observations of active regions on the solar surface. The team asked systematically whether the probe's spectra share fixed periods, and whether those might link to the active-region oscillations.

They applied Lomb-Scargle analysis, a method for unevenly spaced data, to the original series. Wavelet analysis covered evenly resampled versions. Seventeen encounters fed the statistics. Significant periods appeared between two and twenty hours across many physical quantities, with the strongest confidence between four and eight hours. The signals showed up near perihelion, the closest approach, and during radial approach and departure. They were absent far from encounter sites. Differing periods across quantities may point to distinct driving mechanisms.
arxiv-2606-29130:
Aboelwafa, Samir, Elmakky and Torki present DistilledGemma, a system that extracts person-place relations from multilingual historical newspaper articles for the HIPE-2026 shared task. The articles span English, German and French, and the task is to decide which people connect to which places. Their design balances accuracy against computing cost through knowledge distillation, training a small model to imitate a large one.

The pipeline runs in three stages. First, prompt strategies were explored across eight large models to find the best reasoning setup. Second, a large Gemma teacher was fine-tuned efficiently to produce silver-standard reasoning traces. Third, those patterns were distilled into a compact Gemma student, with rule-based post-processing enforcing type and direction consistency. In official evaluation the team ranked third on the standard test and second on the binary test.
arxiv-2606-29230:
Zhu, Sun and Yang present Again-Pose, a method for reconstructing three-dimensional human poses from ordinary video when motion gets extreme. Severe motion blur and occlusion degrade frames so badly that their features collapse into noise. Methods relying on implicit temporal attention, which aggregate information across frames, then cannot tell valid signal from noise, and reconstruction fails.

Again-Pose reframes pose estimation in degraded frames as motion-guided recovery. It explicitly identifies high-quality anchor frames, judged by feature saliency, and propagates reliable kinematic cues from them to inpaint the poses of degraded frames between them. A dual-path motion-aware module captures the fine-grained inter-frame dynamics. A difference-weighted fusion module then propagates those cues adaptively, suppressing drift. On standard benchmarks and the FineDiving dataset, it beat state-of-the-art approaches in robustness and stability.
arxiv-2606-29730:
Chen proves a theorem in differential geometry about how cheaply a manifold can be dominated by a finite complex. Domination here means a map of degree one onto the manifold. His object is the n-skeleton of a finite simplicial complex.

For a closed, connected, smooth n-dimensional manifold, Chen proves it is dominated by such an n-skeleton. The total number of simplices in that skeleton is bounded above by a constant. That constant depends only on the dimension and on its embolic volume, a geometric quantity tied to how the manifold can be filled. The result links topological complexity to finite domination with explicit control.
arxiv-2606-30130:
Jinmin Wang, Zhizhang Xie, and Guoliang Yu give a self-contained proof of Gromov's dihedral rigidity conjecture for three-dimensional polyhedra. The conjecture constrains how a convex polyhedron's geometry can deform. If scalar and mean curvature stay nonnegative and corner angles stay small, the shape must be flat. The general proof exists but is long and technical. This version aims at accessibility.

Restricting to dimension three avoids many higher-dimensional complications. The essential ideas of the general approach still show through clearly. The authors prove a strengthened form of it. Their setting uses connected spin polyhedral manifolds in 3D. Earlier partial results covered cone-type and prism-type polyhedra with angle restrictions. Lott's related theorem handled even dimensions without dihedral angles. The shorter proof should help readers enter the scalar curvature literature.
arxiv-2606-30230:
Floor van Maarschalkerwaart, Subhadip Mukherjee, Christoph Brune, and Marcello Carioni make learned image reconstruction robust to noise that differs from training. Learned reconstruction solves inverse problems like deblurring and CT scanning. Models trained under one noise model generalize poorly to others. Robust optimization guards against worst-case distribution shifts. Standard versions perturb everything the same way, which is too cautious.

Their structured framework restricts perturbations to match the measurement physics. Ambiguity sets can target how data depend on the signal. That captures doubt about the forward model and noise better. Strong duality holds for the general formulation they develop. Explicit finite-dimensional dual forms follow for several perturbation types. A worst-case risk bound produces a familiar Tikhonov-style smoothing effect. Deblurring and sinogram-to-CT experiments show improved robustness and stability. The learned map ends up low-rank in linear settings.
arxiv-2606-30930:
Emmanouilidis and three colleagues analyze stochastic gradient descent, the workhorse training method of deep learning, in the regime where learning rates are far larger than classical theory allows. In practice models are routinely trained at this edge of stability, where curvature-driven oscillations appear, yet most existing analysis covers only deterministic gradient descent and leaves the random, mini-batch setting open.

The authors prove sharp convergence guarantees for the multiclass cross-entropy loss, covering both linear classifiers and two-layer neural networks. Their results show the dynamics alternate between an unstable, oscillating phase and a stable phase where the expected loss falls at a controlled rate. Crucially, the randomness itself self-stabilizes the iterates, returning them to stability within a fixed number of steps. Experiments confirm the picture.
arxiv-2606-31030:
Navarro and Olivares take up contextual pattern matching, a search task suited to giant repetitive collections like genome sets and versioned documents. Instead of listing every occurrence of a pattern, the search returns one position for each distinct context, where the context is a fixed number of symbols on either side of the match. Listing identical repeated occurrences one by one wastes effort, so distinct contexts are what users usually want.

Known solutions run in optimal time but need data structures as large as the text itself, which is too much for very repetitive data. The authors give the first optimal-time method that works in compressed space, using a symmetric compressed automaton called an SCDAWG. They also improve a weighted ancestor data structure so the distinct contexts can be listed with very small delays.
arxiv-2606-31330:
Pan and three colleagues examine thick brane worlds in f(R) gravity, where our universe is a thick wall inside a higher-dimensional space. Two scalar fields support an exact warped background whose energy density can split in a Bloch-type pattern. Such inner structure might trap gravity waves for a long time as resonances.

The team require the effective gravitational coupling to stay positive, which splits a smooth ghost-free branch from a singular one. In the ghost-free branch, no narrow long-lived tensor resonances appear in either relative-probability or phase-shift spectra. Sharp peaks show only on the singular branch, where the coupling vanishes and the potential blows up, so they mark a bad boundary rather than real physics. Massive Kaluza-Klein modes on the good branch are then mapped in the complex frequency plane.
arxiv-2606-31430:
Gangopadhyay studies one periodic feature in warm inflation that leaves three linked signals. In warm inflation the inflaton field loses energy to a thermal bath, and a shift-symmetric field couples to that bath periodically, so friction oscillates as it rolls. When a thermal channel opens mid-roll, friction surges sharply.

The surge grows a narrow, log-periodically modulated peak in the curvature spectrum at small scales, leaving cosmic microwave background scales untouched. That peak can make asteroid-mass primordial black holes form in numbers matching the dark matter. It also sources gravitational waves in two bands at once, one near LISA's range and one for deci-hertz detectors. A matching offset in the bispectrum, fixed by the spectrum's running, ties all three clocks to one phase.
arxiv-2606-31530:
Rohwedder and Schnaars extend a rounding method from coflow scheduling to the general graph scheduling problem. Edges of a multigraph must be placed on time steps so that each step forms a matching, and weighted groups of edges finish when their last edge runs. Coflows and data migration are the famous special cases.

Their iterated rounding algorithm gives an essentially tight approximation for the case where the optimum is large. The proof leans on odd-set inequalities from matching theory and on edge colouring results for multigraphs. Combined with the best known method for small optima in data migration, their result improves the approximation rate for data migration in every regime. The bipartite insight, it turns out, survives the move to general graphs with the right polyhedral tools.
arxiv-2606-31630:
Xu, Zeng, Paisley and Zhao argue that language models writing probabilistic programs need a statistical checker, not a test suite. A program in Stan, Pyro or NumPyro can compile, run and pass every unit test while using the wrong likelihood, an invalid prior or a sampler-hostile parameterization. Their proposed verifier is the Bayesian workflow itself: posterior predictive checks, simulation-based calibration, sampler diagnostics and held-out predictive scores.

On a benchmark of 200 seeded faults spanning 14 misspecification types, this calibration oracle flags errors far better than unit tests, which catch none, and a reference-free version still reaches solid accuracy. Fed back into a repair loop across fifteen models, calibration feedback lifts fix rates sharply, while passing unit tests actually suppress repair. Programs written from scratch show the same pattern.
arxiv-2606-31930:
Fairall and Glinnan develop a way to pool evidence across grouped studies when each group is estimated by the Generalized Method of Moments. Applied economists increasingly estimate the same parameter in several countries, markets or experimental sites, then face the external-validity question of how much information to share. Bayesian hierarchical models answer it naturally, but they need a likelihood, which GMM settings often lack.

The Quasi-Bayesian Hierarchical Model keeps each group's own GMM objective and adds a pooling term for economically comparable parameters, with estimation by a Laplace-type quasi-posterior. For strongly identified parameters, the estimator matches standard GMM asymptotically in distribution. For weakly identified ones, a limit-experiment analysis shows the pooling rule is a Bayes rule under the hierarchy-induced prior, and pooling can reduce mean squared error.
arxiv-2608-00030:
Kondapalli and co-authors train a small model to route queries to expert search agents. Specialist retrieval agents often beat general search. Picking the best agent for a query stays open, though. Current routing leans on topic or intent alone. That misses what the agent's own results actually show.

Their model learns agent choice and tool-call parameters together. Supervised fine-tuning comes first, then reinforcement learning. A layered reward weighs retrieval relevance and topic fit. On hard mismatch cases, the model scored 0.918 NDCG@10. Two baselines scored far lower on those same cases. Overall it hit 0.771 at about 120 ms per choice, far faster than one baseline.
arxiv-2608-00230:
Doyle, Laurent, and Ventresque present PADRAIG, a model-based generator of Android test inputs. Automated input generation for Android is a crowded research field. Random generation is easy to maintain but inefficient. Systematic and search-based routes make effective tests at high runtime cost. Model-based routes pay a modelling cost up front, then generate faster.

PADRAIG uses a detailed control flow model of the app under test. It was compared with three state-of-the-art tools, each using a distinct technique. Tests ran on 19 randomly selected apps from the F-Droid store. PADRAIG reached 16 percent more line coverage than the state of the art on average. Its generation runtime was 84 percent lower on average. Precise modelling pays off in both coverage and speed, they conclude.
arxiv-2608-00330:
Cutler and co-authors test new ways to assess visualization literacy beyond multiple choice. Literacy spans decoding data, building charts, and spotting design flaws. Standard tests target lower-order skills like chart reading. They show ceiling effects, where modest skill scores near the top. Higher-order skills like critique and design go unmeasured.

Their two web-based assessments use think-aloud critique and sketching tasks. Participants critique designs and sketch charts from data plus a prompt. Three groups took part: crowdworkers, course students, and researchers. The new tests captured skills distinct from CALVI and Mini-VLAT scores. They also split experienced individuals more finely than choice-based tests. Qualitative, multimodal tests are a promising complement, they conclude.
arxiv-2608-00430:
Wan and Yang construct self-similar solutions of the three-dimensional Muskat problem with surface tension. The one-phase problem gets a one-parameter family of small solutions. Each solution scales with time to the one-third power times a profile. The initial data are conical, proportional to the norm of x. The profiles perturb the linear capillary smoothing of the cone.

They identify the leading quadratic correction to that profile. A raywise inverse estimate for the linear similarity operator anchors the proof. A favorable cancellation in the quadratic term helps as well. Tame estimates for the Dirichlet-Neumann operator on conical graphs complete the toolkit. A contraction argument then yields the solutions. The conical singularity rounds instantly for positive time, they show.
avicenna-canon-medicine-gruner-1930:
Avicenna, the Persian physician and philosopher of the eleventh century, wrote the Canon of Medicine as a vast encyclopedia of healing. Gruner's 1930 English translation covers Book One of the Canon. It is the first English rendering of the medical system that ruled East and West for six centuries.

Book One lays out the theory: elements, humors, temperaments, and the causes and signs of disease. Avicenna sorts fevers, pulses, and diets with a calm, orderly mind that trusts both reason and long practice. European universities taught from the Canon into the seventeenth century, so its first book shaped doctors for ages.
boas-the-religion-of-the-kwakiutl-indian:
Boas spent decades recording the Kwakiutl, now known as the Kwakwaka'wakw, of British Columbia's coast. This 1930 study, drawn from dictated native texts, presents their religion as they described it themselves, in the Columbia University Contributions to Anthropology series.

The heart of the book is the winter ceremonial, the great season of dances, feasts, and secret societies. Boas explains shamanism, guardian spirits, and the rituals by which dancers took on spirit power. Because the texts came from native speakers, the work gives an insider's view rare for its time. It remains a core source on Northwest Coast religion.
budge-amulets-talismans-1930:
E. A. Wallis Budge, keeper of Egyptian works at the British Museum, wrote this wide survey of charms in 1930. The book was later reprinted with the title Amulets and Talismans. His ground was Egypt and the Near East, where charms had a long, rich past.

Budge sorts charms by kind, tells what each was meant to do, and gives old texts with translations. Stones, rings, and writ charms each get their place, with drawings to show their forms. It stays the classic English survey of the charm lore of the old east.
cia-0000009930:
Hoa Lo, the detention and interrogation center for American prisoners in Hanoi, is detailed in a July 1971 CIA paper. Hoa Lo's French-built walls held the war's most famous group of captives. Unlike the sketch report filed the same month, a detailed paper works in prose: routines, staff, and methods.

Two files on one prison in one month suggest a deliberate study effort that summer. Analysts merged prisoner accounts, photographs, and source reports into a single picture. That picture served debriefers when men came home in 1973. This paper is the fuller half of the pair, the system's center described at length.
cia-0000013230:
Would North Vietnam refuse to comply fully with settlement terms on prisoners? A CIA paper from October 1970 thinks the question through as personal views. The analysts' private doubts ran ahead of any peace talks. They weighed Hanoi's record and its uses for captives. They considered the leverage unreturned men would give Hanoi. That leverage could last long after the guns stopped, in talks not yet begun in earnest.

The paper's doubts proved prescient in ways its writers could not enjoy. The homecoming, when it came, was shadowed by the missing. For readers, the page shows the war's hardest question asked early and honestly.
cia-0000013830:
Information concerning American prisoners of war is gathered in a CIA compilation from November 1966. The compilation pulls the early files' fragments into one place. Names, sightings, camp reports, and rumors all entered this first accounting. Each scrap was a stone in a structure that would grow for decades, as the missing men's files thickened into the war's longest unfinished business.

The compilation's care shows in its plain gathering of small facts. The fragments were all the files had, and they were entered without decoration. For readers, the page is the accounting's foundation layer: the captives, glimpsed and recorded, one report at a time.
cia-0000013930: North Vietnam's policy on prisoners of war sits beside a second topic, the draft, in a CIA report dated January 6, 1968. One half covers how the north said captives would be held. The other covers how the north called up its own young men. The pairing shows the war's manpower and prisoner questions side by side.
cia-0000015330: A letter to Coral Lorenson from John Warner fills a CIA file dated November 2, 1960. Warner refers her letter on to the Air Force, per the title. Most saucer mail that reached the agency was sent on just this way. The file holds the polite hand off given to one more citizen writer.
cia-0000015430: Declassifying a CIA report on UFOs was requested by the Air Force in a record dated July 2, 1966. The two services had shared the saucer problem for years, with the Air Force in the public lead. Opening an agency report would expose how the CIA had judged the same reports. The file keeps the request itself, a small marker of a wider push for openness.
cia-0000020430: Chile's government meant to step up its diplomatic, commercial, and propaganda work abroad, a CIA record dated in 1972 reports. The clipped title lists three fields of effort in a row. Salvador Allende's government was then seeking friends and trade under growing strain. Reading a rival government's plans to sell itself abroad was standard work for the agency's Chile watchers.
cia-0000022330: A Soviet article claimed the United States buys spies, and the CIA kept it in a record dated in 1960. The piece belonged to the press war around the Powers trial that year. Moscow used the case to paint American intelligence as a market in hired men. Filing enemy articles let analysts track the lines being sold to Soviet readers at home.
cia-0000028530: Two American pilots held captive in Laos were transferred to North Vietnam, a CIA record dated in 1968 reports. A transfer moved the men farther from any rescue and into the main prison system. Such moves were tracked closely, since a man's place shaped every plan for him. The entry adds one hard journey to the long record of the Laos missing.
cia-0000044430:
Havana blamed the Salvadoran army for the priest killings, in a CIA record dated October 5, 1989 in the catalog. Cuba supported the rebels in El Salvador's civil war. Its charge against the army came as no surprise to any reader.

Inside, the Cuban accusation is preserved as Havana delivered it. Expected or not, the charge added a foreign voice to the chorus. It also served Cuba's own contest with the United States by proxy. The file shows the murders entering the region's wider argument, in which each capital used the crime to score points against its enemies abroad.
cia-0000045930: An official arrived for talks about Americans missing in Vietnam, and a CIA item dated June 5, 1991, noted the visit.
