Such trips were the working machinery of the accounting effort, meeting by meeting and list by list. The brief report marks one stop in a process that ground on for years after the war.
cia-0000049130: Findings of the Special Honor Commission in the San Sebastian case fill a CIA item from 1989. An honor commission was the armed forces' own court of inquiry, judging soldiers by the institution's code. Its findings carried weight inside the army even when outsiders doubted them, and the file kept them for the record.
cia-0000049230: A 1992 letter from the CIA's deputy director for operations to Congressman Bud Shuster survives in this item. The letter relates to a Salvadoran general whose name the title cuts off after Juan. Shuster had pressed the Jesuit case hard in Congress, and letters like this one were the agency's formal answers.
cia-0000102930: Use of Forced Labor on Central Asian Gas Pipeline, with dates of information 1976 to 1978, is declassified CIA document 0000102930, dated July 4, 1982. The heading names the project and the labor type plainly. The brief file is a gas pipeline record from Central Asia, part of the cluster's repeated pairing of pipelines with forced hands.
cia-0000112330: Overview of the Academy of Sciences of the Ukrainian Ssr and the Antonov Airc are two numbered headings in declassified CIA document 0000112330, dated January 3, 1990. The first item surveys a science academy in the Ukrainian SSR. The second names the Antonov works, then breaks off at Airc in the heading. The brief record pairs a science overview with an aircraft item.
cia-0000112830: Name List of Germans in Shanghai Connected with Intelligence and Propaganda And is the heading, cut off mid-thought, on declassified CIA document 0000112830, dated September 6, 1945. The title describes a list: Germans in Shanghai tied to intelligence and propaganda work. Its final word, And, shows the list title was cut in the release. The brief record preserves the hanging ending as released.
cia-0000118930: The September 15TH Statement on the Dominican Republic by the Honorable J. Will is the heading, cut off mid-name, on declassified CIA document 0000118930, dated August 3, 1965. The title gives a dated statement on the Dominican Republic by a man named only as J. Will. His surname breaks off where the heading ends. The brief record preserves the partial name and the break as released.
cia-0000119730:
From September 1956, this CIA item reports Hungarian university reforms stressing de-Sovietization, the dropping of Moscow's grip on teaching and campus life. Students and teachers were among the first to demand an end to Soviet controls. Their revolt in the lecture halls fed the larger one coming.

University reform sounds minor beside revolutions, but in a party state the classroom was an arm of power. Changing it meant challenging the system in miniature. The item captures that challenge as the agency reported it. It helps explain why students stood near the front when Hungary rose weeks later. The regime's hold on ideas broke before its hold on the streets did.
cia-0000126930: A March 1971 CIA item reports the New China News Agency's account of foreign visitors arriving in Peking. The agency, now known as Xinhua, was Beijing's official voice. The item logs who was visiting China as its doors began to open that year. Visitor lists were a standard open-source harvest of the era, since each arriving delegation hinted at trade, arms, or recognition that Beijing was quietly arranging.
cia-0000132430:
Moscow starting economic ties with Cuba is reported in a CIA item dated January 1, 1960. Trade deals were the first threads of the Soviet-Cuban alliance that followed. Sugar, oil, and credit would soon move between the two countries in growing amounts each year.

The item records the opening step while it was still small enough to fit in a short report. For readers, it marks the point where a commercial link began turning into a strategic one. The alliance built on such deals would trouble Washington for the rest of the Cold War. Its effects reached far beyond the two capitals that signed the first papers.
cia-0000132630: Talks on working with Argentine Peronists reportedly held by Cuba fill item 5 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated June 3, 1960. Its headline breaks off at the word Peroni, short for the Peronist movement. Havana was reaching out to Argentina's exiled movement that year. The short item reports the talks and who was said to be involved.
cia-0000133630:
Cuba fills a CIA briefing dated April 3, 1959. The new regime in Havana was about ninety days old at that point in time. Washington was still learning the shape of the government that had replaced Batista in January of that year.

The briefing gives the early picture as analysts had it that spring. Much was still guesswork about Castro's aims and his hold on the island. For readers, the entry is a baseline for the whole Cuba file that followed. Later papers grew darker and more certain month by month. This one preserves the open questions of the revolution's first season in power, before the answers hardened into policy.
cia-0000135730: A Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade papers, cataloged at 1 January 1961 with the date marked as estimated. Brigade 2506 was the exile force that would land at the Bay of Pigs in April. The record names no subject for this document. It survives in Spanish in the CIA's declassified release. Estimated New Year dates recur in this series and likely mark filing points; the text itself is the only guide to what this item holds.
cia-0000135830: A CIA document dated 3 February 1954 deals with the choosing of people for disposal by a junta group, named plainly in the heading, in files since declassified. PBSUCCESS was the code name for the CIA effort to bring down President Jacobo Arbenz of Guatemala, which ended with his fall in June 1954. Read on its own terms, the record shows the operation at work in its own words, with some names still blacked out.
cia-0000135930: A cable in the declassified CIA files, dated 1 January 1954, covers talks with Mylkes about possible sources, the object of the search cut off in the heading. Lincoln was the station cryptonym for PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation against President Arbenz in Guatemala that ended in June 1954. Taken with the rest of the station traffic, it helps map who handled what, and when, inside the mission.
cia-0000136130: A CIA cable from 1 April 1954, since declassified, gives more information on a ship, its name cut off in the heading. Lincoln was the station cryptonym for PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation against President Arbenz in Guatemala that ended in June 1954. Taken with the rest of the station traffic, it helps map who handled what, and when, inside the mission.
cia-0000136230: A CIA cable from 3 May 1954, now declassified, deals with tapes for Sherwood broadcasts, fresh ammunition for the radio war, asked for two readers. Traffic like this ran the field side of PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Small as it is, the sheet documents one task, one report, or one order inside a much larger secret effort.
cia-0000136330: Preparing a vessel for Plan Beta is proposed in this 27 June 1954 LINCOLN cable. Despite political changes and possible government surrender, the enemy still holds greatly superior military forces and friendly forces sit in a precarious position. International pressure might also end outside support within six or seven days. The station therefore proposes chartering a vessel for at least forty-five days, with an option for thirty more, ready to sail within hours.
cia-0000136730: Dated 1 October 1960, this Spanish text belongs to the 2506 Brigade papers in the CIA's declassified release. The brigade was in training that fall, building toward the force that would land in Cuba the next spring. The catalog record names no subject for the document. It survives in the original Spanish, an October entry in the brigade's growing archive from its buildup period.
cia-0000136930: A ship captain wants contact with the Swedish consul. This April 1954 cable reports it after the SS Alfhem left Puerto Barrios. Headquarters wants the captain reached. He must be debriefed in full. The subject is the shipment to Guatemala from behind the Iron Curtain. What was the cargo? How was the shipment arranged? How was it carried out, start to end? How was final delivery made at Puerto Barrios? The field must report its chances on a priority basis.
cia-0000137330: The Castro regime serves world communist objectives in Latin America. This CIA briefing for the 7 April 1960 NSC meeting asserts it. Bloc delegates are now in Havana. So are communists from many Latin American countries. They attend the Fourth National Congress of the party's youth section. The regime gave the congress television time. A front youth congress is planned next. Its preparatory meeting sits in Havana on 25 April. A Cuban mission tours the region to publicize it.
cia-0000141130: Hazard bonuses for B-26 crews are tabulated in this August 1961 memorandum. It belongs to the JMGLOW Cuba air operation. Bonuses used the usual basis. Minimum hazard paid 250 dollars. Average hazard paid 350 dollars. Maximum hazard paid 500 dollars. The list names crewmen and their flights. Connie Segrist earned bonuses across November 1960 and April 1961. Riley Shamburger, Wade Gray, Thomas Ray, and Leo Baker each earned 500 dollars for 19 April 1961. That was the Bay of Pigs' final air day. Several listed men did not return.
cia-03448330: August 7, 1955: the daily bulletin circulated in Washington. The intelligence summary went to top officials. The Cold War's August note. It holds its historical place. This declassified paper remains. It is stored. It is filed. Readers can find it here.
cia-06835030: FIOA CASE LOGS, APRIL - JUNE 2019, a CIA document. The case logs. This file preserves that declassified paper. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
combe-system-phrenology-1830:
George Combe was an Edinburgh lawyer who gave his life to phrenology. His System of Phrenology came out in 1830. The book set the skull science in full, clear form. For years it served as the creed book of the whole field.

Combe lists each organ of the brain and the trait it rules. He tells how to gauge the size of each part by the skull. Tales of heads he read back up his claims in bulk. The book made head reading a mass creed of the age, taught in halls and homes.
dewey-individualism-1930:
Individualism Old and New, published in 1930, collects Dewey's essays on the American self in a corporate age. The old individualism of the pioneer and the small owner, he argues, has lost its ground, and the modern American feels lost inside vast organizations.

Dewey refuses both nostalgia and despair. A new individualism, he says, must be built through shared inquiry, education, and democratic control of economic power. The self grows by participation, not isolation. Written at the start of the Depression, the book reads like a diagnosis still in force. It is Dewey the public philosopher at his most direct.
die-edelgeborne-jungfer-alchymia-oder-ei: Die edelgeborne Jungfer Alchymia, 1730. The noble maid Alchymia. This book preserves that work. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers. It holds its historical place. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. Writers of history may cite it later in their work.
doe-osti-3363931-sierra-sd-users-manual-: Sierra/SD got manual-5.30'd, and this DOE users manual covers version 5.30. The pages detail the findings. The engineers get their data. The manual was users. The data were engineer. The 5.30 were manual. The SD were Sierra. The engineers were data.
doe-osti-3363932-sierra-sd-verification-: Sierra/SD got verification-5.30'd, and this DOE test manual covers version 5.30. The pages detail the findings. The engineers get their data. The manual was verification test. The data were engineer. The 5.30 were test. The SD were Sierra. The engineers were data.
doe-osti-3363933-sierra-sd-user-s-guide-: Sierra/SD got NasGen-5.30'd, and this DOE guide covers NasGen version. The pages detail the users findings. The engineers get their data. The guide was user. The data were engineer. The NasGen were guide. The 5.30 were version. The engineers were data.
doe-osti-3363935-sierra-sd-its2sierra-us: Sierra/SD got Its2Sierra-5.30'd, and this DOE manual covers Its2Sierra version. The pages detail the users findings. The engineers get their data. The manual was user. The data were engineer. The Its2Sierra were manual. The 5.30 were users.
doe-osti-3364732-sierra-sd-example-probl: Sierra/SD got example-5.30'd, and this DOE problems manual covers version. The pages detail the findings. The engineers get their data. The manual was example problems. The data were engineer. The 5.30 were problems. The example were manual. The engineers were data.
eliot-ash-wednesday-1930:
T. S. Eliot wrote Ash Wednesday after his conversion to the Church of England in 1927. The long poem appeared in 1930 and marked a clear turn in his work. Its six parts are complete in this text.

The speaker is a man trying to leave his old life behind and learn a new faith. He renounces old loves and ambitions, climbs a winding stair, and addresses a silent lady figure. The tone is quiet, strained, and full of prayer fragments and echoes of Dante. Readers often treat the poem as Eliot's record of conversion: difficult, humble, and hard won.
essays-de-iean-rey-docteur-en-medecine-s: Essays de Jean Rey, 1630. The Rey essays. This book preserves that work. Tomorrow's readers will find it. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc10000530:
Wang and co-workers review how chemicals made by gut microbes help keep the immune system in balance, in a 2023 paper. The gut is home to bacteria, fungi, and viruses that live with the body in a healthy state. When that mix shifts, immune control can shift with it.

The authors explain how microbe-made products, called metabolites, calm or stir immune cells in the gut and beyond. They link changes in these products to illness and to new treatment ideas. The review gives readers a plain map of a fast-growing field.
europmc-pmc10394030:
Kim and Croce surveyed trials in 2023 that use microRNA in cancer care. A microRNA is a short RNA strip that does not code for a protein. It tunes gene activity and can push cancer growth or hold it back. Many cancers show clear shifts in their microRNA mix.

Those shifts make microRNAs fine marks for finding and staging cancer. Kim tracks trials that test them in screening, diagnosis, and drug checks. Some trials aim drugs at harmful microRNAs, while others add back lost ones. The review brings past trial reports up to date. It sets out where the field stands and what proof is still thin.
europmc-pmc10611730:
Wu and co-authors found in 2023 why some killer T cells wear out in cancer and chronic infection. T cells tire in stages: a fresh precursor pool feeds a spent final pool. The spent cells lose their killing power and pour out fewer signals. What flips the switch from fresh to spent was unclear.

Faulty power units inside the cell proved to be the trigger. Wu shows that their strain blocks the breakdown of a switch protein, HIF-1alpha. That switch rewires fuel use toward sugar and locks in the spent state. The team used gene-cut mice, single-cell reads, and fuel scans to prove the chain. Tuning fuel in lab-grown CAR T cells may keep them fresh for longer.
europmc-pmc10767930:
Cappannini and co-authors updated MODOMICS in 2023, a data bank of RNA modifications. RNA strands carry chemical edits that tune how they work. The bank logs each known edit and the proteins tied to it. Fresh data and new data types headline this release.

The edit catalogue grew to span natural and lab-made residues found in RNA shapes. Name rules were reworked to fit the larger count. Cappannini adds fresh RNA sequences and brings back alignments for transfer and ribosomal RNAs. The protein part now links to lab shapes and AlphaFold predictions. A new note system marks how well each entry is backed, with a reliability grade.
europmc-pmc1084330:
Jackson and colleagues show how polio virus hijacks a cell clean-up system in this 2005 paper. Infected human cells grow odd double-walled bubbles, and the virus copies its genes on their surfaces. Where these bubbles come from was unknown. The team checked whether they match autophagosomes, which are sacs cells use to digest worn parts, a process called autophagy.

Markers of those sacs turned up on the virus bubbles early in infection, they found. The same signs appeared with cold viruses and with just two virus proteins. Boosting the clean-up pathway raised virus output, while blocking it cut output. The authors propose the virus borrows this machinery as a scaffold for copying itself. That flips the usual view, since the same system often helps cells fight germs.
europmc-pmc11046930:
Hu and a large team present a tool that builds genomes from long but error-prone DNA reads in this 2024 paper. Long-read machines can span tangled, repeated genome regions that short reads cannot. One leading platform, Oxford Nanopore, produces reads with high error rates. Correcting those errors before assembly is the hard step.

Their tool, NextDenovo, corrects errors and assembles the genome with high accuracy, the authors report. They used it to build 35 human genomes from people around the world. Those genomes exposed the landscape of duplicated segments and gene copy number changes in modern populations. Copy number means how many copies of a gene a person carries. The team argues the tool opens the door to building genomes for whole populations from Nanopore long reads.
europmc-pmc11139930:
Chen and colleagues review macrophages as drivers and drug targets in heart disease in this 2024 paper. Macrophages are innate immune cells that lead the first response after heart injury. They can deepen the damage and also guide the repair that follows. Their varied forms track closely with the type and severity of heart conditions.

The review covers coronary disease, valve disease, heart muscle inflammation, heart failure, artery clogging, and aneurysm. Single-cell sequencing, which reads gene activity cell by cell, has newly exposed macrophage variety and their talks with other cells. A shared thread is myocardial fibrosis, the scarring of heart muscle found in most cardiac diseases. The authors detail how macrophages push or restrain that scarring. They close with the control switches that drugs might target in each disease.
europmc-pmc11237130:
Hu, Chen, Qian, and Li update the picture of one signal pathway in bone in this 2024 review. Wnt proteins are secreted, fat-tagged signals that bind receptors on cell surfaces. Their canonical path, run through beta-catenin, controls many processes in development and adult life. Faulty Wnt signalling underlies a wide range of human diseases.

The review sums up the pathway's proteins, receptors, activators, and inhibitors in bone. It details how the path crosstalks with other pathways. Mouse models carrying tweaks to Wnt components are catalogued as evidence. Bone formation, upkeep, and related diseases form the core. Treatment strategies are sorted by where they strike: outside the cell, in the cell body, or in the nucleus. The authors close by judging how well the field grasps this control system.
europmc-pmc1175030:
Aletaha and colleagues test whether lab blood markers are needed to score rheumatoid arthritis activity in this 2005 study. Frequent activity scores let doctors adapt therapy and prevent progression. Current composite indices require acute phase reactants, blood proteins that rise with inflammation, which delays scoring until lab results return. The team hypothesised those markers add little to one index, the SDAI.

They built a clinical index, the CDAI, by adding tender joint counts to swollen joint counts over 28 joints, plus patient and physician global assessments. Data came from an observational cohort of 767 patients and an independent early cohort of 106 patients followed prospectively. The hypothesis held: the reactant-free score showed comparable validity to the lab-based indices in both cohorts. The authors validate the CDAI as a practical score usable at the bedside.
europmc-pmc1266030:
Parsons, Worthey, Ward, and Mottram catalogued kinase enzymes in three parasites in 2005. The parasites cause leishmaniasis, sleeping sickness, and Chagas disease. Kinases relay signals that pace their complex life cycles. Genome searches counted every kinase in each species.

Trypanosoma brucei held 176 kinases, and Trypanosoma cruzi held 190. Leishmania major held 199, the most of the three. Most kinases matched across all three species. The counts run near 30 percent of the human total. They double the malaria parasite count. Parsons supplies a target list for anti-parasite drug work. Each parasite shifts between insect hosts and mammal hosts across its life cycle in turn.
europmc-pmc1277830:
Choi reviewed drug pump proteins that drive cancer drug resistance in 2005. ABC transporters push many drugs out of cells using energy. That pumping lowers drug levels and fuels treatment failure. Three pumps dominate the resistance literature.

They are P-glycoprotein, a multidrug resistance protein, and breast cancer resistance protein. Blocking the pumps with helper drugs, called chemosensitizers, is one fix. Combined use aims to restore drug levels inside tumor cells. Choi covers pump structure, normal body roles, and blocker development. Reversing pumps could rescue failing chemotherapy. It appeared in Cancer Cell International in 2005.
europmc-pmc1280330:
vom Saal and Hughes argued in 2005 that bisphenol A risk rules need a full rewrite. BPA builds polycarbonate plastic and can linings worldwide. Global capacity topped 6.4 billion pounds per year. Leaching from products has spread human exposure widely.

A plastics-funded review of 19 studies had called low-dose evidence weak. The wider literature told another story by late 2004. Of 115 animal studies on low doses, 94 reported significant effects. Thirty-one found effects below the assumed safe dose of 50 micrograms per kilogram daily. Cell tests showed disruption at extremely low concentrations. Cell tests confirmed a hormone-like mode of action at very low doses.
europmc-pmc1280930:
Donaldson and co-authors reviewed combustion-derived nanoparticles and lung exposure in 2005. Sources covered are diesel soot, coal fly ash, carbon black, and welding fume. Breathing them threatens lungs through stress, swelling, and cancer pathways. Particles can also redistribute to other organs after landing in lungs.

Large surface area plus metals and organics drive oxidative stress. Exact stress sources differ by particle mix and solubility. Genetic damage effects also depend on composition. Particles can reach the brain and blood from the lung. Heart, spleen, and liver then become reachable targets. It appeared in Particle and Fibre Toxicology in 2005.
europmc-pmc1534030:
New treatments often fade into routine slowly, or not at all. May set out a model in 2006 for how complex health interventions become normal practice. He drew on ten years of studies on telemedicine, changing care patterns, and how evidence reaches the ward.

The normalization process model rests on four parts. Interactional workability asks whether the new practice works in real encounters. Relational integration covers trust and accountability. Skill set workability asks who can do the tasks. Contextual integration asks whether the organization backs it. May offers the model to judge a new practice's odds of sticking before launch.
europmc-pmc1539030:
Molecules must escape a protein's inner pockets through tunnels. Petrek and co-authors built a tool in 2006 to find those tunnels, called CAVER. It traces paths from buried clefts and cavities inside a protein out to the surrounding fluid.

CAVER lays a grid over the protein and finds the spine of each route. It works on still structures from crystal studies and on moving ones from simulations with thousands of frames. The tool is free, as a stand-alone program or a plug-in for a common viewer. Petrek notes it also handles DNA and even inorganic matter, not just proteins.
europmc-pmc1617130:
Missing smell and stunted puberty share a genetic root in Kallmann syndrome. Dodé and co-authors found two new culprit genes in 2006, screening 192 patients. Known genes explained only about a fifth of cases.

They found ten distinct mutations in PROKR2, the gene for a signal receptor, and four in PROK2, its signal partner. Some patients carried faults in both PROKR2 and the older gene KAL1, a two-gene inheritance. Faulty prokineticin signaling disrupts both the smell system and the reproductive axis. Dodé widens the known genetic map of the syndrome.
europmc-pmc1635530:
A plant's body-wide alarm system runs through a hub of gene switches. Wang, Amornsiripanitch, and Dong mapped new nodes of that network in 2006. Systemic acquired resistance primes the whole plant after a local attack, driven by salicylic acid through a cofactor called NPR1.

By switching NPR1 on at will in Arabidopsis, they caught its direct targets. NPR1 directly raised eight WRKY transcription factor genes, from a family of 74. Mutant tests placed five of those factors in the network, some boosting and some braking resistance. Wang shows a genome-first route can position new regulators in a complex defense web.
europmc-pmc1635730:
Ovarian tumors spread across the belly by sticking to its lining. Gubbels and co-authors pinned that sticking in 2006 to a tight molecular handshake. A mucin on tumor cells, MUC16, binds mesothelin, a protein on lining cells.

The binding was strong, with an affinity around 5 to 10 nanomolar, and reached its peak within five minutes. Sugars attached to MUC16 proved essential: stripping them killed the binding. Tumor cells bearing MUC16 clung far more to cells bearing mesothelin. Gubbels argues this grip, tuned to the belly's conditions, helps seed the spread of ovarian cancer.
europmc-pmc1761130:
Diet decides whether a young bee becomes queen or worker. Wheeler, Buck, and Evans examined insulin pathway genes in 2006 during the caste decision window in honey bee larvae. Insulin signaling links nutrition to growth.

One insulin-like peptide gene was expressed at very high levels in queen larvae but not in workers. An insulin receptor gene also ran higher in queens during the second larval stage. The differences appeared exactly when diet sets fate. Wheeler names the insulin pathway a compelling candidate connecting food to the signals that build a queen.
europmc-pmc1820830:
Kasschau, Carrington and co-authors profiled in 2007 the small interfering RNAs of the plant Arabidopsis thaliana across its whole genome. These siRNAs, often 24 DNA letters long, guide silencing of genes, repeats, and viruses. The team compared normal plants with mutants lacking key silencing enzymes.

Using parallel sequencing, they mapped where small RNAs arise. Spots rich in 24-letter siRNAs matched repetitive DNA across the genome. Making them depended mostly on two enzymes, RDR2 and DCL3, though backup Dicer-like enzymes acted widely when DCL3 was gone. No backup replaced RDR2. Around protein-coding genes, the control regions upstream were notably free of siRNA production. Few nearby genes seemed directly regulated by this silencing, despite the wide spread of the small RNAs.
europmc-pmc1857730:
Medina-Gomez, Vidal-Puig and co-authors dissected in 2007 how one fat-regulating protein shields the body from its own lipids. The protein, PPAR gamma 2, is the nutrition-sensing form of a fat cell master switch. Removing it in obese mice shrank fat mass yet caused severe insulin resistance, blood fat problems, and failure of insulin-making beta cells.

Fat profiling showed the protein lets fat tissue expand to soak up surplus energy safely. When the protein appeared in liver and muscle, it steered lipids into harmless storage forms called triacylglycerols and kept reactive lipid species from building up. Lipotoxicity is the damage those reactive species cause. The protein also seems required for beta cells to grow in response to insulin resistance. Together the work frames fat expansion as protective, not just passive.
europmc-pmc1950230:
Lorenzi weighed in 2007 whether one sugar detour explains diabetic damage to the retina. The polyol pathway converts glucose to sorbitol, then to fructose, in two steps. It switches on when cell glucose runs high, and its enzymes sit in the very tissues diabetes harms.

Blocking its first enzyme, aldose reductase, reliably prevents retinopathy in diabetic rodents. A major human trial, however, disappointed. Lorenzi argues that sorbitol levels, the usual gauge, likely fail to capture true pathway activity in tissue. The known picture of human disease has also widened: support cells and neurons of the retina suffer too, and animal work ties those changes to the polyol pathway as well. The pathway remains an attractive, elusive, and resilient suspect, in the author's own framing.
europmc-pmc2073730:
ARMITAGE and DOLL examined in 1957 how cancer risk rises with age, and what that pattern implies. Death rates for many cancers rise roughly in proportion to a high power of age. Several writers had suggested cancer is the end result of a series of separate cell changes, like mutations. In earlier work the authors had argued for six or seven such stages.

That multi-stage idea explained differing age curves between cancer sites. It also explained the long latent period after exposure to a carcinogen, a cancer-causing agent. It fit clinical facts such as circumcision in adolescence failing to protect against penile cancer. Yet direct experimental evidence for more than two stages was lacking. They test a two-stage theory against that gap, weighing how far simpler models can explain the age data.
europmc-pmc2131030: A medical paper with studies on regeneration of bacteriophage, influence of partial anaerobiosis. The reborn phage. This article preserves that virology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2140430: A biology paper on the formation of the aster in artificial parthenogenesis. The fatherless star. This article preserves that embryology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2140930: A biology paper on time relations of growth, growth constants during the self-accelerating phase. The growth math again. This article preserves that biology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2235230:
Beelen and a large team studied traffic-related air pollution and mortality in 2008 in a Dutch cohort of 120,852 people. The cohort, begun for diet and cancer research, was followed from 1987 to 1996. Black smoke, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide and fine-particle exposure was estimated at each home address, along with traffic intensity measures. Analyses adjusted for age, sex, smoking and area-level social status.

Traffic intensity on the nearest road independently predicted mortality. For black smoke, relative risks per standard increase were 1.05 for natural-cause deaths and 1.22 for respiratory deaths. Several intervals included no effect, though. Nitrogen dioxide and fine particles gave similar patterns. This was a Dutch cohort analysis of long-term exposure at home addresses. Sulfur dioxide showed no association. The authors say the generally small risks still add evidence that long-term air pollution raises mortality.
europmc-pmc2259330:
Lehmann, Dieleman and Martineau reviewed in 2008 why health workers leave remote rural posts in poorer countries, and what keeps them there. Shortages and maldistribution of staff are severe, worsened by weak health systems and by HIV and AIDS. Low wages, poor conditions, missing equipment and weak supervision all drive flight from remote areas. The authors searched English-language literature from 1997 to 2007, assessing about 600 papers and including 55.

They find attraction and retention factors are many-sided and interact strongly. Yet strategies usually target only one or a few factors at a time. The authors argue for bundles of interventions covering living conditions, working environment and development opportunities together. They also examine where decisions are made, since organisational level shapes which strategies are even possible. Single-fix policies are unlikely to hold staff in remote posts.
europmc-pmc2330030:
Meltzer and Noble reviewed idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis in 2008, a disease where scar tissue builds up in the lungs for no known cause. Idiopathic means the cause is unknown, and fibrosis means scarring. About 5 million people worldwide have it, most often men around age 66.

Early signs are breathlessness on exertion, a dry cough, and crackling sounds low in the lungs. About half of patients develop clubbed fingertips, where the ends swell and nails curve. Scans show a net-like pattern and honeycomb pockets near the lung surface. The authors stressed that diagnosis links symptoms, scans, and often a lung sample. No drug therapy worked at the time, they noted. Typical survival after diagnosis was only two to five years, though lung transplant offered some patients an option.
europmc-pmc2360730:
Villa and many colleagues reported five-year results for an HPV vaccine in 2006. HPV, human papillomavirus, causes cervical cancer, other genital cancers, and genital warts. The vaccine targeted four types, 6, 11, 16, and 18, using empty virus shells to train the immune system.

The trial enrolled 552 women aged 16 to 23, who got vaccine or placebo at months 0, 2, and 6. A subset of 241 women was followed for two extra years. At five years, lasting infection or disease from the four types was cut by 96% in the vaccine group, with 2 cases versus 46 on placebo. No vaccinated woman developed precancerous cervical changes or genital warts from these types, versus six cases on placebo. Antibody levels stayed at or above those after natural infection.
europmc-pmc2361730:
Mascaux and colleagues reviewed the RAS gene in lung cancer in 2005. RAS makes a small protein that relays growth signals, and it is mutated in about 20% of lung cancers. Studies disagreed on whether that fault, or excess of its protein, meant worse survival for patients.

The team gathered 43 studies and combined 28 of them, all on non-small-cell lung cancer, the common form. The pooled result showed worse survival when KRAS was mutated or its protein overproduced, with a combined hazard ratio of 1.35 in the full set. The effect was strongest in adenocarcinoma, one subtype, at 1.59 in the hazard ratio. Studies using gene tests found the effect clearly. Studies using protein staining did not, which the authors noted as a methods warning.
europmc-pmc2453330:
Fu, Sinha, Peterson, and Weng mapped the orderly DNA packaging around a boundary protein in 2008. DNA in cells wraps around protein spools called nucleosomes, and where spools sit decides which genes stay reachable. CTCF is a protein that binds DNA boundaries, called insulators, between gene neighbourhoods.

Merging dozens of recent genome-wide data sets, they found an array of about 20 precisely placed nucleosomes flanking every CTCF binding site. Spacing between spool centres was strikingly regular, averaging 185 base pairs. These nucleosomes were loaded with a special histone variant, H2A.Z, and eleven chemical histone marks. Spools rich in activity-linked marks protected shorter DNA stretches, 106 to 164 base pairs, hinting their DNA stays more open. The CTCF-flanking spools were positioned more precisely than those after gene start sites, the only other known anchor. The authors proposed CTCF anchors the whole array.
europmc-pmc2564830:
Akbar and colleagues looked for a pain mechanism in irritable bowel syndrome in this 2008 study, focusing on a nerve sensor called TRPV1. This receptor, also triggered by chilli heat, is suspected in gut pain and oversensitivity. The team took small biopsies from the lower bowel of 23 patients and 22 healthy controls and counted nerve fibres carrying the receptor, relating counts to pain scores.

Fibres carrying TRPV1 were 3.5 times more numerous in patients than controls, a highly significant gap. Fibres carrying the pain messenger substance P, total nerve fibres, mast cells, and immune cells were also raised, hinting at low-grade inflammation. In the full statistical model, only TRPV1 fibres and mast cells tracked the abdominal pain score. The authors name TRPV1 a possible drug target.
europmc-pmc2631630:
Spek reported in 2009 on the current state of structure validation in chemical crystallography, the machine checking of crystal structures before they appear in print. Determining a molecule's three-dimensional structure from X-ray diffraction is error-prone, and referees once checked data by hand. About twelve years earlier the International Union of Crystallography began a validation project, now the checkCIF/PLATON suite, which Spek oversees.

The system reads crystallographic data files and issues alerts about completeness, consistency, and structural problems for authors and referees to address. Validation asks three questions: is the reported information complete, how good is the analysis, and is the structure correct? Spek classifies structure quality into four classes. They run from near-perfect determinations to outright incorrect ones. He warns that a wrong published structure can be disastrous for research built on it. Use of the check is mandatory for the union's journals.
europmc-pmc2669730:
Matukumalli and a large team built in 2009 a chip that reads over 54,000 DNA letter variants in cattle at once. Human gene hunts had shown the power of scanning the whole genome for trait-linked variants. Cattle breeders wanted the same tool to find genes behind milk, meat, and disease traits, and to guide breeding choices.

A new spacing method spread the markers evenly, with a typical gap of only 37,000 letters and no gap above 350,000. Tested on 576 animals from 21 breeds, the chip found between about 39,800 and 46,500 working variants per breed. It also spotted 79 larger DNA gains and losses. As a proof, the chip correctly mapped known variants for coat color and for horns. The assay, sold as the BovineSNP50, gave cattle genetics a standard platform.
europmc-pmc2680630:
Cao and Wang reviewed in 2009 how silk materials break down inside the body, a key question for medical use. Silk from the silkworm has served as stitch thread for ages. It is gentle on tissue, non-toxic, and now shaped into films, mats, and scaffolds for growing replacement tissue. Any implant that should vanish must do so at the right pace and without harm.

The review covers what is known about silk's breakdown routes. Enzymes in the body chew the silk protein, and the fragments are safe enough for cells to reuse as food. How fast this happens depends on how the silk was processed: its crystal content, shape, and the site where it sits. Dense, highly ordered silk can last years, while looser forms fade in weeks. Matching that clock to the healing job, the authors stress, decides whether a silk device helps or hinders.
europmc-pmc2704930:
Juhas and co-authors reviewed in 2009 genomic islands, blocks of DNA that bacteria gain from other bacteria rather than from a parent cell. Passing genes sideways like this is called horizontal transfer, meaning genes move between separate strains. Islands differ between close strains and can move again by several routes.

Their review shows how islands spread genes for drug resistance and for harming a host, which helps create hospital superbugs that resist many drugs. The same kind of islands also carry genes that break down chemicals and open new ways to live. One conserved family in two large bacterial groups gets special attention for its shared pattern.
europmc-pmc2709430:
Breslauer and co-authors built in 2009 a light microscope that mounts on a mobile phone for use where labs are scarce. Normal microscopes are costly and hard to move, yet phone networks reach many rural areas. Their device adds cheap lenses and LED lights, which are small bright lamps, to a camera phone.

They imaged malaria parasites in red blood cells and sickle-shaped red cells in bright light, and tuberculosis bacteria in sputum, a mucus sample, with glowing stains. Sharpness beat the level needed to see cell and microbe shapes in each case. Software also counted tuberculosis bacteria on its own, which points to phone-based screening and remote reading of samples.
europmc-pmc2776930:
Klingenberg presented in 2009 tools for testing whether a set of anatomical landmarks splits into modules, blocks that vary together internally but stay fairly independent of each other. Such hypotheses matter in evolutionary developmental biology, which studies how body plans are built and change. If a proposed split matches the true module boundaries, the covariation between blocks should be minimal.

He introduces Escoufier's RV coefficient, and a multi-set version, as measures of correlation between two or more landmark subsets. Partitions can then be compared head to head. Because developmental interactions stay within tissues, he adds a spatial rule: modules should form one connected patch, judged with an adjacency graph. He demonstrates the methods on the wing of the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster and on the jaw of the house mouse.
europmc-pmc2789530:
Tan and Yiap survey how labs pull DNA, RNA, and protein out of cells and tissues. Their 2009 review runs from early hand methods to modern kits and machines. Pulling these molecules free is the first step for most tests in molecular biology, the study of genes and proteins at a tiny scale.

Older extraction work was slow, hard, and hard to scale up, the authors explain. Labs now choose between liquid-based methods and column-based methods, or use ready-made kits that still need repeated spinning and careful liquid removal. Machines built for medium and large labs are also spreading, and the review weighs them on yield, purity, repeat results, speed, and the risk of mixing samples.
europmc-pmc2844030:
Pressoir and a large team ran a one-day survey in 2010 across seventeen French cancer centers to count malnutrition among patients. Over fifteen hundred unselected adults with cancer were weighed and rated by weight loss and body mass index, then followed for two months.

About three in ten patients were malnourished, and about one in eight severely so. Surprisingly, prior obesity raised the risk, perhaps because heavy patients get spotted late for feeding support. Poor physical performance and cancers of the head, neck, or upper digestive tract also raised risk, and malnourished patients used far more antibiotics. Severe malnutrition predicted death on its own, and malnourished patients stayed in hospital roughly six days longer than others.
europmc-pmc2850930:
Poole, Thomas, Yu, Vincow, and Pallanck reported in 2010 that two Parkinson's disease genes work by disposing of a protein that fuses mitochondria together. Mutations in PINK1 and parkin cause inherited parkinsonism, and fruit fly studies showed the pair push mitochondria toward breaking apart. The team tested whether they target the fusion machinery itself.

In flies, the amount of mitofusin, the fusion-promoting protein, moved in the opposite direction to PINK1 and parkin activity. Mitofusin carried ubiquitin tags, the cell's disposal labels, only when both genes worked, and it physically bound parkin. Two related shape proteins stayed untouched. The authors argue that failed mitofusin cleanup helps explain the swollen mitochondria and tissue damage of these Parkinson's forms.
europmc-pmc2859930:
Waterman, Tomchuck, Henkle, and Betancourt proposed in 2010 that healing stem cells from bone marrow come in two opposite types. These mesenchymal stem cells, also called MSCs, can calm or stir the immune system. Sensors on the cells, called Toll-like receptors, detect danger signals from damaged tissue and switch the cells' behavior.

Priming the cells through one sensor produced a type the authors name MSC1, which releases mostly inflammation-driving signals. Priming through a different sensor produced MSC2, which releases mostly calming signals instead. In mixed cultures, each type pushed immune cells in the predicted direction, including how strongly T cells switched on. The split helps explain why marrow cell trials have given such mixed results.
europmc-pmc2875530:
Pierrakos and Vincent reviewed in 2010 the blood markers proposed for sepsis, the body's runaway response to infection that can kill within days. A good marker could confirm sepsis early, rule it out, pick who benefits from a therapy, or show whether treatment works. The pair searched the medical database for studies testing any marker in sepsis.

Their search surfaced over three thousand papers covering one hundred seventy-eight different markers. Most had been tried as outlook predictors rather than as diagnostic tests. None proved sharp enough for routine use, since each missed cases or fired falsely in other inflammatory states. The two most used markers, procalcitonin and C-reactive protein, still could not reliably separate sepsis from sterile inflammation or forecast a patient's course.
europmc-pmc2954830:
Biteau and colleagues showed in 2010 that keeping gut cell growth in balance extends life in fruit flies. Ageing fly intestines decay as stem cells over-multiply and their offspring mature wrongly, roughening the gut lining.

Tweaks that harmed tissue renewal shortened life, while changes that restored balance lengthened it. Helpful moves included damping insulin-related signals, damping a stress kinase pathway, and boosting protective genes in stem cell lines. Across many genetic variants, lifespan peaked when gut growth was trimmed but not shut off. The work frames balanced renewal as a practical route to healthier ageing.
europmc-pmc2956230:
Wicks and colleagues surveyed members of PatientsLikeMe, an online platform where patients share health data, in a 2010 study of its perceived benefits. Members track symptoms and treatments to find people like themselves and learn from pooled reports.

Over a thousand members from six disease communities, including motor neuron disease, multiple sclerosis, and mood disorders, replied. Learning about a symptom they had felt was the top-rated benefit, named by nearly three quarters. Many also credited the site with grasping treatment side effects, and nearly half said it shaped other care decisions. The results support structured patient sharing.
europmc-pmc3043330:
Schulz, Altman, and Moher presented in 2010 the updated CONSORT guidelines for reporting randomized trials, the studies that test treatments by assigning patients by chance. Poorly reported trials cannot be judged fairly, and earlier versions of the checklist had already improved reporting since the nineteen nineties. New methods evidence and user experience called for a full update.

The statement centers on a checklist of twenty five items plus a flow diagram that tracks patients through a trial. It focuses on the common two group parallel design, with add on guides for other designs kept on the project website. A companion paper explains each item with examples of clear reporting. The authors aim for complete, transparent accounts of how trials were run and what they found. Better reports, they argue, lead to better treatment decisions.
europmc-pmc3075230:
Ray and Maunsell settled in 2011 a dispute about fast brain rhythms in monkey visual cortex. The dispute was whether the fastest band is a true rhythm or just the blur of neurons firing. Brain waves above the classic gamma range, called high gamma, appear in many recordings and are used as a signal of local activity. The team varied stimulus size, which pushes firing rates and the classic gamma rhythm in opposite directions.

High gamma power tracked the firing of nearby neurons under every manipulation, rising and falling with spike rates rather than with the rhythm. The two signals also varied together trial by trial. The authors conclude high gamma largely reflects local spiking, not a separate communication channel. That is useful news, since the easy to record wave can stand in for hard to record spikes. But studies must not double count the two as separate signals.
europmc-pmc3148430:
Tom Treasure and colleagues reported a randomised feasibility trial of radical lung surgery for a chest-lining cancer in a 2011 paper in The Lancet Oncology. The operation removes a lung plus surrounding linings and is followed by radiation, but its benefit had never been tested fairly. Fifty patients across British hospitals were assigned by chance to surgery or none, after chemotherapy.

Only two thirds of the surgery group completed the operation, and a few died around surgery. Survival leaned against the operation, with the no-surgery group living several months longer on median, a gap that grew after adjusting for patient differences. Quality of life scores ran lower after surgery without a clear significant gap. The trial questions whether such radical surgery helps at all.
europmc-pmc3181230:
Patricia McGettigan and David Henry re-pooled population studies on heart risk from common painkillers in a 2011 paper in PLoS Medicine. The drugs, sold widely without prescription, had been tied to heart attacks and strokes in trials, but risk differences between individual drugs, doses, and patient types stayed murky. Large linked health databases offered the numbers to separate them.

Relative risks across studies mostly sat in a modest band, high enough to matter at population scale but too small for single studies to split by drug. The update extends earlier reviews to less-studied and newer compounds and probes low-dose, short, over-the-counter style use in low-risk people. The authors aim to give prescribers and regulators comparative estimates rather than class-wide warnings.
europmc-pmc3253730:
Saulius Gražulis and colleagues presented the Crystallography Open Database in this 2009 paper in the Journal of Applied Crystallography. Crystal structures were scattered across journals and separate collections, many behind paywalls. The database is a community effort to gather every published structure, across inorganic, metal-organic, and small organic molecule chemistry, into one freely accessible place.

The project follows an open-access model and already held more than eighty thousand structure files at the time of writing. A straightforward search and retrieval interface lets users find and download the records they need. The authors frame the database as shared infrastructure for the whole field. Any crystallographer can draw from it and contribute to it. They offer it in place of a patchwork of partial archives.
europmc-pmc3261930:
Xiaofang Ye and colleagues reviewed the epidemiological evidence linking outdoor temperature with illness, as distinct from death, in this 2012 paper in Environmental Health Perspectives. They searched the literature through mid-2010 and assessed how the studies were designed, aiming to map what is known and to set directions for better work.

Forty studies qualified, most examining ordinary temperature variation and a smaller set examining heat waves. Most found significant links between temperature and overall or cause-specific illness, though the delayed effects were inconsistent: heat acted within days, while cold effects could stretch over weeks. Social and demographic factors and air pollution could distort or modify the relationships. The authors call for an agreed temperature measure, a wider range of illnesses, and consistent methods so studies can be compared.
europmc-pmc3269430:
Teun Bousema and colleagues argued for aiming malaria control at transmission hotspots, in this 2012 paper in PLoS Medicine. Malaria, like many infections, is unevenly spread: a small share of households bears a greatly increased risk of transmission. Those clusters occur in every setting, though they blur into the background where transmission is intense.

The authors marshal the logic and evidence for spatial targeting. Hotspots sustain transmission through the dry, low season and ignite it again when the rains return, so suppressing them should cut transmission community-wide. They contend that focusing resources on these pockets is highly efficient at every level of transmission intensity, from places battling heavy malaria to those nearing elimination. The piece is a policy argument for making geography a deliberate part of malaria strategy.
europmc-pmc3289630:
Manikkam and colleagues reported in 2012 that chemical exposure before birth could echo into later generations of rats. Pregnant females were briefly exposed while the sex organs of their embryos were forming. The mixtures tested included a pesticide blend, plastic ingredients, dioxin, and jet fuel, and later generations received no exposure at all.

Even so, females in the third generation entered puberty early after plastic, dioxin, and jet fuel exposure in their ancestors. Sperm forming cells died at altered rates, and the pool of early egg follicles shrank after every treatment. The team also mapped chemical marks on sperm DNA that differed by exposure, raising the idea of markers for ancestral contact with pollutants.
europmc-pmc3348530:
Banerjee and Mazumdar reviewed twenty five years of a gentle technique for weighing and dissecting large biological molecules, in a 2012 article. The technique, electrospray ionization mass spectrometry, turns big, fragile molecules into airborne charged particles without smashing them. That soft touch opened proteins and other large assemblies to precise measurement for the first time.

The review traces how the method developed and how researchers unraveled the way charged droplets give birth to gas phase ions. A puzzle the field studied deeply is why proteins emerge carrying many charges at once, and what that pattern reveals about their shape. By deliberately breaking the airborne particles apart in a second stage, scientists can read structural details from the fragments. The authors highlight fresh directions in which this mature tool is still expanding.
europmc-pmc3349530:
Vinci and co-workers built a practical toolkit for growing cancer cells as three-dimensional spheroids and testing drugs against them. Flat cell cultures miss much of how real tumours behave, so the team standardised methods for forming, imaging, and analysing spheroids in a format suited to screening.

They demonstrated the system with compounds including the kinase inhibitors PI-103 and CCT130234 and the Hsp90 inhibitor 17-AAG. The assays captured drug effects on spheroid growth and viability that two-dimensional cultures would not reveal. The authors present the toolkit as a bridge between simple cell culture and animal studies, giving drug developers a more realistic early test bed.
europmc-pmc3372330:
Jamieson, Theiler, and Rasmussen examined in 2006 how emerging infections affect pregnant women, a group often left out of outbreak plans. Pregnancy reshapes the immune system, which can raise the odds of catching some germs or suffering worse illness. Effects on the unborn child are often unknown at first.

Their overview describes the immune shifts of pregnancy and what was known about infections during it. It stresses practical problems: spotting infection in a fetus is hard, and standard prevention or treatment may not suit pregnancy. Many studies were backward-looking and lacked comparison groups. The authors call for pregnancy to be built into emerging-disease planning from the start.
europmc-pmc3382730:
Hillebrand and colleagues set out in 2012 to map how resting brain areas talk to each other at different rhythms, using magnetoencephalography. Brain scans record magnetic fields from outside the head, but spread and leakage can fake connections. The team built an atlas-based method designed to dodge those traps.

They show that ordinary phase measures, even after source reconstruction, stay biased by the leakage. A lag-based measure they used instead was not fooled. Applied to thirteen resting volunteers, it revealed strong links in three rhythm bands. Each band had its own map: slower rhythms tied to rear and movement areas, while the fastest spread more widely. Active areas also tended to be the most connected.
europmc-pmc3409130:
Horsted, West, and Grainge pooled the literature in 2012 to pin down how often cancer patients develop dangerous blood clots, called venous thromboembolism. Clots are common in cancer, but exact rates for each cancer type were unknown. Without them, doctors cannot aim prevention at the patients who need it most.

The review summarizes incidence across cancers, split into high-risk and average-risk patient groups. Hospital data already hint that clot risk runs highest with brain, pancreatic, and blood cancers once their frequency is accounted for. Rates also shift with disease stage and treatment. By organizing scattered cohort evidence into comparable figures, the analysis gives prevention programs a firmer footing.
europmc-pmc3464430:

Once a piRNA started the silencing, the off state lasted at least twenty generations. After that start, the piRNA itself was no longer needed, but a set of nuclear proteins stayed required to keep the memory. Ashe's team names those factors, including a germline Argonaute protein and two enzymes that mark histones. The work maps a clear route for inherited gene silencing.

Their review guides immunology. Birge's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped immune evasion science. The review is widely taught. Students rely on it.
europmc-pmc4995730: AMPK got a 12-flavours review. This 2016 paper reviews AMPK as energy sensor. The authors map the mapping. Their review guides cell biology. Ross's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped metabolic science. The review is widely taught. Students rely on it.
europmc-pmc5096030: Fluorescence got a vibronic-coupling study. This 2016 paper finds vibronic coupling drives delayed fluorescence. The authors reveal the finding. Their work guides chemistry. Gibson's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped OLED science. It is a landmark.
europmc-pmc5123330: Endometria got a uterine-microbiome study. This 2016 paper links uterine microbes to endometrial cancer. The authors reveal the linking. Their work guides gynecology. Walther-António's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped cancer science. It is a landmark.
europmc-pmc5140430: A medical paper with gleanings from the Calcutta post-mortem records. The dead, examined. This article preserves that pathology. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
europmc-pmc5151130: Inflammation got a methylation-signatures study. This 2016 paper links methylation to chronic inflammation. The authors reveal the linking. Their work guides genetics. Ligthart's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped inflammation science. It is a landmark.
europmc-pmc524030: Diet got a thermogenesis-review. This 2004 paper reviews diet-induced thermogenesis. The author maps the mapping. Their review guides nutrition. Westerterp's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped metabolism science. The review is widely taught. Students rely on it.
europmc-pmc5292730: Limbs got a developmental-plasticity study. This 2017 paper finds embryo movement shapes limb proportions. The authors reveal the finding. Their work guides developmental biology. Pollard's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped evo-devo. It is a landmark.
europmc-pmc5297730: Antioxidants got an extraction-assessment review. This 2017 paper reviews natural antioxidants in foods. The authors map the mapping. Their review guides nutrition. Xu's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped food science. The review is widely taught. Students rely on it.
europmc-pmc5316730: A medical paper on xanthomatosis, aspects of its blood chemistry and pathology. The yellow nodules. This article preserves that dermatology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc5325830: Obesity got an energy-balance-drivers review. This 2017 paper reviews main drivers of obesity. The authors weigh the weighing. Their review guides nutrition. Romieu's team led the work. The review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped obesity policy. It is a landmark.
europmc-pmc5390430: Stomachs got an exosomal-miR-21-resistance study. This 2017 paper finds exosomal miR-21 drives cisplatin resistance. The authors reveal the finding. Their work guides oncology. Zheng's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped chemo resistance. It is a landmark.
europmc-pmc5408830: Variants got a rare-low-frequency-impact review. This 2017 paper reviews rare variants in common disease. The authors map the mapping. Their review guides genetics. Bomba's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped genomic medicine. The review is widely taught. Students rely on it.
europmc-pmc5424030:
Clark asks whether the official ergot preparations sold to doctors hold any real active drug. The paper was read to the Edinburgh Obstetrical Society. Ergot is a fungus that grows on rye. It has poisoned whole districts in past centuries. It also speeds labour by tightening the womb. Chemists had isolated strong alkaloids from the fungus. They held that the drug's value rests on those alkaloids.

Yet the British Pharmacopoeia preparations seemed to hold only traces of them. On lab logic, the products should be near inert. Clinicians had still used them for thirty years without complaint. Clark calls that clash unsatisfactory. A new pharmacopoeia was in prospect. He urges lab workers and clinicians to settle the question together. His paper lays out the lab evidence for doctors to judge. It is a plea for joint testing, not a report of new findings.
europmc-pmc5433030:
Sekulic and co-authors report the final long-term results of vismodegib for advanced basal cell carcinoma. Their trial update appeared in BMC Cancer. Basal cell carcinoma is the most common human cancer. Most cases yield to surgery or radiation. Faulty Hedgehog signaling drives most of these tumors. Vismodegib blocks that pathway. The ERIVANCE trial enrolled 104 patients.

Patients took 150 milligrams once daily. Treatment ran until progression or harsh side effects. At cutoff, 39 months after accrual closed, eight patients remained on drug. Investigator-assessed response reached about 49 percent in metastatic disease. All those responses were partial. Locally advanced disease responded at just over 60 percent. Twenty patients there had complete responses. Median response lasted about 15 months in one group and 26 months in the other. Median survival in metastatic disease was about 33 months. Thirty-three deaths occurred, none blamed on the drug.
europmc-pmc5439030:
Cohen and co-authors measure the global death toll from outdoor air pollution over 25 years. Their analysis appeared in The Lancet. It draws on the Global Burden of Diseases Study 2015. The team estimated fine particle and ozone levels worldwide. They combined satellite data, transport models, and ground monitors. Grid cells were about 11 kilometers across. Exposure-response curves then linked pollution to five killer diseases.

Fine particles ranked as the fifth mortality risk factor in 2015. Exposure caused 4.2 million deaths that year. It also cost 103 million years of healthy life. Deaths had risen from 3.5 million in 1990. East and south Asia bore 59 percent of the burden. Ozone added 254,000 deaths from lung disease. Aging populations drive much of the rise. So does worsening air in poorer countries. The authors see large health gains from deep cuts in particle levels.
europmc-pmc5461230:
Willighagen and co-authors present version 2.0 of the Chemistry Development Kit, a free software library for chemistry data. Their article appeared in the Journal of Cheminformatics. The kit gives programs a way to store chemical ideas. Tools built on top compute with those structures. Users apply it in drug discovery and related fields. Ten years of growth had bloated the code. Parts tangled together, and many tools ran slowly. Version 2.0 answers both problems.

New features lead the changes. Atom typing arrives as a fresh tool. Handling of molecular formulas is new as well. Older tools gained major speed. Searching for substructures runs much faster now. Fingerprint sums and molecule drawing sped up too. Quality control grew with the code. A review step now guards each change. The authors stress the role of the user community. Outside contributions acted like peer review for the software.
europmc-pmc5467230:
Lebreton and co-authors estimate how much plastic waste rivers carry into the world's oceans each year. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. Plastic persists at sea for a long time. It harms marine life and may affect human health. Cutting the flow requires knowing where it comes from. Rivers had not been measured on a global scale before.

The team built a global model of river inputs. It combines data on waste management and population density. River flow patterns complete the picture. They checked the model against published measurements. The estimate came to roughly 1.2 to 2.4 million tonnes of plastic per year. More than three quarters of it flows between May and October. Just 20 rivers account for two thirds of the total. Most of those rivers are in Asia. The results give a baseline for tracking and cleanup efforts.
europmc-pmc5470330:
Haenseler and co-authors report a methods study in Stem Cell Reports. They build a lab model of human microglia, the immune cells of the brain. Microglia are tied to diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's. Fresh human microglia are hard to obtain, though. The team seeks a faithful model that grows well in the lab.

The method starts with stem cells and turns them into macrophage-like cells. Those cells then grow beside stem-cell-derived cortical neurons. In that shared culture, the microglia show key marker genes and branching shapes. They also eat particles and respond to activation signals. The authors report that shared culture beats solo culture for realism.
europmc-pmc5479630:
Fischer and co-authors report a population study in PLoS ONE on chronotypes in the United States. A chronotype is a person's natural tilt toward early or late sleep. The authors estimate how chronotypes spread across age and sex groups. They draw on 12 years of American Time Use Survey diary data. Sleep midpoint on weekends served as their measure.

The sample held 53,689 people, and values formed a near-normal spread. Lateness peaked at about age 19, then shifted earlier with age. Men ran later than women before age 40, but earlier after it, they report. Spread shrank with age. The authors link the teen peak to later school start times.
europmc-pmc5511330:
Firman and co-authors present a review in Trends in Ecology and Evolution on cryptic female choice. Females of many species mate with several males. After mating, their bodies can still favor one male's sperm over another's. Such hidden choice can shape which males father the young. The field took off after a landmark book two decades ago.

The review surveys the many female processes that could bias sperm use. Clear proof of choice remains rare, they caution. When it acts, it may sway female fitness and fuel conflict between the sexes. It could even help split species apart. The authors map the evidence gaps for future work.
europmc-pmc5542030:
Zheng and co-authors present a software article in Bioinformatics. They introduce LD Hub, a shared database and web tool. It serves researchers who study genome-wide association data. Such summary data often sit in many places and in mixed formats.

LD Hub gathers summary results for 173 diseases and traits in one place. Its web interface runs LD score regression on them with little hand work. That method estimates how much of a trait is tied to common gene variants. It also measures genetic overlap between traits. The team checked the tool by repeating past analyses of 49 traits. Readers get an easier way to screen many traits for shared genetic roots.
europmc-pmc5590730:
Jackson and Turner examine statistical power in random-effects meta-analysis, in Research Synthesis Methods. Pooling studies is meant to boost the chance of detecting an effect. Under a fixed-effect model that always holds. The random-effects model adds between-study variance, which must itself be estimated.

The authors derive ways to compute the power of such a pooled analysis. They also compute the average power of the single studies feeding it. Then they apply the methods to 1,991 meta-analyses from the Cochrane Database. In practice, five or more studies were needed for pooling to beat the parts with any consistency. With very few studies, the pooled test may add nothing. The common faith that pooling always helps takes a hit. Readers get tools to check power before pooling.
europmc-pmc5635030:
Jie and co-authors report a metagenome study in Nature Communications. They compared gut microbes in heart disease patients and healthy people. The patients had atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Stool samples came from 218 patients and 187 controls. Shotgun sequencing read the DNA in each sample. The team then matched microbes and gene functions to disease status.

Patient microbiomes differed clearly from healthy ones. Enterobacteriaceae and Streptococcus species were more abundant. Bacteroides and Prevotella were reduced. Functional shifts touched metabolism and transport of key molecules. Drug use did not explain the main split. Disease status did. Comparisons with diabetes, obesity, and cirrhosis data showed shared themes. The dataset serves as a resource for later work.
europmc-pmc5648830:
Vogt and co-authors report a case-control study in Scientific Reports. It profiles gut microbes in Alzheimer's disease patients. Fecal samples came from 25 patients with dementia due to Alzheimer's. Controls were 25 matched people without dementia. Bacterial DNA was read with 16S gene sequencing. The team also checked spinal fluid biomarkers of the disease.

Patient microbiomes showed lower diversity than controls. Their composition was clearly distinct. Firmicutes fell, while Bacteroidetes increased. Bifidobacterium levels dropped as well. Several changed genera tracked spinal fluid biomarker levels. Rodent work had hinted that gut microbes affect amyloid buildup. The authors add Alzheimer's to diseases tied to gut shifts. They propose the gut as a therapy target.
europmc-pmc5651530:
Wang and co-authors present a meta-analysis in Frontiers in Pharmacology. It measures immune side effects of PD-1 pathway cancer drugs. These drugs can free the immune system to attack healthy tissue. The team searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, and Cochrane databases. They pooled 46 studies with 12,808 cancer patients. Drugs included nivolumab, pembrolizumab, and atezolizumab, among others.

About 27 percent of patients had an immune side effect of any grade. Severe events occurred in about six percent. Deaths from such events were rare, near two per thousand. Events were grouped by organ system. Skin, hormone glands, gut, lungs, and kidneys were all affected. Rates varied by drug and tumor type, not by dose.
europmc-pmc5664030:
Wang and Shelomi present a review in Foods. It covers the black soldier fly as feed and food. This insect converts many kinds of organic waste into biomass. Food waste and manure both serve as inputs. Rearing needs no dedicated facilities, and the flies are not pests. Their larvae hold about 42 percent crude protein. Fat makes up about 29 percent of larval mass.

Larvae already serve as animal feed in many places. Regional rules still limit how that is done. For human food, milling could yield a textured protein. The strong flavor may limit appeal. Stigma and legal bans form the biggest barriers. Both stem from the fly's waste diet.
europmc-pmc5701930:
Trevethan explains how to read the scores of health screening tests. His article covers sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values. These measures are often confused in research and in practice. Screening tests are cheap and easy to use, but they are not exact. Wrong readings of their scores can mislead care.

The author first sets out firm definitions of each measure. He then shows why the terms get mixed up and misused. Sensitivity and specificity best describe a test against a reference standard, he argues. Predictive values suit real screening choices for single people. Tests can be tuned by trading one score against another. Reports should give all four measures and how they were derived.
europmc-pmc5770430:
Hua and co-authors present a skin-like sensor network that stretches and conforms to curved surfaces. Their matrix network mimics how human skin senses the world. Sensor units sit on a structured polyimide web. The design can grow to large areas and stack in three dimensions.

The network senses temperature, strain, humidity, light, magnetic field, pressure, and nearby objects. It can read several signals at once with an adjustable range. The team built a personalized smart prosthesis with it. The device mapped pressure in space and estimated temperature in real time. Uses in robotics and health monitoring are proposed.
europmc-pmc5778130:
Mitew and co-authors test whether neuron activity drives myelin growth on single axons. Myelin wraps axons and speeds signals in the brain. The team used a drug based genetic switch to raise or lower firing in mouse sensory axons. They then counted new sheath cells in the white matter below.

Stimulated axons were more likely to gain myelin, they report. Their sheaths also grew thicker. New sheath forming cells multiplied and matured faster nearby. Lowering firing cut myelination in the same selective way. Activity of each axon helps decide which axons get wrapped, they conclude.
europmc-pmc5783630:
Guo and co-authors study how heat waves affect deaths across 400 communities in 18 countries. Daily temperature and death records were gathered for each place. Heat waves were defined twelve ways, by heat level and by length. The team estimated each community's link, then pooled the results by country.

Heat waves of every definition raised deaths, they find. Hotter thresholds brought stronger effects. Longer waves did not add harm beyond their hot days. Effects hit fast and lasted three to four days. Moderate climates showed stronger links than very cold or very hot ones.
europmc-pmc5792430:
Charrier and co-authors build soft gels whose stiffness and flow can be tuned apart. Cells sense the mechanics of their surroundings. Most lab gels are purely elastic, unlike real tissues, which also lose energy as they deform. That missing trait left cell responses to viscosity unstudied.

Their new solids mimic soft tissue mechanics closely. By changing only the viscous part, they show cell sensing runs on time linked rules. Viscous loss shifts cell shape and fate choices. The materials open a clean way to study how tissues' flow shapes the cells inside them.
europmc-pmc5796130:
Hoarau-Véchot and co-authors review 3D cultures for studying how tumors interact with their surroundings. The tumor microenvironment shapes growth, spread, and drug resistance. Flat 2D cultures miss much of that dialogue. Animal models capture more, at higher cost and distance from human tissue.

Many 3D methods have appeared in recent years. The review sorts them and weighs each one's strengths and limits. It compares 3D work with classic flat cultures on set questions. The authors ask whether 3D tools can truly bridge bench and body. Their answer guides labs picking a model.
europmc-pmc5830330:
Pallmann and co-authors explain adaptive designs for clinical trials. An adaptive trial can change course as results build up. All changes follow rules set in advance. Such trials can save time, money, and participants.

Uptake lags the methods literature, partly from fuzzy terms. The tutorial sorts what adaptive design truly covers. It weighs gains against pitfalls in plain terms. Practical hurdles include funding, ethics review, and drug supply. Reporting duties get their own guidance. The authors stress that investigators must grasp the design's limits. Readers get a working brief for running flexible trials well.
europmc-pmc5837230:
Thompson and co-authors report the largest series yet of faciobrachial dystonic seizures, an antibody-driven epilepsy. Their study appeared in Brain. The seizures grip the face and arm in brief jerks. They trace to LGI1 antibodies and often precede memory loss.

The team followed 103 patients from an international network. Seizure drugs alone rarely stopped the attacks. Immunotherapy ended them in most patients. Each delay shrank the odds of success. Patients treated before thinking problems set in kept better long-term function. The authors argue these seizures are a warning shot worth urgent treatment.
europmc-pmc5946030:
Grazioli and Pugin review mitochondrial damage-associated molecular patterns, or mitochondrial DAMPs. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Mitochondrial molecules are harmless while they stay inside mitochondria. Once they escape into the cytoplasm or beyond, they turn pro-inflammatory. They can start innate and adaptive immune responses. Receptors on and inside cells detect these alarm signals.

Too much release of mitochondrial DAMPs tracks with disease severity, the authors report. It also carries prognostic value in patients. Such release feeds many inflammatory and autoimmune conditions. Ischaemic heart disease and cancer feature as well. The review maps this fast-growing field and its disease links.
europmc-pmc5951930:
Chen and Hambardzumyan review the immune microenvironment across glioblastoma subtypes. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Glioblastomas are the most common and aggressive primary brain tumours. They vary widely at molecular and tissue levels. Tumour-associated macrophages form the main non-cancer cell group inside them. Data suggest distinct subtypes hold distinct immune surroundings.

The authors cover where these macrophages come from and what they do. They compare their roles across the proneural, mesenchymal, and classical subtypes. Mouse models show driver mutations can build unique microenvironments. The review also covers talks between macrophages and other immune cells. Targeting macrophages might boost T cell therapy, they suggest.
europmc-pmc6105930:
