Behr and co-authors revisit the timetable of tuberculosis infection. Their analysis appeared in The BMJ. A quarter to a third of humanity carries the bacterium. Standard teaching calls most infection latent for life. The authors challenge that picture with follow-up data.

Most disease, they show, strikes soon after infection. Cases rarely appear more than two years later. Old pre-antibiotic studies pinned the timing closely. Remote infection dominates only where spread has nearly stopped. The authors propose three simpler terms for the stages. They urge research money toward recent transmission. Vaccine trials should also plan around early disease. Readers get a sharper clock for a global killer.
europmc-pmc6191530:
GBD 2016 Headache Collaborators report a systematic analysis in The Lancet Neurology on migraine and tension-type headache. Headache disorders have emerged as a major global public health concern. This study refreshes the estimates of how many people live with them. It covers the years 1990 to 2016.

Data came from population surveys across all countries and regions. A Bayesian model produced prevalence by sex and age, and years lived with disability. In 2016 the two disorders together caused 52.3 million years lived with disability, 6.5 percent of the world total. Rates per person changed little, so growth reflects population change. The authors present methods and results in a form clinicians can use.
europmc-pmc6225430:
Cianciosi and co-authors review phenolic compounds in honey. Honey has been valued for healing since ancient times. Its flavonoids and phenolic acids drive much of that value. They give strong antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects. The review appeared in Molecules.

Honey can kill microbes and slow some tumour growth. It acts on pathways that control cell growth. It also shows anti-diabetic effects in studies. Reported effects include lower blood glucose levels. Honey protects the heart system in part by guarding LDL from oxidation. Effects on nerves, lungs, and gut are also covered. The authors update evidence on honey in health and disease. They note benefits reported for athletes as well.
europmc-pmc6259430:
Soković and co-authors tested herb oils against bacteria that sicken people. Their study appeared in Molecules. Ten common culinary and medicinal herbs were used. The set ran from lemon and lavender to oregano, thyme, and sage. Oils were checked against ten bacterial species. Targets included E. coli, Salmonella, and Staphylococcus aureus. Two lab methods measured the strength of each oil.

Oregano oil showed the broadest and strongest action. Among single compounds, carvacrol ranked highest. Other strong parts included thymol, linalool, and menthol. Food makers face pressure to drop chemical preservatives. Plant oils could serve as natural guards against spoilage and poisoning. Rising drug resistance adds a medical reason to study them too. The authors give full chemical profiles for each oil tested.
europmc-pmc6315530:
Chun and Kim review autophagy, the cell's main recycling and cleanup program. The review appeared in Cells. Autophagy delivers worn proteins and organelles to lysosomes. There they are broken down and reused. The program answers many kinds of cell stress. It is conserved across species and guards cell balance.

Faulty autophagy is tied to cancer and brain diseases. The authors trace the proteins that run the pathway. They also cover chemical tags that tune those proteins. Such tags add layers of control to the system. Each layer may offer a drug target. The review maps the machinery for cell biologists. It also points to paths for new treatments.
europmc-pmc6397230:
Huang and co-authors report a prognostic study in Scientific Reports on cervical cancer. A blood score called the systemic immune-inflammation index mixes counts of platelets, neutrophils, and lymphocytes. It had not been tested in cervical cancer before.

Patients with a high score before surgery had worse survival in both study groups. High scores also tracked with larger tumors. Among several blood indexes, this one alone predicted outcome on its own. It beat the ratios doctors more often use, tests showed. The cheap blood score may help flag patients who need closer care.
europmc-pmc6426830:
Stancu and co-authors test whether clumped Tau protein switches on the NLRP3-ASC inflammasome, an immune alarm already tied to amyloid damage in Alzheimer's disease. Tau tangles spread through the brain in a prion-like way as seeds template new clumps. Whether those seeds also drive inflammation was unknown.

Tau seeds taken up by microglia did activate the inflammasome in culture. In Tau transgenic mice, lacking ASC sharply reduced seeded Tau pathology, and the NLRP3 blocker MCC950 had the same effect when given into the brain. Even unseeded Tau disease eased without ASC. Blocking this immune pathway could therefore slow three harmful processes at once.
europmc-pmc6447530:
Shen and co-authors present MetDNA, an algorithm that names far more small molecules in broad mass spectrometry runs by leaning on the network of reactions that links them. Standard naming matches spectra against libraries, yet most known compounds have no reference spectrum, so most signals stay unnamed. Reaction partners, though, tend to look alike in shape and in spectrum.

Starting from a few firmly named seed compounds, MetDNA lends their spectra to their reaction neighbors, then steps outward through the network again and again. About 2,000 compounds could be named in all from a single run, across machines and sample types. Fuller naming makes pathway-level reading practical for studies of body chemistry.
europmc-pmc6466530:
Zicari and co-authors review why people with HIV on effective antiretroviral therapy still live with chronic immune activation and inflammation, and pay for it in non-AIDS illnesses. Some 36.9 million people live with HIV worldwide, and therapy has turned infection into a chronic condition without eradicating the virus. Several engines keep the immune system idling high.

Residual low-level viremia, a damaged gut lining leaking microbial products, co-infections, thymic decline, and the cumulative toxicity of the drugs themselves form a self-reinforcing cycle. The fallout includes metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular disease arriving early. New approaches aimed at the inflammation itself, not just the virus, are surveyed as the next therapeutic frontier.
europmc-pmc6524730:
Huang and co-authors present the NCATS BioPlanet pathway platform. Their paper appeared in Frontiers in Pharmacology. Chemical genomics seeks to predict how small molecules affect living systems. That work must span all pathways active in human cells.

BioPlanet joins 1,658 human pathways from public, hand-curated sources. The team cross-checked the set for overlap and consistency. Users can browse, search and analyse pathways online. Pathways appear on a 3D globe. Distance there reflects shared gene content. Search runs by gene target, category, or linked assay. From the full set, the authors propose 362 assays. That minimal set could probe the whole pathway universe.
europmc-pmc6561930:
Favaro and co-authors test whether mitochondria must keep splitting to keep muscle alive, writing in Nature Communications. The fission protein DRP1 falls in ageing and wasting muscle, but cause and effect were unclear. The team deleted Drp1 only in mouse skeletal muscle and watched what failed.

Mice born without muscle DRP1 grew poorly and died. Deleting it in adults brought atrophy and degeneration instead. Their mitochondria swelled into oversized, malfunctioning forms. The distress signaled the nucleus to switch on protein-breakdown machinery and a stress response, while the enlarged mitochondria soaked up excess calcium, killing fibers. The work shows mitochondrial shape is not cosmetic: fission helps set calcium balance, nuclear programs and muscle mass itself.
europmc-pmc6598430:
Espíndola and co-authors review caffeic acid, a plant compound with activity against liver cancer. Their review appears in Frontiers in Oncology. Caffeic acid occurs in coffee, wine, tea, and propolis. It fights oxidation and inflammation in lab studies. Liver cancer is common, aggressive, and often deadly. The authors gather the chemistry behind the compound. They also track how the body absorbs and processes it.

Gut microbes break caffeic acid down after intake. The gut wall then tags it with sulfate and other groups. Against tumor cells, the compound cuts reactive oxygen damage. It also slows new blood vessel growth in tumors. It blocks signals tied to cancer spread, including MMP enzymes. The review weighs this evidence for future drug design.
europmc-pmc6612530:
Tian and co-authors hunt the genetic cause of a rare brain disease. Their research article appears in the American Journal of Human Genetics. Neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease, or NIID, creeps forward over years. It leaves telltale inclusions inside nerve cells and other tissues. Its symptoms vary so widely that cases were long missed.

Linkage mapping pointed the team to a stretch of chromosome 1. Exome sequencing found no culprit mutation there. Long-read genome sequencing revealed the answer instead. A GGC repeat in the gene NOTCH2NLC had grown far too long. The team confirmed it in three more families and five single cases. Screening 456 other families found the same expansion in Alzheimer and parkinsonism cases. They propose one label, NIID-related disorders, for the whole group.
europmc-pmc6718830:
Lewis and co-authors profiled the genes active in early rheumatoid arthritis. They sequenced RNA from joint tissue, called synovium, and matched blood in a large group of patients who had not yet been treated. The goal was to find patterns that predict how the disease will run. A public website lets others explore the data.

Synovium fell into three types. One was rich in fibroblasts, one in macrophages, and one in both lymph and myeloid cells. Myeloid-heavy signatures tracked with a good response to first drug therapy. Plasma cell genes marked a group whose joints worsened over time. Blood patterns were far less clear than tissue ones.
europmc-pmc6756230:
Leuzy and co-authors review tau PET imaging in diseases called tauopathies. A misfolded protein, tau, builds up in the brain in Alzheimer's disease and related disorders. New tracer compounds now let PET scanners picture tau in living patients. First-generation tracers had flaws, and second-generation ones were built to improve on them.

The review collects lab and clinical findings for both generations. It relates tau images to amyloid markers, brain shrinkage, and thinking test results. Disorders covered include progressive supranuclear palsy and corticobasal syndrome, among others. Measuring tracer binding fairly across studies takes care. The authors close with trial uses and future applications of tau imaging.
europmc-pmc6826930:
Hubrecht and Carter introduce a special issue of Animals on the 3Rs of animal research. The 3Rs stand for replacement, reduction, and refinement. They were set out by William Russell and Rex Burch in a 1959 book on humane technique. The framework now guides lab animal welfare law and practice around the world.

The authors trace how the ideas spread, helped by the Universities Federation for Animal Welfare. Laws such as the European Directive of 2010, in full force from 2013, wrote the 3Rs into rules on housing and review. The piece then previews the issue's papers on putting the principles into daily practice.
europmc-pmc6834330:
Gutiérrez and co-authors review omega-3 fatty acids and immune cells, in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Omega-3 fats, found in oily fish, have been known for 30 years to alter immune behaviour. They sit inside cell membranes and change how those membranes flex and cluster. Their breakdown products also act as signals in their own right.

The review works through the major immune cell types one by one. Omega-3 fats such as EPA and DHA generally quiet the activation of both innate and adaptive cells. A few functions, though, are boosted rather than damped. The authors set out the molecular steps proposed for each effect, and where the proof stands.
europmc-pmc6864930:
Zhou and co-authors report results of a community challenge in Genome Biology. No one can test every protein in the lab, so computers predict what proteins do from their sequences. The CAFA challenge scores those predictions in the open. Its third round, CAFA3, expanded both the data volume and the kinds of analysis over earlier rounds.

Predictions also steered new experiments for the first time. Whole-genome mutation screens in the yeast Candida albicans and the bacterium Pseudomonas aeruginosa tested predicted gene functions directly. The loop produced fresh, verified annotations for more than 1,000 genes. Overall accuracy improved over past rounds, though no method passed a key score threshold the authors track.
europmc-pmc6878630:
Liu and co-authors report a study in Stem Cell Research and Therapy on calming inflammation in sepsis. Mesenchymal stem cells can push macrophages, the immune system's big eaters, toward a healing state called M2. That shift reduces harmful inflammation. Signals the stem cells release do the pushing. Which signal mattered most was unclear.

Working with mouse macrophages stirred up by a bacterial toxin, the team traced the effect to TGF-beta secreted by the stem cells. Blocking its receptor undid the benefit, while adding the pure protein copied it. The signal acted through the Akt and FoxO1 pathway inside the macrophages. The authors name a precise route for a therapy often described only in general terms.
europmc-pmc6961830:
Chang and co-authors review how ageism damages older people's health across the world. Their systematic review appeared in PLoS ONE. Ageism can sit in social institutions, which bake in bias. It can also live inside older people themselves, who absorb their culture's gloomy views of aging. Past reviews had not tracked both levels at once.

The search screened 13,691 papers and kept 422 studies, covering over 7 million participants. Ageism linked to worse health in 95.5 percent of studies. Effects showed in all 45 countries, across 11 health domains and 25 years, and grew more common over time. Findings were stronger in less-developed countries. Older people with less schooling were hit hardest. Bias came from targeters of every age, sex, and background, the authors found.
europmc-pmc6966330:
Knecht and co-authors review enzymes that bacteria-infecting viruses use to chew through bacterial coats. Their mini-review appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology. Many bacteriophages carry depolymerases as tail spike proteins. These enzymes slice the sugar coats that armour host bacteria.

A phage first locks onto coat sugars, then cuts repeating units to burrow through. At the cell wall, it injects its DNA and infects. Similar enzymes have now turned up in several phage families beyond the first one studied. The review sorts them by which coat type they attack: capsule, slime layer, or surface lipopolysaccharide. Substrate choice and precision are described in detail. Uses in biotechnology close the piece, since such enzymes can help detect or control harmful bacteria while sparing neighbours.
europmc-pmc7016530:
Bajan and Hutvagner review RNA-based medicines in the journal Cells. The first DNA oligonucleotide drug won approval in 1998, and the first RNA-based oligonucleotide followed in 2018. Antisense drugs and RNA interference drugs are now reaching patients. One class is missing from that progress: medicines based on microRNAs, small RNAs that tune gene activity.

The review asks why microRNA drugs lag behind. Disease states change the levels of many microRNAs, so mimics and blockers look promising on paper. Yet only a handful have entered clinical trials. Bajan and Hutvagner weigh the benefits against delivery and safety obstacles, and judge what the search for microRNA targets has actually delivered so far.
europmc-pmc7070030:
Gee and co-authors build a delivery packet for genome editing in Nature Communications. CRISPR-Cas9 delivered by viral vectors keeps expressing for a long time, raising off-target damage and immune reactions. A short-lived delivery of the ready-made protein, with its guide RNA, would be safer. The team packs that ribonucleoprotein cargo into extracellular nanovesicles, a system named NanoMEDIC.

Two homing tricks load the cargo. A chemical dimerisation step recruits the Cas9 protein into forming vesicles, while a viral packaging signal plus self-cleaving riboswitches tether the guide RNA and then release it inside. The vesicles edited genomes efficiently in cell types that are usually hard to transfect, including human induced pluripotent stem cells, neurons, and myoblasts. In muscle cells grown from a Duchenne muscular dystrophy patient's stem cells, exon skipping passed 90 percent. One injection into mouse muscle produced permanent exon skipping, pointing toward in vivo therapy.
europmc-pmc7098030:
Zheng wrote a review of SARS-CoV-2, the new coronavirus behind the COVID-19 outbreak, in the International Journal of Biological Sciences. The virus was then new, and little was known about it. Zheng gathers the key early events and the basic facts known by late February 2020.

The review covers signs and symptoms in patients, and the likely paths of transmission. It weighs the origin and evolution of the virus. Bats look like the natural reservoir, and pangolins may have been an intermediate host, though Zheng notes both roles need more proof. The review closes with early drug options under development. Readers get a compact early brief on an emerging global threat.
europmc-pmc7132130:
Matsuyama and co-authors show that lab cells engineered to carry the protein TMPRSS2 grow SARS-CoV-2 far better than standard cells, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Isolating the virus from patients is a first step for research and test development. Ordinary VeroE6 cells work, but poorly.

Their VeroE6/TMPRSS2 cell line proved highly susceptible to infection, making it useful for isolating and multiplying the virus. The result also shows TMPRSS2, a protein that clips the viral spike, helps this virus just as it helps the SARS and MERS viruses. A reliable growing system underpins drug screening and antibody testing, so the method mattered early in the pandemic.
europmc-pmc7139330:
Martínez-Limón and co-authors review the p38 signalling pathway from basic biology to cancer therapy, in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. The p38 pathway carries stress signals from the cell's surroundings into changes in gene activity. It touches many cell processes, and its role in cancer cuts both ways.

First described as a tumor suppressor that blocks RAS-driven transformation, p38 can also promote tumors in other settings. That dual nature has confused drug development: inhibitors reached clinical trials for several cancers without much success so far. The review maps the pathway's main functions, weighs isoform-specific roles, and surveys current and alternative treatment strategies that might exploit the pathway more cleverly.
europmc-pmc7146530:
El-Saber Batiha and co-authors review the chemistry and medicinal activities of garlic, in Nutrients. Garlic has been eaten and used as a remedy worldwide for centuries. Its active chemistry centres on sulfur compounds such as alliin, allicin, and ajoenes, plus flavonoids like quercetin.

Extracts and isolated compounds have been tested against bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protozoa, and for antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anti-diabetic, and anti-cancer effects. Allicin, garlic's best-known compound, killed tumor cells in the lab as far back as 1960. The review also covers how the body absorbs and clears these compounds. It is a wide survey of why a kitchen staple keeps attracting pharmacological attention.
europmc-pmc7157630:
Ashour and co-authors review the 2019 novel coronavirus against the record of past human coronavirus outbreaks, in Pathogens. SARS emerged in 2002 and MERS in 2012, each showing coronaviruses' knack for jumping into humans. SARS-CoV-2, first identified in Wuhan in December 2019, caused severe viral pneumonia.

By late February 2020, tens of thousands of cases and several thousand deaths were reported in China alone. Its death rate looked lower than SARS, but it spread far more readily. The review covers virus structure, genome organisation, and cell entry, then looks ahead: future outbreaks will depend both on how the viruses evolve and on how well prevention and treatment are built.
europmc-pmc7228430:
Satici and co-authors test how discomfort with uncertainty wore down mental wellbeing during COVID-19. Their study appeared in the International Journal of Mental Health and Addiction. The sample held 1,772 Turkish adults from 79 of the country's 81 cities. Ages ran from 18 to 73 years. Each person rated wellbeing, tolerance of uncertainty, repetitive thinking, and fear of the virus.

People who hated uncertainty reported worse wellbeing. The link ran through two middle steps in sequence. First came rumination, the habit of chewing over worries. Then came fear of COVID-19 itself. Together they carried much of the harm. The authors suggest that calming repetitive thought and fear could protect mental health. Their model maps one route by which a crisis gets inside daily mood.
europmc-pmc7242730:
Grzywa and co-authors review how arginase from myeloid immune cells blunts the body's fight against cancer. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. T cells need the amino acid arginine to activate and multiply. Tumors often swarm with myeloid cells that release arginase, an enzyme that destroys arginine. Starved of it, T cells falter.

Two forms of the enzyme, ARG1 and ARG2, appear in tumors. Higher activity usually tracks with later disease and worse prognosis. Tumor cells can even trigger neutrophils to dump their arginase outside. Suppressor myeloid cells and macrophages are the main sources. Blocking arginase is now a candidate partner for immunotherapy. The review gathers the evidence across cancer types. It frames amino acid control as a real lever on immune response.
europmc-pmc7286230:
Fisk, Livingstone and Pit examine how three countries rushed to promote telehealth in the first weeks of the COVID-19 pandemic. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. The World Health Organization declared the pandemic on March 12, 2020. The authors review government and professional actions in Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States over the following 2 weeks.

Older people were the focus: they use telehealth most and faced the highest risk of dying from the virus. The three countries differed in how far and how fast they moved, reflecting their different health systems. Telehealth was promoted to spot possible infections in older people living alone, support those isolating, and keep treatment going at a distance. The paper records that early policy scramble in detail.
europmc-pmc7288430:
Kieft, Zhou and Anantharaman present a program, spelled V-I-B-R-A-N-T, that finds viruses hidden in mixed DNA data. Their paper deals with metagenomes, where DNA from microbes and viruses is jumbled in one set. Old tools often miss odd viruses or tag plain bacterial DNA as viral.

The program mixes machine learning with protein matching. It uses neural nets fed on protein signs, plus a new score for genome quality. It can find viruses that live free and viruses built into a host genome, and it flags genes that help viruses change host chemistry. In tests it beat tools such as VirSorter, VirFinder, and MARVEL. On 120,834 viral sequences from human and wild settings, it found on average 94% of the viruses present.
europmc-pmc7325630:
Rodríguez-Rey and co-authors surveyed adults in Spain for Frontiers in Psychology during the first weeks of the COVID-19 outbreak. Spain had declared a state of alarm in March 2020, and most people were confined at home. The team asked 3,055 adults about stress, anxiety, depression, and daily life changes.

About 36 percent reported moderate to severe psychological impact from the crisis. Roughly 41 percent reported depressive symptoms, and a similar share felt stressed. Women, younger adults, and people who lost jobs showed the worst symptoms. Worry about an economic crisis ranked highest among concerns. Feeling well informed, keeping up leisure activities, and feeling healthy were linked to better mental health.
europmc-pmc7338530:
Doi and co-authors report a pre-clinical safety study in Nature Communications on stem cell treatment for Parkinson's disease. Parkinson's kills dopamine-making brain cells, and lab-grown replacements are a hoped-for therapy. The team tested dopamine progenitor cells grown from a clinical-grade human induced pluripotent stem cell line.

Lab checks confirmed the cells' identity and found no leftover undifferentiated stem cells and no worrying changes in cancer-related genes. In immune-deficient mice, the cells caused no tumors or toxicity. Transplanted into rats with a Parkinson-like lesion, the cells improved the animals' behavior. On the strength of these results, the group began a clinical trial in patients in 2018.
europmc-pmc7347130:
Zhang and co-authors report a case series in PLoS ONE on deaths from COVID-19. It covers 82 patients who died at one hospital in Wuhan, China. Their records came from the hospital's electronic medical files. All had lab-confirmed infection with the new coronavirus.

Most of those who died were men, and most were over age 60. Many had other health problems, most often high blood pressure, heart disease, or diabetes. Breathing failure was the main cause of death. Harm to the heart, liver, kidneys, and blood was also common. Only a small share got intensive care, and fewer than half had a breathing machine. The median time from first symptoms to death was 15 days. Readers see how strained care and organ-wide harm shaped these early deaths.
europmc-pmc7350730:
He and co-authors test a cell-free treatment for knee osteoarthritis in Stem Cell Research and Therapy. The treatment uses exosomes, tiny parcels shed by stem cells from rat bone marrow. Earlier work suggested the cells themselves help cartilage, but parcels might carry the benefit with fewer risks. The team tested them in dishes and in rats.

Cartilage cells took up the exosomes, which blunted the damage signals sent by an inflammatory molecule, IL-1β. Treated cells grew and moved better, and kept making cartilage matrix proteins. In rats with induced joint damage, injections raised matrix protein levels and lowered a cartilage-chewing enzyme. Pain responses improved from week 2 onward. The authors frame exosomes as a promising repair signal for worn joints.
europmc-pmc7402630:
Candido and co-authors trace the evolution and spread of SARS-CoV-2 in Brazil in Science. Brazil's epidemic was among the world's fastest growing, yet data were scarce. The team sequenced 427 new viral genomes and combined them with mobility data and a representative genomic dataset.

They identified more than 100 separate international introductions into Brazil. Most Brazilian strains, 76 percent, fell into three clades that arrived from Europe between late February and mid-March 2020. Early spread stayed local and within state borders; later, big cities exported the virus widely. Control measures cut the reproduction number in São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro from above 3 to between 1 and 1.6. Genomics, the study shows, can reconstruct an epidemic's hidden routes.
europmc-pmc7424030:
Lochhead and co-authors review the tight junctions that seal the blood-brain barrier. This barrier lets the brain pull in nutrients while it blocks toxic substances. Tight junction proteins stitch the barrier cells together and keep gaps shut.

The review shows that these protein seals are not fixed. Disease and stress can change which proteins are made or where they sit. That shifts how much can pass into the brain. The same seals block most drugs, which makes brain treatment hard. The authors map ways to loosen the seals in a safe, brief way so drugs can slip through. Readers gain a full picture of barrier design, control, and drug delivery.
europmc-pmc7445430:
Bourdely and co-authors identify a new subset of human dendritic cells and trace what it does. Dendritic cells present antigens and steer T cell activation. Their full range in humans was not well mapped.

The subset, named DC3, carries CD1c and CD163 but not CD88. DC3s are the direct forerunners of inflammatory dendritic cells found in tissue. They grow through a GM-CSF path apart from other known lineages. Like classic dendritic cells, they can switch on naive T cells. They excel at priming CD8+ T cells that home to tissue, through TGF-beta signals. In breast tumors, DC3 entry tracked with tissue-resident memory T cells. The findings mark DC3s as a lineage with strong power over tumor immunity.
europmc-pmc7447230:
Hamadani and co-authors measure the instant effects of COVID-19 stay-at-home orders in rural Bangladesh. Lockdowns can hurt income, food access, and mental health. The team compared survey data from before the pandemic with data gathered during lockdown in Rupganj.

Mothers of 3016 children were invited, and 2424 joined the study. Nearly all knew and followed the stay-at-home advice, yet family paid work fell sharply. Median monthly family income dropped from US$212 at baseline to $59 during lockdown. Far more families fell below the basic income line and faced food insecurity. Mothers reported more depression and anxiety symptoms. Among women facing partner violence, over half said it had grown since lockdown. The orders carried deep social costs.
europmc-pmc7515030:
Delgado-Bonal and Marshak write a full tutorial on approximate entropy and sample entropy. Both algorithms judge how regular a data series is by hunting for patterns. Their theory differs, though users often ignore that fact.

The tutorial needs no prior knowledge from the reader. It explains the ideas through information theory and chaos theory. Simple source codes show how to compute each measure. A step-by-step example walks through proper use of both. The methods began in physiology work on body signals. They now serve medicine, telecommunications, economics, and Earth sciences too. The authors stress correct use over listing past applications. Misuse, they warn, flows from skipping the theory behind the tools.
europmc-pmc7538930:
Hou and co-authors present NATMI, a toolkit for predicting how cells signal each other. Single-cell sequencing now profiles thousands of cells at once. Knowing which cells talk helps explain tissue behavior.

NATMI draws on a database of 2293 ligand-receptor pairs. Each pair has literature support behind it. The tool builds and shows communication networks from expression data. Tests on published datasets found the busiest cell pairs. They also found the most active signaling pairs. Results pointed to strong self-signaling in many cells. The toolkit works with single-cell and bulk data. It also compares networks across conditions.
europmc-pmc7695830:
Parayath and co-authors design tiny carriers that reprogram T cells inside the body. Cell therapies that give T cells new receptors work well against cancer. But making them outside the body for each patient is costly and slow. The team sought a shortcut: send the receptor blueprint direct to blood T cells.

The carriers hold mRNA, made in the lab, for a cancer-targeting receptor. In mice with leukemia, prostate cancer, and liver cancer, repeat doses created enough armed T cells to shrink disease. Gains matched those from lab-made cells given as a bolus. The authors say such carriers are easy to make, ship, and give.
europmc-pmc7773630:
Bhaskaran and co-authors test whether HIV raises the risk of COVID-19 death in England. It used the OpenSAFELY platform, which links primary care records with death records. The study held 17,282,905 adults. Of these, 27,480, or 0.16%, had a record of HIV infection.

During the study span, 14,882 COVID-19 deaths occurred, 25 of them in people with HIV. After age and sex were taken into account, HIV linked to higher death risk, with a hazard ratio of 2.90. Full adjustment lowered it to 2.59, still high. The link looked larger in Black groups. The authors urge care in shielding this group.
europmc-pmc7779030:
Blake and co-authors describe the Mouse Genome Database, or MGD, the shared knowledge base for the laboratory mouse. MGD is the authority for mouse gene, function, and trait data. It also holds mouse models of human disease. MGD sets the official names for mouse genes, alleles, and strains.

Curators gather facts from papers and from datasets sent in by researchers. New features improve the Multi Genome Viewer, which compares genomes across mouse strains. Many more strains now have their own pages with wider query options. Variant data for strains were integrated in depth. The team also sped up literature curation. A new portal focuses on mouse models and genes for COVID-19 study.
europmc-pmc7815730:
Wei and co-authors build microparticles that boost anti-PD-1 therapy for cancer. Checkpoint drugs face three barriers. Too few T cells enter the tumor. The tumor setting suppresses immunity. Antibodies gather and sink into tumors poorly.

The particles come from macrophage membranes. They carry the drug metformin and wear a mannose coat. That coat steers them to M2-like tumor macrophages. Metformin then flips those cells to the attack-minded M1 form. Flipped macrophages drew in more CD8+ T cells. Suppressive cell types fell back. The particles also broke down collagen in the tumor. Anti-PD-1 antibody then reached deeper and worked better. Treated animals gained stronger, longer-lasting tumor control.
europmc-pmc7839230:
Rethlefsen and co-authors present PRISMA-S, a guide for reporting literature searches in systematic reviews. Searches form the base of every systematic review. That base is often described too thinly to repeat. Older guidance was scattered and vague.

PRISMA-S extends the main PRISMA statement. It tells authors exactly what to report about a search. Database names, full strategies, and dates all belong in the report. Peer review of searches and record handling are covered too. The group behind it includes review and library experts. Their aim is searches that readers can check and rerun. Better reporting should lift trust in review findings.
europmc-pmc7872030:
Zafar and Saier review gut Bacteroides species in health and disease. The gut microbe world out-codes its host by far. Helpful gut residents can turn harmful in the wrong place. Bacteroides rank among the top helpful groups. They digest complex plant sugars for the host.

These bacteria feed vitamins to the host and neighbors. They shape gut immunity as well. Yet some can drive abscesses and infection outside the gut. The authors set out both faces in detail. Molecular contacts behind each effect are named. The picture that emerges is rich and two-sided. Context decides whether these microbes help or harm.
europmc-pmc7936330:
Cinelli and co-authors report a study of the echo chamber effect on social media. Echo chambers form when users mostly meet views that match their own. Platforms differ in design, and those designs may shape how far views spread. The team compared the main platforms on shared measures to test that idea.

They analysed more than 100 million pieces of content on hot topics such as gun control, vaccination, and abortion. The data came from Gab, Facebook, Reddit, and Twitter. Two measures led the work: sameness within user networks, and bias in how content flows toward like-minded peers. Clustering into like-minded groups dominated the dynamics on all platforms. A direct check of news use showed stronger segregation on Facebook than on Reddit. The study gives hard shape to a widely claimed effect.
europmc-pmc8085630:
Chadha and co-authors summarize the World Health Organization's first world report on hearing. The World Health Assembly asked for the report in 2017. It was built through wide consultation and released in March 2021. By 2050, nearly 2.5 billion people will live with some degree of hearing loss. At least 700 million of them will need rehabilitation services.

Much hearing loss can be prevented across a lifetime. Over a billion young people risk damage from loud personal listening devices. Cost-effective fixes for finding and treating loss already exist. Yet services show an 83% gap between need and access worldwide. Unaddressed loss cost close to 1 trillion international dollars in 2020. An extra 1.33 United States dollars per person each year could lift coverage to 90%. That spending could help 1.3 billion people. Each dollar could return around 16 over a decade.
europmc-pmc8160230:
Jarczak, Kluge, and Nierhaus review the pathophysiology of sepsis and its treatment concepts. Sepsis is a life-threatening syndrome of organ failure. A disordered host response to infection drives it.

The review updates how immune failure unfolds in sepsis. It then sorts treatment choices, from basic causal and supportive care onward. Added measures such as blood purification lack firm proof so far. Targeted immune therapy also remains unproven. The authors stress that proven care still rests on early basic steps. They frame where new trials should aim next. Basic steps include treating the infection source and supporting failing organs.
europmc-pmc8163330:
Anthony and co-authors argue that metallodrugs are a class apart in drug discovery. Metals bring chemical traits that pure organic compounds cannot offer. At least 10 metals are essential for human life.

About 46 other metals also serve in drugs and diagnostic agents. Platinum drugs feature in half of cancer chemotherapies. Lithium, silver, and bismuth each fill known roles. The authors show why pipelines built for organic drugs fit metal drugs poorly. They map chances and hurdles in finding and testing new metallodrugs. The field needs its own screening habits, they argue.
europmc-pmc8168830:
Lee and co-authors set out a framework for handling missing data in observational studies. Missing values are common in medical research, yet choices about them stay murky. Poor reporting threatens trust in results.

Their framework runs in three steps, starting with a clear analysis plan. The plan states the model and how gaps will be handled. A case study from a long-running parents and children cohort shows each step. The authors also press for open reporting of each choice. The work comes from the STRATOS initiative. It aims to lift standards across observational research.
europmc-pmc8371430:
Panchal and co-authors review how COVID-19 lockdowns affected the mental health of children and teens. Lockdowns began after the pandemic was declared in March 2020. The systematic review covers young people aged 19 years or younger who lived through lockdown.

The review included 61 articles with 54,999 children and adolescents, with a mean age of 11 years. Anxiety and depression symptoms were common across the studies, though rates varied widely between them. Irritability and anger were also reported often. Risk factors included special needs, past mental disorders, and heavy media use. Good parent-child communication protected against anxiety and depression. The authors call for clear support plans for young people at risk.
europmc-pmc8399130:
Burguin and co-authors update the treatment picture for breast cancer, the most common cancer in women worldwide. The disease splits into four molecular subtypes based on hormone receptors and HER2 status. Care is matched to subtype, but side effects and resistance remain common.

Standard care joins hormone therapy, anti-HER2 drugs, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy. Triple-negative cancers still lack a standard targeted treatment. New paths include immunotherapy, antibody-drug conjugates, and attacks on metabolic routes. The review walks through current treatments first. It then weighs the new strategies from a personalized care view. The authors also flag the challenges each new path brings.
europmc-pmc8455130:
Tian and co-authors show that the N501Y spike mutation helps SARS-CoV-2 grip its human receptor more tightly. Variants carrying this change, including Alpha, Beta, and Gamma, spread faster between people. The team asked what the mutation does at molecular level.

They mixed cell binding tests, kinetics, single-molecule force work, and computer models. The mutated binding domain latched onto ACE2 faster and let go more slowly. Force tests showed a higher binding chance and a stronger hold. Simulations found new chemical contacts that explain the grip. The authors argue this tighter bond drives the higher transmission of these variants. Future mutations may act the same way.
europmc-pmc8538030:
Martini and co-authors run a meta-analysis on ultra-processed foods and diet quality. Such foods, classed by the NOVA system, may threaten health through their nutrient mix. National survey data can show how they reshape whole diets. The team gathered such samples from many countries.

The search covered studies published before July 2021. Diets were sorted by the NOVA classes in each survey. Ultra-processed foods supplied up to 80 percent of calories in the United States and Canada. Sweets and sweet drinks led the list. As their share rose, fresh and lightly processed foods fell. Free sugars and fats rose too, while fiber, protein, and key minerals dropped.
europmc-pmc8604730:
Friedrich and co-authors identify tissue patterns in inflammatory bowel disease that link to poor drug response. Current drugs fail for many patients, and the reasons were unclear. The team combined bulk and single-cell gene data with tissue measures. Three patient groups took part, with 376 people in total.

One pattern stood out: deep ulcers with many neutrophils and active fibroblasts. Fibroblasts in the ulcer bed drew neutrophils in, driven by interleukin-1 signals. This gene pattern was higher in people who did not respond to several drugs. Four more groups, with 343 people, showed the same link. The authors suggest blocking interleukin-1 for this ulcer type.
europmc-pmc8651630:
Scott and co-authors test if better sleep leads to better mental health in a meta-analysis of trials. Whether sleep causes mental health problems was not clear. The team pooled randomized trials where a treatment improved sleep. They then checked if mental health improved too.

The pool held 65 trials with 8,608 people in total. Better sleep gave a medium gain in overall mental health. Gains showed for depression, anxiety, and rumination. Stress and psychosis symptoms gained less but still improved. Larger sleep gains tracked with larger mental health gains. The authors say sleep care could join mental health services.
europmc-pmc8660730:
Ali and co-authors review global trends in type 2 diabetes complications and deaths since 2015. An earlier review found most data came from a dozen rich countries. Rates of heart attacks, amputations, and deaths were falling there. The new review asks if those trends held and spread.

Most data still come from rich countries with strong tracking systems. Some data now come from Africa and Latin America as well. Rich countries saw more falls in heart complications and deaths. In some poorer countries, those rates rose over time. The authors also flag flaws in data capture and reporting. These flaws shape what the global trends seem to say.
europmc-pmc8836030:
Akbarian, Khani, and Eghbalpour survey bioactive peptides and what they can do. These small molecules hide inside parent proteins. Cutting the protein free releases their activity. Other peptides are made directly by microbes and body tissues. Many are now sold as chemical or lab-made products. Interest spans medicine, food, and cosmetics.

The review covers how such peptides are produced. It lists natural sources, from foods to venom-like secretions. It then walks through their uses one by one. Effects include killing microbes, lowering blood pressure, and fighting oxidation. Others help control blood lipids, appetite, and blood sugar. A section treats cyclic peptides as a step beyond straight chains. The authors close with computer methods and future prospects.
europmc-pmc8888930:
Guo, Wang, and Yin review how shifting microglia states could treat neurodegenerative disease. Microglia are the brain's resident immune cells. Their inflammation appears in Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and other such diseases. Microglia come in two broad modes. M1 cells release inflammatory signals and can harm neurons. M2 cells calm inflammation and protect tissue. A spectrum lies between the two.

The review argues for pushing cells from M1 toward M2. It explains microglia functions and phenotypes first. It then covers the shift itself in each major disease. Receptors that steer the shift get a section. Cytokines and ion channels follow. Bioactive compounds and drugs that induce the shift are cataloged. The authors close with other steering factors. Balance, they argue, is the therapeutic prize.
europmc-pmc8982030:
Gramates and co-authors lead a guided tour of FlyBase, the fruit fly genetics resource, as it enters its fourth decade. Drosophila melanogaster is a pillar model organism. FlyBase centralizes its genetic and genomic data. Curators and developers stock it from papers and big projects. Alleles, constructs, phenotypes, and interactions all live there. Reagent information joins them. This paper highlights the features users miss most often. Some tools are unique to FlyBase.

Tools for finding data come first. Reports that organize data follow. Several grew from one curator's side project. Community and external resources earn a section. Help pages and contact routes are mapped. Coming attractions close the tour. The authors write for fly researchers first. Other model organism communities may borrow ideas. Thirty years of history inform the design.
europmc-pmc9186530:
Nurk and co-authors present the complete sequence of a human genome from the Telomere-to-Telomere Consortium. The reference genome in use since 2000 covered only part of the genome. About 8% stayed unfinished, mostly repetitive regions. The new sequence, T2T-CHM13, fills those gaps.

The complete sequence holds 3.055 billion base pairs with gapless assemblies for all chromosomes except Y. It corrects errors in prior references and adds nearly 200 million new base pairs. Those new regions hold 1,956 gene predictions, 99 of them protein coding. Centromere arrays and recent duplicate segments are now readable. The authors say the finished regions open complex genome areas to variation and function studies.
europmc-pmc9191730:
Shumate and co-authors improve transcriptome assembly by mixing long and short sequencing reads in StringTie. Short reads are accurate but rarely span many exons. Long reads capture full transcripts but carry more errors, which can misplace splice sites. A hybrid approach can take the best of both.

The new StringTie release does hybrid-read assembly in one tool. On some data sets it more than doubled the count of correctly assembled transcripts. It also beat long-read-only assembly on precision by a wide margin. Tests covered simulated data and real data from a plant, a mouse, and humans. Fixing long reads first was slower and less accurate. The software is free and open source.
europmc-pmc9252830:
Galaxy Community gives the 2022 update on the Galaxy platform for biomedical analyses. Galaxy is a browser-based workbench that lets scientists share, analyze, and visualize their data. It asks little technical skill from users. A global community maintains it, with free services on several continents.

More than 8,000 analysis packages have been wrapped as Galaxy tools. A training network offers over 230 free tutorials for self-directed learning. Recent gains include a better interface for large jobs and a full machine learning suite. Galaxy workflows powered the Vertebrate Genome Project and global SARS-CoV-2 work. Engagement metrics grew across users, jobs, and contributions. The update shows a mature open platform still expanding.
europmc-pmc9337830:
Zhang and co-authors review cellular senescence as a treatment target in aging and disease. Senescent cells have left the cell cycle for good after damage or stress. They release a harmful mix of signals that spreads senescence and breaks tissue balance. Mouse models where these cells can be deleted show they drive much age-related decline.

Two drug families aim at these cells. Senolytics kill them; senomorphics mute their harmful signals. Early trials in people suggest real benefit, and more trials are under way. The review covers how the cells form and mark themselves. It also tracks how candidate drugs are found and tested. The authors see senescence control as a core strategy against aging diseases.
europmc-pmc9400730:
Troup, Fallan, and Baud give a critical review of how linkers are designed for PROTAC drugs. A PROTAC joins two ligands with a chemical linker. One ligand binds a target protein, and the other binds an E3 ubiquitin ligase. The pair marks the target for destruction inside the cell.

The authors survey the main linker classes in print. They cover plain alkyl and polyethylene glycol chains. They also cover newer clickable and light-switchable designs. Linker length and makeup shape how a PROTAC acts, they note. The review faults the old trial-and-error habit in linker choice. It urges more use of computing and structure work to guide design.
europmc-pmc9493130:
Rastogi and co-authors examine the role of B cells as antigen presenting cells. B cells are best known as antibody makers. They can also switch on antigen-specific CD4 and CD8 T cells. That presenting job has drawn far less study than antibody work.

The review sets out how B cells take up and process antigens. Presentation can run through the B cell receptor or bypass it. The authors compare B cells with other presenting cells, such as dendritic cells. B cell populations and their traits get a survey. Outside agents that shift presentation are also covered. Interest is rising for two reasons, they note. B cells shape the tumor microenvironment in key ways. They are also being tested as cellular therapies. Regulatory and killer roles of B cells round out the picture.
europmc-pmc9931230:
Kung and co-authors test ChatGPT on the United States Medical Licensing Exam. The exam has three parts: Step 1, Step 2CK, and Step 3. ChatGPT took all three without special training or added reinforcement. The study asks what large language models could do in medical training.

ChatGPT scored at or near the passing line on each exam. Its answers also showed strong agreement and insight in explanations. The authors read this as a sign of real promise. Such models may help students learn core medical knowledge. They may later aid clinical choices as well. The paper became an early benchmark for AI in medical education. Its limits are noted beside its strengths.
europmc-pmc9949730:
Barroso and co-authors set out the Brazilian Guidelines of Hypertension for 2020. The document gives national advice on finding and treating high blood pressure. A large panel of Brazilian specialists drafted and approved the guidance. It reflects local practice needs and current evidence.

The guidelines cover how blood pressure should be measured and classed. They address risk scoring, organ damage checks, and treatment thresholds. Drug choices and combined therapy form a core part. Advice also spans special groups and hard cases such as resistant hypertension. Lifestyle steps sit beside drug care throughout. Clinicians get a single reference for daily decisions in Brazil. The panel aims to cut heart and vessel harm from uncontrolled pressure.
faulkner-as-i-lay-dying-1930:
As I Lay Dying, published in 1930, is one of William Faulkner's most famous novels. Addie Bundren, a poor Mississippi farm wife, dies after asking to be buried in Jefferson. Her husband and five children load her coffin onto a wagon and set out to honor that wish.

Fifteen voices take turns telling the story, each in short, intense sections. Flood, fire, and decay beset the journey, and each Bundren reveals private griefs and motives. Cash, Darl, Jewel, Dewey Dell, and little Vardaman all see the same events differently. Faulkner turns a grim family errand into a bold, dark, and often funny portrait of pride and endurance.
fisher-genetical-theory-1930:
Ronald Fisher was a British statistician and biologist who set Darwin's theory on a firm math base. His 1930 book The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection joins Mendel's laws of inheritance to selection in wild populations. It is a dense book that changed its field.

Fisher shows with math how small inherited differences spread or vanish across generations. He treats topics from mimicry in moths to the balance of the sexes with the same tools. Later scholars call the book a founding text of population genetics and of the modern synthesis. He wrote for biologists, so the math comes wrapped in farm and field examples.
fortune-psychic-self-defense-1930:
Dion Fortune wrote the classic defense against occult attack in 1930. Psychic Self-Defense draws on her own cases from years of work in the field. Fortune was a trained nurse and a leading figure in British occult circles.

She tells how to spot the signs of a psychic attack and how to tell them from nerves or fraud. Then she gives the means of defense: rites, prayer, and plain steps of daily care. Her tone is calm and practical where others wrote fog. Every later book on guarding the mind against such harm cites hers.
fortune-training-and-work-of-an-initiate:
Fortune laid out the course of occult training step by step in 1930. The Training and Work of an Initiate is the mate to her Esoteric Orders, the how to that book's what. It maps the road from first study to full work in a lodge.

Meditation, symbol study, and rite craft form the spine of the course. Fortune tells what each stage does to the student and what can go wrong on the way. Her counsel is strict, sane, and shaped by her years as a teacher. The book still serves as a guide to the initiate's road.
freud-civilization-discontents-riviere-1:
Sigmund Freud published Civilization and Its Discontents in German in 1930. The English text here is Joan Riviere's translation of the same year. Freud asks why civilized life brings so much unhappiness. Culture, he argues, demands that we curb aggression and sexual drives. The curbs save us from chaos but leave guilt and malaise.

He studies religion, love, work, and the sense of guilt with bleak clarity. The death drive returns as a force behind war and cruelty. Written as Europe darkened, the book is Freud's darkest social theory. It remains his most read work of cultural criticism. Few essays on modern discontent match its reach.
frus-1861-d130:
On 12 June 1861, William Dayton reported the new French stance to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 130 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Dayton reported a Paris that had now stated its neutral course. The task shifted from shaping the stance to policing it. His mid June letter marks that turn, from the drama of decision to the grind of watching its use. Policing a neutral stance meant protests, claims, and proof, week after week. Proof, in such work, was a matter of ship names, dates, and sworn words. The turn he marks governed the file from then on.
frus-1861-d230:
In a letter dated 14 September 1861, William H. Seward gave Mr. Fogg his latest word from Washington. It was printed as Document 230 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d30:
Henry Sanford sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 18 July 1861. It is document 30 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Sanford wrote three days before the battle of Bull Run was fought in Virginia. His letter crossed the ocean in a world that did not yet know the result. That gap between event and report is the true pace of diplomacy in 1861, and this letter marks it plainly. The steamship mails set the pace of his work, each packet bringing a fresh batch of tasks. Each packet from home reset his tasks, and he worked through them in order.
frus-1862-d130:
Seward wrote again on 18 August 1862, this time to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It was printed as Document 130 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d230:
William Stuart wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 2 September 1862, in a letter printed as Document 230 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It was one of two Stuart letters under that date.

Stuart wrote in the immediate wake of Bull Run, with Lee's army about to cross into Maryland. British policy turned on whether the South could prove itself a lasting nation in the field. A legation letter from this week reached London as ministers there weighed that proof. Its place in the file marks how closely diplomacy tracked the armies. Britain's first concern in Washington was the blockade and what it cost British trade.
frus-1862-d30:
In a letter dated 10 March 1862, William H. Seward gave Charles Francis Adams his latest word from Washington. It was printed as Document 30 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It belongs to the winter of the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d330:
William H. Seward, as Secretary of State, resumed the Paris mail on 3 October 1862 with a dispatch to William L. Dayton, printed as Document 330 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It was one of two Seward letters to Dayton under that date in the wider file.

Early October found France ready to propose a truce jointly with Britain and Russia, waiting only for London's word. Seward's letters to Paris in this window carried the Union's refusal in advance: no foreign plan for the war would be accepted. This dispatch belongs to that firm autumn line. French mills wanted Southern cotton, and French yards watched the Union blockade with care.
frus-1862-d430:
On 28 June 1862 Gabriel García Tassara, Spain's minister in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. His note is Document 430 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Tassara had served in Washington for years and knew American politics well, which made his notes a fair test of Spanish feeling. In the summer of 1862 Spain was pulling out of the joint Mexican venture while France pressed on alone. The questions between Madrid and Washington ran from that expedition to Confederate activity near Cuba. A note like this one kept those matters in formal channels, where Seward preferred to handle them.
frus-1862-d530:
A second note of 7 June 1862 went from Roest van Limburg to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 530 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, beside its same-day companion.

Same-day pairs were common when a minister transmitted separate enclosures or took up two questions that protocol kept apart. The Dutch business of that week in Washington ran alongside the Hague correspondence of Minister Pike, and the two files illuminate each other. Van Limburg wrote as the resident voice of a small maritime power dealing with a great republic at war. His notes, formal and exact, are the Washington half of one of the volume's most complete small-country records.
frus-1862-d630:
Edward Joy Morris wrote from Constantinople to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 March 1862. His report is Document 630 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Spring 1862 found Morris reporting the Levant's quiet: American commerce moving, citizens protected, the war a subject of curiosity rather than policy at the Porte. Such reports had a negative value Washington appreciated, the assurance that one whole region required nothing. They also carried the minister's observations on the Eastern Question. That was the standing rivalry over Ottoman lands. American merchants felt it in every port from Smyrna to Beirut. The letter sustains the Turkish file's calm, expert tone.
frus-1863p1-d130:
London's late-March mail includes this dispatch from Charles Francis Adams to Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 26 March 1863. A second Adams letter in the volume shares the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 130 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Late-March mail from London came as the ship fight neared its peak. Adams reported talks, press, and the state of the yards for Washington's use. This dispatch is one of a pair sent that day. In the run of the volume it stands in one of the thickest weeks of the file. Both capitals wrote hard on the same points that week.
frus-1863p1-d230:
Reporting on 9 July 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The report is document 230 in the 1863 diplomatic papers. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

Union wins at Gettysburg and Vicksburg in early July 1863 weakened the case for aiding the South. British leaders grew more careful, and Adams's post grew a little less tense. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d30:
Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 15 January 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 30 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Mid-January letters from Adams weighed how Britain was taking the new year of the war. The freedom edict had stirred the British public, and the legation tracked that stir with care. Adams's cool style suited the work: he reported what he saw, not what he hoped. This dispatch is a fair sample of his craft, and of the file that made his name as the Union's man in London.
frus-1863p1-d330:
Writing in Washington on 29 November 1862, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, addressed Secretary of State William H. Seward on British business. The paper is document 330 in the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Taken as a run, these notes chart Britain slowly accepting that the Union would not collapse. That judgment, formed in Washington, helped keep Britain out of the war. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d430:
A 28 March 1863 dispatch from William H. Seward, the Secretary of State reached Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the spring of 1863.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d530:
A dispatch dated 23 May 1863 went from Secretary William H. Seward to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d630:
From William H. Seward, Secretary of State to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons: a letter dated 14 October 1863. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the autumn of 1863.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d130: Wallace Murray, the State Department's Adviser on Political Relations, wrote a memorandum dated November 15, 1943, preserved as Document 130 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Murray's office handled the Near East among other regions, a desk with much at stake that autumn. The record gives the author and the date and no topic. The memorandum is printed in the Foreign Relations series, in the voyage sequence of papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d230:
The United States Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 400 aboard the Iowa on 18 November 1943. It tackles one command problem: how to get the most from American strategic bombing flown from bases across the whole European and Mediterranean area, in support of the Pointblank bombing plan.

The paper concludes that all such forces, including the power to shift units between areas, should sit under a single command, working closely with RAF Bomber Command. Base services and day-to-day running would stay with the local army commanders. It recommends a new United States Strategic Air Force headquarters in the United Kingdom, since the heaviest bomber forces and the best facilities were already there.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d30: Stalin replied to Roosevelt on September 8, 1943, the day Italy's surrender was announced to the world. His message is Document 30 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The catalog record does not tie the letter to that news or to any topic, and it should not be made to. It survives in the Foreign Relations series as part of the September exchange that set up the Moscow foreign ministers' meeting.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d330:
General Patrick Hurley, the President's personal representative, telegraphed Roosevelt from Tehran on 26 November 1943 about where the President would stay during the conference. Sent by Army channels, the message tracks a Soviet invitation delivered that same day.

That morning Hurley had told the Russian chargé d'affaires that Roosevelt would reside at his own legation, a decision he believed final and made before any Russian invitation arrived. At three that afternoon the chargé returned with a cordial invitation from his government for Roosevelt to be its guest at the Russian Embassy instead. Hurley promised to convey it, while doubting a change could still be made, since all preparations followed the legation plan. An agent, meanwhile, was inspecting the offered embassy quarters so every detail would be in hand.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d430:
Ambassador Laurence Steinhardt telegraphed Secretary of State Hull from Ankara on 3 December 1943, number 1968, repeating his most secret message to Cairo for the President. It gives the travel plan and the full party for President Inönü's journey to the second Cairo Conference.

Ambassador Hugessen received authority the night before to give Inönü the assurance he wanted, of a free discussion among equals. The president plans to leave Ankara at four that Friday afternoon by special train. He would reach Adana by noon on Saturday. He would fly on to Cairo at once if the planes have arrived. His party numbers fourteen: the president, his secretary, his physician, two aides, the foreign minister and his staff, the under-secretary, and four servants. The British, Soviet, and American ambassadors travel with them.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d530:
Ambassador Averell Harriman sent another report to President Roosevelt from Moscow on December 23, 1943, his second direct cable of the week. Harriman was then the central figure in Soviet-American relations on the ground. The State Department printed the report in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Frequent direct reports from Harriman meant the President was watching Moscow closely in the first weeks after Tehran. The ambassador's judgments about Soviet intentions carried into every major choice of 1944. For readers, this cable is another panel in the best reporting stream Washington had from inside the Soviet Union, written by a man who dealt with Stalin's government face to face.
frus-1944-quebec-d130:
A second message from Mikołajczyk, also dated September 10, 1944, reached Roosevelt through the Polish ambassador in Washington. The news had changed: the Soviet government had now agreed to collaborate on aid to Warsaw. The Polish premier seized on that opening and pressed the president to act on it at once, before talks could eat up the remaining time.

His request was specific. Roosevelt should direct General Eisenhower to begin air operations for Warsaw's defenders immediately. If the Soviets opened discussion of the plan and raised reservations, Mikołajczyk warned, so much time would pass that saving the city might become impossible. The message is a study in urgency from a leader watching his capital die.
frus-1944-quebec-d230:
C.C.S. 618/3, the British Chiefs' memorandum of September 12, 1944, gives the settled allied answer on coordinating with the Soviet military. Stalin had raised the matter in June, and Marshal Vassilievsky had asked for the chiefs' proposals in July. A United Chiefs of Staff committee remained unacceptable, as agreed at Sextant. Something narrower was needed.

The conclusion proposes a Combined Military Committee in Moscow. It would be purely consultative and advisory, with no power to decide without reference to the respective chiefs of staff. It would deal only with strategic and operational matters, keeping clear of the European Advisory Commission's civil affairs work. A senior Soviet General Staff officer was essential, and the mission heads in Moscow would serve for the Western allies.
frus-1944-quebec-d30:
Churchill wrote to Harry Hopkins on August 26, 1944. Paris had been liberated the day before. The message appears in the pre-conference papers. Those papers fill the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

The two men corresponded that week about the coming meeting. Roosevelt would host Churchill at the Citadel in Quebec City. The letter belongs to the final arrangements. Those arrangements were made against a backdrop of triumph in France. For readers, it shows the alliance's personal wiring at work. That wiring carried speed, candor, and friendship. Formal diplomacy alone could not carry that load.
frus-1945-50-intel-d130:
Strategic Services Unit General Orders No. 16, dated 19 October 1946, is among the SSU's last papers in the volume. General orders announce a unit's internal acts: postings, honors, and endings. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

By October 1946 the SSU's secret operations had largely passed to the Central Intelligence Group, and the remnant was winding down. A numbered order from that season has the flavor of a colors ceremony in prose. Readers who followed the unit from Magruder's first letters will feel the thread close. The OSS's last ember was kept alive for a year by careful paper. Here it dims toward its end, as its work lives on in a new house.
frus-1945-50-intel-d230:
A memorandum from the Secretary of the Army (Royall) reached the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers) on 26 November 1947. Readers meet it as document 230 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The old board and its group were gone, replaced that fall by the CIA under the new National Security Council.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d30:
General Clayton Bissell, the Army's assistant chief of staff for military intelligence, wrote to Secretary of War Patterson on 22 October 1945. Bissell spoke for the Army's own intelligence arm, G-2. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

The Army's intelligence chief had his own claims in the postwar settlement, separate from the SSU remnant housed in his department. His memorandum to the secretary shows G-2 stating its case at the top. Readers should keep the Army's threads distinct: Magruder's leftover OSS men and Bissell's uniformed service were rivals inside one building. The volume prints both sides, and the friction between them shaped what the Army finally asked for.
frus-1945-50-intel-d330:
On 18 November 1947, the Director of the Policy Planning Staff (Kennan) sent a memorandum to the Under Secretary of State (Lovett). It survives in print as document 330 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. The old board and its group were gone, replaced that fall by the CIA under the new National Security Council.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d430:
National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 11, dated 6 January 1950, is document 430 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The directive opened the rule making of a new decade. By 1950 the CIA had rivals, partners, and a record of its own to defend. A fresh standing order at that point shows the Council still tuning the balance among them, three years after the agency began. The 1950 directives speak to a system that now had to manage success and strain alike. A new decade found the rule book still open, still being written by use.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d130:
British views on Germany's economy, gathered from London embassy cables, are summed up for the President on 29 November 1944. Stettinius's memorandum is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It tests the State Department's own draft of 10 November against the reports.

British officials, the cables show, strongly oppose sweeping de-industrialization and extreme impoverishment of Germany. They are testing selective controls instead, and finding most of them hard to work. London wants measures that will hold public support and still be enforceable a generation later, when wartime feeling has cooled. The British back conversion to peacetime production and payment of reparation in kind, and they are keen to start talks on returning looted property.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d230:
Washington answered Iran's oil freeze with a carefully even hand on 16 October 1944. Secretary Hull's cable to Ambassador Morris, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, tells him what to say to the Iranian government. It was repeated to London and Moscow.

The United States has taken note of the decision to put off all petroleum talks. The two American firms that spent a year, and much effort and expense, pursuing a concession are naturally disappointed, having expected a contract. Still, Washington voices confidence that the Iranian authorities acted in good faith. One expectation is stated plainly. When Iran is ready to hear applications again, American firms must get treatment no less favorable than that given to any other country's nationals.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d30: Roosevelt wrote to Churchill on 23 December 1944, with the Battle of the Bulge then raging in Belgium. The message is document 30 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on Malta and Yalta. Wartime Christmas brought no break in diplomacy, since the coming conferences at Malta and Yalta still needed the two Western leaders aligned on every major question.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d330:
Strangely, the heading on this record calls it a Combined Chiefs of Staff session, yet the room held the three leaders themselves. At Yalta at 5 p.m. on February 4, 1945, Stalin asked Roosevelt to open the meeting. The President thanked him for the comforts arranged in the midst of a war. He said the three delegations would understand each other better as they went along.

Roosevelt proposed that they proceed without stiff form, speaking frankly and freely on what the common cause required. The whole map of Europe, he said, needed discussion. The text that follows matches the first plenary session, whatever the heading says — a mismatch worth knowing about.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d430:
One added clause carries the Soviet mark on the Declaration on Liberated Europe. Molotov proposed the amendment at the plenary of February 9, 1945. At the end of the fourth paragraph, the period would give way to a comma. Then new words would follow.

Strong support, the added words say, will be given to those people in these countries who took an active part in the struggle against German occupation. The change looks small on paper. In practice it pointed aid toward partisan movements, most of them friendly to Moscow. The amendment survives in the Bohlen collection, attached to the next day's minutes.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d130:
