Acting Secretary Grew relayed a private message from Churchill to the President on July 7, 1945. The long telegram, sent through Lord Halifax, is document 130 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Britain had just voted, and Churchill shared his reading of the election and his plans if he lost.

Churchill sends warm regards and expects his government to win a majority, though elections hold surprises. Even on a bad result he would not resign at once; he would wait for a confidence vote in the Commons. The British political members will leave the conference on July 25 to await the count at home, returning July 27 if needed. He also urges that the conference not be hurried, recalling how abruptly the Crimea meeting ended.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d230:
The Joint Civil Affairs Committee proposed winding down the European Advisory Commission in an undated memorandum printed as document 230 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. The committee argued that the London-based body had outlived its purpose now that the fighting in Europe had ended.

Hostilities have terminated, the paper says, and in Germany the four national commanders now speak for their governments, with Austria to follow. The commission was once the one place the powers could regularly consult on Germany and Austria; that is true no longer. Keeping it would only duplicate the Control Council's work. The paper also urges that the national commanders get broad authority to decide day-to-day questions, since slow delegations, above all the Soviet one, had been the chief cause of delay.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d30:
Now that Harry has left, Harriman reported the mission to Truman on June 8, 1945. There was no doubt, he wrote, that Stalin had been gravely concerned at their first meeting. Adverse developments of the past three months in relations between the two countries weighed on him. Firm positions taken by Roosevelt before his death, and by Truman since, had had their effect.

Stalin did not fully understand the basis of the difficulties, Harriman judged. In the early talks he took the offensive, complaining of American misdeeds. He warned that if America did not wish to deal on a friendly basis, the Soviet Union was strong enough to look after itself. Yet he was clearly glad to see Harry. The report balances hope and warning.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d330:
George Elsey, an aide to the President's naval aide, traced the tangled history of cutting Germany into pieces in an undated memorandum. At Tehran in December 1943, he recalls, Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin had briefly agreed Germany should be dismembered. Roosevelt proposed five parts. Churchill, after some doubt, suggested two: Prussia and a southern Germany.

Stalin, Elsey writes, sided with the President's view and disliked a large southern state. Yet the Tehran talk settled nothing firm. The memo follows the idea through Yalta and through Churchill's Moscow visit of October 1944. It gave Truman the record of an idea his predecessor had floated but never fixed.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d430:
Agreements for governing Berlin are reported in General Clay's message from Frankfurt of July 9, 1945, signed by General Bradley. At a Saturday conference with Marshal Zhukov in Berlin, the commanders had settled the city's government by Kommandatura. A formal paper was being prepared for signature at Berlin on Tuesday.

The arrangement provides a three-power government of Berlin as a unit in all respects, with French liaison until the French zone is defined. Each commander keeps responsibility for law and order in his own sector. The city's government will run through eighteen departments, covering such matters as education, religion, and the press, though the Kommandatura may merge or change them.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d530:
Repatriation rules are spelled out in Grew's secret cable to Tittmann at Vatican City on July 11, 1945. Under the Yalta Agreement, American policy is to repatriate to the Soviet Union all claimants of Soviet citizenship whose claims the Soviet authorities accept. In practice, that means Soviet citizens originating within the 1939 boundaries of the Soviet Union are repatriated irrespective of their individual wishes.

The Baltic peoples stand outside that rule. The United States has not recognized the incorporation of the Baltic states into the Soviet Union, so Lithuanians, Latvians, and Estonians are not considered Soviet citizens by this government. It is contrary to American policy, Grew adds, to facilitate the involuntary repatriation of Baltic nationals, Poles, Croats, Slovenes, and Slovaks.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d630:
Harold Minor, acting chief of the Middle Eastern desk, recorded a talk with the Iranian minister on June 18, 1945. His memo is document 630 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The minister had come at his own request to press for Allied withdrawal from Iran.

Minor reports the words of Iran's foreign minister, sent by wire that day. Iran, the minister said, lay in confusion and disruption, with no government secure in place. He himself did not know how long he would stay in his post. He spoke, he said, as an Iranian citizen voicing what Iranians felt. The root of the trouble, he argued, was the presence of foreign troops on Iranian soil. Until those forces left, he held, Iran's state could not improve.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1030: Ambassador John Winant sent this fragment of a telegram from London to Philip Mosely at Potsdam on July 18, 1945. Only an extract is printed here; the full text appears later in the volume. Winant reports a delay in London. No word has yet reached the Soviet embassy there from Moscow. Without that word, the Soviets cannot clear or sign the agreement amending the occupation zones agreement for Germany. The fragment shows the French zone settlement waiting on a single missing approval from the Soviet capital.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1130:
Draft words lay before Truman, Stalin, and Churchill on 21 July 1945, in a text the three leaders weighed but had not yet approved. The volume prints it as a text considered by the heads of government. Considered is the key word: the language was still open to change.

Drafts of this kind were the raw stock from which the Potsdam Protocol was built. Lines were added, cut, and fought over before any of them bound the three powers. Read beside the approved text printed next to it, this draft shows the deal mid-formation. A reader can watch single phrases carry the weight of nations.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1230:
A second Togo cable to Sato is dated 21 July 1945. Two instructions in a day show Tokyo leaning hard on its Moscow channel. The summit in Germany was moving toward a public word on Japan, and Tokyo sensed its time shrinking.

Togo's messages balanced two needs: keep the Soviet door open, and keep Tokyo's own hard-liners from shutting the whole bid down. That balance runs through his words to Sato. This cable is one piece of it. Preserved through American codebreaking, it lets readers watch a beaten empire's last diplomacy from inside its own wires.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1330:
Britain's team tabled this proposal on 21 July 1945. It came from the end of the summit's first week, while Churchill still led the British side. The paper set London's stand on its point for the other teams to answer.

British papers of the first week carry a poignancy their writers could not feel. The government behind them was about to fall, and new men would own the stands taken here. This proposal is part of that first-week British hand. It survives in the American record, where readers can set it against the final terms and judge what the change of leaders cost or saved.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1430:
A second Soviet text dated 29 July 1945 follows in the closing run of the volume. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

The Soviet habit of tabling full drafts forced the other sides to argue on Moscow's paper or spend time writing their own. This text is part of that pressure, applied as the talks neared their end. For readers, the run of Soviet drafts is a study in negotiation by document: claims fixed in ink, defended clause by clause. What survived into the protocol can be checked line by line from these pages.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-130:
Thompson's minutes record a Potsdam session of July 28, 1945, the day the British delegation returned under a new prime minister. Thompson kept one of the steady American records throughout the conference. His minutes for this date were printed in the second Potsdam volume. The talks now entered their final, decisive stretch.

The minutes let readers watch the reshaped conference at work. Old points were reopened with new men across the table. Thompson wrote it down in sequence, without ornament. That plainness makes his record a firm base for judging later claims. The day's page adds to a run that covers nearly the whole conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-30:
For one Potsdam gathering, the only witness the editors can cite played the piano. The meeting left no official record at all. Its editorial note is the thirtieth unnumbered item following document 710, in the sequence of conference records for July 1945.

The editors report that fragments of the conversation were recalled by Sergeant Eugene List. List had played the piano for Truman and his guests at the gathering in question. His recollection was reported in The New Yorker of December 29, 1945, page 15. The note itself preserves nothing of what was said at the meeting. It stands as the thinnest entry in this stretch of the volume, a pointer to a published magazine piece in place of a record.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d730:
Dated July 26, 1945, document 730 is a further proposal from the United States delegation at Potsdam. The date places it in the conference's second week. By then the talks had settled into hard trading on the largest questions. The proposal entered the numbered record of the second Potsdam volume.

Later proposals differ from opening ones. They are written against known resistance. Readers can sense the narrowing room in a second-week text. The document helps trace how the American side adjusted its aims. It stands as a dated marker between the first drafts and the final protocol.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d830:
Barnes wrote from Bulgaria on July 31, 1945, in document 830. The representative in Sofia reported to the Acting Secretary on Potsdam's last full day. His letter closes his conference-span run in this part of the volume. It was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

A final-day report from the field has a settling quality. Barnes stated Bulgaria's state as the great decisions landed. Readers can set his ground truth beside the protocol's smooth lines. The document shows the distance between a settlement's text and a country's life. His mission would now work inside that distance, and his letters map it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d930:
Edwin Pauley sent William Clayton these estimates of wealth in the Soviet zone of occupation on July 25, 1945. His short letter says the figures should interest Clayton during the current talks. Two attachments give American and Soviet percentages side by side, within Germany's 1937 borders.

The American estimate puts the zone's average share at 49.1 percent, against a Soviet figure of 40.9 percent. Both sides agree on farming at 48 percent. They differ on industry, at 39.3 against 35.3 percent. A second table breaks down factory branches. Electrical work and clothing top the list, each above 60 percent in the Soviet zone.
frus-1952-54v16-d1030:
The American delegation at Geneva cabled this statement home on July 21, 1954. General Smith read it at the eighth plenary session on Indochina. The United States would not join the joint declaration. It spoke alone instead.

Washington took note of the July 20 and 21 accords. It vowed to use no force to disturb them. Renewed attack would be viewed with grave concern. On votes, it restated its June 29 stand for unity through free elections watched by the United Nations. The cable asks for instant release of the text. The memo sits among the Dien Bien Phu crisis papers of that spring.
frus-1964-68v30:
China is the subject of Volume XXX in Foreign Relations of the United States, 1964-1968. The main sequence runs to 336 documents. Short closing sections treat Tibet and Mongolia. The papers follow the U.S. stand against seating Beijing at the United Nations. They also cover the Warsaw talks, trade controls, and the Cultural Revolution. China's nuclear tests and the war in Vietnam shape much of the record.

Cables from posts abroad report votes at the UN year by year. Memos weigh whether to soften travel and trade rules. The tone stays wary throughout. The volume shows a policy of containment held firm, with only small probes toward contact.
frus-1969-76v02-d130: A memorandum from the State Department's Executive Secretary, Theodore Eliot, to Under Secretary John Irwin protests diplomacy run by the NSC staff. It is document 130 in Volume II of the 1969-1976 Foreign Relations series. Eliot cites three cases where NSC aides dealt with foreign officials without State's knowledge. They touch the Indian Ocean, Pakistan, and Brazilian coffee. He asks that State be consulted unless the President directs otherwise. He warns the Secretary may take the matter to the President.
frus-1969-76v30:
Greece, Cyprus, and Turkey from 1973 to 1976 fill Volume XXX of the 1969-1976 series. The Greece section runs to 71 documents. Cyprus takes the largest share, with documents 72 through 194. Turkey closes the volume. The Cyprus chapters cover the 1974 coup on the island and the Turkish intervention that followed. The Greece chapters trace the fall of the junta and the return of civilian rule.

The Turkey chapters deal with the U.S. arms embargo and the strain it caused. Talk records show Kissinger with Archbishop Makarios and Greek and Turkish leaders. The volume is the main U.S. record of the Cyprus crisis and its long wake.
frus-1977-80v30:
Public diplomacy fills Volume XXX of the 1977-1980 Foreign Relations series. Its 215 documents run in one sequence. They cover the work of the USIA and its successor agency: broadcasts, exhibits, exchanges, and press work abroad. One memo urges quick sharing of interview and press conference texts through the Wireless File. USIA, it notes, did not then receive such texts on a regular basis. Advance notice of interviews would let posts use them at once.

The papers track the merger of USIA with State Department cultural work in 1978. They weigh how to speak to foreign publics in the Cold War's late phase. Budgets and staffing run throughout.
gao-gaoreports-b-295530:
CW Government Travel, Inc., attacked a contract term in GAO file B-295530, dated March 7, 2005. The Army's solicitation for travel office services, under the Defense Travel System program, set a guaranteed minimum for its indefinite-quantity contracts. The firm said the sum was too small to be real. GAO denied the protest. The digest is one line: the record showed the minimum was more than nominal. A floor that is more than a token figure meets the law for such contracts.

The purchase looked toward multiple awards for Defense-wide travel services. This ruling cleared the minimum; the price scheme fell in the next round.
gao-gaoreports-b-298730:
ALATEC Inc. protested an Army award to The Analysis Group, LLC. The contract covered engineering and technical support services at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. The buy was set aside in full for small firms. GAO ruled in B-298730 on December 4, 2006.

The size status of the winner drove the case. The Small Business Administration found the firm other than small. Its appeals office later backed that call. A protest stay had paused the work in the meantime. GAO said the Army should end the large firm's contract. Letting it run would clash with the Small Business Act. No sound counterweight was shown. GAO sustained the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-309530:
Web database renewals split on timing in this GAO decision, B-309530, dated September 17, 2007. The National Labor Relations Board renewed seven web database deals. It charged the cost to fiscal year 2006 funds in September 2006. Five deals had to be in place on October 1, 2006. Their old terms ran out the day before.

GAO upheld the five renewals. The Board had fair ground to order them before the old terms lapsed. Two renewals broke the rule, though. Those deals ran to October 31, 2006. They were a need of fiscal year 2007, not 2006. The Board should have paid for them with fiscal year 2007 funds.
gao-gaoreports-b-310230:
Sunrise Medical HHG, Inc. lost its protest; the GAO decision is B-310230, dated December 12, 2007. The Veterans Affairs office sought manual wheelchairs and parts. The award went to Invacare Corp. The deal ran one year with four option years. Sunrise fought the scores for tech plans and past work. It also fought a brush-off of its late price cut.

GAO denied the protest. The scores were fair, or any flaw did no harm to Sunrise. The late price cut got a fair no as well. Sunrise was not the firm that would have won but for the flaw. Late cuts earn no grace for a firm out of the lead.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-230:
Space Shuttle, GAO-05-230 of March 9, 2005, warns of a staff trap in NASA's plan to retire its shuttle fleet. The fleet will fly till the space station stands done, near the end of the decade. Then it stops. Thousands of skilled civil and firm staff keep the fleet safe. If they leave too soon, safe flight is at risk.

GAO asks how far NASA has got with a plan to hold that crew till the last flight. It names the drags on the plan so far. More steps are needed to set the agency up well, the title holds. Pay, pride, and clear dates all play a part.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-730:
Report GAO-05-730, released July 14, 2005, examines the Defense Department's new personnel system. The system would reset rules for more than 700,000 civilian staff. It covers hiring, pay, promotion, and discipline. A 2004 law gave the department wide power to make the change. GAO described the design process and weighed it against sound change practice.

GAO found the first design plan was rushed and not well suited. After a rethink, the department slowed down and brought in more voices. The new process met four of six key practices GAO checks. One gap was outreach. Messages did not reach all staff groups or speak to their concerns. GAO warned that the launch still faced hard tests.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-930:
Foreign airline safety in code-share deals is graded in GAO-05-930, a report dated August 5, 2005. U.S. airlines sell seats on partner airlines' flights under their own codes. A 2000 federal program makes U.S. airlines audit their foreign partners' safety. That audit is a condition of approval. GAO judged whether the program gives sound assurance of safety and security.

From fiscal years 2000 through 2004, the transport department approved such deals 270 times. It suspended none for known safety concerns. The aviation agency and the security agency raised no safety objections in that span. Sometimes a U.S. airline dropped a deal expecting an objection. The Defense Department runs its own reviews of the same foreign carriers for its own travel. It reads many of the same audit reports, GAO found. Oversight of the program should be strengthened, it concluded.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-230:
Four federal compensation programs are profiled in GAO-06-230, a report dated November 18, 2005. Since 1969 the government has taken a growing role in paying people hurt by toxic exposures. The Black Lung Program, built for coal miners, was meant to end in 1976. Instead it became permanent, and new programs followed. They cover vaccine injuries, radiation exposure, and illness among energy workers. As Congress weighs a program for asbestos victims, it asked GAO for a close look at the four.

For each program, GAO lays out the design: its purpose, funding, management, and benefits. The four differ in who pays and how claims get judged. Promises made as temporary have a way of lasting. Costs and claimant pools grow past early guesses. The report gives lawmakers a grounded base for the asbestos debate and for judging the true price of such pledges.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-330:
Lessons from the Oil for Food scandal drive GAO-06-330, a report issued April 25, 2006. The program began in 1996 to ease Iraqi hardship under sanctions. It moved more than $67 billion in oil revenue. It delivered $31 billion in humanitarian aid to Iraq. A 2005 defense law ordered GAO to review the UN's stewardship. GAO tested the program against five key internal control standards. It judged the control environment and the other standards' core parts.

Weak controls let a vast program drift, the lessons show. GAO urged U.S. diplomats to press the UN toward reform. Programs with heavy financial risk should follow accepted control standards. Risk checks must be full and timely, the report stresses. Controls should grow stronger across the whole UN system. The case became a byword for aid without oversight. This report turns scandal into a checklist. It asks what honest stewardship of billions requires.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-530:
Work finished late in one year but paid in the next is called carryover. The report numbered GAO-06-530, issued June 27, 2006, checks carryover in the Defense Working Capital Fund. Budget estimates put carryover at about $6.3 billion. That sum covers depot maintenance, ordnance, and research work moving from fiscal year 2006 into 2007. Defense committees accept some carryover for smooth workflow. They worry the amount may exceed what is needed.

GAO tested whether the services figured carryover under the department's new policy. It checked whether customers sent orders late in the year and how that swelled carryover. The services did not calculate amounts correctly, GAO found.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-730:
Recovery of endangered species is studied in GAO report GAO-06-730, issued on September 6, 2006. The Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service run the Endangered Species Act of 1973. The act generally requires recovery plans for species facing extinction. Those plans name the threats to each species and the steps to remove them. GAO reviewed 31 selected species and the time their recovery was taking.

GAO found that many factors shape how long recovery takes. Success can hinge on removing the main threat, guarding habitat, or even grasping what the threats are. Timelines for the reviewed species ranged widely. GAO warned that some species may not be recovered at all. The report shows why recovery is slow, costly work measured in decades.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-830:
Pilot training by contract is examined in GAO report GAO-06-830, issued on September 22, 2006. The Air Force hired firms to run simulator training for the F-15C, F-16, F-15E, and airborne warning aircraft. The Army did the same for helicopter training at its Flight School XXI. Contractors own, operate, and maintain the simulators. The services count on industry to fund the large upfront investment in the equipment.

GAO found that the approach had perceived benefits but was not adequately supported at the start. Training itself had improved under the contracts. Yet the expected number of simulator sites had not been activated. GAO also found that the return on taxpayer dollars was not effectively tracked. The report urges better proof that the model pays off.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1030:
Marine Corps special operations forces, newly placed under a joint command, are assessed in GAO report GAO-07-1030, dated September 5, 2007. Demand for special forces grew with wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, and with training of foreign troops. A Marine component was set up under U.S. Special Operations Command.

Acting on his own authority, the Comptroller General had GAO test the join. GAO asked if the new Marine command knows the force shape it needs. It checked the Corps' workforce plan for those troops. It asked if the joint command has judged whether Marine training readies them for their missions. Action is needed, GAO found.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1130:
Help for new farmers needs proof it works, GAO reports in GAO-07-1130, dated September 18, 2007. The Department of Agriculture counts a beginning farmer as one with 10 years or less on a farm, at any age, who takes a real part in the work. Its farm agency lends to those who can not get bank credit, and holds funds back for new farmers.

Its conservation arm pays new farmers at higher rates in two programs. GAO reviewed the key steps the department has taken to aid new farmers. It then judged how the department shows if those steps work. More steps are needed, the title states, to prove the aid's worth.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-430:
Early-phase missile defense choices need better facts, and GAO-07-430, issued April 17, 2007, tells the Pentagon what is missing. The Defense Department had spent about $107 billion since the mid-1980s on ways to destroy incoming missiles. A March 2006 Missile Defense Agency report weighed systems that kill missiles just after launch. Congress asked GAO to grade that report.

GAO found the report held some useful work but clear gaps. Life-cycle cost figures were thin and hard to trust. Two costly systems, the Kinetic Energy Interceptor and the Airborne Laser, were set to prove themselves in 2008 and 2009. Funding both at once raised hard questions. GAO listed the added data that future choices will need, so lawmakers can weigh cost against worth.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-830:
Enforcement work at the Securities and Exchange Commission is graded in GAO-07-830, dated August 15, 2007. The Enforcement Division probes violations of securities laws. It can seek fines and repayment of ill-gotten gains. It also runs the Fair Fund program, which returns money to harmed investors. Recent cases brought record fines against firms and top officers. GAO studied how the division plans, tracks, and closes its cases. It asked whether planned upgrades fix known flaws.

Case files were tracked in systems with clear limits, GAO found. In March 2007, the division set one central gate for new probes. It has not yet written the rules and criteria for that gate. A new data system due in late 2007 needs timely, uniform entries to help. In May 2007, the division moved to close stale cases faster. Fair Fund work also needs stronger management. The agency agreed with GAO's conclusions and advice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-130:
Louisiana's vanishing coast and lessons from past repairs fill GAO report GAO-08-130, issued December 14, 2007. The state holds 40 percent of the coastal wetlands in the lower 48 states. It stands to lose almost 17 square miles of coast each year for the next 50 years. Wetlands blunt storm surge and support wildlife and fishing. A 1990 act set up a joint repair program.

Over 17 years, that program built or designed 147 projects to guard over 120,000 acres. GAO drew lessons from that record for far larger efforts now funded. It made no recommendations. Its stress falls on care in design as spending grows.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-30:
Fusion energy bets are audited in GAO report GAO-08-30 (October 26, 2007). On November 21, 2006, the United States joined five nations and the European Union to build a giant test reactor in France. The project aims to prove that magnetic fusion can yield power. The Energy Department plans to spend $1.12 billion over 9 years on the U.S. share. About 44 percent would buy U.S.-made parts.

GAO warns that the figure is a sketch, not a firm estimate. The design is still unfinished, and the joint project's own hurdles may raise costs. At home, two fusion research lines run side by side with weak coordination. GAO urges firm cost figures and a joined research plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-730:
Aid pacts with poor countries rest on forecasts of jobs, income, and growth. The Millennium Challenge Corporation makes those forecasts for each pact. GAO-08-730, dated June 17, 2008, checks the math behind pacts with Armenia, El Salvador, Lesotho, and Mozambique.

Forecast methods shifted from project to project. Of 20 projects, 9 used a 20-year span and 11 used other spans. For 2 projects, the standard span would drop returns below the agency's own bar. Papers behind three of the four pact choices were not kept. GAO urged written steps, a second set of eyes on the math, and one standard method.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-930:
Bringing U.S. forces home from Iraq will be a huge and costly job. GAO-08-930, a September 2008 report, reviews the Defense Department's planning for that drawdown, which DOD calls reposturing. As of March 2008, about 173,000 pieces of equipment worth about $16.5 billion sat in Iraq awaiting return. The Desert Storm pullout, after a much shorter war, took at least 14 months.

Commands began planning in fall 2007, and DOD started tying the efforts together in May 2008 around three assumptions. Any move would rest on ground assessments, allow lead time once a timetable is set, and flow out gradually, at no more than 2.5 brigades' worth of gear a month. But roles for running the retrograde are still not clear. GAO urges a clarified chain of command.
gide-immoralist-bussy-1930:
André Gide published The Immoralist in French in 1902, and Dorothy Bussy translated it into English in 1930. Its narrator, Michel, is a scholar who falls gravely ill on his honeymoon in North Africa. As his body recovers, his old dutiful life begins to feel like a kind of death.

Michel learns to prize health, sensation, and freedom above duty and convention. His wife Marceline sickens even as he grows strong, and he cannot turn back. Gide tells the tale in spare, lucid prose, without direct judgment. Readers must weigh Michel's liberation against its cost themselves. The short novel made Gide a central, and scandalous, figure in French letters.
gould-case-for-the-sea-serpent-1930:
Rupert Gould, a naval officer of exact habits, pled the sea serpent's case in 1930. The Case for the Sea-Serpent is the most methodical brief for the beast made in its century. Gould had won fame sorting out sea mysteries and odd tales of the deep.

He answers the great Dutch treatise of Oudemans case by case, report by report. Where the proof is weak he says so; where it is strong he presses it home. His claim is plain: some sightings point to a real beast not yet in the books. Friend and foe of the serpent alike must pass through Gould.
herschel-preliminary-discourse-1830:
John Herschel, son of the astronomer William Herschel, published his Preliminary Discourse in 1830. It is a survey of how science should be done, written for general readers. The book quickly became the great statement of scientific method for its century.

Herschel walks through each branch of natural study, from astronomy to geology. He argues that laws come from careful watching, testing, and honest doubt. Charles Darwin read the book as a young man and took its standards to heart. Few works did more to shape how Victorians thought about science. It first reached readers as part of a popular series on useful knowledge.
history-of-the-english-people-volume-ii-:
John Richard Green continues his History of the English People in this second volume. Its two spans are the Charter, 1216 to 1307, and the Parliament, 1307 to 1400. Green keeps his eyes on the people and their growing institutions. Kings matter as they shape, or miss, that growth.

Edward's great host marches north against Bruce in these pages. Thirty thousand men, with wild levies from Ireland and Wales, face a Scots army of footmen near Stirling. Green tells Bannockburn as a people's triumph, not a king's. Parliaments, towns, and friars fill out the century. The volume shows England becoming a political nation.
hughes-not-without-laughter-1930:
Langston Hughes published Not Without Laughter in 1930, his first novel, written in his twenties with the support of a patron. Hughes grew up largely in Kansas, in towns much like the novel's Stanton. He set out to show Black American family life from inside, with its humor intact.

Sandy Rogers grows up in a house run by his grandmother, Aunt Hagar, a washerwoman of iron faith. His mother drifts, his father chases work and music, and his aunts choose opposite paths: respectability and the blues life. Tornado, school, and first jobs shape Sandy's education. Laughter, as the title insists, runs through hardship without denying it. The novel is the classic story of the Harlem Renaissance's Midwestern roots.
jeans-mysterious-universe-1930:
James Jeans published The Mysterious Universe in 1930, based on his Rede Lecture at Cambridge. Jeans surveys the new physics of relativity and quantum theory. He argues that the universe looks more like a great thought than a great machine. Its laws, he suggests, may be the laws of a cosmic mind.

The famous line that God appears as a pure mathematician comes from these pages. Critics praised the prose and debated the philosophy. The book sold widely and spread a sense of quantum mystery to the public. Jeans did not claim proof for his idealism. He offered it as the best reading of strange new facts.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-30:
Huronia falls in Volume 30, from 1898, the climax of the set so far. Thwaites covers the Hurons across 1648 and 1649, the years of ruin. Brébeuf and Lalemant die at St. Ignace after hours of torture.

Witnesses who lived through the attacks tell the shattering story here. The Huron nation scatters to the winds as its towns burn. Priests burn Sainte-Marie themselves rather than leave it to foes. Loss on this scale stuns even readers who saw it coming. The volume reads as the mission's Good Friday, with no Easter yet in sight. It is the hardest book in the series to put down.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-ben-eliez: Aaron ben Eliezer, a German Talmudist of the thirteenth century, is treated in this Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. Meir ben Baruch of Rothenberg, the greatest rabbinical authority of that age, deferred to him in a responsum. The matter is under consideration by great men, namely the high court of Rabbi Aaron, Meir wrote. Abigdor ha-Kohen, chief rabbi of Austria, corresponded with him and called him my teacher. Another source calls Aaron the only man who combined scholarship, ripe experience, and authority in one.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abelites-called:
The Abelites were a North-African Christian sect, most likely of gnostic roots. They lived in a few small groups near Hippo in the time of Augustine, late in the fourth or early in the fifth century. Their name points to Abel, Adam's son, who was thought to have died without children. Their rule of life matched that belief in an odd way.

They did marry, the entry says, but held back from the act of marriage itself. They held the bearing of children to be unlawful. To keep their group alive, each pair adopted a boy and a girl, who would inherit their goods and live the same way. The last of the sect was wiped out under the emperor Arcadius in 407.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abishua-father-: Abishua, a name glossed as "Father is Riches," covers two men in the entry. One was a son of Phinehas and great-grandson of Aaron the high priest. He appears in the line of Aaron's priestly heirs and as an ancestor of Ezra. The second Abishua was a grandson of Benjamin, named in First Chronicles viii. 4. The entry gives no deeds, dates, or other detail for either man beyond these family links.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-eli:
German ritualist Abraham ben Elijah ha-Kohen flourished in the fifteenth century. His short guide to forbidden foods was first printed in 1599. It appeared as an appendix to the Basel edition of Isaac Düren's Sha'are Dura.

He wrote for lay readers, not scholars, and kept the rules brief and clear. A letter to the Halberstadt community asks them to spread the booklet nearby. They were to explain it in German to those who could not read Hebrew. He seems to be the Abraham who put the Passover rules into rhyme. His activity ran not much past the year 1470.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abravalla-samue: Samuel Abravalla, called the Great, was the richest Jew in Valencia. In the attacks of 1391 he was forced to accept baptism. City leaders reported the rite on July 14, 1391. He took the name Alfonso Ferrandes de Villanueva. The entry says he soon went back to Judaism. Later he went to Rome as an envoy of the Spanish Jews. There he met with the pope, alongside Don Solomon ha-Levi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-acheron-or-ache:
Acheron is the fiery river of Hades in Greek myth. Plato names it in the "Phædo," 113 a. Jewish end-time lore takes it up as well. In the Sibyllines and in Enoch, the dead cross Acheron to reach the realm of bliss. The river thus works as a gate between death and rest.

In the Book of Adam and Eve, a six-winged seraph casts Adam's body into the lake. God then lifts it after three hours and gives it to Michael. Michael is to take it to the third heaven. In the Apocalypse of Paul, the lake has waters white as milk. Those who repent are cast into it by Michael. They then pass into the city of God. The entry links the lake to the river of fire in Enoch. Souls must bathe in it to be made clean for paradise.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adler-samuel-83:
Samuel Adler was a German-American rabbi and Talmud scholar. He was born at Worms on December 3, 1809. He died in New York on June 9, 1891. His father Isaac, a fellow rabbi in Worms, gave him his first Hebrew lessons. Isaac died on December 23, 1822. Samuel, then thirteen, kept up his studies in want. He read at Worms and Frankfort, then at Bonn and Giessen. He took his degree in 1836.

His first post was as preacher and aide rabbi in Worms. In 1842 he became rabbi at Alzey. He held that post to 1857. That year Temple Emanu-El in New York called him. He led that flock to 1874, then held the post in name with rest from work. In Germany he fought the civil bars on Jews, above all the Jewish oath. He won equal room for Jewish teaching in Worms schools. His essays and a book of gathers show his wide learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aha-ahai-ii-930:
Aha II, a Palestinian amora of the first amoraic generation in the third century, was surnamed Berabbi, Ha-Gadol, or Roba, meaning "the Great." He systematized Baraitot at the academy of Hiya ha-Gadol and taught Samuel ha-Zaken.

The Midrash preserves his homily on Numbers xiii. 2, built on the promise of the land to Abraham. A king promises a gift to a friend; the friend dies, but the king keeps the promise to the friend's son. So, Aha argues, God's promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob stands for their children, since God's word stands forever.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-i-pav:
Alexander I., Pavlovich, was emperor of Russia from 1801 to 1825. He was born at St. Petersburg on December 23, 1777. He died at Taganrog on December 1, 1825. His reign brought more internal reform than any since Peter the Great. In 1802 he set up a commission on the Jews. Its work became the Enactment concerning the Jews of December 9, 1804.

Under that law, Jews could buy and rent land in the western and southern provinces. They could enter all schools, build factories, and travel on business. The price was German dress for them and their families. The first Jewish farming colonies in Russia grew from these rights. Alexander gave 3,000 rubles in 1805 toward a Jewish hospital in Wilna. In 1818 he ordered three Jewish deputies to sit in St. Petersburg. Yet the Pale still fenced most Jews in, and village life stayed barred.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ali-ha-levi-ben:
Ali ha-Levi ben Solomon held the rank of Gaon at Bagdad. He headed the academy there in the first half of the twelfth century. His name shows up in an old Arabic responsum. Benjamin of Tudela also names him in his travel book. There he is the master of David al-Roi. David was a false messiah of the time.

Much of the entry sorts out the spelling of his name. Some writers give Eli and others give Ali. A second puzzle fills the later pages. Poems praise a later Ali from the same line. The entry argues that this Ali was a grandson. He held the same high post in his turn.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-altenkunstadt-j: Jacob Koppel ben Zebi Altenkunstadt was a rabbi at Verbo in Hungary. He was known as Koppel Harif as well. He lived in the first half of the nineteenth century. He wrote new notes on the tractate Hullin. That work came out at Presburg in 1837. In his preface he states its source. It is drawn from a larger set of notes. That larger set covered the whole Talmud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amram-hayyim-14: Hayyim Amram was a writer who lived in Palestine. He worked in the first half of the nineteenth century. He wrote a note on the Passover Haggadah. The Haggadah is the book read at the Passover meal. His book bears a title that means Passover offering. It came out at Leghorn in 1836. The hosted entry runs to two short lines. It names no other work or fact for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-angyal-engel-an: Anna Angyal, born Engel, was a Hungarian author born at Veszprim in 1848 who died in 1874. She was a teacher's daughter from Hod-Mezö-Vasarhely. Well read in Hungarian, French, and German letters from a young age, she began to publish at sixteen. Her first novel, Adventures of a Hungarian Family, ran in a Hungarian magazine. In 1865 her short novel Prejudices described the state of the Jews in Hungary. A historical novel, Jlonka es Elemer, followed in 1868.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-apelles-of-asca:
Apelles of Ascalon was a counselor and close companion of the emperor Caligula, who reigned 37-41. After a wild youth he went on the stage and became a tragic actor. Philo, as cited here, makes him a man with a deep hatred of the Jews.

Constant access let Apelles pass that hatred to Caligula, aided by Helicon, the emperor's Egyptian fool, who mocked Jews for sport. When Philo led an Alexandrian Jewish embassy to plead for equal rights, Apelles backed the rival anti-Jewish side, and Caligula dismissed the Jews in anger. The entry ends with doubts about how and when Apelles died under his whimsical master.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-archeology-bibl:
Biblical archeology, as the entry defines it, is the science that presents the home, civic, and religious life of the Hebrews in the lands of the Bible. Its field runs through Judaic history down to the fall of Jerusalem in the year 70, when Judaism ceased to be a power in Palestine.

Josephus already used the word archeology for the whole history of his people in his Antiquities of the Jews. That broad sense held until the Reformation, the entry says. No true treatise on biblical archeology appeared until after the Middle Ages. Carlo Sigonius, who died in 1584, first gathered the matter under heads of sacred places, persons, and rites. The entry traces how the field's scope and methods grew from that start.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-artemion-1830:
Artemion led the Jewish revolt in Cyprus against the emperor Trajan in the year 117. Details are scant, and the entry says so. Roman sources report that the Jews destroyed Salamis, the island's capital, and killed 240,000 Greeks. Trajan's general Martius Turbo put the rising down, and the cruelty of that suppression points to heavy Jewish losses in return.

Hatred outlived the fighting. A law made after the revolt barred any Jew from setting foot on Cyprus at all. Even a Jew cast onto the island by shipwreck was to suffer death. The entry rests on Dion Cassius and on Gratz's history, and it leaves the story at that stark end: a revolt, a sack, a crushing answer, and a ban.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ma-aseh-books-1:
Ma'aseh books, collections of tales in Judeo-German, are surveyed in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. These books were printed in Hebrew script and filled with stories and legends. They arose around the start of the fifteenth century among Jews of the Rhine provinces. The literature later grew during migrations into Russia and Poland.

The article explains who the books were for and what they held. They gave entertainment and instruction to women and girls, who were not bound to learn Hebrew. Early writers borrowed freely from King Arthur, the Nibelungenlied, and Till Eulenspiegel. Elijah Levita's Bovo book of 1501 retold the romance of Bevis of Hampton. Jewish tales from the Bible and tradition soon took the larger share. Over time the collections became anthologies of short stories, each ending with a moral. The entry charts a popular literature in a mixed Jewish-German tongue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-malekar-moses-b:
Moses Bapujee Malekar, a Bene-Israel soldier of Bombay, receives a short entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Bombay about 1830, he enlisted in the Twelfth Regiment of Native Infantry in April 1851. He rose through the ranks over nearly three decades. He became subahdar in 1865 and subahdar-major in 1878.

The article records his honors and his fighting. He was present at the siege and capture of Kotah and at the action of Bunnas. For that service he received a medal and clasp. In 1879 he won the second class of the Order of British India. Later came the first class, with the title Sirdar Bahadur. On retirement he was made a justice of the peace. The brief notice preserves one of the Indian Jewish soldiers whose careers the empire decorated.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marmorek-alexan:
Alexander Marmorek was an Austrian physician and a Zionist leader. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Mielnica, in Galicia, on February 19, 1865. He took his medical degree at Vienna in 1887. He then moved to Paris and trained at the Pasteur Institute, where he later served as an assistant.

In 1900 he claimed a serum could cure puerperal fever, but it did not prove effective. In 1903 he claimed an antidote for tuberculosis. One reviewer praised that claim, and another condemned it. The entry also tracks his Zionist work in Paris. He had joined Kadimah, a student society, led the French Zionist Federation, and founded a Jewish popular university.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-me-assefim-coll:
The Me'assefim, the “Collectors,” were the young Hebrew writers who launched the first successful Hebrew periodical. Richard Gottheil and Moses Löb Bamberger tell how it happened in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. The spark was the German translation of the Pentateuch by Mendelssohn in 1782. Its commentary praised the beauty of Hebrew. Two tutors in a Königsberg household, Isaac Abraham Euchel and Mendel Bresslau, resolved to make Hebrew a living literary language again.

Backed by the Friedländer brothers, they issued an appeal in the spring of 1783. They founded a society for the study of Hebrew. Their journal “Ha-Me'assef,” the Collector, ran from 1784 to 1811. It moved from Königsberg to Berlin, Breslau, Altona, and Dessau as money and editors allowed. Mendelssohn himself contributed, anonymously, and the article tracks every volume's wanderings, the raw record of the Haskalah learning to publish.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-ben-jos:
Menahem ben Joseph of Troyes was a thirteenth-century liturgical compiler. The Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 notices him in an article from the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Max Schloessinger. He succeeded his father, Joseph Hazzan ben Judah, as cantor of Troyes. To him the Jewish liturgy owes the collection of the order of prayers used by that community. The collection was quoted ever after as "Siddur Troyes."

His pupil Judah ben Eleazar arranged the collection. Judah may be the author of a commentary, "Minhat Yehudah." That work was written about 1313. It quotes Menahem's work. The manuscripts survive in the Bodleian and at Parma. The notice is brief. It rests on Gross's "Gallia Judaica," on Steinschneider, on Luzzatto, and on Zunz. Still, it fixes the man to whom a regional rite, that of one of the great Champagne communities, owes its written form.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moloch-molech-1:
Moloch — Molech in the Hebrew text — is the god to whom children were sacrificed, examined in a Jewish Encyclopedia article by Isidore Singer and George A. Barton, published in 1906. Leviticus names him first, forbidding any Israelite to give his seed to Molech on pain of death. First Kings adds that Solomon built him a high place on the hill before Jerusalem.

The article collects the dossier: Molech is called an Ammonite god; the rite lived at Topheth in the valley of Hinnom; Manasseh's reign let it in, and Josiah's reform stamped it out. The writers signal early that an uncritical reading of these passages misleads, and the piece proceeds as critical scholarship — testing what the texts actually prove about the cult and its name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mortara-marco-1:
Marco Mortara was an Italian rabbi and scholar who led the Mantua congregation for over fifty years. Isidore Singer and Gotthard Deutsch wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Born at Viadana on May 7, 1815, he graduated from the rabbinical college of Padua in 1836. Mantua called him as rabbi in 1842, and he stayed until his death in 1894.

Mortara held conservative views and fought a plan to drop the second day of the holy days. As a disciple of S. D. Luzzatto he opposed the Cabala, which brought a heated dispute with Elijah Benamozegh. He wrote sermons, textbooks, and essays in four languages. His best known work lists the names in Italian Jewish history, the Mazkeret Hakme Italiya of 1887.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-murcia-11230:
Murcia, capital of the old Spanish kingdom of Murcia, had Jews from the days of Moorish rule. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on them. When James of Aragon besieged the city, he treated with it through an embassy that included his Jewish secretary Astrue.

Alfonso the Wise granted Murcia's Jews the privileges of Toledo and Seville, with their own judges for cases between Jews. They worked in commerce and industry and asked Solomon ibn Adret whether trade in animal skins was lawful. The persecution of 1391 struck them, yet the community was still large in 1474. They lived in a ghetto by the Orihuela gate until the expulsion of 1492.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nasi-lit-prince:
Nasi is a Hebrew title that means prince or president. Its entry was written by Joseph Jacobs and Kaufmann Kohler for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The article treats the nasi as head of the Sanhedrin. It asks who held the title in ancient Jewish life. It also asks how the office changed over time.

Rabbinic texts pair the nasi with the ab bet din. The first pairs run from the Maccabean age to Hillel and Shammai. Later, the house of Hillel kept the title for generations. The article weighs rabbinic claims against Josephus and the New Testament. Some modern scholars doubted the old picture, and others defended it. Readers get a close debate on early Jewish leadership.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nehushtan-11430:
Nehushtan was a bronze serpent broken by King Hezekiah. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Second Kings dates the act to his reign's start. Tradition linked it to Moses' desert serpent. That serpent had healed Israelites bitten by poisonous snakes.

The rabbis read the name as a word in dual form. Worship of it, they held, cost both lives: this and the next. A baraita adds that the people cheered its destruction. Modern scholars split on the name's true sense. Some see a bronze image, apart from the word for serpent. Others hear a long form of that very word. All agree the tradition is no older than Hezekiah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nunez-vaes-isaa:
Isaac Joseph Nuñez-Vaes was a rabbi at Leghorn, in Italy, who died before 1788. His short life sketch was written by Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He followed the Cabala, the Jewish path of mystic thought. Those who knew him held him in high regard for his learning and his piety.

His chief book was Siah Yizhak, printed at Leghorn in 1766. It gave new notes on Yoma, a tract on the Day of Atonement. A second part dealt with Hagigah and with prayer. It stressed the Shemoneh Esreh, the main daily prayer. His son Jacob brought that part out after his death. It came out in 1788 with Jacob's own notes added.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oppenheim-heinr:
Heinrich Bernhard Oppenheim was a German jurist and writer on wealth. Isidore Singer and Max Cohen wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Frankfurt am Main in 1819. He died at Berlin on March 29, 1880. His father was a rich jeweler of Frankfurt.

Heinrich read law at Göttingen, Heidelberg, and Berlin. He sought a post as a teacher at Berlin first. No post came, though friends of rank spoke for him. A Jew could not win that right at Berlin then. He won it at Heidelberg in the end. There he taught state craft and the law of nations. He taught those fields from 1841 to 1845. His first books on home rule came out in those years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-orient-der-1003:
Der Orient was a German weekly on Jewish life and books. Herman Rosenthal and Schulim Ochser wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Julius Fürst founded it and put it out at Leipzig. It ran from January 1840 to June 1851. Its writers were some of the best Jewish minds then.

The weekly came in two parts for its readers. One part dealt with the daily life of the Jews. One part, a book sheet, dealt with their past and works. Jost, Graetz, and Frankel were among its writers in chief. A new press law in Saxony struck in 1851. The first part then ceased at the start of that year. The book sheet ceased five months after that date. Its aim was to spread knowledge of the Jewish past. It sought to lift the lot of Jews by wide reform.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ox-or-bullock-h:
The ox, or bullock, was a farm beast held as sacred. Morris Jastrow, George A. Barton, and others wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. M. Seligsohn and the board were among those others. Among the farm folk of the Semites, it held that rank. At Tyre a goddess was shown with a bull's head.

In Israel too, the bull was held sacred in old days. Proof lies in the cult of God in a calf's form. That cult may have come from the Canaanites near by. Twelve bronze oxen held up a great basin in the Temple. That basin stood in the court at Jerusalem for wash use. The bull was a chief beast for gifts at the altar. Its roles in food and in cult gave it that rank.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pass-aaron-de-1:
Aaron de Pass was a South African merchant and shipping pioneer. He worked in Cape Colony with his brother Elias from 1846. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Their firm was called De Pass, Spence and Company.

The firm helped build the whaling, sealing, and fishing trades of the colony. It leased the guano islands from the government. It also brought in the first patent slip for ship repair. De Pass traded dried fish to Mauritius and brought back sugar. He owned a large sugar estate in Natal as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-perfume-12030:
Perfume in ancient Israel came from plants, not animals. Emil G. Hirsch and Wilhelm Nowack wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Gum resin and balsam formed the base of most scents. Wood, bark, and leaves were used at times.

The prized plants included myrrh, cinnamon, and cassia. Saffron and aloes also appear on the list. Israel knew nothing of distillation as a craft. Makers poured hot oil over the scented matter instead. Beds and royal robes were perfumed for delight. Women carried small scent bottles on long chains.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pichler-adolf-1:
Adolf Pichler was an Austrian painter of Bible scenes. He was born in 1834 at Cziffer, in Hungary. Isidore Singer and Rosalie Perles wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. At thirteen he went to Budapest to earn his bread.

Pichler tutored while he trained as a teacher. At the Academy he won first prize for a head study. He became a favorite drawing teacher in Budapest. Munich gave him masters like Kaulbach and Volz. His best known canvas shows Moses finding the calf worship. Other works show Spinoza and Judah ha-Levi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pseudo-messiahs:
Pseudo-messiahs are men who claim to be the sent saviors of Israel. Kaufmann Kohler and H. G. Friedmann wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Each claims a call from God to free his people. Each aims at the promised messianic kingdom. Some were cheats who farmed the trust of the crowd.

Others were fooled by their own strong beliefs, they say. All shared one goal, the return of Israel to its land. Some sought it by prayer, fasting, and penance. They looked for wonders to help them on the way. Others took bolder paths to the same end. The article marches through these men age by age.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-publican-12430:
Publican was the name for a local farmer of taxes. Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The office stood among Jews under Roman rule. Rome let out its customs dues to such men. The term of the farm was most often five years. The dues fell on goods sent out of the land.

The dues turned on the worth set on the goods. That worth could be bent to squeeze the payer. So publicans were hated men in their towns. They were worst hated when Jews farmed Jews. Echoes of that hate sound in the New Testament. There publicans are paired with sinners again and again.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ragoler-abraham:
Abraham ben Solomon Ragoler was a Lithuanian Talmudist of the eighteenth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Wilna. He was also a brother of Elijah ben Solomon.

The article says Ragoler preached at Shklov. It names his book Ma'alot ha-Torah, printed again at Königsberg in 1851. That book gathers Talmud passages that praise the Torah. It also praises those who study the Torah. A short list of sources ends the entry. Readers learn how one preacher turned respect for study into a book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ree-julius-1263:
Julius Ree was a Danish merchant and political author born on June 1, 1817. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Aarhus in Jutland. He died in Copenhagen on September 3, 1874.

The article says he was a son of Hartvig Philip Ree. In 1842 he set up a wholesale business at Randers. He held town offices there, including alderman. He also spoke for the local Jewish congregation. In 1857 he moved his business to Copenhagen. He entered the lower house of Parliament in 1864. His writings cover economics and Norway's position in 1814. He helped found a loan society for small farmers. The entry joins trade, politics, and farm credit.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosebery-hannah:
Hannah, Countess of Rosebery, was an English social leader and giver to charity. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote her entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born in London in 1851, she was the only daughter and heir of Baron Meyer de Rothschild.

In 1878 she married the Earl of Rosebery, yet stayed a practicing Jew. She belonged to London's Central Synagogue and backed many Jewish causes. Her gifts aided deaf children, trained nurses in Scotland, and working girls in Whitechapel. There she founded the Club for Jewish Working Girls, one of her best known projects.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rufus-12930: Rufus was a Roman general of the first century of the common era. Isidore Singer and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. After Herod's death he led the cavalry of the 3,000 men of Sebaste. That troop was the flower of the royal army against the Jews. With Gratus, who led the infantry, he held out until the legate Varus reached Jerusalem with reinforcements. Josephus tells the story in his Jewish War.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saloman-geskel-:
Geskel Saloman was a painter born of German parents at Tondern, Sleswick, on April 1, 1821. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. His parents soon moved to Copenhagen, where he attended art school.

A portrait by Saloman won the Neuhauser prize in 1848, while still a student. After Paris he settled at Göteborg, in Sweden, and painted in Algiers. From 1870 he lived at Stockholm and taught at its art academy. His canvases include The Emigrants and The Blessing of the Sabbath Lights. He wrote on classical statues too, and stayed a pious Jew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-mose:
Samuel ben Moses was a Russian cabalist of Swislotz, in the Grodno region. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He lived in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, in Russian Poland.

His Shem Shemu'el gives cabalistic readings of the whole Pentateuch, verse by verse. It also supplies hidden, cabalistic reasons for the commandments found there. In its preface Samuel quotes another work of his, Yad Shemu'el. That book applies the same mystical method to the Psalms of David. The two titles together show a lifetime given to Cabala.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saul-ben-david-:
Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Saul ben David. He was a Russian rabbi who died in 1623. The entry is short. It lists the three works he left behind. All three deal with points of Jewish religious law.

His Ṭal Orot, printed at Prague in 1615, is written in verse. It treats the thirty-nine main classes of work forbidden on the Sabbath. An appendix discusses the rules of erubin. His Ḥanukkat ha-Bayit followed at Prague in 1616. It covers the laws tied to Ḥanukkah, the Feast of Lights. He also wrote an elegy for his teacher, Solomon ben Judah. That poem, in twenty-two stanzas, appeared at Amsterdam in 1697.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schultens-alber:
Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Albert Schultens, a Dutch Orientalist. Schultens was born at Gröningen on August 23, 1686. He died on January 26, 1756. He studied Arabic at Leyden under Van Til. At Utrecht he studied under Reland. He took his doctorate at Gröningen in 1709.

Schultens taught Hebrew at Franeker from 1713. He later settled at Leyden as keeper of the Warner manuscripts. He was the first modern scholar to use Arabic to explain Hebrew. People call him the father of modern Hebrew grammar. His Institutiones of 1737 set out that method. He also published a grand edition of Job in two volumes. His edition of Proverbs followed in 1748. Critics attacked his approach, and he defended it in letters of 1749.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sephardim-calle:
Sephardim are the descendants of Jews driven out of Spain and Portugal. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on them. They settled across Europe, North Africa, Turkey, and the Americas. Many came from rich and learned families of Iberia.

Some had served as state officials, bankers, doctors, or teachers. Years of suffering for their faith left them proud and self-aware. For long they saw themselves as the nobility of Jewry, and others agreed. The entry traces how that pride shaped their dress, manners, and standing. It opens the story of a diaspora that kept Spanish Jewish culture alive for centuries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sheftall-shefta:
Sheftall was an American family long known in Savannah, Georgia. Cyrus Adler, Frederick T. Haneman, and L. Hühner wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the family. Benjamin Sheftall reached Savannah from England in July 1733. He was one of forty Jewish immigrants on that arrival.

Benjamin began a family manuscript telling of that 1733 migration. His son Mordecai completed the record years later. Benjamin opposed slavery and helped found Savannah's Union Society. His son Levi led in the local congregation's affairs. Another son, Mordecai, fought as a patriot in the Revolution. He was among the first white children born in the colony. The entry traces one family through Georgia's founding age.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sicarii-greek-a:
Sicarii, or daggermen, were Jewish zealots who fought Roman rule before Jerusalem fell. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on them. They hid small daggers, called sicae, under their cloaks. From those blades they took their feared name.

At crowded festivals they stabbed men friendly to Rome. Then they wailed loudly over the deed with the crowd. That show of grief hid them from detection. Governor Felix cleared robbers out, but the Sicarii proved harder. Felix even used them to kill the high priest Jonathan. Under Cumanus they murdered an imperial servant on the highway. The entry shows terror tactics growing inside a nation sliding toward revolt.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simhah-b-isaac-:
Simhah ben Isaac ben Kalonymus ha-Kohen was one of the Worms Jews killed in the First Crusade. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died on May 25, 1096. Crusaders had just slain his father Isaac and his seven brothers.

Simhah swore he would not die without striking back. He pretended to accept baptism and was taken to a church. As the rite was about to begin, he drew a hidden knife. He stabbed the bishop's nephew, and was then killed in the church. The brief entry preserves a stark tale of revenge and martyrdom.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sosius-caius-13:
Caius Sosius was a Roman general who aided Herod in Judea. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Herod had been made king by Rome but lacked full power. He still had to wrest the country from Antigonus by force. Antony ordered Sosius, legate of Syria, to support him actively.

Sosius reached Jerusalem with a large army in spring 37 BCE. Rams battered the northern walls for forty days of siege. The first wall fell, then the second fifteen days later. Defenders made a last stand by the Temple and upper city. Antigonus surrendered on his knees and was put in chains. Sosius received a triumph for his victory over Judea.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stern-hermann-b:
Hermann de Stern was an English financier born in Frankfort-on-the-Main in 1815. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He settled in London with his brother David in 1844. The brothers founded the banking house of Stern Brothers. He died in London on October 20, 1887.

Stern Brothers soon ranked among London's most trusted banking houses. Hermann focused mainly on Portuguese finance deals. He also helped float the Danubian loan of 1864. Spanish mortgage and Italian tobacco loans bore his hand too. Portugal made him a baron in 1869, as his brother became a viscount. He supported the Anglo-Jewish Association and the Jews' Free School. The entry profiles a banker active in public Jewish life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tanhum-bar-hani:
Tanhum bar Hanilai was a Palestinian amora of the third century. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. His father's name hints at Babylonian roots. He transmitted sayings of Joshua ben Levi and Johanan. Bar Kappara's teachings also passed through him.

Some decisions appear under Tanhum's name in the Babylonian Talmud. The Jerusalem Talmud credits the same rulings to older men. His own legal sentences survive in several tractates. Abbahu and Tanhuma later transmitted his words. He preached publicly, once alongside Abba bar Zabdai. He died during a Hanukkah festival, sources say. His sayings carry a high ethical tone. One pictures Torah and soul as daughters held in trust. The entry sorts a preacher's tangled attributions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-terah-14330:
Terah, father of Abraham, Nahor, and Haran, is profiled in this short entry. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia, published in 1906. Terah came from Ur of the Chaldees. He moved with his sons to Haran, where he died.

Joshua told Israel that Terah had worshiped idols. Scholars still debate what his name means. Some link it to a word for wild goat. Others see a worn form of a moon word. The Midrash adds that Terah made and sold idols. It says Abraham minded the shop in his father's absence. Later tales made Terah a general of Nimrod.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-todros-ben-mose: Todros ben Moses Yom-Tob, also called Bondia, was a French physician at Cavaillon. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He worked in the second half of the fourteenth century. Steinschneider identified him with Todros of Cavaillon. In 1394 he made a Hebrew translation of a Latin fever treatise. The original was by Johanan ibn Masuyah, with commentary by Peter of Spain. His most valued translation treated digestive and purgative medicines. Its author was Arnold of Villeneuve.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trumpet-hazozer:
The trumpet, or hazozerah, must not be confused with the shofar, this article insists. Cyrus Adler and I. M. Casanowicz wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia, published in 1906. Later ages mixed up the two instruments' names. Hebrew Scripture keeps them clearly apart. Psalm 98 names shofar and trumpet side by side.

Numbers orders two trumpets of beaten silver. Solomon's Temple raised their number to 120. The Arch of Titus shows two trumpets again later. Josephus describes a tube nearly a yard long. It flared into a bell at the end. The trumpet served signals more than music. It called assemblies, broke camp, and sounded alarms. Priests blew it at offerings and new moons.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-voltaire-14730:
Voltaire was a French poet, historian, and essayist. He was born at Paris on November 21, 1694. Gotthard Deutsch wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His birth name was François Marie Arouet. He took the name Voltaire about 1718. He became a champion of free thought and liberty.

The entry stresses one sharp contradiction. Voltaire defended Jean Calas, a victim of Catholic fanaticism. Yet he also spread anti Jewish views. Two bad dealings with Jewish bankers fed his bias. In London a banker's failure cost him money. At Potsdam a bond scheme with Abraham Hirsch went wrong. The article weighs his tolerance against his prejudice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weil-simeon-hir: Simeon Hirsch Weil was a German scholar, son of Nethaneel Weil. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote this brief entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at Carlsruhe in the eighteenth century. He published his father's works on the Law. They include the Netib Hayyim and the Torat Netan'el. He also issued his father's legal answers. His own book retells the tale of Eldad ha Dani. A German translation accompanies that work, printed in 1769.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-william-of-norw:
William of Norwich was a boy at the center of a false charge. Joseph Jacobs wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In 1144 his family claimed Jews had killed him. He is the first alleged victim of the ritual murder myth. His body was found in Thorpe Wood near Norwich. It bore marks of thorns on the head.

His uncle accused the Jews at the next synod. No action was taken against the accused. A converted Jew named Theobald spread a wider tale. He claimed Jews chose a town by lot each Passover. Norwich, he said, was that year's lot. This is the first record of the blood accusation. The entry exposes how the myth began.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yudan-ben-simeo:
Yudan ben Simeon was a scholar of Palestine in the third century. Joseph Jacobs and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In the Babylon books he is called Judah ben Simeon. He was a peer of the great Johanan in that age.

Johanan passed on a rule of his on heir law. A talk that passed twixt the two is kept as well. Men oft cite their feud on writ law and mouth law. More of his tale words live on in the books. Many treat the birth of the world and its frame. Some treat the beasts and birds of the wide earth. One tale tells of the phoenix bird of old myth. It lives a thousand years and is born from an egg. Great beasts, he said, will feed the good in the next world.
lawrence-assorted-articles-1930:
Assorted Articles, published in 1930, the year of Lawrence's death, is his final collection of essays and journalism. It gathers pieces written for newspapers and magazines in his last years, on subjects from his childhood to censorship.

'Nottingham and the Mining Countryside' returns to the world of his youth and measures what industry did to it. 'The Novel' defends his art, and 'Pornography and Obscenity' attacks the censors who had hounded his work. The voice is tired, funny, and undefeated. Read as a farewell volume, it shows the range of a writer who argued with his whole age.
liutprand-works-wright-1930:
Liutprand, bishop of Cremona, was a Lombard courtier and envoy whose histories sparkle with wit and spite. F. A. Wright translated his works into English in 1930. The volume holds his three surviving books: the Antapodosis, the Deeds of Otto, and his famous report of an embassy to Constantinople.

The Antapodosis, his book of payback, tells the tangled wars of Italy and the empire in his century. The embassy report of 968 mocks the Byzantine court, its pomp, its food, and its emperor, in scenes still funny after a thousand years. Liutprand gossips, flatters, and settles scores on every page. No other tenth-century writer gives so lively a picture of courts East and West.
long-odds-pg2730:
This second Gutenberg version prints Haggard's Quatermain tale again. Its note points readers toward the earlier etext, number 1918. Quatermain narrated the story to Haggard in Yorkshire. The old hunter's son had just died when he told it.

He then departed for Africa with Curtis and Good. A white people, rumored all his life, drew the quest onward. Haggard doubts the party will ever return from it. One letter from the Tana River reported hardships and hopeful traces. Magnificent and unexampled discovery, the letter hopes, may still await. Haggard shrewdly suspects the quest will claim them permanently.
mathnawi-nicholson-vol-4-1930:
Book Four of Nicholson's Mathnawi came out in 1930. R. A. Nicholson's set gives Rumi's poem in Persian text with English dress. The Mathnawi is the great Sufi poem of Jalaluddin Rumi. His set of dress books is the stock one in English.

This book rounds out the pre-1931 parts of Nicholson's long work. The Mathnawi's six books of tales form a sea of Sufi lore. Each tale turns on love, loss, and the soul's hunt for God. Nicholson spent years of his life on the poem, and it shows in the care of each page.
mckeon-selections-medieval-philosophers-:
Richard McKeon published Volume 2 of Selections from Medieval Philosophers in 1930, editing and translating the texts himself. The anthology runs from Roger Bacon to William of Ockham. McKeon, a scholar at the University of Chicago, built the two volumes as a gateway to medieval thought.

Writers here include Bonaventure, Aquinas, Matthew of Aquasparta, and Duns Scotus, alongside Bacon and Ockham. The Scotus selections from his Oxford Commentary and Ockham's Quodlibetal Questions were the only public-domain English versions. McKeon chose texts that show medieval thinkers arguing, not just concluding. For a generation of students, this volume was their first real meeting with scholastic philosophy in its own words.
measure-for-measure-pg1530:
William Shakespeare's Measure for Measure is set in Vienna, in five acts. The contents list each scene, from the Duke's palace to a nunnery. A cast list names the men and women of the play.

Vincentio, the Duke, leaves Angelo as his deputy in act one. Isabella, sister to Claudio, pleads in the rooms of power. Mariana, once betrothed to Angelo, waits at her house in act four. Constable Elbow and Abhorson, the executioner, add low life to the court plot. A public place near the city gate hosts the last act. Mercy and strict law clash in each scene the contents map out.
meyerson-identity-reality-1930:
Identity and Reality, published in English in 1930 in Kate Loewenberg's translation, is Emile Meyerson's masterwork. It is a classic of French writing on science. Meyerson argues that science, beneath its variety, does one thing: it reduces difference to identity.

To explain, for science, is to show that the varied is the same. The falling stone and the moon obey one law; heat is motion; species are one life. Meyerson traces this drive through the history of physics and chemistry, and marks where reality resists it. His rationalism is deep and unfashionable in the best way. The book rewards slow reading.
newton-opticks-1730:
Isaac Newton's Opticks appears here in its fourth edition of 1730, the last Newton oversaw in his lifetime. First published in 1704, Opticks set out his experiments on light and color in English rather than Latin. The 1730 printing became the standard form of the work.

Newton showed that white light is a mix of colors, split by prisms and joined again by lenses. He studied thin films, diffraction, and the rings that bear his name, and pictured light as streams of tiny bodies. The closing Queries range from gravity to God's action in the world. The fourth edition preserves the founding text of physical optics as Newton finally left it.
ockham-de-sacramento-altaris-birch-1930:
T Bruce Birch published his edition and translation of William of Ockham's De Sacramento Altaris in 1930. Ockham, the English Franciscan thinker of the 1300s, wrote the work on the sacrament of the altar, the Eucharist. Birch printed the Latin text with facing English, a critical edition.

Ockham applied his famous razor, the rule against needless entities, to questions of quantity and presence in the sacrament. His nominalism, which denied real universals, shaped the argument throughout. The edition was the only complete work of Ockham in public-domain English. Scholars of medieval philosophy use it to study both his logic and his theology of the Eucharist at first hand.
openalex-w1989372330:
Nigel Beebe and co-authors traced an invasive mosquito's spread. Their paper appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2013. The Asian tiger mosquito is expanding its range worldwide. It can carry dengue and chikungunya viruses to new places. It was detected in Papua New Guinea's Fly River region.

Population genetics can reveal where invaders came from. The team used genetic markers to trace the mosquito's routes. Knowing sources helps target surveillance and control efforts. Early detection in new regions raises the stakes, they note. Genetic tracing turns specimens into invasion history. The study aids Pacific and Australian biosecurity planning.
openalex-w1997128330:
Lorenzo Galluzzi, Jose Manuel Bravo-San Pedro, Ilio Vitale and many colleagues wrote shared guidance on cell death. Their review appeared in Cell Death and Differentiation in 2015.
