It came from the Nomenclature Committee on Cell Death. The paper asks which parts of cell death are core and which are side effects.

The authors set out clear terms for the field. They defined accidental cell death, where harsh harm breaks cells at once. They also covered controlled forms of death that cells can adjust. The review sorted key traits from traits that only sometimes appear. Shared terms help labs compare results and avoid confusion. The guidance updated earlier advice from the same committee.
openalex-w2007354430:
Sijia Wang, Cecil Lewis, Mattias Jakobsson and colleagues mapped gene variation in Native American peoples. Their paper appeared in PLoS Genetics in 2007. They studied samples from North, Central and South America. The team asked how these populations differ and relate to each other.

They tested hundreds of gene markers in over four hundred people. The people came from twenty-four Native American populations. The team studied the data together with world samples. Their work traced patterns of diversity across the Americas. Such patterns bear on how people first spread through the continents. The data give a baseline for later health and history studies. Careful sampling across regions was central to the design.
openalex-w2091494430:
Wieland Meyer, Alexandra Castaneda, Stuart Jackson and colleagues typed a dangerous yeast across Ibero-America. Their paper appeared in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2003. The yeast, Cryptococcus neoformans, causes life-threatening infections. It occurs worldwide in patients and the environment. A research network was built to map it regionally.

The team collected hundreds of isolates from nine countries. Samples came from clinics, animals and the environment. Two fingerprint methods sorted them into types. Eight known molecular types were found. One type dominated, matching worldwide infection patterns. A smaller share belonged to related species types. Nine isolates showed an unusual gene pattern. Shared typing helps track outbreaks across borders.
openalex-w2102348230:
Marianne Sinka, Yasmin Rubio-Palis, Sylvie Manguin and colleagues mapped the main malaria mosquitoes of the Americas. Their paper appeared in Parasites and Vectors in 2010. Malaria rates in the Americas are the world's lowest. Strong mosquito control helped achieve that. Targeting control needs current maps of each vector species.

The team built a database of mosquito occurrence records. It covered the region's dominant vector species. Thousands of records came from twenty-five countries. Expert range maps were refined with specialist advice. Climate and environment data accompanied the records. Short profiles summarised each species' ecology and behaviour. The maps help programmes aim control where vectors thrive.
openalex-w2114151630:
Helen Sian Crosweller, Baneet Arora, Sarah Krystyna Brown and colleagues built a world database of giant volcanic eruptions. Their paper appeared in Journal of Applied Volcanology in 2012. Hazard planning needs records of past eruptions. The database covers the recent geological period. It forms part of a global volcano risk project.

The database lists nearly three thousand volcanoes. It holds over eighteen hundred eruption records. Each record gives size, date and rock type. Deposit volumes are included where known. A web search tool lets users filter by region. Data can be downloaded into spreadsheets freely. Many volcanoes still lack linked eruption records. The structure allows easy growth as data arrive.
openalex-w2289209130:
Kaustubh Adhikari, Tania Fontanil, Santiago Cal, and colleagues published this genome scan in Nature Communications in 2016. They searched admixed Latin American genomes for DNA loci shaping facial and scalp hair features. Hair appearance is strongly heritable and differs sharply between continental populations, yet earlier gene studies covered mostly Europeans and East Asians.

Latin Americans blend Native American, European, and African ancestry, offering fresh genetic ground. The scan links specific genome regions to traits like hair shape, color, and balding patterns in this population. Past work elsewhere had tied balding to the androgen receptor region and color to pigment genes. Comparing results across ancestries shows which hair traits evolved along separate paths in different peoples.
openalex-w2741980530:
Dan Joseph Stein, Carmen C. W. Lim, and Annelieke M. Roest lead the World Mental Health Survey collaborators on this 2017 study in BMC Medicine. It maps social anxiety disorder across countries. Most earlier data came from rich Western nations. This study pools twenty-eight community surveys with over one hundred forty thousand respondents, spanning rich, middle-income, and poor countries.

The disorder starts early in life almost everywhere and tends to persist. Prevalence runs highest in high-income countries and in the Americas and Western Pacific. Sufferers everywhere share similar profiles: younger, female, unmarried, with less education and income. Social anxiety also travels with other mental disorders in consistent patterns. Treatment rates are lowest where incomes are lowest. The authors conclude that national differences are real, but the disorder's basic shape is strikingly global.
openalex-w2743010030:
Sandra Milena González, Natalia A. Taborda, and María Teresa Rugeles reviewed CD8+ T cell subgroups in HIV infection in Frontiers in Immunology in 2017. Most people exposed to HIV repeatedly still become infected. A puzzling minority, called exposed seronegatives, never show infection despite repeated exposure. Among infected people, progress toward AIDS also varies enormously.

CD8+ T cells are immune cells that kill virus-infected cells, and their subgroups behave differently. The review examines what these subpopulations do during exposure and at each infection pattern. Some infected people stay healthy over ten years without treatment, while controllers keep virus nearly undetectable. Genetic traits, blocking antibodies, and microRNAs have all been tied to resistance. Understanding protective T cell patterns could guide vaccine design. The authors gather the evidence on which subgroups help and which fall short.
openalex-w2793038730:
M. Gabriela Kramer, Martín Masner, and Fernando A. Ferreira, with Robert M. Hoffman, assessed bacterial cancer therapy in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2018. Using bacteria against tumors has a long, interrupted history. In the 1800s, surgeon William Coley treated patients with bacterial preparations after noticing tumors shrink during infections. His work was shut down, and the field slept for half a century.

Today several bacterial species are again in development as cancer treatments. How well they work depends on the strain, its genetics, and its behavior inside tumors. This perspective updates the most promising results from animal models, alone and combined with other therapies. It weighs routes of administration and how bacteria interact with cancer cells. Modern mouse models, genetics, and imaging could sharpen the approach. The authors map what must be proven before bacterial therapy reaches patients broadly.
openalex-w2942506530:
David Bertioli, Jerry Jenkins, Josh Clevenger, and colleagues report the genome sequence of the cultivated peanut in Nature Genetics in 2019. The peanut, Arachis hypogaea, is a major food crop grown around the world. Its genome is a segmental allotetraploid, meaning it formed from the joining of two related genomes.

Reading a peanut genome is hard because its two subgenomes are very much alike. The team assembled the full sequence despite that challenge, working across many research centers. A complete reference genome gives breeders and biologists a map for finding genes behind traits such as yield and disease resistance. It also lets scientists study how the peanut's doubled genome evolved.
openalex-w2992752930:
André Devaux, Jean-Pierre Goffart, Athanasios Petsakos, and colleagues wrote this book chapter, published in 2019. It argues that sustainable potato farming systems can strengthen global food security. Feeding a growing world population well, with the same or fewer resources, is the central challenge they address.

Food security, they note, has four parts: food supply, access to food, food quality and use, and stability over time. The potato fits all four, thanks to its wide spread and strong demand in poorer countries facing hunger and malnutrition. The chapter first surveys world hunger and farm growth. It then reviews the potato's importance and how its farming systems can be made more durable.
openalex-w3005400930:
Marc Zapatka, Ivan Borozan, Daniel Brewer, and colleagues published this study in Nature Genetics in 2020. It maps links between viruses and human cancers across the full Pan-Cancer genome project. The data cover more than two thousand six hundred cancers of thirty-eight types.

Three separate analysis pipelines searched the genome and gene-readout data for viral traces, and their agreed results were kept. Viruses turned up in hundreds of samples, most often known cancer-linked ones such as Epstein-Barr virus, hepatitis B virus, and human papillomavirus. In head and neck cancer, the virus and key driver mutations rarely appeared together. Viral DNA woven into the genome also matched local changes in gene copy numbers.
openalex-w3043746530:
Camila Perera, Alicia Salamanca-Sanabria, Joyce Caballero-Bernal, and colleagues published this methods paper in Conflict and Health in 2020. Its title states its thesis: no implementation without cultural adaptation. The team describes a process for adapting simple psychological therapies for use in humanitarian crises.

They applied a four-step process to a World Health Organization program called Problem Management Plus. The target users were displaced Venezuelans and Colombians living in Colombia. Steps ran from a rapid review of local population traits, through screening the manual for parts needing change, to local consultation and outside expert review. Cultural fit is widely praised but rarely spelled out as a method. This paper supplies that missing recipe.
openalex-w3081768530:
H. Fabrice Dannon, Ayitondji Dannon, Ouorou Douro-Kpindou, and colleagues wrote this review in the Journal of Cotton Research in 2020. It examines the fungus Beauveria bassiana as a living pesticide for cotton pests. In Benin, chemical sprays against cotton caterpillars have contaminated farm land, pushing growers to seek alternatives.

The fungus infects insects and has shown killing power against several pest species, but its record on cotton caterpillars was thin. The review covers how the fungus attacks, how it interacts with plants, other insects, soil, and microbes, and what control programs tried over the last decade. It weighs the gains and limits of fungal sprays and the hurdles to selling them. Application methods and target pests get special attention.
openalex-w3119128530:
Francesco Schettini, Núria Chic, Fara Brasó-Maristany, and colleagues published this study in npj Breast Cancer in 2021. It profiles HER2-low breast cancer, tumors with faint levels of the HER2 protein but no gene amplification. The group drew little attention until new drugs began to work on it.

Fresh antibody-drug conjugates aimed at HER2 show strong activity in these supposedly HER2-negative cancers. Yet the clinical and molecular traits of HER2-low disease were still unclear. The team gathered case data on symptoms, tissue features, and gene activity patterns from a standard fifty-gene test. Their portrait helps doctors recognize this in-between category and judge who may gain from the new drugs. It marks a shift in how breast cancer is split.
openalex-w4210980530:
Bekele Shiferaw, Melinda Smale, Hans-Joachim Braun, and colleagues review wheat's role in feeding the world, in Food Security in 2013. Wheat supplies about a fifth of all dietary calories and protein on Earth. Demand in developing regions keeps climbing, and those regions grow about half of the world crop. The Green Revolution from the nineteen sixties raised yields sharply and held food prices down.

Modern wheat varieties spread faster than almost any farm innovation before them. Yet yield growth has since slowed, and the old methods caused environmental damage of their own. Replacing ageing varieties with better ones is a central challenge. The authors argue that future gains must come from sustainable intensification, not a simple repeat of the past.
openalex-w4211229530:
Ulf Gustafsson, Michael Scott, Martin Hübner, and colleagues present the 2018 ERAS Society recommendations for colorectal surgery, in the World Journal of Surgery. ERAS, or Enhanced Recovery After Surgery, is a package of care steps before, during, and after an operation. Used together, the steps help patients recover faster with fewer complications. These guidelines cover planned, or elective, surgery on the colon and rectum.

This is the fourth updated edition of the society's colorectal guideline. The authors searched the medical literature for each step in the pathway. They graded the evidence behind every recommendation using the GRADE system. Best evidence came from careful trials, pooled analyses, and large patient cohorts. The result is a shared standard that surgical teams can audit.
openalex-w4226083230:
R. Abbott and the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA collaborations inferred the population of merging compact binaries from gravitational waves, in Physical Review X in 2023. Their catalogue, GWTC-3, covers the first three observing runs of the detectors. It holds signals from three merger classes: two black holes, two neutron stars, and one of each. The question is how often each class merges across the universe.

The team estimated merger rates for neutron star pairs and mixed pairs within wide ranges. Black hole mergers, they found, grow more frequent at greater distances, looking back in time. Their local rate is pinned down more tightly than the others. Such population figures test how massive stars live, die, and pair up.
openalex-w7208704330:
Wilson Correa Borges and three colleagues examine the political and electoral role of the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God in today's Brazil, working through its link with the Republicanos party. Their historical and documentary study draws on electoral court data, parliamentary research, party documents, and the church's own institutional publications. The guiding question is how this church-party tie expanded the party and shaped a distinct kind of religious presence in Brazilian party politics.

The authors read the case through classic thinkers on power and religion as well as recent work on faith, politics, and the reshaping of the Brazilian right. Their material lets readers follow the mechanics behind headlines: how a large neo-Pentecostal church organizes voters, candidates, and discourse inside a national party. For students of religion and politics, the study maps one of the clearest cases of the two worlds merging.
openalex-w7214147330: Ester Kamile da Silva Leite and Liane de Rosso Giuliani report a case on diagnosing an inborn error of metabolism. The sample's abstract sets out the condition group and the study aim, but the individual case details do not appear in the excerpt. These genetic disorders, mostly enzyme defects, can block a metabolic pathway and mimic sepsis in emergencies, above all in newborns. The article aims to show why screening before symptoms appear is needed to prevent related complications. On that limited evidence, this record is flagged as thin.
openalex-w7215034230:
Maria Jaqueline Vieira Santos and Kyrlian Bartira Bortolozzi listened, in a 2026 qualitative study, to older adults who had gone to school in rural Brazil. Reanalyzing semi-structured interviews with four people aged between sixty and eighty-one, they traced several threads. They followed the material and family conditions that shaped schooling, the uses of reading and writing across a lifetime, and the knowledge built outside school walls.

Schooling in these lives was marked by scarce school supply, long distances, mixed-age classes, and work woven together with study, yet the narrators valued education highly. Difficulties with reading and writing coexisted with rich social uses of language and knowledge gained in family, work, and daily life. Interrupted schooling, the authors conclude, did not mean interrupted learning: the learning continued for a lifetime, in places no school record captures.
openalex-w7215106830:
Cintya Gabryelle da Silva de Rezende led a 2026 review on two underdiagnosed conditions of old dogs: osteoarthritis and cognitive dysfunction. Searching four databases for studies from 2017 to 2025, the team kept fifteen sources on how planned preventive check-ups can catch these conditions. Owners and vets alike often dismiss their signs as just aging, the authors note, which is exactly how they stay hidden.

Active clinical screening routines reveal far higher rates of both than routine formal records show. Cognitive dysfunction was linked with greater muscle and bone damage alongside it, a sign the two are related. Veterinary physiotherapy stands out as a treatment path after early osteoarthritis diagnosis. Building tested screening tools for cognition, pain, and joint mobility into every geriatric visit, the authors conclude, is vital to cut underdiagnosis and protect old dogs' quality of life.
openalex-w7221065430:
Giovanna Azevedo Rodrigues and Marcelo Caixeta propose a new way to sort borderline personality disorder by its causes, in a 2026 theoretical essay from a Brazilian psychiatric hospital. Patients with this disorder differ widely and respond unevenly to treatment, and the authors argue that two sources of instability explain much of that variety.

One form, called familiopathic, is kept alive by a harmful family environment still acting on the patient, so family work matters more than medicine alone. The other, thymopathic, grows from a built-in disorder of mood regulation, where they hypothesize a slow response to lithium. Mixed cases combine both. The essay offers a classification method and testable predictions, while admitting the drug claims outrun present evidence.
parrington-main-currents-vol-3-1930:
Parrington died before he could fully finish his history, and the third volume came out in 1930 from his notes. It covers the years after the Civil War, when realism began to push back against polite, genteel taste. Mark Twain and other plain-spoken writers lead the story.

The volume shows authors turning toward city life, business power, and the hard facts of a changing country. Parrington praises writers who faced those facts and faults those who hid behind pretty manners. Even unfinished, the book completes one of the boldest surveys of American thought ever written.
perjurd-free-mason-detected-1730:
The Perjur'd Free Mason Detected appeared in London in 1730, the same year as Prichard's Masonry Dissected. It answers Prichard directly. The author signs himself a Free Mason and writes in righteous anger at the betrayal of the fraternity's secrets, calling the exposer perjured for breaking his obligation.

The pamphlet is the earliest Masonic counter-pamphlet in print. It defends the Craft's honor and disputes the exposé's claims point by point. As the fraternity's first printed self-defense, it holds a pivotal place. The quarrel shows Masonry learning to fight in the new arena of cheap print. Both pamphlets together stage the birth of a very modern argument about secrecy.
phrenology-article-of-the-foreign-quarte: A hosted sample showing only the Google Books digital-copy notice pages that precede this scan, with no page of the work itself visible. The catalogue record names the piece as Phrenology, an article of the Foreign Quarterly Review, attributed to Richard Chenevix and dated 1830. It notes the copy's source as the YA Pamphlet Collection of the Library of Congress, a great gathering of early nineteenth-century pamphlets.
pickthall-meaning-glorious-koran-1930:
Marmaduke Pickthall was a British novelist who embraced Islam and spent years in India in Muslim service. His Meaning of the Glorious Koran, published in 1930, was the first Quran translation by a native English-speaking Muslim. It ranks among the two most widely used English renderings ever made.

Pickthall aimed at a plain, dignified English that echoes the Arabic without copying its form too closely. He adds short notes and a life of the Prophet by way of introduction for new readers. Muslim readers praised the version for joining sound English style to loyalty toward the source text.
plos-pbio-0020030:
Simon K. Cheng, Felix Olale, Ali H. Brivanlou, and their group untangled a signaling path in PLOS Biology in 2004. TGFβ signals guide how embryos grow. A protein family called EGF-CFC helps some of those signals reach their targets, and a blocker called Lefty can shut them down.

The team shows that Lefty works by jamming the EGF-CFC helpers. It stops some TGFβ signals, such as Nodal, while leaving others alone. That fine control matters in the early embryo, where signal strength sets body axes. The work explains one way embryos keep strong growth signals on a short leash, and why losing that leash can distort development.
plos-pbio-0020130:
Patrick Seale, Jeff Ishibashi, Anthony Scimè, and co-workers tested stem cells from hurt muscle in PLOS Biology in 2004. A marker protein called Pax7 is the sign of muscle stem cells. The team worked with a blood-linked stem cell group found in injured muscle and asked what Pax7 does there.

Adding Pax7 was enough to steer those cells toward becoming muscle, and without it they could not take that path. So Pax7 is both needed and sufficient for the switch, a strong claim in stem cell work. The result points to a master control for muscle fate. If that control can be used safely, it might one day help repair muscle lost to injury or disease.
plos-pbio-0020230:
Margaret J. Mackinnon and Andrew F. Read modeled a hard trade-off in malaria in PLOS Biology in 2004. Malaria parasites grow inside red blood cells, and the immune system fights them. The authors ask how that fight shapes the evolution of the parasite's virulence, meaning how sick it makes the host.

Their model suggests strong immunity can favor tougher, faster-growing parasites, since only those thrive under attack. That is a warning for vaccine design. A vaccine that cuts symptoms without blocking growth might, in theory, select for more harmful strains. The paper does not claim this has happened. It shows the risk is real enough that malaria programs should track parasite change as vaccines roll out.
plos-pbio-0020330:
Konrad P. Körding, Izumi Fukunaga, Ian S. Howard, and their team applied economics logic to movement in PLOS Biology in 2004. In economics, a utility function scores how much each outcome is worth. The authors ask whether the brain, while controlling a reach or a step, acts as if it used such a score.

By studying how people adjust to forces and errors, they infer the hidden costs the motor system seems to weigh, like effort and accuracy. If movement follows a utility rule, then many odd habits of motion fall into place. The approach also gives engineers a principled way to model human control. That helps prosthetics and robots that must move with people, not just near them.
plos-pone-0000030:
Markus Ralser, Gino Heeren, Michael Breitenbach, and co-authors corrected an old assumption about a rare enzyme disease in 2006. Triose phosphate isomerase deficiency damages blood and nerve cells. The faulty enzyme was long blamed on catalytic inactivity, a broken working site that can no longer do its chemical job.

The team showed the real cause is different: altered dimerization. The enzyme works in pairs, and the mutant versions pair up wrongly, which wrecks their stability while the chemistry itself can still run. That correction matters for any future therapy, because fixing a pairing problem is a different task from fixing a dead active site. Small distinction, large consequences for patients.
plos-pone-0000130:
Nicholas Valmas and Paul R. Ebert published this pest control study in PLOS ONE in 2006. It compares fumigants, gases used to kill insects in stored grain, along with a phosphine booster. To run the tests safely, the authors built a new containment chamber for making concentrated phosphine gas.

Phosphine is effective but dangerous to handle, and insects keep evolving resistance to it. The authors measure how toxic the fumigants and the booster are under controlled conditions. Safer, well-measured testing helps the grain industry protect stored harvests while keeping workers safe and staying ahead of resistant pests.
plos-pone-0000230:
Bernard Le Foll, Carrie Wertheim, and Steven R. Goldberg published this addiction study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Tobacco is clearly addictive in humans. Yet experts long argued over whether nicotine by itself makes laboratory animals work to get more, as truly addictive drugs do. The authors tested nicotine's reinforcing power in non-human primates.

The title states the result: nicotine showed high reinforcing efficacy in the primates, meaning the animals worked hard to obtain it. That settles a long controversy in the authors' favor: nicotine alone can drive drug-seeking. The finding underpins tobacco regulation and the design of quitting aids.
plos-pone-0000330:
Sophie Agaugué, Laure Perrin-Cocon, Patrice André, and colleagues published this hepatitis C study in PLOS ONE in 2007. The hepatitis C virus travels in blood partly as lipo-viro-particles, virus joined with fat particles. Using particles from chronically infected patients, the authors show they interfere with TLR4 signaling in dendritic cells, damping an immune alarm pathway.

A virus that quiets the alarm can persist for decades, as hepatitis C does. The paper identifies one of its silencing tricks in real patient material. Understanding that interference helps explain chronic infection and suggests where therapies might restore the alarm.
plos-pone-0000430:
Lilian Ricaud and colleagues exposed the plant Arabidopsis to gamma rays and mapped its responses, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Gamma rays damage DNA, and plants, which cannot flee radiation, must repair or adapt. The team tracked ATM-mediated responses: ATM is a master protein that senses DNA damage and switches on defense programs, in both gene activity and development.

Arabidopsis is the standard lab plant, so its damage responses stand in for those of crops and wild plants. Knowing which genes ATM controls after irradiation helps explain how plants survive radiation in soil and seed. The work also feeds space biology, where radiation is a constant hazard for growing food.
plos-pone-0000530:
Richard P. Meisel and Stephen W. Schaeffer tracked how fruit fly chromosome arrangements pass through egg formation, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Drosophila pseudoobscura carries chromosomal arrangements, flipped segments called inversions, whose frequencies vary in nature. The team studied meiotic transmission: whether arrangements are passed on fairly or gain an edge during meiosis.

Unfair transmission, called meiotic drive, can spread a chromosome variant even if it harms the fly. Testing for drive explains otherwise puzzling patterns in wild populations. Inversions in this species are a classic system from the early days of population genetics. Modern transmission tests refine what the pioneers could only infer.
plos-pone-0000630:
Joanne Miles, Jennifer A. Mitchell, Lyubomira Chakalova and colleagues mapped gene activity around the human beta-globin locus for PLOS ONE in 2007. The locus holds the globin genes used to build hemoglobin. Strong links were already known between transcription, the copying of DNA into RNA, and chemical marks on histones, the proteins DNA wraps around.

Using a method called RNA FISH in red-blood-cell precursors, the team showed copying also runs through the stretches between genes. They tracked how that intergenic transcription and the locus's epigenetic profile change with the cell cycle and development. The picture is of a whole region switching on in a coordinated, timed way.
plos-pone-0000730:
Esmeralda A. J. M. Soares, André F. A. Santos, Thatiana M. Sousa and colleagues compared how two HIV subtypes gain drug resistance, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Subtype C is the most prevalent HIV-1 form worldwide, dominating countries with the highest HIV rates. Few studies, though, had evaluated how antiretroviral therapy performs against it. Southern Brazil was the first developing region to offer free, universal therapy.

That setting lets the authors compare resistance acquisition in subtypes B and C under real treatment programmes. If subtypes resist differently, treatment guidelines written for subtype B may fit subtype C poorly. The comparison matters most where subtype C is common and resources are thin.
plos-pone-0000830:
Anne Bergeron, Mahdi Belcaid, Grieg F. Steward and colleagues offered a divide-and-conquer plan for sequencing whole microbial communities. In environmental sequencing projects, DNA from an entire community is fragmented and sequenced, with goals including reconstructing partial or complete genomes of its members. In communities rich in species, a large fraction of the data resists assembly, because similar fragments from many species tangle together.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE method enriches the data by splitting the problem into parts it can handle. Ocean and soil samples hold most of Earth's microbes, almost none cultured. Better assembly turns raw fragments into genomes, letting science name and study organisms it cannot grow.
plos-pone-0000930:
Anna Okvist, Sofia Johansson, Alexander Kuzmin and colleagues studied a gene control system in the brains of people with alcohol dependence, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Long term drinking reshapes the brain, and those changes involve many genes at once. The NF-kappaB family of factors switches whole sets of genes on and off.

The team asked whether that system is dysregulated, thrown off balance, in chronic alcoholics. Changes there could help explain lasting cognitive problems tied to drinking. Brain tissue studies like this are hard to do and rarely direct. They still offer the closest look at what years of alcohol do inside the human brain.
plos-pone-0001030:
Satoru Yamagishi, Yoshihisa Koyama, Taiichi Katayama and colleagues built a cell model of inclusion bodies seen in inherited ALS, in PLOS ONE in 2007. In familial ALS tied to mutant SOD1, neurons and astrocytes grow hyaline inclusions, glassy clumps holding the faulty protein. How those clumps form was not known.

The team induced similar inclusions in vitro by stressing the cell's protein handling system, in cells carrying the ALS linked mutation. A lab model lets researchers test what starts clumping and what might stop it. Inclusions are a visible mark of the disease process, so a model of their birth is a useful tool.
plos-pone-0001130:
Diseases move at different speeds in a mouse and in a human, and body size is part of the reason. Jessica Cable, Brian Enquist, and Melanie Moses took up this scaling problem in a 2007 PLOS ONE article on the allometry of host-pathogen interactions. Allometry is the study of how body traits change with size.

The authors examine how body size and metabolic rate shape the pace of infection and disease progression across species. That matters for epidemiology and for a practical worry in medicine: how to translate results from small lab animals to people. A sound scaling rule makes animal studies more useful.
plos-pone-0001230:
Nigersaurus taqueti was a sauropod dinosaur that fed at ground level, cropping low plants like a lawn mower. Paul Sereno and colleagues described its skull from Early Cretaceous fossils in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The fossils document, for the first time, the cranial anatomy of a rebbachisaurid sauropod, Nigersaurus's family.

Its adaptations for ground-level herbivory are extreme: a wide, squared-off muzzle and batteries of small teeth among them. The authors argue these features challenge current ideas about feeding function and strategy among sauropods. Nigersaurus has become a textbook example of how far a plant-eating dinosaur's skull could specialize.
plos-pone-0001330:
Dental pulp from animals infected with prion diseases can carry infectivity, raising a worry for dentistry. Nadège Bourvis and colleagues assessed the risk of transmitting sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in endodontic practice, root canal work, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The concern is that the disease could spread to patients through reused instruments when prion inactivation is inadequate.

The authors model that risk in the absence of adequate prion inactivation. Prions resist standard sterilization, which makes the question more than theoretical. Their assessment helps dental regulators weigh single-use instruments and cleaning standards.
plos-pone-0001430:
Daniela Contu and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on the roots of people on the island of Sardinia. The island has high rates of some immune ills, such as type 1 diabetes. Knowing its gene past is key to sound disease gene hunts there. The team read markers on the male Y chromosome across the island.

Their data point to roots that predate farming on the island. The people look gene alike in some ways, yet diverse in others. That mix shapes how gene scans should be planned there. It also adds a chapter to the tale of how island peoples formed in Europe.
plos-pone-0001530:
Xinhua Yu and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a DNA variant and multiple sclerosis. This ill harms nerve fibers, and risk runs in part through families. A variant in the DNA of the cell power units had been eyed as a risk factor. The team tested it in six European case control groups.

They report the variant does raise the risk of the disease in their data. A power unit link fits the nerve harm, since nerves hunger for energy. Each firm risk variant adds a clue to how the ill starts. It also helps sort which patients share a common root cause.
plos-pone-0001630:
Augustin Zoungrana, Boubacar Coulibaly, Ali Sié, and their co-authors ran a clinical trial in Burkina Faso on a new pairing of malaria drugs. Their 2008 PLOS ONE research article tested methylene blue combined with either artesunate or amodiaquine against uncomplicated falciparum malaria. The team looked at both safety and how well the treatment worked.

Existing drug pairs based on artemisinin are the standard cure, but safe, effective, and cheap backups are still needed as the parasite adapts. Methylene blue was the first man-made malaria drug ever used, and newer studies had hinted it could help again. The full text gives the trial design, the patient results, and the side effects seen. Trials like this tell health programs which drug pairs deserve wider use.
plos-pone-0001730:
Julia J. Day, James A. Cotton, and Timothy G. Barraclough studied how cichlid fishes multiplied in Lake Tanganyika in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Why some groups and regions hold far more species than others is a basic question in evolutionary biology. Answering it needs densely sampled family trees and good study systems. The lake's cichlids, famous for their variety, offer both.

The authors examined the tempo and mode of diversification: how fast new species arose, and whether the pace changed over time. The full text gives the family tree, the timing estimates, and the pattern of bursts or steady growth. Lake radiations like this are natural tests of how new species form, and Tanganyika is the oldest of the great African lakes.
plos-pone-0001830:
Michael L. Clawson, Juergen A. Richt, Thierry Baron, and their co-authors tested cattle genes for links to atypical mad cow disease in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Atypical bovine spongiform encephalopathies are recently recognized prion diseases of cattle. They are rare, with about 30 cases identified worldwide at the time.

The team tested prion gene haplotypes, inherited variants of PRNP, for an association with atypical BSE and report an association. The full text gives the cattle cases and the haplotype statistics. If certain PRNP types predispose cattle to spontaneous prion disease, surveillance and breeding programs gain a genetic risk marker for a feared food-safety disease.
plos-pone-0001930:
David Whitaker, Dennis Levi, and Graeme Kennedy tested how the eye judges a change in a moving object's path, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Vision guides how we reach for, catch, or dodge things in motion. A key skill is spotting when a moving object veers off its line, by even a small amount.

The team measured how well people spot that veer, and how the skill builds as the object is watched over time. Their title gives the theme: what the eye gleans across time sets how fine the judgment can be. Results of this sort ground models of motion vision used in science and in display design.
plos-pone-0002030:
Ali Kinkhabwala and Calin Guet shuffled gene switches to crack their code, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. A promoter is the DNA stretch that sets when a gene turns on, by adding up signals from many binding proteins. Reading that code at single promoters is key to grasping how cell networks are wired.

The pair built synthetic promoters by shuffling parts, then watched how each mix behaved. Shuffled versions act as controlled tests of the code, free of the clutter of natural genes. Rules learned this way can guide the design of gene circuits with set behavior.
plos-pone-0002130:
Maria Tsirigotis, Mitchell Baldwin, Matthew Tang, and co-authors traced a cell signal that worsens damage from faulty proteins, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Some brain diseases are caused by proteins with an expanded stretch of the amino acid glutamine, called polyglutamine repeats. How these proteins kill cells was not well understood when the study began.

The team showed that the harm from expanded polyglutamine proteins runs mainly through a stress signal switch called p38MAPK. Blocking that pathway reduced the cell damage in their tests. The work points to a possible drug target for a group of diseases that includes Huntington's disease. In those diseases, slowing cell death would matter a great deal.
plos-pone-0002230:
Laith Abu-Raddad, Amalia Magaret, Connie Celum, and co-authors weighed the role of genital herpes in Africa's HIV epidemic, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Observational studies had long suggested that herpes simplex virus type 2, the usual cause of genital herpes, helps HIV spread. At the time, herpes vaccines were in development and trials were testing whether treating herpes with acyclovir could slow HIV.

The authors assessed how large a share of HIV infections herpes may have driven. They conclude herpes played a bigger part than any other sexually transmitted infection in raising HIV prevalence in Africa. That ranking shapes where prevention money can do the most work.
plos-pone-0002330:
Matthias Möllenbeck and co-authors followed the path a ciliate takes to unscramble one of its genes, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Some single-celled ciliates rebuild their genomes as they develop a working nucleus. In the process, internal eliminated sequences are cut out and the coding pieces of genes, sometimes stored in scrambled order, are rejoined.

The team traced the pathway used to detangle a scrambled gene step by step. A cell that can cut, shuffle, and reseal its own DNA with precision performs a feat of natural editing. Understanding its rules informs both genome evolution and the design of DNA-based computing.
plos-pone-0002430:
In 2008, Lynn and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Francis C. Lynn, Lidia Sanchez, Ramon Gomis, and others. Its subject is identification of the bHLH Factor Math6 as a Novel Component of the Embryonic Pancreas Transcriptional Network. Basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factors play important roles in differentiation processes during embryonic development of vertebrates.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002530:
A research team led by Owusu-Agyei reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Seth Owusu-Agyei, Kwaku Poku Asante, Ruth Owusu, and others. Its subject is an Open Label, Randomised Trial of Artesunate+Amodiaquine, Artesunate+Chlorproguanil-Dapsone and Artemether-Lumefantrine for the Treatment of Uncomplicated Malaria. Artesunate+amodiaquine (AS+AQ) and artemether-lumefantrine (AL) are now the most frequently recommended first line treatments for uncomplicated malaria in Africa.

Artesunate+chlorproguanil-dapsone (AS+CD) was a potential alternative for treatment of uncomplicated malaria. Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002630:
Ursula Schwab led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was triacylglycerol fatty acid composition in Diet-Induced weight loss in subjects with abnormal glucose metabolism – the GENOBIN study. Authorship is credited in the record to Ursula Schwab and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. The effect of weight loss on different plasma lipid subclasses at the molecular level is unknown. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002730:
Tatiana N. Badaeva led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was genetic variation and de novo mutations in the parthenogenetic caucasian rock lizard darevskia unisexualis. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Tatiana N. Badaeva, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Unisexual all-female lizards of the genus Darevskia that are well adapted to various habitats are known to reproduce normally by true parthenogenesis. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002830:
Jeffrey A. Lyon led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was protection induced by plasmodium falciparum MSP1 42 is Strain-Specific, antigen and adjuvant dependent, and correlates with antibody responses. The catalog record names Jeffrey A. Lyon first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Vaccination with Plasmodium falciparum MSP1 42 /complete Freund's adjuvant (FA) followed by MSP1 42 /incomplete FA is the only known regimen that protects Aotus. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002930:
Nathan Morrell, Philipp Leucht, Ludan Zhao and co-authors found a way to deliver Wnt protein in the body in 2008. Wnt signals drive strong growth and repair effects that could have real medical value. Yet there were no specific Wnt boosters and no method to deliver purified Wnt protein in a living animal.

Wnt proteins carry lipid tags needed for their activity, which makes them hard to handle. Packaging Wnt in liposomes, tiny fat bubbles, kept it active, as the title reports. Published in PLOS ONE, that step opens tests of Wnt therapy for repair in living tissue.
plos-pone-0003030:
Esteban Gurzov, Fernanda Ortis, Latifa Bakiri and co-authors studied the factor JunB in pancreatic beta cells in 2008. In type 1 diabetes, cytokines help drive beta cell death by rewiring gene networks. The AP-1 transcription factor family is a key regulator of inflammation and cell death in that setting.

The team evaluated JunB, one AP-1 subunit. Its title-level finding is that JunB inhibits endoplasmic reticulum stress and apoptosis in beta cells. Published in PLOS ONE, a protective factor inside insulin-making cells is a candidate worth guarding in early diabetes. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003130: Pradeep K. Gupta and colleagues published a PLOS ONE study in 2008 on anthrax lethal factor, one of the toxins of the anthrax bacterium. The title states its narrow question: what role the amino acids at the start of the protein play in how potent the toxin is. No abstract beyond the title was supplied, so no findings are stated here.
plos-pone-0003230:
Lidia Ruiz, Magali Traskine, Irene Ferrer and colleagues characterize the p53 response to senescence in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. P53 activation can trigger various outcomes, among them reversible growth arrest or cellular senescence, the permanent stop of division. It is a live debate whether these outcomes are influenced by quantitative or qualitative mechanisms. The relative contribution of p53 to Ras-induced senescence is also at issue.

Readers follow an attempt to define what kind of p53 response a stress signal produces. Senescence is a barrier against cancer, so its triggers matter for therapy. Knowing whether dose or quality decides the outcome changes how drugs might be used.
plos-pone-0003330:
Paul E. Dux and René Marois study the attentional blink in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The attentional blink is the impaired ability to detect the second of two targets. The targets appear in a rapid serial visual presentation stream of distractors. The blink occurs if the second target appears within two hundred to six hundred milliseconds of the first. The team examined whether the ability to inhibit distractors predicts this effect.

The title reports that distractor inhibition predicts individual differences in the attentional blink. Readers learn why some people miss the second target far more than others. Individual differences can reveal the mechanism behind a classic attention limit.
plos-pone-0003430:
Kumar Selvarajoo and co-authors modeled alarm signals inside immune cells in this 2008 paper. Surface sensors called Toll-like receptors spot molecules from germs. They pass signals through a web of pathways toward the nucleus. A change in one molecule can reroute signals through that web.

The team treated each junction in the web as a traffic point. Their model showed how signal flow shifts when one route changes. That redistribution can alter which genes the cell turns on. The work helps explain why one sensor can cause many outcomes. The same junction logic may apply well beyond this one set of receptors.
plos-pone-0003530:
Hugues Dardente and co-authors added a part to the mammal body clock in this 2008 paper. The circadian clock runs on loops of genes switching each other off and on. Changes after proteins are made control their traffic and breakdown. Those steps are keys to keeping daily time.

The team implicated an F-box protein, FBXL21, in pacemaker function. F-box proteins help tag worn proteins for removal. Clearing clock proteins at the right pace sets rhythm speed. The finding gives chronobiology a new gear to study. A clock that runs at the wrong speed disrupts sleep and health in many ways.
plos-pone-0003630:
Jason D. Fridley published this ecology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It places plant invasions in the eastern United States in a world context. Fridley asked where the invading plants came from and why some floras supply so many invaders.

He compared the alien flora of the eastern states with plant patterns across the globe. The sources traced back in large part to the forests of Asia and the fields of Europe. By splitting mere alien plants from fast-spreading invaders, the study sharpens the who, where, and why questions of invasion science.
plos-pone-0003730:
Katia Cortese, Macarena Sahores, Chris D. Madsen, and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The urokinase receptor, uPAR, sits on cell surfaces and is common on malignant tumors. It works with partners that help break down tissue barriers. How the receptor cycles on and off the surface was the question.

The team found uPAR is taken into cells and recycled back without using clathrin or LRP-1, two usual routes. This steady traffic runs on its own pathway. The alternate plan helps explain how tumors keep this aggressive marker on display at the surface.
plos-pone-0003830:
Tiaza Bem, Pierre Meyrand, Pascal Branchereau, and colleagues published this neuroscience modeling paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. Networks of rhythmically active cells drive many body functions, from breathing to swimming. The team studied networks linked by fast inhibition and by electrical synapses, which pass current directly.

Their model and hybrid networks could settle into several different stable activity patterns. Nothing in the wiring or settings changed between patterns; brief inputs switched the network from one to another. The multi-stability shows a single wiring diagram producing many behaviors. Real brain circuits may use the same trick to switch tasks.
plos-pone-0003930:
Martin Hromada, Marcin Antczak, Thomas J. Valone, and co-authors watched how shrikes pick where to settle in 2008. Animals often settle near rivals, a choice that defies standard habitat theory. Two ideas could explain it, the authors note. Birds may gain safety or other benefits from a rival's presence.

Or the settlers may copy clues from other species that are doing well. Their PLOS ONE study tested social information use between species in shrikes. The work shows animals read other species' success when choosing home ground. Such copying links species' fates more tightly than once thought.
plos-pone-0004030:
Sarah Cherian, David A. Forbes, Angus G. Cook, and co-authors studied anemia in refugee children in 2008. Hepcidin is the body's key controller of iron balance. It rises with inflammation and some infections. Its role in children with iron deficiency anemia was unclear.

Their PLOS ONE article measured hepcidin alongside infection and inflammation markers. The children studied were pediatric refugees in a cross-sectional design. Links among the measures clarify why iron treatment sometimes fails. Inflammation can lock iron away even when diet supplies enough. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004130:
Jean-Louis Herrmann and colleagues published this clinical study in PLOS ONE in 2009. New blood tests that measure interferon gamma, a signal released by T cells, had opened fresh ways to detect hidden tuberculosis infection in adults. Far fewer studies had tried these tests in children, and none had been done in France.

The team followed how interferon gamma responses change over time in children being checked for tuberculosis. Tracking the response, rather than taking one reading, matters because children can be hard to diagnose with standard tests. The paper adds child-specific evidence on a test that doctors increasingly use to find latent infection.
plos-pone-0004230:
Matthias Becker and colleagues published this lung cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The team had already built a transgenic mouse model of non-small-cell lung cancer driven by the RAF oncogene. Here they ask whether those tumours need Bmi1, a factor that stem cells use to renew themselves.

They bred the cancer model with mice lacking Bmi1 and watched tumour initiation and growth. They report that Bmi1 is required for the growth of RAF-driven lung tumours. A gene that a tumour cannot grow without is a candidate target for future drugs. The model lets researchers test such questions without patients.
plos-pone-0004330:
Andrew Collins and colleagues published this exercise study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The team had shown before that exercise benefits stress resistance and coping. They had also reported that epigenetic changes, chemical marks on DNA that tune gene activity, are involved in forming memories of stressful events.

Putting the two lines together, they studied how exercise helps the brain answer stress. They link the benefit to stronger epigenetic marking and gene activity in the dentate gyrus, a memory-forming part of the hippocampus. Exercise, on this account, literally re-marks the brain's stress machinery. The work ties a daily habit to changes deep in the memory system.
plos-pone-0004430:
Spots of melanoma that spread to new sites decide how long a patient lives, and Sharon Huang, Marlene Darfler, Michael Nicholl, and co-authors hunted for protein clues in PLOS ONE in 2009. They worked with melanoma samples kept in paraffin blocks, the standard way hospitals store tissue. Such archives are plentiful, but reading proteins from them is hard.

Using a method called LC/MS, the team measured proteins in the stored tumors in a precise, counted way. They compared tumors by whether the cancer had spread. The goal was to find protein markers tied to that spread. Markers like these could one day help doctors spot risky melanomas early and choose stronger treatment for the patients who need it most.
plos-pone-0004530:
Young ravens forage in gangs near big communal roosts, where rich food is easier to find, report Sasha Dall and Jonathan Wright in PLOS ONE in 2009. Ravens feed mainly on carcasses of large animals, rich food that does not last long. Those carcasses are usually defended by pairs of territorial adults.

Young, non-breeding ravens feed socially and gather in communal winter roosts. The roosts seem to work as information centers, where birds learn where food is. Dall and Wright show the pickings near large roosts are rich enough to favor this gang foraging. The study ties a striking social habit to plain economics: share news of carcasses, and everyone eats better than a lone young bird could.
plos-pone-0004630:
Chemotherapy helps antibody-guided radiation find its tumor targets, show Fares Al-Ejeh, Jocelyn Darby, and Michael Brown in PLOS ONE in 2009. Radioimmunotherapy uses antibodies to carry radioactive atoms to tumors. Its clinical utility is limited by inefficient delivery of therapeutic doses of radiation to solid tumors.

The antibody targets the La autoantigen, exposed on dead and dying tumor cells, as the team's earlier work showed. They aimed to test the therapeutic utility of yttrium-90 radio-conjugates of that antibody. Chemotherapy synergizes with the treatment, on their evidence: killing some tumor cells first exposes more target for the antibody. A combination that makes each part work better is exactly what solid tumor therapy needs.
plos-pone-0004730:
Billow Ahmed and colleagues showed that a changed cell scaffold can trap the serotonin transporter in the wrong place, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The transporter clears serotonin from gaps between nerve cells and shapes mood signals. Its tail end holds docking sites for other proteins and is vital for its work at the surface.

Using protein scans and cell tests, the team found the transporter tied to a scaffold filament. When serotonin changed that scaffold, the transporter spread was blocked. The finding links mood signals to the cell frame itself. It may help explain some drug effects on mood.
plos-pone-0004830:
Ken Kron and colleagues discovered novel hypermethylated genes in prostate cancer using genomic CpG island microarrays, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Promoter methylation regulation of tumor suppressor genes is a common feature of many cancers. Such silencing may contribute to cancer development, including prostate cancer. Prompting genome wide searches for newly methylated loci that could serve as biomarkers or reveal pathways.

Microarrays scanned CpG islands for abnormal methylation gains. Novel candidates emerged for validation as markers. Methylation tests could aid early detection. Some genes may also be therapeutic targets. The study gives researchers concrete leads that later work can verify and extend.
plos-pone-0004930:
People feel what others feel more strongly when those others seem similar. Andrea Serino, Giulia Giovagnoli and Elisabetta Làdavas examined this effect in PLOS ONE in 2009. They tested whether social representation shapes shared feeling. Social representation is how the brain pictures another person.

Judged similarity can rest on physical traits. It can also rest on group membership, such as ethnic or political identity. The study tested whether similarity changes how strongly states are shared. Its results speak to the biology of empathy. They also bear on why group divisions can dull our response to other people's pain.
plos-pone-0005030:
Cells crawl by spending energy at their leading edge. That energy is ATP, the cell's fuel. Jan Kuiper and colleagues studied a local fuel source in PLOS ONE in 2009. The source is brain-type creatine kinase, or CK-B. The enzyme transfers high-energy phosphate groups between ATP and phosphocreatine.

CK-B makes ATP right where the cell moves. Local generation facilitates cell motility. Fuel made far away would arrive too slowly. Deficiency of CK-B is coupled to lost function in neural circuits. The finding explains how moving cells keep energy close. It connects an old energy enzyme to the mechanics of crawling.
plos-pone-0005130:
Fascin-1 bundles actin into spikes that help cells move. It is absent from most normal epithelia. Many carcinomas switch it on, and its presence predicts poor outcomes. Yosuke Hashimoto and colleagues asked what turns its gene on. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They studied the fascin-1 promoter in human carcinoma cells.

Two regulators control that promoter. One is CREB, a common gene switch. The other is the aryl hydrocarbon receptor, a sensor for environmental chemicals. Together they drive fascin-1 expression in these cancer cells. The switches reveal how cancers arm their invasion tool. Blocking them could blunt spread. The finding also links chemical sensing to cancer cell movement.
plos-pone-0005230:
Nerve cells send messages by releasing packets from tiny vesicles, and a protein family called SV2 rides on those vesicles. One member, SV2B, is the most distinct of the three forms in mammals. Morgans and colleagues studied mice lacking SV2B in PLOS ONE in 2009, focusing on the retina.

Without SV2B, signaling in the retina grew weaker, as the title states. The mix of other vesicle proteins also changed. The results show this quiet vesicle protein matters for crisp signaling in the eye, and they guide work on how release sites are stocked.
plos-pone-0005330:
People who eat deer killed with lead bullets may swallow lead fragments along with the meat. Studies of subsistence hunters have shown raised blood lead levels, and ammunition residues persist in carcasses. Hunt and colleagues examined venison from rifle-killed deer in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The study assessed how much lead bullet fragments contribute to human dietary exposure. Even small fragments matter, since lead harms nerves and development at low doses. The findings inform hunters, processors, and health advisers about a risk that is invisible in the meat. Lead does its worst harm to the young brain, so meat shared with kids. With women who may bear kids is where this quiet risk should be cut first and with most care.
plos-pone-0005430:
Rebekah Bartelt and colleagues compared two kinds of T cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. T cells help clear germs from the body, but when they switch on at the wrong time they can cause disease. Labs often study long-lived T cell lines grown in dishes instead of fresh cells from blood.

The team set off the T cell receptor in both kinds of cells and compared the signals that followed. They also compared what the cells did next, such as making signals and dividing. Any gaps between the two warn workers not to trust cell lines too far when studying real immune responses.
plos-pone-0005530:
Jing Du and co-authors studied chemicals released by brain cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Chemicals made by nerve cells affect how nearby cells work and stay healthy. Whether those chemicals play a role in Alzheimer's disease was unknown.

The team compared chemicals from two brain cell types: cells of the cerebellum and cells of the hippocampus. The two sets had opposite effects linked to the disease process. That contrast hints that where a chemical is made in the brain may decide whether it helps or harms in Alzheimer's disease. The result warns against treating all brain regions as one in studies of this disease.
plos-pone-0005630:
Claudio Marinho and co-authors studied malaria in pregnant mice in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Malaria in pregnancy harms the placenta and leads to poor outcomes for mother and baby. The ways the parasite expands during pregnancy are hard to study in people.

Using new mouse tools, the team tracked parasites that returned after a first infection in pregnancy. Those parasites bound more strongly to the placenta. Mothers who had been through it once gained protection in later pregnancies, a pattern the model can now be used to explain. Malaria in pregnancy is a leading cause of low birth weight in the tropics, so models of it carry weight.
plos-pone-0005730:
Yervand Karapetyan and colleagues sped up the typing of prion strains in 2009. Prions are misshapen proteins that cause fatal brain diseases, and each strain behaves in its own way. Old typing methods took months of watching disease in mice, plus detailed brain checks.

The new method grows prions fast in special mice, then reads the strain with a panel of test cells. Faster typing matters when a new case appears in cattle, deer, or people. It can show quickly whether the strain matches a known threat. The team details how the shortcut holds up against the slow standard.
plos-pone-0005830:
Tammy Westmoreland and co-authors screened yeast in 2009 for genes that protect against the chemo drug doxorubicin. The drug breaks DNA double strands, which kills cancer cells but also harms healthy ones. Finding resistance genes in yeast can reveal the same defenses in human tumors.

The team tested a full set of yeast strains, each missing one gene, in its diploid form. Hundreds of strains proved sensitive to the drug, outlining a conserved repair network. Because the network is shared with humans, its members are leads for making tumors more drug-sensitive. Yeast again serves as a fast first draft.
plos-pone-0005930:
A tuberculosis vaccine can fail or succeed on dose alone. Claus Aagaard, Truc Hoang, Angelo Izzo and colleagues showed that in a 2009 PLOS ONE study of the vaccine Ag85B-TB10.4 given with the adjuvant IC31. Earlier work had paired the same vaccine with a different adjuvant built on charged fat particles.

With IC31, protection against the bacteria and the rise of hard-working T cells both hinged heavily on how much antigen was given. Dose is thus a dial that can tune the whole vaccine. The finding tells trial designers that picking the amount is as vital as picking the ingredients, a lesson for TB vaccines still in testing.
plos-pone-0006030:
Psoriasis patches almost never turn into skin cancer, a fact that puzzles doctors. Sari Suomela, Outi Elomaa, Tiina Skoog and colleagues followed one gene from that puzzle in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies CCHCR1, a gene inside the main psoriasis risk region, which is switched on in some cancers, and looks at its levels in skin cancer.

CCHCR1 is up-regulated in skin cancer and tied to expression of EGFR, a growth receptor, the title reports. A psoriasis gene with a second life in cancer links two skin stories that seemed opposed. The work may help explain the strange guard psoriasis offers, and it adds a fresh suspect to the study of skin tumors.
plos-pone-0006130:
A coronavirus enters cells by its spike, and small changes there can rewrite its reach. Yoshiyuki Yamada, Xiao Bo Liu, Shou Guo Fang and colleagues proved that in cultured cells in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies the avian coronavirus infectious bronchitis virus, adapted to eggs and to chicken and monkey kidney cells, and the spike protein substitutions it gained along the way.

Gaining cell-cell fusion activity through those substitutions determined whether the virus could infect, the title reports. Entry is the first gate every virus must pass, so its rules are basic to outbreak science. The work shows how a poultry virus tunes its key, a lesson that reads across the whole coronavirus family.
plos-pone-0006230:
Music feels stronger with eyes closed, and Yulia Lerner and colleagues wanted to know why. Their 2009 PLOS ONE study links the effect to the amygdala, a brain region tied to emotion. The value people feel from a stimulus depends partly on how the brain is processing at that moment.

Brain imaging showed the amygdala mediating the boost in emotional experience when eyes stay shut. Context, not just sound, sets the strength of feeling. The finding helps explain everyday habits like closing eyes at concerts. It also guides studies of emotion, which must account for such processing styles.
plos-pone-0006330:
Potassium channels that open near a neuron's resting voltage help set how excitable the cell is. Sinead Clancy and colleagues studied Kv12.2 channels and two small partner subunits, KCNE1 and KCNE3, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The channel is highly expressed in the nervous system, but its functional variety is poorly understood.

The subunits regulate how many channels reach the membrane surface in lab tests. Together the three proteins form a tripartite complex in living animals. Partner subunits multiply channel behaviour from the same pore. The finding helps explain diversity in neuronal signalling.
plos-pone-0006430:
Miaozong Wu and co-authors studied aging muscle in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper centered on a protein called Akt. Old skeletal muscle shows more metabolic and functional problems. Left unchecked, these problems raise illness and death rates. The team looked at why Akt, also called protein kinase B, works less well as muscle ages.

They linked the decline to a chemical change called S-nitrosylation. They also tested acetaminophen, a common pain drug, as a way to intervene. The study connects a basic cell signal to the weakness of old muscle. It hints that a familiar drug might help protect aging muscle function.
plos-pone-0006530:
Paige Davies, Anne Powell, John Swain, and colleagues studied cell fusion in the intestine for PLOS ONE in 2009. Cell fusion between circulating bone marrow-derived cells and other cells is well documented in various tissues. It has recently been suggested to occur in the intestine as well. The team examined how inflammation and proliferation act in this process.

Their title reports that inflammation and proliferation act together to mediate intestinal cell fusion. Two signals together may create the conditions fusion needs. Fusion could contribute to gut repair, or to disease when misdirected. The study clarifies when bone marrow cells merge into gut tissue.
plos-pone-0006630:
Kheng Chheng and co-authors reported drug-proof staph infections in Cambodian children in PLOS ONE in 2009. In rich lands, community-linked MRSA, a form of Staphylococcus aureus that resists key drugs, is on the rise. It has seemed rare in poor lands, but data there are thin. The team studied the rise of this form in infections of children in Cambodia.

Finding this form on the rise there changes how doctors should treat staph cases. First-choice drugs must now cover the drug-proof strain. Watch systems in less studied places often find such problems late. Their report is an early warning for the whole region.
plos-pone-0006730:
Tao Dao and colleagues hunted for immune targets on a common cancer protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is cyclin D1, overproduced in many human tumors. Excess cyclin D1 helps drive uncontrolled cell division. That makes it a possible target antigen for immunotherapy. Only a few T cell targets on it were known.

The team identified a human cyclin D1 peptide that triggers killer-helping T cells. The peptide induced human cytotoxic CD4 T cells. CD4 cells are usually helpers, so cytotoxic ones are notable weapons. A defined peptide target could support vaccine-style cancer treatments. The work widens the list of cyclin D1 fragments the immune system can be taught to attack.
plos-pone-0006830:
Fang Chen and Yongqun He studied how a rough strain of Brucella kills mouse macrophages in PLOS ONE in 2009. Brucella bacteria live inside host cells and cause brucellosis. Surviving inside macrophages is critical for chronic infection. Smooth virulent strains block the death of their host cells. Rough strains behave differently.

The rough Brucella abortus strain induced both apoptotic and necrotic death. An enzyme called caspase-2 mediated the killing. The contrast with smooth strains highlights a survival strategy. Blocking cell death lets smooth bacteria persist quietly. Understanding the switch may expose ways to break chronic brucellosis.
plos-pone-0006930:
Stefanie Müller, Monika Götz, and Dagmar Beier studied acid sensing in a stomach bacterium in PLOS ONE in 2009. The bacterium was Helicobacter pylori, a human gastric pathogen. Its ArsRS two-component system is the master regulator of acid adaptation. Low pH was thought to trigger the sensor protein ArsS into action.

The team focused on one building block of ArsS, histidine residue ninety-four. They tested whether that single residue does the pH sensing. Pinpointing the sensor helps explain how the bacterium survives stomach acid. That survival is the first step in infections that can lead to ulcers and stomach cancer.
plos-pone-0007030:
Shelton Bradrick and Matthias Gromeier identified a new cap-binding protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. RNA made by RNA polymerase II carries a special cap at its start. The cap is a modified building block called 7-methylguanosine. Proteins that grip this cap help control the RNA's fate, from export to translation.

The authors showed that a protein named Gemin5 binds this cap. That was a new role for a protein known from other RNA work. Cap binding places Gemin5 at a control point for gene expression. The finding may reshape views of how messenger RNA is handled.
plos-pone-0007130:
Sean Rice and Anthony Papadopoulos modelled chance in evolution in PLOS ONE in 2009. The movement of animals and plants between local groups shapes how species adapt and split. It also helps keep gene variety alive. That movement is not a steady flow, and part of it is pure chance. Fitness, too, can shift by luck from year to year.

Their model joined chance in fitness with chance in movement. It asked how the double dose of luck changes the fate of groups. Fixed models can mislead when groups are small and luck looms large. This work gives a more honest base for how species change over time.
plos-pone-0007230:
Lluís Armengol, Sergi Villatoro, Juan R. González, and colleagues searched human genomes for group-defining differences in 2009. Understanding genetic contributions to trait variation matters for health. Populations differ in disease risk and in response to medicines, and genetics explains part of those differences.

The authors profile structural variation across the genome. They focus on copy number variants, stretches of DNA gained or lost between people. They identify variants that define genomic differences among major human groups. Their catalog helps researchers study population history and plan medical genetics studies more fairly.
plos-pone-0007330:
Hong-Wen Liu, Yun-Cin Luo, Chia-Lin Ho, and colleagues studied how cells follow their substrate in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Cells navigate by soluble chemical gradients, but that guidance fades if the signal stays unchanged. Whether guidance by the extracellular matrix, the material cells crawl on, also adapts was obscure.

The authors test locomotion guidance by immobilized matrix cues. They report the guidance is adaptive, like chemical guidance. They also show a transient change in calcium levels can restore faded guidance. Their finding reveals a reset mechanism for cells moving through tissues.
plos-pone-0007430:
Chetan Hans and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how high blood fats damage blood vessels and the nerves that regulate them. They used mice lacking the ApoE gene and fed them a high-fat diet, a standard model of artery disease. The question was whether a DNA-repair enzyme called PARP-1 helps drive the damage.

Mice without PARP-1 were protected against much of the harm. Their blood vessels worked better, and their autonomic nerve control stayed steadier. The protection involved eNOS, an enzyme that keeps vessels relaxed, and lower oxidative stress. The results suggest that blocking PARP-1 could shield vessels from fat-driven injury. That idea may matter for diseases where cholesterol harms both arteries and nerves.
plos-pone-0007530:
Hiroyuki Nakagawa and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on Lasp-2, a protein that grips the cell's actin skeleton. Lasp-2 gathers in actin bundles and at focal adhesions, the anchor points where cells grip their surroundings. The protein has three structural regions. Which regions do the gripping was unknown. The team tested the LIM domain and the nebulin-repeat region in particular.

Both regions proved to contribute to the interaction. They help Lasp-2 bind actin filaments and settle into focal adhesions. Knowing the division of labor explains how the protein organizes cell shape. Actin anchors underlie movement, division, and a cell's sense of place. A protein that manages those anchors matters in development and in cancer spread. The study assigns its parts their jobs.
plos-pone-0007630:
Dhruv Sareen and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 with a safety warning for stem cell medicine. Growing human neural progenitor cells in dishes is the foundation of future cell therapies for the brain. Such therapies need cells with a normal chromosome set. Abnormal cells raise the risk of tumors after transplant. The team checked the chromosomes of cultured human neural progenitor cells over time.

During culture, some cells gained an extra copy of chromosome 7 and of chromosome 19. Those trisomies appeared as the cells expanded in vitro. A therapy grown from such cells could carry hidden danger. The warning matters now, before these cells reach patients widely. Routine chromosome checks should accompany long culture. The study is a guardrail for a promising field: growth in a dish must not quietly rewrite the genome.
plos-pone-0007730:
Yuan-Ping Pang and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It reports a new drug candidate against botulinum neurotoxin serotype A. That toxin causes botulism, a life-threatening paralysis. Current antibody treatments can only catch toxin still outside nerve cells.

Once the toxin slips inside, antibodies cannot reach it. The active part is an enzyme that cuts key proteins. The team used computer-aided design, then built the molecule they designed. The result is a potent small-molecule blocker of that enzyme. Such a drug could treat poisoning after exposure, not just prevent it.
plos-pone-0007830:
Massimiliano Baldassarre and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It studies filamins, proteins that link the cell's actin skeleton to its surface. Mammals have three filamins, and the founding member, FLNa, was tied to cell migration. Mutations in FLNA cause a brain disorder where neurons fail to migrate.

The authors tested how filamins control the first steps of movement. Filamins regulate how cells spread on a surface. They also govern how migration gets started. Those early steps decide much of what follows. The findings matter for development and for cancer spread.
plos-pone-0007930:
Hong Choi and colleagues named a new player in bone control in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is Lrp4, found on osteoblasts, the cells that build bone. They showed it acts as a receptor, a docking site, for two known bone signals, Dickkopf 1 and sclerostin.

Tests in living mice linked Lrp4 to both bone growth and bone turnover, the steady renewal of the skeleton. When this docking step fails, the balance of building and breakdown shifts. The finding adds a handle for research on weak bones and on drugs that aim to strengthen them.
plos-pone-0008030:
Takehiko Ogura and colleagues gave the silkworm its first full Ras gene survey in PLOS ONE in 2009. Ras proteins are growth switches found in nearly all complex life, famed for their role in human cancer. In most insects, the family had barely been charted.

The team found three Ras genes in the silkworm and read where and when each one works. The silkworm is both a farm animal and a lab model, so the survey serves two masters. It also lets scientists compare the insect switches with the human ones that go wrong in tumors.
plos-pone-0008130:
Manuela Basso and colleagues cataloged the proteins locked in clumps in ALS tissue in PLOS ONE in 2009. ALS kills the nerve cells that run muscles, and clumps of protein are a hallmark in those cells. Which proteins fill the clumps, and why they gather, stayed murky.

The stubborn clump proteins, washed free of all that dissolves, pointed to nitrative stress, a form of chemical damage from nitrogen-based radicals. The damage looks like a cause of the gathering, not a side effect. That chain gives drug hunters a place to cut in, before clumps form.
plos-pone-0008230:
Patrick D. Schloss presented a DNA sequence aligner in PLOS ONE in 2009 for microbial ecology. Surveys of microbes keep growing as sequencing capacity grows. Analysis then hits a bottleneck: building a meaningful multiple sequence alignment. Common aligners differ in quality and speed. A poor alignment can distort every later conclusion about a community.

Schloss offered a high-throughput tool built for these large surveys. Faster, reliable alignment lets researchers handle far more sequences. That helps studies of bacteria in soil, water, and the human body. The paper is a practical methods contribution for a fast-growing field.
plos-pone-0008330:
Paul Zak and his team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about how a hormone can change how kind men are. How we choose to be kind or to act for self is a deep point in the study of acts. The team gave the male hormone testosterone to 25 men. Each man took both the drug and a fake drug at set times, and no one knew which was which at the time. Blood tests checked that the hormone did rise as planned.

Kind acts were scored with a trade game in which one man splits cash and the next can turn the split down. Men on the hormone gave less in the game than men on the fake. A body-made drug thus swung a choice of cash and kind acts in a clear way. The work links the body's own drugs to day-to-day social choice.
plos-pone-0008430:
Xiaolong Wang, Deming Gou, and Shuang-yong Xu present a lab method in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their method makes short bits of DNA called antisense oligonucleotides. Such bits can block small RNAs or their targets. Labs use them as tools, and doctors may one day use them as drugs. But bits made by chemists often hold flawed copies that are hard to remove.

The method, called PEAR, uses two enzymes to copy and cut DNA in a loop. It can make large amounts of clean product in the lab. The paper shows how the loop works and why purity improves. That could lower cost for research use.
plos-pone-0008530:
