Christine Bell and co-authors track two factors in early mouse embryos in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The factors are SNAI1 and SNAI2. They initiate epithelial-to-mesenchymal transitions in development and cancer spread. Those transitions let stationary cells become mobile ones. The team find both factors expressed in preimplantation embryos. Their pattern at the two-cell stage is asymmetric, meaning uneven between cells.

Later, the factors become segregated to the trophectoderm in the blastocyst. The trophectoderm is the outer layer that forms the placenta. This segregation hints at an early role in lineage choice. The work reveals an unexpected place for these transition factors.
plos-pone-0008630:
Josephine V. J. Lightowler, Graham S. Cooke, Portia Mutevedzi, and colleagues reported a clinical study from South Africa in PLOS ONE in 2010. It deals with cryptococcal meningitis, a fungal infection of the membranes around the brain. Among people with HIV in sub-Saharan Africa, few illnesses kill more of them. The study site was KwaZulu-Natal province.

More patients there were gaining access to drugs that fight HIV itself. Yet surviving also depended on how well the meningitis was treated. So the team examined which patient and care factors were linked to how cases turned out. Their findings show where local treatment fell short. They also point to changes that could help more patients live.
plos-pone-0008730:
Azad Kumar, Elisa Greggio, Alexandra Beilina, and colleagues tested the aim of a Parkinson-linked enzyme. Their work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mutations in LRRK2 are the most common known cause of inherited Parkinson disease. LRRK2 is a kinase, an enzyme that tags proteins with phosphate. One possible target is 4E-BP, a protein that controls protein making. Whether LRRK2 truly tags it was disputed.

In test-tube assays, the enzyme tagged itself far more strongly than 4E-BP. That weak aim casts doubt on 4E-BP as a natural target. Clearing up false targets saves Parkinson research from dead ends.
plos-pone-0008830:
Eric Wooten, Lakshmanan Iyer, Maria Claudia Montefusco, and colleagues used gene networks to find suspects for a heart defect. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. A bicuspid aortic valve has two flaps instead of three. The defect runs strongly in families. Only about one person in a hundred has it, limiting classic gene hunts. The team instead preselected promising gene variants.

Network-guided analysis flagged variant patterns in AXIN1, PDIA2, and endoglin. Those patterns tracked with the valve defect. Smart preselection can rescue studies of rare traits. The suspects now await confirmation in larger groups.
plos-pone-0008930:
Brett Zani, Laura Indolfi, and Elazer Edelman described tiny tubes linking airway cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. The cells they studied line the bronchi, the air passages inside the lungs. Cells often talk by sending signals through body fluids over long distances. They can also touch directly when they sit side by side.

Under the microscope, the team saw bronchial cells grow thin bridges toward each other. Cells used these tubes to move and to pass signals between neighbours. The bridges formed a direct line of contact that fluid signals cannot match. Such links may help the airway lining repair itself after injury.
plos-pone-0009030:
Sumanti Gupta and co-authors watched a fungus attack chickpea plants at the earliest moment, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fusarium oxysporum causes wilt disease that devastates chickpea crops. Plants often resist invaders by killing their own cells around the entry point. Wounding the plant lets this fungus in, starting the contest.

Rather than the defence burst coming first, the fungus struck the plant's core metabolism. Basic processes that keep the plant's cells running were its initial target. That early hit may weaken the plant before defences can organise. Crop breeders could use the timing to build chickpeas that react faster.
plos-pone-0009130:
Ido Yosef and co-authors starved E. coli of its protein-delivery crew and watched membranes suffer, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Membrane proteins must be built straight into the cell's membrane. A delivery system called SRP guides them there as they are made. Two parts, Ffh and FtsY, are each essential in this bacterium.

The team drained each part in turn and tracked membrane protein production. Some earlier work had hinted the system might be partly optional. Depletion confirmed the SRP route as central to membrane biogenesis. The result firms up a basic chapter of bacterial cell biology.
plos-pone-0009230:
Kim Brolin, Kristina Persson, Mats Wahlgren, and co-authors published this malaria study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Malaria parasites that infect pregnant women can pile up in the placenta. A parasite surface protein called VAR2CSA drives that pile-up. Women pregnant for the first time are hit hardest, while mothers in later pregnancies often carry protective antibodies.

The team studied how those natural antibodies recognize different parts of VAR2CSA. They used samples from pregnant women in a malaria-endemic area. Knowing which parts of the protein antibodies actually target is vital for a vaccine. A pregnancy malaria vaccine would need to copy the protection that repeated pregnancies build naturally.
plos-pone-0009330:
Paul Azzopardi and co-authors published this mineral study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Osteopontin is a protein that blocks the growth of hydroxyapatite, the mineral of bone and teeth. In dishes it stops crystals from forming and growing. In the body it is thought to keep soft tissues from hardening with mineral.

The team studied how osteopontin interacts with the crystal surface. They weighed the roles of electric charge and of the protein's shape in that grip. Details matter because the same control system fails in diseases of unwanted calcification. The study separates two forces that earlier work had lumped together.
plos-pone-0009430:
Martine Humbert and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2010 on a hard to treat cancer of the pancreas. Some growth signals run too high in these tumors. One drug, masitinib, blocks several of those signals. The team paired it with gemcitabine, a drug long used for this cancer.

The pair was tested on human tumor cells grown in the lab. It was also tested in mice that carried human tumor tissue. The authors report how the two drugs acted together in both settings. Their work tests whether a paired approach could do more than a single drug alone.
plos-pone-0009530:
Annette O'Connor and colleagues reviewed health studies near large animal farms in PLOS ONE in 2010. Animal feeding operations house many livestock in a small area. People who live nearby often report health complaints. The review gathered studies on breathing, gut, and mental health in such neighbors. It weighed how strong and consistent the evidence is.

Pulling the studies together shows where links are firm and where they are weak. Many reports rely on what people say about their own health, which can bias results. The authors set out what better studies would need. Their map helps officials judge real risks around these farms.
plos-pone-0009630:
Theresa Manful and co-authors hunted for a better test for sleeping sickness in PLOS ONE in 2010. The East African form is caused by Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense. Diagnosis still rests on finding the parasite in blood under a microscope. That method misses cases and needs skilled staff. The team screened the parasite's proteins for ones that patients' antibodies recognize strongly.

Proteins picked out by patient blood are candidates for a simple antibody test. The team also cloned the genes for the most promising ones. A field friendly test would speed treatment of a disease that is fatal if missed. The study supplies the raw material such a test needs.
plos-pone-0009730:
Fibrocytes are blood-born cells that help build scar tissue after injury. S. John Curnow and colleagues grew them from mononuclear blood cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. They compared growth with serum present and with serum absent. Mononuclear cells include the white blood cells that patrol the body.

Serum is the liquid part of blood left after clotting. Distinct types of fibrocyte grew under both conditions, not just one. That result clarifies the conditions that steer blood cells toward the scar-building fate. Knowing the rules matters for research on wound healing and fibrosis.
plos-pone-0009830:
Some HIV drugs work by blocking the virus from fusing with human cells. Pedro Matos and colleagues studied two such fusion inhibitor peptides, enfuvirtide and T-1249. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The team watched how the peptides interact with cell membranes. They used membranes from erythrocytes, red blood cells, and lymphocytes, white blood cells of the immune system. How a drug peptide meets the membrane affects how well it can work. Membrane contact is the first step in blocking fusion. The details help chemists design stronger fusion blockers.
plos-pone-0009930:
Amanda G Oglesby-Sherrouse and Michael Vasil describe a new small RNA in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper on Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The bacterium infects people with weak defenses and needs iron to cause disease. It can pull iron from heme, the iron-carrying part of blood.

Two known small RNAs from one gene spot help the cell save iron. The authors found a third, longer RNA from the same spot, named PrrH, and mapped its full length. Heme, not just iron, turns PrrH down. That change then alters which other genes switch on. Readers see a fresh control layer that lets the germ sense heme directly.
plos-pone-0010030:
The authors were Olga Gil, Ivan Díaz, Cristina Vilaplana, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study built a tuberculosis model in minipigs. A low dose of the TB bacterium was given through the chest. The pigs were then watched for twenty weeks as infection took hold.

Immune readings showed a strong Th1 type response and a weak antibody response. Tissue checks showed how granulomas, tight balls of immune cells, formed around the germs. The title names the key point: walling germs inside granulomas helps contain TB in this model. The model gives TB researchers another animal system to study.
plos-pone-0010130:
The authors were Reyhan Nergiz-Unal, Judith Cosemans, Marion Feijge, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study looked at blood clots on ruptured artery plaques. When plaque breaks, platelets build a clot, and a signal called ADP helps stabilize it. That signal works through receptors named P2Y12 on platelets.

Most earlier models damaged healthy vessels, which may not match real heart attacks. Studying clots on ruptured plaques under flow, the team confirmed a stabilizing role for P2Y12. The result supports drugs that block that receptor to prevent dangerous clots. The work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.
plos-pone-0010230:
The authors were Lawrence Bish, Kevin Morine, Meg Sleeper, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study asked what a muscle growth brake does in the heart. Myostatin is well known for holding back skeletal muscle growth. Its role in heart muscle, though, was controversial, with studies pointing in different directions about benefit and harm.

The team studied heart cells under stress, in culture and in a mouse model. Stress raised myostatin through a route that depends on the Erk signal. The raised myostatin then held back heart cell growth, naming a control loop worth watching in heart disease.
plos-pone-0010330:
Arnaud Bertrand, Michael Ballón and Alexis Chaigneau used sound to map life in the ocean for PLOS ONE in 2010. Deep water in some regions holds very little oxygen. These low-oxygen zones are growing as the climate warms and human effects add up. Most sea animals cannot live far down into such water. Their depth limit, though, is hard to watch directly.

Echo sounders, which bounce sound off animals below, offered a way. The reflections showed where living things stopped as depth increased. That stopping line marked the top edge of the low-oxygen zone. Tracking that edge over time could reveal how fast the zones expand. For fish and the people who depend on them, the stakes are direct.
plos-pone-0010430:
Patrycja Dubielecka and colleagues studied how cells gulp fluid, and how two protein versions steer that gulping, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gulping process, macropinocytosis, lets cells take in fluid and large molecules. It depends on the cell's inner skeleton reshaping near the surface. A protein called Rac1 was thought to trigger that reshaping through a partner complex. The authors focused on two forms of a related protein, Abi1.

The two forms regulated the gulping process differently. Small differences in one protein can thus tune a whole cell behavior. Cells use gulping to feed, to sample their surroundings, and sometimes to let viruses in. Cancer cells also exploit it to fuel growth. Sorting the regulators may reveal ways to block those abuses.
plos-pone-0010530:
Anna Liisa Suominen-Taipale and colleagues checked whether eating fish tracks with fewer depressive episodes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fish and their omega-3 fats are often said to protect mental well-being. The evidence behind that claim, though, was conflicting. The team ran a cross-sectional analysis in a Finnish population sample. They compared fish intake, omega-3 intake, and blood levels of these fats against depression history.

Looking at diet and blood measures together strengthens the check. Blood levels show what the body actually absorbed, not just what people report eating. Cross-sectional data cannot prove cause, and the authors treat it accordingly. Still, large population analyses help settle whether the fish-mood link deserves trials. Mental health nutrition needs exactly this kind of careful accounting.
plos-pone-0010630:
Jin-Hyeok Hwang and colleagues searched for a marker that predicts chemotherapy success in pancreatic cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Surgery can remove the tumor, yet the cancer often returns. Added drug treatment helps some patients and only burdens others.

The team measured a tiny molecule, microRNA-21, in tumor samples. Patients with high levels fared worse and gained less from added treatment. Low levels marked a group that benefited more. A simple tumor test of this kind could spare some patients harsh drugs that would not help them, and focus care where it works.
plos-pone-0010730:
Jatin Shah and colleagues gathered studies on why people in India join clinical trials, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Trials have globalized fast, with many now run in India. That growth raised fair questions about consent, trust, and whether local customs are respected during recruitment.

The meta-analysis combined findings from many interview-based studies. Hope for better care, trust in doctors, and family advice recurred as motives. Payment mattered less than outsiders often assume. Knowing real motives helps ethics boards write rules that protect volunteers without blocking research that local communities actually welcome.
plos-pone-0010830:
Yair Fisher, Anna Nemirovsky, Rona Baron and colleagues reported this mouse study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Alzheimer's disease fills the brain with clumps of a protein fragment called amyloid-beta. The team tested whether vaccinating mice against that fragment would draw immune T cells to the plaques and help clear them away.

Vaccination with amyloid-beta sent T cells to gather at plaques in the brain, and the plaques were almost fully cleared. A comparison vaccine using a spinal cord protein sent its T cells to the spinal cord and caused harmful inflammation there instead. The amyloid-targeted cells also raised markers linked to cleanup activity in the brain. Fisher and colleagues offer early evidence that a carefully aimed immune response might remove plaques without attacking healthy tissue.
plos-pone-0010930:
Por Ir, Chean Men, Henry Lucas and co-authors published this health survey in PLOS ONE in 2010. Serious illness is a known route into poverty in developing countries, through treatment bills and lost work, but measuring that impact well is difficult. As part of an international project, the team surveyed rural Cambodia to find households hit by major illness.

Nearly six thousand households across three rural health districts were interviewed after random cluster sampling. In more than a quarter of them, at least one person had suffered a serious illness during the recall period. Those households were flagged for deeper interviews about costs, coping, and livelihood damage. Ir and colleagues supply the screening half of a poverty-and-illness study, showing how common the shock of major sickness is in the Cambodian countryside.
plos-pone-0011030:
Lee Yee Choong, Simin Lim, Poh Kuan Chong and co-authors published this breast cancer proteomics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tracking how breast cancer develops is hampered by the genetic and environmental noise between patients. The MCF10AT model avoids that noise: four cell lines descended from the same source, each mimicking a later stage of progression, grown as grafts.

Using isotope-tagged mass spectrometry, the team measured more than twelve hundred proteins across the model. Nearly a hundred proteins changed significantly between stages, spanning twenty functional groups including kinases, proteases, adhesion, and skeleton proteins, and the number of changed proteins grew as disease advanced. Choong and colleagues supply a stage-by-stage protein map of breast cancer progression, a cleaner hunting ground for markers and drug targets than patient samples alone.
plos-pone-0011130:
Madronal, Lopez-Aracil, Rangel and colleagues raised mice in varied settings for PLOS ONE in 2010. Some mice lived in rich spaces with more room to move, objects to explore and cage mates to meet. The team then tested movement, learning and new brain cell growth.

Mice from rich settings performed better and grew more new cells in a brain region tied to memory. The gains show how daily surroundings shape the brain in lasting ways. That supports the value of active, social settings for brain health. It also gives lab studies a warning: plain cages may understate what a brain can do.
plos-pone-0011230:
Pond, Delport, Muse and colleagues corrected a gene analysis bias in PLOS ONE in 2010. Models of how the genetic code evolves need starting estimates for how often each code word appears. Common shortcuts guess those rates instead of measuring them, and the guesses can bias results.

The team showed how to correct that bias in empirical estimators used by the models. Sharper estimates improve family trees built from gene data. Better trees give better dates for when genes and species split. The fix is a small change with wide use, since codon models are a daily tool in evolution research.
plos-pone-0011330:
Tamar Dvash, Neta Lavon, and Guoping Fan studied female human stem cells in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Female cells carry two X chromosomes, and early in growth one X is normally shut down so gene doses stay balanced. The team used stem cells taken from early embryos to watch when and how that shutdown begins.

They found that cells in their earliest passages do not all shut down the X in the same way. Some had started the process, others had not, and the pattern shifted as cells were grown longer. That uneven start matters for anyone using these cells in research. A lab that assumes all female stem cells behave alike may misread its results, so the paper urges care in checking each cell line.
plos-pone-0011430:
Hedley Grantham, Robert Pressey, and Jessie Wells tested in 2010 how well conservation shortcuts actually work. Planners cannot map every species, so they protect areas rich in a few well-known groups and assume the rest of life is covered. Earlier tests of that assumption disagreed wildly, and the team asked why the verdict kept changing.

They found that the answer depends on which measure of success is chosen, producing a kaleidoscope of different results from the same plans. A reserve network can look excellent by one yardstick and poor by another. The humbling lesson is that planners must state their yardstick openly and test several. Otherwise a protected map may guard only the stand-in species while the life it was meant to represent slips away uncounted.
plos-pone-0011530:
Susanna Marg and co-authors characterized in 2010 a mouse whose cell glue cannot grip properly. Vinculin is a protein that anchors cells to their surroundings by binding actin, the cell's cable protein, at adhesion sites. The mouse carries a splice variant of vinculin, missing two segments, that is produced constantly and cannot bind actin at all.

Studying what breaks in such a mouse reveals, by subtraction, exactly what the grip does for tissues under mechanical load. Heart, skin, and vessels all pull on their cells, and weak anchoring shows first where the pulling is hardest. The mutant is a precise tool rather than a curiosity: one defined defect, present from birth, in a protein found in nearly every tissue. Cell biologists can use it to test which adhesion jobs truly need vinculin's grip and which have backups.
plos-pone-0011630:
Steven Cannon and colleagues revisited the deep history of legume plants in PLOS ONE in 2010. Legumes, including beans and peas, host soil bacteria in root nodules and gain nitrogen from the air. Evidence suggested the whole legume genome doubled early in their history, and many assumed that doubling came before the nodule partnership.

The authors tested that order across legume groups. They found the doubling did not predate nodulation in all lineages, so the partnership arose without waiting for it everywhere. The revised timeline changes the standard story of how one of farming's most valuable plant alliances began.
plos-pone-0011730:
Ruolin Yang and Bing Su compared gene teamwork in human and mouse tissues, in PLOS ONE in 2010. High-throughput tools now let scientists watch many genes at once. While many single genes behind species differences have been characterised, far less is known about how whole tissue-level gene groups evolved.

Yang and Su identified modules of genes tied to specific tissues in each species and compared them side by side. Some teamwork proved conserved, while other modules were rewired between human and mouse. Knowing which networks stayed stable warns against assuming mouse results always transfer to human biology.
plos-pone-0011830:
Carlos Caicedo-Carvajal, Troy Shinbrot, and Ramsey Foty published this 2010 study on how groups of cells change from flowing masses into firm tissue. Growing embryos and healing wounds both need cells that can first move past each other, then settle and hold still. The team focused on bonds between two proteins, integrin and fibronectin, that link cells to the material around them.

Working with three-dimensional clumps of cells, the authors show that the strength of those integrin and fibronectin bonds decides whether a clump behaves like a thick liquid or like a soft solid. Weak bonding lets cells keep trading places, while strong bonding locks the group in place. That switch helps explain how a loose crowd of cells becomes stable, organized tissue.
plos-pone-0011930:
Subhadip Raychaudhuri proposed in 2010 a stripped-down model of how cells decide to die. Real signaling networks are large, but the essential logic of sensing a stimulus and adapting to it can be captured in a minimal network. The model was built to respond in proportion to signals of different strengths.

Applied to apoptosis, the cell's orderly death program, the model explains why genetically identical cells facing the same signal do not all die at once. Random differences between cells emerge naturally from the network's structure. A simple model that reproduces that variability gives researchers a test bed for ideas about drug resistance, where a few cancer cells survive treatment that kills the rest.
plos-pone-0012030:
Roger Chung and co-workers reported in 2010 that a natural metal-handling protein can stop amyloid clumping driven by copper. Alzheimer's disease is marked by insoluble plaques of beta-amyloid, and evidence suggests copper and zinc help the amyloid aggregate. The protein tested was metallothionein, the main human protein that binds copper and zinc for safekeeping.

In rat cortical neurons, metallothionein blocked the copper-driven aggregation of amyloid and its toxicity. A built-in defense that neutralizes the metal trigger is an appealing lead: rather than attacking plaques after they form, boosting this guard could prevent the clumping chemistry from starting. The work also ties brain metal balance more firmly to Alzheimer's damage.
plos-pone-0012130:
Brad Reynolds, Sean Powers, and Mary Anne Bishop tracked fish around built and natural reefs in Alaska's Prince William Sound, reported in PLOS ONE in 2010. Damage to nearshore habitat has pushed many groups to build artificial reefs, hoping fish will settle there. Copper rockfish and lingcod are key fish in this sound, and both were fitted into the study using sound-based tracking tags.

The tags let the team follow where each fish stayed and how far it roamed, at created sites and natural ones alike. Knowing whether fish truly live at built reefs, or just pass through, decides whether reef building is worth the cost. The results feed into how Alaska manages habitat repair after damage.
plos-pone-0012230:
Leah Gerber, Manuela González-Suárez, Claudia Hernández-Camacho, and co-authors studied breeding California sea lions in PLOS ONE in 2010. In this mating system, males fight to hold groups of females, gaining more mates through aggression. Their observations during the June to August breeding season covered how both male and female behavior across that season shapes how many pups females produce.

Aggression carries a price: effort spent fighting and guarding is effort not spent elsewhere, and turmoil can cost females and pups too. Measuring that price in a wild colony tests a core claim of evolutionary theory with real animals. It also helps managers predict how disturbance at crowded breeding beaches affects the next generation.
plos-pone-0012330:
Antariksh Tyagi, Sumit Bag, Virendra Shukla, and co-authors tested a shortcut for identifying species from short DNA reads, in PLOS ONE in 2010. DNA barcoding identifies a species from a snippet of a standard gene region, and it normally judges identity by genetic distance or signature characters. With snippets so short, those judgments can blur between close species.

Their approach counts how often each short word of DNA letters appears in the barcode region, a frequency fingerprint that separates species across kingdoms, from fungi to animals. A method needing only short reads works with damaged museum specimens and gut or soil samples alike. Faster, cheaper identification feeds everything from food fraud detection to biodiversity surveys.
plos-pone-0012430:
Giuseppe Nicastro, Sokol Todi, Ezgi Karaca and colleagues dissected the working head of the ataxin-3 protein, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Ataxin-3 faults cause Machado-Joseph disease, a brain disorder that steals movement control. The protein normally trims ubiquitin chains, the tags that mark other proteins for disposal, and its Josephin domain does the gripping and cutting.

The team mapped how the domain binds ubiquitin chains and where it cuts them. Those details explain how the healthy protein works and what may misfire in disease. A clear map of the cutting head helps chemists think about drugs that could tune its activity in patients.
plos-pone-0012630:
Lee, Singh, Tsark and co-authors altered a control region that keeps two growth genes apart in mice. The genes H19 and Igf2 sit side by side, and a boundary element works only on the copy from the mother. There, a protein called CTCF blocks distant enhancers from reaching the Igf2 promoter.

Their 2010 change made the boundary work on both copies at once. Pups then grew poorly before birth and many died around delivery. The harsh outcome shows how fine the balance of this gene pair is, and why its faults appear in human growth disorders.
plos-pone-0012730:
Benn, Weaver, Billet and co-authors mapped how much of the deep North East Atlantic seafloor humans have touched. Most past checks stopped at waters shallower than two hundred metres. Their 2010 assessment went deeper, tallying fishing, cables, litter and other marks across a wide ocean area.

Knowing the true footprint is the first step to protecting deep habitats that recover very slowly. Trawling and other deep uses were still growing when they wrote. Their map gives regulators a baseline against which later damage or recovery can be judged.  Deep sea floors hold species found nowhere else on earth.
plos-pone-0012830:
Hanson and Ballantyne tested whether the colour of dried blood can betray how long a stain has sat at a scene. Knowing when blood was shed would fix the time frame of a crime for investigators. Their 2010 study tracked the hemoglobin Soret band, a strong light-absorption feature of blood pigment, as stains aged.

The band shifted toward blue wavelengths as time since deposition grew. A steady shift tied to age could turn a bloodstain into a rough clock. Forensic teams would still need care with heat and light effects.
plos-pone-0321830:
Hung-Yun Lu and five colleagues solve a tracking problem in brain research in this 2026 methods study. Scientists recording neurons over weeks face a basic question. Is that the same cell as yesterday? Electrode drift and shifting signals make identity uncertain. The team built a waveform-based tracker tuned for standard electrode arrays. It recognises cells by their spike shape alone, without needing overlapping recording sites.

With identities secured, they followed several properties over time. Waveform shape itself stayed stable, which validates the tracker. Firing patterns were mostly steadier than not. Yet intervals between spikes and tuning preferences drifted gradually in some neurons. Brains, it seems, keep a stable cast while quietly reassigning some roles. That balance of stability and plasticity fits how animals keep old skills while learning new ones. The method opens long-term single-cell studies to ordinary laboratory arrays.
plos-pone-0335830:
Oratai Kanlayawut and colleagues ran a randomized trial in 2026 with older adults who were overweight or obese. Everyone followed the same twelve-week program of progressive strength training using exercises that work several joints at once. Half the group also received confidence-building strategies woven into each session, based on the idea that believing you can exercise helps you keep doing it.

Both groups finished stronger, with better balance, endurance, and mobility, and neither pulled clearly ahead on body composition. The confidence group did gain extra ground on knowledge, self-belief, and expectations about exercise, and their resting heart rate stayed steadier. The authors suggest that adding mindset support to strength training may help older adults stick with it, even when physical gains look similar.
plos-pone-0343430:
Moslemipour and colleagues, in a 2026 paper, build a decision model for cloud manufacturing, where factories share machines and jobs across distance through a central platform. In such systems, scheduling, shipping, pricing, and quality choices tangle together, and studies usually treat them one at a time. Fairness between customers is also often ignored.

Their model pursues three goals at once: profit for the system, satisfaction for customers based on price and quality, and fairness, so no customer is served far worse than another. A standard solver cracked small and medium cases exactly. A genetic algorithm, which breeds better solutions over generations, handled the large cases with near-equal quality in far less time. Leaving out shipping choices, satisfaction, or lateness penalties all produced worse plans. The authors present the framework as a way to run shared factories without quietly sacrificing some customers.
plos-pone-0344330:
Pragya Singhal, Priyanka Srivastava, and Liza Rajasekhar examine the mental health of people in India living with lupus, a long-term disease in which the immune system attacks the body's own organs. Their 2026 study gives patients questionnaires on stress, low mood, worry, and quality of life, and compares results with healthy people and with how severe the disease runs.

Stress, depression, and anxiety were all common among patients. Quality of life lagged behind healthy peers in body comfort, friendships, and surroundings. Worse disease went with worse mental health. Older patients who were homemakers fared poorest, while younger students fared better. The authors argue lupus care in India should treat the mind as part of the disease.
plos-pone-0345530:
Morris and colleagues refined a delivery system that ferries proteins into cells in a 2026 study. Tiny carrier peptides can cross cell walls, but cargo often stays trapped in pockets inside the cell. Their adaptor grabs cargo with a calcium-dependent grip that loosens once inside, freeing the cargo to work.

Test cargos carried rising positive charges, letting the team map where charge helps or hurts entry. A refined adaptor worked across all cargos at very low doses. Two extra-positive adaptors, though, blocked entry of the most positive cargos. Matching adaptor charge to cargo charge thus decides success, a design rule for future cell-delivered medicines.
plos-pone-0347030:
Tuan-anh Tran, Tamás Ruppert, György Eigner, and János Abonyi propose a conceptual model linking the content of factory work to how stressed workers feel and how well they perform. Managers need such tools to design jobs that do not burn people out, yet existing models mostly ignore what the work itself contains. Drawing on a broad literature review, the team built a system dynamics model with feedback loops between workload, stress, and output.

Trial runs in simulation software produced patterns matching real-world reports. Because the model is qualitative and conceptual, the authors present it as a scaffold: a basis for future human digital twins, pending experiments to pin down its numbers.
plos-pone-0347330:
Shaoguang Ren and colleagues followed nearly half a million adults in the UK Biobank to test whether mobile phone use is linked to rheumatoid arthritis, a painful joint disease. Over a median of about fourteen years, roughly six thousand participants developed the disease. The team compared non-users with users and looked at years of use, weekly calling time, and hands-free habits.

Phone users showed a modestly higher risk of developing the disease than non-users, and risk rose with some patterns of use. The differences were small, and an observational study cannot prove phones cause joint disease. Still, the size of the cohort makes the pattern hard to ignore and worth checking with other methods.
plos-pone-0347430:
Yanina E. Tena Garcia, Bianca R. Baltaretu, and Katja Fiehler studied how people judge the position of single objects versus the average position of a whole group. Volunteers in their 2026 experiment saw six kitchen objects, either inside a kitchen scene or against a plain texture, for a brief flash or several seconds. They then clicked where one object, or the group's centre, had been.

A realistic kitchen setting helped people locate single objects when they had more time to look, and their eyes ranged more widely across the scene. For group averages, the plain background worked better at the shortest flash. Viewing time changed eye movements in both tasks. The results show context shapes even basic visual judgements.
plos-pone-0347730:
Anis Nurwidayati and seven colleagues examine the hidden genetic structure inside a malaria mosquito complex across Indonesia, in this 2026 study. Members of the Anopheles tessellatus complex look identical under a microscope, yet only some spread malaria, so telling populations apart matters for control. The team collected mosquitoes on five islands and sequenced one nuclear and two mitochondrial gene regions, building family trees and haplotype networks.

The mosquitoes formed one family group split into three well-defined lineages: one in Sumatra, one in Sulawesi, and one spanning Java and the Nusa Tenggara islands. Diversity of gene variants ran high while overall sequence differences stayed low, and several Sulawesi populations showed strikingly strong local structure. The authors say targeted molecular identification is key before control programs can know which populations actually transmit malaria.
plos-pone-0348130:
Baoxu Ma and co-workers map how China licensed laboratory monkeys and other nonhuman primates over five recent years. Primates are used in medical research because their bodies are close to ours, and China runs a national license system for raising and using them. Their 2026 study pulls every license record from the national system for the years from twenty twenty to twenty twenty-four.

Most of the licenses covered use of primates rather than breeding them, and totals rose until one year then fell sharply. Beijing and Jiangsu led in use licenses, while breeding centered in Guangxi and Yunnan. Companies held most licenses, ahead of universities and research institutes. The map gives planners a clearer view of where this research capacity sits.
plos-pone-0348430:
Farzin Shama and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One electronics paper on a compact microwave filter cell built on a standard circuit-board material. The cell acts as a low-pass filter, letting signals below its cutoff through while blocking an unusually wide band above it, stretching across five harmonics of the cutoff frequency.

Built and measured in the lab, the device showed a sharp transition from passing to blocking, very low signal loss in its passband, and unusually steady timing behavior. Its footprint is small enough for dense microwave circuits. The authors pitch the design for communication and radar hardware that must reject harmonic interference across a very wide range without bulky extra filtering stages.
plos-pone-0348530:
Julia Heisig and colleagues published a 2026 interview study in PLOS ONE on why German doctors order routine monitoring scans for patients with coronary heart disease or past stroke. Such check-ups, including heart and neck-artery ultrasound, aim to catch worsening disease early, yet evidence for the right tests and timing is thin. The team interviewed twenty-two doctors, general practitioners, cardiologists, and neurologists across two states, and analyzed the conversations thematically.

Doctors generally saw monitoring as beneficial, a chance to spot progression and adjust treatment in time. They also named its risks: overdiagnosis, overuse, and overtreatment when scans come too often. Motives for ordering ultrasound ranged from reassurance and safety worries to financial incentives, and doctors disagreed about whether routine scanning is justified. Many reported too little guidance on intervals. Clearer evidence on when monitoring helps, they say, would cut both missed decline and needless testing.
plos-pone-0349030:
Rosychuk and colleagues tested whether sewage data could track COVID-19 cases across Alberta communities in a 2026 study. Sewage testing helps most when personal testing is limited. Samples from eleven treatment plants over nearly two years were matched to daily case counts for each sewershed.

Flexible models that allow delayed, curved links fit case patterns well, especially in smaller communities. The link's shape was similar across sites, but strengths differed by site. That means each town needs its own calibration rather than one shared rule. With local tuning, sewage signals can warn officials as case testing rises and falls.
plos-pone-0349130:
Ross A Hamilton and colleagues hunted for the helper proteins that switch on the androgen receptor, the engine of prostate cancer, including a stubborn variant that shrugs off modern drugs. Using DNA bait in a test tube, they fished out the protein teams that gather on the receptor's docking sites and identified the members by mass spectrometry.

One helper, CAND1, had not been linked to the receptor before. Silencing it in prostate cancer cells dimmed the receptor's target genes, and patient data tied higher CAND1 levels to spread disease and worse survival. A partner enzyme strengthened the receptor partly by locking CAND1 into place. The authors nominate this helper system as a fresh drug target for treatment-resistant prostate cancer.
plos-pone-0349230:
Bong Kyun Kim and Soo Hyung Eo built a scoring system to help wildlife rescuers decide when a rescued raccoon dog should be treated, watched, or humanely put down. Such calls are often made on gut feeling because no scientific standard exists. Their 2026 study analyzed thirteen years of records for nearly fourteen hundred raccoon dogs at a Korean rescue center, looking for what predicted a successful release.

The strongest predictors were what caused the accident, the season, and how badly the animal was hurt. From those factors the team built a three-band score: low-risk animals get active treatment, medium-risk animals get monitoring and reassessment, and high-risk animals may be euthanized promptly because release is so unlikely. The system uses only information available at intake, aiming for faster, fairer decisions.
plos-pone-0350130:
Tomofumi Yamazaki and co-authors mapped how close Tokyo residents live to health facilities and to public transport. Japan's aging, shrinking population makes fair access to care harder, even in the capital. Their 2026 geographic analysis measured walking-distance zones around pharmacies, hospitals, clinics, dental offices, and elder welfare facilities, then checked how many sat near bus stops, bus routes, and train stations.

Facilities of every kind clustered near bus stops in both central Tokyo and the western Tama region. Proximity to rail stations, by contrast, varied sharply between areas. The authors stress that walkable closeness is not the same as real access to a needed service. They argue health planning and transport planning should be done together, neighborhood by neighborhood, rather than assuming density alone guarantees access.
plos-pone-0350230:
Hadley Jaramillo and co-authors asked a simple question in 2026. Can plain bicarbonate make an old drug work again? The target was a tough hospital germ that resists most drugs. The germ sits high on world lists of threats that need new treatments.

In lab tests, bicarbonate at levels found in blood made the drug far stronger. Dozens of patient strains became much easier to kill. In mice, the pair helped in blood infections but not in lung infections. The team links that split to local bicarbonate levels at each site. Body chemistry, it seems, can switch a drug on or off.
plos-pone-0350430:
Short Instagram videos now shape how many people learn about illness, so Sankirth Madabhushi and colleagues graded seventy-eight popular reels about Crohn's disease. Their 2026 PLOS One study scored the top-viewed English clips tagged for the condition on accuracy and basic quality marks.

Only about one in six came from medical professionals, and their clips taught more and scored higher on quality checks. Popularity, measured in likes and views, said nothing about accuracy. Videos giving medical advice scored worst for possible harm, and a surprising share of harmful clips came from professionals. The authors urge viewers to treat advice in reels with care.
plos-pone-0350730:
Dong Yan and colleagues studied winter comfort outdoors for older people in a park in Nanyang, China, in 2026. Cold season park use supports health and social life, but comfort limits differ for frail elders, who are often designed for as if they were robust.

The team grouped visitors by a frailty scale, measured the park microclimate, and matched comfort votes to a standard heat index. The neutral temperature fell as frailty rose, meaning frailer visitors felt cold less keenly in sensation yet adapted in fewer ways. Knowing these thresholds helps designers add shelter, seating, and sun traps where older park users need them.
plos-pone-0350830:
A muscle running down the front of the shin helps hold the foot's arch, and Naoki Aizu and colleagues tested exactly what it does to the arch and the big toe. Their 2026 PLOS One study electrically stimulated the muscle in twenty-five healthy young adults without letting the ankle bend.

Sensors tracked the arch bone's movement and toe angles. The arch bone shifted upward, backward, and inward, briefly raising the arch. The big toe straightened slightly in nearly every participant, moving away from the bunion direction. The higher the arch rose, the more the toe corrected, and bent toes corrected most. The results support training this muscle in foot care.
plos-pone-0351130:
Ni Luh Saddhwi Saraswati Adnyani and colleagues interviewed seventeen general practitioners in Indonesia about telemedicine apps for remote care. A fit model guided the talks: do the tools match the tasks doctors actually do? Remote visits cover history taking, advice, prescribing, and follow up, each with distinct needs for chat, records, and service links.

Doctors found apps broadly helpful for speed and reach, yet named gaps in clinical communication, joined up records, and task support. Fit broke down where apps forced workarounds for exams or referrals. Rich interview detail, the authors argue, shows builders what to fix first: tools shaped around real clinical tasks, not around video calls alone.
plos-pone-0351230:
Jordan Twombly Ellis and four co-authors report this 2026 PLOS One ecology study. It asks how researchers should sample the links among bees, flowers, and microbes. Honey bees make a handy test case. Scientists can sample honey from the hive, bees working inside it, or single bees caught while foraging. Using DNA tests, the team compared what each sample type reveals. They looked at the plants and microbes bees meet.

Honey and hive bees each carried richer mixes than single foragers. But single-bee samples were not just smaller versions of the hive picture. They captured variation among bees that the other samples missed. The authors conclude that each method tells a different, partial story. Studies should choose sampling with care, rather than treat the methods as interchangeable.
plos-pone-0351330:
Dentists grade tooth wear with scoring systems, but do two dentists reading the same digital scan agree? Maria Lorens and Iwona Tomaszewska tested two wear indices on about two hundred forty-six anonymized mouth scans, in this 2026 PLOS One reliability study.

Two trained examiners scored every section of each mouth independently under both systems. The simpler erosion index showed good agreement, with matching scores across the whole mouth. The fuller evaluation system landed in the moderate to good range. Checks also looked for one examiner consistently scoring higher. The authors conclude scans support dependable wear screening, with the simpler index the steadier of the two.
plos-pone-0351430:
Melissa Cantrell and four co-authors report a 2026 qualitative study of how researchers at four large American universities feel about open access publishing fees. Journals increasingly charge authors a fee to make articles free for anyone to read, and the study asks how even well-funded scholars experience that system.

Drawing on more than one hundred fifty open-ended survey responses, the team shows that many researchers feel trapped. They support open access in principle, yet resent the charges and feel powerless to change them. Feelings differed by career position and background. The authors argue the fee model is unsustainable even for privileged researchers, not only for those at poorer institutions.
plos-pone-0351630:
Jiaxin Peng and colleagues tested a dietary compound, ergothioneine, as a shield for kidneys sliding from sudden injury toward chronic disease. That slide often follows chemotherapy drugs like cisplatin, which scar the kidney's tubules. In mice given cisplatin, the team combined tissue checks, blood tests, and single-cell gene reading to see what the compound changed.

Treated mice kept better kidney function and showed less scarring. Inside tubule cells, genes for the cell's power plants, which injury had scrambled, moved partway back toward normal. In dish-grown tubule cells, the compound cut damaging stress gases, preserved the power plants' charge, and kept energy levels up. The picture points at mitochondria as the compound's protective site, and suggests a food-derived molecule worth testing as kidney medicine.
plos-pone-0351730:
Riwei Wang and colleagues used network toxicology, a mapping method that overlays a chemical's likely protein targets on a disease's gene web, to ask how bisphenol F might feed fatty liver disease. The chemical replaced the notorious bisphenol A in plastics and linings and now turns up widely in the environment. Database mining produced twenty-eight shared candidate targets between the compound and the disease.

Two candidates stood out when patient liver data were checked: a drug-processing enzyme and a hormone-carrying protein, both raised in diseased livers. Docking simulations showed the chemical binding its targets stably, and pathway analysis sketched the routes it could disturb. All of this is computational, a suspicion with an address rather than proof of harm, but it tells laboratory toxicologists exactly which liver proteins to test first in bisphenol F.
plos-pone-0351930:
Aliaa Gouda, Muhammad Arshad, and Jan Andrysek test whether a metronome-like beat can straighten the walking of prosthesis users. Their 2026 study applies rhythmic auditory stimulation during gait training. Uneven step timing is a common problem after leg amputation. The beat aimed to improve temporal symmetry. Motion analysis then checked the whole body's movement patterns, not just timing. Both above-knee and below-knee amputees took part, plus able-bodied volunteers in a special beat-matching task.

Timing did improve. Overall movement patterns, though, did not change significantly for either amputee group. Individuals varied a lot. Some gained symmetry cleanly, while others compensated elsewhere in the body. The able-bodied task revealed the hidden adjustments people make to chase an uneven beat. Experience with a prosthesis strongly shaped each user's response. Therapists should therefore expect personal, not average, reactions when adding rhythm to rehabilitation.
plos-pone-0352330:
Yizhou Lan, Jeroen van de Weijer, and Albert Lee present this 2026 PLOS One study of how Mandarin and Cantonese speakers in mainland China judge English accents, including each other's. More than one hundred sixty English learners rated recorded passages for how strong the accent sounded, how easy they were to understand, and social qualities such as status and friendliness.

Native English recordings were judged least accented and socially superior by everyone. Both listener groups rated Cantonese-accented English as more strongly accented than Mandarin-accented English, even though the two were equally understandable. Cantonese-accented speech was heard as friendlier but lower in class, while Mandarin-accented speech was rated more dynamic and superior. The authors show that even closely related language backgrounds carry a pecking order of accent prestige.
plos-pone-0352430:
Preechaya Wongkrajang and three colleagues compare five ways to detect lupus anticoagulant in this 2026 lab study. These antibodies disturb clotting tests and signal autoimmune risk. Detection is inconsistent, as every lab knows. The team analysed one hundred thirty-five plasma samples sent for testing. Four integrated assays skipped the traditional mixing step. A fifth followed the international stepwise algorithm faithfully, mixing study included. Two venom-based reagent brands were among the contenders.

Positive rates disagreed substantially. Depending on the assay, between about nineteen and thirty-six percent of samples counted as positive at one cutoff. A stricter cutoff trimmed some assays' rates sharply. Agreement between methods and links to related immune proteins were also mapped. For patients, the assay choice can decide whether they carry a lupus label at all. The comparison gives laboratories concrete grounds for picking, and questioning, their routine procedure.
plos-pone-0352930:
Chaofeng Niu led a team of eight authors on this 2026 analysis of heart failure across Asia over the years from 1990 to 2021, drawn from a worldwide disease burden database. Heart failure, where the heart cannot pump well enough, disables millions. The team counted cases and years lived with disability in forty-eight Asian countries.

Asia carried tens of millions of cases by 2021, a burden up by well over half since 1990, and China alone held more than two fifths. Severe cases drove most disability. Niu urges targeted action as the regional load keeps climbing.
plos-pone-0353130:
Kaibin Wei and four colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One methods paper on forecasting time series when training data are scarce. Their system turns number sequences into short written descriptions, lets a language model read those descriptions for extra context, and then adjusts a standard forecasting model's output accordingly. Most of the underlying model stays frozen, so adapting it to a new domain is cheap.

Across four datasets, including weather records, the prompt-guided system often beat the plain forecaster, with error reductions of around a tenth in some low-data settings. Gains were not uniform across every dataset and measure, which the authors note openly. The work suggests that written context can help forecasting models adjust to new fields without full retraining.
plos-pone-0353230:
Nichaporn Khumduang and three colleagues evaluate this 2026 PLOS One study of a balance test used to screen people with inner-ear disorders for fall risk. Forty-two patients took the Mini-BESTest balance battery plus walking and stand-up tests, and were classed as low or higher fall risk using their fall history and physical performance. The authors looked for a score cut-off that best separates the groups.

The total score separated the groups only modestly. A chosen cut-off caught almost all higher-risk patients but also flagged many low-risk ones, making it sensitive rather than precise. Among the subscores, reactive postural control, the ability to recover from a sudden push, showed the clearest signal. The authors suggest therapists pay special attention to that domain when planning rehabilitation.
plos-pone-0353630:
Ciaran Fairman and seven colleagues pilot a strength-training programme, with or without creatine, for people treated for colorectal cancer, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Twenty-seven participants trained three times a week for ten weeks, mixing clinic sessions with virtual ones; half took daily creatine and half a placebo powder. The trial's real question was feasibility — could such patients be recruited, kept, and kept safe?

Recruitment was hard: only a small share of those assessed enrolled. But those who joined stayed, trained faithfully, took their powders, and reported no serious harms. Strength and physical function improved modestly in both groups, with no clear creatine advantage. A bigger trial is justified, the authors say — with better recruitment plans.
plos-pone-0353930:
Yuan Li and Ningning Wang present a neural network that sorts sleep into stages. It works from brain and eye signals. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Sleep staging normally takes an expert hours of reading traces by hand. Their framework listens at several time scales at once. It pays close attention to the most telling moments. It ignores redundant stretches. It also blends brain-wave and eye-movement channels. Each channel is weighted moment by moment.

On two public sleep datasets the system did well. It classified stages with accuracy in the low-to-mid eighties. The authors also show which signal drove each decision. Clinicians need that kind of openness. Only then can they trust automated scoring in real sleep clinics.
plos-pone-0354030:
Hongwei Li and co-authors build an AI system that cleans up underwater photographs blurred and tinted by water itself. Robots and divers need clear images, but many enhancers either invent detail or run too slowly on large frames. Their design steers a fast sequence model with variables drawn from the physics of underwater light loss, and merges detail across scales without letting the model balloon in size.

Across four public test sets, the system scored near the top on standard quality measures while staying compact. The authors report it handled even very large frames thanks to its step-by-step cost growing gently with image size. Li and colleagues pitch the design for subsea robots that must see clearly in real time.
plos-pone-0354130:
Nagarajan Vasugi and Madurakavi Karthikeyan present a tiny antenna designed to live inside the body, in this 2026 PLOS ONE engineering paper. Implanted medical devices, from pacemakers to glucose monitors, need to send data out through tissue safely. Their design, smaller than a fingernail, combines a rhombus centre, keyhole cut-outs, and a reversed L-shaped patch to broadcast on two bands used for medical telemetry.

Bench tests in minced pork and salt water matched the computer simulations well. Safety checks on how much radio energy tissue absorbs, plus link calculations, stayed within accepted limits. A dependable in-body antenna is one of the quiet parts that makes remote patient monitoring possible.
plos-pone-0354330:
Nader M Hanna and four colleagues published this 2026 population study of lung cancer care in Ontario, Canada. Linking health records for well over a hundred thousand patients diagnosed between 2007 and 2023. They asked how income, having a family doctor, immigration, and distance to a cancer center related to late diagnosis and receiving surgery.

Over half arrived with stage four disease. Patients lacking a family doctor were far more likely to be diagnosed late, and surgery rates fell steeply with age and illness burden. Hanna calls the gaps social inequities needing upstream fixes.
plos-pone-0354430:
Janice Park and four colleagues ask the people who would actually carry out emergency pig depopulation what they think of two newer methods, in this 2026 survey study. When disease outbreaks strike, whole herds sometimes must be killed quickly, and water-based foam and high-expansion nitrogen foam have been developed as alternatives for large operations. The researchers surveyed farm owners, veterinarians, and staff after they watched demonstrations of both methods.

Respondents rated the nitrogen foam as harder to perform and implement than the water-based foam. Their written comments dwelled most on ease of use and cost, and some asked for pre-assembled kits or outside services. The authors conclude that demonstrations alone will not prepare the industry; training pathways and practical support need building before an emergency forces the issue.
plos-pone-0354930:
SiLing Ren led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of a healthy woman's vaginal microbes across one menstrual cycle. Her community was dominated by Lactobacillus crispatus, a species tied to good vaginal health. Samples at six points in the cycle underwent full-length gene sequencing and activity profiling to see whether the microbe's behavior changed.

The species stayed dominant by numbers, but its gene activity rose and fell in rhythmic, phase-specific waves, reshaping its metabolism over the cycle. Ren argues this flexible activity, not just abundance, explains how the species holds its ground.
plos-pone-0355130:
Gang Zhou, Shishi Liao, and Qi Jiang wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on wireless power transfer, sending electricity without cables. The system design is called LCC-S, one layout of compensating circuits. Working from an equivalent circuit model, the authors carry out multi-objective parameter design, tuning several goals at once.

Pareto analysis then maps the trade-offs, showing which designs cannot improve one goal without losing on another. Wireless charging designers must balance power, efficiency, and size, so a trade-off map is more honest than a single best answer. Engineers building charging pads and vehicle systems are the readers for this design method.
plos-pone-0355230:
Shiho Miyata led a team of eight authors on this 2026 cattle genetics study of mastitis, a costly udder infection in dairy herds. They defined susceptible Holstein cows as those suffering three or more bouts in one lactation, then scanned the genomes of fifty susceptible and healthy cows and checked candidate markers in another hundred.

Most candidate markers sat on the X chromosome, hinting that inherited variation there shapes udder immunity. A small marker panel was rarely wrong when it cleared a cow as low risk. Miyata says bigger herds must confirm the markers before breeding programs use them.
plos-pone-0355730:
Martin Ackah and colleagues build a questionnaire that measures what rest actually feels like for adults living with long-term fatiguing illness. Rest is prescribed often in rehab, yet it is poorly defined, and no tool captured its full experience. The team drafted questions with expert input, then tested them on adults with such conditions, checking structure, consistency, and links with existing coping scales.

The final scale holds a compact set of items in six themes. They cover rest habits, how restoring rest feels, and planning rest. They also cover barriers, emotions about rest, and the risk of resting too little. Several themes lined up sensibly with older coping measures. Ackah and colleagues say clinicians can now track rest quality instead of just telling patients to rest more.
plos-pone-0355830:
Maria Pérez and co-authors trace the careers of tens of thousands of United States medical school graduates to find who leaves academic medicine before reaching senior rank. Women and several minority groups remain scarce among senior faculty, and the leak points matter for fixing that. The study follows graduates appointed as junior faculty over two decades and models which traits predict early exit.

Women, Asian faculty, and underrepresented groups each left at higher rates than white male peers, as did those carrying debt or starting at the lowest rank. A year of research during residency and a research-heavy first institution both protected against leaving. Department mattered too. Pérez and colleagues argue that retention fixes must start long before promotion decisions arrive.
plos-pone-0355930:
XueRu Li and co-authors mapped how a traditional Chinese herb, Isatis root, might act against liver inflammation tied to hepatitis B. The herb is prized for antiviral and anti-inflammatory use, yet its molecular routes were murky. Their 2026 study used network pharmacology, docking calculations, and motion simulations rather than bench experiments.

Screening found seventeen active compounds in the herb. Their predicted targets overlapped with hepatitis B disease genes at well over a hundred points. Network analysis highlighted hub genes, and pathway checks pointed to inflammation and survival signalling. Docking and simulation runs supported stable binding for key pairs. Li and colleagues present the map as a hypothesis generator for later laboratory testing, not as proof of clinical effect.
plos-pone-0356630:
Zhuwen Yan and coauthors published a 2026 engineering paper in PLOS ONE on keeping steel strip flat during cold rolling under very high force. When a mill squeezes strip hard, ordinary roll bending controls can fail, leaving wavy edges and uneven thickness. The team studied a six-high tandem mill and replaced slow physics simulations with fast statistical stand-ins, then searched them with two optimization algorithms for the best roll bending settings.

Under the heaviest rolling force they tested, the optimized combination of work-roll and intermediate-roll bending cut the thickness variation across the strip to about a third of its former value. Surface crown errors shrank as well, pressure became far more even, and edge waves nearly disappeared. Analysis also shows how extreme force shifts the best settings, and why intermediate rolls resist certain wave defects better. The approach offers mills a route to flatter, high-strength strip.
plos-pone-0356730:
Sandra Pamela Cangui-Panchi and colleagues tested whether the liquid left behind by growing Lactobacillus bacteria, with no living cells in it, can kill dangerous germs on its own. Their 2026 study brewed supernatants from thirty strains and challenged fifteen bacterial and yeast pathogens, including drug-resistant isolates, measuring killing power, then probing what in the liquid does the work.

A third of the liquids worked well, cutting viable microbes by a hundred- to ten-thousand-fold, and effectiveness varied by strain batch rather than species label. Neutralizing the acid removed only part of the punch, and enzymes removed another part, implying a cocktail of acids and protein-like weapons. Liver cells tolerated the liquids; immune cells showed some stress. The results support these brews as food and health preservative candidates.
plos-pone-0357030:
Juan Felipe Valdés-López and colleagues published a 2026 laboratory study in PLOS ONE on how the COVID-19 virus turns off a calming immune pathway. Severe COVID is driven by runaway inflammation, especially the signal interleukin 6, from immune cells called mononuclear phagocytes. The team combined gene profiles from patients' blood cells with dish-grown macrophages, and tested what the active form of vitamin D could do.

Infection switched on an inflammatory program tied to disease severity, flooding the cells with interleukin 6 and its signaling machinery. At the same time, the virus dimmed the vitamin D receptor and the genes it normally controls, leaving the cells less able to respond to vitamin D's braking effect. Adding that active vitamin D form strongly suppressed the inflammatory output in their functional tests. The findings sketch a mechanism for the cytokine storm, and why vitamin D status may matter in severe infection.
plos-pone-0358130:
Jae Ho Shim, Ji Yeon Lee, Jihye Han, and Hyeon Soo Kim published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It concerns muscle wasting during spaceflight, where weightlessness weakens astronauts. Using integrative transcriptomics, the study identifies an eighteen-gene candidate panel measurable in blood.

A blood-accessible biomarker panel would let flight surgeons track muscle loss with a blood draw instead of scans or biopsies. Genes whose activity can be read in blood and that change over time suit the longitudinal monitoring the title describes. Space medicine teams planning long missions are the readers who need such a simple tracking tool.
plos-pone-0358330:
Faith Walker and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on conservation genetics. Their subject is the spotted bat, a rare North American species. The team draws on three kinds of samples: ancient, historical, and modern, spanning a long stretch of the species' past and present.

Comparing DNA across eras shows how bat populations have changed in size and connection over time. Museum specimens and old remains let genetics reach back before modern surveys began. Wildlife agencies deciding how to protect a scarce bat need this long view to judge whether today's populations are shrinking or holding steady.
plos-pone-0359330:
Guy Rubin and three colleagues report a small laboratory test of a new enzyme treatment for Dupuytren's disease, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The disease builds collagen rich cords in the hand that slowly pull fingers into a bent position. An injected bacteria made collagenase already treats it without surgery, and the team asked whether a lab made version of a related enzyme could do the same job.

They took cords removed during surgery from five patients, injected the test enzyme or a plain buffer, and pulled the tissue apart on a measuring machine. Enzyme treated cords tore under clearly less force, roughly a third lower in this tiny series. The authors call it early proof of concept and say dose, timing, and safety work must come before any patient use.
plos-pone-0359530: Hormenu and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on heart and metabolic health in Cape Coast, Ghana. They measured how common cardiometabolic disease is among informal sector workers, who often lack steady pay and health cover. They also looked at what raises the risk. The data came from the CarMeR study. Street traders and casual workers are easy to miss in health planning.
plos-pone-0359630:
Jiayi Peng and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. Named RCTE, it is a piece of AI software, an object detection framework that sorts what it finds into many classes. Its job is reading dental panoramic radiographs, the wide X-ray images that show all the teeth at once.

Object detection software draws attention to specific findings in an image and labels what they are. A framework built for dental panoramas must handle crowded, overlapping teeth and varied problems in one scan. Dentists and imaging researchers could use such tools as a second set of eyes, and this work adds one more candidate system to compare.
pmc-13197330:
Gautam Panwar and colleagues set out a 2026 trial protocol on yoga for fatty liver disease. The disease, called MASLD, is the most common long-term liver problem in the world. It links closely to obesity, high blood pressure, and type 2 diabetes, and yoga may help on several fronts at once.

The trial enrolled seventy-two adults at a hospital in Dehradun, India. Half get standard care plus a sixty-minute online yoga module five days a week for three months. Half get standard care alone. Checks cover liver fat on ultrasound, liver enzymes, blood sugar, weight, mood, and quality of life. As a protocol, it reports no results yet; findings will test yoga as an add-on therapy.
pmc-13198030:
Franziska Lezius and colleagues surveyed staff in an international tele-intensive care network in 2026. Tele-intensive care links expert hubs to smaller units by video and data feeds. Hard outcome data are tough to gather across borders, so the team asked frontline staff about benefit and acceptance.

Thirty staff at ten spoke sites in four countries answered an online survey. Most felt well supported, both clinically and personally. Trust and working ties with the hub rated high. Ethics and data protection stood out as top concerns throughout. Views were alike across quite different health systems. The authors see room to grow and call the model well accepted, with privacy care as a lasting priority.
pmc-13202130:
Digital health is a fashionable label, and a 2026 conceptual article by Brigitte Séroussi argues the science underneath it has an older name. Writing alone, Séroussi compares digital health with biomedical and health informatics and asks which should anchor education, research, and professional identity in healthcare technology.

Her analysis portrays informatics as a mature science covering data representation, knowledge modeling, decision support, safety, and ethics. Digital health, by contrast, is framed as an applied layer that turns that science into products and services like telehealth and mobile apps. She recommends reintegrating digital health within informatics as its translational arm, rather than letting the newer term absorb the discipline.
pmc-13212630:
Șerban Talpoș leads a team reporting in 2026 on long-term satisfaction after jaw surgery that corrects deformities of face and bite. Patients were followed for at least three years after operations on both jaws planned by an interdisciplinary team.

The cohort held 126 patients, who answered a customised twenty-item questionnaire about appearance, function, and feelings. Satisfaction ran high, especially for smile appearance and self-confidence, and stayed steady across patient groups. Complications affected about one patient in nine, most often plate infection in the lower jaw, and they were the main factor linked to lower satisfaction. All complications were resolved without lasting harm.
pmc-13213130:
Biset Asrade Mekonnen and co-authors ask in 2026 how homes in Bahir Dar City, Ethiopia, store and throw out old drugs. Medicines kept too long or dumped with care can poison kids and foul soil and water.

The team spoke with more than 400 homes. Only a third knew the safe way to deal with old drugs, though more than half felt keen to do right. Most homes kept spare drugs, chiefly pain pills and antibiotics, left when a course ended or side effects hit. Old stock most often went out with the trash. Few homes took drugs back to a pharmacy. Age, schooling, health cover, know-how, and outlook each linked to safer habits.
pmc-13215530:
Huibo Yan and co-authors present a 2026 analysis of HIV and AIDS among Chinese adults of reproductive age, drawing on Global Burden of Disease 2023 estimates. The study covers 1990 to 2023 and projects trends forward to 2035.

Age-standardized incidence, prevalence, mortality, and disability rates all rose steeply across the period, with prevalence up about eightfold. Unsafe sex accounted for 70 percent of HIV deaths in 2023. The projections suggest male incidence will level off near five per hundred thousand while female rates keep climbing, which widens the gap between the sexes. The authors argue for prevention strategies that differ by gender and for care planning aimed at a growing chronic burden.
pmc-13215630:
Amalie Skovgaard and co-authors present a 2026 protocol for a scoping review on how round-the-clock movement patterns relate to mental health in frontline workers. Sleep, sitting, and activity are usually studied separately, and the authors want the combined picture.

The review will follow established scoping methods, include English-language studies from 2000 to 2025, and chart how movement was measured alongside outcomes such as burnout, depression, and sleep quality. By May 2026 the searches had already identified 527 studies for charting. The authors expect the finished map to expose methodological and occupational gaps and to guide policy for workers in high-stress, irregular-schedule jobs.
pmc-13216330:
Safaa Ragab and co-authors present a 2026 study on turning rice husk waste into cellulose acetate, a widely used biodegradable material. Their twist is a copper perchlorate catalyst that drives the acetylation under mild, solvent-free conditions.

Working with cellulose taken from rice husks and with commercial microcrystalline cellulose, the team varied catalyst amount, temperature, and reaction time. The refined material converted almost fully, with yields near 98 percent at room temperature, while husk cellulose reached about 87 to 93 percent, the figure set by temperature. The degree of substitution tracked catalyst dose, heat, and time in a strong, steady way. Product identity was checked by spectroscopy and diffraction, and the authors present the method as a tunable route to di- and tri-acetates.
pmc-13217430:
Rogers Makonje and co-authors present a 2026 survey of diabetes self-care among 385 adults attending a regional hospital clinic in Mbale, eastern Uganda. Managing type 2 diabetes day to day, through medication, diet, activity, and monitoring, decides long-term outcomes, and local performance was unknown.

Only about a third of patients, 34.6 percent, reached the study's bar for good self-management on a standard questionnaire. Doing well clustered with advantage and support: higher education, employment, and higher income each raised the odds, as did having diabetes for fewer years, knowing its complications, and having family backing. General diabetes knowledge alone showed no link. The authors argue that interventions should target money, family, and complication awareness, not just information.
pmc-13217930: In 2026 BMC Medical Imaging published a short correction to an article on Alzheimer's disease detection from MRI images, by Pande Sandeep Dwarkanth and co-authors. The notice is a correction only: it fixes the spelling of one author's name, which appeared as Hanen Karamati instead of Hanen Karamti, and confirms that the original article has been updated. No data, methods, or conclusions are changed.
pmc-13218030:
Tatjana Kvitkina and colleagues set out a 2026 study protocol on long COVID in people with diabetes in Germany. Diabetes clearly worsens the acute course of COVID-19 infection, but whether it also raises the risk of lingering post-COVID illness is unresolved. Nationwide population data on that question are missing, and the protocol fills the gap.

The planned study will use billing records from Germany's statutory health insurance, which covers nearly the whole population. The team will compare how often long COVID was diagnosed between 2021 and 2023 in people with and without diabetes, and look for risk factors behind any difference. They will also track deaths and hospital stays, including admissions for heart attack, stroke, and diabetic foot problems, over the three years after a long COVID diagnosis. Sensitivity analyses will test how under-diagnosis might distort the results.
pmc-13218130:
Ambrose Okello and colleagues studied critically ill patients with electrolyte imbalances at a Ugandan referral hospital in a 2026 prospective cohort study. Abnormal blood levels of sodium, potassium, and chloride are common in severe illness and shape survival, yet data from sub-Saharan Africa are scarce. The team worked in the emergency department of Mbarara Regional Referral Hospital.

Over four months in 2023, the study enrolled 400 non-trauma adults judged critically ill by early warning score, measured their electrolytes on arrival, and followed them for 14 days. Electrolyte imbalances were widespread, most patients had several at once, and 14-day mortality reached 59.9 percent, with most deaths in the first three days. Being referred from another facility raised the risk of death, as did heart failure and past alcohol use. Care from specialists, correcting electrolytes before referral, and prompt ward admission were protective, giving concrete priorities for emergency care in similar settings.
pmc-13219230:
Kaitlin Hellier and co-authors examine what four years does to selenium-tellurium evaporation material in a 2026 study. Alloys of selenium and tellurium are laid down as thin films for photodetectors and optoelectronic devices, valued for their light sensitivity and phase-change traits. Their stability as stored feedstock had barely been studied, even though spoiled material degrades every film made from it.

Pellets stored in plain air for four years were compared with fresh pellets under inert gas. Microscopy showed the surface sprouting protrusions and crystals, and analyses found surface crystallization plus oxygen-bearing phases, chiefly tellurium oxide and crystalline selenium. Fresh pellets aged under heat and humidity developed the same defects, confirming oxidation and crystallization as the decay route. Devices from the spoiled material showed higher resistivity, unstable dark current, and weaker light response.
