The authors warn controlled storage and handling are essential for reliable devices from these alloys.
pmc-13220830:
Austin M. Breaux and colleagues compare two ultrasound-guided nerve blocks for pain after surgery in a 2026 review. Splitting the breastbone, the median sternotomy, gives surgeons access for bypass and valve but leaves pain that drives opioid use and slows breathing and recovery. Blocking the nerves of the chest wall through fascial planes has become a component of gentler pain plans.

The two contenders, the pecto-intercostal fascial block and the transversus thoracic plane block, reach overlapping territory by routes. The studies suggest comparable pain relief and opioid sparing, with hints that the pecto-intercostal approach may cut opioid consumption or delay the first request for medication. The review widens to pharmacogenomics: how a patient's drug-handling genes and physiology bend their response to the anesthetics and opioids. Technique depth, coverage, risk, and experience shape the choice, and the authors recommend individualizing block selection rather than crowning a winner.
pmc-13221430:
Mirashini Swaminathan and collaborators report a 2026 United Kingdom cohort study of gut and liver inflammation caused by cancer immunotherapy. Checkpoint inhibitors help many cancers, yet they can trigger colitis and hepatitis. Records covered 2,049 patients treated at twelve NHS centers between 2016 and 2018 for melanoma, lung, or kidney cancer.

Colitis appeared in about one patient in eleven, hepatitis in about one in fourteen. Steroids handled most cases, though a minority needed stronger immune suppression. Patients who developed either condition survived longer on average than those without such side effects. Suppression treatment did not worsen survival in colitis, which supports its use when steroids fall short.
pmc-13222630:
Maopei Chen and co-authors reappraise arterial infusion chemotherapy combined with whole-body treatment for inoperable liver cancer, in a 2026 study of 302 newly diagnosed patients treated between 2018 and 2023. The approach delivers chemotherapy straight into the liver's artery while systemic drugs, including immune and targeted agents, work throughout the body. Survival was tracked and modeled for influencing factors.

Median time without progression passed eleven months, and median survival reached thirty months. Survival rates at one, two, and three years fell gradually from about two thirds to about two fifths. Liver enzyme levels, inflammation ratios, spread beyond the liver, and treatment mix all tied to outcomes. The regimen was well tolerated overall.
pmc-13227030:
Keith Bodger and the VEST Study Group report a 2026 real-world study of vedolizumab, a gut-targeted antibody drug for inflammatory bowel disease, across twenty-two United Kingdom centres. Trial results do not always match routine practice, so 364 patients receiving the drug as standard care were followed with activity scores, physician assessments, and patient questionnaires at each infusion.

Fifty-eight percent were still on the drug after a year. Among those who persisted, quality-of-life scores improved markedly by fourteen weeks and held at one year. Remission rates at fourteen weeks hovered near thirty percent for both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, including steroid-free remission. Side effects forcing a stop were rare, at about three percent, and earlier health status predicted who stayed on treatment.
pmc-13229930:
Andrew Kerwin and colleagues describe in 2026 a young boy whose rare ankle growth kept returning after surgery. The condition, called Trevor disease, makes extra cartilage and bone grow from one side of a joint end in children. He was three years old when care began, with pain, stiffness, and trouble walking.

Over five years he needed three operations to remove the growth, even though each removal looked complete during surgery. Symptoms guided each decision to operate again rather than a fixed schedule. Growth returning more than once shows how long watchful follow-up must last in a growing child. Families can use the timeline to understand that one operation may not end the problem.
pmc-13232630:
Jan Erik Bellingrath develops in 2026 a formal theory for why the felt present moment stretches and shrinks. His self-simulational theory ties the width of subjective time to how the brain models itself. The work rebuilds that theory from the free energy principle, a broad account of how living systems stay organized.

A computer model of layered time inference then reproduced two classic quirks without extra assumptions. Voluntary actions and their effects feel closer together in time than they are, a pull called intentional binding. Deep meditation states, where time sense nearly vanishes, also fell out of the same machinery. Mood, boredom, flow, and near-death states are folded into the same frame, which could be rebuilt inside artificial agents.
pmc-13233030:
Ambre Sibari and colleagues issued a 2026 study testing a kinder way to measure how well flea and tick products stop sand fly bites in dogs. Sand flies can pass on Leishmania parasites, so anti-feeding performance matters. Standard tests expose sedated dogs to live flies, which conflicts with the replacement, reduction, and refinement principles for animal research.

Twelve dogs received either a dinotefuran, permethrin, and pyriproxyfen spot-on or no treatment. Flies fed on the dogs directly and, in parallel, on hair samples through an artificial feeding system. The treated product kept anti-feeding efficacy above 80 percent for a month in both setups, and fly survival also fell. The matching results support the hair-based model as a humane substitute for live-dog testing.
pmc-13233630:
Kimberly A. DiMauro and colleagues published a 2026 cohort study of paraneoplastic neurological syndromes tied to the anti-Hu antibody, also called ANNA1. In these syndromes, the immune response to a cancer, most often small cell lung cancer, attacks the nervous system instead. The single-center study followed 45 patients, tracking disability, wheelchair dependence, and survival.

The syndrome's opening form mattered greatly. Patients starting with limbic encephalitis, inflammation of the brain's memory centers, faced much higher hazards of serious disability and death. A surprising result emerged among lung cancer patients. Those with the syndrome survived longer than 1,513 patients with the same cancer alone. Their hazard of death ran about forty-one percent lower after adjustment. The authors read this as evidence that the anti-tumor immune response also restrains the cancer.
pmc-13233730:
Xiuli Wang and Lior Goldberg published a 2026 article on why CAR T cell therapy cures some leukemia patients for good while others relapse. The treatment re-engineers a patient's T cells to hunt CD19-marked cancer cells, and first responses in relapsed B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia are strong. Yet between thirty and eighty percent of patients eventually relapse with cancer that still carries the target.

The authors describe their trial-based study comparing long-term responders with patients who relapsed within months, matched carefully for clinical factors. Their team profiled the infused cells and later bone marrow samples across metabolism, mitochondrial shape, single-cell proteins, and metabolites. The framing idea gives the article its title: fit T cells need fertile ground, meaning a supportive bone marrow niche, for responses to last.
pmc-13234830:
Mingchen Zhang and colleagues created in 2026 an injectable gel dressing for infected diabetic wounds, which heal slowly and often become reinfected. The gel starts from hyaluronic acid, a natural skin-related molecule, carrying an attached antibiotic called polymyxin B. Iron ions linked through a helper molecule hold the network together with reversible bonds. Those reversible links let the gel thin under pressure and pass through a needle.

Laboratory tests killed nearly all Escherichia coli bacteria and most Staphylococcus aureus bacteria on contact. The material proved compatible with living tissue in safety checks. In diabetic mice, treated wounds shrank much further by day seven than wounds covered with a commercial dressing. Microscope examination showed better skin regrowth and more collagen laid down in treated wounds. The authors propose the gel for clinical development.
pmc-13234930:
Abeer Salama and co-authors tested in 2026 whether chestnut fruit extracts can calm fits brought on in mice by a stimulant. Epilepsy involves oxidative stress and inflammation in the brain, so plant compounds are studied as add-on options. Fruits were extracted twice, once with weaker ethanol and once with pure ethanol. Lab profiling matched the two fractions before animal testing.

More than seventy compounds appeared, mainly phenolic acids and flavonoids with known protective effects. The pure ethanol fraction held richer chemistry and showed much stronger power in test tube assays. In mice, that fraction delayed fit onset nearly threefold and shortened fits compared with untreated animals. Brain measures moved in a protective direction, with calming signals up and damage markers down. Results came close to those of a standard sedative drug.
pmc-13235230:

pmc-13236230:

pmc-13236830:

pmc-13236930:

pmc-13239330:

pmc-13239630:

pmc-13239930:

pmc-13240230:

pmc-13241330:

pmc-13241430:

pmc-13262530:

pmc-13262730:
Liqing Yu comments on a new finding about how dietary fat enters the gut's lymph vessels in a 2026 journal article. pmc-13262830:

Girls gained slightly more height, less weight, and about half a point of body mass index. The largest height gains came between 2005 and 2010 in both sexes. Girls' weight and body mass rose until 2015, then declined, while boys' kept rising.
pmc-13262930:
Eric Nyarko and colleagues ask Ghanaian health workers what a snakebite phone app must do first. Their rankings give developers a priority order grounded in end users, not guesses.
pmc-13263330:

pmc-13263430:

pmc-13263530:
Jack S. Hardman and co-authors present a 2026 systematic review of ways to improve antibiotic use in children with suspected infections in poorer countries. A diagnostic algorithm helped in Ghana and Burkina Faso but not Uganda. The authors call for adaptable tools tested for both safety and prescribing quality.
pmc-13263730:
Whitney Jin and colleagues give radiation oncologists a three-dimensional map of the tumor they just removed. After head and neck surgery, shifted anatomy makes aiming adjuvant radiation guesswork. Target volumes changed in three cases for the main zone and three for the boost zone, expanding or shrinking with better margin knowledge. Doses to nearby organs shifted only slightly. pmc-13263930:

One hundred patients aged eighteen to sixty-five will be randomized across hospitals in Sweden, Norway, Denmark, and Finland.

pmc-13264130:
Hanyang Yu and a large engineering team create titanium implants whose surfaces generate small electric fields in a 2026 study. Plain titanium is body-friendly but biologically quiet, so bone often bonds slowly without complex coatings. Their printing method varies how tantalum melts into titanium during laser fabrication, leaving a patterned mix reminiscent of Damascus steel across the implant surface.

After simple oxidation, the pattern yields steady surface voltage differences tunable across the range found in living tissues. Cell and animal tests showed bone-forming performance nearly double that of a standard titanium control in cranial defect repair. Migration and differentiation of bone cells both improved. The built-in field survives later machining, which suits real implant manufacturing.
pmc-13264230:
Ivan Cherrez-Ojeda and a very large international team ask why doctors underuse patient questionnaires in eczema and chronic hives care in a 2026 study. Standard patient-reported measures capture itch, sleep loss and daily burden that brief visits miss. Earlier network research showed low routine use across specialist centers, so this follow-up surveyed thousands of physicians in forty-five centers about barriers, habits and personal characteristics linked to reluctance.

The excerpt outlines the cross-sectional design using the network questionnaire across reference centers for urticaria and related swelling disorders. Linking perceived obstacles to actual use patterns can reveal whether time, training or doubts about value drive the gap. Findings aim to guide practical fixes so patient voice enters treatment decisions more consistently in allergy and skin clinics.
pmc-13264530:
Chandreyee Roy and Ahmed Sameer published a 2026 survey study on pornography use and thoughts of suicide among young adults. Past work often assumed more use means worse mental health, but results have been mixed. The pair asked whether the reasons for use matter more than the amount.

Amount of use showed a small negative link once mood was counted. Using pornography to avoid feelings linked to higher suicidal thoughts, while use for sexual pleasure linked to lower ones. The authors stress the study shows links, not causes, and urge focus on emotion control.
pmc-13264630:
Omnia Mahareek and co-authors published a 2026 study on a natural carrier that ferries a cancer drug to liver tumors. The carrier is surfactin, a soap-like molecule made by a common bacterium, which can fold into tiny spheres on its own. They loaded it with doxorubicin, a widely used cancer drug.

The particles held a strong share of drug, 36 percent by their measure, and released more of it in acid conditions like those in tumors. In dish tests, the loaded carrier killed liver cancer cells at a far lower dose than the dose that harmed normal cells. The authors see a safer, targeted route for this drug.
pmc-13264930:
Juliana Soares Tenorio de Araújo led a 2026 national study of COVID-19 vaccination among people experiencing homelessness in Brazil. This group faces steep barriers to care, and how many finished their vaccine schedule was unclear. Interviewers met participants face to face in every state capital and the federal district during 2022 and 2023.

Finishing the schedule linked most strongly to a prior COVID-19 diagnosis, trust in vaccine efficacy, and support for mandatory vaccination. Visits from street clinic health agents more than tripled the odds of completion, and receiving government aid also helped. Trust in federal authorities and community information sources mattered too. The authors say outreach and trust are the levers for closing the remaining gaps.
pmc-13266030:

Dietary exclusions and eating orientations were recorded as controls. Age and gender are included for each participant. pmc-13266230:
Jessica A Atkinson and the team compare two blood pressure drugs in pregnancy using Australian linked data (2026). Labetalol and nifedipine are both common oral choices, with unclear comparative safety. The target trial emulation covered Victorian pregnancies from 2009 to 2020. Results ran from first prescription to four weeks after birth.

A total of 7,416 pregnancies qualified, and most got labetalol first. After adjustment, nifedipine linked to higher risk of the combined maternal harm outcome. Event rates differed by several percentage points between groups. Neonatal results formed the second primary measure. The design mimics a trial using routine data.
pmc-13266830:
Jean-Pierre Frat, Rémi Coudroy, and Arnaud W Thille comment in 2026 on the NAVIGATE trial of early breathing support outside intensive care. The trial enrolled 523 ward patients with mild acute low-oxygen respiratory failure across hospitals in Italy, Greece, and Kazakhstan. Half received scheduled sessions of mask ventilation added to standard oxygen, while the others received usual care.

Patients varied widely, from pneumonia to heart-related fluid in the lungs and problems after surgery. Most had low oxygen without clear distress signs. Frat and colleagues use that mix to question when early mask support truly helps and for whom timing matters most.
pmc-13267830:

pmc-13268230:

The authors call the findings exploratory and say larger, clinically realistic studies must confirm them before any test reaches practice.
pmc-13268630:

pmc-13268930:
Jing-Yan Song and Feng-Yi Dong explore in 2026 how electroacupuncture might rescue failing embryo implantation, working through a tiny RNA carried between cells. pmc-13269030:

The authors say these lab values may help flag the sickest newborns early.
pmc-13270030:

pmc-13271730:

pmc-13272230:

pmc-13272330:

pmc-13272430:

pmc-13272530:

pmc-13272630:

pmc-13272830:

pmc-13273530:

pmc-13273630:

pmc-13274130:

pmc-13274430:

The finished domain will join a larger public database for mapping health risks and strengths together across the state.
pmc-13276030:
Vivian Pascal Willers and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on making amino acids without farms. pmc-13276230:

pmc-13276430:

pmc-13276530:

pmc-13276930:

pmc-13277530:

pmc-13277630:

pmc-13278530:

pmc-13278930:

pmc-13279030:

pmc-13279430:

pmc-13280330:

At three years, their infection odds stayed near four fold as well. Side effect odds rose by about one third, and revision surgery odds rose too. pmc-13280530:
Qing Liu and colleagues published a 2026 review of SREBPs, a family of transcription factors that act as master switches for fat and cholesterol production in cells. Tumors lean on these switches to build membranes and signaling molecules for growth. Abnormal SREBP activation shows up across cancers. The review notes the family's reach into obesity, atherosclerosis, diabetes, and neurodegenerative disease. That reach makes its regulation a medical concern.

The authors explain how the proteins sit inactive in a membrane until cleavage frees them. They then enter the nucleus and switch on genes for cholesterol, fatty acid, and triglyceride synthesis or uptake. The authors map how tumors hijack that machinery and how activation pushes malignant progression, and which drug strategies aim at the pathway.  Their verdict is that blocking SREBP activity is a promising anticancer direction. The regulatory networks are intricate, and need fuller mapping before treatments can exploit them.
pmc-13280630:
Po-Ting Lin and colleagues published a 2026 study on liver cancer tied to hepatitis B, a virus that harms the liver. The team asked whether small gene differences could predict how patients fare on immune therapy. Their chart review covered ninety-six patients treated between 2020 and 2023. All got two immune drugs given as standard care.

One gene form stood out. Patients who carried it went close to twenty months before their cancer grew again. They also had a lower chance of a sharp rise in a liver enzyme, a sign of liver strain. Four other gene variants showed no link. The authors say a simple gene test might help doctors plan care for these patients.
pmc-13280730:
Li PingGen and colleagues published a 2026 study of a dissection strategy for skull surgery that chooses instruments by the properties of each tissue layer. In frontotemporal cranioplasty, the skin-muscle flap often sticks tightly to the membrane covering the brain, and tearing that membrane is a major risk. The team reviewed 124 operations from 2020 to 2025. Of these, 55 used their biophysics-based strategy, which uses blunt expansion along a loose natural plane and low-power heat cutting tuned to the electrical difference between muscle and membrane. The other 69 were conventional cases.

The strategy group lost less blood, averaging about 128 milliliters against about 277, and finished operations fifty minutes sooner. Membrane tears dropped from 39.1 percent to 12.7 percent, and blood collections under the skull after surgery fell. Infection and seizure rates did not differ. The authors present tissue-aware instrument matching as a practical, teachable way to make a reoperation safer and faster.
pmc-13281030:
Zhu Mao and colleagues used gene data to test a link between blood pressure and hay fever in a 2026 study. Hay fever, or allergic rhinitis, makes the nose run and itch with dust or pollen. Genes can act as a natural test, since they are set before habits form. The team checked the link in both directions with several math methods. They used more than four hundred gene markers tied to the top blood pressure number.

All methods agreed on one direction. People whose genes pointed to lower top pressure had a slightly higher risk of hay fever. The rise was small but steady across methods. The flip test found no sign that hay fever genes move blood pressure. The authors say low pressure itself may open the door to hay fever, a claim that needs more work.
pmc-13281330:
Min-Ho Lee and colleagues reviewed how to give less blood-thinning drug in heart bypass surgery in a 2026 paper. Bypass needs strong thinning so blood does not clot in the machine. At the end, a second drug cancels the first to restore normal clotting. Too much of either drug can raise bleeding after surgery. The review homes in on the bedside test that times how fast blood clots. Readings vary by the brand of test device in a steady, known way.

Ignoring that device gap can push drug doses higher than needed. Newer plans dose the canceling drug by the measured level of the first drug, not by a fixed rule. Such plans use far less on average. Leftover free canceling drug is itself a risk. The authors urge teams to match doses to device and to measured levels, aiming for the smallest safe amounts of both drugs.
pmc-13281630:
Laura Sheard and colleagues wrote a 2026 editorial on story-based research in a health journal they help run. Their field, implementation science, studies how to get proven care into daily use. Work based on talks, notes, and lived detail is pouring into the field. The editors welcome it, and they call for deep, self-aware studies. They also urge a wider mix of such methods and freer ways of reporting them.

The editorial sets fresh guiding rules for this kind of work in the journal. One change stands out. Authors will no longer need to attach a standard checklist to these submissions. The editors argue that stiff forms can squeeze out the very depth they want. They ask instead for clear thought about how knowledge was built. Rigidity, they say, should give way to judgment, as long as the reasoning is shown.
pmc-13281730:
Scott H Wirth and colleagues weighed two centuries of proof on a sore throat germ in a 2026 review. The germ can trigger acute rheumatic fever, a swelling illness that scars the heart. The review grades the chain of proof with two standard tools. One scores cause-and-effect clues, and one ranks study quality. It walks from early case notes in the 1800s to modern population studies. The stakes are live, since vaccines against the germ near approval.

Proof is strong that untreated infection raises fever risk. It is also strong that antibiotics cut that risk in many settings. Support is fair for the timing of the chain and for this germ as the sole trigger. The inner mechanism, an immune misfire after infection, rests on thinner though coherent proof. The authors flag two gaps: fresh forward-looking data in high-risk groups, and the role of skin infections.
pmc-13282130:
Xiaoyue Yang and co-authors demonstrate a 2026 surgical technique on video for fixing pelvic organ prolapse in several compartments at once. Prolapse means organs such as the bladder or womb slip downward from their normal place. Their method uses keyhole surgery through a single port and hangs a tailored mesh sideways inside the pelvis. One change fixes the mesh to a deep tissue layer at the back, adding support older methods lacked.

The patient shown was a seventy-two-year-old woman with the most severe stage of prolapse. Surgeons dissected to clear landmarks and tunnelled under the lining to place the mesh. The authors say the method rebuilt the front, middle, and back compartments while keeping the vagina intact. They present it as an option that may bring fewer problems than mesh placed through the vagina.
pmc-13282230:
Ana Martínez-Serrano and co-authors present a 2026 trial testing a phone app that helps nurses dose emergency drugs for children. During resuscitation, reviving a child whose heart has stopped, doses must be worked out fast by weight, and errors are common. The Spanish app, PEDIDOSIS, was compared with usual aids such as printed tables and calculators. One hundred five nurses from several hospitals took part in realistic simulations.

Wrong doses occurred in about half of drug rounds with usual methods. With the app, that fell to about a quarter. Large dose errors and repeated errors by the same nurse also dropped sharply. Nurses using the app reported higher satisfaction and lower stress, and rated its usability well. The authors say a focused dosing app can cut errors in a rare but high-stakes task. Real emergencies, not just simulations, would be the next test of the benefit.
pmc-13282430:
Suha Abdulateef Aloosi presents a 2026 clinical pilot study from Iraq on a tissue-handling step added to wisdom tooth surgery. Forty patients at a university dental clinic in Sulaimaniyah had partially erupted lower third molars removed between January 2024 and June 2025. All operations used a modified three-sided flap, a shaped cut in the gum. Half the patients, chosen at random, also received sulcular deepithelialisation, careful renewal of the gum crevice lining.

The added step did not change pain, swelling, or limited mouth opening after surgery. Yet dry socket, impaired healing, and sensitivity in the neighbouring molar, each seen in the control group, were absent in the treated group. Pain tracked with tooth splitting and a surgical difficulty score. Limited opening also tracked with splitting. The author concludes the lining step can improve soft-tissue healing and may prevent socket complications.
pmc-13282630:
Rafael Jordana and co-authors describe a 2026 taxonomy paper naming three new springtail species from Romania. Springtails are tiny soil arthropods, and the family covered here is among the most diverse and hardest to classify. Two new species belong to a large genus whose past descriptions were often incomplete. A third belongs to a scaled genus of forty-four known species found worldwide, and it lives alongside humans.

The authors use modern methods based on the pattern of bristles on the body, which have greatly sharpened species diagnoses in this group. Standardised terminology from recent global revisions also underpins their descriptions. Each species is formally characterised so other researchers can recognise it. The Romanian finds add to the known diversity of this family in the Palaearctic region, the northern Old World. The authors argue careful morphology still anchors biodiversity discovery, even as DNA tools spread.
pmc-13283130:
Drill selection for placing brain electrodes in children is compared head to head in a 2026 series from Mahalia Dalmage and partners. The surgery, called sEEG, maps seizure zones through small skull holes. Drill feel, ease, and speed affect safety, yet bone drills are often borrowed from orthopedics.

Charts covered patients treated in 2022 and 2023 at one center. Twelve patients got a new drill made for brain surgery, and five got a standard bone drill. The new drill gave steady hole times and clear feel of bone layers. No problems arose in that group. One patient in the bone drill group got a skin burn that led to wound breakdown and infection.
pmc-13283930:
LuYi Tang and colleagues combined two big United States data sources in 2026 to weigh high systolic blood pressure as a stroke driver. Systolic pressure is the top number in a blood pressure reading. Global Burden of Disease estimates gave the population picture, while the national NHANES survey gave person-level readings and histories across 1999 to 2023.

The burden data named high systolic pressure the leading risk factor for stroke burden in 2021, with its share growing since 2010, mainly among older people and women. Survey modelling tied a history of high pressure to clearly higher stroke odds even after many adjustments. Higher readings also linked to higher death risk among stroke survivors. A U-shaped curve appeared, with risk dipping at low pressures and climbing steeply above a turning point.
pmc-13284430:
Saad Bouchlarhem and co-authors describe a 2026 case of a fast-growing gum lesion in a 15-year-old patient. The lesion, called angiomatous epulis or gingival pyogenic granuloma, is benign and linked to irritation, trauma, swelling, or hormone shifts. Its red mass and easy bleeding can look like a malignant gum tumor at first sight.

The mass had grown over two months. X-ray and CT showed a well-defined soft-tissue lesion limited to the gum, with no bone loss or spread to nearby tissue. Full surgical removal was done, and tissue study confirmed the benign diagnosis. The case shows how imaging helps rule out cancer, judge extent, and plan safe removal.
pmc-13284830:
Eren Sakarcan, Jeanette Fulton, and Shashank Kaushik present a 2026 case report linking a rare syndrome with unusual breast duct growths. A 34-year-old woman with Maffucci syndrome, a rare condition with cartilage tumors, blood vessel growths, and bone deformity, developed diffuse papillomatosis inside breast ducts. Fewer than 300 Maffucci cases have ever been reported.

The woman had prior cartilage cancers at three bone sites and first came in during 2016 with bloody nipple discharge. The authors explore a shared gene pathway, since IDH1 and IDH2 changes drive Maffucci syndrome and also mark a rare breast cancer subtype. They offer the link as a hypothesis to raise clinical awareness, not a proven cause.
pmc-13285630:
Farmyard soil can hide a drug-proof germ with high harm power, Sonia Akther and co-authors warn in a 2026 genome data report. The team pulled Klebsiella pneumoniae strain KP-S-66 from dirt near a cattle shed in Dhamrai, Bangladesh, and read its full gene set with a high-throughput machine.

The draft genome spans about five million letters in thirty-four chunks. Annotation found thirty-two resistance genes, most tied to pumps that spit drugs back out of the cell. A harm scoring tool rated the strain near the top of the scale, despite its soil home. Files now sit in a public gene bank, giving trackers a reference for watching resistant germs move between farms, animals, and people.
pmc-13285830:
Guwani Liyanage leads a 2026 multi-centre survey of drug allergy in Sri Lanka, a topic with thin data across lower-income countries. Wrong allergy labels can block the best drugs and push doctors toward weaker choices. Interviewers asked clinic patients about past reactions and checked which traits came with a drug allergy label.

Face-to-face talks covered 12,491 adults at second- and third-level hospitals between late 2024 and spring 2025. About one in seventeen people reported a drug allergy, with antibiotics named most often and penicillins at the top of that list. Labels grew more common with age and with other long-term illness, and less common among men. The authors call for allergy services and clear referral paths, noting that demand for testing far outruns supply.
pmc-13285930:
Ghanshyam Kacha and co-authors review team care and drug taking in type 2 diabetes in a 2026 narrative review. Many patients skip or drop the pills that keep blood sugar in range, which blunts the gains drugs promise. The review gathers proof on whether care from a mixed team of health workers helps patients stay on track.

Searches across three databases yielded mostly original studies, plus a handful of reviews, on team models for adults with the disease. Pharmacist-led checks with follow-up most often lifted adherence, and nurse-led coaching on habits added modest gains. Care that also dealt with low mood, diabetes stress, and money strain showed promise for both adherence and health. Gains ran strongest where teams shared work closely and kept contact going, though self-reported measures cloud much of the proof.
pmc-13287130:
Jingmeng Cui and co-authors offer a 2026 tutorial for psychologists who build formal models of changing mental processes. Such models turn verbal ideas into equations, yet teams often judge them only by running simulations, which can hide why a model behaves as it does.

Two worked examples, covering panic and suicidal thinking, show how plotting system states and mapping shifts across parameter values can reveal stable points and tipping behaviour. A free R package with a visual interface, called deBif, supports the steps. The authors argue that these checks help locate where a model departs from clinical observation.
pmc-13287230:
Francisca Leila Araujo dos Santos and co-authors fed 21 young Anglo-Nubian goats in 2026. Three diets were compared. The question was whether whole millet grain can stand in for whole corn in rations without forage. One group kept a hay-based control diet, while the others received pellets plus either whole corn or whole millet.

Grain-only diets lowered total intake, and the corn group grew more slowly and reached lower slaughter weight, though carcass measures did not differ. Millet gave the highest fat intake and kept growth and carcass traits acceptable. Body measures such as temperature were unaffected. The authors conclude that millet can replace corn in such rations for growing kids.
pmc-13287330:
Weiting Wang and colleagues tested electrical acupuncture in 2026 in rats recovering from a heart attack that led to heart failure. Needles at the Neiguan point on the forelimb delivered mild current daily for fourteen days, starting one week after a blocked heart artery was tied off.

Treated rats pumped blood better and showed less chamber stretching, scarring, and tissue death than untreated rats. Nerve balance improved as well. Signals along a vagus nerve pathway rose, including a receptor and growth factors tied to new vessel growth. The authors present the pathway as a plausible route for the repair effect seen in this small animal study.
pmc-13288030:
Yuan Zhao and colleagues review validation work on the ICOPE screening scale in a 2026 scoping review. The World Health Organization built ICOPE to spot early decline in older adults across memory, movement, mood, and other capacities. Countries have adopted the tool at different speeds and in different forms. The review compares study designs, screening results, and test accuracy across global settings.

Positive screening rates varied widely between studies, driven by design, population, and cutoff choices. The tool's reliability and accuracy also shifted across cultural settings. Common problems included a gap between screening and follow-up care, uneven access to digital versions, and little long-term outcome data. The authors urge shared core measures and standard paths that link screening to assessment and care. They see special value in adapting the path for places with few resources.
pmc-13289130:
Ruth M Escalona and colleagues study a protein in ovarian cancer in 2026. The protein is called ADAMTS1. It plays roles in swelling and tissue shaping. The team checked tumors at many stages. They also tested cancer cells in the lab.

Protein levels rose in later, higher-grade tumors. Spread tumors held more than first tumors. In high-grade tumors, it sat in cell nuclei. Fluid-borne tumor cells held more of its message. Silencing it did not slow cell growth. It did cut cell sticking and raise movement. Matrix changes and a cell switch drove that shift. Blocking one switch reversed the extra movement.
pmc-13289430:
Saleh Khairy Saleh and colleagues describe a 2026 single-center review of cancer return after mesopancreas removal during pancreatic surgery in Egypt. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma spreads early, and clearing fatty tissue behind the pancreas, called mesopancreas, may improve cancer control. Full data on where cancer returns after that step were still limited before this cohort.

Surgery took place at Minia University's Liver and GIT Hospital from February 2018 to February 2024, covering 86 patients followed at least 24 months. Mean age was 58.4 years, and clear-margin surgery succeeded in 84.9 percent of cases overall. Cancer returned in 60.5 percent at a median of 11.3 months after surgery. Distant spread led, then local return, then both together.
pmc-13289930:
Sofie Jespersen headed a 2026 randomized trial on high-intensity interval training in chronic hepatitis B with fatty liver. Having both conditions raises liver harm and death risk. Patients were assigned evenly to twelve weeks of intense interval exercise or no intervention. Liver fat by magnetic imaging was the main outcome. Fitness, metabolism, and well-being were secondary checks in the trial.

Recruitment ran slow, so the trial stopped early with only nineteen patients included and fourteen finishing, seven per group. Liver fat change differed by about two percentage points between groups, a gap that was not statistically firm in this tiny sample. Exercise did raise maximal oxygen uptake clearly and lifted emotional well-being scores. Larger trials are still needed.
pmc-13290230:
Why actin bundles end up the size they do, without any precise ruler, is taken up by Christian Vanhille-Campos and Anđela Šarić in a 2026 commentary. They discuss new work by Rosario and colleagues reporting universal length fluctuations in actin structures found in cells.

Bundles of actin filaments shape what cells can do, from the staircase-like stereocilia that let the inner ear detect sound to the thin filopodia that probing cells extend. The commentary explains how bundle size and shape emerge from filaments assembling together rather than from strict size-control machinery. Placing the new findings in that wider frame, the authors show how a simple statistical pattern might underlie structures whose dimensions are tuned tightly to their jobs.
pmc-13290430:
Anesthesia for a child born with stiff, fixed joints demands extra planning, as Sivalakshmi Ramesh and colleagues illustrate in a 2026 case report. The condition, arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, can distort the airway and face, disturb temperature control, and raise fears of malignant hyperthermia.

Their patient was a 10-year-old boy with a recessed jaw who needed corrective leg surgery and had overheated during a past operation. On top of standard checks, the team used entropy readings for sleep depth, a device tracking muscle relaxants, and an arterial line. Drugs were given by target-controlled infusion, the airway was secured with a video scope, and a caudal block supplied pain relief. Sugammadex brought full muscle recovery before he woke, and his recovery was smooth.
pmc-13290530:
Iman Ahmed and colleagues take stock in 2026 of a global manifesto for cancer care in war zones. Two years on, they find it still lacks machinery for follow-through. The manifesto, issued in August 2024 after a first-of-its-kind global summit on war and cancer care, set out seven recommendations for conflict-impacted populations.

Drawing on public sources and the authors' professional networks in crisis settings, the paper builds baseline information on how far each recommendation has actually moved. Its central complaint is structural: the manifesto named goals but no implementation framework, progress metrics, or plan for clearing obstacles. Ahmed and colleagues contrast the promise with stark gaps in cancer response across humanitarian settings and argue that measurement must come before the pledges can mean much.
pmc-13290730:
A lung tumor announced itself through blistering skin and mouth sores in a 2026 case report by Yi Dong and colleagues. Their patient, a 68-year-old woman, arrived with a generalized rash, oral ulceration, and fever, and chest imaging found a thoracic mass of uncertain origin.

Surgery settled the source: the mass was an inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor of the lung carrying an SQSTM1-ALK gene fusion, an uncommon, rarely metastasizing growth. Mouth tissue findings plus the clinical picture supported paraneoplastic pemphigus, a dangerous autoimmune companion of such tumors. The authors present the case as a diagnostic reference and add a caution. Follow-up was short and no systemic immune suppression was given, so the course should not be read as a treatment recommendation.
pmc-13290830:
A zinc-handling protein shields artery wall cells from an iron-driven death in aortic dissection, Wenxin Lin and colleagues show in a study from 2026. Dissection tears the aorta as its middle layer degenerates and smooth muscle cells die, and zinc imbalance had been spotted in patients without a known role.

Lin and colleagues name the zinc-MT3-GPX4 axis a candidate drug target.
pmc-13290930:
Allergy drops taken at home under remote supervision worked in the real world, Chet Tharpe and colleagues report in a retrospective cohort study from 2026. Over a median 20 months of follow-up, symptom severity fell steadily, and the share reaching a large improvement climbed from 28% at one year to 45% at two. Medication use shrank, quality-of-life gains spread to over 90% of patients by 30 to 36 months, and self-reported adherence stayed above 90%. Side effects were uncommon and mostly mild, with no anaphylaxis. Patients with asthma also gained control and used inhalers less. The authors back the model as feasible and scalable.
pmc-13291230:
Solar power in space needs lighter, tougher panels. Mei Gao, Narges Yaghoobi Nia, and Nina Vaidya discuss new paths in a 2026 viewpoint piece. Spacecraft now serve calls, Earth watching, and deep probes. Each task demands more power from less weight.

A second route uses perovskite cells, a cheap and light class. A third pushes special thin materials to extreme thinness. Past lessons from the Hubble telescope show both promise and risk. Thermal strain once shook its early roll-out wings badly.
pmc-13291330:

Twenty tired patients wore two glass types in turn. One gave bright blue-rich light each morning. The other gave dim red light as a control. Each phase lasted one week with a washout gap. Both types cut fatigue scores by week’s end. Blue light gave a larger quick drop in tiredness. Comfort and sleep were checked for safety. A bigger trial is the clear next step.
pmc-13291730:

Eight patients joined and all stayed through the six-week study.

pmc-13291830:

Baseline questionnaires captured each woman's usual patterns first.

Negative feelings showed no forward link to any eating behavior measured. Regulation use also failed to predict later choices in the momentary data. pmc-13291930:

Answers used 0-to-100 scales or open numbers.

Women in 2018 stood out for higher bodyweight and more weight training than later cohorts. Many other measures, from supplement knowledge to social indicators, drifted without reaching significance. pmc-13292330:
Nuzul Sri Hertanti and Yeu-Hui Chuang deliver a 2026 Indonesian version of the Dengue Preventive Attitudes Questionnaire for public health nurses. Internal consistency reached 0.75 on Cronbach's alpha, and two-week test-retest reliability matched at an ICC of 0.75 in their checks. They recommend wider validation before national rollout.
pmc-13292430:

Human relevance still needs testing.
pmc-13292830:
Ahmed Kassem Khater leads a 2026 study of root bacteria that help cowpea plants fix nitrogen on small farms in eastern Kenya. Samples came from Machakos and Kitui counties, where dry conditions limit yields and local strains may suit local soils.

Those helpful strains varied widely, and eight beat the nitrogen-fed control plants, with the best three reaching well above that level. Gene reads placed most in Rhizobium or Bradyrhizobium groups. Close relatives often performed very differently, so strain testing matters for future seed coatings.
pmc-13293430:

Seven surgical groups across three hospitals took part, with 700 patients in all, split evenly between checklist and standard information. Data were gathered from March 2022 to February 2024, and reply rates sat below half. Mean scores across nine literacy areas did not differ between groups. One area, actively managing health, hinted at a time-linked gain, yet the checklist alone did not lift overall literacy.
pmc-13293730:
Jiaqing Feng and co-authors blend blood fat profiling, immune cell gene data, and machine learning in a 2026 study of retinal artery occlusion. The condition is a sudden blockage that blinds an eye and signals wider vessel risk, and its fat and immune links were poorly joined up.

Samples came from 66 patients and 66 cataract controls. Long-chain fats ran high in patients and marked out cases. One fat, C20:2n-6, best split patients with and without blood fat disorder, and lab tests showed it spurred regulatory T cells to make a calming signal. That chain may serve as both marker and treatment lead.
pmc-13293830:

One group had spectral CT, which builds pictures at different energy levels, while the other had standard contrast CT. In total 340 adults with confirmed cancer were included, treated between September 2023 and September 2025.

Gains were clearest for tumor depth and lymph node spread, while distant spread detection was similar. After adjustment, spectral imaging still predicted correct staging, supporting its wider use before treatment planning.
pmc-13294230:

Alzheimer disease and tau-driven frontotemporal degeneration were compared with TDP-driven disease, synuclein disease, and controls. pmc-13294330:
Vjosa Preniqi and colleagues track moral language in hit song lyrics across six decades, in a 2026 study. Two large lyric sets, one reaching back to 1960, let them compare trends by artist gender and genre.

pmc-13294430:
Hassan Masood and colleagues scope mouse models for studying von Willebrand factor in inflammation for a 2026 review. Searches through October 2024 gathered studies that measured the factor directly or via its trimming enzyme ADAMTS13, with dual screening and extraction.
