Factor levels rose in 75% of studies, while activity rose in only 31% in the reported shares. Method choices swing results, so model picking needs care.
pmc-13294830:
Sebastiaan Van Dyck and colleagues report new ways to excite long-lived nuclear spin states in a 2026 physics study. These states hold population imbalances between spin arrangements and can outlast normal relaxation times. Work at low magnetic fields is hard because nearby chemical shifts crowd together.

Selective radio-frequency fields, applied singly or in combination, created spread-out states in paired protons along fatty chains. Five molecules were tested, including ethanolamine, lysine, and vitamin B1, with two reported for the first time. Measurements at both 1.4 tesla and 11.7 tesla compared state lifetimes with ordinary relaxation, and the authors give practical advice for tuning conditions when signals sit close together.
pmc-13295230:
Katie Lawther and colleagues feed red seaweed to dairy cows to cut methane in a 2026 study. Ruminants release large amounts of the gas from rumen microbes, yet how seaweed feeding rewires those microbes was unclear. Nordic Red cows ate grass silage and concentrate with or without a small seaweed share.

Methane yield fell by more than half when seaweed was included across the rotating feeding periods. Gene surveys showed fewer routes toward acetate and methane and more toward propionate, a useful energy product. Genes for making vitamin B12, needed by methane makers, also dropped, pointing to wide network reshaping rather than simple poisoning of one germ.
pmc-13295530:
Yu Liu and colleagues grade meat from Mongolian horses and hunt the genes behind tenderness, in a 2026 study. Horse meat is gaining fans as a lean protein rich in minerals, and the Mongolian breed is prized for hardiness and eating quality. The team set meat from three regions side by side, two in Mongolia and one in Inner Mongolia, then dug deeper into the Inner Mongolian animals.

Meat from Inner Mongolia carried more healthy fats and minerals such as iron and selenium. Within those horses, front leg meat proved more tender, kept better color, and lost less water in cooking than hind leg meat. Gene activity profiles pointed to switched-on genes for fat storage and muscle fiber type in the foreleg. The authors offer the results to breeders who select for meat quality.
pmc-13295630:
Mingxin Zhang and colleagues watch energy use in hunting horseshoe bats in a 2026 study. Calling loudly and often during echolocation should cost dearly, yet bats hunt all night on tight budgets. Five bats wore tiny sensors recording heart signals and calls across 34 prey-tracking sessions.

As prey drew near, call rates climbed steeply during the approach phase of each hunt. Heart rate and total energy spending, however, held steady compared with the quieter search phase. Bats grouped pulses into sonar bursts and reshaped single calls to save effort. The strategy shows how evolution can fund intense sensing without blowing the energy budget.
pmc-13295830:
Bixuan Yan and a large team interview lung fibrosis patients across China in a 2026 study. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis steadily scars the lungs, yet how patients live the illness at different stages was little recorded. Interviews ran across six regions between November 2024 and March 2025.

Fifty-three patients shared experiences grouped by time since their diagnosis. Effects spread across symptoms, sleep, eating, activity, social life, mood, and money worries in the accounts. Cough and breathlessness troubled patients most at every stage, joined by strain around diagnosis and decline. The authors call for care that treats emotional and social burdens alongside lung symptoms.
pmc-13296130:
Bo-Yang Zhang and colleagues trace how bisphenol F, a stand-in for the curbed bisphenol A, harms mouse testes through the gut, in a 2026 study. Male mice got the compound daily for twenty-eight days at three doses. Their testes showed shrunken sperm-making tubes, hollow patches, and a weakened barrier that guards sperm, and the team dug into gut microbes and body chemistry for the chain behind it.

Gut microbe mixes shifted, helpful kinds thinned, and histidine handling in the gut was damped, leaving the testes short of histidine. Signs of ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death, rose in the testes: hurt mitochondria, iron buildup, and fat damage. A histidine transporter mark also fell, though direct blocking of transport was not shown. The authors frame gut imbalance and histidine loss as the path from exposure to harm.
pmc-13296930:
James D. Jentsch, Shawn M. Aarde, and Jared R. Bagley separate hormonal from chromosomal influences on teenage drinking in a 2026 mouse study. The four core genotypes model lets gonadal sex and sex-chromosome set vary independently. Adolescent mice chose freely among water and two strengths of alcohol during short daily sessions.

All groups preferred the stronger alcohol, and total intake differed sharply by group. Gonadal males drank more than gonadal females, with the gap widest in animals carrying two X chromosomes. Chromosome effects surfaced mainly in gonadal females, where XY animals drank more than XX animals. Drinking came in fast early bouts, resembling binge patterns. The pattern partly mirrors human adolescent sex differences.
pmc-13297430:
A mitochondrial protein that rises after a blocked brain artery may itself drive further injury, argues a 2026 study led by Shuyue Cheng. The work examines two complex I subunits, NDUFA4 and NDUFB3, in ischemic stroke and in cells starved of oxygen and glucose.

Proteomics and blotting showed both proteins increased in the tissue bordering mouse brain infarcts, and similar rises appeared in treated PC12 cells. Lowering NDUFB3 protected the cells: energy output recovered, harmful reactive oxygen fell, membrane voltage steadied, and fewer cells died through a JNK-linked pathway. Forcing extra NDUFB3 caused the opposite harm. The authors flag the protein as a candidate drug target needing further validation.
pmc-13297630:
Yuexi Liu and colleagues review a family of signalling pathways, called MAPK, in vitiligo, the skin condition that leaves white patches, in a 2026 article. In vitiligo the immune system destroys the pigment cells of the skin. MAPK pathways steer cell growth, survival, and inflammation, and they act inside several cell types at once.

When these pathways misfire, they feed pigment loss from three sides: faulty pigment making, oxidative stress, and immune attack. Drugs that tune the pathways might blunt stress damage, calm the immune assault, and help pigment return, the authors argue. The review gathers candidate agents as a guide for treatment research.
pmc-13297730:
Luis Herrera and Alicia Di Prisco study what happens when a collapsing ball of glowing fluid suddenly gains a symmetry in time, in a 2026 theory paper. Such fluid spheres model stars shedding heat as they fall inward under their own gravity. A tool called the asymmetry factor lets a time symmetry appear at one chosen instant of the fall.

Every physical quantity was tracked through that instant. Even a symmetry lasting a vanishingly short time changed the later course of the collapse in a drastic way, the maths shows. A thermal effect also emerged, linking the asymmetry factor to the fluid's relaxation time. The results may sharpen models of how real stars collapse.
pmc-13298030:
Muhammad N. Mahmood and Eunice Y. Chow present a 2026 case report on a rare, harmless skin growth that blends features of a melanocytic nevus and a perineurioma. First described in 2011, the lesion is easy to overlook and can be mistaken for blue nevus, dermatofibroma, neurofibroma, or even desmoplastic melanoma. Their patient was a man in his seventies with a lesion on his right forearm.

Clinical and laboratory findings from the case are laid out to help clinicians separate this growth from look-alike spindle-cell lesions. The authors stress that rarity plus resemblance drives misdiagnosis, so careful pathology matters before treatment choices are made.
pmc-13298130:
Rongbao Kang and others propose a method for judging cyber defence plans in factory control systems before deployment, in a 2026 study. Defenders face limited visibility, unknown attacker plans, and random state changes that spread between connected devices. Their dynamic Bayesian network models four uncertainty sources explicitly.

Expected effectiveness is paired with information entropy so results and prediction uncertainty are judged side by side. A substation automation case study, plus ablation tests removing parts of the model, showed the method could separate plans and stay stable under moderate noise in its probability tables. The tests also revealed coupling between knowledge-based and random uncertainty.
pmc-13298430:
Almost every UK household lives within a short drive of a family doctor, quantifies Mathieu Di Miceli in a 2026 geospatial study. The analysis located all 7,965 active GP practices as of December 2023 and computed straight-line distances from 1.78 million household postcodes.

Some 98.8% of postcodes sat within 10 km of a practice; the farthest was in the Shetland Islands. Practices together served over 73 million registered patients. How strongly practice counts tracked population density varied by district, with the tightest link in Northern Ireland. The author suggests future work add staffing levels and public transport, which distance alone cannot capture.
pmc-13298730:
How a yeast is killed before becoming a winemaking additive changes what it does in the bottle, show Valentina Civa and colleagues in a 2026 study. They prepared derivatives of the unconventional yeast Saccharomycodes ludwigii by heat, high pressure, or partial lysis plus pressure, and added them to two Spanish white wines.

All derivatives raised polysaccharide levels within two days. The high-pressure version best protected proteins, cutting heat-induced haze by 21% after fifteen days, while none improved tartrate stability. Sensory effects showed clearly in the neutral Garnacha Blanca and were partly masked by Tempranillo Blanco's stronger aroma. Short contact with pressure-treated derivatives looked most promising.
pmc-13299230:
Tereza Růžičková and others review the gene-level picture of Waldenström macroglobulinemia, a rare slow-growing blood cancer, in a 2026 survey. The disease fills bone marrow and produces a single antibody type, yet its biology is complex. Recurrent mutations in two genes reshaped understanding of how the cancer develops and responds to treatment.

Chromosome changes, epigenetic marks, and small regulatory RNAs add further layers, alongside support from the marrow environment. New targeted drugs, especially Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors, improved therapy, though resistance persists. Other drug classes offer personalised options. The authors expect joined gene and surroundings data to sharpen risk grouping and treatment tailoring.
pmc-13299330:
Kanono Comet Manesa, Simiso Dube, and Mathew Muzi Nindi improve silk sericin films by blending and crosslinking them with a synthetic polymer, in a 2026 biomaterials study. Pure sericin films are brittle and dissolve too easily. Sericin from three moth species was combined with polyvinyl alcohol and crosslinked to reduce separation and solubility.

Crosslinking raised heat stability and tensile strength while controlling dissolution. The films regulated wound moisture, swelled in a pH-sensitive way, and showed antibacterial activity against several bacteria over a day of testing. Surface images revealed a rough granular network suited to cell attachment. Differences among species show that polar chemical groups drive film performance.
pmc-13299630:
Aging cells that refuse to die may drive a common form of heart failure, argue Qiu-Cheng Zhu and colleagues in a 2026 review. In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, senescent cells accumulate and broadcast a cocktail of inflammatory signals known as the SASP, stiffening the heart muscle.

The review traces how those secreted factors promote scarring, starve the microvasculature, and injure heart muscle cells. Two treatment ideas follow: senolytic drugs that clear senescent cells outright, and senomorphic drugs that mute their output. The authors flag practical barriers, including delivering senolytics precisely and lacking blood markers to track whether treatment is working.
pmc-13300730:
Irina Vlasova-St. Louis and Svetlana Khaiboullina review next-generation sequencing for mucolipidoses and related lysosomal disorders in a 2026 article. These conditions, passed down in families, blur together in the clinic, which long made exact diagnosis slow and uncertain. The authors survey how larger variant lists, genotype-to-phenotype links, and functional evidence now feed standard judgments of pathogenicity across the mucolipidosis types and nearby membrane and transport disorders.

Coverage in practice includes targeted gene panels as a first step, exome and genome sequencing for harder cases, and RNA or long-read methods that catch splicing defects and complex rearrangements. Newborn screening and population genomics are covered too. The authors argue that sequencing has redrawn disease lines and cut the long wait for answers for families. Work that remains centers on sorting the flood of variants that are hard to classify, and on wiring results into daily clinical workflows.
pmc-13301030:
D Valente and co-authors present the HF REMAP study on using signal frequency analysis to judge ablation quality during ventricular tachycardia treatment, published in 2026. Peak frequency analysis reads the frequency content of heart signals as a proxy for healthy local activity, and burning should reduce it. The team reanalyzed forty-three patients with complete before and after high density maps from a 247 patient ablation series, measuring how much high frequency signal remained in the area.

Over a median follow-up past a year, eleven patients suffered recurrence or an arrhythmic storm. Patients left with under seventy percent residual high frequency signal enjoyed about ninety percent freedom from tachycardia at twelve months, against roughly twenty-five percent for the rest. Adjusted modeling confirmed heavy residual signal as an independent predictor of relapse. The authors promote the remap measure as an operator independent check that a lesion set worked.
pmc-13301230:
R Haase and co-authors dissect how randomized trials define atrial fibrillation recurrence after ablation in a 2026 scoping review. If every trial counts relapse differently, comparing them is guesswork. Searching three databases, the team gathered 374 trials and pulled apart 700 endpoint definitions, component by component, from episode length thresholds to drug rules.

Most arrhythmia endpoints, 535 of them, hinged on an episode duration cutoff, while only sixty used total burden, and quality of life endpoints clustered in selected trial categories with two questionnaires. The biggest sources of divergence were how the blanking period was handled, how hard anyone looked for the rhythm, and what drugs were allowed. How repeat ablations counted also split the field, as did whether results were framed as time to event or yes no outcomes. Some pieces, like the three month blanking period, standardized over time. The authors offer their component map as groundwork for harmonized reporting.
pmc-13302530:
A simple blood ratio flags how much muscle a brain-injured patient is burning, Valentina Blažinčić and colleagues report in a 2026 rehabilitation study. Records of 291 patients treated within six months of traumatic brain injury supplied lab values and functional independence scores at admission and discharge. The urea-to-creatinine ratio served as a marker of protein breakdown.

Patients whose ratio reached eighty or higher left with markedly lower independence scores, a median of 27 against 40. Yet once feeding route, consciousness level, and admission function entered the model, the ratio lost its independent pull. The authors read it as a gauge of overall catabolic burden rather than a standalone predictor, still worth watching during rehabilitation.
pmc-13302730:
A Guareschi and co-authors compare, in a 2026 two-centre study, the two main forms of conduction system pacing: left bundle branch pacing and deep septal pacing. Both aim to keep the ventricles contracting together, but they target slightly different anatomy. Real-world comparisons of heart function after each were limited.

The analysis covered 124 heavily paced patients followed for a median of nine months. Bundle branch pacing produced a narrower paced trace and clearly better recovery of pumping strength than deep septal pacing. Stroke volume and cardiac output also ran higher in that group, and mechanical synchrony was tighter. Complication rates matched, leaving deep septal pacing as a dependable fallback when bundle capture fails.
pmc-13303330:
Solid parts could give sulfur batteries their huge energy without their fire risk, Yoonha Hwang and colleagues review in a 2026 survey of all-solid-state lithium-sulfur designs. Sulfur promises a theoretical 2600 watt-hours per kilogram, yet liquid cells leak capacity through the polysulfide shuttle. A solid electrolyte blocks that leak and adds safety. The review walks the three battlegrounds: cathodes, electrolytes, and the seams between parts.

Cathode plans span sulfur-carbon mixes, lithium sulfide, metal sulfides, and organosulfur compounds. Electrolytes split into inorganic, polymer, and hybrid families. Seam fixes range from stack pressure and soft layers to built-in stabilizing skins. Slow chemistry and cracking cathodes remain the chief blocks, the authors conclude.
pmc-13303630:
Jelena Micić leads a 2026 study of job and lifestyle factors in couples receiving assisted reproduction at a Belgrade referral center. Age, egg reserve, and cause of infertility are known influences, but daily habits and work exposures may also matter.

All couples treated from January 2019 to January 2022 who met set criteria were included, totaling 501 couples. Questionnaires covered habits and social background, and records supplied cycle details. About one couple in five reached clinical pregnancy. For women, younger age and vitamin or mineral use linked to success. For men, younger age and no chronic illness mattered most.
pmc-13303730:
Andreia Bandeira Luís leads a 2026 laboratory study of hydroxyapatite coatings on titanium dental implant surfaces. How the coating is hardened may change how gum cells grow on the implant and how well soft tissue seals around it.

Titanium discs were laser-textured in two pattern sizes, then coated by standard heating or by laser heating. Human gum fibroblast cells were grown on seven surface types for up to seven days. Texture alone left cell survival unchanged. Standard-heated coatings lowered survival, while laser-heated coatings did not and scored higher overall. Inflammatory signals stayed low across groups, favoring the laser route.
pmc-13304130:
Martin Storr and Martin Gschwender test a gut bacterium's protection of the bowel wall in a 2026 cell study. Irritable bowel syndrome often involves a leaky gut lining that lets harmful germs cross and stir symptoms.

The strain Bifidobacterium bifidum MIMBb75 is known to ease the syndrome alive or heat-killed, likely by clinging to gut surface cells. In a lab gut cell layer, both living and heat-killed forms stuck well thanks to a water-repelling surface that survived heating. Electrical resistance across the layer rose under both forms, supporting a physical shield effect much like a plaster on the wall.
pmc-13304630:
Shula Shazman applies machine learning to predict which women gain full lipid benefits from diet plans in a 2026 pooled analysis. Blood fat responses to the same diet vary widely between people, complicating heart prevention advice.

Data came from 284 women with overweight or obesity across three trials and seven diet styles. A combined win required all four fat ratios to improve over twelve weeks. About one third of women hit that full mark, with two diet styles scoring highest. A tree-based model predicted the outcome best, guided mainly by starting triglycerides, body mass, age, and weight.
pmc-13305030:
Maria Sofia Fede leads a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of oxycodone levels measured after death. The widely used pain drug often appears in postmortem tests, yet judging whether it caused a death stays hard for forensic teams.

Two databases were searched through March 2026 under standard review rules. Twenty-three studies covering 4,335 drug-positive deaths entered the summary, with fourteen pooled numerically. Deaths judged fatal poisonings carried far higher blood levels in the pooled average than deaths from other causes. Single-drug deaths ran higher than mixed-drug deaths, and breakdown product ratios added context.
pmc-13306830:
Zhaohui Fan corrected shore radar errors with a vision transformer trained on ship broadcast data in a 2026 study. Shore radars carry steady range and angle errors that blur vessel tracking for safety and security work.

About 80,000 paired radar and AIS records from a public tracking dataset taught the model nonlinear error patterns through self-attention, without hand-built physics rules. Range error fell from 514.76 m to 7.77 m, a 98.5% cut in reported figures, while angle error fell by 89.8% in the same tests. Part-by-part checks confirmed each design piece added gains.
pmc-13309030:
Kofi Effah and co-authors run in 2026 a joint cervical precancer screening drive across Ghana, pairing HPV gene tests with visual checks by trained alumni of one centre. Their drive screened 1636 women aged 25 years and up at 29 sites in all 16 regions in January and February 2025.

High risk HPV showed in 26.6 percent of women, while visual checks flagged 4.0 percent in the same drive. Types 52, 58, and 51 led, while types 16 and 18 made up under 5 percent of infections found. HIV raised the odds of both flags by a wide margin. Same visit heat care reached over a third of flagged women.
pmc-13309230:
Q Ma, J Licinio, and ML Wong pinpoint in 2026 which part of the epigenetic reader PHF21B grabs a key active-gene mark on histones. The protein shapes genes tied to synaptic plasticity and social memory, and its gene sits in a region deleted in Phelan-McDermid syndrome. Mutant versions missing candidate parts were tested in human cells.

Deleting the tail coil region still allowed binding, although somewhat weakened. Mutating the PHD zinc finger wiped out the interaction completely across five repeated experiments. Normal protein bound strongest of all. The mark in question, H3K36me3, decorates gene bodies while they are being read and guides splicing and chromatin layout. Naming the finger domain as the essential reader module focuses future work. Neurological disorders tied to this chromosomal region may hinge on exactly such reading failures.
pmc-13309530:
Davut Deniz Uzun led a 2026 simulation trial comparing two tools for placing a breathing tube when the airway is flooded with vomit. Breathing in stomach contents during airway care raises harm and death, so first-try success matters. A standard routine pairs suction with tube placement to clear the view.

Two hundred doctors were split evenly between a camera tool with a steep curve and the classic direct tool, using a set soiling model. First-try success was far higher with the camera tool, at 94 percent against 58 percent for the direct tool in the trial. Tube placement and first breath also came faster. The authors favor the camera tool for heavily soiled airways.
pmc-13309830:
Sumaira Riffat and co-authors compare oxidative stress in 2026 across one hundred women in Karachi who could not conceive, for varied causes: polycystic ovary syndrome, endometriosis, unexplained cases, and male-factor cases. Blood levels of a fat-damage marker and a mitochondrial defence enzyme were gauged with fertility signals.

Women with polycystic ovary syndrome carried higher body mass than the male-factor and unexplained groups. Their damage marker also ran higher against the defence enzyme, pointing to stronger lipid peroxidation and redox skew. Across that group, the two readings moved in flipped ways, sharpening the picture of failed antioxidant defence. Other causes showed less marked skew. The authors single out PCOS for oxidative treatment research. Infertility carries heavy social and mental weight, and they frame oxidative balance as a piece of it that can be gauged and treated.
pmc-13310230:
Michael Peter Mayrhofer and co-authors assess whether old window glass can be reused in new facades in a 2026 study. Reuse cuts waste and carbon, yet old glazing varies in size, build, and performance. What stock actually sits in standing buildings decides whether reuse is practical at scale.

Glazing in nine education and research buildings, built or refitted between 1967 and 2013, was catalogued by count, size, assembly, and layer thickness. On-site measures of heat and light passage were set against software estimates. Selected assemblies were also checked against current structural design rules. The authors map where reuse looks feasible and where standards or sizes block it.
pmc-13310530:
Francesca Thaden and co-authors measure in 2026 how bonding position affects the forces produced by fixed lingual retainers, the wires glued behind front teeth after orthodontic treatment. Three commercial retainers, two steel and one computer-designed nickel-titanium, were loaded in a biomechanical rig. A standard vertical displacement was applied at three bonding heights: near the biting edge, mid-crown, and near the gum.

Forces and twisting moments grew with loading in every setup. Retainer type separated the results significantly, while bonding height did not. The softest response came from one steel retainer bonded high; the stiffest from the nickel-titanium wire bonded mid-crown. Multistrand steel wires may deform more under biting loads, the authors note. Fixed retainers occasionally trigger unwanted tooth movements, which motivated the study. Whether bonding height matters clinically, they conclude, still needs patient-level research.
pmc-13310630:
Swati Madhulika and co-authors investigate in 2026 a chromatin-remodelling protein called HELLS in acute myeloid leukaemia, where database analysis showed it switched on too strongly in several cancers. Cell models of blood-cell development and patient data from a large leukaemia cohort were combined. Experiments removed HELLS from leukaemia cells and tracked growth, death, and gene marks.

Without HELLS, leukaemia cells matured more readily, arrested their cycle, and died more easily, with unstable chromatin as part of the picture. Chemotherapy drugs worked better on deficient cells as well. In patient data, high HELLS tracked with adverse risk classification and poorer survival, while low expression meant better remission chances. Stem-like leukaemia cells taken from patients also carried less disease-marker burden once HELLS was removed. The authors propose HELLS as both a prognostic marker and a drug target in this aggressive blood cancer.
pmc-13310930:
Timna Hitrec and colleagues test whether torpor disturbs body clocks in mice in a 2026 study. Torpor saves energy by dropping heat and activity when food is scarce, and daily clocks time its start. Whether the deep rest itself shifts the clock was poorly known.

Torpor was triggered by food removal or by switching on torpor neurons in the brain. Mice then woke in constant darkness so clock phase could be read from wheel running. Rhythm stayed intact in both cases. Waking from fasted torpor advanced the clock by about 40 minutes of shift, which suggests arousal acts as a non light cue. Activity rose before torpor as mice sought food.
pmc-13311330:
Suthakaran Vivian Trishan, Jesuthasan Mithushan, and Peethambaram Jeepara report a 2026 case of a benign kidney tumor in a teen that also raised her red blood cell count. Telling such tumors from cancer in young patients is hard.

The 14-year-old girl had flank pain and blood in her urine seen only under the microscope. Scans showed a clear-edged mass at the top of one kidney. A needle sample hinted at metanephric adenoma but could not settle it. Surgeons removed part of the kidney, and lab study confirmed the benign tumor. Her blood count settled to normal and kidney function held.
pmc-13311830:
Ayan Abdullahi Mohammed and co-authors write a 2026 letter on the return of Bundibugyo Ebola in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, confirmed on 15 May 2026. The strain kills fewer patients than the Zaire strain but still spreads hard.

The authors recall the 2012 Isiro outbreak, with 38 confirmed cases and 34 percent deaths among them, and pooled figures putting this strain's death rate near a quarter. Heavy cross-border movement with Uganda, Rwanda, and other neighbors, plus displacement and insecurity, hamper case finding. They urge regional surveillance and readiness before the outbreak widens, given past detection delays.
pmc-13312130:
Mohammad Amin Hadavi and colleagues report a 2026 feeding study on what the aromatase inhibitor exemestane does to Japanese quail. Estrogen steers reproduction and liver fat handling in birds, so blocking its production could shift laying performance, blood lipids, and egg quality in ways producers need to understand.

The team fed 192 young female quail diets with 0, 0.5, 1.0, or 1.5 milligrams of exemestane per kilogram for 56 days. Egg production and egg weight did not change significantly overall. At the highest dose, though, shell share fell, a liver enzyme rose, and yolk fat oxidation increased sharply, alongside shifts in yolk fatty acid makeup. The authors read the pattern as dose-related metabolic effects without major harm to laying output, while noting hormone levels themselves were not measured.
pmc-13312930:
Alexis V. Schmid and James A. Gagnon identify, in a 2026 study, the signal that summons neutrophils to an injured zebrafish heart in the first act of its scar-free regeneration. The team had earlier spotted injury-triggered interferon signaling as a feature separating regenerating zebrafish from a non-regenerating fish relative, and now they trace which interferon does the work.

A single family member, interferon-phi1, switches on within hours of injury and drives the interferon-stimulated gene program that peaks three days later. Mutant fish unable to make it lost that response and recruited far fewer neutrophils to the wounded heart muscle, while macrophages and new blood vessel growth carried on normally. Later, the mutants cleared fibrotic tissue a little more slowly. The authors cast interferon signaling as an early choreographer of the inflammatory phase that regeneration depends on.
pmc-13314030:
Alle Mahamood Rashid, Zaid Khalaf Khidhir, and Eman Dhahir Arif document, in a 2026 study, E. coli contamination across poultry wet markets in Sulaymaniyah Province, Iraq. Poultry meat picks up bacteria readily during slaughter and processing where sanitation is poor. The researchers gathered 210 specimens from carcasses, equipment, workers, and market water. They confirmed the species with a marker gene and checked for two virulence genes, then sequenced selected isolates to place them on a family tree.

Contamination was widespread: 116 samples, or 55.24 percent of those tested, carried E. coli. Machine surfaces were the dirtiest source at 86 percent positive. Carcasses contributed the largest share of positive finds. Both virulence genes turned up among the confirmed samples, though overall levels stayed low. One sequenced isolate clustered separately from known lineages. The authors call the results a clear public health hazard and press the markets to adopt stricter cleanliness standards.
pmc-13314130:
Hussein Ali Hussein and Inam Bader Falih evaluate, in a 2026 rat study, two immune stimulants against Candida krusei, a fungal pathogen known for antifungal resistance and invasive infection. One candidate was galectin-3, a sugar-binding protein involved in innate antifungal defense. The other was a sonicated preparation of the fungus itself, used as a broad immune trigger. One hundred twenty rats were allocated across treatment and control groups, immunized under the skin, then challenged with infection, with blood and lung measurements at days 15 and 30.

Antibody levels rose in every treated group, peaking at day thirty. The fungal preparation and the combination drove the interleukin-17 and interleukin-23 signals of a Th17-style response. Galectin-3 instead turned up two lung defense genes tied to neutrophil call-up and surfactant protection. The combination muted one gene while keeping the other raised. The authors conclude the two agents enhance antifungal immunity through different routes.
pmc-13314430:
Sanne Peeters and co-workers test whether time with a pet lifts mood in daily life, in their 2026 study. Pets are often said to aid emotional wellbeing, but proof is mixed, and the idea that pets buffer stress needed a real-life check.

The team used phone prompts with 188 dog and cat owners. They rated mood, stress, and pet contact at random moments up to 10 times a day for five days, as the design states. Models that account for repeated measures found pet contact tied to higher positive and lower negative mood, the same for dogs and cats. No clear proof showed that pets softened the mood hit of stress moments. The work supports a small daily mood gain from pets, shared across species, without backing the stronger buffer claim.
pmc-13314730:
Brooklyn VanDerWolde and colleagues report a 2026 case of Merkel cell carcinoma on the hand. This rare, fierce skin cancer of nerve-like cells usually grows on the head and neck, and the hand is an odd site where early spotting makes a real difference.

Their patient was a 79-year-old woman with a mass on her left hand for 1 month, as the history states. A punch biopsy proved the cancer. Care paired wide cutting with margins of 1.5 cm as given in the report, a split-thickness skin graft, and a check of the sentinel node, which came back clear. One round of added radiation followed. The case stresses quick biopsy of odd hand lumps and notes a shift in radiation practice for this cancer.
pmc-13314930:
Hind Qajia and colleagues report a child thigh mass that hid a cancer behind a bruise story, in a case study published in 2026. Rhabdomyosarcoma is the soft-tissue sarcoma seen most often in childhood, and it can mimic a benign blood clot after a knock, which delays care.

Their patient was a 5-year-old child with a fast-growing painful thigh mass after minor trauma. The first guess was a post-trauma hematoma. Ultrasound, X-ray, and MRI told a darker tale: a big muscle mass with cell-death zones, uneven dye uptake, and wrapping of the thigh vessels, as the report describes. Tumor seeds had also spread along the biopsy track. Tissue study proved the sarcoma. The case warns teams to image odd post-trauma masses with full care before accepting a benign story.
pmc-13315230:
Yaru Xu and colleagues surveyed mothers in 2026 about breastfeeding when mother and baby had been kept apart. The cross-sectional study ran at Shanxi Bethune Hospital in late 2024 and used a standard questionnaire on knowledge, attitude, and practice around feeding.

In total, 513 mothers took part, and more than half used mixed feeding. Most said separation had hurt breastfeeding, with work setting and family support named as key factors. Knowledge scores linked in unexpected ways with attitude and practice scores, while type of birth and whether separation had ended also mattered. The findings point to support needs for separated mothers.
pmc-13316130:
Chiara D’Alterio and Stefania Brozzetti report in 2026 a gallbladder case that looked exactly like metastatic cancer but was not. A 66-year-old woman arrived with weight loss, upper belly discomfort, and a felt mass, and scans showed a thickened gallbladder wall plus a 33 millimeter vascular mass at the fundus.

Imaging suggested spread to liver, colon, and abdominal wall, with many liver cysts also present. Keyhole exploration at first seemed to confirm cancer, with infiltration and swollen nodes. Final tissue study instead named xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis, a rare fibrosing inflammation, with diffuse biliary hamartomatosis, underlining why tissue proof decides such cases.
pmc-13316230:
Saeed Mohammadzadeh and co-authors pooled studies in 2026 on MRI radiomics for predicting response to chemotherapy given before surgery in head and neck squamous cancer. Four databases were searched to July 2025 for work judging how well image-derived features sort responders from non-responders, with quality scored by a standard radiomics scale.

Twenty-one studies entered the pool. In validation sets the summary area under the curve was 0.84 in the reported pooling, separating complete or partial response from stable or progressive disease. Wide variation between studies was explored with regression and subgroup checks to find its sources.
pmc-13316430:
Eunju Nam and colleagues, in 2026, study how the transcription factor SNAIL boosts removal of acetyl groups from nucleosomes by the CoREST complex. SNAIL helps guide development and also plays a role in cancer. It binds the enzyme LSD1 through one end and DNA through zinc fingers at the other end.

Using a purified system, the team measured deacetylation by a complex containing LSD1, HDAC1 and the CoREST scaffold. SNAIL increased activity at several sites on histone H3, and the effect needed both its binding regions. Work with models and targeted mutations also implicated the acidic patch on the nucleosome surface. The results show how several weak contacts combine to steer chromatin change.
pmc-13317330:
Yang Liu and co-authors pooled, in a 2026 review, trials asking whether core training actually boosts game performance in team-sport athletes, beyond the trunk strength it surely builds. Team sports demand bursts, stops, and turns that lean on a stable middle.

Four databases yielded 22 controlled studies with 588 athletes, checked with standard bias and certainty tools. Balance improved moderately with core work, with a pooled effect of 0.67 in the combined analysis, though study results varied widely. Jump, sprint, and direction-change outcomes were also pooled for the verdict. The review gives coaches a firmer sense of where trunk training pays off in match skills, and where proof stays thin.
pmc-13317630:
Ehsan Ullah Rashid and colleagues report, in 2026, a single organic molecule that can emit either blue or white light depending on how its molecules pack. White light devices usually stack several coloured layers. A single-component emitter would simplify construction and avoid heavy metals.

Their molecule joins a phenoxazine donor to a ring-shaped acceptor through a twisted bridge. In solid form it showed two emission bands and produced white light. When molecules sat close together, a low-energy emission from paired molecules switched on. When a host material kept them apart, only the blue monomer emission remained. Calculations supported the paired-state picture. Devices without a host emitted broadly across the visible range, while diluted devices gave pure blue, proving the tuning idea.
pmc-13319030:
Maximilian Jacobi and colleagues present a 2026 national analysis of German hospital data for tracking cosmetic surgery from 2006 to 2023. Four common procedures were traced through mandatory quality reports: liposuction, eyelid surgery, breast augmentation, and tummy tuck. Volumes were compared with national market estimates. A cosmetic-purpose diagnosis code was also checked.

Recorded inpatient procedures totalled 352,468 over the period studied. Annual volume tripled, from 11,593 to 33,170 cases per year. Liposuction surged by 611 percent, while breast augmentation fell by a third. Hospitals captured only a small slice of the national market, though: 2.0 percent of breast augmentations and 13.5 percent of liposuctions by 2023. The cosmetic code appeared in just 0.4 percent of cases.
pmc-13319530:
Hadi Jafarimanesh and co-authors ask new nurses what helps or blocks settling into ward work in a 2026 study from Tehran teaching hospitals. Many new nurses leave within their first year, most of all on busy medical and surgical wards. Knowing what smooths the shift from school to full duty could help keep them in post.

Deep talks were held with 21 nurses who each had less than one year on the job, and their words were sorted into themes. Drive, school readiness, kind peers, and firm backing from the hospital all helped. Stress, thin welcome training, poor ward culture, and heavy loads all hurt. Stronger support at each level could ease the shift and cut early leaving.
pmc-13320030:
Esther Cerdan-Hernandez and co-authors test a vessel scan for telling true disc swelling from a look alike in a 2026 eye study. A swollen eye disc from raised brain pressure needs fast care, while a disc that only looks swollen from buried deposits needs a far calmer path. Blood flow measures around the disc from a light based scan were tried as a sorting tool.

Careful checks sorted 65 patients into 14 with true swelling and 51 with the look alike, with most eyes scanned in both groups. Flow and fill measures ran higher in true swelling, most clearly on the nose side of the disc. Sorting power was fair rather than strong, so the scan can aid but not replace full work ups.
pmc-13320430:
Isanka U. Ratnasekera and a large team ask, in 2026, why patients with advanced liver cirrhosis develop a serious abdominal infection. Fluid collecting in the abdomen, called ascites, should kill gut bacteria that leak across the bowel wall. In cirrhosis that defence fails, causing spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

Cell-free ascites fluid rapidly killed a harmless lab strain of Escherichia coli. Strains that actually cause peritonitis, including harmful E. coli and Klebsiella, resisted the fluid. A genome-wide screen showed both germs needed surface sugar coat genes, controlled by one regulator, to survive. Immune cells taken from ascites, by contrast, swallowed and killed resistant strains with ease. Cirrhotic mice also cleared a coat-flawed mutant quickly. Targeting bacterial coats or boosting those immune cells may cut infection risk.
pmc-13321830:
Gabriela da Silva Collar and colleagues test a drug pair against resistant hospital germs in Brazil in a 2026 study. Carbapenem resistant Acinetobacter baumannii causes deadly infections with few treatment options left. The team checked the pair, sulbactam plus durlobactam, against 94 isolates from a high burden Brazilian setting.

Adding the second drug sharply lowered the dose of the first drug needed and restored its effect in every isolate. The germs spanned seven types, led by ST730 and ST79, with varied drug defence genes. Activity held steady across that mix. The authors present the pair as a strong option where this germ is common.
pmc-13322030:
Binyi An and co-authors test whether published heat killing methods for a fungus truly work in a 2026 study. Heat killing of Cryptococcus neoformans is common in immune research and vaccine work. The team reviewed 50 papers and found 23 distinct protocols varying in heat, time, cell density, and sample volume.

Using two virulent strains, only 9 protocols killed every fungus, while 14 left survivors. Just 34 percent of papers reported complete killing, and only 20 described plating checks, so failures may often pass unseen. Sample volume and cell density strongly shaped results. The authors give evidence based guidance for safer, more reliable heat killing.
pmc-13322630:
Ramya Boddepalli, Harsh Chhajer, and Rahul Roy build a joint mathematical model of virus growth and innate immunity in a 2026 study. Positive sense RNA viruses use many tricks to dodge host defences, and forecasting their course inside a cell needs both sides modelled together. The model links the viral life cycle to RIG-I sensing and JAK-STAT signalling pathways.

Comparisons showed Japanese encephalitis virus falling sharply because fast growth triggers strong RIG-I defence, while hepatitis C virus stays poorly controlled. Outcomes flipped sharply at a boundary, where small shifts in immune strength decided whether infection cleared or persisted. Two steps, immune gene translation and viral copying, governed that split most strongly.
pmc-13322830:
Daxia Cai and a large clinical team describe a lung cancer case in 2026 where the tumour changed type after surgery. The man first had mixed adenosquamous cancer and adenocarcinoma, both with an EGFR Exon-21 L858R change, and had radical surgery followed by afatinib.

The disease later came back, and a new biopsy showed pulmonary sarcomatoid carcinoma, a rare and aggressive form thought to arise through a shift in tumour cell character. Treatment with combined immune therapy and chemotherapy then brought a lasting complete response. Alongside the case, the authors review reports of similar change after EGFR-targeted drugs, to help clinicians spot this pattern and choose care when standard lung cancer plans no longer fit.
pmc-13322930:
Weiya Ma and co-authors gather prediction models for delirium after stroke, in a 2026 systematic review with a pooled look at predictors. Searching nine databases to April 2026, they kept 16 studies holding 24 models, with sample sizes from 100 to 14,475 patients.

Model accuracy ranged from moderate to good, and the pooled area under the curve sat near 0.83 in their analysis. Age, stroke severity on the NIHSS scale, a neutrophil-to-lymphocyte measure, vision problems and infection recurred as predictors. Every study carried high risk of bias under the PROBAST tool, mostly from weak analysis methods. Few studies checked calibration or real clinical use, so the authors treat current models as unreliable for practice.
pmc-13323030:
Yilin Chen and co-authors report low-dose dasatinib for chronic-phase chronic myeloid leukaemia in later lines of care, in a 2026 real-world cohort study. They reviewed 53 patients who switched to a low dose because of weak response, intolerance or a push for deeper response.

Among 37 patients without a major molecular response before switching, about a third reached deep response levels after the change in the reported counts. All three patients switched to deepen response regained the deepest level tracked. Side effects that had forced a switch cleared in all 13 intolerance cases, with no new severe worsening seen. The authors judge low dosing a workable option for selected patients.
pmc-13323130:
Tuo Zhang and co-authors chart suicide deaths linked to substance use disorders in the United States, in a 2026 analysis of CDC WONDER data from 2001 to 2023. Each death counted once, with suicide as the underlying cause and a substance disorder listed among contributing causes.

The age-adjusted rate rose from 0.45 to 0.74 per standard unit across that span in their figures, a rise of about two thirds. Men carried higher rates throughout, women showed steeper relative growth, and the heaviest burden fell on adults aged 45 to 54 years, non-Hispanic White groups, the Midwest and nonmetropolitan areas. Two forecasting methods diverged, one near flat and one rising modestly toward 2035.
pmc-13324830:
Osman Fehmi Beyazal, Nihan Kayalar, and Mehmed Yanartaş tested whether cell salvage pays off in cardiac reoperations in Türkiye. Their 2026 study compared 45 patients operated on between 2024 and 2025: 31 with cell salvage, which collects and returns the patient's own blood, and 14 without. Baseline traits, comorbidities, risk scores, and operative data were similar between groups, and the team compared blood use, bleeding, outcomes, and costs.

Intraoperative and postoperative blood product use and bleeding amounts were statistically similar with and without cell salvage, making routine use not cost-effective in the Turkish economy, though the technique proved safe. The authors advise against routine adoption while preserving a role for selective intraoperative decisions, where the potential to cut transfusion needs in a given patient justifies its use. They note this is the first cost-effectiveness evaluation of cell salvage specifically in cardiac reoperations.
pmc-13325930: A 2026 retraction notice withdraws a 2019 Cell Proliferation article by Chen and colleagues on the long non-coding RNA HCG11 and glioma growth through a miR-496 and CPEB3 axis. Editor-in-chief Qi Zhou and publisher John Wiley & Sons agreed the move after a third party raised concerns. Checking found Cyclin D1 bands in Figure 6C duplicated from another group work and reused for a different protein. The authors never answered or shared raw data, so the editors judge the findings unreliable.
pmc-13327530:
Francine Forbes systematically reviewed the brain-guarding and immune-tuning proof for three Caribbean healing plants. Her 2026 review covers bitter melon, soursop, and guinea hen weed, long used for swelling, body chemistry, and nerve disorders. She hunted PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library for lab-stage proof. Though plant chemistry research grows, a joined-up review of these plants' effects on nerve and swelling paths had been missing.

Early data hint the plants' active parts can tune oxidative stress, steer cytokine webs, and sway nerve cell survival. Bitter melon gives polysaccharides, proteins such as MAP30 and alpha-momorcharin, momordicine, and peptides. Soursop gives acetogenins, phenolics, flavonoids, and food fibers. Guinea hen weed gives dibenzyl trisulfide and water fractions with immune-tuning action. Forbes weighs clinic and public health value for Caribbean and low-resource settings, while noting the proof stays lab-stage and needs joined-up review.
pmc-13327930:
Edward J Filippone and John L Farber give a contemporary review of primary membranous nephropathy in a 2026 article. The kidney disease is an autoimmune attack on podocyte targets, most often the PLA2R receptor. Fourteen other targets are now known, and the culprit stays hidden in 5 to 10 percent of cases. It usually appears as nephrotic syndrome.

About a third of patients remit on their own, a third head toward kidney failure, and the rest keep leaking protein, so treatment follows risk level. Low-risk patients can be watched, the highest-risk receive alternating steroids and cyclophosphamide, and mid-to-high-risk patients get rituximab with a 60 to 80 percent response expected on their summary. Antibody levels guide follow-up and flag relapse.
pmc-13328030:
Dongchu Wang, Xiangwu Ding, and Aixiang Wang test whether stomach lining shrinkage predicts H. pylori treatment success in a 2026 hospital study. Patients with chronic atrophic gastritis received a four-drug bismuth regimen as first treatment, and scope images graded their atrophy by the Kimura-Takemoto system into closed and open types. A total of 154 patients completed follow-up breath testing.

Overall cure reached 76.6 percent, but the open-type group cleared the infection in only 42.3 percent of cases against 83.6 percent for closed-type patients. Open atrophy independently predicted failure, with an odds ratio of 8.287 after adjustment in their model. A quick scope grade before treatment could warn doctors to plan stronger or longer therapy.
pmc-13328430:
Ziwen Wang and co-authors review plant medicines for antipsychotic movement side effects in a 2026 article. Extrapyramidal syndrome, stiff and shaky movements from blocked dopamine, is a frequent cost of long antipsychotic use. Searching four databases, the team gathered clinical reports and a larger body of animal work on herbal treatments.

Most clinical reports found herbal medicines eased the side effects in schizophrenia patients, and animal studies largely showed prevention or relief of drug-induced movement problems. Proposed routes include rebalancing brain transmitters, cutting oxidative stress, guarding mitochondria, and calming inflammation, with the KEAP1 and Nrf2 control pathway recurring. Better human trials are the obvious gap before clinics can lean on these remedies.
pmc-13329330:
Megan E Gately and colleagues ask in a 2026 study how clinicians decide whom to offer home video visits. Video care grew fast during the pandemic, yet older and rural patients use it less. The team interviewed 16 clinicians from 11 Veterans Affairs hospitals, covering doctors, nurses, therapists, psychologists, and other roles.

Clinicians weighed their own experience and views of video, the goal of each visit, and what they believed about each patient. Age and assumed tech skill often shaped offers, even before patients were asked. The authors argue that clearer guidance could stop capable older adults from being passed over. Fair access needs offers based on need and patient choice, not on assumptions alone.
pmc-13330430:
Binglian Qin and a large team report first proof of Rickettsia bacteria in a kissing bug species in southern China in a 2026 study. The bug, Triatoma rubrofasciata, is known for spreading Chagas disease, not Rickettsia. In total, 362 bug specimens were screened across body parts and droppings with nested gene tests for six targets.

Rickettsia DNA appeared in eight bugs, a rate of 2.2 percent in the reported counts. Four held Rickettsia felis, while four could not be typed. Fleas nearby carried the bacterium far more often, and rats carried it at low rates. Ticks held a distinct type. Gene trees split bug and rodent strains apart from tick strains. Separate spread cycles are likely, the authors argue.
pmc-13330530:
Marko Vinceković and a large team study alginate mixes for wrapping probiotic bacteria in a 2026 report. Mixes paired alginate with casein, with carrageenan, or with both, formed by calcium gel steps. The cargo was a Lactobacillus bulgaricus strain called LB12. Tests covered chemistry, flow, heat, shape, swelling, and release.

Spectra confirmed crosslinked networks held by hydrogen bonds and charge forces. Adding bacteria loosened those links and raised swelling. Particles stayed sturdy under force and heat in the reported checks. Release began after a lag, then ran by diffusion for one mix and by swelling for another. The authors see food, supplement, and farm uses for such carriers.
pmc-13330630:
Michèle Morfouace and a large international team map radiation dose and eye harm in child cancer survivors in a 2026 study. Survivors of head and neck rhabdomyosarcoma often face late eye problems, from cataracts and dry eyes to retina and optic nerve damage. The cross-sectional work links doses to each eye organ with later harm.

Retina damage appeared after top doses above 40 Gy-equivalent in the reported highlights, while optic nerve damage followed top doses above 52 Gy-equivalent in those summaries. Adult dose limits may not fit children, whose tissues react differently. Organ-specific limits drawn from child data could guide safer treatment planning, the authors argue, without weakening cancer control.
pmc-13332330:
Heckemann and colleagues studied the craft of facilitating co-design workshops in health care in 2026, where patients and the public help shape solutions to complex problems. Toolkits cover project organization, but the relational work of running the sessions is rarely described, and most facilitators learn on the job. Two of the authors ran five workshops with people living with chronic pain and recorded solo reflections and paired discussions after each one.

Three linked spaces emerged from their analysis: a planning and learning space, the workshop-holding space with its structural, emotional, physical, and activation sides, and a tacit space of unspoken reading and response. Facilitation meant holding these spaces together through constant interpretation amid unpredictability. The authors offer a reflection model, holding complex spaces through relational work, as a flexible aid for facilitators rather than a step-by-step guide.
pmc-13332430:
Bowen Cai and colleagues engineer a 2026 suture coating meant to heal the tendon-bone junction after rotator cuff repair. Repair often fails because that junction regenerates poorly under persistent inflammation and excess reactive oxygen species at the implant surface. The team coated polyethylene terephthalate sutures with gelatin and tannic acid holding cerium-doped bioactive glass nanoparticles. The layered coating stuck firmly, looked uniform, and scavenged reactive oxygen species well.

In lab tests, coated surfaces pushed marrow stem cells toward bone and cartilage fates and steered immune macrophages toward a calm, anti-inflammatory state with far less internal oxygen stress. In a rat rotator cuff repair model, high-load coated sutures improved regrowth of the fibrocartilage junction and raised bone mineral measures. The work offers surgeons a suture that does more than hold tissue: it actively calms the local immune response while the junction rebuilds.
pmc-13333330:
Sakawrut Poosri and colleagues develop a 2026 rapid genotyping assay for FTO and PPAR-gamma nutrigenetic variants in Thai adults with overweight or obesity. Diet-gene research links fat mass and obesity-associated variants and PPAR-gamma variants to dietary response and obesity risk. Accessible gene testing tools are needed, notably for population studies in low- and middle-income countries. Current methods are often limited to single or duplex formats, raising cost and time for multi-variant screening.

The team built and validated a cost-effective four-plex high-resolution melting assay for simultaneous detection of four obesity-linked variants, using standard lab equipment and allele-specific primers with distinct melting temperatures. Lab validation against Sanger sequencing in thirty samples tested diagnostic accuracy by sensitivity measures detailed in the full paper. The assay gives population researchers a faster, cheaper route to nutrigenetic screening in Thai adults.
pmc-13336030:
Zhaoyi Wu and colleagues study 2026 melatonin easing graft biliary scarring by blocking VIM+ bile duct cell subgroup via hypoxia/TGF-beta-CREM-VIM axis. NAS, a severe liver transplant complication, is defined by biliary scarring, with unclear mechanisms and limited drug plans. Single-cell RNA reading was done on bile duct tissues of NAS patients, ongoing or succeeding in endoscopic treatment.

Combined analysis showed that biliary lining shift and scarring were reduced in the fibrosis easing group than in the fibrosis ongoing group. VIM+ biliary lining cell, a novel shift-related subgroup, exhibited strong shift pathway action and decreased during biliary scarring easing. Outside-cell hypoxia and TGF-beta signals enhanced CREM activity in VIM+ biliary lining cells, promoting shift by controlling VIM levels. CREM knockdown in biliary lining cells greatly suppressed hypoxia- and TGF-beta-induced VIM levels.
pmc-13336230:
Maria Adelane Monteiro Silva and co-authors studied fathers' time around childbirth during the COVID-19 pandemic in a 2026 qualitative study from Ceará, Brazil. Pandemic restrictions reshaped who could be present at births, and fathers' health weak spots in that period are rarely examined.

Eleven fathers who stayed with their partners through childbirth and the weeks after at two maternity hospitals were interviewed between August 2020 and July 2021. Thematic analysis, framed by a health vulnerability model, yielded two categories: one on fathers' support role and emotional state during the pandemic, another on gender issues, reading skills, and fathers' participation. The accounts portray men stretched between supporting their partners, navigating rules they barely grasped, and managing their own distress with little institutional attention.
pmc-13336730:
Leyla E Dogan and colleagues reported a bioprinting method in 2026 for growing large, self organising blood vessel constructs. Lack of blood vessels limits engineered tissues, since cells deep inside starve without a supply network. The team printed centimetre scale mother vessel constructs in one step from stem cell derived progenitor cells.

Within a week the cells formed both lining cells and wall muscle cells, building a wall with inner, middle, and outer layers. The wall reached about 150 micrometres thick in ten days, with collagen and elastic fibres, and its lining cells showed a key vessel enzyme. The method offers a step toward lab grown tissues with their own working vasculature.
pmc-13337830:
Ambra Sedran and co-authors examine whether teeth grinding breaks front tooth repairs after braces in a 2026 study. Patients had received added composite restorations on upper front teeth after orthodontic care. Some repairs fractured, while others held, forming the comparison.

Forty restorations from 20 patients were reviewed with a standard bruxism tool and muscle recordings. The fracture group showed higher jaw muscle activity on several measures in the reported tests. Microscope study of broken surfaces found cracks starting where the opposing tooth struck. Results tie grinding forces to repair failure and argue for screening grinders before cosmetic rebuilding.
pmc-13339130:
Lucia Trevisan, Kathryn S. Foster, and Jonathan Clayden probe folding molecules that pass signals along their length in a 2026 chemistry study. Their oligothiourea chains fold through hydrogen bonds whose direction can flip. Fluorine tags let nuclear magnetic resonance watch that network in detail.

Temperature and two-dimensional NMR mapped bond direction and strength in chains of two to five units. Fluorine readings still worked inside micelles and bicelles that mimic cell membranes. Longer chains revealed middle steps during full direction reversal as reported. Knowing how the network holds or flips helps design molecular wires for use in membrane settings.
pmc-13341230:
Bond strength of a new two-bottle dental adhesive is tested by Ahmet Özlü and colleagues in a 2026 study. Thirty extracted human molars received one of three systems: the new G2-Bond Universal, the reference two-step Clearfil SE Bond, or the one-step G-Premio Bond.

Composite was built up, specimens were cut into small sticks, and bond strength was measured right away and after 6 months in water. Aging did not significantly weaken any group. Clearfil SE Bond scored highest and beat G-Premio Bond, while G2-Bond performed comparably and formed the thickest glue layer. The authors suggest that thickness may add toughness under chewing stress.
pmc-13341330:
Abby Q. Y. Li and colleagues modelled cost value in 2026 of NT-proBNP guided heart failure risk sorting in Hong Kong patients with type 2 diabetes. Heart failure is among the costliest harms of the condition, adding about 12,800 US dollars per patient per year in Hong Kong. The team built a four state Markov cohort model from Hong Kong Diabetes Biobank data from 2014 to 2019.

Patients were classed as low or high heart failure risk by NT-proBNP cutoffs of 400 and 125 picograms per millilitre. The model ran over a lifetime from a payer view with 2023 costs. Life years, quality adjusted life years, and cost ratios were weighed. The work tests whether blood test guided heart care spending buys enough health to justify its cost.
pmc-13341430:
A scoring chart for nerve damage risk in type 2 diabetes is built by Shangren Xie and colleagues, in their 2026 study. Data from 570 patients were split evenly into training and validation sets, and logistic regression hunted independent predictors of diabetic peripheral neuropathy.

Eight factors qualified: older age, body mass index at or above 24.0 kg/m2, smoking, drinking, hypertension, abnormal blood lipids, diabetic kidney disease, and diabetic eye disease. The resulting nomogram predicted well, with areas under the curve of 0.795 in training and 0.857 in validation, and calibration matched observed risk. Such a chart could help clinics flag patients for foot and nerve checks.
pmc-13341530:
A newborn's yellow skin led to one of the earliest diagnoses of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, reported by Vinson James's team in a 2026 case report. The 4-day-old boy, born small at 2,150 g, came in cold, with low blood sugar and a weak cry.

Sepsis was suspected first, but direct bilirubin peaked at 2.6 mg/dL, a liver enzyme hit 632 U/L, and alpha-1 antitrypsin measured under 20 mg/dL. Genetic testing confirmed the PiZZ type by day 8 of life. Supportive care sufficed, and gastroenterology follow-up was arranged. The case notes this condition escapes standard newborn screening panels.
pmc-13341630:
A leftover guidewire can fake a perfect aneurysm repair, warn Yang Liu and research partners in a 2026 case report. During endovascular aneurysm repair, the final angiogram is trusted to confirm sealing, yet a stiff wire still sitting in place can mask a type Ib endoleak at the distal attachment.

The authors walk through how the masking happens, what the deceptive images look like, and why the oversight matters: a missed leak can later rupture the aneurysm sac. Practical lessons target the closing steps of the procedure and future reinterventions. It is, they note, the first detailed report of repair failure traced to this specific trap.
pmc-13342130:
Lactate does more than feed tumors; it may armor them against radiation, in a 2026 review by Yuxiang Zhang and colleagues. Lactylation, a chemical tag lactate leaves on proteins, is emerging as an epigenetic layer linking metabolism to DNA repair, redox balance, and survival after irradiation.

Evidence tiers vary: metabolic rewiring and repair effects rest on direct radiotherapy data, while chromatin, immune, and RNA-level mechanisms lean on related models. Threads to RNA stability and binding proteins are flagged as hypothesis-grade. Sorting strong from speculative links is itself a service, guiding which parts of this axis deserve drug development first.
pmc-13343530:
Dianzhe Tian and co-authors chart world research on the metabolic syndrome and cancer link in 2026, mixing publication mapping with gene network analysis. Output from 2000 to 2024 was mined from Web of Science and PubMed to see who publishes, what themes rise, and which molecules connect metabolic disorder to tumors.

China and the United States drove most growth, while Europe held strong collaboration centrality. Topics moved from single metabolic problems toward whole syndrome profiles, cancer outlook, and interventions. Network work flagged hub genes and pathways around inflammation, insulin signaling, and metabolic rewiring. The authors argue the link runs both ways and that fixing metabolic dysfunction could improve cancer treatment tolerance and survival.
pmc-13344230:
Tetsuya Kawakita and co-authors compare severe childbirth complications across sickle cell genotypes in a 2026 national study. Sickle cell disease raises pregnancy danger. How much each genetic form contributes at population scale was unclear. The team mined a readmissions database covering over 20 million delivery stays from 2016 to 2022.

Severe morbidity hit 6.0 percent of HbSS deliveries and 7.9 percent of HbSC deliveries, both roughly six times the risk without the disease, while sickle thalassemia and even simple trait also raised risk in a graded ladder. Transfusion and readmission followed the same pattern. Care teams, the authors argue, should plan peripartum care around each patient's genotype.
pmc-13345830:
Carlos F. Lagos and co-authors recount finding a pinpoint blocker of connexin hemichannels in 2026. These half-channels leak signals between cells and their surroundings in health and disease. Drugs kept hitting the full gap junctions built from the same proteins. The team screened molecules against a structural model and validated hits in cells.

One small chiral molecule, D4, passed every check. Its right-handed form shut Cx43 hemichannels at about 5 nanomolar. It spared gap junctions, ignored Cx36 channels, and left three unrelated channel types alone. Its mirror twin did nothing. Single-channel recordings confirmed complete block at 10 nanomolar. The scaffold opens a cleaner way to probe and perhaps treat hemichannel-driven disease.
pmc-13346030:
Jennifer Lee and co-authors guide small-biopsy diagnosis of front chest-center masses in 2026. Thymic tumors, lymphomas, nerve hormone tumors, and germ cell tumors crowd this space. They mimic each other on tiny samples. The review weighs needle aspiration, core biopsy, and ultrasound-guided sampling for pathologists and treating teams.

Core samples and a newer freezing biopsy through the airway scope usually yield enough tissue. With careful sorting plus stains and gene tests, they beat thin needle draws on accuracy for most tumor types. Picking the right sampling tool for the suspected lesion matters. So does taking enough tissue and layering confirmatory tests. Together they decide whether a small sample can carry a big diagnosis.
pmc-13348030:
Graham S. Collier reflects, in a 2026 account, on building light-active polymers from a simple ring unit while starting a lab during the pandemic. Conjugated polymers serve solar cells, switches, and body-linked devices, yet chasing records has bred tangled syntheses. So his group centred work on dihydropyrrolopyrrole scaffolds that stay modular, scalable, and easy to tailor.

Keeping designs simple cut green costs and let students with tight resources run real projects, a dual gain the author frames as strategy, not compromise. Early-career hurdles, from picking a topic to growing it under COVID limits, shape the advice, with student success treated as a design goal beside device numbers.
pmc-13350630:
Runjie Shui and co-authors tested in 2026 whether PSMA PET/CT joined with multiparametric MRI lifts prostate cancer diagnosis. The focus was intermediate PI-RADS 3 to 4 lesions. There, benign and malignant disease are hardest to split. True sorting avoids needless biopsies. It also catches cancers that need treatment.

One hundred thirty-five patients scanned from early 2024 to late 2025 were studied in look-back. Fluorine-18 PSMA-1007 PET/CT was weighed against MRI. Age, antigen measures, prostate volume, and scan uptake values fed a multi-parameter model. The joined path beat either mode alone for spotting cancer in this murky group. The model gives a step toward fewer missed cancers and fewer needless biopsies.
pmc-13352130:
Shaik Mohamed Shamsudeen and Smitha Naik map research on cell harm from dental X-ray imaging in a 2026 bibliometric study. Radiation can damage cells, but harm from routine dental scans gets less attention. Three databases were searched for original studies of cone beam CT and panoramic imaging effects on cheek cells.

Thirty-five articles were included and sorted by year, country, imaging type, sample size, and analysis method. Institutional output, journals, funding, dose used, and top-cited papers were also tallied. No prior mapping of the field existed. Results show where work concentrates and where gaps remain for safer imaging practice and future study design.
pmc-13353530:
Andrew J Sullivan led a 2026 study of sex gaps in drug giving after deep angiography for heart artery disease, covering 2017 to 2024. Women who have a heart attack and undergo angiography have historically faced higher illness and death than men of similar age, and gaps in optimal medical care may contribute. The team asked whether giving gaps have narrowed over time.

Records from a high-volume centre were studied for giving of rule-urged care after angiography for obstructive disease, comparing women and men across the study years. Trends showed how the gap changed, rather than a single snapshot. The results help cardiology services judge whether equity in post-procedure giving is improving and where notice is still needed.
pmc-13353930:
Dan Wu and co-authors engineer a layered 3D scaffold that speeds bone regrowth by tuning surface roughness in 2026. Human bone heals small breaks alone but not critical-sized defects, and graft options carry donor risks. Their nano- and micro-scale scaffold presents a tunable surface texture to marrow stem cells.
