The gain traced to stronger force sensing by cells at the layered surface, a process called mechanotransduction. A mechanics-first design route may beat chemistry-heavy grafts for large defect repair.
pmc-13356530:
M Gregory Grewal and others engineered packed hydrogel microfibers as scaffolds for dynamic cell conduct and 3D printing inks, in 2026. Particle-based gels serve as injectable scaffolds, printing inks, and permissive culture systems, thanks to bulk yielding and porosity. Spherical microparticles, however, limit design control over interparticle links and group.

The team built gels from discrete electrospun microfibers, segmented to a defined length, whose packing creates a scaffold with tunable yielding and porosity. Cells behave on the fly within the fibrous network, and the stuff prints as a biomaterial ink. Bioengineers gain a scaffold platform whose layout can be tuned for both cell culture and bioprinting.
pmc-13358330:
Xinxin Guo and Baoji Song report a 2026 study of surgery for gynecomastia, the growth of breast tissue in men. The condition is common and can cause deep shame and stress. Fat removal by liposuction alone often leaves firm gland tissue behind, so the team paired it with gland removal through a small cut around the nipple.

They reviewed 177 patients treated from 2019 to 2025. Most results were good, with high patient satisfaction scores, and side effects were mostly mild, such as fluid buildup or brief numbness. The study supports the paired method as a safe option that can give a flatter, more natural chest shape.
pmc-13358530:
Bingyuan Zhou and co-authors report a 2026 study on a small blood cell that may hint at lung cancer outlook. Basophils are the rarest white blood cells, and their share in the blood can shift around surgery. The team asked whether a drop in that share after surgery warns of a worse future.

They followed 468 lung cancer patients at one center and split them by whether the basophil share fell or rose after the operation. The groups were then compared on survival over time. The team also built a wider model that joins this sign with other patient facts, aiming for a cheap blood-based clue to who needs closer watch.
pmc-13358830:
Sarah Reddy and co-authors test online symptom reporting for lung cancer patients in a 2026 paper. Modern drug treatments extend life but bring complex side effects that need close watching. A web platform called eRAPID lets patients report symptoms from home, receive instant advice matched to severity, and send the data straight to their care team.

The project checked whether lung cancer patients starting drug treatment would join, stay, and report as asked. It also logged which symptoms came up, what advice the system gave, and how patients and staff felt about it. Showing the platform works in daily care is a first step toward wider use.
pmc-13359730:
Mehmet Akif Bozdayi and co-authors profile vitamin D in a Turkish city in a 2026 study. Vitamin D levels are read against cut-offs, but what counts as normal depends on whose blood built the reference range. The team used routine hospital laboratory data from Şanlıurfa, in southeastern Türkiye, to set local benchmarks for adults.

After cleaning the data, they analyzed 48,826 records from people tested during 2025. Levels were broken down by age, sex, and season, and the middle range of values was set out as a local reference. Regional data like this keep doctors from judging local patients by ranges drawn from distant populations.
pmc-13359930:
Anıl Kaya and co-authors measure the thalamus in epilepsy in a 2026 study. The thalamus is a hub deep in the brain with many small nuclei, heavily wired to the cortex and involved in seizures. The team compared the volumes of these nuclei between people with generalized epilepsy and healthy matches, and between men and women.

They analyzed MRI scans from 232 participants using an automated brain segmentation tool. Volumes were compared side to side within each person and across groups, with care taken for head size and age. Mapping which nuclei shrink or swell could clarify how epilepsy takes hold and whether the changes differ by sex.
pmc-13361330:
Sezer Akgöl and Fatih Kocabaş hunt for drugs against a deadly fever virus in a 2026 study. Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus kills a high share of its victims and has no approved drug. One viral enzyme, called OTU protease, helps the virus mute the host's first immune alarms. The team targeted a side pocket of this enzyme to build blockers.

They first made the enzyme in the lab and confirmed it works, stripping ubiquitin tags in cells as the real virus does. Computer screening of a drug library then picked candidates that fit the pocket well. Lab checks followed to test the best fits. Blocking this enzyme could free the immune system to fight back, so even early leads matter for a virus this dangerous.
pmc-13362330:
Kuen Su Lee and co-authors ran a 2026 trial on preventing sickness after anesthesia. Nausea and vomiting after surgery are common and miserable. Ramosetron is a standard shield drug, but whether adding dexamethasone strengthens it in this setting was not settled. The team enrolled 385 adults across several hospitals and surgery types, from gynecologic to plastic surgery, all without patient-controlled pain pumps.

Patients were assigned by chance, with neither side knowing who got what. One group got dexamethasone right after anesthesia began plus ramosetron at the end; the other got ramosetron alone. The team compared how often nausea and vomiting struck, their severity, pain scores, and the need for rescue drugs. A clear answer helps anesthesia teams build the best anti-sickness plan for mixed surgery lists.
pmc-13362730:
Agnieszka Nemś and colleagues present a 2026 food study on snacks enriched with button mushroom powder. They mixed the powder into snack pellets at 5 and 10 percent, then puffed the pellets two ways: deep frying in oil or microwave heating. The team measured nutrition, health-linked compounds, taste signals, color, and crunch for each batch.

Mushroom powder raised protein, fiber, and polyphenol levels, and the microwave batch with 10 percent mushroom scored best overall, with very low fat. Microwaving also kept more of the useful compounds than frying. The trade-offs were a darker color, less puff, and stronger bitter and earthy notes. The study backs mushroom powder as a useful snack add-in, with microwave puffing the cleaner route.
pmc-13363730:
Nico Surantha, Hanfei Zhang, and Daiki Watanabe present a 2026 study on drone-style inspection of power line parts with lean artificial intelligence. Hand labeling of field photos is slow and costly, so their framework learns from a few labeled images plus many unlabeled ones. The framework uses the model's own confident guesses as extra teaching data. A second stage squeezes the model to run in real time on small edge computers.

Their debiased semi-supervised method beat the standard version on detection scores across two datasets. Among hardware trials, a tiny YOLO model in low-precision mode on a Raspberry Pi 5 earned the best balance score on their new deployment scale. They offer that scale as a steadier yardstick for judging edge readiness.
pmc-13364030:
Andrey Altynov and colleagues present a 2026 study on turning polypropylene waste into gasoline blending parts by pyrolysis and hydrogen treatment. Heating the plastic without air gave liquid fuels, and the gasoline cut was then hydrosaturated over a standard refinery catalyst. The team varied heat and feed rate to learn how each setting reshapes the fuel's makeup, and used blending software to judge the products.

Pyrolysis at 450 degrees gave the best feed for upgrading. One upgraded sample ran cleanest, with the least olefins and benzene, but its octane was low, suiting it as a base blend part. A second sample, made cooler and faster, scored higher octane for use as a booster, though its olefins need balancing. The work maps a waste-to-fuel route.
pmc-13364630:
Lei Han and co-workers review 2026 work on plant and herb goods that may calm the scar niche in stiff lung disease. In this ill, scar grows and can not be undone, and lung immune cells steer the harm. Past care hits one mark at a time and gains little.

Plant goods hit many marks at once, they note, shifting lung immune cells from harm to heal states and blocking scar signals. Old herb blends add joint effects. The team urges hard lab proof, from raw cell maps to tiny dose ships, before clinic hopes rise. The field needs proof, not just network guesses.
pmc-13366030:
Bjorn Meijers and Thomas Mavrakanas weigh in 2026 if a low dose blood thin drug can guard the hearts of folks with far gone kidney ill. Three past trials show the low dose drug plus aspirin cuts heart and limb harms in artery ills. But those trials shut out folks with the worst kidney loss.

A new trial, named TRACK, takes on that gap with a blind test in stage four and five kidney ill. Hints from past sub groups give hope, but no firm proof. The pair frame what the trial must show to change care for this high risk crowd.
pmc-13367530:
Rajesh Venkitakrishnan and co-workers write in 2026 on calm of harsh wheeze ill in India with a shot drug that cuts a white cell type. Harsh wheeze with high counts of that cell type drives much harm, stay, and cost, yet plain puffs can fail to hold it. New shot drugs aim at the cell's growth cue.

Trials show such shots cut flare rates, ward stays, and puff drug load, and lift lung work and life feel. Some folks reach full calm of the ill. Gaps in who gains most stay. The team frames the shots as exact care for a set wheeze type.
pmc-13370830:
Laurin Bixby and co-workers open in 2026 a look at pay gaps for US nurses who live with a disability, a group the nurse work force can not spare. Such gaps are known in broad work, but not for the biggest care crew. Poor fits and harsh wards push such nurses out, past work shows.

Their study reads two decades of a huge US house poll for work age nurses who name as reg or adv nurses. Pay reads in log wage form split by disability state. The work sets up proof for rules that keep such nurses in post with fair pay.
pmc-13373830:
Henriette Leicher and colleagues show that a plant's own signalling peptides help powdery mildew colonise its host in a 2026 study. The receptor kinase FERONIA is a susceptibility factor for powdery mildew in Arabidopsis, but the mechanism was unclear. The work reveals a host weakness that fungi exploit, and a possible target for mildew-resistant crops.
pmc-13374230:
Chunhua Wei and colleagues compare fall risk across new androgen receptor blockers for prostate cancer in a 2026 meta-analysis. Androgen receptor pathway inhibitors are mainstays for advanced prostate cancer, yet fall risk is a serious concern, especially for older men. Eleven phase 2 and 3 randomised trials covering 12,239 patients compared enzalutamide, apalutamide, and darolutamide against placebo or non-steroidal antiandrogens.

Overall, the blockers doubled the risk of falls of any grade, with drug-specific and stage-specific subgroups examined. Prediction intervals were used to show how effects might vary in future trials. The analysis gives oncologists drug-by-drug fall data for counselling, monitoring, and choosing agents for patients already at high fall risk.
pmc-13380730:
Chakravarthy and colleagues check how often fibrosis develops under two ways of delivering a drug for wet age-related macular degeneration, in a 2026 analysis of the Archway trial. One arm received monthly injections of ranibizumab; the other received the Port Delivery Platform, an implant releasing the drug, refilled every 24 weeks. Fibrosis, scarring under the retina, is a cause of vision loss in this disease, and 248 implant patients and 167 injection patients were graded from photographs over 96 weeks.

Fibrosis rates stayed low in both arms: at week 96, 7.7 percent of implant eyes and 5.4 percent of injection eyes showed fibrosis on the photographs. Among eyes with no fibrosis at baseline, new fibrosis by week 96 appeared in 2.4 percent of implant eyes against 0.7 percent of injection eyes. Eyes with fibrosis in the implant arm gained 3.2 letters on average, while injection-arm counterparts lost 9.9 letters. Chakravarthy supports the implant as burden-reducing without a fibrosis penalty.
pmc-13382030:
Zi-Lun Ruan and colleagues report a 2026 study identifying a fat-making enzyme as a brake on anti-tumour immunity. Switching on a tumour's own alarm signals can draw in immune cells and help immunotherapy work. The enzyme in question, called GPAT4, is abundant in many tumours, including pancreatic and breast cancers, where immune entry is poor.

In mouse experiments, tumours lacking the enzyme grew more slowly and filled with more killer immune cells. The reason was stress in the tumours' energy centres, which leaked their DNA into the cell and triggered an alarm pathway. Notably, this effect did not depend on the enzyme's usual chemical job. Blocking it could be a new way to warm up cold tumours.
pmc-13382530:
Heather Hanson led a 2026 study of how HIV-2's Vpx protein wakes innate immune alarms in infected cells. Vpx, absent from HIV-1, boosts HIV-2 growth by destroying host antiviral proteins, including SAMHD1 and parts of the HUSH silencing complex. The team asked whether that destruction also trips nucleic acid sensing.

The work reveals a trade-off: Vpx frees viral genes from silencing, but the same act alerts innate defenses that could shape infection outcomes.
pmc-13383530:
Joyce Berkumwin Der's team examined what drives successful tuberculosis contact tracing in Ghana, in a 2026 cross-sectional survey. Ghana detects only 29 to 34 percent of estimated tuberculosis cases, below the African average of 47 percent and the World Health Organization target of 70 percent. Contact tracing could find exposed contacts and undiagnosed cases earlier.

The team systematically sampled adult tuberculosis patients from treatment registers across three districts in three regions, using structured interviews and logistic regression. Patient-reported factors linked to tracing success were analyzed, with variables passing a liberal bivariable screen carried into multivariable models. The findings aim to strengthen tracing where detection lags most.
pmc-13383930:
Rafael Calvo Rodríguez and co-authors describe a two-step drilling method for precise tibial tunnels in knee ligament surgery in 2026 work. Tunnel position strongly affects graft success, and repeated drilling wastes bone. Their method first places a guidewire at the target spot under camera view, guided by known landmarks.

If the spot needs shifting, a small 6 mm tunnel creates a corridor to move the wire with fine control. Surgeons then widen that corridor to a final 10 mm tunnel at the corrected site, adding only about 5 percent to the tunnel area. The authors present the approach as a reproducible way to fix placement while sparing bone stock.
pmc-13385430:
Iba and colleagues define a conserved population of vessel-lining stem cells marked by the protein CD157, in 2026 vascular biology research. Endothelial cells carrying CD157 help renew and maintain blood vessels, but their identity was vague. Comparing gene profiles from mouse and human tissues, the team found these cells share a transcriptional signature enriched for growth genes. CD157-positive cells from muscle proliferated more vigorously than their negative counterparts in culture, evidence of stem character. Analysis suggested these cells communicate with neighbors through the CXCL12-CXCR7 signaling axis, a known vessel guidance pathway. Iba proposes the shared signature as a handle for harnessing the vessel's repair crew in regenerative medicine.
pmc-13386030:
Rongrong Hu and co-authors review extracellular vesicles in acute myeloid leukaemia, a cancer of blood-forming cells where many patients relapse or resist standard treatment. Vesicles are tiny parcels cells release to carry molecular cargo. Their 2026 review covers both how leukaemia vesicles help the disease and how vesicles might be turned into treatments.

Vesicles shed by leukaemia cells reshape their surroundings to favour tumour survival and progression, a role now under intense study as researchers look for the mechanisms behind treatment failure. At the same time, engineered vesicles could deliver cargo that triggers cancer cell death or silences cancer genes through their RNA payload. The authors synthesise recent discoveries on both fronts and discuss the obstacles facing vesicle-based therapy, aiming to show where the approach is realistic for blood cancers.
pmc-13386830:
Akinbami R. Adenugba and colleagues find hidden variety inside a lab strain of mouse pneumonia virus in 2026 work. The virus serves as a stand-in for human RSV in a natural host, and strain J3666 was thought to be one virus. One form lengthens the main gene, while the other adds a small upstream reading frame that lowers gene output. Rebuilt viruses differing only in that gene tip proved the longer form more virulent. The authors argue that attachment protein levels tune severity, a caution for labs sharing the strain.
pmc-13388430:
V J Garrido Hernández's team printed bone-repair scaffolds from polylactic acid mixed with hydroxyapatite, a mineral close to natural bone, using digital light processing, a form of high-detail 3D printing. The scaffolds carried linked square pores and a planned porosity near four fifths. Hydroxyapatite content ranged from none to five percent.

Computer modelling showed the shapes held up well under body-like loads. Lab tests found cells thriving best on the four and five percent mixes, both classed as highly biocompatible. The paper presents these printed scaffolds as a tunable alternative to bone grafts, which are limited by donor harm and scarce supply.
pmc-13389030:
Jie Yu and a clinical team report, in 2026, on going home the same day after combined keyhole surgery for infertility. All patients received enhanced recovery care, a package of steps meant to lower stress on the body and speed healing, but same-day discharge after this combined procedure had rarely been studied.

Among 104 women, 51 went home the same day, and problem rates were low and similar in both groups, with no repeat surgery or return visits within 30 days. Living more than 30 kilometres away lowered the chance of same-day discharge, while finishing surgery before mid-afternoon raised it. Hospital teams planning day surgery will find practical factors that shape a safe discharge plan.
pmc-13390430:
Sundas Khan's team presents the plan for a stepped trial testing whether nudges can lift doctor take-up of a lung clot choice-support tool. A pilot found take-up of 39.1 percent with a nudge at order entry versus 20.7 percent without. The full trial will assign twelve ER units across three health systems over nine steps and thirty months, testing a record-free web tool with rollout and impact results.
pmc-13390730:

pmc-13392330:
Gabriel C Roth and co-authors examine, in 2026, whether cholesterol levels affect five-year survival in Parkinson's disease, with or without brain stimulation therapy. Cholesterol metabolism has been implicated in Parkinson's development, but its role in long-term mortality was unclear.

The records-based study held 212 patients, split by care type. One group had deep brain stimulation; one had best drug care. Thought, mood, and movement were scored with standard scales. Fat levels in blood, taken near test day, were tied to death over five years. Brain doctors gain long-term data on a cheap blood test. The data are split by care type, which is how wards must use them.
pmc-13392630:
Abhishek Vadher heads a ten-author review of whether artificial intelligence can pick chemotherapy plans better than doctors working from guidelines alone. Models drew on clinical details, tissue images, scans, and molecular data together. Reported gains included longer survival and better tumour shrinkage in several studies, and some models flagged patients unlikely to benefit, opening the door to gentler care. Early signs of fewer side effects appeared too, though the evidence base stays small.
pmc-13393330:
Chengjin Li leads an eleven-author team presenting DDSurfer, a deep learning system that rebuilds the brain's cortical surfaces straight from diffusion MRI scans. Surface rebuilding normally depends on a different scan type with better contrast, then warps the result into the same space, and alignment errors creep in. Diffusion data alone are coarse and low-contrast, which is why the detour existed.

The framework runs two processing streams that fuse matching fine features and learns a smooth deformation to shape the folds for each person. Training used machine-made stand-in shapes rather than hand-marked truth, a weakly guided approach. Tests across varied datasets showed stronger shape accuracy and steadiness than older pipelines, and it held up on fresh data. The authors release the code and an interactive module, pitching the tool for connectomics work built around this imaging.
pmc-13393630:

Six hundred eighteen patients treated between 2010 and 2020 were followed for survival by stage, tissue type, and treatment. The disease struck at a rate of roughly one and a half cases per hundred thousand woman-years.

Survival reached about three quarters at one year and well under half at five years, driven mainly by stage, age, and histology. Added chemotherapy after surgery showed no survival benefit in either localised or advanced disease, including the commonest subtype. Keyhole surgery looked better than open surgery in early disease at first glance, but careful balancing of the groups erased the difference, leaving the approaches comparable with bias still possible.
pmc-13393730:
Sipei Cheng and colleagues compare a low-cost pork belly model with traditional training for ultrasound-guided nerve blocks in a 2026 study of anesthesiology residents. The transversus abdominis plane block numbs the abdominal wall, and trainees need safe practice before working on patients.

Thirty residents received the same theory lessons, then half added pork belly simulation while half trained traditionally. Each resident later performed blocks on surgical patients under supervision and one block independently, scored by blinded instructors. Training programs gain a cheap, hands-on option that may sharpen skills before live cases.
pmc-13394030:
Aicee Dawn Calma leads an seventeen-author prospective study. The rest had mimic conditions.

The authors propose the combined bundle for earlier, firmer diagnosis and faster trial recruitment.
pmc-13394730:

Seizures fell more on the drug than on the dummy pill, with the clearest gain at the top dose. Dizzy and sleepy spells were more common on the drug, but no serious harm gap appeared. Most who finished stayed on the drug for months. The authors call the results a proof of concept.
pmc-13395330:
Gemma C. Sharp and a large team sift, in 2026, how parents' habits before birth shape child health. Four long studies from the United Kingdom and Norway gave records on more than two hundred thousand births. The team tested smoking, alcohol, caffeine, and low income against 72 child outcomes up to age eleven. They cross-checked cause with gene scores and by comparing mothers with partners.

Few links proved strong or wide. Effects for mothers and partners were alike in most tests, which hints at home factors, not womb effects. Maternal smoking still tied firmly to small babies, higher child weight, and mood and behaviour issues. A free web tool lets readers browse all results.
pmc-13395430:
Roberto M. Benzo and co-authors ask, in 2026, what helps or blocks heart symptom tracking during cancer care. Many cancer drugs strain the heart, and early signs can slip between visits. The team interviewed twelve patients on heart-straining therapy and twelve of their care staff at a cardio-oncology clinic. Answers were sorted by skill, chance, and drive.

Both sides saw tracking as shared work. Patients often felt unsure which symptoms matter and when to worry. Time pressure and competing demands squeezed tracking chances. Ties with staff and family support shaped the effort. Gains from tracking, such as early action, fed drive. The authors map fixes for each factor.
pmc-13395530:

Failing hearts make too many reactive oxygen species, which push cells toward death. The review traces a chain through cell power plants: poor calcium handling starves energy cycles, which drains the cell's antioxidant shield. Harmful species then escape in greater force.

One drug family raises calcium inside the power plants and has shown promise. Other drugs sop up the harmful species directly, deep in the power plant. A third path tops up raw material for the shield itself. The authors sort these levers as targets for trials.
pmc-13396030:
Franz Rubel and co-authors issued an updated atlas of ticks in Germany in 2026, adding newly located records for species that live in the country and for kinds carried in from abroad. The atlas now maps 26 species in all, based on records tied to exact places.

The common castor bean tick, Ixodes ricinus, gained 271 new locations, while imported Hyalomma species, which arrive on migratory birds and can carry serious viruses, added many records as well. Rare bat and bird ticks contributed only a handful each. By tracking where each species turns up, the update helps health and veterinary services judge where tick-borne disease risks are growing.
pmc-13396230:

The team built a library of 64 antioxidant ionizable lipids, screened them, and landed on a lead particle, AO12LNP, whose lipid carries a 4-hydroxyphenyl group that scavenges reactive species.

The particles stayed uniform at roughly 150 nanometers across and packed over 80 percent of their mRNA cargo. That improved regeneration outcomes and genome editing efficiency in the reported experiments.
pmc-13396430:

That paragraph presented a 35-year-old man with HIV and substance addiction who arrived with ulcerated skin sores and a painless testicular lump. The correction leaves the review's account standing while flagging the overlap for readers and indexers.
pmc-13396730:

With a loaded cathode at 47.4 milligrams per square centimeter, the cell reached a specific energy of 201.5 watt-hours per kilogram counting all components. pmc-13396830:
Fella Chennou and others gauge biomarker-based eligibility rules in acute kidney injury trials in a 2026 systematic review and methodological meta-analysis. Hunting six data stores for trials from 2010 to 2023 with biomarker eligibility and kidney or death outcomes, the team compared expected versus seen primary event rates and modeled power effects. The read shows how enrichment shifts event rates and what that means for trial sizing. Trial designers gain a methodological fix for biomarker-enriched kidney studies.
pmc-13397330:
Delfina R. Msanga and co-authors tested healthy-looking children at Bugando Medical Centre in Mwanza, Tanzania, for past infection with the parasite Toxoplasma gondii. Finding that background rate, and the household habits tied to it, guides prevention.
pmc-13397530:
William M Tian and colleagues ask whether immune-calming biologic drugs raise risks for people having breast enlargement or rebuilding. Their 2026 study uses the TriNetX health record database. The team then compared wound healing, infection, fluid build-up and implant problems between groups. Past evidence was scattered and mostly borrowed from other kinds of surgery, so a direct look at breast cases gives surgeons firmer ground for planning and for honest talks with patients.
pmc-13397630:
Chongjing Li and others build a machine learning framework to predict atypical hyperplasia and endometrial cancer in women past menopause in a 2026 study. The framework backs tailored diagnostic sorting. Clinicians gain a validated tool for sparing low-risk patients invasive workup.
pmc-13397730:

Fifty-five patients were tracked again after surgery to watch changes over time. The fracture group proved frailer and showed a distinct signal pattern tied to their lower killer cell counts, hinting at targets for protecting recovery.
pmc-13398130:
Zhi Xu and co-authors build a smart gel dressing for diabetic wounds, which suffer low oxygen, corrosive oxygen by-products, stubborn inflammation and infection all at once. Their 2026 study forms the gel from chitosan, a boronic acid linker and polyvinyl alcohol, then loads it with manganese oxide particles wrapped in an algal pigment. The dressing can be injected, heals its own cuts, sticks to tissue and walls the wound off.

When corrosive molecules attack, the gel breaks down and frees its particles, which mop up the harmful oxygen species and release fresh oxygen in place. Near-infrared light then heats the particles to kill bacteria. The layered design aims to fix the wound's whole hostile climate rather than one fault at a time.
pmc-13399330:
Shriya Saha and a large team examined how killer T cells find their way into the skin lesions of Indian patients with post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis, in a 2026 immunology study. The condition follows apparent cure of visceral leishmaniasis. Its skin lesions still harbor parasites, making patients a reservoir that keeps transmission going. What summons those cells was poorly mapped.

Comparing patients with healthy controls, the team found far more CD8 T cells in the lesions. Those cells looked worn out. They carried the senescence marker CD57 and had lost the killing proteins perforin and granzyme. Blood and skin both showed raised levels of the messengers that attract T cells, including CCL5, CXCL9, and CXCL10, plus matching receptors on the cells. The authors argue that strong homing signals deliver exhausted cells that cannot finish the job. They propose host-directed therapies that restore T cell strength.
pmc-13399930:
Isadora Brandão Pelucio and colleagues compared antibiotics for Clostridioides difficile infection in people who also have inflammatory bowel disease, in a 2026 review and meta-analysis. Searching five databases through October 2024 under PRISMA rules, the team gathered studies that compared regimens head to head in adults with both conditions.

Nine studies covering 643 patients qualified. Recurrence struck 17.4 percent of patients on metronidazole against 8.2 percent on vancomycin. Pooling the four studies that allowed it leaned the same way, an odds ratio of 0.55 favoring vancomycin, though the difference was not statistically significant and the studies disagreed considerably with each other. Deaths were few and similar across groups, and every colectomy occurred in colitis patients. The authors conclude that vancomycin may protect higher-risk IBD patients from recurrence, but the evidence is thin and patchy, and prospective trials designed for this population are the real need.
pmc-13400230:
Pu and team report, in 2026, a hybrid bypass for complex femoropopliteal occlusive disease in patients who lack usable vein for a conventional graft. Their approach relines the above-knee popliteal artery from inside, using balloon angioplasty and a covered stent graft to build an outflow segment. A surgical bypass then runs from the femoral artery to that segment, avoiding a below-knee prosthetic graft with its poor record.

Three patients with chronic limb-threatening ischemia and failed interventions received the hybrid procedure. Operations took about three hours with mean blood loss of 300 milliliters, and technical success came in every case without perioperative complications or death. All three achieved limb salvage and symptom relief, with grafts patent for at least two years and one patient followed beyond three years. Popliteal arteries in the series were often under 5 millimeters, against a smallest 6-millimeter prosthetic graft, motivating the relining strategy.
pmc-13400530:
Meng-Tian Li and co-authors review, in 2026, how cereal crops can be engineered to make valuable fats in their seeds. Plant oils have wide uses, but getting rare lipids from natural sources can be costly and hard to scale. Synthetic biology now lets scientists rewire seed fat pathways in grains.

The review first lays out how seeds build fatty acids and assemble storage oils, plus the gene editing and transfer tools available for major cereals. It then covers progress making omega-3 fats EPA and DHA, wax esters and even insect sex pheromones in engineered plants. Cereals, the authors argue, could become large, sustainable factories for nutrition, farming and bio-based industry.
pmc-13401330:
Ying Liu and co-authors wrote a 2026 retrospective case-control study on chalazion history. They asked whether a past chalazion, a blocked oil gland lump on the eyelid, leaves lasting meibomian gland loss and dry eye disease. The glands in question supply the oily layer of the tear film.

Sixty patients with a past chalazion at one hospital between June 2021 and June 2024 were compared with 90 patients without that history. The team measured tear film height, tear break-up time, and surface staining, then split the chalazion group into 42 patients with gland loss and 18 without. Regression analysis hunted for factors driving gland loss. Within the gland-loss group, mild-to-moderate loss was compared with severe loss, above two-thirds of gland tissue, and loss severity was correlated with dry eye measures.
pmc-13401530:
Ana Carolina Silva Barros and co-authors present a 2026 protocol for a randomized trial pairing an extract of Terminalia fagifolia with light therapy for diabetic foot ulcers. The tree is a medicinal species from Brazil's Cerrado savanna. Diabetic wounds inflame persistently, heal slowly, and raise amputation risk.

The single-blind trial will enrol 102 people with type 2 diabetes and non-infected lower-limb ulcers, assigned at random to three groups. One group receives the plant extract with wound occlusion alone, while another combines the extract with photobiomodulation from a gallium arsenide laser, with further comparison treatment. Natural products are attractive add-ons for their anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, antimicrobial, and regenerative actions, but this species has never been tested clinically for wound healing. The protocol sets out the first such trial of the extract, alone and with light.
pmc-13401630:
Amy D Shapiro and co-authors wrote a 2026 plain language summary of long-term treatment with intravenous plasminogen concentrate for type 1 plasminogen deficiency. The condition is ultra-rare, and the body makes too little plasminogen protein. Without it, thick fibrin layers called lesions build up in different parts of the body.

The medicine, sold as RYPLAZIM, is the first approved treatment and works by replacing the missing protein. Adults and children in the study had already got the concentrate in the trial that led to approval or through expanded access programmes. Researchers tracked safety and effectiveness over the long term and tested whether dosing more or less often changed how well it worked. Members developed no new deficiency-related lesions and saw no return of earlier ones during treatment.
pmc-13402230:
Hajibadali and Allahverdipour propose, in 2026, that low- and middle-income countries institutionalize health literacy as a governance mechanism rather than a classroom goal. The Middle East and North Africa region is their case. Frameworks for health-literate groups come mostly from rich countries, while MENA systems face top-down governance, fragile public trust, and tight resources, calling for a home-grown roadmap instead of templates.

Their framework rests on five linked pillars: structural reform with advocacy, building social capital and trust, training for health workers, primary care overhaul, and lasting financing. Drawing on World Health Organization frameworks, the Ottawa Charter, and Health in All Policies, they argue health literacy should function as an accountability mechanism. It should sit inside state architecture, not as a patient-education add-on. The model, they contend, is astute and transferable to low- and middle-income settings wrestling with health equity and governance.
pmc-13402730:
Agrawal and co-authors test, in 2026, whether HIV envelope proteins engineered from viral clades can engage the germline precursors of VRC01-class broadly neutralizing antibodies. Those precursors are the rare immune cells a vaccine must awaken. The unmutated antibody forms do not bind the envelope at all; designed immunogens must coax them onto a maturation path. The team built envelope variants that remove glycan shields such as the site in about 80 percent of strains, and tracked responses in knock-in mice carrying the receptors.

Every such envelope woke the B cells. The receptors accumulated mutations at key positions depending on which immunogen was used, meaning identical cells followed different maturation pathways. Glycan occupancy underlined the design sensitivity: one built site sat at 78 percent versus above 90 percent at like sites on wild-type cores in assays. The authors say vaccine designers must choose immunogens by the route they induce, not activation.
pmc-13403030:
Chao Xiong and colleagues link epidural-related maternal fever, the temperature rise that follows labor epidurals in up to a third of mothers, with structural shifts in the vaginal microbial community. Epidurals remain the most used labor pain method, yet fever after placement tracks with worse newborn outcomes, from acidosis and low Apgar scores to encephalopathy, plus more cesarean deliveries. Why the fever happens is still unsettled.

The vaginal microbiome guards both mother and the newborn first microbial seeding, which shapes immune and nervous development. The study examines how fever episodes align with changes in that floral balance, its diversity and stability, among women giving birth. Xiong and the team frame the work as a step toward separating harmless epidural fever from infection risk without reflexively escalating care for mother and baby.
pmc-13403330:
Jing Hu and colleagues measure what rotting city waste breathes out during a week of storage, tracking ammonia and volatile organic compounds across three temperatures. A seven-day fermentation rig held simulated municipal waste at 30, 40, and 50 degrees Celsius, with online ammonia monitoring and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry for the organic vapors. Pile heat rose and moisture fell as microbes worked, confirming active breakdown.

Ammonia built steadily and rose faster at higher temperatures, and its calculated odor activity made it the priority stink to control. Vapor families took turns: aromatics early and mid-run, oxygenated compounds surging mid-run, alkanes leaking steadily, halogenated compounds spiking where plastics sat, and alkenes varying by stage. For incineration plant storage pits, the authors translate the timetable into ventilation and odor control priorities.
pmc-13403530:
Long-hao Jia and co-authors reviewed in 2026 a family of protective proteins in the kidney that can also do harm. These proteins, called peroxiredoxins, clear harmful oxygen by-products and keep cells in balance. Under strain they can change shape and act as helpers or as signal hubs.

In kidney tissue they guard power centers and damp swelling and scarring pathways. Yet some members, once changed or released from cells, can stir more injury instead. That two-faced behavior makes drug design tricky. Future work must boost the guard role at the right place and time while muting the harmful side.
pmc-13403730:
Renjian Li and a big team paired a new microscope with a smart cleanup program in 2026 to film living tissue in many colors at once. Splitting faint glow across many color bands leaves each band starved of light. Noise then swamps the true signals in live animals.

Their scope sweeps a thin sheet of light across the sample for cleaner starting images. The program then rebuilds sharp color layers, even for dyes whose colors nearly match. Whole live zebrafish could be imaged at fine scale. The team even tracked tiny plastic bits as they moved through the fish body.
pmc-13404630:
Gebremariam Wulie Geremew and many colleagues track heart patients in Ethiopia after acute coronary syndrome, reporting in 2026. Their question was how soon serious events return and what predicts them. The events counted were repeat heart attack, stroke and heart failure.

Charts covered 400 adults sent home on preventive medicines from Gondar university hospital between January 2020 and December 2024. During follow-up, 33.8 percent of patients had at least one major event, and the middle time to an event was 1.5 years in the reported follow-up. Cox modelling linked higher risk to female sex, other chronic illness and worse Killip class, a grade of heart failure severity. Findings point to closer follow-up for the highest-risk patients after discharge.
pmc-13405730:
Yangyang Shi and colleagues ask why social media users push back against the algorithms that feed them, in a 2026 survey study in China. Recommendations can feel pushy, repetitive and hard to escape. The team models resistance as a reaction to power, not just to bad suggestions.

Two perceptions anchor the model: algorithmic power, the sense that the system controls the user, and algorithmic technicality, its data-driven coldness. Both linked to stronger resistance through two routes, lower fairness judgements and stronger negative emotions. Survey data from users of algorithm-driven platforms support the parallel paths. The authors frame pushback as a response to platform control itself.
pmc-13406130:
Kyoung Yeon Moon and Taeeun Shim sort South Korean students by how they relate to chatty artificial intelligence, in a 2026 Q-method study. Fifty-six university students who use conversational AI ranked forty statements built from literature and interviews. The method reveals shared viewpoints rather than average opinions.

Four viewpoints emerged, together explaining 55 percent of the variation in the reported analysis. Groups ranged from students who treat AI as a mere tool and deny any relationship, to autonomy defenders guarding their independence. In between sit selective emotional users and reflective distancers. No group saw AI as a full substitute for human relationships, though they differed on emotional use and boundary setting.
pmc-13406630:
Hidehiko Hara reviews blood-thinning treatment after structural heart procedures in a single-author 2026 article. Catheter repairs such as valve placement, leak sealing and appendage closure have transformed care, but clots and bleeding must be balanced afterwards. Trial and registry evidence from mainly 2015 to 2025 is gathered.

Choices range from one antiplatelet drug to two, or full anticoagulation, with different answers per procedure. In valve replacement, early practice favoured dual therapy, while later trials shifted the picture, the review explains. Stroke, device clots and major bleeding anchor the outcome comparisons. Guidance is still evolving, and Hara maps where certainty ends for each intervention.
pmc-13407130:
Micol Massimiani reviews, in 2026, the signalling cast that lets an embryo implant and the placenta form. A ready embryo and a ready womb lining must arrive in step. Signals pass between mother and embryo to sync the meeting. Failures in that exchange sit behind failed implantation, repeated miscarriage, and infertility.

Once attached, the growing embryo needs a working interface for nutrients, gases, immune tolerance, and hormones, which the placenta provides. Its building involves dedicated cells invading and blood vessels remodelling. Growth factors and hormone signals steer the whole build. When placentation goes wrong, preeclampsia, restricted fetal growth, and early birth can follow. The review gathers decades of progress on these processes for readers in fertility medicine.
pmc-13407330:
Xiaobing Zhang and co-authors review, in 2026, how failing quality control inside cell power plants may drive Parkinson's disease. Damaged mitochondria, the cell's energy units, normally get repaired, reshaped, or recycled through systems including the PINK1 and Parkin pathway, and when control slips, faulty units pile up and stress the cell.

The review connects that pile-up to oxidation chemistry that encourages the clumping protein alpha-synuclein, dopamine breakdown products, and membrane changes. Fragments of mitochondrial DNA escaping their compartment can also trip innate immune alarms, feeding long-running brain inflammation. Newer hints involve chemical marks on RNA. Treatments aiming to boost recycling, shield mitochondria, or calm immune signalling are gaining attention, likely in combination rather than alone.
pmc-13407630:
Heeyeon Son and co-authors examine, in 2026, how family life relates to symptom distress in Korean adolescents and young adults with cancer. Symptom distress in this age group is common yet often overlooked. Family support shapes coping. The team reused existing data from young patients and their parents. They tested which family factors track with lower distress.

Parents and young patients did not always see the family the same way, especially on support, which the young people rated lower than their parents did. Among every factor tested, only the patients' own perception of family strength was linked to lower symptom distress, with the connection clearest during active treatment. The authors urge supportive care built around the young person's viewpoint rather than the parents' alone.
pmc-13407830:
Hadeer Ali and co-authors produce, in 2026, melanin from a sea-associated bacterium and cook it into glowing carbon dots for medical use. Melanin protects against light and oxidation but is scarce from sustainable sources and dissolves poorly, so the team optimised production from a newly isolated Bacillus strain, reaching 0.208 grams per litre with a statistical design.

Heat treatment in water converted the pigment into dispersible dots 9 to 15 nanometres across that absorb ultraviolet light, fluoresce in tunable colours, and stay stable under illumination. The dots spared healthy skin cells, keeping over 70 percent alive, while killing breast cancer cells selectively, with potency differing between two cancer lines and strong suppression of long-term colony growth. Computer modelling predicted interactions with several cancer-related targets, supporting combined therapy-and-imaging potential.
pmc-13408230:
Makoto Kondo, Hanae Fujita, Koji Habe, and Keiichi Yamanaka present a 2026 case report of a factory worker whose hands turned yellow-brown after phenol contact. Phenol normally causes an irritant skin burn with that characteristic staining. The patient, newly assigned to resin adhesive production, reused contaminated work gloves for about two hours.

Painless discoloration appeared after his first shift, followed by pain and swelling, then red plaques spreading to his forearm, thigh, and chest. Doctors read the distant rash as an id reaction, a secondary flare away from the original contact site. Symptoms settled with conservative treatment once exposure stopped. The case reminds clinicians that the yellow-brown stain is a diagnostic clue and that a quick work history can clinch the cause.
pmc-13408430:
Andi Praja Wira Yudha Luthfi and co-authors report in 2026 a rare benign tumour removed from a 54-year-old woman's ankle. The growth, an osteochondrolipoma, mixes mature fat with cartilage and bone inside a fatty tumour, and it almost never appears in the hindfoot. It had enlarged slowly without pain but was starting to interfere with footwear.

Scans showed a tidy, mixed soft-tissue mass with hardened parts and no attachment to bone, and surgeons removed it completely. Microscopy confirmed fat laced with cartilage and mature bone, sealing the diagnosis. Three months later the patient wore shoes comfortably, her ankle function score had risen, and nothing had regrown. The authors remind clinicians to keep this harmless entity in mind when a calcified foot mass could otherwise suggest something more sinister.
pmc-13409730:
Marina Axentii and colleagues, writing in 2026, test whether a rapeseed protein and fiber mix can lift the food value of wheat pasta. They made rigatoni with five mixes, swapping in the rapeseed blend for none, 5, 10, 15, or 20 percent of the flour. Dough handling, inner structure, and cooking quality were all tracked.

Rheology tests and a Mixolab device showed how each dough stretched, held water, and stayed stable during mixing. Moderate amounts, from 5 to 15 percent, made the dough firmer and more springy. Higher shares broke up the gluten network, so more solids were lost in cooking water and the cooked pasta turned softer. The middle range looks like the best trade-off for now.
pmc-13411430:
Zhili Lu and colleagues grade in 2026 answers from six large language models to patient questions about age-related macular degeneration, a leading cause of vision loss in older adults. Patients increasingly ask chatbots about their eyes, yet accuracy, transparency, and reading level were untested for this condition. Thirty real-world questions were put to each model.

Two senior eye doctors, blinded to which model wrote what, scored all 180 answers with four standard quality tools. Agreement between the raters ran strong to near-perfect. No model met the reading benchmark discussed in the study, and gaps between trustworthy content and readable content are the paper's theme. Patients may get sound facts written well above their reading level.
pmc-13411930:
Andrew D. Meyer and colleagues set out a 2026 pilot trial protocol, nicknamed TEAPOT, for children who bleed after tonsil surgery. Tonsillectomy ranks among the most common operations in American children, yet up to five percent return to emergency care with bleeding. Surgeons usually take these children back to the operating room for cauterization. Earlier chart reviews hint that nebulized tranexamic acid, a drug that protects blood clots, might lessen the bleeding.

Children arriving with secondary bleeding will get three nebulized doses of either the drug or salt water, assigned at random. The pilot tracks enrollment pace, protocol adherence, return trips to surgery, pain, anxiety, drug levels in the body, and side effects. Results will shape a larger confirmatory trial.
pmc-13412130:
Stanley Innes and colleagues write a 2026 commentary on how hands-on therapists can work safely with people who live with borderline personality disorder. The condition often comes with long-term pain and muscle or joint trouble. So physios, chiropractors, osteopaths, and massage staff meet these patients a lot. Few, though, are trained in how mood swings, past trauma, and sharp feelings about trust shape hands-on care.

The authors borrow from the NICE guide for the condition and adapt its core ideas to the treatment room. Joint planning, steady care from the same staff, and clear limits all earn a place. Touch can help, yet the same closeness can do harm when handled with poor care. They call for trauma-aware practice and for studies planned with patients.
pmc-13412330:
David Livingston and colleagues published a 2026 bedside algorithm for lower gut bleeding in adults arriving at emergency departments. The working group of the Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery built the stepwise guide to standardize first checks and treatment choices, while stressing that it never replaces bedside judgment.

Lower gut bleeding strikes about 33 to 87 people per 100000, accounts for 3 percent of emergency surgery referrals, and hits older patients with more coexisting illness than upper gut bleeding. Hospitals can adapt the annotated algorithm into local protocols, giving emergency teams a shared, evidence-based starting path.
pmc-13413330:
Sheng Chen and colleagues compare in 2026 two strains of a fungal partner living inside a wild barley grass, with opposite effects on the plant's photosynthesis. Epichloë endophytes often help host grasses, yet strain differences from separate populations were poorly understood. One strain came from Gansu and one from Xinjiang; each was placed into fungus-free plants and also studied in its natural pairing, with leaf structure and gas exchange measured.

Plants carrying the Gansu strain kept healthy chloroplasts, richer pigments, and stronger photosynthesis than fungus-free controls. The Xinjiang strain deformed chloroplasts and depressed the same measures in its hosts. Both new pairings stored extra starch grains in leaves. Since the fungal strain alone flipped the outcome, the authors urge strain-level selection for forage use.
pmc-13415230:
Kang Shu and co-authors review gold nanoparticles as antiviral tools in 2026, organizing the field by design, surface, and mechanism. Gold particles can be tuned in size and shape, and their surfaces accept many attachments. Methods covered range from citrate reduction and seed growth to greener plant based routes.

Surface coatings include polyethylene glycol, nucleic acids, antibodies, peptides, sugars, and antiviral drugs. Coated particles can block a virus at entry, slow its copying, hinder its exit, or destroy it with light driven heat. Gaps remain in linking structure to effect, plus safety and scale-up hurdles. The review offers a framework for building the next generation of such particles.
pmc-13416130:
Annika Hettich, Morten A. Karsdal, and Nicholas Willumsen measure collagen made by tumor linked fibroblasts to expose how they differ, in 2026. Fibroblasts around tumors lay down matrix that helps cancers spread, yet these cells vary widely. Four cell lines were grown for up to twelve days with growth cues and anti scar drugs.

Two lines were scar prone by nature and barely changed with extra cues. Two quiet lines ramped up three collagen markers strongly when pushed. One growth factor chiefly drove type three collagen output, another drove type six. Two anti scar drugs pushed output back to its start level or below. Matching care to cell type looks key.
pmc-13417330:
Fang Yuan and colleagues screen bacteria from traditional Chinese fermented vegetables for removing aflatoxin B1, a potent mould toxin, in a 2026 food safety study. Six strains showed removal ability. One strain of Lactiplantibacillus plantarum, coded YS-718, removed about 78 percent of the toxin in liquid fermentation tests.

Work with separate cell parts showed the bacterial cells themselves adsorb the toxin most strongly, rather than a released substance breaking it down. Binding survived repeated washing and hours in simulated stomach fluid. Fermenting peanut meal with the strain cut toxin while raising protein and amino acid content, suggesting a greener way to rescue contaminated feed.
pmc-13417730:
The EFSA PPR Panel weighs whether routine dog toxicity studies can be waived in pesticide approval, in a 2026 scientific opinion. European rules require 90 day feeding studies in rats and dogs for new active substances. The dog study's added value has been questioned, prompting a retrospective review by the panel.

Across past cases, nearly all species differences in safe dose levels traced to study design, natural variation, or body size scaling, not true dog sensitivity. A tiered strategy with set data criteria is proposed to justify waivers case by case. The approach also promotes non animal methods in safety testing.
pmc-13418130:
Hongjun Han and colleagues followed 46 children with lupus in 2026 through 48 weeks of belimumab added to standard therapy. The drug targets a B-cell signal, and the team tracked natural killer cell counts alongside complement levels, disease scores, and steroid doses.

Killer cell counts more than doubled by week 48, disease scores fell from 16.4 to 2.1, most children reached low disease activity, and over 90 percent cut steroids. The paper links rising killer cells to complement recovery and calmer disease, while calling for controlled trials to confirm the pattern in larger cohorts of children with lupus.
pmc-13419030:
Holly Childs and colleagues studied soy metabolism and heart risk in 148 midlife American women in 2026, using data from the Study of Women's Health Across the Nation. Gut bacteria convert soy daidzein into O-desmethylangolensin in some women only, splitting them into producer and non-producer types with possibly different heart profiles.

Non-producers averaged 7.6 points higher systolic blood pressure than high producers after adjustment, with fasting glucose also trending higher. The paper supports checking gut metabotype when judging soy's heart effects, while noting the small non-producer group of 23 women.
pmc-13419230:
Salazar and colleagues studied in 2026 how changing tongue base size affects chewing and swallowing in minipigs. A growing tongue base, as in weight gain, and surgical shrinking of it both occur in patients with breathing problems during sleep.

Both groups showed delayed timing of palate and tongue muscles during chewing at all checks after baseline. The fattened pigs used stronger tongue and jaw muscle activity than the surgery group. Swallowing timing was delayed mainly in the surgery group, hinting at impaired swallowing after the operation. The fattened group showed weaker breathing, with slower airflow and smaller breath volumes. The authors conclude that both enlargement and reduction force feeding and breathing to adapt. Each route carries its own risk: swallowing problems after surgery, and airway problems with weight gain.
pmc-13419330:
Park and co-authors compared two ways of measuring brain chemistry with magnetic resonance spectroscopy, a scan method that reads chemical signals instead of anatomy. They set a fast spiral imaging technique against the established single-voxel method in the same brain region, the posterior cingulate cortex, in five healthy volunteers at 3 Tesla.

By eye, spectra from the two methods looked comparable in overall quality when scan times were matched exactly. Quantitatively, the imaging method produced a lower signal-to-noise ratio and wider uncertainty bounds on its chemical estimates than the single-voxel scans. Measured levels of glutamate and of glutamate plus glutamine also came out lower with the imaging approach. The team attributes the small gaps to differing tissue weighting and sensitivity, and calls the techniques broadly comparable overall.
pmc-13421330:
Ramon Cohen and seven colleagues report, in a 2026 cohort study, that antibody levels at the low end of normal can foreshadow chronic lymphocytic leukaemia many years later. Rather than a deficiency diagnosis, these low-normal immunoglobulin readings may betray early immune disturbance or a hidden precursor condition.

The study followed 294,712 adults aged 40 to 80 with routine antibody testing for up to ten years. Low-normal IgA carried the strongest link to later leukaemia, roughly two and a half times the risk, ahead of IgM and IgG. Checking people with low lymphocyte counts separated the signals: IgA stayed predictive while the others faded, suggesting different mechanisms. The authors read IgA's long reach — over a decade — as a constitutional susceptibility marker.
pmc-13421430:
Junnan Fang leads a nine-author review, published in 2026, of a soil fungus genus called Gongronella and its prospects for farming. The genus lives in many habitats, colonises plant roots, and appears to feed crops while protecting them, which raises hopes for a biological fertiliser and pest-control ally.

The fungus secretes enzymes that free nutrients from urea and organic phosphorus, and it recruits helpful bacteria to share that work, improving what plants can take up. It also tolerates environmental stress well. The authors balance this promise against open questions about how its partnerships with plants actually work. They argue that answering those questions is the step between a promising microbe and a reliable farm input.
pmc-13421530:
Yi-Wen Bao leads a ten-author team studying, in a 2026 paper, a specific class of white matter damage in Alzheimer's disease: bright spots on scans that hug the brain's fluid-filled ventricles. Such lesions reflect small vessel disease and may mark processes at the boundary between brain fluid and tissue.

Automated lesion mapping ran on two cohorts, both with MRI, amyloid scans and cognitive testing. One held 295 participants from an Australian imaging study. The other held 82 people seen at a memory clinic. The ventricle-adjacent lesion volume separated impaired from normal participants in both cohorts, predicted later decline, and tracked fluid volume closely. Statistical mediation suggested it carries part of the link between brain fluid volume and cognition. The authors argue lesion location deserves as much attention as total burden.
pmc-13421730:
Jay Prakash, Tonny Veenith, Bram Rochwerg and Kalavathy Swarna write, in a 2026 commentary, on sharpening ambulance care for supraventricular tachycardia, a fast heart rhythm often first treated before hospital. Responding to a recent scoping review, they accept its map of prior work. Their focus is the wide variation it exposed in diagnosis and treatment between ambulance services.

Their proposals start with sending electrocardiograms for remote expert reading. They add artificial intelligence decision support. They urge wider use of the modified Valsalva manoeuvre, a straining technique that can reset the rhythm. They also want better-judged use of the drug adenosine. They warn that most evidence is observational and spans changing eras of care. Prospective multicentre studies with standard outcomes top their research agenda.
pmc-13422330:
Mohamed and colleagues examine in 2026 whether the formula used to size breathing machine settings treats male and female lungs fairly in acute respiratory distress syndrome, a severe lung failure. Tidal volume is set by predicted body weight, which is calculated from sex and height.

Pooling individual data from seven landmark trials gave 5,367 ventilated patients, 46 percent of them women. Women received smaller absolute breath volumes than men, but once scaled to predicted weight the volumes were nearly equal. Raw driving pressure, the pressure swing that inflates the lungs, ran slightly higher in women. Yet after adjustment for age, severity, and settings, sex showed no firm link to driving pressure. Women did show a slightly higher blood pH and a clearly lower ventilation ratio, a measure of how efficiently carbon dioxide is cleared.
pmc-13422930:
Jing Yuan and five colleagues audit, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, the orphan drugs China approved between 2005 and 2022 — what they treat, what they add and what they cost. Fifty-nine drugs covering thirty-two rare-disease indications passed the national regulator in that window.

Where data existed, disease frequency varied enormously, from under one case per million people to about twenty-six per hundred thousand for prevalence. Using French health-authority ratings as the yardstick, most drug-indication pairs were judged medically important, a small share weak or insufficient. Approval in China trailed the first global launch by a lag the team measured, and monthly treatment costs were tallied alongside reimbursement-list coverage. The authors offer the audit to policymakers balancing access against price.
pmc-13423030:
Aguilar and co-authors tested a Spanish-language version of the Pain Self Efficacy Questionnaire, adapted culturally for Spanish-speaking Mexican Americans living with chronic pain. The questionnaire measures pain self-efficacy, a person's confidence in staying active despite pain, which predicts engagement in daily activities but had lacked a validated tool for this population.

The study enrolled 182 adults with chronic pain, of whom 56.6 percent were women, with a mean age of 38.3 years at enrollment. The adapted scale showed high internal consistency, with reliability coefficients near 0.92 on both standard measures reported. A factor analysis supported its underlying structure, and scores correlated modestly in the expected directions with pain anxiety, pain catastrophizing, and pain interference. The authors conclude the version is reliable and preliminarily valid, while calling for further work before routine clinical use.
pmc-13423930:

pmc-13424130:

pmc-13424730:

pmc-13430730:

pmc-13430830:
