Hohenhaus and colleagues follow neck movement after two-level cervical fusion surgery. Their 2026 prospective trial studies 69 patients having anterior cervical discectomy and fusion at two levels for degenerative disease. Bending range was measured with a goniometer. Patients rated their own mobility before surgery, at three months, and at one year. Pain and quality-of-life scores accompanied the ratings.

Measured mobility dipped at three months across bending, tilting, and rotation, then recovered to essentially the preoperative range by one year. Patients' own ratings told a kinder story earlier: subjective mobility had already improved significantly at three months and stayed improved. Neck and arm pain fell significantly by three months at rest and under strain, quality-of-life components rose, and about 93 percent of patients were satisfied with the surgery. The authors conclude two-level fusion does not cost lasting neck mobility.
pmc-13452830:
Stefanie N Hakkesteegt and a large team test whether scan features can flag which desmoid tumors will break a watch and wait plan. Desmoid type fibromatosis is a rare growth that does not spread, and doctors often watch it first rather than treat at once. Their 2026 study pools 200 patients from the Netherlands, Italy, and Canada who began with watching alone.

The watching plan failed for 26 percent of patients, who then needed active treatment. A model built on MRI scan features reached fair skill at home, and it held up better in the Italian and Canadian groups than in the Dutch one. Adding basic clinical facts did not sharpen the model at all. The authors see promise in the scan based tool, while noting it needs more work before clinics rely on it.
pmc-13453030:
Prashant Acharya and nine co-authors lay out a trial plan to curb antibiotic overuse among junior doctors in Nepal. Drug resistance grows when antibiotics are handed out too freely, a pattern seen in many lower income countries. Their 2026 protocol tests two cheap nudges that add little to a doctor's workload.

The trial plans for about 60 doctors in five hospitals and roughly 3,600 patients over six months. In a stepped rollout, hospitals first require doctors to write the diagnosis on each prescription, a prompt to pause before prescribing. Later, each doctor gets personal feedback on how often they in fact prescribe antibiotics. The main yardstick is the share of visits that end with an antibiotic, tracked across the rollout steps.
pmc-13453530:
Huang and co-authors ask whether menopausal hormone therapy changes liver cancer risk. Their 2026 Swedish cohort study compares 217,878 women who received the therapy between 2006 and 2023 with over a million age-matched women who did not. The analysis separated the two main liver cancer types and adjusted for smoking and alcohol diagnoses, fatty liver disease, diabetes, obesity, and several medications.

Hormone users had about half the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma, the most common liver cancer, with a hazard ratio of 0.46 indicating the reduction. The reduction appeared for estrogen-only and combined preparations alike, and looked strongest in users aged 60 and over. No association appeared for the second cancer type, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, where the hazard ratio sat near one. The authors report an association, not proof of protection, within this observational design.
pmc-13453730:
Marcelo Pedrosa Gomes, Leila Teresinha Maranho, Letícia Estela Cavichiolo Espindola, and Flávia Yoshie Yamamoto review how new kinds of pollution stress plants and shape their use as living cleaners. The pollutants span drugs, pesticides, PFAS chemicals, nanomaterials, and plastic bits in soil and water. Their 2026 review links how each pollutant enters and moves in the plant to the harm it does.

What counts is the dose inside the plant, not just the dose around it, the authors stress. Stress replies swing widely: defense enzymes rose 1.5 to 4.6 fold in some studies, while a key protective chemical fell by 20 to 50 percent. Hormone shifts ranged from mild to a ten fold surge under hard stress. Microbes living on roots also sway how plants cope. The review warns that mixed pollutants plus climate stress break simple one factor predictions.
pmc-13454030:
Shengnan Tian and five co-authors review a gut to ovary signaling chain that may help explain premature ovarian insufficiency, early loss of ovarian function. The condition affects about 1.1 to 3.7 percent of women and lifts later risk of heart disease and bone loss. Current care mostly means hormone replacement, which eases symptoms without restoring the ovary. Their 2026 review centers on butyrate, a fatty acid made by gut microbes.

In their model, butyrate travels as a metabolic messenger and switches on a protective pair, SIRT1 and FoxO1, inside egg supporting cells. That switch curbs cell death signals and steadies the cells' power plants, helping follicles survive. Animal work backs parts of the chain: butyrate restored ovarian function in models, and stool transplants from healthy donors slowed ovary aging in mice. The authors call the axis a route toward disease changing care.
pmc-13454130:
Fady Khoury and others studied how active conflict and national identity mold intergroup bias in Israel in 2026, among Arabic and Hebrew speakers. Prosocial choices weigh self versus others and are shaped by identity and conflict, yet how war and language affect bias in real time was little tested. Participants completed a social value orientation task for in-group and out-group recipients.

Across 338 participants, people were more generous toward in-group than out-group members, and bias intensified during the Israel-Hamas war. Language of presentation did not significantly change bias. Among Arabic speakers only, national identity correlated with bias during the war, not before it. The findings show bias is dynamic, tied to minority-majority status and active conflict, not fixed by language alone.
pmc-13454230:
Jiaojiao Fu, Chuanxi Zhu, and Zhenzhen Fan review the two way street between alpha-synuclein clumps and failing lysosomes in Parkinson disease. The clumped protein fills the Lewy bodies that mark the disease, while lysosomes are the cell's recycling centers that should clear it. Their 2026 review pulls together molecular, cell, and animal work on the loop.

When lysosomes falter, the cleanup path stalls and clumps build faster; the clumps in turn jam the recycling machinery further. The review maps the enzymes and control switches where the loop can be cut. Candidate therapies aim to restart lysosome work, from gene and drug approaches to boosters of the cleanup path. The authors frame the axis as a central target for treatments that might slow the disease rather than mask symptoms.
pmc-13455230:
Daiki Mori and others told of loxoprofen overdose with no harm in 2026. Loxoprofen is a much-used anti-inflammatory prodrug. Overdose reports are scant, with no past symptom-free massive-dose cases.

A forty-three-year-old woman took over eight thousand milligrams of loxoprofen and came in two hours later in stable shape. Labs and heart tracings were plain, and belly CT showed no stomach contents. She stayed symptom-free with plain labs through her stay. She went home on day three. Drug-level tests showed sky-high blood levels two hours past intake. Loxoprofen hit one hundred fifty-nine micrograms per millilitre, trans-hydroxy sixty-four, and cis-hydroxy twenty-nine. Levels fell fast soon after. The case hints high blood levels need not mean harm. Fast drug breakdown may explain it. Toxicologists gain a symptom-free massive-dose profile.
pmc-13456830:
Coşkun and colleagues study what accompanies cyberbullying among teenagers in this 2026 school-based survey. Online bullying, both suffering it and doing it, is a growing mental health concern in adolescence. The team questioned 600 students aged 14 to 18. Five established scales covered cyberbullying, emotion regulation, and metacognitive beliefs. Metacognitive beliefs are habits of thinking about one's own thoughts. Loneliness, social support, and time on social media were also measured.

Being targeted online was linked with greater difficulty regulating emotions, stronger unhelpful thinking beliefs, and more loneliness, and with less perceived social support. Emotion regulation difficulty was the strongest single predictor of both victimization and perpetration in their regression models. Modeling suggested loneliness carries part of the connection: struggling with emotions and feeling unsupported fed loneliness, which in turn was tied to involvement in cyberbullying on both sides.
pmc-13456930:
Ubaldo Miranda-Soberón and colleagues test how well hats shield the face from sun in Peru in a 2026 field experiment. Ultraviolet light drives skin cancer on exposed face areas, and farm workers rely on hats, yet brim width and shape change protection site by site. Twenty head coverings, four caps, eight medium-brim walking hats and eight wide-brim peasant hats, were mounted on a mannequin in Ica and measured hourly from 09:00 to 15:00 in February 2024.

Wide-brim peasant hats blocked a median of 83.1 percent of facial ultraviolet light, well ahead of walking hats at 62.0 percent and caps at 44.5 percent, and led at the nose, lips, neck and chin and during peak hours from 11:00 to 13:00. Ears were best protected overall at 92.9 percent. The mannequin test cannot capture movement or fit, but it gives a clear ranking for workers choosing headwear under strong sun.
pmc-13457030:
Qianyu He and four colleagues ask, in a 2026 data study, whether one metabolic enzyme tells the same story in arthritic joint lining and in aging muscle. The enzyme, NAMPT, feeds the cell's NAD supply and stirs inflammation. The team re-analyzed public gene datasets for knee osteoarthritis synovium and older skeletal muscle, keeping discovery and confirmation rounds apart.

In the discovery round, the enzyme's signal trended downward in both tissues, though arthritis studies disagreed enough to blur pooling. Outside datasets partly backed the fall, in arthritic lining and in muscle from patients with true sarcopenia. Gene pathway scoring linked the enzyme to immune and metabolic activity in tissue-specific ways. The authors conclude that NAMPT sits in different company in joint and muscle, a caution against one-size theories of aging tissues. They frame the work as hypothesis building for targeted follow-ups.
pmc-13457630:
Gunchan Paul writes an editorial on paraquat, the emerald-green herbicide behind an outsized share of fatal poisonings in India's farm belts. National crime data for 2024 place Telangana first in insecticide suicides, the two Telugu states together accounting for about one in four such deaths nationwide. Paraquat is frequently the substance involved, killing 50 to 90 percent of those who swallow it.

The poison concentrates in the lungs, where it generates oxygen radicals that scar the tissue into irreversible fibrosis, so patients suffocate slowly while fully conscious. Removal treatments such as dialysis or hemoperfusion help only inside a golden window of two to four hours, before the lungs lock the toxin away. Commenting on a South Indian intensive care study in the same issue, Paul credits improving hospital protocols. Yet he insists the real fix is upstream: public awareness and government restriction of a chemical this lethal, this easy to buy.
pmc-13457730:
Samra Beyene and six colleagues published this 2026 methods study introducing CLARI-O, a tissue-clearing technique adapted for brain organoids, the lab-grown brain tissues used to model human development. Studying these 3D balls of cells usually means slicing them thin, which destroys their spatial layout. Clearing makes whole organoids transparent instead, so microscopes can map cells, connections and shapes through the intact structure.

The team show CLARI-O imaging glial cells, including oligodendrocytes and microglia, which are scarce in organoids, and their contacts with neurons. They applied it to forebrain assembloids, fused organoid pairs, to chart the border between regions. They also cleared mouse brains carrying transplanted human organoids to trace cell migration, blood vessel growth and integration. They also cleared samples after live calcium imaging, a first, matching recorded activity to the structure seen afterwards. The authors position CLARI-O for disease modelling and drug screening.
pmc-13457930:
Fleetwood and colleagues compare survival after heart attack for people with and without mental disorders in England. Their 2026 cohort study covers 131,075 patients with the milder heart attack type and 79,045 with the severe type, treated between November 2019 and February 2023. Diagnoses of schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and depression came from linked health records, and deaths from national registers.

Thirty-day mortality was higher for several groups: after the milder attack type, schizophrenia carried about 73 percent higher odds of death and depression about 17 percent higher. After the severe type, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and depression all raised thirty-day risk. Every disorder was tied to higher one-year mortality, though adjusting for differences in guideline-based care shrank the gaps. The authors report the pandemic generally did not widen these disparities.
pmc-13458030:
Ribeiro and colleagues in Canada read in 2026 a live cohort of hard to treat psoriatic arthritis patients put on two strong drugs at once. The ill flares joints and skin, and one drug leaves some folk still raw. The cohort sits in a world research pool tracked ahead of time. Thirty nine patients took a pair for two months or more. Most had burned through five strong drugs first. Joint, skin, and self scores were logged each few months.

The pair of a base drug plus a fast pill did the clear work. Sore and swollen joint counts fell, and skin scores fell with them. Self felt pain and life marks rose too. Ill turns on the pairs were few and mild. The team backs pair use case by case, and calls for strict long trials on safe pairs.
pmc-13458730:
Federica Battistini and the Ascona B-DNA Consortium, fourteen research groups strong, model DNA at a scale meant to expose a physical code written into its sequence. DNA's flexibility and shape shift with the letters it carries, steering protein binding, nucleosome placement, and genome evolution, yet the combinations explode beyond piecemeal study. Their 2026 hexABC effort embeds all 2,080 DNA hexamers inside 190 chosen 20-base-pair duplexes and simulates each in replicate for at least ten microseconds in explicit solvent.

The runs produced a quarter-petabyte of data, ensembles spanning milliseconds at fragment level and a tenth of a second at base-pair level. Mining them maps sequence-dependent behavior, including rare backbone transitions, reversible base-pair opening, and partial unfolding events short runs miss. The consortium releases the results as checked, FAIR data, raw material for training coarse-grained and AI models aiming to simulate DNA at cellular scale.
pmc-13459030:
Wang and co-authors present the first survey of natural radioactivity in soils across Gansu Province, China. Their 2026 paper measured three naturally occurring radionuclides, thorium-232, radium-226, and potassium-40, in 115 soil samples from farmland and uncultivated sites. A high-purity germanium detector counted the gamma rays each sample emitted.

Average activity came to about 27 becquerels per kilogram for thorium-232, about 46 for radium-226, and about 567 for potassium-40. The calculated outdoor dose rate and annual effective dose for residents sat near world background levels, and the external hazard index was well below the safety threshold. Levels resembled those in neighbouring Sichuan Province. The authors conclude Gansu soils pose no significant radiological threat to local residents, and they offer the data as a baseline for future monitoring.
pmc-13459430:
Zhang-le Zhu and Hui-fen Hu compared fourteen versions of the triglyceride-glucose index, a cheap insulin-resistance estimate from blood fat and sugar, for predicting new cardiovascular disease in older adults. Their 2026 study combined two national aging cohorts, China's CHARLS and England's ELSA, totaling 5,028 middle-aged and older participants. Seven indices used a single measurement and seven used cumulative averages across two waves, and the team assessed each against heart disease and stroke events.

Follow-up ran a median of 5.0 years in the Chinese cohort and 13.5 years in the English one, during which 1,067 cardiovascular events occurred. All fourteen indices were significantly associated with new disease, but versions blending the index with obesity measures performed clearly stronger than the base index alone. Cumulative averages added only modest gains over single measurements. The team packaged the results into a nomogram and web tool.
pmc-13459530:
Belkadi and colleagues introduced a derived blood trait in 2026 that sharpens genetic reading of lipoprotein data from a widely used scanning platform. The platform measures fat-carrying particles in blood by size, but its readouts overlap heavily, which blurs biological meaning. The team computed each particle class's total fatty acid content from its lipid building blocks and checked the result against directly measured fatty acids in more than 274,000 UK Biobank participants.

The computed and measured values matched almost exactly. At the size-resolved level, the new trait gave stronger gene signals than the raw lipid measures at eight gene locations. Five of those genes act directly in fatty acid handling, including known fat-processing genes. The authors argue that adding the computed trait to future studies on this platform will make genetic and health findings easier to interpret.
pmc-13459630:
Fatma Özcan Sıkı and co-authors reviewed a decade of childhood solid organ trauma care to argue that the injured child, not the injury grade on a scan, should drive treatment decisions. Their 2026 study covered 1,043 children aged up to eighteen admitted to a Turkish tertiary center between 2014 and 2024. The injuries hit organs such as the liver and spleen. Mechanisms, transfusion needs, operations versus watchful management, and outcomes were analyzed against the graded severity of each injury.

Blunt trauma accounted for 97 percent of cases, with falls from height and traffic accidents the leading causes. Penetrating injuries made up the remaining 3 percent. The cohort's management patterns show how often children recovered without surgery under modern non operative protocols, reserving operations for the unstable rather than the highly graded. The authors frame their decade of experience as support for physiology first care.
pmc-13459830:
Koji Nozaka and Naohisa Miyakoshi report saving a dialysis patient's leg after free flap failure in a 2026 case report. Severe open tibial fractures in haemodialysis patients heal poorly, and flap loss in a single-vessel limb leaves few options. A 65-year-old man on maintenance haemodialysis sustained a severe open shin break, Gustilo IIIB, with major soft-tissue loss; first cleaning, outside bracing and back-muscle flap cover ended in flap death.

With only the posterior tibial artery supplying the leg, surgeons avoided another flap. They instead shortened the limb by 75 mm to close soft tissue with local muscle, then gradually lengthened it by the Ilizarov method. Bone union and alignment followed, the fixator came off at 17 months, and at eight years the patient was pain-free and back to agricultural work. Surgeons gain a vascular-independent salvage strategy for complex limb-threatening injuries.
pmc-13460230:
Jeffrey W. Ramos-Santiago leads a large team piloting in 2026 a text messaging program, A todo pulmón, meant to raise lung cancer screening among Latino adults in the United States. Latinos screen at particularly low rates despite strong interest when access improves, and they use texting heavily. Forty eligible adults who had missed annual screening received the bilingual program, built with a community advisory board, and answered surveys at the start and at three months.

Most participants had never heard of lung cancer screening, and nearly three quarters did not know they qualified. Follow-up was completed by thirty-five people. Verified screening reached twenty-five percent by three months, and a third completed shared decision-making talks. The team judges the approach feasible and acceptable for a fuller trial.
pmc-13461930:
Filippo Carannante and colleagues lay out, in a 2026 technique article, a keyhole approach for reversing a Hartmann operation in a patient with several past belly surgeries. The original operation leaves the colon ending in a stoma; reversal rejoins the bowel. Scar tissue, shifted anatomy, and fragile planes make reversal one of the hardest bowel operations. Most surgeons choose open surgery.

Entry was gained through the stoma site with a ring retractor, giving access and stable air pressure. Scar tissue was freed with a cold blade to limit heat injury. After the rectal stump and upper colon were freed, a stapled join was made. Dye imaging checked bowel blood flow, and an air test checked the join for leaks, with extra stitches where needed. Care followed an enhanced recovery plan. The operation finished without switching to open surgery, no stoma was needed, and the patient went home on day three.
pmc-13462230:
Philippa Jennifer Ayiku leads a 2026 lab study of a molecule that may make cisplatin hit cancer harder. Cancer cells survive DNA damage by copying past damaged spots, a tolerance trick called translesion synthesis. That route also breeds instability and drug resistance. The molecule, C#3, breaks a protein partnership, MAD2L2 and Rev1, that the trick needs. The team tested it in cells and mice.

Treated cells grew sensitive to cisplatin across cell lines, with stronger damage signals after treatment. A plasmid test showed the molecule blocked copying across damage spots in mammalian cells. Direct measures confirmed fewer pairs formed. Cells exposed during recovery kept damage signals on longer, as if repair had stalled. In mice with melanoma or triple-negative breast tumors, the drug pair shrank tumors more than either alone. The authors back this pathway as a drug target for boosting DNA-damaging chemotherapy.
pmc-13462330:
Jungang Tan leads a 2026 study of the gene TARDBP in liver cancer, formally hepatocellular carcinoma. The gene makes a protein, TDP-43, known to feed cancer processes, yet its meaning here was unclear. The team read cancer databases, then checked tissue with lab tests. They mapped where the gene is active cell by cell and tested its links with immune features and drugs.

TARDBP ran high in liver tumors and rose with stage, marking worse survival. Single-cell mapping showed little activity in immune cells but activity in tumor cells with invasive, fast-growing traits. Lowering the gene dampened a survival pathway and cut levels of PD-L1, a protein tumors use to hide from immunity. Patients with high TARDBP had weaker immune scores, more mutations, and poorer responses to checkpoint drugs. The authors name it a marker of bad outlook and a target for making immunotherapy work better.
pmc-13463630:
Di Xu and colleagues designed a catalyst in 2026 that turns carbon dioxide and hydrogen into ethanol, a fuel and industrial solvent. Carbon dioxide conversion could cut emissions and store green hydrogen, but past catalysts gave low ethanol yield from tangled reaction paths. Their design traps palladium-copper alloy particles inside Y zeolite, pairing metal and mineral sites to split competing steps.

The paired sites steered carbon-carbon joining and carbon-oxygen breaking in balance, reaching over 93% ethanol selectivity and over 200 milligrams per gram of catalyst per hour. That pace beats most earlier solid catalysts for this reaction. The recipe offers a route to high-value liquids from waste gas, though scale-up and hydrogen supply will decide its real climate value.
pmc-13463930:
Li Zhang and colleagues assessed nutrition in 2026 among women newly diagnosed with cervical cancer in Tanzania, where it is the most common women's cancer. Poor nutrition can worsen cancer outcomes, yet no local picture existed for these patients. The team studied 184 patients at the Ocean Road Cancer Institute from May to September 2023, scoring diet, blood markers, and food intake.

Nearly two fifths ate less after diagnosis, cutting cereals, leafy greens, orange vegetables, and fats, and 84.8% needed nutrition help. Moderate or severe malnutrition struck 48% of early-stage patients and 78% of late-stage patients, with late-stage scores clearly worse. The gap argues for routine nutrition screening and support alongside cancer treatment, especially for late-stage cases.
pmc-13464030:
Jakob Knold and co-authors present a case report, published in 2026. It describes one 83-year-old man with a very large aneurysm. An aneurysm is a balloon-like swelling in a vessel. His sat in his right coronary artery. A fall brought him to hospital, where it was found. Earlier scans showed it had grown to sixty millimetres. The heart team judged the rupture risk high.

The patient wished to avoid open-heart surgery. The team closed the aneurysm through a catheter. They used the condom technique. This balloon-based method seals off a vessel segment. The procedure succeeded. The approach suits aneurysms on arteries already fully blocked beyond the swelling. The authors note long-term durability is unproven.
pmc-13464130:
Fangzhou Ran, Dan Zhang, and Lingen Wang weigh how motorized food shopping links to household food waste in rural China. The team tracked 204 households in Shandong for three days in 2017, weighing edible food thrown away. Each household got a motor score based on how it fetched each kind of food.

Waste rose as motor scores climbed from low levels, then tended to fall at the top end. Storage waste showed the bend most clearly, while plate waste rose in a straight line. Motor scores foretold whether a household wasted at all, more than how much it wasted. Shopping more often sharpened the link, and plant-based staples drove the pattern more than perishable foods.
pmc-13464430:
Chen and colleagues read in 2026 the skin of high oil scalps in Asian adults who claim oil and flake woes. Scalp oil, or sebum, feeds itch and dandruff, yet its links to skin water were murky. The team read oil, water, shield, and a rust stress mark at three sites. One wash with an anti flake brew came last.

The scalp held the most oil, the least water, and the weakest shield of the three sites. Oil in the pores ran against skin water. The rust mark rose with oil, and with how much itch and flake folk claimed. One wash cut oil on the skin and in the pores, and the rust mark fell with it. The team urges brews that lift oil but spare the shield.
pmc-13465030:
Fekonja and co-authors interviewed a 2026 qualitative study of triage nurses in a Slovenian university hospital emergency department, asking how they perceive safety errors during triage. Triage sorts arriving patients by urgency, and mistakes there can delay care and cause harm. Accuracy studies abound, but nurses' own perceptions were rarely explored.

Nineteen triage nurses gave semi-structured interviews between September and December 2024, analysed thematically by Fekonja. Nurses described administrative errors such as misidentifying patients and wrong data entry, plus wrong urgency categories in both directions. Causes spanned human factors, organisational strain, and high patient volume pressing on the desk. Consequences included delays in care and potential patient harm for those mis-sorted. Prevention ideas centred on training, staffing, communication, teamwork, and systematic identification checks.
pmc-13465230:
Jiang and colleagues surveyed 336 Chinese patients in 2026 about life with neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder. The autoimmune disease attacks the optic nerves and spinal cord. It strikes women about nine times as often as men. An online questionnaire in mid-2024 collected medical details plus the standard EQ-5D health scale. That scale converts problems with movement, self-care, activities, pain, and mood into one quality-of-life score.

Patients averaged about 40 years old. Their mean score landed near two thirds of full health, a substantial loss. Mood was the hardest-hit dimension, with only about 15 percent reporting no anxiety or depression problems. Self-care held up best, untouched in about three quarters. Disability, walking difficulty, more accompanying diseases, older age, and greater caregiving needs dragged scores down. Higher income and satisfaction with treatment lifted them. Whether the disease was currently relapsing mattered less than the lasting functional damage.
pmc-13465430:
Satish Singh and three co-authors show that alpha2-antiplasmin, the body's chief clot-dissolution brake, also blunts the stroke drug tenecteplase. The engineered drug lasts longer than its parent and shrugs off one brake, yet this second brake was untested against it. Human clots in dishes and mouse stroke models carried the tests.

Tenecteplase dissolved clots dose by dose, and an antibody blocking the brake multiplied that effect. In mice lacking the brake gene, drug treatment after stroke left smaller dead zones, less swelling, and less bleeding. Behavior scores after stroke also ran better in the brake-free mice. Pairing a brake blocker with the clot drug, the authors propose, could widen its benefit window.
pmc-13465530:
Recep Ünal and Yeliz Kılınç compared plate materials in 2026 for jaw joint fractures below the condyle, where access is tight and the upper fragment is small. Titanium plates dominate, yet they cloud imaging and mismatch bone stiffness, while carbon-fibre PEEK bends more like bone and stays invisible on scans. Six computer models paired three plate shapes with titanium or 30% carbon-fibre PEEK under two bite loads.

Carbon-fibre plates cut stresses in plates, screws, and surrounding bone, but let fragments shift more than titanium. Molar-side loading stressed models most, and the lambda shape in carbon-fibre gave the lowest hardware stress while the rhombic shape spread bone stress most evenly. Surgeons must balance rigidity against stress relief, since the stiffest construct is not always the kindest to bone.
pmc-13465730:
Bingbing Li and colleagues trace a two-gene switch that helps potatoes resist early blight, a fungal disease that cuts yield and quality, in a 2026 plant study. Infection by the fungus Alternaria solani makes hydrogen peroxide build up in the plant, and adding extra peroxide speeds the disease along. A catalase gene named StCAT1 works against that damage.

Plants with StCAT1 silenced lost antioxidant strength and sickened more easily, while plants making extra copies resisted better. A second factor, StABI5, switches StCAT1 on, and silencing it weakened resistance as well. The pair forms a working module through reactive oxygen signaling, offering breeders concrete genetic material for hardier potato lines.
pmc-13466430:
Behzad Banihashemi and colleagues ask what a heart attack without a blocked artery means for survival in very old patients, in a 2026 analysis of a Swedish population study. Among more than thirty thousand cohort members, 925 people had a first coronary event between 2009 and 2018, at an average age of eighty-one. Events were classed as treated blockage, the unobstructed pattern called MINOCA, or other acute heart injury.

Only a small slice had MINOCA, forty-nine people among the non-revascularized group whose charts were reviewed in detail. Death rates over a median two and a half years were high in every category, passing four fifths overall. Unadjusted survival did not differ clearly between the event types.
pmc-13466830:
Serdal Arslan and colleagues profile circular RNAs in the blood of patients with Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, a severe tick-borne viral disease, in a 2026 study. These ring-shaped RNA molecules steer gene activity and had never been mapped in this illness, which kills many patients and has no approved drug or vaccine. Blood from patients and healthy controls was treated to keep only the rings, then read on a gene chip.

Fifteen rings ran higher in patients while more than two hundred ran lower, a lopsided pattern. Follow-up lab checks confirmed selected changes. Because some profiles may track fatal outcomes, the authors see groundwork here for both understanding the disease's course and spotting the patients in greatest danger early.
pmc-13467330:
Tomislav Sušac and co-authors examine in 2026 what makes tinnitus, or ringing in the ears, feel more disabling to some patients than to others. The study enrolled people who had both tinnitus and hearing loss, and compared them with hearing-loss patients who had no tinnitus. Each person completed hearing tests plus standard questionnaires on tinnitus burden, mood, stress, and personality.

The patient group numbered 127 people, with 119 in the comparison group. Patients who rated their tinnitus as catastrophic scored far higher on depression, anxiety, and stress than those with slight to moderate grades. More schooling was weakly tied to lower burden scores, while louder perceived ringing tracked with greater distress. The findings support screening tinnitus patients for emotional distress as part of routine care.
pmc-13467630:
Huang and colleagues reviewed in 2026 ways to make biodegradable polymer films block oxygen and water better. Such films must protect food, drugs, and electronics. These green films are plentiful and break down after use, but they still leak far more than oil-based plastics, which limits their use in sensitive packaging. The review gathers the main strategies and the hurdles that remain.

Huang covers surface coating, blending, layered stacking, chemical redesign, nano-scale composites, and filler reinforcement. For each, they map how the fix changes molecular structure and how that change lifts the oxygen and water barrier, in both natural and synthetic green polymers. The goal is design guidance that links a chosen method to a target barrier level. Remaining challenges include cost, scale-up, and holding barrier gains in humid real-world storage, which the authors set out for future work.
pmc-13468230:
Ioana Muller and colleagues measure in 2026 how often sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass and strength, and malnutrition persist in people living with transplanted lungs. Ninety-nine adult recipients were assessed during routine follow-up using the EWGSOP2 definition for sarcopenia and the GLIM criteria for malnutrition, applied both before transplantation and at follow-up.

Sarcopenia was found in 17 recipients, or 17.2 percent, and most of those cases were severe. Malnutrition was common before transplantation, affecting about 53 percent, and still affected about 23 percent afterward. Sarcopenia clustered with the diseases that led to transplant, mainly COPD and interstitial lung disease. The numbers show that a successful transplant does not end nutritional vulnerability, and that muscle health merits a standing place in follow-up care.
pmc-13468530:
A Posthumus and a large Dutch team report a cohort study, published in 2026. It covers blood pressure control one year after organ transplantation. High blood pressure affects most transplant recipients. It drives heart disease. Yet it receives little attention. The team analysed 1,112 recipients in the TransplantLines cohort. They had received heart, liver, lung, or kidney transplants.

Nine in ten recipients had hypertension. In nearly three quarters of those, it was above target. A fifth received no blood pressure treatment at all. This was despite raised readings. Poor control was common across all organ types. It linked to older age and diabetes. The authors frame these as missed chances to protect transplant patients.
pmc-13468830:

pmc-13469030:

pmc-13469130:

pmc-13469230:

pmc-13469830:

pmc-13470130:

pmc-13470230:

pmc-13470330:

pmc-13470730:

pmc-13471330:

pmc-13472130:

pmc-13473830:

pmc-13475730:

pmc-13476730:

After fixes such as hands-on training, believable peer scores, and clearer peer labels, the second group responded better. pmc-13476930:

pmc-13478030:

pmc-13478430:

pmc-13479630:

pmc-13479930:

pmc-13480230:

pmc-13480730:

pmc-13480830:

pmc-13482130:

pmc-13482830:

pmc-13483430:

pmc-13483530:

pmc-13483730:

pmc-13487930:

pmc-13488130:

pmc-13490530:

pmc-13490730:

pmc-13491930:

pmc-13492030:

pmc-13492330:

pmc-13492430:

pmc-13493830:

pmc-13495230:

pmc-13495330:

pmc-13495730:

pmc-13498630:

pmc-13499130:

Tagging rose while transport ran and loosened the link with that partner, suggesting site-by-site tagging tunes how carriers form, open, and deliver their cargo.
pmc-13499530:
Garcia-Olivares and colleagues test where the ADHD drug viloxazine acts in the living brain. The drug is known to raise two brain signal chemicals by blocking their uptake. Tests in glass dishes also hinted at action on serotonin receptors, which help set mood and focus.

The team used PET scans, which track a tagged tracer in the brain, in macaque monkeys. Viloxazine blocked tracer binding at one serotonin receptor type at far lower blood levels than at its close cousin. At blood levels like those in treated patients, the drug filled about sixty to seventy percent of that receptor. This action may add to its known uptake effect.
pmc-13499930:
Julieth Bibiana Espinel-Porras, Laura Daniela Arenas, and Victor Manuel Mora-Bautista report in 2026 a child who developed a rare immune attack on the optic nerves and spinal cord after COVID-19 infection. The disorder, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, targets a water-channel protein in support cells of the central nervous system. Their patient was a nine-year-old boy whose illness began with a week of unstoppable vomiting six weeks before admission, a recognised opening syndrome.

He then developed progressive leg weakness, slurred speech, and multiple eye and cranial nerve failures over twenty days. Scans showed widespread lesions in brain white matter and long stretches of spinal cord inflammation. Blood tests confirmed the signature antibody and past COVID infection, with spinal fluid largely normal. High-dose steroids restored walking yet vision lagged, so five plasma exchange sessions followed. They brought full visual and neurological recovery before maintenance treatment began.
pmc-13500530:
Shahnawaz Ahmad and co-authors present in 2026 a security framework that marries federated learning with blockchain records to protect Internet of Things networks without gathering private data centrally. Connected devices now number in the billions, and centralised training pools sensitive data in one breachable place. Federated learning trains models on the devices themselves, while a blockchain log verifies model updates and builds trust among participants, with the combined system aimed at spotting crypto-mining malware.

On the mining malware dataset the model scored accuracy and specificity both in the high ninety percent range under tenfold cross-validation in the reported evaluation, beating current practices according to the authors. Added encryption that computes on sealed data is discussed as a route to regulatory compliance. Smart healthcare and smart city deployments are named as fitting application areas.
pmc-13501530:
van Susante and colleagues follow heart surgery patients for a year to see whether a remote preparation program leaves lasting change. The program, delivered by phone and video before elective surgery, targets fitness, breathing muscle training, mental support, nutrition, and quitting smoking. Their 2026 report reanalyzes a randomized trial that compared the program with standard care. It tracks risk factors and quality of life before surgery, then at 3, 6, and 12 months afterward.

Both groups cut every risk factor over the year and felt better, except on one nutrition measure. The program group still did better on two fronts: smoking stayed lower at every check, and nutrition risk ran lower, clearly so at three months. Quality of life scores were higher in the program group at all follow ups. Remote preparation, the authors conclude, can seed habits that outlast the surgery itself.
pmc-13501630:
Mengjiao Yang leads a twelve-author team reporting a 2026 longitudinal study of how physical frailty and social relationships evolve together in older Japanese adults. Three survey waves ran between 2014 and 2020 in suburban Japan. Of 1,004 adults aged 65 or older, 704 who were initially independent and had at least two waves of data entered the analysis. Frailty was scored from the physical strength part of the Kihon Checklist, social life from an interaction index, and latent class growth models traced the pair jointly.

Three combined paths emerged: low frailty with rich social ties covered 78.0 percent of participants, while two smaller groups showed progressive frailty with social ties either maintained or rapidly declining. Over six years, 103 participants came to need long-term care. Against the healthiest group, adjusted hazard ratios were 2.33 where social ties held up and 3.85 where they collapsed. Sensitivity analyses using imputation, matching, and competing-risk models confirmed the pattern.
pmc-13501730:
Hoang and a large Vietnamese team analyse the 2021 STEPS survey to measure high blood pressure and its behavioural drivers in Vietnam. The survey, run to World Health Organization design, recorded blood pressure in 3,809 adults aged 18 to 69 and smoking, drinking, activity, and diet. Their 2026 analysis asks not just which single habits matter, but how risk stacks when unhealthy behaviours cluster in the same person.

Just over a quarter of adults had hypertension, with men higher than women and prevalence climbing steeply with age. Drinking alcohol and eating too little fruit and vegetables each kept an independent link with hypertension after adjustment. The clustering result was stark: odds rose step by step with each added risk factor, peaking in people carrying all four. The authors say the burden looks worse than in earlier Vietnamese surveys and argue for prevention programmes that tackle behaviours together.
pmc-13503730:
Khalid Alkhattabi and three co-authors set out a defense plan for linked medical devices, in a 2026 paper. Watches, sensors, and monitors that track patients can be hacked, which puts health data and safety at risk. Old guard tools based on fixed rules miss new attack styles.

The plan pairs a virtual twin of the device network with shared training across sites, so raw patient data stays put. Smart models watch for odd behavior in real time. One model scored near the top on a ward data set, with precision and recall both near one. The full setup held up when test attacks tried to fool it, and key checks ran in under a twentieth of a second.
pmc-13503830:
Md. Nazmussakib Shuvo leads a team testing whether neem leaf extract can fight two drug-resistant germs, in a 2026 study. The germs were taken from pus in skin boils and can cause stubborn infections. Neem has a long record in folk care for skin ills.

The team grew the germs, tested the extract on discs, and used gas tools to list its active compounds. Sixteen compounds were screened on paper for drug-like traits and safety; five passed. Computer docking placed those five into key germ proteins, and motion runs checked that the grips held. Two compounds bound best and stayed stable in the runs. The authors say tests in living animals must come before any medical claim.
pmc-13503930:
Farshad Taiyari and Jamal Roshani test a replaceable pipe damper meant to shield steel frames in earthquakes, in a 2026 paper. The damper sits inside a brace and yields like a fuse, soaking up quake energy so the main frame stays sound. Spent pipes can be swapped after a quake.

Computer models of frames with and without the system ran under many quake records. Two layouts for placing pipes in the braces were compared. A layout shaped by the frame's main sway mode raised the design response factor by about 87 percent over a bare frame. It also matched the even layout's strength while using less pipe overall. Damage odds curves showed lower risk for damped frames. The authors give design factors for code use.
pmc-13504830:
Tadesse Tarik Tamir leads a team gathering world evidence on what pushes pregnancy diabetes into lasting type 2 diabetes, in a 2026 umbrella review. About one in six pregnancies worldwide involves pregnancy diabetes, and mothers face a high later risk of the chronic form. Past reviews each covered single factors.

The team merged twelve reviews and pooled analyses spanning more than four hundred studies and six million women. The steadiest risk factors were insulin use in pregnancy, high body weight, and a family history of diabetes. Blood sugar measures during pregnancy also flagged higher risk, as did older age and high blood pressure. Breastfeeding pointed the other way, with lower later risk across reviews. The authors frame prevention around weight, screening, and nursing support.
pmc-13505030:
Shunya Ogawa leads a team watching how a fast-clearing anesthetic behaves when liver blood flow is clamped during surgery, in a 2026 pilot study. The drug, remimazolam, is broken down by a liver enzyme. The Pringle maneuver, a clamp that cuts bleeding in liver surgery, might slow that breakdown and deepen sedation.

Ten patients having liver removal with the clamp gave blood samples around each clamping round. Drug levels tended to rise after clamping in six cases but not in the rest. Overall, levels after the last clamp did not differ clearly from levels before the first. A brain-based depth-of-sleep score also held steady. All patients had well-preserved liver function, and the authors judge the drug safe in that group.
pmc-13505130:
Jason M Aubrey and colleagues describe a woman in her fifties who suffered a full-thickness tear of the esophagus after restarting the weight-loss drug semaglutide. She had been off the drug for months and resumed at the highest weekly dose without building up gradually. Within a day she developed severe vomiting, chest pain, shock, and breathing failure.

Scans showed air around the heart and fluid around both lungs, and a swallow study confirmed the perforation. Doctors treated her with an endoscopic stent, chest drainage, and tube feeding, and she improved enough to go home. Two months later she returned with a severe lung infection and a fistula, needing major chest surgery. At ten months she ate normally with the esophagus healed, and the authors warn clinicians to suspect this rare injury when vomiting and chest pain follow a restart.
pmc-13506530:
Emilia and colleagues mapped the evidence in 2026 on digital and AI tools across the care pathway for preeclampsia, a dangerous blood pressure disorder of pregnancy. Their scoping review covered four linked tasks: predicting risk, educating patients, monitoring blood pressure at home, and escalating care when readings worsen.

From nearly 1,400 records, 34 studies met the criteria. Prediction models sorted high-risk from low-risk patients well, but checks of accuracy, outside validation, and fairness across groups were uneven. Home monitoring results were mixed; one large trial found no earlier detection, while some care models cut visits without more harm. No study had yet tested all four functions together as one coordinated service, which the authors flag as the key gap.
pmc-13507230:
Raleb Taher leads a 2026 team that uncovers how nitrogen starvation creates antibiotic-tolerant persister cells in E. coli without draining their energy. Persisters are rare dormant cells that survive drugs by keeping drug targets idle, and they drive stubborn chronic infections. Earlier work blamed energy loss, yet nitrogen-starved cells kept normal energy levels while persisters surged.

Cell tracking in a microfluidic mother machine, a device that watches single cells over generations, showed persisters carry low levels of PyrBI, an enzyme for nitrogen use and building block synthesis. Forcing steady PyrBI levels cut persistence sharply. Biofilm persisters showed the same low pattern. Random dips in key enzymes may be a general route into dormancy under many nutrient shortages.
pmc-13507330:
Sheng-Ming Qu and Bing Wang show, in 2026 work, that pushing support fibroblasts toward fat-cell identity restrains infantile hemangioma, the common benign blood-vessel tumor of infancy. These tumors grow fast, then usually shrink, and their vessel cells take cues from neighboring fibroblasts. Single-cell profiling revealed heavy talk between the two cell types inside tumors.

Fat-shifted fibroblasts strongly curbed vessel cell growth, movement, invasion, and tube building while raising cell death. The brake ran through the Hippo pathway, which parked growth drivers YAP and TAZ outside vessel cell nuclei. A fat-program switch, PPARγ, in fibroblasts started the chain, and silencing it released the brake. Stromal reprogramming offers a fresh angle on hemangioma therapy.
pmc-13507430:
Mihatsch and Menzel model a quiet puzzle of cell biology: how do proteins squeeze through membrane mazes whose pores are narrower than the proteins themselves? Many organelles and synthetic soap-like systems fold into triply periodic membranes, regular three-dimensional lattices full of cavities joined by tight throats. Their 2026 theoretical study uses a phase-field model, a mathematical membrane that can wobble, with a rigid spherical particle forbidden to cross it, and works out the statistics of the membrane's fluctuations.

The particle's motion falls into two free-wandering regimes separated by a long plateau, the fingerprint of trapping. The particle rattles inside one cavity until a random membrane fluctuation widens a throat at the right moment. Then it hops to the next cavity and waits again. The authors verify their fluctuation mathematics both analytically and numerically.
pmc-13508430:
Donglin Li and six co-authors document the herbal bath tradition of the Hakka people in Guangdong, China, in 2026 fieldwork. Medicinal baths aid recovery after childbirth and care for newborns in traditional Chinese practice, yet Hakka customs were barely recorded. Teams visited nineteen Hakka settlements in the north of the province during 2023 and 2024. They interviewed 138 local informants and watched practices in homes. Scoring tools measured how strongly people agreed on plants for each use and how central each plant was.

The survey logged 108 bath plant species, most of them herbs, with whole plants, leaves, and stems used most often. Knowledge clustered among older women, who lead care for mothers and babies. The plants served over thirty health needs, with the strongest agreement for recovery after birth, breathing troubles, and skin problems. Hakka baths proved milder and simpler than a neighboring group's, built around family care.
pmc-13509630:
Beifen Pan leads an eleven-author team studying schooling, mood, and memory in adults aged sixty to seventy-four in China, in work published in 2026. The group drew on a national family survey from 2022, with 3666 people in the final set. Mood was scored with a short standard depression scale, and memory was rated by each person in a single question.

About one in four participants scored in the probable depression range. More schooling went with milder symptoms and with better self-rated memory, while poorer self-rated memory went with worse mood. Tests of the pathway suggested that part of the schooling link runs through how people judge their own memory. The authors say early checks of memory concerns could help flag older adults at risk of deeper low mood.
pmc-13510830:
Carlos A. Toro and Giulio Maria Pasinetti use machine learning to model thinking test scores in older United States adults, folding in urine markers of pesticide exposure, in 2026 work. The data came from a national health survey run from 2011 to 2014 and covered adults aged sixty and over with full thinking tests and exposure measures. Models also took in background, lifestyle, and mood information, plus scores on a depression questionnaire.

Sex, racial and ethnic group, and schooling ranked among the strongest predictors of test performance. Two breakdown products of a common insect repellent kept negative links to a speeded symbol test in tightened models, most clearly among adults in their sixties. The authors say exposure markers may add useful context to aging models, yet only long-term studies can tell whether the links reflect cause, shared exposures, or leftover mixing of factors.
pmc-13510930:
Qiu and colleagues review in 2026 how non-coding RNAs, RNA molecules that do not build proteins, shape cancer and might be turned into treatments. Once dismissed as transcriptional noise, these molecules make up about ninety-eight percent of all RNA transcripts. The review covers microRNAs, long non-coding RNAs, and circular RNAs, the three best-studied families, drawing on experimental and computational studies.

Across cancers, these RNAs help switch genes on and off and drive hallmarks such as cell proliferation, resistance to cell death, spread to distant organs, and metabolic rewiring. The authors survey the translational landscape, examining clinical trials now running or completed, the delivery methods used to get RNA drugs into tumors, and emerging technologies. Aiming to separate fact from fiction, they offer a balanced view meant to guide future research and clinical development in RNA-based cancer medicine.
pmc-13511930:
Qiaolian Feng, Yanfei Li, Yongbao Liu, Xiao Liang, Mingyang Liu, Duo Qu, and Yue Cen build a learning system that spots faults in ship chilled water units, in 2026 work. It works across different machines and conditions. Ship chillers face shifting sea conditions, few labeled fault examples for the target machine, and noisy vibration in sensor signals. The design improves an earlier domain adaptation network with a doubled attention setup.

Two encoder branches handle the differing sensor sets of two chiller types. Attention modules boost fault-sensitive parts of the signal and damp noise, while shortcut links keep deep training stable. A two-layer alignment scheme, mixing an adversarial game with a distance measure, pulls the two machines' signal patterns together so fault knowledge transfers. The authors report the system can flag subtle faults of varying severity under few-example conditions, a setting where plain models often fail.
pmc-13512430:
Beloslava Malakova and colleagues built a gene-level score that measures how loaded a gene is with harmful variants in autism. Standard tools grade single variants alone, dropping the gene size and variant frequency context needed to compare gene sets.

The score blends three inputs: how often both gene copies differ, the gene's coding length, and per-variant harm grades from a standard predictor. Tested on 55 high-confidence autism genes against a public reference set, it flagged raised harmful burden in 48 of them. It also beat simply adding up variant scores per gene, and repeat sampling checks confirmed the signal was real. Malakova offers the score as an added layer for ranking genes and comparing burden across gene sets.
pmc-13513730:
Güney Sarıoğlu, Yakup Yiğit and Abdulmecit Afşin wrote this 2026 comment on a study by Li and colleagues. That study linked the triglyceride-glucose index to chronic total occlusion, a complete blockage of a heart artery. Li's team studied 1,157 people having coronary angiography, an imaging test of the heart arteries, and found higher index values tied to occlusion. The comment questions how far that link should be trusted.

Sarıoğlu and co-authors argue the index marks an unhealthy metabolic setting rather than directly causing blockage. They note other studies found straight-line or U-shaped risk patterns, so a single cut-off may mislead doctors. Because patients sent for angiography are already high risk, they add, results may not apply to general screening of healthy people. They suggest combining the index with inflammation markers and plaque imaging for a fuller picture of risk.
pmc-13515430:
Wang and colleagues showed in 2026 that adding steam sharply boosts gas sorting in an electrochemical membrane reactor built for making benzene from methane. That reaction runs best at high heat, yet most membrane reactors cannot pull out hydrogen and let in oxygen at the same time in that heat range. Removing hydrogen helps the reaction, and oxygen curbs carbon buildup on the catalyst.

The team used hollow ceramic fibers that carry both protons and oxygen ions, and tried feeding steam to one side of the membrane or both. Steam raised the flow of both gases a lot. At the top heat tested, hydrogen flow rose about eightfold over dry runs, and oxygen flow rose about fourfold. Feeding steam to both sides worked best. The results support using such reactors alongside methane conversion plants.
pmc-13515530:
Vlad-Florin Oiegar leads a ten-author team reviewing lung rehabilitation for post-COVID syndrome in a 2026 systematic review. The syndrome leaves lasting breathlessness, fatigue, and weakness across several organs. Following standard review rules, the team searched three databases for trials from 2021 to early 2026. Twenty randomised trials with 2,101 adults qualified, and two reviewers screened and graded them independently.

Rehabilitation clearly improved walking capacity and peak oxygen use. Breathing and limb muscle strength rose as well. Quality of life, breathlessness, and fatigue improved across most programmes. Results for lung mechanics, anxiety, and depression were mixed, which points to reconditioning rather than rebuilt lungs as the main engine of benefit. Remote rehabilitation by video or phone worked as a practical alternative. Oiegar's team urges programmes tailored to each patient, with muscle training at the core.
pmc-13517330:
Xinyi Lu and six colleagues dissect heavy metals in coastal wetland mud on China's Bohai Bay in a 2026 study. Wetlands trap metals washing off the land, but how much arrives, from where, and with what risk are separate questions. The team sampled three depth layers at twenty-eight sites and measured eight metals, then ran pollution scores, source modelling, and risk assessments in one linked framework.

Average levels sat below the strictest marine sediment limits, with copper and arsenic mildly enriched. Depth profiles were mostly flat, stirred by tides and burrowing life. Sources split three ways: natural rock background near thirty-nine percent, air deposition near thirty-one, and local human activity near thirty. Mercury drove most ecological worry. Risk to people stayed within acceptable bounds, though children near homes and adults near industry faced the higher ends. Source shares and risk shares did not match.
pmc-13517630:
Yaolong Xu, Fujun Ma, and Hong Chang survey forever chemicals in electroplating wastewater in a 2026 review. China's plating industry, the world's largest, releases PFAS chiefly through chrome plating, where the chemicals tame toxic mist. The authors gather monitoring from fifteen industrial parks and ninety-seven firms, where twenty-nine PFAS turned up and the banned PFOS still hit extreme levels.

Long-chain compounds dominated, and screening keeps finding hidden cousins nobody targeted. Treatment options disappoint one by one: settling removes almost nothing, microbes can raise dissolved levels, and resins grab long chains but let short ones slip through fast. Membranes block nearly all long-chain PFAS yet foul and leave a concentrate problem behind. Xu's team concludes that no single technology cleans this stream, and they offer the survey as a control-planning reference for the industry.
pmc-13518630:
Yang Bo, Cai Hongyi, and Li Hao review progress in 2026 on deep learning models that combine several kinds of patient data to predict outcomes in stomach cancer. Single sources such as scans, tissue slides, genes, or clinical records each capture only part of a tumor. Fusion models join those layers to sort patients by risk in a more personal way.

The review covers core methods, current prognostic models, shared datasets, and ways of judging model quality. Yang and co-authors also weigh hard problems: uneven data, hard-to-explain model choices, and slow movement into clinics. Readers get a map of where combined-data prediction stands and what must improve before hospitals can rely on it.
pmc-13518730:
Kenichiro Hiraoka and colleagues followed pregnancy results for a gentler sperm-injection method that uses tiny pulses to open the egg, rather than a sharp needle that draws up cell fluid. The 2026 study covered 1,822 cycles from 1,072 patients under age forty at two fertility centers in Japan, using frozen single embryos warmed for transfer. Standard IVF cycles served as a comparison.

About half of the pulse-method cycles led to a clinical pregnancy, and just under two fifths ended in a live birth, figures close to those of the comparison group. Birth weights, lengths of pregnancy, and rates of birth defects were also similar across the two groups. One clear gap stood out, with more girl babies born after the pulse method than after standard IVF. For patients and clinics, the findings back the method as a sound choice while leaving that sex-ratio gap open for further study.
pmc-13518830:
Joao Antonangelo and four colleagues test in 2026 how soil moisture affects a handheld X-ray tool used to predict soil fertility. Portable X-ray fluorescence gives farmers fast nutrient readings, yet water in the sample can distort element signals. How moisture interacts with other soil traits was less clear.

Regression models were built under four moisture states, from dry soil to saturated paste. Potassium, calcium, and magnesium predictions were strong in dry and saturated samples, while copper and zinc fared worse. Adding soil pH and organic matter lifted accuracy sharply, improving fit up to about sixfold in some cases. Antonangelo and co-authors call for standard sample preparation so readings stay comparable.
pmc-13518930:
Lisa Abegglen and colleagues hunted for a new way to save young elephants dying of a fast-moving herpesvirus bleeding disease. Published in 2026, the work asked whether sticky DNA webs released by immune cells, already blamed for clots in other bleeding diseases, also drive harm in infected calves. The disease strikes calves whose immune defenses are still immature, making it a major threat to elephant survival.

Elephant immune cells released these DNA webs when triggered in the lab, including by blood plasma from sick animals, and tissue from fatal cases held large amounts of them. Drugs known to block web formation stopped the response in lab tests. The authors propose pairing web-blocking drugs with current care, such as fluids, antivirals, and plasma transfusions, to lift survival odds. Readers get a clear biological lead for a disease that has long lacked one.
pmc-13519030:
Gaochen Zhu and Guan Yang built a stool-based test for multiple sclerosis that reads the whole gut microbe community, not just bacteria. Published in 2026, the study analyzed gene-sequence data from stool samples, with 1,152 people in the discovery group and 1,306 in total across three regions. Machine learning models then learned to separate patients from healthy controls using microbes from several kingdoms plus their genes and metabolic pathways.

The models flagged 90 bacterial species, a handful of fungal and viral species, 119 gene families, and 17 metabolic pathways tied to the disease. In the discovery data the models scored near the top of the accuracy scale for both men and women, though scores fell on outside test sets. A shorter 30-marker version held up better externally. Low levels of Faecalibacterium microbes and a methionine-making pathway tracked with the disease. The work points toward a noninvasive stool marker, still needing wider validation.
pmc-13519430:
Varsha Patil and colleagues tested which implant abutment material best keeps its screw tight under chewing. Published in 2026, the lab study ran 45 implant-abutment units through half a million load cycles at a set force. Fifteen units each used titanium, zirconia, and a plastic called PEEK, simulating six months of chewing. Reverse torque, the twist needed to loosen each screw, was measured before and after cycling.

Titanium held the highest loosening torque after cycling, followed by zirconia and then PEEK, with clear gaps among all three groups. The result favors titanium for lasting joint stability, while zirconia offers a tooth-colored option with somewhat weaker grip and PEEK trails on torque hold. Clinicians gain a ranked guide for balancing looks against the risk of a screw working loose.
pmc-13520230:
Eshetu Molla leads a large team evaluating an improved rapid malaria test in 2026 at Ethiopian health centers. Ethiopia hosts two malaria species needing different treatment, and gene deletions forced a switch away from the older test type. Some 1,200 patients with suspected malaria at two centers gave blood for the new test, microscopy, and precise PCR as the reference.

PCR found malaria in 40.6 percent of patients. The rapid test caught 89.7 percent of PCR-confirmed infections, far above microscopy's 59.8 percent, with similar accuracy at ruling infection out. Sensitivity reached 100 percent at high parasite densities but slipped for mixed infections. Agreement with PCR was strong, supporting routine clinic use.
pmc-13520330:
Batuhan Turgay and colleagues compare in 2026 two start times for hormone support in frozen embryo transfer using a natural cycle. Support with progesterone began either two days before transfer or on transfer day itself, and pregnancy outcomes were compared.

The review covered 246 transfer cycles from 2022 to 2024 at one university centre. Blood progesterone on transfer day was higher when support started earlier, yet pregnancy and live birth rates were higher when support started on transfer day. Adjusted analysis kept that link. The counterintuitive pattern invites caution, since treatment choice was not random and centre routines may explain part of the gap.
pmc-13520430:
Dan Ye and colleagues show in 2026 that a signalling protein called DLL1 helps ovarian cancer resist the chemotherapy drug cisplatin by blocking a form of iron-driven cell death. Ovarian cancer often returns after cisplatin, so understanding resistance routes matters for new combinations.

DLL1 levels were higher in tumour tissue and tracked with poorer outlook. Lowering DLL1 slowed growth and movement while triggering the iron-driven death pathway, with more lipid damage and faulty mitochondria. A protective Nrf2 and GPX4 axis sat downstream. In animals, targeting DLL1 alongside a death inducer shrank resistant tumours, nominating DLL1 as both marker and drug target.
pmc-13520530:
Şebnem Zeynep Eke Kurt and colleagues check in 2026 whether a standard chest pain score called HEART performs equally during off-hours and regular hours in an emergency department. Staffing and case mix change overnight, so score behaviour might drift with the clock.

Records covered 2,800 patients seen in Istanbul from 2020 to 2025, with most arriving off-hours. Serious heart events within thirty days occurred in roughly one in seven patients. Sorting accuracy was nearly identical between time groups, well within the preset similarity margin. Both groups showed systematic overestimation against older reference risks, suggesting local recalibration matters more than shift timing.
pmc-13521430:
Karleena Snow and Arindam Sharma launch in 2026 a short symptom form for heart failure clinics. The form is free and quick to fill in. Older tools can feel long and complex. Some also cost clinics money to use.

The pilot used the form with over 1,000 patients in routine visits. Three case stories show the form at work across heart failure types. Patients got brief teaching on form use. Feedback from patients and staff drove three rounds of fixes. Patients took to the form well. Staff said talks dug deeper into symptoms, and care plans fit each patient better. Big validation work comes next.
pmc-13521530:
Nikhita and colleagues tested in 2026 how cleaning methods affect how deeply a root canal sealer soaks into tooth dentine. Sealer penetration into tiny dentine tubules helps seal the canal. Sixty-three single-rooted teeth were split among three activation methods: sonic, passive ultrasonic, and diode laser. Each group also used one of three final rinses, including the standard chelator EDTA and two newer options.

Diode laser activation drove the sealer significantly deeper than sonic or ultrasonic methods. Among rinses, EDTA gave the highest penetration, especially combined with the diode laser. The newer rinses, HEDP and chitosan, allowed comparatively shallow penetration. The authors conclude that irrigant choice and activation method jointly decide sealer reach. For the bioceramic sealer tested, EDTA plus diode laser activation was the strongest pairing in this lab study.
pmc-13522930:
Jing wrote in 2026 a close read of fresh work on a plant gene hush system that guards against viruses. The system, short named S-PTGS, chops matching RNA into bits that then hunt their kin. Two steps rule it: a first spark, and a spread that can cross the whole plant. The study under read, by Lacroix and co-workers, split the steps with bred plant lines and a pale leaf marker that shows the hush at work.

Their key find is that each step has its own bar. The spark fires when stray, flawed RNA tops a set load, more than the cell's clean up crew can clear. The spread fires only when the target's sound RNA runs high too. If sound RNA runs low, the first bits just chew it up. No second wave forms then.
pmc-13523230:
Antonio Giulio Napolitano and a large team study leftover air space after surgery for collapsed lung in a 2026 multicenter analysis. Records covered four hundred sixty-three patients treated with keyhole surgery for primary spontaneous pneumothorax at three Italian centers over a decade. The residual space at the top of the chest was measured on the discharge X-ray, and recurrence was compared across four surgical approaches.

Overall recurrence was just under seven percent. Removing the lung apex combined with chemical pleurodesis, a treatment that sticks the lung to the chest wall, gave the strongest protection, while mechanical pleurodesis alone carried higher risk. A larger residual space predicted recurrence in adjusted analysis, especially in older patients and in one surgical subgroup. The authors suggest the measurement could guide procedure choice and follow-up.
pmc-13523430:
Fulei Zhao leads a large team identifying a protein that fuels sugar burning in lung cancer in a 2026 study. Non-small cell lung cancer often rewires its metabolism toward glycolysis, meaning rapid sugar breakdown, yet the regulators are incompletely understood. The protein SerpinB7, normally a protease blocker, was found at high levels in tumor tissue and linked to poor prognosis. Mechanistic experiments traced its partners in cancer cells.

SerpinB7 binds a second protein, Annexin A2, and shields it from destruction, keeping its levels high. That partner in turn boosts the growth driver c-Myc, which switches on glycolytic genes. Tumor specimens confirmed both proteins are raised together. Silencing SerpinB7 with RNA packed in ferritin shells suppressed tumor growth and spread in models. The authors propose the axis as a metabolic target for this cancer.
pmc-13523530:
Ronald Opito leads a large team in a 2026 prospective protocol to profile disease burden in Uganda's Teso subregion through community-based medical education at Soroti University. The program places medical students in primary care facilities to build skills in community service, teamwork, leadership, and ethics. Little epidemiological data existed for Teso.

The plan mixes surveys on noncommunicable, neglected tropical, and infectious diseases with cohort studies of trends over time. Focus groups and key informant interviews will explore community views, health system capacity, and prevention practice. A participatory approach will co-design each phase with community members, practitioners, and local authorities, while students collect data under faculty supervision. The team expects prevalence, trend, and risk factor evidence to guide local interventions and health policy.
pmc-13525730:
Washington and colleagues published a 2026 report on closing a stubborn stomach-wall leak. Feeding tubes placed through the stomach wall can leave a leak after removal. The channel's skin lining keeps it from sealing on its own. Two men, aged 63 and 30, leaked for months despite standard care.

Both underwent a burn-and-stitch fix done through an endoscope. A plasma beam first scorched the channel lining to trigger fresh healing. Stitches then pulled the opening shut from inside the stomach. Drainage stopped within a week for both men after the procedure. No leak returned during the follow-up time the team recorded. Larger studies are needed before the fix becomes standard practice. One patient had leaked for about a year before the fix.
pmc-13526730:
Meredith Grace Smith, Nadine Smith, Georgia McKenzie, and Adrienne Harvey check, in a 2026 study, whether two pain questionnaires for young people and children with cerebral palsy give stable results over time. Both tools were adapted so respondents with varied abilities can self-report pain interference and pain-related fear or avoidance. Reliability over a repeat interval is essential before trials use them to judge change.

Participants aged five to thirty with ongoing pain, recruited at four Australian sites, completed each questionnaire twice, two to four weeks apart. Reliability was moderate for both instruments, with correlation coefficients in the sixties and seventies across subscales. Measurement error and smallest detectable change values were reported for each scale. The authors conclude both tools are stable enough for clinical and research use centered on self-report.
pmc-13526830:
Gao and colleagues published a 2026 study on gene switches that release medicine on demand. Gene therapies often run at one fixed level once delivered. The team built switches from a cell system that tags proteins for disposal. A licensed pill, taken by mouth, pauses the disposal and frees the protein.

With disposal paused, therapeutic proteins poured into the blood of treated mice. The release was tunable by dose and reversed when pills stopped. The design rode along with standard virus delivery used in gene therapy. The team showed uses for heart disease and chronic pain control. Simple parts, they argue, beat complex circuits for clinic-ready control. Remote control like this could steady hormone or pain treatments.
pmc-13527130:
Tan and co-authors map brain immune cells across time in this 2026 mouse study of neuroPASC, the neurological fallout of long COVID that includes brain fog and mood symptoms. Building on their earlier model, the team sequenced single immune cells from brains at four points. The points were before infection and at 6, 30, and 100 days afterward. In the earlier model, infected mice showed behavior changes and brain inflammation lasting 120 days.

The atlas shows a relay of cell types. Resident microglia expanded into inflammatory, stress-response, and metabolic states that persisted to the latest time point. Border-associated macrophages, stationed at the brain's edges, switched on monocyte-attracting signals during acute infection. Blood-derived monocytes and neutrophils then surged in transiently, priming the long-lived microglial reaction. The authors argue this coordinated handoff, rather than any single cell type, sustains chronic neuroinflammation, and they nominate microglia as the key therapeutic target.
pmc-13528030:
Zetian Chen and six colleagues test whether two blood markers together can flag stomach conditions that precede cancer. The markers are pepsinogen levels and antibodies to Helicobacter pylori, a common stomach bacterium. The cohort study ran from 2016 to 2019 and screened 19,879 people. Participants were split into four groups by their two test results.

A total of 1,152 people went on to endoscopy and tissue checks. The group positive on both markers had about double the odds of atrophic gastritis versus the fully negative group. In the upper stomach, odds of wasting and of intestinal-type change were five to nearly seven times higher. The authors say pairing the tests sharpens detection. That could help target endoscopy where stomach cancer is common.
pmc-13528130:
Liu and colleagues published a 2026 study on RNA tags that track with sepsis severity. Sepsis is a runaway body response to infection that can kill quickly. Cells also rewire sugar burning during sepsis, a shift tied to outcomes. The team pooled several sepsis datasets to map RNA-tag regulators.

Most tag regulators ran lower in sepsis patients than in healthy people. Two reader proteins ran higher, standing out from the general fall. One eraser protein, ALKBH5, tracked closely with sugar-burning activity levels. Its removal in lab models shifted many of the same genes as sepsis. A risk model built on these regulators may help forecast outcomes. One validation set agreed with the model's calls nearly nine times in ten.
pmc-13531530:
Mark Harris and colleagues reviewed international evidence on paying general practices for quality. Published in 2026, the review of reviews searched major databases for systematic reviews and meta-analyses from 2010 onward, keeping twenty reviews. Australia's fee-for-service model faces strain, prompting interest in blended payments that mix service fees, capitation, and performance bonuses for complex chronic care.

Blended models with performance pay showed small quality gains, mainly in multidisciplinary settings and incentivized activities, with the clearest intermediate gains in diabetes care. Evidence for other conditions stayed inconclusive, and capitation alone showed no quality benefit. Gains appeared larger in weaker study designs, with ceiling effects and wide variation across systems. The authors urge careful, equity-aware evaluation of each incentive before adoption.
pmc-13531830:
Mingwei Tong leads a 2026 mouse vaccine test against the pork-borne parasite Trichinella spiralis, which has no licensed vaccine. The candidate protein is an antioxidant enzyme found on the parasite surface across its life stages. Mice received the lab-made protein with an adjuvant, then swallowed live larvae as a challenge.

Vaccinated mice built strong antibody responses mixing two immune styles and raised gut defenses, including protective mucus and surface antibodies. Adult worms in the gut fell by 65 percent and muscle larvae by about 62 percent. Gut and muscle damage also eased, marking a promising candidate.
pmc-13532130:
P. Romeo and colleagues used internal ultrasound scans to test whether polycystic ovarian shape and endometriosis often appear together in the same patients. Endometriosis means tissue like the womb lining grows outside the womb, while polycystic shape means an ovary holds many small follicles.
