The clinic reviewed 165 patients scanned for suspected or known endometriosis between February and June 2023. About 62 percent had endometriosis, 37 percent showed the polycystic pattern, and 35 percent of the endometriosis group had both. Patients with both findings were younger and lighter, and deep endometriosis appeared less often in the polycystic group. Once age was accounted for, most gaps faded, so Romeo treats the overlap as a lead for further study, not proof.
pmc-13532330:
Yingying Hu and colleagues report in 2026 on a model for self-healing cracks in rock. Cracks in mines and tunnels can leak water and weaken walls, and normal repair can cost a lot and harm nature. The team studied germs that make calcium carbonate, a hard mineral that can fill gaps.

Lab work found the best yield near pH 9 with set levels of urea and calcium. A particle flow model then traced how the mineral fills a crack and lifts load strength. Readers get both the lab recipe and a model for safer, lower-impact repair of underground works.
pmc-13534430:
Bruno Kamarowski and colleagues introduce in 2026 a dataset and detector for active face liveness checks using close-up movements. Systems must tell a live face from photos or videos shown to fool login checks, yet public data for active tasks are scarce. Volunteers performed close-up moves while spoof samples used celebrity images on varied devices.

Their detector blends distortion traits with spatial embeddings from the face images. It posted the lowest error among recent active models across all four test protocols on the new dataset. Access rules for research use are shared, helping others reproduce and build on the work.
pmc-13534530:
Xinhua Dong and colleagues study in 2026 how fulvic acid contamination changes the shear strength of red clay in Guilin, China. Acid pollution can weaken soils under buildings, yet dose and time effects were unclear. Repeated shear tests, mineral checks, and microscope imaging tracked clay soaked at varied strengths and durations.

Low acid strength with short soaking raised strength by boosting cohesion and friction, as particles clumped and pores filled. Higher strength with longer soaking cut both measures sharply and loosened the soil fabric. A dual binding model explains the switch from help to harm.
pmc-13536830:
Nicholas J Short leads a 2026 phase II trial of a dual-target antibody for low-blast blood diseases with few options. Vibecotamab links a marker on cancer cells to T cells so the immune cells can kill them. Two groups took part, covering 21 patients with leftover measurable leukemia and 27 patients with related marrow disorders after standard drug failure. Treatment ran from 2022 to 2025 with rising first-cycle doses.

Leftover leukemia cleared in about one in five patients in the first group. About two thirds of the second group responded overall. Survival medians differed by group, with longer survival in the leukemia group. Infusion reactions or cytokine release affected most patients, usually at mild levels. The authors call responses real yet short-lived and urge further study of the approach.
pmc-13538230:
Carrancho and a large Spanish team publish the protocol for the SPAIN Trial, a national randomised comparison of robotic versus open pancreatoduodenectomy. That is the formidable Whipple operation that removes the head of the pancreas. Robotic surgery promises smaller wounds and faster recovery for one of the most morbid operations in medicine, but hard evidence lags behind adoption. Their 2026 protocol describes a trial in busy Spanish centres with established robotic pancreas programmes.

Patients needing the operation for disease, benign or malignant, of the pancreatic head, bile duct, duodenum, or ampulla will be assigned two-to-one toward the robot. The main yardstick is total complication burden within ninety days, summarised by a standard index that weights every complication. Secondary measures span operating time, blood loss, conversions to open surgery, the specialty's defined complications, cancer clearance and lymph node counts, time to chemotherapy, and full costs.
pmc-13538530:
Ida Romano and co-authors isolate and evaluate cellulose-breaking bacteria for green industry in a 2026 combined lab study. Plant fiber breakdown by enzymes underpins biofuel making and waste reuse, so fresh strains matter. Isolates were screened by clearing halos and ranked by enzyme assays on model and real plant feeds. The team then sequenced them for fiber genes and trialed them in small fermenters on a soluble fiber feed at two loadings.

Four strains led early enzyme rankings across two bacterial genera. Two finalists advanced, one Bacillus strain peaking within hours in warm culture and one Streptomyces strain peaking after many days in cooler culture, each reaching solid enzyme levels. Genomes confirmed fiber breakdown gene sets. The authors nominate both strains for scale-up work toward fuel and waste applications.
pmc-13539630:
Mar Lozano-Casanova and colleagues adapt and validate a caregiver feeding style questionnaire for Spanish parents in a 2026 study. Feeding styles shape child eating behavior and family well-being, so a sound local tool matters. The English questionnaire underwent translation checks with twenty parent interviews, then 194 Spanish parents of children aged 7 to 10 years completed it within a cohort followed since hospital discharge. Two factor models were tested.

Both a two-dimension and a single-dimension model fit acceptably, with adequate internal consistency each. A few items were lightly reworded for cultural fit. The authors recommend the shorter single-dimension version for its simplicity and performance, judging the Spanish edition structurally sound for research and practice.
pmc-13540930:
Jinfeng Ma leads a 2026 pig genetics study mapping the DNA regions that set teat number in American Large White and Landrace sows. More teats mean more piglets can nurse, making the trait directly economic for breeders.

Nearly sixty-seven hundred pigs with teat counts were genotyped on a dense chip, then statistically upgraded to whole-genome resolution. Genome scans found significant spots on several chromosomes, with one region on chromosome seven explaining about three percent of variation. Fusing gene activity and chromatin data from embryonic mammary tissue elevated four candidate genes, including PTPN13. Feeding the top markers into selection models is reported as improving prediction for breeding programmes.
pmc-13543630:
Ting Gao and colleagues published a 2026 study of how the fragrant ginger lily Hedychium coronarium controls its scent, focusing on a ubiquitin ligase, an enzyme that tags proteins for disposal. An earlier finding showed a transcription factor, HcWRKY1, switches on the gene making the flower's main scent chemicals. Screening the ligase family produced seven candidates, and interaction tests singled out HcPUB30 as the one that physically binds that factor.

Laboratory assays confirmed the ligase tags the factor and sends it to the cell's shredder. The ligase peaks in petals as flowers fade. Silencing it in petals unexpectedly lowered scent output and lowered the factor's gene activity too, a twist suggesting feedback in the circuit. Scent, this work shows, is governed not just by which switches exist but by how fast they are thrown away.
pmc-13547230:
Shrinivas Pundlik and co-authors built in 2026 a processing pipeline that mines ordinary driving recordings for how drivers scan with their heads at intersections, where about half of all crashes happen. Cars carried cabin and forward cameras plus speed and location logs. Software clipped the footage around intersections, read signs and maneuvers from the road view, and estimated head turns from the cabin view with a custom model built for wide angles.

Against 365 hand-checked intersection clips from six vehicles in three states, the pipeline spotted signage in 99 percent of cases and maneuvers in 95 percent. Estimated entry points landed within about a meter of the truth, and head pose error averaged under seven degrees. The authors aim at automated study of very large driving datasets.
pmc-13548530:
Na An and colleagues describe two patients with multiple myeloma who developed a dangerous blood and kidney complication during treatment with proteasome inhibitors, in a 2026 case report with a literature review. These cancer drugs are usually well tolerated, yet a small number of patients develop thrombotic microangiopathy, where damaged vessel linings trigger clotting, low platelets, and anemia. Telling the drug reaction apart from other causes in myeloma is difficult.

In both cases, suspicion of the drug led doctors to stop it promptly, and plasma exchange helped selected patients. The authors review how the injury may arise and which treatments, including the antibody drug eculizumab, might be considered. Their central message is speed: early recognition and stopping the drug give patients the best chance of recovery.
pmc-13548630:
Mohammed Abdeljawad and colleagues survey mothers of premature babies in Gaza about what they know of caring for fragile newborns, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Mothers handle feeding, warmth, infection prevention, and light therapy safety, yet knowledge in strained neonatal units was little documented. Interviewers asked 170 mothers across four government hospitals thirty questions spanning temperature control, feeding, phototherapy, and infection and skin care.

Average knowledge sat in the moderate range, though nearly a third of mothers scored poorly. Feeding was the weakest area, while infection and skin care scored highest. Missing specialist antenatal follow-up for the premature pregnancy predicted lower knowledge. Detailed answers exposed risky gaps around feeding tolerance, tube feeding, light therapy safety, handling, and cord care. The authors use the map of gaps to propose focused teaching before discharge.
pmc-13550430:
Sina Gouran and colleagues solve the equations of fine particles swirling in a forced vortex, in a 2026 applied mathematics paper. Vortex flows separate particles in devices from blood plasma separators to petroleum equipment, and knowing where a particle drifts decides how well hazardous material can be stripped from coal and oil processes. Using an analytic technique that avoids building computational grids, the team solved the nonlinear motion equations for particles of differing sizes and drag properties.

Particle position grew over time under all conditions tested. Raising the drag-to-inertia ratio pushed particles further along, as did shrinking the starting radius. Spin speed around the vortex behaved oppositely for the two knobs: it fell as particles started larger and rose with the drag ratio. The authors judge their grid-free method a reasonable, efficient solver for such transport problems.
pmc-13551730:
Na-Noom Jeong, Hyun Joung Lim, Won-Ho Kim, and Min-Ju Kim published a 2026 analysis of Korean national survey data on lifestyle and fatty liver disease tied to metabolic dysfunction. The study covered 23,111 adults aged 19 to 80 surveyed from 2016 to 2021. A healthy lifestyle score from zero to four combined diet quality, physical activity, smoking, and sleep duration.

About a quarter of participants met the disease definition used, with the highest rates in the least healthy lifestyle group. Risk fell stepwise as healthy factors accumulated, and the lowest risk appeared in people combining good diet, activity, and non-smoking in the reported models. Because the data are cross-sectional, the authors note that cause cannot be proven, yet the pattern supports combined lifestyle prevention.
pmc-13551930:
Manoj Pandey published a 2026 essay on a new threat to medical journals. Cheap AI tools let writers mass-produce letters to the editor. Each letter is a citable unit. Floods of such letters can inflate citation scores like the h-index. The author calls the tactic letter-bombing. Data-heavy fields such as surgical oncology look most exposed, since fake critiques of trial statistics are easy to draft.

The essay sets out how to spot abnormal letter volumes. It then proposes a layered defense for journals. Labels in article metadata would close indexing loopholes. Checks of author history would flag repeat offenders. Criticized authors would gain a right to reply at the same time. The author frames the package as a baseline rule set for guarding the record.
pmc-13554130:
Anita Kumari leads a five-author team mapping how moso bamboo cells turn into embryo-like growth in a 2026 study. Growing bamboo from such cells could speed breeding, yet the inner changes stay poorly known. The team tuned three growth recipes for stem pieces: starting a callus, growing it, and coaxing embryos from it. Chemical and gene scans then tracked each stage.

Callus that could form embryos brimmed with fatty compounds, plant defence chemicals, and growth hormones. Callus that could not form embryos leaned toward other compound families, such as bitter plant alkaloids. Genes steering cell identity and embryo growth also switched on during the key stage. The maps give bamboo growers a resource for future breeding and gene work.
pmc-13554330:
Vu Hoang Nguyen and Ngoc Quyen Nguyen charted the heavy treatment burden of deep wound infections after lower back surgery at one Vietnamese hospital. The study followed early infections, meaning those found within 90 days of the first operation.

Of 1,923 spine patients screened, just 16 had a deep infection, about 0.83 percent, usually spotted around two weeks after surgery. Those 16 patients needed 52 repeat spine operations between them, and ten needed vacuum wound dressings with many changes. Eight patients hit a major burden event, such as implant removal, intensive care, or a treatment-related injury. Median infection-related hospital time reached 46.5 days for those with a major event, against 23 days without, Nguyen reports.
pmc-13554430:
Jeong-Won Kim leads a twelve-author team testing a ginseng compound against radiation damage to the gut in a 2026 mouse study. Radiation harms the gut lining during cancer treatment and after accidents, and few drugs help. Mice given strong abdominal radiation received the compound, called ginsenoside Rb1. Gut structure, bacterial leakage, and immune shifts were all measured.

Treated mice showed less damage to the gut's tiny folds and pits, and fewer bacteria crossing into the body. The compound raised calming regulatory T cells and their signal, IL-10. That signal, not the compound itself, switched on a growth path in gut cells in dish tests. Blocking IL-10 wiped out the benefit in mice, confirming the chain.
pmc-13554630:
Chunhui Ni and five colleagues test whether two platelet ratios predict death within 28 days in sepsis. The platelet-to-neutrophil ratio and platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio may add value beyond standard prognostic scores. Their 2026 single-center cohort covers 287 adults with sepsis by Sepsis-3 criteria. Patients were split into high and low groups at the median of each ratio.

Multivariate Cox models tied lower platelet-to-neutrophil ratio to higher 28-day mortality, with a hazard ratio near zero point nine seven. Higher platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio also tied to higher mortality, with a hazard ratio near one point zero one. The team built models from SOFA alone, APACHE II alone, each score plus one ratio, and a composite model. Results support the ratios as added prognostic markers.
pmc-13556030:
Kyle J Farrell and three colleagues surveyed fellows in 2026 about how fellowship programmes' social media shapes recruitment. Programmes increasingly post online to reach applicants, especially after application cycles moved partly virtual. The team sent a 24-question web survey to fellows across specialties at one large academic medical centre spanning three United States regions, after programme directors granted permission to contact them.

Nearly two hundred fellows replied. X and Instagram were the platforms used most to research programmes, and close to half said a virtual cycle made them lean more on programme websites and accounts. Posts about wellness and work-life balance drew the most interest, ahead of education quality and fellow achievements. Programmes reading the results learn what applicants actually look for when they scroll.
pmc-13557030:
Charleston F. Christie and twelve colleagues described in 2026 a staged screening route that tests seizure drug candidates in zebrafish of increasing age before moving to mice. Epilepsy affects more than fifty million people, and many candidate compounds fail because they cannot reach the brain. Young zebrafish larvae are a popular first screen, yet their blood-brain barrier is still immature at the usual testing age.

The team screened 31 vitamin K relatives in seven-day-old fish against chemically triggered seizure-like activity, and seventeen compounds calmed it. Three advanced to dose testing in older fish, two stayed active at the later ages, and both protected mice in a standard seizure test, with brain levels confirming central exposure for each. One compound held up even at the stronger stimulus setting. Later-stage fish screening, the authors argue, gives a practical filter before costly mammal work.
pmc-13558730:
Nosrat Madadi Mahani, Narges Ghadiri, and Fatemeh Banifatemeh computed in 2026 how well a boron nitride cage can carry a lung cancer drug called sunvozertinib. The cage, a hollow sphere of boron and nitrogen atoms, was tested in four forms with quantum chemistry calculations: plain, stuffed with the drug inside, and doped with nickel or platinum atoms. Measures covered sticking energy, charge movement, energy gaps, light absorption, and electron sharing maps.

Nickel doping won decisively, gripping the drug far more strongly than the plain or stuffed cages, narrowing the energy gap, and shifting light absorption in ways that signal real chemical coupling. Platinum doping helped less, while the plain cage barely held the drug at all, a loose grip the authors recast as a feature for slow, sustained release. Nickel-doped cages are their pick for loading and delivery.
pmc-13559130:
Chao Ma, Pengling Huang, Guanghua Pei and Zhaowei Meng published this 2026 study building a prediction tool for hepatic portal venous gas in children. The gas appears in the liver's portal vein and can signal a surgical emergency or a harmless finding. Sorting the two is a challenge. The authors reviewed 107 children with confirmed cases and built a nomogram, a scoring chart, from features separating children who needed surgery or died from those who recovered without it.

Twenty children fell in the high-risk group and 87 in the benign group. Two features predicted danger: loss of the layered look of the bowel wall, and abnormal spread of intestinal gas. Widespread gas carried the highest odds. The model discriminated well, scoring 0.899 on the accuracy curve, and 0.879 after bootstrap correction. Decision analysis showed net benefit across risk thresholds. The authors offer the chart as a bedside aid for urgent decisions.
pmc-13560130:
Yanquan Wei and colleagues fish antibody fragments against feline calicivirus from a phage display library built from immunized cats. Their 2026 study targets the VP1-CDE region, a neutralizing patch on the virus's main capsid protein. No specific antiviral drug exists for this common cat pathogen, which causes respiratory disease and sometimes fatal systemic infection.

The library held over two hundred million independent phages with good diversity. Three rounds of selection yielded five unique fragments, and all five bound both the purified target protein and virus-infected feline kidney cells. Converted into fusion proteins, one fragment neutralized the genogroup II isolate strongly, and a second worked weakly, while the remaining three showed no useful neutralization. The authors nominate the two active fragments as candidates for diagnostic reagents and antiviral development, with all evidence so far from laboratory assays.
pmc-13560330:
José Lascano Contreras tells how bedside ultrasound by the treating nephrologist caught a risky pseudoaneurysm in a dialysis patient's arm graft. His 2026 case report follows a 53-year-old woman on hemodialysis since 2013 for kidney failure caused by lupus nephritis. She arrived with pain, swelling, fever, and a rapidly growing pulsatile lump over her synthetic brachioaxillary graft.

The dialysis-unit scan showed the outpouching connected to the graft through a narrow neck, with the swirling yin-yang flow pattern classic for pseudoaneurysm. Fast proof sped her move to a vessel center, where CT angiography found active contrast leakage. Blood cultures later grew Enterococcus faecium, and scans showed heart valve infection as well. Despite antibiotics, the graft had to come out in surgery marked by severe bleeding. The author argues nephrologist-run ultrasound enables fast spotting of access crises.
pmc-13560430:
Kevin Bassey and three colleagues pool the prevalence of left ventricular systolic dysfunction, a weakening of the heart's main pumping chamber, in children living with HIV in sub-Saharan Africa. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis follows PRISMA guidance across five databases. Twenty studies covering 3,994 children reported the condition by echocardiography.

The pooled prevalence was 6.0 percent, but studies disagreed wildly, with heterogeneity at ninety-five percent in the reported statistic. Era explained much of the spread: studies from before or early in the antiretroviral era found 27.8 percent, against 3.6 percent in the treatment era in the subgroup comparison. Clinics with at least eighty percent treatment coverage reported far less dysfunction than those below that mark. Measurement method also shifted estimates. The authors conclude the complication persists in a real minority and urge standardized definitions in future longitudinal work.
pmc-13560630:
Ema and co-authors announced a 2026 draft genome sequence of Ligilactobacillus agilis strain SY88, a lactic acid bacterium taken from traditional yogurt in Rajshahi, Bangladesh. Such bacteria drive food fermentation and are generally regarded as safe. The strain was isolated from yogurt bought at a local confectionery shop in 2025.

Colonies were grown on standard MRS agar without oxygen at body temperature for forty-eight hours, then purified by repeated streaking. DNA was sequenced on an Illumina platform with paired reads and assembled with the SPAdes programme, Ema reports. The draft genome spans just under two million base pairs with a GC content, the share of G and C letters, near forty-two percent. Publishing the sequence expands genomic resources for dairy associated lactic acid bacteria.
pmc-13562130:
Behrooz Mamandipoor and four colleagues teach machine learning models to fill in hourly blood gas and metabolic panel values for intensive care patients between real laboratory draws. Their 2026 study feeds prior labs, medications, clinical events, fluid balance, hemodynamics, and ventilator settings into the estimators. A downstream task, predicting who will need kidney replacement therapy, tests whether the filled values help.

The gradient boosting estimator cut imputation error by about a third for blood gas targets and about a fifth for metabolic ones, against simply carrying the last value forward. A bidirectional memory network fed the machine-filled series predicted dialysis need better than the same network fed carried-forward values, on both discrimination measures reported. The authors argue continuous imputation turns sparse lab data into a live signal for deep learning at the bedside.
pmc-13562530:
Hao Hu and ten colleagues package a plant-derived protective compound into a self-assembling gel that slowly releases it inside the eye. Glaucoma kills the nerve cells of the retina, and pressure control alone does not stop that loss. Carnosic acid, drawn from herbs, guards nerve cells, yet getting it to the retina and keeping it there is hard. The 2026 team loaded it into RADA16, a peptide that forms a soft, porous gel, and tested three strengths to pick one soft enough for injection.

The chosen gel released the compound over 72 hours. In cell tests the loaded gel supported growth and proved gentle at working doses. In rats with a sudden pressure spike in the eye, the treatment thinned the damage: fewer stressed cells, lower inflammatory signals, and better cell survival. The authors see a route toward long-acting eye protection from one injection.
pmc-13562630:
Zezhong Ding and colleagues built a compact vision system to grade rose tea, a product whose uneven quality hurts sellers and buyers alike. Grading still relies on manual labour, which is slow and inconsistent, while large AI models are too heavy for factory equipment. Their 2026 paper adapts a small object-detection model, YOLOv12n, with a leaner design and pruning that trims unneeded connections.

The finished model, RTD-YOLO, graded tea with an F1 score near 90 percent and a detection accuracy near 96 percent, while shrinking to just 2 megabytes. It ran at 55 frames per second on a small edge device, fast enough for a production line. The authors offer it as practical support for standardising rose tea and helping high-quality products stand out.
pmc-13563730:
Huilin Liu and eleven colleagues track a combined blood marker over time to see how its accumulated burden forecasts heart disease and stroke. The marker, TyG-CVAI, blends triglycerides and glucose with a Chinese visceral-fat index, capturing insulin resistance and belly fat in one number. Their 2026 study used the national CHARLS cohort: 4,338 middle-aged and older adults free of cardiovascular disease, measured in 2011 and 2015, then followed for about five years. People were grouped by whether the marker stayed low, rose, fell, or stayed high.

New disease struck 845 participants. Every unfavourable pattern raised risk, and the stay-high group fared worst, with a hazard ratio of 1.77 against the stay-low group. Even the group whose marker fell kept extra risk, at 1.64, hinting that past exposure leaves a mark. Each standard rise in cumulated marker added 10 percent risk. Repeated measurement, the authors argue, beats a single snapshot for spotting danger early.
pmc-13563830:
Kristi E. Gamarel and three colleagues give dissemination science a missing vocabulary: eight named outcomes that spreading research findings is supposed to produce. Without shared terms, studies cannot say why a spread strategy worked, and results cannot accumulate. The 2026 paper draws on communication theory, innovation diffusion, public policy, and organisational readiness thinking, plus two decades inside a national HIV research network. The ladder runs Exposure, Comprehension, Credibility, Salience, Perceived Fit, Leadership Endorsement, and Action Readiness, ending at the Decision to Implement.

That final decision is also the border fence: the authors place the start of implementation science exactly there, separating outcomes from the mechanisms that cause them. Three studies from an adolescent HIV trials network illustrate each rung in action. The taxonomy is offered as a starting language, not a rulebook. Clearer targets, the authors argue, let future studies compare strategies honestly and build the cumulative evidence the field lacks.
pmc-13568730:
Ahmad Alwazzan leads a 2026 retrospective study of 126 ovarian cancer patients asking whether routine blood tumor markers measured before treatment can forecast when cancer will return. Three markers were compared across tumor subtypes in patients treated with major surgery plus chemotherapy.

One marker, CA-125, was raised in about three quarters of patients, far more often than the other two. Surprisingly, raised CA-125 came with a longer time before recurrence in survival analysis, while a third marker carried independent weight in adjusted models. The mixed signals show why single markers mislead, and they argue for combining marker profiles with tumor type when counseling patients about outlook.
pmc-13569430:
Aline Zarea and colleagues tested whether new mutations explain sporadic early-onset Alzheimer's disease, publishing the trio study in 2026. Most early-onset cases lack a family history, and new mutations cause some such cases in other neurodegenerative diseases, but their role in Alzheimer's was largely unknown. The team recruited 37 new patient-parent trios nationwide and combined them with 12 previously reported trios.

Only three patients carried a disease-causing new mutation in known genes APP or PSEN1, while candidate new mutations in other genes might explain a small extra share. No excess burden of rare variants emerged in large case-control data, and risk scores looked no more enriched than chance. The authors conclude most sporadic early-onset disease reflects complex inherited risk rather than single new mutations.
pmc-13571330:
Mayara Marques and colleagues report a patient whose dangerous heart rhythm kept returning after earlier burn treatment inside the heart. The rhythm problem, ventricular tachycardia, is a fast heartbeat from the lower chambers that can prove fatal if it persists.

The patient had prior bypass surgery, which blocked the usual route to the heart's outer surface for treatment. Mapping showed the faulty circuit ran deep in the heart wall, beyond the reach of normal burns. Doctors stacked two energies at one inner spot, pulsed electric field and heat, until the burns reached deep enough. The rhythm stopped at the seventh pulse application and could not be restarted, Marques reports.
pmc-13572330:
Agustin Vaccaro and colleagues present, in a 2026 surgical case, a 46-year-old man treated for a mid-rectal growth through a transanal endoscopic operation. The operation dissected between the two muscle layers of the rectal wall. Colonoscopy had found a roughly five-centimeter leafy growth, tissue tests suggested a benign glandular polyp type, and MRI staged it as an early tumor with clean margins.

The operation took three hours, lost minimal blood, and the patient went home the next day without complications. Cutting between muscle layers reaches the deepest safe margin while keeping the rectal wall intact, which can cure early rectal cancers and preserves later surgical planes. The case demonstrates the technique in a favorable lesion.
pmc-13573230:
William Lammons, with ten colleagues, reports a study of creative workshops that helped patients shape research on frailty. The word names a state of low reserve in older age, yet the word can sting and carry stigma. A linked project asks how an electronic frailty score can serve clinics best, and public input was sought in fresh ways.

Three workshops used group blackout poetry, where people black out words in a text to leave a poem, and quilt-making. Twenty-two people took part across the two poetry sessions and one quilt session. The work changed the main project's topic guide and analysis plans. Themes covered unease with the word frailty itself, the need to tailor how it is raised with each patient, and time strain in health services. Two poems and a quilt photo stand as outputs.
pmc-13573330:
Xiaoyun Liu, with two colleagues, reports a 2026 cohort study of a combined metabolic index and heart disease risk over time. The index joins a blood fat ratio with the waist-to-height ratio, so it reflects both harmful fats and belly fat. A single reading may miss how risk builds, so the team tracked change across years.

Data came from a national ageing study in China, with 9,120 adults aged 45 and up at the start and 6,164 in the change analysis. People whose index stayed high faced the top risk, about a third above the steady low group. Those who rose from low to high also faced raised risk, while those who fell from high to low showed no extra risk. Total exposure over time added risk clues beyond one reading. The authors urge repeat checks.
pmc-13578230:
S Prejesh, Tamilarasi Kathirvel Murugan, and Logeswari Govindaraj present a 2026 system for spotting risky drug mixes before patients are harmed. Taking many drugs at once is now common, and harms from pairs that clash are hard to catch with single models, which can also miss events where many drugs appear together.

The team blended three learning methods and fed them reports from the United States adverse event system, with drug details mapped from a drug database. Each flagged mix also gets a risk score meant to guide clinical judgment. The blend scored high on accuracy and caught nearly all true risky cases in testing, which the authors offer as support for drug safety teams.
pmc-13578830:
Agnes Karingo Karume and colleagues ask women living with HIV in Kenya, and their care providers, how a tablet based family planning guide worked in practice, in a 2026 study. The self guided tool ran inside a larger trial at clinics. Ten group talks gathered views from 95 women who used it, and ten providers sat for deep interviews.

Women said the tool sharpened their choices, taught them about less known methods, and cleared up myths. Talks with providers also went better, women reported. Providers found it handy for tailoring advice, above all for new users and teens, though it fit poorly when a woman already knew her method. Users called the tool long, so the authors suggest trimming it and letting some groups skip it.
pmc-13579230:
Yan Zhou and colleagues review batteries built to live inside the body and treat disease while they power care, in a 2026 paper. Normal batteries must be sealed tight against their toxic innards, which caps how small a device can shrink. Body friendly batteries skip the hard shell and join the therapy itself, making mild electric fields and releasing helpful chemical products at the site.

The review sorts uses into three lanes: electric stimulation that nudges tissue to heal, chemical products that do the treating, and drug delivery paced by the battery. Heart pacing, cancer care, and tissue regrowth all appear as test beds. Working principles get a short tour before the authors turn to what blocks wide use, from material safety to steady output, and what the next wave of designs must solve.
pmc-13579730:
Nader Hashemi and colleagues mapped human papillomavirus in Tehran over 14 years, to guide vaccination and screening. HPV, a common sexually transmitted infection, causes most cervical cancers and a share of other anogenital cancers. Their retrospective study examined 6,418 people tested at one pathology laboratory between 2011 and 2024, 5,988 women and 430 men, using several genotyping methods over the period.

Overall positivity reached 40.8 percent in women and 63.3 percent in the smaller male group, peaking in the 20–30 age band. The top genotypes were 6, 16, 52, and 31. Nearly three-quarters of patients had no symptoms and came for routine screening. The authors present the genotype map as baseline data for national prevention planning in Iran.
pmc-13582130:
Properzi Luca and colleagues pool sixty studies to map how the voice box nerve travels past a neck artery, in a 2026 review for thyroid surgeons. Cutting this nerve is a feared slip in thyroid operations, and the artery below the gland is the usual landmark for finding it. The pooled set covered over nine thousand patients and nearly fifteen thousand neck sides.

The nerve ran behind the artery most often, in just over half of sides. It ran in front in about three in ten and threaded between branches in the rest, too often to assume the classic path. A rare variant that skips the usual loop appeared only on the right side, in under one percent of right sides. Spread between studies ran huge, so the authors insist surgeons verify the nerve by sight before tying any vessel.
pmc-13584430:
Congcong Jin and colleagues revisit a cheap blood test in women with polycystic ovary syndrome, often shortened to PCOS. The test, ESR, measures how fast red blood cells settle, a rough sign of body-wide inflammation. Their 2026 study compared 2,006 women with PCOS, a hormone condition that disrupts periods and fertility, against more than ten thousand women with regular ovulation.

ESR ran higher in the PCOS group at every age and weight band, and more of those women crossed the high-value line. The test tracked with harmful blood fats and with shifts in kidney and liver measures, and with hormone patterns in both groups alike. Yet on its own it sorted new PCOS cases poorly. The authors pitch it as a low-cost way to watch inflammation, not as a stand-alone diagnosis.
pmc-13589130:
Wei Wei and co-authors search in this 2026 study for the liver genes that control blood triglycerides, the fats that shape belly fat in growing chickens. Excess belly fat wastes feed and lowers carcass value, so breeders want its genetic levers.

The team measured blood fat in Wannan chickens at three ages and profiled liver gene activity in twenty-four birds. Blood fat tracked belly fat closely. Network analysis grouped genes into modules, and one module tied strongly to both traits. Six genes involved in building and modifying fats stood out as central regulators. The authors say these genes give breeding programs concrete targets for leaner birds, though each candidate still needs direct functional testing.
pmc-13591230:
Yobsan Tamiru and nine colleagues investigate outbreaks of Marek's disease, a virus driven cancer of chickens, in central and western Ethiopia. The disease drains poultry farms through deaths and higher care costs. Between late 2021 and late 2022 the team gathered 94 pooled samples from sick birds in four areas. Birds came from both farm and backyard flocks; unvaccinated birds were found only in backyard settings.

Gene tests found the virus in about four of five pooled samples, with feather samples and organ tissue both scoring high. Imported breeds tested positive more often than local ones. Three fifths of positive samples grew the virus in cell culture. Tamiru and the team call for deeper gene work to tell vaccine strains from wild ones and to guide control.
pmc-13592130:
Chunting Wu leads a team testing broccoli sprout extract against kidney harm in mice fed a fat rich diet. Fat overload can stuff the kidney with lipids, sparking oxidative stress and inflammation that erode its filtering work. Mice received the extract in their food for twelve weeks. Blood and kidney measures of function, fat content, and antioxidant strength were tracked, plus a broad scan of kidney lipids.

Extract fed mice showed far better kidney numbers, with key waste markers down by roughly half or more. Kidney fat fell, antioxidant defenses rose, and four harmful lipid species returned toward normal. Wu and the team trace the gain to a switched on energy sensor pathway, stronger antioxidant gene programs, and a quieter inflammasome alarm.
pmc-13592630:
Harsh Vivek Harkare leads a team costing two community tuberculosis screening routes in South Africa and Lesotho. One route read chest X-rays with computer aided detection alone. The other added a quick blood inflammation test for people whose X-ray scores fell in a middle band. Inside a large trial, 20,023 people were screened and every cost ingredient was counted from the program's view.

The X-ray only route found 72 cases at about 5,454 dollars each. Adding the blood test found fewer cases, 60, and cost about 7,486 dollars each, over a third more. Staff pay drove costs in South Africa, vehicles in Lesotho. Higher underlying prevalence would cut cost per case sharply, Harkare and the team conclude, while bigger screening volume at current rates would not.
pmc-13593730:
Jutta Pikalo and a team of co-authors screened free-ranging European wildcats from Germany's Harz Mountains for viruses known from domestic cats. Spleen samples from forty-two wildcats collected between 2010 and 2018 were tested with a battery of molecular assays. The assays covered established agents such as feline leukemia virus and feline parvovirus, plus several recently described viruses.

Viral DNA turned up in seven animals. Feline leukemia virus appeared in five wildcats and feline parvovirus in two, while none of the other targeted viruses was detected. The authors caution that long-preserved samples may have dulled the tests, so absences are not proof a virus is missing. Even so, the two positive findings confirm that domestic cat diseases circulate in this wild population, and continued monitoring is needed to judge spillover risk and protect the species.
pmc-13594430:
Ayan Suleimenovich Abdrakhmanov and co-authors report implanting a leadless pacemaker in a woman who was seventeen weeks pregnant, with careful tracking of the radiation dose her fetus received. She had fainting and severe weakness, and monitoring showed dangerous pauses in the signal between the heart's upper and lower chambers, so lasting pacing was needed.

The team implanted a Micra AV device, which sits entirely inside the heart, using X-ray guidance held to strict safety rules. The fetal dose came to a small share of levels tied to harm before birth, and the mother's own dose was also recorded. Her symptoms vanished, the pregnancy went on without problems, and she delivered a healthy baby. The authors offer the case as practical reassurance that leadless pacing can be done in pregnancy when the need is pressing and exposure is kept as low as possible.
pmc-13598430:
Kun-Ming Rau and co-authors tested a water extract of Pogostemon cablin, the patchouli herb of traditional medicine, against triple-negative breast cancer cells, an aggressive type lacking the usual drug targets. Their laboratory study measured growth, death pathways, cell cycle position, and the proteins that drive cell division in the MDA-MB-231 cell line.

The extract slowed growth in proportion to dose and time, yet the expected death machinery stayed quiet: no meaningful apoptosis, no collapse of mitochondrial voltage, no activation of the executioner enzyme. Instead the cells piled up at the gate to division and inside mitosis itself. The reason appeared in the protein readings: the CDC2 and cyclin B1 pair that triggers division was turned down, with its activator's marking altered. The authors conclude the herb stalls cancer cells in mitotic delay, a different and possibly useful way to restrain this tumor type.
pmc-13598930:
Shadab Momin and a team of co-authors describe automating emergency palliative radiotherapy, the urgent radiation given to relieve cancer emergencies, where teams often skip the usual simulation scan and improvise under pressure. Their scripting-driven workflow builds the plan from the cone-beam scan taken on the treatment machine itself, automating prescription handling, beam setup, and dose calculation.

Built-in prompts guard the safety-critical steps, while humans keep control of image checks and field borders. Dose calculations on the treatment-machine images agreed with conventional scan-based plans within a few percent. Automation removed thirty-three manual data entry steps from the older two-dimensional workflow, and average time on the treatment table came to about an hour. Staff backed the change strongly in surveys, with every respondent reporting benefit after training. The system rolled out across several sites in one health network.
pmc-13601630:
Ivar J H G Wamelink leads a thirteen-author team describing IMAGO in 2026, an Amsterdam dataset built for brain tumor research. It gathers imaging, tissue, molecular, and survival records for 1,700 adults with diffuse glioma, a family of aggressive brain cancers. The first release covers 500 patients with structural MRI scans taken before surgery in four standard sequences, plus scans within two weeks after surgery for 381 of them.

Derived images add diffusion-based maps for nearly all patients and blood-volume maps for a subset. Every scan is aligned to a standard brain space and stripped of skull, so files are ready for analysis. Tissue data include IDH mutation status for all 500, a chromosome deletion marker for 170, and tumor grade for all. Automated tumor outlines, checked by humans, are included for some cases. The authors intend the dataset for building synthetic images, training tumor segmentation, and predicting molecular features from scans alone.
pmc-13602730:
Fang Wang leads an eleven-author team testing licorice extract in weaned piglets in 2026, hunting antibiotic alternatives for livestock. Glycyrrhizic acid, the main active compound in licorice, fights inflammation and viruses, yet its farm value was unproven. On a commercial nursery, 225 weaned piglets were split into five groups: plain feed, routine antibiotics, and three licorice doses up to 2.6 grams per kilogram of feed. Growth, illness signs, blood markers, and airway microbes were tracked.

The highest licorice dose improved growth and cough scores modestly, short of significance. Clearer gains appeared elsewhere: diarrhea fell, skin scores improved, and antibody levels IgG and IgM rose. Antioxidant enzymes strengthened while a damage marker dropped. Airway profiling found more Alloprevotella and fewer of twelve disease-linked species, including major swine lung pathogens, at the high dose. The authors back glycyrrhizic acid as a workable non-antibiotic strategy for young pigs.
pmc-13612830:
Yu-Chieh Lin leads a team reporting in 2026 on a computer model that predicts whether early bladder cancer will return after BCG therapy, a standard treatment placed directly into the bladder. The cancer type studied grows on the bladder lining without reaching the muscle layer, yet its course varies widely between patients. Good staging and grading matter for choosing care, but results can differ between hospitals.

The team trained its model on 1,437 cases from hospitals in Lithuania and Taiwan using federated learning, a method that trains across sites without pooling raw data. The shared model beat single-site versions, reaching 86.2 percent accuracy for tumor stage and 79.2 percent for grade. It also grouped tissue features into a new risk signal for relapse, which could help doctors spot patients who need closer follow-up.
pmc-13612930:
Fritz Sterr and colleagues report a qualitative study from Germany on what makes it hard to wean adult intensive care patients off a breathing machine. Taking a patient off mechanical ventilation sounds like one step, yet in practice it involves many people, judgements, and risks. The team ran group talks and workshops over three days in 2025 with 29 intensive care professionals to map how the process really works.

Their analysis produced four themes covering how complex weaning is, what outcomes matter, which actions help, and how those parts link together. The work feeds into a broader program theory that aims to explain why weaning succeeds or stalls. For intensive care teams, the study offers a shared language for a daily task that is often handled by habit rather than by clear shared reasoning.
pmc-13616330:
Jia Feng leads a team designing a living biosensor inside bacteria that lights up when cadaverine, a smelly diamine used as a building block for nylon-like polymers, is present. Cell factories engineered to make such chemicals improve fastest when engineers can spot the best producers at a glance. Gene activity scans revealed a promoter, a DNA switch named PpyrF, that answers to diamines, and a partner protein, Ihfβ, that governs the switch.

Stepwise tweaks to the promoter, the partner protein, and the output's start signals raised the sensor's fold response more than 2.33 times. With the sharper sensor guiding them, the authors ran a multi-level engineering campaign on Escherichia coli to push cadaverine output higher. The design logic, finding a native switch and polishing it, can be reused for other fermentation products.
pmc-13616430:
Camelia López-Deflory, Margalida Miró-Bonet, and Amélie Perron listen to nurses in Spain's Balearic Islands public health system to rethink what fairness at work means in health care. Organisational justice, how fair staff judge their treatment and rewards to be, shapes nurse well-being, yet past research frames it narrowly. Drawing on 31 long interviews and the social justice theory of Nancy Fraser, the authors read nurses' words closely for the deeper pattern.

Nurses described justice not as perks or pay scales but as being able to practise according to their professional ethos, the values they entered nursing to serve. Blocked staffing, voice, and recognition therefore sting as injustice itself. The reframing tells managers that fairness programs will miss the mark until ward conditions let nurses do the job as they believe it should be done.
pmc-13617330:
Zhang Huawei and three colleagues survey music students in China about adopting Internet of Things technology in smart classrooms. Connected sensors and devices are spreading through higher education, yet little work asks how performance students, whose learning is hands-on, feel about them. The team polled one thousand twenty undergraduate and postgraduate music students at twelve universities that already run smart classrooms.

Two frameworks guided the analysis: one on technology acceptance, covering expected performance, effort, social influence, and support conditions, and one on psychological readiness for new technology. Readiness showed the strongest link to intention to adopt and also fed both performance and effort expectations, which acted as parallel bridges to adoption. Social influence, by contrast, had no significant effect, and some links differed between men and women. The authors advise universities to build student readiness and reliable support, not rely on peer pressure.
pmc-13617830:
Merva Güneyli and Emin Murat Canger report a 2026 imaging study of the nasopharynx, the space behind the nose, in people with cleft lip and palate. Early signs of nasopharyngeal cancer often appear in a recess called the Rosenmüller fossa, so knowing how cleft anatomy reshapes that region matters for detection. Using cone-beam CT scans, they compared seventy-eight people with clefts against seventy-eight healthy individuals.

The cleft nasopharynx showed a narrow and long configuration. Several distances and angles differed significantly from controls, including longer torus levatorius and tympanotubal angle measures, with the strongest changes in bilateral clefts, while fossa depth itself did not differ. Even in one-sided clefts, both sides were similarly affected. The authors conclude the cleft is a regional remodeling of the whole nasopharyngeal complex, not a local defect, with implications for throat function and middle ear disease.
pmc-13618030:
Maciej Spiegel and Nino Russo use quantum chemistry calculations to ask how attaching a sugar unit changes the antioxidant power of resveratrol, the much-studied red grape compound. The sugar-bearing form, polydatin or piceid, appears in traditional medicine plants and is sometimes reported stronger and sometimes weaker than plain resveratrol. Their computational protocol modeled attacks by a peroxyl radical in water at body pH and in a fat-like environment.

One hydroxyl group on the molecule's second ring did most of the radical-scavenging work in both settings. The sugar's effect flipped with surroundings: in the fat-like phase polydatin reacted faster than the reference antioxidant Trolox, while in water it fell behind both Trolox and plain resveratrol. The authors explain the dispute in the experimental literature this way: glucosylation helps the molecule where fats dominate and hinders it in watery conditions.
pmc-13618930:
Shahsanam Gheibi and seven colleagues build and test a questionnaire for rating the professional behavior of medical residents in Iran. Professionalism shapes care quality and public trust, but measuring it needs a sound instrument. Starting from literature and existing tools, they drafted sixty-two items and put the pool through expert content review, resident checks, and a field test with two hundred seventeen residents.

Expert review and resident feedback trimmed the pool, and factor analysis settled on a six-factor structure explaining most of the variation, yielding a final eighteen-item tool. Reliability was strong, with internal consistency and repeat-test stability both high. The authors recommend the tool to educators, administrators, and policymakers for assessing conduct in clinical settings, spotting weaknesses, and designing targeted help. They also note it serves general medical students as well as residents.
pmc-13619030:
Lana Tran and seven colleagues report a 2026 Phase 1 drug-interaction study asking whether an acid suppressor changes how the body handles vepdegestrant. The drug is an experimental estrogen receptor degrader being developed for advanced breast cancer. Because the drug dissolves by pH, stomach-acid reduction could cut its absorption. Twelve volunteers took one dose alone in one period, then, in a second period, one dose after five days of esomeprazole, with blood sampled for a week.

Exposure fell with the acid suppressor on board: exposure ran at eighty-four percent of the drug-alone value, and peak concentration at seventy-four percent. A similar dip appeared for the drug's epimer form. All twelve treatment-emergent adverse events across seven participants were mild, and the dose was well tolerated. The authors conclude that combining the two only mildly lowers vepdegestrant levels, information prescribers need when patients take common reflux medicines.
pmc-13621530:
Boyi Chen and six colleagues asked whether a replaced knee feels most forgotten when its slope matches the patient's own anatomy, in a 2026 study of robot-assisted versus manual surgery. The backward tilt of the shin bone's top, the posterior tibial slope, shapes how a new knee bends and feels. Two hundred forty patients, split evenly between robot and manual techniques, had slopes measured on CT and joint awareness scored a year later.

Robots cut placement error to under half the manual group's. Joint awareness peaked near a slope of about five degrees across everyone, tracing an inverted-U. Yet drifting from a patient's native slope independently dragged scores down, no matter which technique was used. Patients rebuilt within two degrees of their anatomy reported clearly better awareness than those further off. The authors urge planning around each patient's original slope rather than chasing one universal target.
pmc-13621830:
Brooke R Shepley and colleagues explore whether age changes how two blood vessel signals respond to hard exercise. The signals, Notch1 and VEGF-A, help keep the inner lining of vessels healthy and react to the friction of flowing blood. The team measured them in healthy adults before and after a peak cycling test.

Twenty-nine adults aged twenty to sixty-five gave blood at rest, right after exercise, and after fifteen minutes of recovery. The measured piece of Notch1 stayed flat across exercise on average, yet it ran higher in older adults and its change after exercise varied with age. That change also tracked the thickness of the neck artery wall. VEGF-A showed no clear pattern at all. The authors read the contrast as a sign that aging alters one vessel pathway while leaving the other largely untouched.
pmc-13623130:
Sinling Tiffany Yu and colleagues review deep learning tools that outline the heart on CT scans of patients with congenital heart disease, meaning heart defects present from birth. Drawing these outlines, called segmentation, helps plan surgery, yet each defect is unique and the anatomy is small. No review had gathered this young field before.

Searching six databases for work from 2004 to 2025 left fourteen studies. The UNet design and its variants dominated, and the best score for a single structure came from a hybrid model with a ResNet backbone outlining the aorta. Reporting was strong on training details and model design. Weak spots were plain: only two studies tested their model on outside data, and none explained how they chose sample sizes or handled missing data. Small vessels consistently scored worse than the whole heart. The authors call for bigger shared data sets and standard reporting.
pmc-13623230:
Marco Brambilla heads a European study of repeat CT scanning, asking how often patients rack up high cumulative radiation doses. Thirty-one facilities in eighteen countries shared exposure records, with 2023 as the focus year and a three-year window around it. The team tested new yardsticks for repeat imaging and a benchmark that flags centres needing attention.

The database held more than seven hundred thousand patients and over 1.6 million scans in the year. The share of patients crossing a high cumulative dose differed widely between facilities, reaching a few percent depending on the measure used. Counting new cases per year proved more honest than counting everyone ever exposed, which badly understates repeat rates. The authors propose a dose benchmark drawn from the spread of centre values, above which a facility should review its habits. They argue that cutting repeat scans is a direct gain for patient care.
pmc-13623330:
Hai-Lin Yao and colleagues studied how smoking, drinking, and body weight relate to semen quality in men seeking preconception care. Male factors drive a large share of infertility, yet dose and shape of lifestyle effects were unclear. Their look-back study analysed 3,336 men at a Chengdu andrology clinic from January 2019 to June 2023, adjusting for age, abstinence, and season.

Smoking showed a clear dose harm: men smoking over 20 cigarettes daily or for over 10 years had lower sperm counts, totals, and motility. Ex-drinkers regained only slight motility. Weight showed a curved pattern, peaking in mildly overweight men, while obesity still impaired quality. Yao and colleagues urge quitting smoking and managing weight before conception.
pmc-13624530:
Xu-Chen Xia and colleagues test a plant sugar chain, drawn from the herb Polygonatum kingianum, as a weapon against Staphylococcus aureus, a germ that often resists standard antibiotics. The team first measured how the extract, called PKP, killed bacteria in dishes. It then gave the extract through the nose to rats with infected sinuses, a model of stubborn sinus disease.

In dishes, PKP killed the target germ more strongly as the dose rose, apparently by breaking its cell membrane. Treated rats showed fewer invading white cells, fewer abscesses, and lower levels of a swelling signal, while a barrier-guarding signal recovered. Blood tests added signs of calmer, better-balanced immunity, which supports plant compounds as helpers beside failing antibiotics.
pmc-13626330:
Noelle Callizot and co-authors test a small molecule, AZP2006, as a shield for the brain cells lost in Parkinson's disease. The drug, already in trials for a related condition, works through two helper proteins, progranulin and prosaposin, that keep lysosomes, the cell's recycling centers, in order. Faulty recycling lets the toxic protein alpha-synuclein pile up, so the team challenged lab-grown neurons and animal models with mitochondrial injury and pre-made synuclein fibers.

The drug blunted both insults and protected dopamine-making neurons, and blocking the progranulin path took that protection away, tying the effect to the recycling system. Restored lysosomal balance is the proposed engine. With synuclein diseases short on protective drugs, tuning this protein pair looks like a promising route worth clinical testing.
pmc-13628430:
Karla A. O. Souza and seven colleagues built a lab method for measuring nitazenes in blood plasma. Nitazenes are a class of very strong lab-made opioids. Their 2026 paper tackles a forensic problem. These drugs turn up in street drugs and fake pills, often without the user knowing. They can poison at very low doses.

The method pairs a tiny extraction step with a fine measuring tool. It reads nitazene compounds across a wide low range. Results proved exact and steady in repeat runs. The team proved it on a real poisoning case, the first reported in Brazil. That patient needed repeated doses of the antidote naloxone. They present the method as practical for hospital and forensic labs alike.
pmc-13629230:
Jonah M. Walker and ten colleagues propose a shared language for reporting reproductive isolation. Isolation is the barrier that stops kin lines from merging back into one. Their 2026 framework tackles a practical problem. Researchers measure isolation in many clashing ways. Results then resist comparison across species.

The scheme sorts its terms into three linked domains. Each domain is a nested ladder that most breeding organisms can fit. Barriers as unlike as habitat choice and sterile hybrids gain steady labels. The authors show the system at work. They invite the field to adopt and extend it. Shared measures, they argue, would let speciation research pool its scattered proof at last.
pmc-13629530:
Katherine A. Fowler and five colleagues summarise the 2023 findings of a United States violent death reporting system. The system links death records with coroner and police files for every violent death. The report covers all fifty states, the capital district, and Puerto Rico. It captured over ninety percent of the nation's homicides and suicides that year.

The system recorded 72,093 deaths in the states and capital district. Suicides made up nearly two-thirds. Homicides followed at just over a quarter. Smaller shares covered unclear deaths, legal action deaths, and accidental firearm injuries. Puerto Rico's pattern ran the other way, led by homicide. Rates and details varied sharply by sex, age, and ethnic group. The authors supply that detail for prevention planning.
pmc-13629630:
Caitlin M. Logan and A. Sue Menko review, in 2026, how the eye keeps its immune system in precise balance. Older thinking cast the eye as simply immune-privileged and sealed off, yet newer work shows resident immune cells living in its tissues, necessary for healthy development and for mounting protection after injury.

Regulation turns out to be layered and far-reaching. Events in one eye can stir responses in the other, calming cells such as regulatory T cells and specialised macrophages steer recovery, and even the microbiome feeds into ocular health. The authors argue that grasping these connections, from the eye through the visual system and beyond, opens routes to treatments that preserve sight by restoring balance rather than merely suppressing inflammation.
pmc-13635130:
Xuliang Wang and colleagues published this 2026 study of a large language model built to triage possible heart attacks at first contact. Emergency triage for acute coronary syndrome starts with a patient's own story, yet firm diagnosis waits on blood tests and heart tracings that smaller clinics may lack. The team built a model that reads only the patient's narrative and vital signs. They tested it on more than sixteen thousand past cases and over five hundred live cases.

The model caught the condition with high sensitivity, meaning few true cases slipped past it. It also processed each case much faster than cardiologists reviewing charts on their own. The authors suggest such a tool could speed and sharpen first decisions in emergency departments, especially where specialists and tests are scarce. Because early treatment saves heart muscle, faster sorting at the door carries real weight for survival.
pmc-13635230:
Naroa Ibarra-Aizpurua and six colleagues published this 2026 study of how inflamed support cells can turn toxic to the neurons lost in Parkinson's disease. The team grew midbrain astrocytes and dopamine neurons from reprogrammed human stem cells. Some cells carried a mutation in a gene called GBA, a common Parkinson's risk factor. Inflammatory signals were used to push the astrocytes into a reactive state, and gene readings mapped their response.

Reactive astrocytes changed thousands of genes, and their calcium handling went badly off balance. Mutant astrocytes released even more calcium under inflammatory pressure. In mixed cultures, the combination of inflammation signals and clumped alpha-synuclein, the disease's signature protein, killed dopamine neurons. Astrocytes alone did not explain it; their inflamed state made the protein clumps deadly. Even healthy donor astrocytes lost their supportive quality under inflammation. The authors argue this helper-turned-harmful switch deserves a place in Parkinson's research.
pmc-13637330:
Cong Huang led a 2026 multicenter cohort study testing whether removing the prostate helps men with widespread hormone-sensitive prostate cancer who have responded deeply to modern drug therapy. Surgery after spread was once reserved for low-volume disease, but stronger drug combinations now push more high-volume patients into deep remission, with prostate-specific antigen below 0.2, opening a window to test added local treatment. The team followed 126 men from 2018 to 2023, comparing surgery plus standard care against standard care alone.

At a median follow-up near forty-seven months, the surgery group lived longer by imaging, overall, and biochemical measures. Among seventy-four high-volume patients, surgery still tracked with longer imaging progression-free survival, overall survival, and biochemical progression-free survival, and matched-pair analysis agreed.
pmc-13639230:
Emma Spotorno and five colleagues report a 2026 materials study on passive daytime radiative cooling, a way to shed heat to outer space even under direct sun. Such coolers must reflect sunlight strongly while emitting heat through the atmosphere's mid-infrared window.

The team pressed thin films of silica-loaded polymer onto silver-coated steel and measured both their light response and cooling power. Strong emission across the full mid-infrared range lined up with higher radiative power near room temperature. The result gives engineers a clear quantitative test for judging candidate coolers, which could support energy-saving cooling in buildings.
pmc-13639630:
Scattered brain-imaging findings in hard-to-treat depression may converge on two control networks. Noda argues this in a note on a study by Han and colleagues. Treatment-resistant depression means failure to benefit from two adequate antidepressant trials of different classes. It has produced mixed maps of brain change. Noda explains how coordinate network mapping, applied to single coordinates rather than broad regions, reframes those inconsistencies as a two-tier pattern.

Depression-linked abnormalities clustered on the frontoparietal network and the cingulo-opercular network, while those specific to treatment resistance were found in the cingulo-opercular network alone. That split, Noda suggests, frames resistant depression not merely as severer depression but as a distinct failure of core systems that maintain goals, spot key signals, and regulate actions. He also warns the brain map came from young adults.
pmc-13641830:
Carmel Williams and three colleagues wrote an editorial marking forty years since the Ottawa Charter for Health Promotion, the framework born at a 1986 World Health Organization conference in Canada. The charter made healthy public policy a central idea in public health.

The authors argue that laws on income, housing, food, and work still shape health more than medical spending does, a point first pressed by Canada's Lalonde Report. Australia helped carry the agenda from Ottawa to Adelaide and beyond. The editorial credits public health research with producing the findings and advocacy that move governments toward fairer policy.
pmc-13642030:
Maya S Bishop and eight colleagues present a 2026 sheep study of megadose vitamin C salt, sodium ascorbate, for brain pressure problems during sepsis. Severe infection often raises pressure inside the skull and dulls the response to blood pressure drugs, yet no treatment targets that brain dysfunction directly.

Sheep received live Escherichia coli infusions until sepsis developed, then either ascorbate or a matched placebo for seven hours. The treated animals' skull pressure returned to normal, blood pressure improved, and responsiveness to norepinephrine was fully restored, while placebo animals stayed impaired. The authors offer the results as first evidence for this approach.
pmc-13645230:
Feng Yu and three colleagues present a mathematical model explaining why the brain's master clock resists temperature shifts that easily reset clocks elsewhere in the body. Daily warmth cycles entrain tissues, yet the suprachiasmatic nucleus stays stubbornly on light-based time.

Their compartment model adds a heat shock pathway and the nucleus's spatial layout. Simulations reproduced the odd split: heat flips peripheral clocks while the master clock holds. The dorsal and ventral clock regions sit at intrinsic phase offsets, so the same heat pulse pushes them in diverging directions that cancel out. Simultaneous input to both regions strengthens the buffering, protecting daily timing.
pmc-13645530:
Abdullah A Aldaeej presents a study introducing the Dynamic Behavioral Feature Predictor, a machine learning model that forecasts which software features users will want by reading their behavior. Product teams struggle to rank feature ideas, and stated wishes often miss real desires hidden in usage data.

The model combines convolutional and memory networks to find layered patterns in interaction records. In comparative experiments it reached ninety-nine percent accuracy, beating the single-network baselines it was tested against, and it sorted varied user behavior types for tailored recommendations. Aldaeej cautions that accuracy may depend on data quality and urges real-world robustness testing before teams lean on it.
pmc-13648130:
Chul Gab Lee, in a 2026 review, takes on the label idiopathic Parkinson's disease when it is pinned on welders in Korea. The word means the cause is unknown. Claims staff often read it as proof that work played no role, so pay claims get turned down.

Lee checks proof from diagnosis, tissue, brain scans, population studies, and the law. New gene-based ways to define the disease do not hinge on cause at all. Long, low doses of manganese from welding fumes can also harm the same brain cells and leave the same protein clumps. Scans and drug response cannot split the two cleanly. Lee urges that heavy lifetime welding exposure earn a fair hearing under the pay law.
pmc-13649430:
Zihua Wang and seven colleagues pooled studies of a drug called telitacicept for adults with lupus, a disease where the immune system attacks the body's own tissues. The drug blocks two signals that keep antibody-making cells alive. The team kept each study design apart rather than mixing trials with weaker designs.

Thirty-nine reports, all from China, were found, and 22 fed into the pooled math. In two placebo trials, the drug plus standard care more than doubled response rates at about one year. Mild side effects rose a bit, while severe ones showed no clear rise. Proof for other outcomes was weak. The authors say long-term safety is still unknown.
pmc-13650130:
Amin Shafiee and three colleagues, publishing in 2026, present LightPro, a computer chip that calculates with light instead of electricity to speed up neural networks. Light-based matrix multiplication promises efficiency, yet older devices lose signal, leak interference between channels, and take up too much room to scale.

LightPro builds its paths from directional couplers made with phase-change material, a substance whose state is set by heat to fix how much light splits at each junction. An automated search method pruned the layout before fabrication choices were locked. Simulations, checked against published experiments, showed sharply smaller footprint and lower power use than standard designs, while accuracy on test datasets slipped only slightly. A prototype run on a commercial photonic processor confirmed the calculations, which the authors offer as a route to larger light-based accelerators.
pmc-13650530:
Dongfang Yang and four colleagues review multifunctional hydrogels designed to stop pancreatic leaks after pancreatic surgery. Such leaks are common and can kill. Older sealants such as fibrin glue break down fast in the enzyme-rich fluid around the pancreas or lose grip on wet tissue, which may explain why trial results conflict.

Newer gels aim to remodel the local environment rather than merely plug it. Designs capture digestive enzymes, rebuild the target using proteins the enzymes cannot cut, and pair a sealing face with an anti-stick face. Others combine leak prevention with antibacterial and healing actions across the whole recovery cycle. One diagnostic gel that flags leaks has reached human testing, while all treatment gels remain proof-of-concept, mostly in rats. The authors list five gaps blocking translation, from animal model differences to manufacturing and sterilization.
pmc-13651530:
Shivani T Shivani and four colleagues use ultrafast infrared spectroscopy to check a structural model of the toxic protein clumps behind type 2 diabetes. The clumps form from islet amyloid polypeptide, and the team had built an atomic model from a tamed variant carrying three substitutions. The substitutions sat near a helical segment whose true shape stayed unverified.

A modified spectrometer interleaved several pulse sequences so spectra could be recorded while aggregation ran. At a carefully chosen timing, the blur from disordered protein fell away, exposing signals from the oligomer's end helix, its adjacent kink, and a disulfide-looped region. Genuine oligomer spectra matched the tamed variant closely, which strengthens confidence that the atomic model reflects the real disease species. The authors offer the workflow as a general test bench for oligomer structures in other amyloid diseases, where these fleeting assemblies resist ordinary structural tools.
pmc-13652530:
Natália Soares da Silva and three colleagues map the research landscape around post-intensive care syndrome, the lasting physical, mental, and thinking problems many patients carry home after critical illness. Using bibliometric methods on the Web of Science database, the team gathered 120 articles on the syndrome in adults and charted keywords, journals, authors, and collaboration networks. The charts show where attention concentrates and where it is heading.

Quality of life, critical illness, and post-traumatic stress stood out as the dominant themes. The most active authors and journals are named, and the United States leads in publication volume. For clinicians building follow-up clinics and for researchers choosing topics, the analysis shows a field still centered on life after discharge. Clear room remains to grow in coordinated, long-term patient follow-up.
pmc-13658030:
Anatoly Kulikov led a 2026 experiment that boosts randomness using quantum devices, turning flawed random bits into ones no one can predict. Real quantum hardware is imperfect, so its random outputs carry bias that drifts with links between bits. Classical cleanup cannot fix that flaw, as a classic result by Santha and Vazirani proved. A device-free method offers a quantum way out. It requires a loophole-free Bell test run at both high violation and high repetition rate.

The team combined new theory, which made the protocol's settings realistic for experiments, with superconducting circuits that reached that regime. The result matters because cryptography depends on unpredictability: flawed randomness has already let attackers rebuild private keys from public ones. Quantum readers get a clear quantum advantage claim, modest in scale but sharp in logic: a task classical processing provably cannot do, done in the lab.
pmc-2631630:
Spek reviews the state of structure validation in chemical crystallography in 2009. Crystallographers build atomic models from diffraction data, and journals publish thousands each year. A model can look plausible yet still contain errors that mislead later work.

Validation means testing a reported structure against checks for geometry, fit, and internal consistency. Spek, known for widely used checking software, sums up current practice and its gaps. Stronger routine checks protect chemistry and materials science, since one flawed structure can waste other teams' experiments and misdirect drug or material design.  Journals increasingly expected such checks before accepting a new structure report.
pmc-3043330:
Schulz, Altman, and Moher present the journal version of the CONSORT 2010 statement on reporting randomised trials. The statement gives updated guidelines for reports of parallel group trials, where patients are assigned by chance to treatment or control. Clear reporting lets readers judge a trial's fairness.

The 2010 update refreshes the checklist using new evidence about bias and reporting quality. Authors must show how the trial was designed, run, and analysed. This version appeared across leading medical journals at once, underlining its role as the shared standard for trial reports. The same text appeared in several leading journals so no reader would miss it.
pmc-3632530:
McMurdie and Holmes present phyloseq, an R package for shared analysis and graphics of microbiome census data. Studying microbial communities by way of DNA sequencing brings many challenges. Work must integrate ecology, genes, species history, statistics, pictures, and testing in one single flow.

Phyloseq joins those pieces in a single environment built for sharing and repeating analyses. As study designs grew broader, a common toolkit kept results alike between labs. The package became standard equipment in microbiome science, from gut health studies to soil and ocean surveys.  Shared data forms also let ecologists and coders speak the same language.
pmc-3690530:
Scheres presents RELION, a Bayesian approach to cryo-electron microscopy structure determination. RELION is an open-source program for refining macromolecular structures from single-particle cryo-EM data. Alternative approaches often rely on user expertise to tune parameters and steer the process by hand.

A Bayesian method instead weighs many possible structures by likelihood, regularising the result to avoid overfitting noise. That statistical discipline helped cryo-EM produce reliable, near-atomic models of large complexes. RELION became a central tool in the cryo-EM revolution that reshaped structural biology.  Drug-sized complexes once beyond reach became routine targets after such software matured.
pmc-5439030:
Cohen, Brauer, Burnett, and their co-authors estimated the global burden of disease from ambient air pollution in 2017. Breathing polluted outdoor air raises illness and death rates and ranks among the top causes of disease burden worldwide. The team used data from the Global Burden of Diseases Study 2015.

They charted how deaths and disease burden tied to dirty air changed between 1990 and 2015, worldwide and country by country. Fine particles from traffic, industry, and fuel burning drive most of the harm. The trends show where cleaner air policies are winning and where exposure still rises. Such estimates press governments to treat air quality as a health priority.
pmc-5467230:
