Lebreton, van der Zwet, Damsteeg, and their co-authors estimated river plastic emissions to the world's oceans in 2017. Plastics in the marine environment had become a major concern because they persist at sea. They harm marine life and potentially human health as well.

Cutting that flow first requires knowing where marine plastic comes from and how much each source adds. The team modeled how much plastic rivers carry into the oceans and which rivers contribute most. Rivers collect waste from whole inland regions, so they are natural points for intervention. Ranking them helps governments and cleanup programs target the flows where action cuts ocean plastic fastest.
pmc-5648830:
Nicholas Vogt and colleagues published this study in 2017 on the gut microbes of people with Alzheimer disease. Alzheimer disease is the most common form of dementia, and its causes are still not fully known. Animal work had hinted that gut bacteria might affect the sticky brain deposits seen in the disease.

The team compared stool samples from patients and healthy controls and found clear differences in which bacteria were present. Some bacterial groups were less common in patients, while others were more common. The results support a link between the gut and the brain in dementia, and they point to new paths for research on prevention and care.
pmc-7108130:
Xueting Yao, Fei Ye, Miao Zhang, and coauthors studied hydroxychloroquine against SARS-CoV-2 in the lab in 2020. The virus had broken out in Wuhan and spread worldwide. Chloroquine, an old malaria drug, was being tried sporadically in patients.

Hydroxychloroquine shares chloroquine's action but is generally less toxic. Cell tests showed it blocked the virus effectively. Modeling of drug levels in lung tissue suggested a dosing plan for trials. The authors presented it as a candidate to test, not a proven cure; later large trials found no benefit for patients. The dosing model was offered as a starting point for clinical trials, which later settled the question.
pmc-7839230:
Melissa Rethlefsen and colleagues introduced PRISMA-S in 2021, a reporting checklist for the literature searches behind systematic reviews. A systematic review stands or falls on its search, since a missed study can tilt the conclusions. Yet searches are often described so briefly that nobody can repeat or judge them.

PRISMA-S extends the well known PRISMA reporting statement with items specific to searching, covering databases, full search strategies, and how records were handled. The authors explain why earlier guidance left gaps and how the new items close them. The checklist gives reviewers, editors, and readers a way to see whether a review's evidence hunt was thorough enough to trust.
pmc-9186530:
Sergey Nurk, Sergey Koren, Arang Rhie, and the Telomere-to-Telomere Consortium presented in 2022 the first complete sequence of a human genome. The reference genome released in 2000 covered only the euchromatic share of our DNA, the gene rich portion that older methods could read. The remaining portion, rich in repeated sequences, stayed unfinished for two decades.

The consortium sequenced those last regions end to end, assembling a gapless genome of just over three billion letters. The new sequence adds whole stretches of DNA never read before, including regions around centromeres. A truly complete reference sharpens every use of the genome in medicine and biology, from variant hunting to understanding how chromosomes behave.
pmc-9931230:
Tiffany Kung, Morgan Cheatham, and colleagues tested in 2023 how well ChatGPT, a large language model, could perform on the United States Medical Licensing Exam. The licensing exam has three parts, taken across medical school and early training, and it sets the bar for practicing medicine in the United States. The team fed the exam questions to the model without any specialized training or help.

They report that ChatGPT scored at or close to the passing line on all three parts. That result landed early in the public life of such models and drew wide attention. The authors discuss what it could mean for medical education, including both the promise of AI study support and the questions it raises about assessment.
prichard-masonry-dissected-1730:
Samuel Prichard, a disaffected former Mason, published Masonry Dissected in London in 1730. The pamphlet sets out the catechism of the three Craft degrees in plain question and answer. It is the first and most famous Masonic exposé, and it founded the literature of exposure that has followed the fraternity ever since.

Prichard claims to print what lodges swore their members to hide. His catechism runs through signs, words, and the story of Hiram in order. Masons denounced him, and the public bought the pamphlet eagerly. Historians still treat it as the era's best evidence for early ritual. Few exposures have been reprinted so often or believed so widely.
proust-sweet-cheat-gone-moncrieff-1930:
The Sweet Cheat Gone is the sixth volume of In Search of Lost Time, published in French in 1925. C. K. Scott Moncrieff translated it into English in 1930, the year of his own death. Albertine has fled the narrator's rooms, and word soon comes that she has died in a riding accident.

Grief at first floods the narrator, then slowly thins into forgetting. He tests his memories, pursues old suspicions, and finds them fading anyway. Travel to Venice with his mother brings beauty without healing. Proust shows how time erases even the sharpest pain. The volume clears the road toward the final recovery of lost time.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-158-19:
June 30, 1920, closes volume 158 of Punch with Charivaria at the front, the standing column of brief jokes on the news. Summer items on motoring, bathing, and golf share space with graver hints from abroad.

Ireland records fewer births, and the column professes no surprise. A London firm makes the smallest motor-car on the market, already once knocked down by a walker. Ealing citizens demand Sunday bathing if Sunday concerts are allowed. A North Berwick score card calls golf a science no one can exhaust, and headmistresses hear that girls have broadened out, with the home-made jumper blamed.
regardie-stephensen-legend-of-aleister-c:
Two young men rose to defend Aleister Crowley when the press made him a byword in 1930. The Legend of Aleister Crowley, by Percy Stephensen and Israel Regardie, answers the scandal tales with the record. Regardie would soon serve as Crowley's secretary and student.

The book takes up the charges from the Abbey years and the drug and vice stories, point by point. It prints letters and facts meant to show a poet and thinker, not a monster. The fight over Crowley's name starts in earnest on these pages. The volume is the prime source for that fight's first round.
russell-conquest-happiness-1930:
The Conquest of Happiness, published in 1930, is Russell's practical philosophy of happiness: a self-help book by a logician, written with uncommon sense and no cant. He divides it between the causes of unhappiness and the causes of happiness.

Among the miseries he names envy, boredom, fear of opinion, and the sense of sin, each treated as a habit of mind that reason can break. The cures are equally plain: affection, work, wide interests, and effort rightly aimed. Russell writes from experience of despair in his youth. The book has comforted readers for ninety years by treating them as adults.
santayana-realm-matter-1930:
The Realm of Matter, published in 1930, is book second of Realms of Being. After the timeless essences of the first volume, Santayana turns to substance: the material world that exists, changes, and underlies every appearance.

He presents a frank materialism, honored without reduction: matter is the realm of power and fact, while spirit merely witnesses it. The book discusses space, time, and the flux of nature in his measured prose. Santayana called his stance that of a materialist who knows matter only by its signs. This volume gives his late system its solid, physical base.
scott-letters-on-demonology-and-witchcra:
Walter Scott took a cool look at witches and ghosts in Letters on Demonology and Witchcraft, his book of 1830. Scott, the great tale smith of Scotland, wrote the work as notes to a young kin. He tells famed cases of witch hunts, spooks, and deals with the dark in his rich, warm voice.

Scott doubts most of it, yet loves the tales. He blames fear, fraud, and sick minds for the bulk. His book set the tone for all cool pasts of the theme. It is a joy to read still. Scott wrote the book while his health and funds both waned. Its warmth and ease give no hint of the strain back of its birth.
senior-three-lectures-wages-1830:
Senior delivered his Three Lectures on the Rate of Wages at Oxford in 1830. Wages were the sorest question in the new industrial England, and the young professor faced it directly. The lectures gave the wage-fund doctrine its classic form, the theory that ruled Victorian economics for decades.

Senior argues that wages depend on the size of the fund set aside to pay labor, divided by the number of laborers seeking it. From that frame he draws lessons about population, machinery, and poor relief. The doctrine was preached to undergraduates who would govern an empire, which spread its reach far beyond Oxford. Later economists, Mill among them, first defended and then abandoned the wage fund. The lectures remain its first full statement, clear enough to teach and strong enough to fight over for forty years.
shepard-lore-of-the-unicorn-1930:
Odell Shepard wrote The Lore of the Unicorn in 1930. Shepard was a US scribe and a man of the woods and of books. The book traces one beast through tale, fact hunt, and art. No beast of myth has left so long a trail in print.

Greek and Latin scribes first tell of a fierce one-horned beast of India. The mid ages made its horn a cure for all poisons and a mark of Christ. Kings paid huge sums for horns that proved to be whale teeth. The book is the great tale of one beast in the mind of man.
sinclair-mental-radio-1930:
Upton Sinclair was a famed US scribe of tales with a bite. His Mental Radio came out in 1930 and took a strange turn. The book tells of tests with his wife Mary and her gift of mind sight. Albert Einstein wrote a kind word at the front of the book.

Mary would draw a sketch of a thing hid from her sight in a sealed wrap. Her hits came far too oft to be mere chance, Sinclair holds. Scores of the draws stand in print for the reader to judge. The book is the most famed first-hand tale of mind tests of its kind.
smythe-kangchenjunga-adventure-1930:
Frank Smythe climbed on Kangchenjunga in 1929 and found marks he could not place. The Kangchenjunga Adventure, printed in 1930, tells that great expedition in full. Smythe was among the finest mountaineers of his generation, calm and exact in all things.

High on the mountain his party found footprints he reports, with care, as those of a Snow Man. A climber's plain word on such a find gave the yeti debate fresh fuel. The rest of the book is a classic of storm, height, and hard won views. Mystery and mountaineering share its pages in equal part.
stahl-philosophical-principles-1730:
Georg Ernst Stahl was a German doctor and chemist who shaped early ideas about fire and matter. Peter Shaw put his main work into English in 1730 as Philosophical Principles of Universal Chemistry. Stahl tried to give chemistry one clear system for the first time.

At the heart of the book stands phlogiston, a fire-stuff said to leave a body as it burns. The theory was wrong, yet it let chemists sort facts and run tests with new care. Later work by Lavoisier swept it aside. Even so, Stahl's search for order marks a real step in science.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5030:
Benjamin Harrison gives four yearly addresses, from December 3, 1889, to December 6, 1892, parted by three stars. The first opens on the openness of American rule. Few acts of the government are held in trust, even for a time, by those who run the public work. Each step is taken under the watch of a keen and wakeful people, and the state of the Union is known day by day.

Good will and warmth have marked ties with other governments, Harrison reports, and the year just closed leaves few world questions of weight unsettled. None, he thinks, need long block a fair and honored settling. Dealings with other states have been and should stay marked by frankness, he argues, with aims owned and methods free of plots. That course has borne rich fruit across a century of right dealing.
stebbing-modern-introduction-logic-1930:
A Modern Introduction to Logic, published in 1930, is Susan Stebbing's landmark textbook, the analytic tradition's standard introduction for a generation. Stebbing, the first woman professor of philosophy in Britain, wrote it to teach clear thinking as a craft.

The book joins traditional logic to the new symbolic methods of Russell and his school, with constant attention to the confusions of ordinary language. Stebbing insists that logic serves criticism: the point is to detect bad argument in newspapers as much as in treatises. Her clarity made hard material teachable. Generations of students learned their logic from her pages.
stendhal-red-and-black-1830:
Stendhal published The Red and the Black in 1830, a French novel about ambition in the years after Napoleon. Julien Sorel is a carpenter's son with a sharp mind and big dreams. He works as a tutor, then in a great house in Paris. Love affairs with two women shape his rise and fall.

Julien plays roles to climb, yet his pride and passion betray him. A sudden act of violence ends his hopes and leads to trial. Stendhal cuts deep into the manners of church, army, and salon. The title points to the two paths open to a young man: the army's red and the church's black.
suzuki-studies-lankavatara-sutra-1930:
Suzuki's Studies in the Lankavatara Sutra, published in 1930, is his landmark scholarly exposition of a dense Mahayana scripture. The Lankavatara Sutra is the text Bodhidharma is said to have handed to his successor in China. Zen counts it among its root scriptures.

The sutra teaches that the world we see is mind-only, a weaving of consciousness rather than a set of solid things. Suzuki maps its terms, compares its Chinese and Sanskrit forms, and links its thought to Zen practice. Scholars of Buddhism still treat his study as the standard guide to a hard text.
svevo-confessions-of-zeno-dezoete-1930:
Italo Svevo published La coscienza di Zeno in Italian in 1923, and Beryl de Zoete Englished it in 1930 as Confessions of Zeno. Zeno Cosini, a Trieste businessman, writes his memoirs at his doctor's order as part of a cure. He promises to quit smoking on page after page, and never does.

His father, his marriage, his mistress, and his business partner all pass through his sly, self-forgiving memory. The reader learns to doubt every excuse while liking the man who makes them. James Joyce, Svevo's friend, championed the novel when Italy ignored it. The de Zoete translation was the book's first English dress. It remains a comic landmark of the modern novel.
synesius-on-dreams-fitzgerald-1930:
Synesius of Cyrene was a Greek bishop and thinker of the late Roman world. Augustine Fitzgerald turned his essays and hymns into English in two parts, printed in 1930. Among the essays is his famed work on dreams, De insomniis in Latin. His hymns, writ in an old style, were prized by Greek scholars of the age.

In that essay Synesius sets out how dreams can show what is to come. He ties dreams to the soul and to a spirit that links men with the divine. The hymns show the same mind at prayer, in rich and bold Greek verse.
tanner-narrative-of-captivity-1830:
John Tanner tells of thirty years as a captive in his Narrative of 1830, shaped by Edwin James. Snatched as a boy, Tanner grew up midst the Ojibwe round the Great Lakes. He hunts, fasts, weds, and roams their lands. His tale gives a close view of their rites, tales, and hard life in the wild north woods of that age.

Midst the lore stands the great thunder bird, whose wings make the storm's roar. Tanner heard its tale from men who held it true. The book is a chief source on that world. Its voice is plain and true.
ternarius-ternariorum-hemeticorum-bezoar: A Latin title page, badly worn and hard to read, is all that can be made out here. It names a work on ternaries of bezoardic agents tied to laudanum, printed at Erfurt by Johann Birckner in the year marked MDCXXX, or 1630. Much of the page is garbled past reading, so no author claim or account of the text can safely be drawn from it.
the-german-classics-of-the-nineteenth-an: Volume nine of The German Classics, in a patrons' edition of 1914, holds Friedrich Hebbel and Otto Ludwig, and only the front matter and contents are present here. Hebbel's part gives his life, his play Maria Magdalena, Siegfried's Death, tales, essays, and scraps from his journal and boyhood. Ludwig's part gives his life, The Hereditary Forester, and Between Heaven and Earth. No full work follows in the pages given here, so the texts cannot be stated here.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: This thirtieth number of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is dated June 3, 1897. The paper is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and a premium offer. The masthead prices a year at $2.50 and six months at $1.25. The offer asks, which is your favorite bicycle? A reader who sends one hundred regular subscriptions may choose any wheel in the market. He buys it from any dealer he likes, and the publisher pays the bill.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2-part:
Cervantes' Don Quixote continues in Volume 2, Part 30, Englished by John Ormsby. Chapter thirty-six relates the strange and undreamt-of adventure of the distressed duenna, alias the Countess Trifaldi, together with a letter Sancho Panza wrote to his wife, Teresa Panza. The opening pulls back the curtain on the duke's house.

The duke's majordomo, a man of a facetious and sportive turn, played Merlin in the late adventure, arranged its verses, and set a page to represent Dulcinea. With his master and mistress helping, he now devises a fresh trick, among the drollest and strangest contrivances in the book. The reader is let into the plot before the knight is.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
Number 274 of the Mirror, dated Saturday, September 22, 1827, continues its Architectural Illustrations series with the Temple Church in London. The twelfth-century church raises an old antiquarian quarrel over who built England's round churches. Four survive in near-perfect preservation: the Temple Church, St. Sepulchre at Northampton, St. Mary at Cambridge, and Little Maplestead in Essex. A Jewish origin was long supposed for them.

Essays by Mr. Essex and Mr. Britton, the article argues, removed that erroneous notion entirely. Essex reasons that the Jerusalem Temple was not circular and that modern Jews do not affect the figure in synagogues. Cambridge's Jews, he notes, had their own synagogue in the quarter called the Jewry. Antiquarians instead trace the form to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre at Jerusalem. The Knights Templars built the London church, the article concludes, to guard pilgrims.

A supplementary number of the Mirror, No. 344, pairs an engraving of Ehrenbreitstein on the Rhine with the completion of its Spirit of the Annuals notices. Byron's lines from Childe Harold head the piece: the fortress's shattered wall, black with the miners' blast, where peace destroyed what war could never blight. The engraving comes from the Literary Souvenir, drawn by J. M. W. Turner and engraved by J. Pye.

The supplement assembles the characteristics of eight annuals in one sheet. Its quotations include fourteen prose tales, sketches, and poems of great merit. The Rhine, the editors add, keeps its pre-eminence among the mightiest and loveliest highways of Europe. Gift-book reviewing here becomes a tour: a ruined German fortress illustrates an English Christmas annual. Readers get the magazine's seasonal roundup framed by Romantic scenery and a famous stanza.

A boat-house at Virginia Water opens volume 17, No. 493, dated June 11, 1831. Virginia Water's rides and walks had lately been opened to the public, and the writers hope visitors will treat the privilege better than in earlier years. Prize-fighters once trained in its quiet alleys, which had caused admission to be withdrawn.

Praise for the grounds runs high. The artificial lake is called the largest in the kingdom except for Blenheim's, and its cascade wins strong approval. The boat-house itself, built by direction of the late king, draws plainer judgement. Its toy-like style and the little bells on its lantern roof strike the writers as prettiness rather than true picturesque taste.

A supplementary number of volume 20, dated December 15, 1832, surveys the Spirit of the Annuals for 1833. First under review is the Picturesque Annual, praised as one of the most splendid works of its kind. It held twenty-six large plates drawn by Stanfield and engraved by leading artists under Mr. Charles Heath's superintendence.

Leitch Ritchie supplied travelling sketches on the Rhine and in Belgium and Holland, written to accompany the plates. The extract chosen matches the engraving of St. Goar on the Rhine, beneath the ruined castle of Rheinfels. It recalls a custom greeting for first-time visitors of standing, who were asked whether they would be baptised in wine or water.
the-tavern-knight-pg3030: A second record of Rafael Sabatini's Tavern Knight repeats the same title and chapter list as its sibling, then runs three chapters further. Its contents reach chapter twenty-one, adding an interrupted journey, a converted Hogan, and the message Kenneth bore, where the other listing stops at eighteen. The front matter shared by both records is stated here plainly: same author, same opening chapters, no story text in either. Readers can compare the two listings' reach, yet the novel itself appears in neither set of pages.
the-united-states-of-america-part-1-1783:
Edwin Erle Sparks wrote the first part of a two-volume history of the United States, covering 1783 to 1830. His preface complains that the national story has been told as boasting, as providence, and as party triumph. Sparks instead seeks a middle ground between views of the Union as creature of the states and as something born in the soil.

The narrative traces how a confederated republic gradually evolved under necessity, departing from first ideals as progress required. Sparks stresses centralising and decentralising forces over familiar detail. His stated aim is explaining how people slowly shifted from saying the United States are to saying the United States is.
thomson-history-chemistry-vol-2-1830:
Thomas Thomson was a Scots chemist and a keen hand at the tale of his science. His History of Chemistry came out in two books in 1830. Book two ends the work and takes the tale to his own day. Thomson taught chemistry at Glasgow and wrote with a clear hand.

The tale runs from the alchemists through Priestley and Lavoisier to Dalton and Davy. New gases, new metals, and the atomic scheme fill the last age. Thomson knew some of the men whose work he tells of at first hand. The set is an early full tale of the science by a man of the trade.
tob-4030:
Miguel de Cervantes published Don Quixote in two parts, presented complete here in John Ormsby's classic English translation. A minor gentleman, his brains addled by chivalric romances, remakes himself as a knight-errant and rides out with the peasant Sancho Panza as squire. Windmills become giants; inns become castles; flocks become armies.

Sancho's earthy sense answers his master's glorious madness in dialogue that deepens across both parts, until each man borrows the other's nature. The 1605 novel effectively invented modern fiction and gave English the word quixotic. Ormsby's version, learned and lively, remains the traditional way in for English readers.
tob-4130:
Volume one of Mead's Thrice-Greatest Hermes, published in 1906, lays the ground before his Hermetic translations. These prolegomena sort out the tangled history of the literature: who Hermes Trismegistus was said to be, which texts bear his name, and what world produced them.

Mead walks through late-antique Egypt and Greece, where temples, schools, and cults blended their gods and ideas. The learning is dense but humane. Readers who want the translations alone can skip ahead; students will bless the map. Checked from the 1919 edition, volume one is the learned foundation of Mead's whole Hermetic project.
tob-4230:
William Gemmell's translation of the Diamond Sutra, the Chin-Kang-Ching, presents the Buddha teaching his disciple Subhuti through questions and negations. Even the highest teachings, the sutra insists, are rafts to be abandoned once the shore is reached. Form is emptiness, in the famous Mahayana formula carried through this text's tradition, and emptiness is form.

The Chinese version prized across East Asia is the form Gemmell translates, the same tradition that produced the dated printed copy of 868 AD. Short enough to read at a sitting, the text cuts at attachment to concepts, merit, and self, as its diamond title promises. Readers should expect repetition used deliberately, like a bell struck again.
tob-9047-60230:
Animals fill volume two of Bostock's Pliny, as the Natural History moves from the heavens to living things. Elephants earn Pliny's respect for their memory and near-human feeling. Lions, crocodiles, and birds follow, each with habits, habitats, and marvels attached.

Sea creatures close the survey, including monsters reported from distant waters. Pliny mixes sharp observation with travelers' tales he had no way to test, and the blend is part of the charm. Roman farmers and generals once used his notes in earnest. Modern readers get a nature program written two thousand years early, credulity and all.
tyndale-pentateuch-1530:
William Tyndale printed his translation of the five books of Moses in 1530, working directly from the Hebrew. The Pentateuch presented here was the first printed English version of Genesis through Deuteronomy. Tyndale's plain, powerful English set the pattern for every Bible that followed in the language.

Let there be light: his simple phrasing became the backbone of the King James Version two generations later. Authorities hunted the translator across Europe for giving common readers the Old Testament in their own tongue. He was strangled and burned in 1536, his work unfinished but unstoppable. This volume holds the books that taught England to read its Bible. Their directness still startles.
un-ga-res-30: Jobs at the new UN Secretariat drew interest from beyond its member states in 1946. Resolution 30, passed on 9 February 1946, tells the Secretary-General to accept and file job requests from nationals of states outside the UN. Governments asking about such posts must be told the papers will be kept on file. Hiring, though, could only follow the rules of the Secretariat itself.
un-ga-res-630:
False news can wound peace, and a world pact to fight it sits in the record as Resolution 630. The Convention on the International Right of Correction rests on a plain wish: that peoples be told the truth, in full and with trust. False or bent reports, the text holds, put friendly ties between peoples at risk, and can feed the threat of war itself.

The pact gives a state struck by a report it holds false a right of reply. Its correction must be given the same reach, by the same channels, as the first report. Terms in the pact fix what counts as a news dispatch, an agency, and a reporter. The deal grew from Assembly calls of the late 1940s, as war-born lies still rang in fresh ears.
un-ga-res-a-69-30:
States without nuclear arms want a pledge: you will not use yours on us. Resolution A/69/30, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, presses that long fight. Till disarmament is won, the text holds, the freedom and land of such states must be shielded from force, and above all from nuclear threat. The nuclear states had each made one-sided pledges of that kind, and talks in Geneva had chased a binding pact.

Drafts of a world pact on the point had been laid on the table, the text notes. Muslim and non-aligned states had backed the call at their own summits, from Kuala Lumpur in 2003 to Tehran in 2012. The Assembly urges fast talks toward firm, binding pledges that all can trust.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: On 9 February 1946, at the twenty-sixth plenary meeting, the General Assembly adopted Resolution 30. It is a short staffing order. The Assembly told the Secretary-General to receive and file job applications for the Secretariat. The applications were from nationals of states outside the United Nations. He was to tell inquiring governments of such states that the applications would be kept on file. Hiring could follow only the Secretariat's own rules, though.

Resolution 630 (VII) of the General Assembly carries an entire treaty: the Convention on the International Right of Correction, opened for signature after the Assembly approved its text. The convention deals with false or distorted news dispatches that cross borders and damage relations between states.

Under the convention, a state whose interests are harmed by a dispatch it considers false or distorted may issue an official communiqué. The communiqué sets out the facts as it states them. Every receiving state must release that communiqué through its usual news channels within five days. If a state fails to do so, the Secretary-General publicizes the text. Disputes about interpretation go to the International Court of Justice. The convention entered into force once six states had ratified or acceded. It was an early attempt to give governments a formal right of reply in foreign press coverage.

Resolution 69/30 of the General Assembly calls for effective international arrangements — negative security assurances — to protect non-nuclear-weapon states against the use or threat of use of nuclear weapons. The Assembly reaffirms the urgent need for an early agreement. It notes there is no objection in principle within the Conference on Disarmament to an international convention on the subject. It appeals to all states, especially the nuclear-weapon states, to work toward a common formula. The formula could be written into a legally binding instrument.
un-sc-res-1030: The decision entered as Resolution 1030 forms part of the Council record catalogued for 1994. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-130:
Resolution 130 is a brief procedural record adopted on 25 November 1958. It notes with regret the death of Judge José Gustavo Guerrero on 25 October 1958. His death left a vacancy on the International Court of Justice for the rest of his term, to be filled under the Court's Statute.

Under Article 14 of the Statute, the Security Council fixes the date of the election for such a vacancy. The Council decided the election would be held during the fourteenth session of the General Assembly, or at a special session before it. Records like this one form part of the steady, formal work by which the world court's bench was kept complete.
un-sc-res-1330: The Security Council's numbered decisions include Resolution 1330, entered in this catalog under the year 1995. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1430:
UNMEE's job was refocused on the border ruling on 14 August 2002. The Boundary Commission had given its delimitation decision on 13 April 2002. Both Ethiopia and Eritrea had accepted it as final and binding under the Algiers Agreements. The Secretary-General's report of 10 July advised how to move from ruling to marking the line on the ground.

The Council adjusted UNMEE's mandate so the mission could help the Boundary Commission carry out its decision swiftly. The technical steps for transferring territory, as the Secretary-General set them out, were endorsed as a broad framework. Both parties had to work fully and promptly with UNMEE and the Commission. They were to hand over the maps and information needed for mine clearance and marking. Unilateral troop or population moves near the border were barred. The Council appealed for restraint from both sides while the long task of demarcation began.
un-sc-res-1530:
The Council took formal action on Spain in Resolution 1530, adopted unanimously on 11 March 2004. Bombs had torn through Madrid commuter trains that same morning. Many riders were killed and many more hurt. The text names the Basque group ETA as the attacker, on the first reports of the day.

The Council condemns the Madrid bomb attacks in the strongest terms. It sends deep sympathy to Spain's people and government and to the victims' families. All states are urged to help find and bring to justice those behind the attack. The text restates a firm resolve to combat every form of terrorism. Later probes blamed a different network, a fact the same-day text could not yet know.
un-sc-res-1630:
Somalia's arms watchers were renewed on 14 October 2005. The Monitoring Group's report of 22 August had landed with the Council. Weapons and ammunition were flowing into Somalia in growing amounts, breaking the 1992 embargo. The Council backed its special representative's road map for dialogue among the transitional leaders. The country still lacked working national rule.

The Council stressed that every member state had to obey the arms embargo in full. It said it meant to weigh steps against those who broke the ban and those who backed them. The Secretary-General was asked to re-establish the Monitoring Group for six months, in consultation with the sanctions committee. The group would keep investigating embargo breaches and list the offenders. Money for the work had to be arranged by the Secretariat. The sanctions committee was asked to review the group's findings.
un-sc-res-1730:
Sanctions fairness came before the Security Council in Resolution 1730, adopted on 19 December 2006. The Council ran many sanctions lists by then, covering people and groups in several conflicts. Those named often had no clear way to plead their case. Critics said names could sit on lists for years without review.

The text creates a focal point inside the United Nations Secretariat to take removal requests. A named person can apply there or through their own state. The office passes the request to the governments involved and tells the person the final choice. All sanctions committees must rewrite their rules to match this new process.
un-sc-res-1830:
Resolution 1830 kept the United Nations Assistance Mission for Iraq, UNAMI, in place for another year in 2008. By then Iraq was slowly pulling back from the worst sectarian violence. The Council renewed the mission's mandate in much the same terms as before.

Inside, UNAMI is asked to advise on elections, borders, and talks between rival groups, and to support aid and refugee returns. The Secretary-General must report on progress at regular intervals. Short renewal texts like this one are how the Council keeps a mission alive, and they record its judgment that Iraq still needed help.
un-sc-res-1930:
Formal Council action on Cyprus arrived as Resolution 1930, adopted on 15 June 2010. Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot leaders were holding full talks on reunifying the island. Both sides had voiced hope that 2010 could be the year of a settlement. Mine clearing and work on missing persons were moving ahead.

The text extends the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, called UNFICYP, until 15 December 2010. It urges the leaders to speed up the talks toward a federation of two zones with equal political standing. More crossing points along the Green Line should open. The Turkish Cypriot side must also restore the earlier military position at Strovilia.
un-sc-res-30:
Indonesia's ceasefire needed watching in the summer of 1947. The Council had told the Netherlands and the Republic of Indonesia to stop fighting on 1 August. Both sides reported that orders to halt had gone out. On 25 August 1947 the Council noted those steps with satisfaction. It also welcomed a Dutch pledge to help form a sovereign, democratic United States of Indonesia. That pledge matched the Linggadjati Agreement between the parties.

Career consuls in Batavia would report jointly on the situation. Indonesia's government had asked for a Council commission of observers. The Council noted that request as well. Its aim was to prevent rows over the ceasefire. Calm on the ground would help a political settlement take shape.
un-sc-res-330:
Pressure on Latin American states over their natural wealth was taken up by the Security Council on 21 March 1973. The General Assembly had affirmed permanent sovereignty over natural resources in resolutions stretching back to 1962. Its 1970 declaration barred states from using economic or political pressure to bend another state's sovereign choices. The Council noted with deep concern that coercive measures were being used against Latin American countries.

The Council urged states to take fitting steps to block firms that deliberately tried to coerce Latin American countries. It asked states to refrain from using, or backing the use of, any coercive measures against states of the region. The aim was to keep and strengthen peace and security in Latin America. The text is short and general. It marks the Council entering the era's fight over control of the developing world's resources.
un-sc-res-430: The text numbered Resolution 430 belongs to the Security Council's official record, catalogued at 1978. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Security Council resolution 1030, adopted unanimously on 14 December 1995, extends the mandate of UNMOT, the United Nations Mission of Observers in Tajikistan, until 15 June 1996. The extension holds only while the Tehran Agreement of 17 September 1994 stays in force. The Tajik parties must remain committed to the cease-fire, national reconciliation and the promotion of democracy.

The Council welcomes the start of a continuous round of inter-Tajik talks in Ashgabat. It regrets the slow progress toward a political settlement. It urges both sides to observe the Tehran Agreement strictly and extend it substantially. It asks the Secretary-General to keep working through his Special Envoy. He is to report every three months on settlement efforts and on UNMOT. The Council stresses an end to hostile acts on the Tajik-Afghan border. It stresses close liaison between UNMOT, the CIS peacekeeping forces, border forces and the OSCE mission.

A judge's death left a seat empty on the International Court of Justice, and this short text from 25 November 1958 deals with filling it. Judge José Gustavo Guerrero had died on 25 October 1958. Under the Court's Statute, the Security Council had to set the date for an election to choose his successor for the rest of his term.

The Council decided the election would be held during the fourteenth session of the General Assembly, or at a special session before it. The text is brief, but it shows the routine work the Council does to keep the world court complete. It also marks how closely the Council and the Assembly share the task of staffing the Court.

Once more, on 5 December 2000, Iraq's oil-for-food programme is renewed. As with the renewal passed the previous June, the programme kept a controlled channel open for Iraqi oil sales while sanctions remained in force. The income was meant to meet the basic needs of people across the country.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council kept the programme's rules in force for 180 days from 6 December 2000. Food, nutrition, and health kept priority funding, and the fixed share for northern Iraq stayed in place. The Council also pushed to have enough United Nations observers working in Iraq within 90 days to confirm that goods were shared fairly and used as approved.

Resolution 1430, adopted unanimously on 14 August 2002, keeps the Ethiopia-Eritrea peace process staffed for another seven months. A Council mission had visited both countries in February. In April the boundary commission delivered its ruling on the disputed frontier, and both parties accepted it as final and binding under the Algiers peace agreements of 2000.

The Council extended the mandate of UNMEE, the UN mission in Ethiopia and Eritrea, to March 2003. It praised the Secretary-General, his special representative, and the mission itself for helping carry out the agreements. Both parties were reminded of their duties under humanitarian and refugee law and of the need to guarantee the safety of UN and Red Cross personnel.

Bombs tore through crowded commuter trains in Madrid on the morning of 11 March 2004. Spain reeled from its worst terrorist attack. The Council met that same day. Resolution 1530 passed unanimously at the 4923rd meeting. Its text blamed the Basque separatist group ETA for the bombings, an early attribution that investigators later revised.

The members condemned the attacks in the strongest terms. They sent sympathy to Spain's people, its government, and the victims' families. Every state was urged to help find those behind the killings. That duty came from Resolution 1373, the sweeping counterterrorism text of 2001. The resolution closed by renewing the Council's pledge to fight terrorism in all its forms.

Resolution 1630, adopted on 14 October 2005, restarts the team that watches Somalia's arms embargo. The embargo had been in place since 1992 and was still widely broken; a monitoring group's August report laid out violations and recommendations. The Council praised African Union and regional support for Somalia's transitional institutions and urged Somali leaders to keep talking instead of fighting.

The Council re-established the monitoring group for a further six months, to track arms flows, name violators, and advise on enforcement. It stressed that the transitional institutions had to keep building real national governance. Expert monitoring, renewed in short cycles like this one, remained the Council's main source of facts about Somalia's war economy.

Fairer sanctions procedures are the subject of Resolution 1730, adopted on 19 December 2006. The Council stresses that sanctions are a key tool for peace and security. But they must be carefully targeted. Clear, fair procedures should exist for putting people and entities on sanctions lists and taking them off. Humanitarian exemptions also needed a clear path.

The Council adopts a de-listing procedure set out in an annex. It asks the Secretary-General to create a focal point in the Secretariat to receive de-listing requests from listed individuals and entities. The focal point checks whether a request is new, passes it to the designating and home governments for comment, and routes recommendations to the relevant sanctions committee, which decides. All sanctions committees must revise their guidelines to match. Petitioners can also apply through their own state instead.

Iraq's assistance mission, UNAMI, is extended for twelve more months on 7 August 2008. Security in Iraq had improved through joint political and military efforts, though the gains had to be made lasting through real dialogue. All communities were urged to reject sectarianism and share resources fairly.

The wider mandate given in 2007 is kept. The mission's head is to advise Iraq on political dialogue, elections, constitutional review, internal boundaries, and regional talks, and to support aid, refugee returns, and human rights. The Secretary-General is to report every three months. Member states are called on to keep giving the mission staff, money, and protection.

Cyprus negotiations reach a hopeful moment in Resolution 1930, adopted on 15 June 2010. The two leaders had made progress in fully fledged talks and hoped 2010 would be the year of a solution. Work was under way to open the Limnitis crossing point. The island stayed stable, demining advanced, and the Committee on Missing Persons kept working.

The Council extends the UN Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, UNFICYP, until 15 December 2010. It urges full use of the opportunity: faster talks, kept trust and goodwill, and open engagement toward a bicommunal, bizonal federation with political equality. It pushes for the remaining confidence measures and more crossing points. It again asks the Turkish Cypriot side and Turkish forces to restore the earlier military position at Strovilia. A report, including settlement contingency planning, is due by 1 December 2010.

Barbados became free of Britain on 30 November 1966. The small Caribbean island was calm and well run. Its leaders sought a UN seat at once. Resolution 230 passed with no dissent on 7 December 1966. The vote came one week after the island's first day of freedom.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit Barbados. The Assembly agreed within days. Barbados soon punched far above its weight in world talks. Its first prime minister, Errol Barrow, spoke with force for small states. The island's seat dates from this text. It is a plain record of the last legal step from colony to state, done in the space of a single short meeting.

Consuls in Batavia became the Council's eyes in Indonesia in 1947. On 25 August, it adopted Resolution 30. Seven members voted yes and none voted no. Four members held back. The same meeting produced the good offices offer of Resolution 31. Both sides had reported ceasefire orders after the Council's 1 August call.

The text notes those steps with warmth. It also notes the Dutch pledge to build a sovereign, democratic United States of Indonesia. That pledge rested on the Linggadjati Agreement. Career consuls in Batavia must now report jointly for the Council. Their reports cover how the truce is kept. They cover life in areas under army occupation as well. Both governments must give the consuls all help they need.

Latin America's resources and foreign pressure meet in Resolution 330, adopted on 21 March 1973 by twelve votes to none with three abstentions. The Council recalled Assembly declarations on permanent sovereignty over natural resources and on friendly relations, which bar states from using economic or political coercion to subordinate another country's sovereign rights. Members said such coercive measures were being used against Latin American countries.

The Council urged states to adopt measures to stop companies that deliberately try to coerce Latin American countries. It also asked states to refrain from using or encouraging any coercive measures against states in the region, for the sake of peace and security there. The text reflects the era's pushback against corporate and superpower pressure.

Cyprus's peacekeeping force received another six months in the summer of 1978. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 31 May, recommended the extension. The parties concerned agreed with the recommendation. Cyprus accepted that the force should stay beyond 15 June. Resolution 430 records that decision.

The Council extended the force's stationing for a further period ending on 15 December 1978. It reaffirmed Resolution 186 of 1964 and its other decisions on Cyprus. The Secretary-General was asked to continue his mission of good offices between the two communities. He had to keep the Council informed of progress. A report on the working of this resolution was due by 30 November 1978.
united-states-census-figures-back-to-163:
United States Census Figures Back to 1630 gathers population tables for the country across more than three centuries. A short guide at the front explains where the numbers came from. Figures for years before 1992 rest on Census Bureau source files, and where sources gave more than one figure for a year, the compilers averaged them. The 1992 figure was an estimate when the tables were made.

Years after 1992 are the compilers' own estimates, built on a steady growth rate of one percent a year. That rate matched the average drawn from the figures for 1972 to 1992. The guide also warns readers to check price index tables before judging money figures across decades, since inflation can make a larger sum worth less. Dates default to July 1, the Census Bureau's usual date, unless a note says otherwise, and the raw data sits in a footnote.
vos-pauline-eschatology-1930:
Geerhardus Vos taught at Princeton and is often called the father of Reformed biblical theology. His Pauline Eschatology, published in 1930, studies how the apostle Paul thought about the end of the age. Vos reads Paul's letters as a connected system, not as loose sayings.

He shows that Paul holds two claims together: the new age has already dawned in Christ, yet its fullness is not yet here. That already and not-yet frame, Vos argues, shapes everything Paul says about church, sacrament, and hope. Later New Testament scholars built whole schools on the structure Vos mapped here.
way-of-a-pilgrim-french-1930:
The Way of a Pilgrim is an anonymous Russian book of the nineteenth century, first Englished by R. M. French in 1930. Its narrator is a wandering pilgrim with a lame arm, a bag of dried bread, and one burning question. He wants to learn how to pray without ceasing, as the Bible commands.

An elder teaches him the Jesus Prayer: the name of Jesus joined to the breath and the heartbeat, repeated thousands of times a day. The pilgrim walks from village to village through snow and hardship, testing the prayer as he goes. Strangers, soldiers, and peasants cross his path, and the prayer slowly changes him. The little book became the classic guide to this prayer in the West.
weber-protestant-ethic-parsons-1930:
Max Weber's The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism appears in Talcott Parsons's translation of 1930. Weber asks why modern capitalism grew first in Protestant lands. He finds an elective affinity between Calvinist faith and the spirit of methodical work. Believers, unsure of salvation, sought signs of grace in disciplined labor and thrift.

Wealth, in this ethic, is a duty to steward, not a license for pleasure. Weber stresses that ideas and interests grow together; he does not claim faith alone caused capitalism. The essays are the most cited work in sociology. Parsons's version made Weber central to English-speaking scholarship. Debate over the thesis has run for a century.
what-to-do-thoughts-evoked-by-the-census: This record holds the same front pages as its twin record for Tolstoy's What To Do?, and nothing past them appears here. Count Lyof N. Tolstoi wrote the essays after the Moscow census, and Isabel F. Hapgood turned them into English. Crowell printed the book in New York in 1887. Her Boston note, dated September 1, 1887, explains that banned essays spread in hand copies and through a Geneva house. She could mark the censor's cuts in the first half only.
widger-s-quotations-from-the-project-gut: Nothing past a Project Gutenberg header is present here, so the court memoir quotations do not appear. David Widger drew the set from The Court Memoirs of France. It is number 14 in his Quotations series. The header dates the release to February 2003, as etext number 3730. First posting was August 12, 2001, and the edition is number 10. A note on corrected editions begins at the end of the part shown. Standard cautions and appeals fill the rest.
winthrop-model-christian-charity-1630:
John Winthrop wrote A Model of Christian Charity on board the Arbella in 1630, during the crossing to New England. The printed title names him leader and governor of the company sailing from Britain. He argues that God has set some rich and some poor, some high and some low, by wise design.

From that order he draws duties of mercy, love, and shared care among the settlers. The colony, he warns, will stand as a city upon a hill, watched by all eyes. Failure would bring shame and judgment, while faithfulness would bring blessing. That image became one of the most quoted phrases in American public life.
